Omnira should learn across projects without turning every project into one dataset.

6.101 Isolation and Executive Reasoning

Executive reasoning must distinguish between:
Project evidence.
Portfolio evidence.
Shared principle.
Founder preference.
Global policy.
Cross-project inference.
A conclusion drawn from one project should not automatically become a rule for another.
The Project Executive should ask:
Is this evidence local?
Is the pattern generalizable?
Does the other project have the same risk profile?
Does the same policy apply?
What evidence is missing?

6.102 Cross-Project Inference Risk

Cross-project comparison can produce misleading conclusions.
Examples:
The Prompt’s successful content cadence may not fit Familje-Stunden.
Familje-Stunden’s support policy may not fit The Prompt.
GainPilot’s retention model may not fit subscription education products.
One project’s Trust Score threshold may not fit another project’s Damage Boundary.
Portfolio learning requires interpretation, not copying.

6.103 Project Boundary Changes

Project boundaries may change through:
Project merger.
Project split.
Ownership change.
Customer transfer.
Product spin-off.
Archival.
Shared service extraction.
Boundary changes should be treated as major executive and governance events.
They should require:
Data mapping.
Permission review.
Memory review.
Knowledge review.
Credential review.
Cost attribution review.
Approval.
Audit.
Rollback plan.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
6.104 Project Merge

Merging projects should not mean blindly combining all data and authority.
A merge should evaluate:
Customer consent.
Data compatibility.
Policy conflicts.
Brand conflicts.
Memory conflicts.
Financial attribution.
Autonomy licenses.
Tool permissions.
Decision histories.
Some boundaries may need to remain even after organizational merger.

6.105 Project Split

A project split should define:
Which data belongs where.
Which customers transfer.
Which Memory is copied or abstracted.
Which workflows move.
Which credentials change.
Which approvals remain valid.
Which autonomy licenses expire.
Which costs and revenue move.
Autonomy should generally be re-evaluated after a split.
New boundaries create new risk.

6.106 Ownership Change

A change in project ownership should trigger:
Access review.
Role review.
Credential rotation.
Portfolio visibility review.
Memory privacy review.
Approval authority review.
Autonomy review.
Audit handover.
Ownership determines executive authority.
It cannot be treated as a cosmetic field.

6.107 Isolation and Crisis Mode

During Crisis Mode, isolation should become stricter, not weaker.
Possible crisis restrictions include:
Suspend cross-project grants.
Require approval for external actions.
Disable shared credentials.
Freeze autonomy escalation.
Increase logging.
Block exports.
Limit Memory promotion.
Restrict tools.
Urgency should not become an excuse to remove boundaries.

6.108 Isolation and Full Autonomy

Full autonomy does not remove project boundaries.
A fully autonomous project must still operate inside:
Project identity.
Project policy.
Autonomy licenses.
Budget mandates.
Customer rules.
Tool permissions.
Data boundaries.
Audit requirements.
Human override.
Emergency brake.
Autonomy describes how much action may occur without repeated approval.
It does not describe freedom from scope.

6.109 Isolation and the Omnira Constitution

The future Omnira Constitution should define non-negotiable boundary principles.
These may include:
Projects do not access one another by default.
Customer data remains tenant-scoped.
Autonomy never grants cross-project authority.
Founder-private data is minimized.
High-impact cross-project access is auditable.
Human authority can revoke access.
Project isolation failures trigger mandatory response.
Executive Intelligence must operate beneath these constitutional rules.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
6.110 The Boundary Decision Test

Before any cross-boundary action, Omnira should ask:
Why is this access needed?
Is the purpose legitimate?
Is the requested scope minimal?
Can a summary replace raw access?
Can the task be completed through a shared service?
Is human approval required?
How long should access last?
What will be logged?
How will access be revoked?
What is the Damage Boundary?
If these questions cannot be answered, access should not be granted.

6.111 The Project Scope Test

Before every project action, Omnira should ask:
Is the project explicit?
Is the actor authorized?
Is the data project-scoped?
Is the workflow project-scoped?
Are the tools project-scoped?
Is the approval valid for this project?
Is the autonomy license valid for this action?
Will cost and performance be attributed correctly?
Is the output going to the correct destination?
This test should become a repeated implementation principle.

6.112 The Summary Sufficiency Test

Before Portfolio Executive receives raw project data, Omnira should ask:
Can an aggregated signal answer the question?
Can a governed summary answer the question?
Can the Project Executive provide a recommendation?
Is raw access actually required?
Would raw access expose customers or strategy unnecessarily?
The preferred answer is the least invasive form that still supports leadership.

6.113 The Authority Test

Before action, Omnira should distinguish:
Can the system see this?
Can the system understand this?
Can the system recommend something?
Can the system prepare something?
Can the system execute internally?
Can the system act externally?
Can the system spend?
Can the system change policy?
These are different authorities.
They must not be treated as one permission.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
6.114 Failure Modes

The project isolation architecture must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Convention-Based Isolation
The system relies on developers or agents remembering to filter by project.
Failure Mode 2 — UI-Only Isolation
Pages appear project-scoped while backend data access remains global.
Failure Mode 3 — Shared Memory Leakage
Project agents retrieve unrelated project memories.
Failure Mode 4 — Shared Credential Leakage
One project uses another project’s external credentials.
Failure Mode 5 — Approval Leakage
An approval from one project is reused elsewhere.
Failure Mode 6 — Autonomy Leakage
A successful workflow grants implied authority to another workflow or project.
Failure Mode 7 — Brand Leakage
The wrong project identity, tone, or promise appears in another project.
Failure Mode 8 — Cost Leakage
Costs are attributed to the wrong project or hidden as shared cost.
Failure Mode 9 — Metric Leakage
A metric is interpreted using another project’s definition.
Failure Mode 10 — Founder Privacy Leakage
Private calendar or personal details flow into Workforce or project agents.
Failure Mode 11 — Portfolio Overreach
Portfolio Executive accesses unnecessary raw project data.
Failure Mode 12 — Cross-Tenant Leakage
Future customer projects expose data to internal or other customer projects.
Failure Mode 13 — Context Drift
A long-running operation silently changes project scope.
Failure Mode 14 — Cache Leakage
Cached project data is served in another project context.
Failure Mode 15 — Search Leakage
Global search exposes unauthorized project information.
Failure Mode 16 — Emergency Overreach
Crisis handling bypasses boundaries without logging or expiration.
These failure modes must be treated as architectural threats.

6.115 Design Requirements

Any implementation of Executive Intelligence must preserve these requirements:
Every project must have a stable identifier.
Every executive object must have explicit scope.
Every mission must identify its project.
Every workflow instance must be project-scoped.
Every agent assignment must be project-scoped.
Every tool call must carry project authority.
Every external action must verify project destination.
Every Memory write and retrieval must be scoped.
Every Knowledge retrieval must be authorized.
Every cost must be attributed.
Every performance event must identify project origin.
Every approval must identify exact scope.
Every autonomy license must remain project- and workflow-specific.
Every cross-project access must be explicit.
Every temporary grant must expire.
Every boundary violation must be logged.
Every high-impact violation must escalate.
Every future customer project must support tenant-grade isolation.
Every Portfolio summary must minimize sensitive data.
Every Founder-private detail must remain restricted.
Every project boundary must survive UI, workflow, model, and infrastructure changes.
These requirements are not optional implementation details.
They define whether Executive Intelligence can safely exist.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
6.116 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines architecture, not a specific technical stack.
Project isolation may later be implemented through:
Project contexts.
Tenant identifiers.
Authorization policies.
Row-level security.
Scoped service interfaces.
Project namespaces.
Separate indexes.
Credential vaults.
Policy engines.
Audit logs.
Approval objects.
Autonomy license objects.
Event envelopes.
Project-specific queues.
Access grants.
Data classification.
Observability systems.
The technical mechanisms may evolve.
The isolation contract must not.

6.117 The Project Isolation Contract

Omnira must guarantee:
A project knows what it owns.
A project knows what it may access.
A project knows what it may do.
A project cannot silently inherit another project’s authority.
A project cannot accidentally publish through another project.
A project cannot reuse another project’s approval.
A project cannot inherit another project’s autonomy.
A project cannot retrieve unrelated Memory.
A project cannot expose customer data across boundaries.
A project cannot hide its costs inside another project.
Portfolio leadership can see enough to lead without seeing everything.
Shared infrastructure can serve many projects without blending them.
Atlas can communicate across scopes without confusing them.
Founder-private context can support planning without spreading downward.
Future customer projects can remain truly isolated.
If these guarantees are not true, Omnira is not ready for broad autonomy.

6.118 Closing Principle

Project isolation is not a database filter.
It is not a route.
It is not a naming convention.
It is not a prompt instruction.
It is not an optional security enhancement.
Project isolation is the organizational boundary that allows Omnira to lead several intelligent businesses without blending their customers, strategies, memories, permissions, costs, risks, or identities.
The Portfolio Executive may see the organization.
The Project Executive may lead the project.
Manager may coordinate the mission.
Workforce may perform the task.
But every layer must know where one project ends and another begins.
Without that boundary, autonomy becomes unsafe.
With that boundary, Omnira can scale from internal projects to a governed portfolio of future customer organizations.
Atlas may see the whole.
Every project must remain its own.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Cadence Is an Executive Control System
text:
7.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Executive Intelligence must operate over time.
Leadership cannot exist only when the founder asks a question.
It cannot depend on random conversations, manually remembered reviews, occasional dashboards, or crisis-driven attention.
Omnira requires a deliberate Executive Operating Cadence.
The cadence defines when Executive Intelligence should:
Observe.
Review.
Prioritize.
Plan.
Recommend.
Delegate.
Request approval.
Measure.
Learn.
Reconsider.
Escalate.
The objective is not to create more reporting.
The objective is to create reliable organizational rhythm.
A good cadence should help Omnira notice important changes early, maintain strategic continuity, protect founder focus, review decisions before they become stale, and translate long-term direction into daily action.
A bad cadence produces noise.
It creates repetitive reports, unnecessary approvals, constant reprioritization, meeting theatre, and executive fatigue.
This chapter defines how Executive Intelligence should operate daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annually, and in response to significant events.

7.2 The Core Thesis

Executive Intelligence should operate through a layered cadence.
Different time horizons serve different leadership purposes.
Daily cadence creates focus.
Weekly cadence creates coordinated execution.
Monthly cadence creates accountability.
Quarterly cadence creates strategic adaptation.
Annual cadence creates long-term direction.
Event-driven cadence creates responsiveness.
These rhythms must connect.
Daily priorities should support the weekly plan.
Weekly plans should support monthly objectives.
Monthly reviews should inform quarterly strategy.
Quarterly strategy should advance annual direction.
Event-driven changes may interrupt any layer, but they must remain governed and traceable.
The Executive Operating Cadence is not a collection of unrelated reports.
It is one continuous leadership system operating at several time horizons.

7.3 Cadence Is an Executive Control System

Cadence is more than scheduling.
It is a control system for organizational attention.
Without cadence:
Urgent work dominates important work.
Old decisions remain active.
Paused projects quietly reactivate.
Workforce activity drifts from strategy.
Approvals accumulate invisibly.
Risks appear only after damage.
Founder capacity is ignored.
Performance data is reviewed too late.
New ideas continuously displace unfinished work.
Cadence creates recurring decision points.
It gives Executive Intelligence defined opportunities to assess whether the organization is still doing the right work.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.4 The Executive Time Horizons

Executive Intelligence should reason across several time horizons.
Immediate Horizon
Minutes to hours.
Used for:
Incidents.
Approvals.
Critical blockers.
Safety issues.
High-impact external actions.
Unexpected operational events.
Daily Horizon
One working day.
Used for:
Founder focus.
Current project status.
Approvals.
Risks.
Immediate priorities.
Do-Not-Start guidance.
Weekly Horizon
One operating week.
Used for:
Goals.
Mission allocation.
Workforce planning.
Project focus distribution.
Dependencies.
Gantt-style sequencing.
Monthly Horizon
One calendar month.
Used for:
Performance accountability.
Revenue and cost review.
Strategy validation.
Autonomy maturity.
Mode review.
Decision review.
Quarterly Horizon
Approximately three months.
Used for:
Portfolio direction.
Project viability.
Strategic sequencing.
Capability investment.
Resource reallocation.
Major autonomy progression.
Annual Horizon
One year and beyond.
Used for:
Organizational direction.
Business portfolio choices.
Revenue ambition.
Founder role evolution.
Major capability goals.
Long-term risk reduction.
Each horizon should influence the others without collapsing into them.

7.5 Cadence Ownership

The Portfolio Executive owns the portfolio-level cadence.
Project Executives own project-level cadence.
Manager owns operational status coordination inside active missions.
Workforce provides task and execution reports.
Performance Intelligence provides measurements.
Memory preserves relevant continuity.
Decision Ledger preserves major decisions.
Atlas communicates the resulting executive outputs.
The responsibilities should remain distinct:
Executive determines what requires review.
Manager gathers and normalizes execution state.
Workforce reports outputs and blockers.
Performance measures outcomes.
Executive interprets and decides.
Cadence must not turn Executive Intelligence into a status collector or queue manager.

7.6 Cadence by Project Mode

Cadence should adapt to project lifecycle and operating mode.
Not every project requires daily executive attention.
Active Projects
May require:
Daily status interpretation.
Weekly planning.
Monthly review.
Quarterly strategy review.
Observer Projects
May require:
Weekly or biweekly monitoring.
Monthly review.
Event-triggered escalation.
Hibernated Projects
May require:
Monthly or quarterly review.
Restart-condition monitoring.
Event-triggered reassessment.
Archived Projects
May require:
Annual retention review.
Compliance review.
Event-triggered access only.
Operating mode also changes cadence.
A project in Crisis Mode may require continuous or hourly review.
A project in Maintenance operating mode may require only exception-based monitoring.
Cadence should reflect need.
It should not generate activity for its own sake.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.7 Cadence Density

Executive cadence should have an appropriate density.
Too little cadence creates drift.
Too much cadence creates noise and executive overhead.
The correct density depends on:
Project mode.
Risk.
Autonomy level.
External activity.
Customer impact.
Performance volatility.
Founder capacity.
Workflow maturity.
Current strategic importance.
A new autonomous publishing workflow may need daily review.
A stable internal workflow may need weekly review.
A hibernated project may need only monthly review.
Cadence should become lighter as reliability improves, unless risk remains high.

7.8 The Daily Executive Brief

The Daily Executive Brief is the first core product behavior of Executive Intelligence.
It should help the founder begin the day with clarity.
The brief should not merely summarize activity.
It should answer:
What changed?
What matters now?
What needs attention?
What requires approval?
What should be done today?
What should not be started?
What risks are emerging?
What does founder capacity allow?
The brief should be concise at the top and expandable underneath.
The founder should be able to understand the day in less than a few minutes while retaining access to deeper evidence.

7.9 Daily Brief Structure

The Daily Executive Brief should use a hybrid structure.
Executive Summary
A short, decision-oriented overview.
Recommended Focus
The primary focus for the day.
Portfolio Status
A concise view of each relevant project.
Material Changes
What changed since the previous brief.
Workforce and Mission Status
What was completed, blocked, or changed.
Approvals Needed
Actions requiring founder decision.
Risks and Escalations
Important emerging issues.
Calendar and Capacity
What the founder can realistically support.
Do-Not-Start
Work that should remain deferred.
Upcoming Decision Points
Reviews or deadlines approaching.
The structure should remain stable enough to become familiar.
Content should remain dynamic.

7.10 The Executive Summary Layer

The top of the Daily Brief should answer the most important questions immediately.
A conceptual example:
Today’s Primary Focus:
Complete the Memory review required before deeper Executive implementation.
Portfolio Position:
The Prompt automation continues.
Familje-Stunden remains Observer lifecycle mode / Learning operating mode.
GainPilot remains hibernated.
Decision Required:
Approve or defer The Prompt newsletter draft.
Risk:
Project isolation validation remains incomplete.
Do Not Start:
No new architecture epic today.
The founder should not need to read the entire brief to understand the recommended direction.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.11 Recommended Daily Focus

Every Daily Executive Brief should include one primary recommended focus.
It may include a small number of secondary items.
It should not present ten equal priorities.
The primary focus should consider:
Portfolio priority.
Project urgency.
Revenue impact.
Risk.
Founder capacity.
Dependencies.
Current commitments.
Opportunity cost.
A leadership brief without a recommended focus is only reporting.

7.12 The Do-Not-Start Section

The Daily Brief should include a Do-Not-Start section when relevant.
Examples:
Do not open another major epic.
Do not restart GainPilot.
Do not increase The Prompt autonomy.
Do not merge production-impacting changes before review.
Do not schedule additional founder work during a high-load day.
This section protects focus.
It should not repeat irrelevant prohibitions every day.
Items should appear only when they are materially useful.

7.13 Daily Portfolio Status

Daily portfolio status should include only projects requiring attention.
It may show:
Project.
Lifecycle mode.
Operating mode.
Current priority.
Material change.
Risk.
Required decision.
Stable projects with no material change may be collapsed.
The brief should not become a repetitive project directory.

7.14 Daily Project Briefs

Active projects may have their own Project Executive Brief.
The Portfolio Daily Brief should summarize them rather than copy them in full.
For example:
The Prompt:
Publishing workflow completed successfully.
One article requires approval.
No serious policy violations.
Website autonomy remains L2.
Familje-Stunden:
No material change.
Support volume normal.
Next scheduled review Friday.
GainPilot:
No change.
Remains hibernated.
The founder may expand any project for deeper detail.

7.15 Daily Change Detection

The Daily Brief should focus on changes.
Executive Intelligence should compare current state against:
Previous day.
Current weekly plan.
Active decisions.
Expected mission progress.
Known risks.
Founder calendar.
Material changes may include:
Mission completed.
Mission delayed.
New approval required.
Performance anomaly.
New customer issue.
Mode change recommendation.
Autonomy violation.
Provider failure.
Founder capacity change.
If nothing changed, the brief should say so.
It should not manufacture novelty.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.16 Daily Workforce Summary

Executive Intelligence should not inspect every task.
Manager should provide a structured summary.
The Daily Brief may include:
Missions active.
Missions completed.
Missions blocked.
Approvals waiting.
Significant failures.
Capacity concerns.
Next executive decision.
Raw task logs should remain available for inspection but should not dominate the brief.

7.17 Daily Approval Queue

The Daily Brief should contain an approval queue.
Approval items should be prioritized by:
Urgency.
Impact.
Deadline.
Dependency.
Risk.
Reversibility.
Each item should show:
Project.
Requested action.
Reason.
Risk.
Recommended decision.
Deadline.
Consequence of delay.
The approval queue should not require the founder to reconstruct context manually.

7.18 Approval Batching

Where appropriate, low-risk approvals may be batched.
Examples:
Five The Prompt short news drafts.
One week of pre-approved social content.
A set of calendar planning blocks.
A group of low-risk workflow configuration changes.
Batching should reduce approval burden without broadening authority unnecessarily.
High-risk actions should remain individually reviewable.

7.19 Daily Risk Summary

The Daily Brief should surface only meaningful risks.
Risks may be categorized:
Critical.
High.
Moderate.
Watch.
Each risk should include:
Project.
Cause.
Potential impact.
Current control.
Required action.
Owner.
Review time.
The system should avoid repeatedly surfacing unchanged low-priority risks unless a deadline or threshold is approaching.

7.20 Daily Calendar Awareness

Executive Intelligence should account for founder availability.
Atlas may understand calendar details.
The Daily Brief should usually present derived capacity signals:
Deep work capacity: High.
Approval availability: Limited after 14:00.
Meeting load: Heavy.
Recommended Omnira workload: Light.
Private calendar detail should not be exposed unnecessarily.
Calendar awareness should influence recommendations.
It should not merely appear as an informational widget.

7.21 Daily Capacity Classification

Founder capacity may be expressed through a simple classification:
High.
Moderate.
Low.
Unavailable.
The classification may consider:
Available time.
Deep work windows.
Meeting density.
Personal obligations.
Recent workload.
Urgent external commitments.
Executive Intelligence should avoid pretending that a free hour equals a useful deep-work hour.
Capacity is qualitative as well as quantitative.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.22 Daily Brief Delivery

The initial Daily Executive Brief should be available through:
Atlas conversation.
Omnira dashboard.
Future delivery may include:
Mobile notification.
Mobile app.
Voice briefing.
Email summary.
Wearable notification.
The content should remain consistent across surfaces.
The depth may vary.
A mobile notification may show only the primary focus and urgent approval count.

7.23 Daily Brief Timing

The brief should appear at a useful time for the founder.
The default may be morning.
However, timing should adapt to:
Founder schedule.
Timezone.
Work habits.
Calendar.
Project activity.
Overnight automation.
If major automation occurs overnight, the morning brief should summarize it.
If the founder starts later, delivery should align accordingly.
Cadence should serve the user.
The user should not serve the cadence.

7.24 Daily Closing Review

A lightweight end-of-day review may be useful.
It should answer:
What was completed?
What changed?
What remains open?
What should carry into tomorrow?
Did today’s focus remain valid?
Did new risk appear?
This review should be brief and optional unless risk or activity requires it.
It should not create a second full Daily Brief.

7.25 Carryover Rules

Unfinished work should not disappear at the end of the day.
Carryover should classify work as:
Continue tomorrow.
Reschedule.
Reprioritize.
Delegate.
Cancel.
Escalate.
Blocked.
Carryover should include a reason.
Silent carryover creates backlog drift.

7.26 The Weekly Executive Cycle

The weekly cadence converts strategy into coordinated work.
The preferred weekly planning point is Sunday.
The Weekly Executive Plan should determine:
What the organization will accomplish.
Which projects receive focus.
Which missions will run.
Which agents or teams are required.
What the founder must do.
What requires approval.
What must remain deferred.
The weekly plan should be realistic.
It should reflect actual capacity.

7.27 Sunday Executive Planning

Sunday planning should be a major executive ritual.
It should review:
Previous week outcomes.
Unfinished work.
Current portfolio priorities.
Project modes.
Founder calendar.
Workforce capacity.
Open approvals.
Dependencies.
Risks.
Performance signals.
Upcoming deadlines.
It should then produce the next week’s plan.
The planning process should not begin from a blank page.
It should begin from continuity.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.28 Weekly Plan Structure

The Weekly Executive Plan should include:
Weekly Executive Objective.
Portfolio Focus Allocation.
Project Goals.
Executive Missions.
Workforce Assignments.
Founder Commitments.
Approval Schedule.
Dependencies.
Risk Controls.
Do-Not-Start List.
Gantt-Style Timeline.
End-of-Week Success Criteria.
The plan should make tradeoffs explicit.

7.29 Weekly Executive Objective

Each week should have one overarching executive objective.
Examples:
Complete the foundations required for The Prompt website autonomy.
Stabilize Memory Stage 1 before opening additional implementation work.
Validate project isolation across active project workflows.
Prepare Familje-Stunden analytics for informed reactivation.
The objective provides coherence across several tasks.

7.30 Weekly Project Focus Allocation

The Weekly Plan should recommend focus distribution.
A conceptual example:
Omnira foundations: 50%.
The Prompt website autonomy: 35%.
Familje-Stunden observation: 15%.
GainPilot: 0%.
These percentages communicate intent rather than exact time tracking.
If actual activity diverges materially, Executive Intelligence should surface it.

7.31 Weekly Project Goals

Each active project should receive a limited number of weekly goals.
A weekly goal should specify:
Outcome.
Owner.
Measurement.
Deadline.
Dependencies.
Approval requirements.
Risk controls.
Goals should be achievable within the week.
Longer initiatives should be broken into weekly outcomes without losing strategic context.

7.32 Weekly Executive Missions

The weekly plan should list the Executive Mission Briefs expected to run.
Each mission should show:
Project.
Objective.
Assigned capabilities.
Cadence.
Expected output.
Approval gates.
Success criteria.
Escalation triggers.
This connects strategic planning to execution.

7.33 Weekly Workforce Planning

Executive Intelligence should define required capabilities.
Workforce Intelligence should determine how those capabilities are instantiated.
The weekly plan may state:
The Prompt:
Research Agent.
Content Writer.
Editor.
QA Reviewer.
Performance Analyst.
Omnira:
Architecture Reviewer.
Implementation Agent.
Security Reviewer.
Test Agent.
The plan should not over-specify operational assignments that belong to Manager.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.34 Weekly Founder Commitments

The weekly plan should identify what only the founder can do.
Examples:
Approve the autonomy policy.
Review the newsletter draft.
Choose between two strategy alternatives.
Complete a major architecture decision.
Attend a customer meeting.
Provide unavailable context.
Founder commitments should be few and visible.
A system that automates work but creates endless founder review is not reducing burden.

7.35 Weekly Calendar Planning

After approval, Executive Intelligence may create calendar events for founder commitments.
The workflow should be:
Executive proposes schedule.
Founder reviews or edits.
Founder approves.
Events are added to calendar.
Changes remain editable.
The plan should account for:
Existing calendar events.
Deep work windows.
Travel or appointments.
Family commitments.
Study schedule.
Recovery time.
Approval deadlines.
The calendar should reflect the plan.
The plan should not ignore the calendar.

7.36 Gantt-Style Weekly Timeline

The weekly plan should include a Gantt-style timeline or equivalent visual sequence.
It should show:
Mission start.
Mission duration.
Dependencies.
Approval points.
Founder work blocks.
Expected completion.
Review point.
The timeline should remain lightweight.
Its purpose is to show sequencing and dependencies.
It should not become false precision.

7.37 Weekly Dependency Review

Sunday planning should identify:
Hard dependencies.
Soft dependencies.
Risk-reducing dependencies.
Optional enhancements.
The plan should not schedule dependent work before prerequisites are realistically available.
It should also avoid overstating every preference as a hard dependency.

7.38 Weekly Risk Review

The Weekly Plan should identify the small number of risks most likely to affect the week.
Each risk should include:
Likelihood.
Impact.
Early warning signal.
Mitigation.
Escalation threshold.
Risk review should influence scheduling and mission design.

7.39 Weekly Do-Not-Start List

The Weekly Plan should explicitly state which work should not be started.
Examples:
No GainPilot implementation.
No new Voice epic.
No autonomous newsletter sending.
No production merge before review.
No new external MCP connection.
The list should protect the week’s objective.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.40 Weekly Success Criteria

The plan should define what success looks like by the end of the week.
Examples:
Project isolation review completed.
Five The Prompt article drafts prepared.
Decision Ledger object finalized.
No serious policy violations.
All founder approvals resolved.
No new epic started.
Success criteria make the end-of-week review objective.

7.41 Weekly Mid-Cycle Adjustment

The weekly plan should not become rigid.
Executive Intelligence may adjust it when:
A crisis appears.
Founder capacity changes.
A mission fails.
A higher-value opportunity emerges.
A dependency is delayed.
Customer harm risk appears.
Performance materially changes.
Adjustments should remain proportional.
Not every small deviation requires replanning the week.

7.42 Reprioritization Threshold

Executive Intelligence should reprioritize only when the expected benefit exceeds the disruption cost.
Before changing the weekly plan, it should ask:
What changed?
Is the evidence verified?
How urgent is the change?
What current work will be disrupted?
Can the issue be handled without changing the plan?
Does the change affect the weekly objective?
Is founder approval required?
This prevents strategic whiplash.

7.43 Weekly End Review

At the end of the week, Executive Intelligence should review:
Goals completed.
Goals incomplete.
Mission outcomes.
Approval delays.
Performance signals.
Risks realized.
Unexpected work.
Founder capacity accuracy.
Carryover.
Lessons learned.
The review should feed Sunday planning.

7.44 Weekly Carryover

Carryover into the next week should be explicit.
Each item should be classified:
Continue.
Rescope.
Reassign.
Defer.
Cancel.
Escalate.
Repeated carryover should trigger examination.
A task that carries over for several weeks may indicate:
Poor priority.
Insufficient capacity.
Hidden dependency.
Weak mission definition.
Avoidance.
Strategy drift.

7.45 The Monthly Executive Review

The monthly review creates accountability and strategic continuity.
It should examine both projects and portfolio.
The monthly review should answer:
What changed?
What worked?
What failed?
What generated revenue?
What consumed capacity?
Which assumptions were wrong?
Which risks increased?
Which decisions require review?
What should change next month?
The monthly review should not simply aggregate weekly reports.
It should interpret the month.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.46 Monthly Portfolio Review

The portfolio-level monthly review should include:
Portfolio objective progress.
Project mode review.
Revenue and cost overview.
Founder capacity trends.
Shared infrastructure health.
Cross-project dependencies.
Major risks.
Autonomy maturity.
Approval burden.
Strategic recommendations.
It should determine whether portfolio focus remains correct.

7.47 Monthly Project Review

Each active or strategically relevant project should receive a monthly review.
The review may include:
Goal progress.
Revenue.
Costs.
Customer growth.
Retention.
Engagement.
Workflow reliability.
Approval rate.
Correction rate.
Policy violations.
Trust Score.
Roadmap progress.
Operating mode suitability.
The level of detail should match project mode.

7.48 Monthly Financial Review

Executive Intelligence should review project and portfolio economics.
The review may include:
Revenue.
Recurring revenue.
Costs.
Model usage.
Infrastructure spend.
Marketing spend.
Refunds.
Cost per result.
Revenue per customer.
Approval burden as operational cost.
Founder time as strategic cost.
The review should identify both direct financial cost and hidden operational cost.

7.49 Monthly Revenue Review

Revenue should remain a primary signal.
The monthly review should ask:
Which project generated revenue?
Which project protected revenue?
Which initiative improved conversion?
Which initiative reduced churn?
Which work had no credible economic impact?
Which platform capability unlocked revenue?
Revenue interpretation should remain contextual.
A project in Learning operating mode should not be judged like a mature Growth project.

7.50 Monthly Cost Review

Cost review should identify:
Unexpected spend.
Cost concentration.
Provider cost changes.
Expensive low-value workflows.
Shared cost allocation.
Approval overhead.
Founder time consumption.
Maintenance burden.
Executive Intelligence should recommend where cost should be reduced, accepted, or increased.
Cheaper is not always better.
Value matters.

7.51 Monthly Autonomy Review

Autonomy licenses should be reviewed monthly or according to their specific review dates.
The review should examine:
Successful runs.
Approval rate.
Correction rate.
Policy violations.
Rollback performance.
Project boundary compliance.
Trust Score.
Performance stability.
Founder overrides.
Possible outcomes:
Maintain autonomy.
Increase autonomy.
Reduce autonomy.
Pause autonomy.
Expire license.
Extend trial.
Request more evidence.
Autonomy should not expand silently.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.52 Monthly Approval Burden Review

The system should evaluate whether approval burden is reasonable.
Questions include:
How many approvals were requested?
How many were approved unchanged?
How many required edits?
How many were rejected?
How long did approvals wait?
Which approvals could be batched?
Which workflows are ready for broader policy approval?
The goal is to reduce unnecessary founder involvement without weakening governance.

7.53 Monthly Decision Review

The monthly cadence should review decisions whose review dates have arrived.
The review should ask:
Is the decision still valid?
Has evidence changed?
Did the expected impact occur?
Did risk materialize?
Should the decision be renewed?
Should it be revised?
Should it expire?
Decisions should not survive automatically.

7.54 Monthly Strategy Review

The Project Executive should test whether the current strategy remains credible.
It should examine:
Customer evidence.
Market evidence.
Performance.
Revenue.
Cost.
Risk.
Execution capability.
Portfolio constraints.
Founder intent.
A strategy should not be changed because of one bad week.
It should not remain unchanged despite persistent contrary evidence.

7.55 Monthly Mode Review

Lifecycle and operating modes should be reviewed.
Possible questions:
Should The Prompt move from Build toward Growth?
Should Familje-Stunden remain Observer lifecycle mode / Learning operating mode?
Should Omnira shift from Build to Stabilize?
Should GainPilot remain hibernated?
Does any project require Crisis Mode?
Mode changes should be evidence-based and traceable.

7.56 Monthly Board-Style Review

The monthly review should feel like an executive and board review.
It should include:
Executive summary.
Financial position.
Project position.
Performance.
Risks.
Major decisions.
Autonomy changes.
Founder capacity.
Strategic recommendations.
Next-month priorities.
It should not imitate unnecessary corporate ceremony.
The purpose is disciplined reflection.

7.57 The Quarterly Strategic Review

The quarterly cadence should examine direction rather than only execution.
It should answer:
Are we operating the right projects?
Are current priorities producing value?
Is the portfolio too broad?
Which capabilities became strategic?
Which projects deserve more investment?
Which projects should pause?
Which assumptions changed?
What should the next quarter optimize for?
Quarterly review is where material strategic changes should normally occur.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.58 Quarterly Portfolio Strategy

The Portfolio Executive should review:
Portfolio composition.
Revenue trajectory.
Project viability.
Strategic sequencing.
Platform investment.
Founder capacity trend.
Workforce maturity.
Autonomy maturity.
Major risks.
New opportunities.
It should recommend the next quarter’s portfolio focus.

7.59 Quarterly Project Viability

Each major project should be assessed for:
Strategic fit.
Customer value.
Revenue potential.
Current traction.
Cost.
Risk.
Founder commitment.
Execution readiness.
Opportunity cost.
Possible outcomes:
Expand.
Continue.
Stabilize.
Observe.
Hibernate.
Prepare for retirement.

7.60 Quarterly Capability Review

Shared Omnira capabilities should be assessed.
Examples:
Memory.
Knowledge.
AI Intelligence.
Performance Intelligence.
Workforce.
Executive Intelligence.
Approval systems.
Project isolation.
Voice & UX.
MCP governance.
The review should ask:
Which capabilities are now production-ready?
Which remain experimental?
Which are underused?
Which have become bottlenecks?
Which should receive investment next?

7.61 Quarterly Workforce Review

The quarterly review should evaluate Workforce capability.
It may assess:
Role coverage.
Mission success.
Agent quality.
Coordination reliability.
Tool capability.
Escalation quality.
Cost.
Reusability.
Project isolation compliance.
Executive Intelligence should identify missing roles or capabilities.

7.62 Quarterly Autonomy Strategy

Quarterly review should examine autonomy across the portfolio.
Questions include:
Which workflows became trustworthy?
Where did autonomy create value?
Where did autonomy create risk?
Which approvals remain necessary?
Which projects are suitable for broader autonomy?
Where should autonomy contract?
The goal is deliberate progression.
Not maximum autonomy.

7.63 Quarterly Risk Review

Quarterly review should examine systemic risk.
Examples:
Provider concentration.
Founder dependency.
Security posture.
Project isolation.
Revenue concentration.
Approval bottlenecks.
Data quality.
Model reliability.
Customer trust.
Regulatory exposure.
Systemic risk may justify portfolio-level work even when no immediate incident exists.

7.64 Quarterly Roadmap Review

The roadmap should be challenged quarterly.
The review should ask:
Which milestones were completed?
Which dependencies changed?
Which initiatives became unnecessary?
Which work should move earlier?
Which work should move later?
Which roadmap assumptions failed?
A roadmap is a strategic hypothesis.
It is not a promise to preserve outdated sequencing.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.65 The Annual Direction Review

The annual review should establish broad organizational direction.
It should not define every task for the year.
It should answer:
Which businesses should Omnira operate?
Which projects should expand?
Which projects should remain paused?
Which projects should be retired?
What revenue direction should guide the year?
What autonomy maturity should be reached?
How should founder involvement change?
Which shared capabilities matter most?
Which risks must be materially reduced?
The annual direction should guide quarterly planning.
It should remain adaptable.

7.66 Annual Portfolio Thesis

The annual review should define a portfolio thesis.
A portfolio thesis may state:
Omnira will focus on proving one fully governed autonomous media project, preparing one family product for informed growth, and keeping non-core projects hibernated until the operating system can support them safely.
The thesis should clarify what the year is about.
It should also clarify what the year is not about.

7.67 Annual Revenue Direction

The annual review should establish revenue priorities.
It may define:
Revenue targets.
Recurring revenue goals.
Priority revenue projects.
Cost constraints.
Investment boundaries.
Validation thresholds.
Time-to-revenue expectations.
Revenue goals should remain realistic enough to guide decisions.
They should not become motivational numbers disconnected from operating capacity.

7.68 Annual Autonomy Direction

The annual review should define autonomy ambition.
Examples:
The Prompt website operates autonomously within approved editorial policy.
Routine comment replies operate autonomously.
Newsletter preparation is autonomous.
Newsletter sending operates under batch approval.
Familje-Stunden support drafting is autonomous but sensitive sending remains approval-gated.
Autonomy goals should specify scope.
“Make Omnira autonomous” is too vague to govern.

7.69 Annual Founder Role Review

The annual review should examine how the founder’s role should change.
Questions include:
Which decisions still require founder involvement?
Which approvals can be delegated?
Which project areas consume unnecessary founder time?
Where is founder judgment uniquely valuable?
Which repetitive responsibilities should disappear?
Executive Intelligence should gradually increase founder leverage.
It should not simply create more sophisticated work for the founder.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.70 Event-Driven Executive Cadence

Not every important event waits for the next scheduled review.
Executive Intelligence must support event-driven cadence.
Events may trigger:
Immediate alert.
Executive reassessment.
Approval request.
Mission pause.
Risk escalation.
Crisis Mode.
New Decision Ledger entry.
Schedule adjustment.
Event-driven response must remain proportional.

7.71 Event Categories

Executive events may include:
Critical risk.
Customer harm signal.
Security incident.
Unauthorized spend.
Major performance anomaly.
Workflow failure pattern.
Provider outage.
Revenue threshold crossed.
Customer growth threshold crossed.
Trust Score change.
Autonomy violation.
Founder capacity change.
Strategic opportunity.
Different events require different response speed.

7.72 Event Severity

Events should be classified.
Critical
Immediate executive action required.
High
Action required within the current operating day.
Moderate
Review in the next Daily Brief or scheduled review.
Informational
Record for trend analysis unless it accumulates.
Severity should reflect impact and urgency.

7.73 Crisis Override

Crisis Mode may override normal cadence.
During crisis:
Review frequency increases.
External actions may pause.
Approvals become stricter.
Founder notification becomes immediate.
Normal missions may be deferred.
Logging increases.
Recovery becomes the primary objective.
Crisis Mode should end only through defined recovery conditions.

7.74 Opportunity-Driven Override

Positive opportunities may also justify cadence changes.
Examples:
Unexpected customer growth.
High-performing content.
New strategic partnership.
Sudden market demand.
New revenue opportunity.
Executive Intelligence should assess:
Evidence.
Urgency.
Capacity.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Reversibility.
Excitement alone should not override the plan.

7.75 Founder-Initiated Override

The founder may change priorities at any time.
Executive Intelligence should support the decision while stating:
What will be delayed.
Which missions are affected.
What opportunity cost is created.
Which approvals or calendar changes are required.
Whether the change conflicts with current strategy.
Founder authority remains ultimate.
Executive honesty remains required.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.76 Cadence and Decision Ledger

Significant cadence outputs should create or reference Decision Ledger entries.
Examples:
Weekly priority changes.
Project mode changes.
Autonomy changes.
Major roadmap changes.
Budget decisions.
Crisis activation.
Project reactivation.
Project hibernation.
Routine brief content should not flood the Decision Ledger.
Only material decisions should be preserved as decisions.

7.77 Cadence and Memory

Memory should preserve:
Recurring priorities.
Lessons from reviews.
Founder preferences.
Repeated risks.
Planning accuracy.
Approval patterns.
Project mode history.
Reasons for strategy change.
Memory should not preserve every sentence of every brief as equally important.
Executive Intelligence should extract durable meaning.

7.78 Cadence and Performance Intelligence

Performance Intelligence should provide time-appropriate measurements.
Daily cadence may use:
Operational status.
Immediate anomalies.
Workflow success.
Approval queue.
Weekly cadence may use:
Goal progress.
Execution reliability.
Output quality.
Capacity.
Monthly cadence may use:
Revenue.
Retention.
Cost.
Customer growth.
Trust Score.
Policy violations.
Quarterly cadence may use:
Strategic trends.
Portfolio viability.
Capability maturity.
Systemic risk.
The measurement window should match the decision horizon.

7.79 Data Freshness

Every executive review should understand data freshness.
The system should identify:
Current.
Delayed.
Incomplete.
Estimated.
Unverified.
Stale.
A Daily Brief should not present week-old operational data as current.
A quarterly review should not overreact to one day of volatility.
Data freshness is part of executive evidence quality.

7.80 Cadence and Founder Feedback

The founder should be able to provide feedback on briefs and plans.
Examples:
This was useful.
This was too detailed.
This priority was wrong.
This risk was overemphasized.
This approval should have been batched.
This recommendation matched my judgment.
Feedback should improve future cadence.
It should influence Trust Score and personalization without weakening governance.

7.81 Cadence Personalization

The Executive Operating Cadence should adapt to founder preferences.
Possible preferences include:
Brief length.
Preferred delivery time.
Voice or text.
Level of detail.
Notification threshold.
Approval grouping.
Weekend planning style.
Calendar block length.
Personalization should affect presentation and timing.
It should not suppress critical risk or required governance.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.82 Executive Depth Levels

Cadence outputs should use different reasoning depths.
Fast Executive Response
Used for simple operational questions.
Standard Executive Review
Used for Daily Briefs and routine priorities.
Deep Executive Analysis
Used for strategy, autonomy, risk, and roadmap decisions.
Board-Level Review
Used for monthly, quarterly, and annual reviews.
The depth should match the impact of the decision.

7.83 Cognitive Budget

Executive Intelligence should not use the same reasoning budget for every event.
A routine successful workflow summary should be inexpensive.
A strategy change should receive deeper analysis.
A major autonomy increase should receive:
Historical evidence.
Performance review.
Policy review.
Risk analysis.
Pre-mortem.
Alternative analysis.
Rollback planning.
Cognitive budget should scale with impact, uncertainty, and irreversibility.

7.84 Cadence and Notification Control

Notifications should be governed.
Executive Intelligence should avoid:
Duplicate notifications.
Repeated unchanged warnings.
Low-value status alerts.
Unnecessary approval interruptions.
Cross-project noise.
Notifications should be grouped where possible.
Critical issues should remain immediate.

7.85 Report Suppression

A report should be suppressed or shortened when:
No material change occurred.
The project is stable.
The same information was already delivered.
No decision is required.
The data is incomplete.
The review would create no executive value.
Silence can be better than repetition.
The absence of a report should not mean the absence of monitoring.

7.86 Materiality Thresholds

Executive Intelligence should use materiality thresholds.
A change is material when it may affect:
Strategy.
Revenue.
Cost.
Risk.
Customer trust.
Founder capacity.
Project mode.
Autonomy.
Major mission outcome.
Portfolio priority.
Minor changes may remain in operational logs.
Material changes belong in executive cadence.

7.87 Cadence Continuity

Each review should connect to previous decisions.
The system should identify:
What was previously decided?
What was expected?
What actually happened?
What remains unresolved?
What changed?
This prevents every review from restarting the conversation.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.88 Planning Accuracy

Executive Intelligence should evaluate its own planning quality.
Metrics may include:
Goal completion rate.
Carryover rate.
Forecast accuracy.
Approval timing accuracy.
Capacity estimation accuracy.
Risk prediction accuracy.
Mission delay rate.
Poor planning accuracy should lead to calibration.
It should not lead automatically to more aggressive planning.

7.89 Founder Capacity Accuracy

Executive Intelligence should compare predicted founder capacity against reality.
Questions include:
Were planned deep-work blocks used?
Were approval windows realistic?
Was workload too high?
Were personal commitments respected?
Was the founder forced into unnecessary intervention?
This helps the system improve scheduling.

7.90 Cadence Health

The Executive Operating Cadence should have its own health status.
Cadence health may evaluate:
Brief usefulness.
Review completion.
Decision follow-through.
Approval backlog.
Report redundancy.
Planning accuracy.
Carryover.
Risk detection.
Founder satisfaction.
Cadence burden.
A cadence that produces many reports but few decisions is unhealthy.

7.91 Cadence Burden

Executive Intelligence should measure the burden it creates.
Burden may include:
Time spent reading briefs.
Time spent approving.
Number of interruptions.
Repeated requests for context.
Planning meetings.
Manual status reconstruction.
Calendar fragmentation.
The purpose of cadence is to reduce coordination burden.
If burden increases continuously, the architecture is failing.

7.92 Review Preparation

Executive reviews should be prepared automatically where possible.
Preparation may include:
Collecting governed summaries.
Retrieving relevant decisions.
Comparing performance.
Checking review dates.
Identifying anomalies.
Summarizing approvals.
Calculating carryover.
Assessing calendar capacity.
The founder should not need to assemble the review manually.

7.93 Evidence Before Opinion

Every major review should distinguish evidence from interpretation.
The structure may be:
Evidence:
What happened.
Interpretation:
What it may mean.
Recommendation:
What should happen next.
Confidence:
How certain the recommendation is.
This keeps Executive Intelligence honest.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.94 Review Alternatives

Significant recommendations should include alternatives.
For example:
Option A:
Continue The Prompt website autonomy work.
Option B:
Pause and prioritize project isolation.
Option C:
Run both at reduced scope.
Recommended:
Option B, because isolation is a hard dependency.
Alternatives make tradeoffs visible.

7.95 Review Dates

Every major cadence decision should define when it should be reviewed.
Examples:
Review after one week.
Review after 30 successful runs.
Review at month end.
Review when revenue reaches threshold.
Review after the next customer cohort.
Review dates may be time-based or condition-based.

7.96 Cadence Conflict Resolution

Cadence layers may conflict.
A daily urgent issue may conflict with the weekly plan.
A monthly strategy recommendation may conflict with annual direction.
Conflict resolution should consider:
Severity.
Evidence.
Authority.
Reversibility.
Opportunity cost.
Time horizon.
Founder decision.
A lower-level event may temporarily override a higher-level plan.
It should not silently rewrite long-term strategy.

7.97 Cadence and Project Isolation

Every cadence output must respect project boundaries.
The Daily Brief may combine governed project summaries.
It must not expose unnecessary raw project data.
Weekly plans must identify project scope.
Monthly reviews must preserve metric definitions.
Portfolio reviews must not become unrestricted data aggregation.
The project isolation contract remains active during every review.

7.98 Cadence and Future Customer Projects

Future customer projects may require customer-controlled cadence.
Customers may choose:
Brief frequency.
Review participants.
Approval timing.
Notification channels.
Data included.
Portfolio summary visibility.
Autonomy review cadence.
Internal Omnira cadence should not automatically govern customer projects beyond contractual authority.

7.99 Cadence and Multi-User Organizations

Future multi-user environments may include:
Owner brief.
Executive team brief.
Project lead brief.
Approver queue.
Operator report.
Board review.
Each view should respect role and project scope.
One organization may have several cadence surfaces without creating several sources of truth.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.100 Cadence Record Retention

Not every cadence artifact requires permanent storage.
Possible retention rules:
Daily Briefs:
Short- or medium-term retention, with durable lessons extracted.
Weekly Plans:
Retained for planning history and accuracy analysis.
Monthly Reviews:
Long-term retention.
Quarterly Reviews:
Long-term strategic retention.
Annual Direction:
Canonical retention.
Crisis Reviews:
Permanent audit retention.
Retention should balance learning, audit, cost, and privacy.

7.101 Cadence Versioning

Plans and reviews may change.
The system should preserve:
Original version.
Updated version.
Reason for change.
Authority.
Time.
Affected missions.
Decision impact.
Silent plan mutation makes accountability impossible.

7.102 Cadence and Voice UX

Future Voice & UX may deliver:
Morning executive briefing.
Approval prompts.
End-of-day recap.
Sunday planning conversation.
Monthly board-style discussion.
Crisis alerts.
Voice should summarize.
Detailed evidence should remain inspectable through visual interfaces.
Voice must not hide important uncertainty.

7.103 Cadence Dashboard

The Executive Cadence dashboard may include:
Today.
This Week.
This Month.
Quarter.
Annual Direction.
Approvals.
Decisions Due for Review.
Risks.
Calendar Capacity.
Do-Not-Start.
The dashboard should make time horizons visible.
It should not become a wall of metrics.

7.104 Cadence Graph

The Intelligence Graph should show relationships between:
Annual direction.
Quarterly objectives.
Monthly priorities.
Weekly missions.
Daily focus.
Decisions.
Outcomes.
Performance.
The graph should allow the founder to trace:
Why today’s work exists.
Which weekly goal it supports.
Which strategic objective it advances.
Which decision authorized it.

7.105 Cadence Automation

Cadence preparation should become increasingly automated.
Executive Intelligence may autonomously:
Collect status.
Prepare briefs.
Detect changes.
Propose plans.
Schedule draft calendar blocks.
Identify decisions due for review.
Recommend approvals.
Generate review summaries.
High-impact decisions remain governed.
Automation should reduce preparation burden without removing founder authority.

7.106 Cadence Approval Model

Different cadence outputs require different approval levels.
Informational
No approval required.
Recommended Plan
Founder may approve, edit, or reject.
Internal Mission Plan
May execute autonomously within authority.
External Action Plan
Requires applicable policy or approval.
Strategic Change
Requires explicit founder approval.
Crisis Action
May execute within emergency authority and must be reviewed.
The cadence should make approval status visible.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.107 The Cadence Escalation Ladder

Cadence escalation may follow:
Operational note.
Daily Brief item.
Weekly Plan issue.
Monthly Review issue.
Quarterly strategic issue.
Immediate crisis escalation.
Not every issue belongs at the highest level.
The system should escalate based on impact and persistence.

7.108 Anti-Meeting-Theatre Principle

Executive cadence should not imitate corporate rituals that create no value.
Omnira does not need meetings merely because companies have meetings.
Every review should produce at least one of:
Decision.
Priority.
Mission.
Approval.
Risk response.
Learning.
Explicit continuation.
A review that changes nothing and teaches nothing should be shortened or eliminated.

7.109 Anti-Report-Spam Principle

More reporting does not equal more intelligence.
Executive Intelligence should avoid:
Repeating stable information.
Reporting every completed task.
Creating several summaries of the same event.
Surfacing metrics without interpretation.
Asking for approval when policy already grants authority.
Generating long reports without a decision.
Executive output should be selective.

7.110 Anti-Whiplash Principle

The cadence should prevent constant strategic changes.
New information should be evaluated against:
Existing evidence.
Decision history.
Current plan.
Review date.
Trend duration.
Opportunity cost.
One unusual day should not overturn a quarterly strategy without strong reason.

7.111 Anti-Staleness Principle

The cadence must also prevent excessive stability.
A plan should not continue merely because changing it is uncomfortable.
Executive Intelligence must challenge:
Expired assumptions.
Repeated failure.
Unproductive projects.
Unnecessary approvals.
Outdated autonomy limits.
Stale roadmaps.
Ignored risks.
The system should balance continuity and adaptation.

7.112 The Daily Focus Test

Before recommending daily focus, Executive Intelligence should ask:
What is the highest-value outcome today?
What is time-sensitive?
What dependency can be unlocked?
What risk needs attention?
What does founder capacity allow?
What should be deferred?

7.113 The Weekly Plan Test

Before finalizing a Weekly Plan, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Does the plan support portfolio objectives?
Is the weekly objective clear?
Are goals achievable?
Are dependencies sequenced?
Is founder capacity realistic?
Is Workforce capacity available?
Are approval points visible?
What will not be started?
How will success be measured?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.114 The Monthly Review Test

Before completing a monthly review, Executive Intelligence should ask:
What actually changed?
What generated value?
What consumed capacity?
Which assumptions failed?
Which decisions require review?
Should any project mode change?
Should autonomy change?
What should be different next month?

7.115 The Quarterly Strategy Test

Before recommending quarterly direction, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Are these still the right projects?
Are we moving toward revenue?
Is platform investment producing leverage?
Is the portfolio too broad?
Where is systemic risk increasing?
Which capability should mature next?
What should be stopped?

7.116 The Annual Direction Test

Before setting annual direction, Executive Intelligence should ask:
What organization are we trying to become?
Which businesses deserve expansion?
What should founder involvement look like?
What autonomy level is realistic?
Which risks could threaten the entire system?
What must be true by year end?

7.117 Failure Modes

The Executive Operating Cadence must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Report Spam
The system produces frequent summaries without decisions or value.
Failure Mode 2 — Cadence Overload
The founder spends too much time reading, approving, and reviewing.
Failure Mode 3 — Daily Myopia
Daily issues dominate long-term strategy.
Failure Mode 4 — Strategic Staleness
Long-term plans remain active despite changed evidence.
Failure Mode 5 — Weekly Overplanning
The plan contains more work than available capacity.
Failure Mode 6 — Constant Reprioritization
New events repeatedly disrupt important work.
Failure Mode 7 — Hidden Carryover
Incomplete work silently accumulates.
Failure Mode 8 — Calendar Blindness
Plans ignore actual founder availability.
Failure Mode 9 — Approval Bottleneck
The cadence generates more approvals than the founder can process.
Failure Mode 10 — Metric Theatre
Reviews show metrics without interpretation.
Failure Mode 11 — Project Cadence Mismatch
Hibernated projects receive excessive attention while active projects are under-reviewed.
Failure Mode 12 — Scope Leakage
Portfolio reviews expose unnecessary project or customer data.
Failure Mode 13 — Meeting Theatre
Reviews occur because they are scheduled, not because they create value.
Failure Mode 14 — False Precision
Gantt plans imply certainty that does not exist.
Failure Mode 15 — Crisis Normalization
Temporary crisis cadence becomes permanent.
Failure Mode 16 — No Decision Continuity
Each review starts from zero and ignores previous decisions.
These failure modes should be treated as architectural constraints.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.118 Design Requirements

Any implementation of the Executive Operating Cadence should preserve these requirements:
Every cadence layer must have a defined purpose.
Every Daily Brief must recommend focus.
Every Weekly Plan must define a weekly objective.
Every major plan must identify Do-Not-Start items.
Every plan must consider founder capacity.
Every project cadence must reflect lifecycle and operating mode.
Every major review must connect to previous decisions.
Every material change must identify what changed.
Every approval item must include enough context to decide.
Every significant decision must have a review date.
Every carryover item must be classified.
Every event-driven interruption must be proportional.
Every cadence output must preserve project scope.
Every portfolio review must use governed summaries.
Every review should produce a decision, priority, mission, approval, risk response, learning, or explicit continuation.
Every cadence artifact should minimize unnecessary burden.
Every strategic horizon must connect to shorter-term execution.
These requirements define the operating rhythm of Executive Intelligence.

7.119 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines architecture, not a specific scheduling system or user interface.
The cadence may later be implemented through:
Scheduled jobs.
Event triggers.
Executive Brief objects.
Weekly Plan objects.
Calendar integrations.
Approval queues.
Decision Ledger queries.
Performance summaries.
Manager reports.
Dashboards.
Mobile notifications.
Voice briefings.
Gantt views.
Review workflows.
The implementation may evolve.
The leadership rhythm must remain coherent.

7.120 The Executive Operating Cadence Contract

Executive Intelligence must:
Create daily focus without creating noise.
Create weekly coordination without overplanning.
Create monthly accountability without metric theatre.
Create quarterly adaptation without strategic whiplash.
Create annual direction without false certainty.
Respond to events without abandoning governance.
Respect project boundaries during every review.
Account for founder capacity.
Reduce approval burden over time.
Preserve decision continuity.
Make carryover visible.
Make opportunity cost explicit.
Adjust cadence to project mode and risk.
Suppress reports that create no executive value.
Increase review intensity during crisis and reduce it after recovery.
Turn time into organizational discipline.
If a cadence feature does not support this contract, it should be reconsidered.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
7.121 Closing Principle

An intelligent organization does not only know what to do.
It knows when to observe, when to act, when to review, when to wait, and when to change direction.
Executive Operating Cadence gives Omnira that rhythm.
The Daily Executive Brief creates focus.
The Sunday Weekly Plan creates coordinated execution.
The Monthly Review creates accountability.
The Quarterly Review creates strategic adaptation.
The Annual Review creates direction.
Event-driven leadership creates responsiveness.
Together, these rhythms prevent Omnira from becoming reactive, distracted, stale, or overloaded.
The goal is not to create more management.
The goal is to make leadership continuous, deliberate, and useful.
Executive Intelligence should not constantly demand the founder’s attention.
It should make every moment of founder attention count.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.1 Purpose of This Chapter

The Daily Executive Brief is the primary daily leadership interface between Omnira and the founder.
It should give the founder a clear understanding of the organization without requiring manual inspection of projects, workflows, agents, dashboards, performance systems, approvals, calendars, or decision history.
The brief must answer:
What changed?
What matters now?
What should receive focus today?
What requires a decision?
What should not be started?
What risks need attention?
What is operating safely without intervention?
What does founder capacity realistically allow?
The Daily Executive Brief is not a status report.
It is not an activity feed.
It is not a collection of dashboards converted into text.
It is not a list of every task completed overnight.
It is a leadership artifact.
Its purpose is to transform organizational state into daily executive clarity.

8.2 The Core Thesis

A Daily Executive Brief must do three things:
Orient.
Prioritize.
Activate.
Orient
Explain the current position of the organization.
Prioritize
Recommend what matters most today.
Activate
Make decisions, approvals, interventions, and next actions easy to execute.
If the brief only describes activity, it fails.
If the brief contains many facts but no recommendation, it fails.
If the brief requires the founder to reconstruct context before making a decision, it fails.
The core rule is:
A brief without direction is reporting.
A brief with direction is leadership.

8.3 The Founder Experience

The founder should be able to open Omnira and understand the day within minutes.
The experience should feel like receiving a competent executive briefing from a trusted Chief of Staff, CEO advisor, and operating leader.
The brief should be:
Direct.
Calm.
Evidence-based.
Prioritized.
Honest about uncertainty.
Aware of founder capacity.
Serious about decisions.
Human in presentation.
Expandable when deeper detail is needed.
The founder should not feel buried under the organization.
The brief should make the organization feel understandable.

8.4 Hybrid Briefing Model

The Daily Executive Brief should use a hybrid model combining three executive perspectives.
CEO Perspective
What matters strategically?
Chief of Staff Perspective
What needs to happen today?
Board Perspective
What risks, decisions, and performance changes require attention?
The brief should not force the founder to choose between a strategic summary and an operational plan.
It should provide a concise top layer with structured depth underneath.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.5 The Briefing Layers

The brief should support three information layers.
Layer 1 — Executive Snapshot
Readable in less than one minute.
Contains:
Primary focus.
Critical decision.
Material risk.
Founder capacity.
Do-Not-Start instruction.
Layer 2 — Executive Detail
Readable in several minutes.
Contains:
Portfolio position.
Project changes.
Mission status.
Approval queue.
Performance signals.
Upcoming decisions.
Layer 3 — Evidence and Traceability
Opened only when needed.
Contains:
Evidence.
Data sources.
Assumptions.
Confidence.
Decision history.
Workflow logs.
Performance detail.
Risk analysis.
The founder should receive clarity first and complexity only when requested.

8.6 Stable Structure, Dynamic Content

The structure of the brief should remain familiar.
The content should change according to organizational state.
A stable structure reduces cognitive load.
The founder should always know where to find:
Today’s focus.
Approvals.
Risks.
Project status.
Calendar capacity.
Do-Not-Start items.
However, empty or irrelevant sections should be collapsed.
A stable structure does not require displaying every section every day.

8.7 Canonical Brief Structure

The canonical Daily Executive Brief should include:
1. Executive Snapshot
2. Today’s Primary Focus
3. Founder Capacity
4. Material Changes
5. Portfolio Position
6. Project Executive Summaries
7. Mission and Workforce Status
8. Approval Queue
9. Risks and Escalations
10. Performance Signals
11. Decisions Due for Review
12. Do-Not-Start
13. Recommended Calendar Blocks
14. Upcoming Decision Points
15. Confidence and Evidence Notes
The order may adapt slightly when urgency requires it.
Critical risk should move to the top.

8.8 Executive Snapshot

The Executive Snapshot should communicate the day in a compact form.
A conceptual example:
Primary Focus:
Complete the Memory Stage 1 review.
Critical Decision:
Approve or defer The Prompt newsletter draft.
Portfolio Position:
The Prompt remains the main autonomy proving ground.
Familje-Stunden remains Observer lifecycle mode / Learning operating mode.
GainPilot remains hibernated.
Risk:
Project isolation validation remains incomplete.
Founder Capacity:
Moderate.
Do Not Start:
No new architecture epic today.
The snapshot should not contain unexplained metrics.
Every item should have executive meaning.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.9 Today’s Primary Focus

Every brief should recommend one primary focus.
The primary focus should be the highest-value founder-directed outcome for the day.
It should consider:
Current portfolio objective.
Weekly Executive Objective.
Urgency.
Revenue impact.
Strategic leverage.
Risk.
Dependencies.
Founder capacity.
Opportunity cost.
Open commitments.
The primary focus should be written as an outcome, not a vague topic.
Weak:
Work on Memory.
Strong:
Complete the Memory Stage 1 review required before implementation continues.

8.10 Secondary Focus

The brief may contain one or two secondary focus items.
Secondary focus should remain subordinate to the primary focus.
Example:
Primary:
Complete the Memory review.
Secondary:
Approve The Prompt article batch.
Review one open autonomy recommendation.
The brief should not present several equally weighted priorities.
Priority requires ranking.

8.11 Focus Recommendation Format

The focus recommendation should include:
Recommended outcome.
Reason.
Time sensitivity.
Expected impact.
Founder effort.
What it unlocks.
What it delays.
Example:
Recommended outcome:
Approve the final Memory Stage 1 contract.
Reason:
It is a hard dependency for deeper Executive implementation.
Founder effort:
Approximately one focused review block.
Unlocks:
Implementation planning for the next Memory stage.
Delays if ignored:
Executive Intelligence roadmap progress.

8.12 Founder Capacity

The brief should include a founder capacity signal.
Capacity may be:
High.
Moderate.
Low.
Unavailable.
The classification should reflect more than free calendar time.
It should consider:
Deep-work windows.
Meeting density.
Personal obligations.
Study commitments.
Family commitments.
Recent workload.
Decision fatigue.
Approval backlog.
Urgent external obligations.
A free hour should not automatically be classified as high capacity.

8.13 Capacity Translation

The capacity signal should affect the recommended workload.
Examples:
Capacity: High
Recommended workload: One deep strategic task and two short approvals.
Capacity: Moderate
Recommended workload: One focused review and routine approvals.
Capacity: Low
Recommended workload: Approvals only. No new deep architecture work.
Capacity: Unavailable
Recommended workload: Existing automation continues. Escalate only critical items.
Capacity should shape leadership recommendations.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.14 Founder Privacy

The brief may use detailed calendar context internally.
It should normally present derived capacity rather than private detail.
Allowed:
Approval availability is limited after 14:00.
Not normally required:
Detailed explanation of the private appointment causing the limitation.
Atlas may know more.
The brief should expose only what is useful.

8.15 Material Changes

The brief should emphasize what changed since the previous briefing.
Material changes may include:
Mission completed.
Mission delayed.
New approval required.
Performance anomaly.
Customer complaint pattern.
Autonomy violation.
Project mode recommendation.
Provider failure.
Revenue threshold crossed.
Risk severity change.
Founder capacity change.
Decision review date reached.
Stable information should be compressed.

8.16 Change Baseline

Material change should be measured against:
Previous Daily Brief.
Current Weekly Plan.
Active Executive Missions.
Expected performance.
Known risks.
Decision Ledger.
Current project modes.
Founder calendar.
A change is meaningful only relative to an expected state.

8.17 No Material Change

When no material change occurred, the brief should say so.
Example:
No material portfolio change since yesterday.
The Prompt workflows remain within approved scope.
No new approvals are required.
The system should not manufacture urgency or novelty.

8.18 Portfolio Position

The portfolio section should summarize the current organizational position.
It may include:
Global objective.
Active project priorities.
Lifecycle modes.
Operating modes.
Portfolio risk.
Shared dependency.
Founder capacity impact.
The section should remain short.
Detailed project information belongs in expandable project summaries.

8.19 Project Inclusion Rules

A project should appear prominently when:
A material change occurred.
A decision is required.
A risk changed.
A mission is active.
A review date is due.
A project mode may change.
Founder attention is needed.
Stable projects may be collapsed.
A hibernated project should not appear daily unless a restart condition or relevant event occurs.

8.20 Project Executive Summary

Each included project summary should contain:
Project name.
Lifecycle mode.
Operating mode.
Top project priority.
Material change.
Mission status.
Risk.
Approval need.
Autonomy state.
Recommended action.
Example:
The Prompt
Mode: Active / Build
Priority: Website news automation
Change: Five drafts completed
Approval: Article batch ready
Risk: No serious violations
Autonomy: L2 — Prepare
Recommendation: Review the batch today

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.21 Project Summary Depth

The founder should be able to expand a project summary into:
Detailed mission status.
Performance data.
Workflow runs.
Approval history.
Risk analysis.
Decision history.
Autonomy license.
Evidence sources.
The top-level brief should not copy all project detail.

8.22 Project Scope Integrity

Every project summary must remain project-scoped.
The brief may combine governed summaries.
It must not expose unnecessary raw data from several projects in one context.
Each item should clearly identify its project origin.

8.23 Mission Status

The brief should summarize active Executive Missions.
Mission status may be:
On track.
At risk.
Blocked.
Waiting for approval.
Completed.
Paused.
Failed.
Cancelled.
Each mission shown should include:
Project.
Objective.
Status.
Material change.
Next executive need.

8.24 On-Track Missions

On-track missions should be compressed.
Example:
The Prompt social publishing remains on schedule.
No intervention required.
The brief should not spend significant space describing healthy execution unless the outcome is strategically important.

8.25 At-Risk Missions

An at-risk mission should include:
Cause.
Potential impact.
Current control.
Recommended action.
Decision deadline.
Example:
Mission:
The Prompt website news automation.
Status:
At risk.
Cause:
Source validation is incomplete.
Impact:
Article approval may be delayed.
Recommendation:
Continue drafting but block publication until source review is complete.

8.26 Blocked Missions

A blocked mission should explain:
What is blocked?
Why?
Who or what must unblock it?
What work can continue?
What happens if it remains blocked?
The founder should not need to inspect task logs to understand the blocker.

8.27 Workforce Summary

Manager should provide a structured summary of Workforce activity.
The brief may include:
Active teams.
Completed outputs.
Significant failures.
Blocked tasks.
Capacity constraints.
Escalations.
Approval dependencies.
The brief should avoid listing every agent action.

8.28 Agent Visibility

Agents should appear in the brief only when:
A role is missing.
An agent failed materially.
An agent produced a high-value result.
A policy violation occurred.
A new role is recommended.
A resource conflict exists.
Routine agent activity belongs in the Operating Graph and execution logs.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.29 Approval Queue

The Approval Queue is a primary action surface.
The founder should be able to make decisions without reconstructing context.
Each approval item should include:
Project.
Requested action.
Action type.
Reason.
Recommended decision.
Risk.
Reversibility.
Deadline.
Consequence of delay.
Supporting evidence.

8.30 Approval Priority

Approval items should be ranked by:
Damage potential.
Urgency.
Dependency impact.
Revenue impact.
Customer impact.
Reversibility.
Deadline.
Founder effort.
The most recent approval should not automatically appear first.

8.31 Approval Categories

Approvals may include:
Publish.
Send.
Spend.
Connect.
Change strategy.
Change project mode.
Increase autonomy.
Create calendar event.
Respond to sensitive customer case.
Deploy production change.
Delete or permanently remove data.
