The category should be visible.
Different categories may have different review interfaces.

8.32 Recommended Decision

Executive Intelligence should provide a recommendation.
Example:
Recommended:
Approve with edits.
Reason:
The article is strategically relevant, but the source wording should be corrected before publication.
Confidence:
High.
The system should not force the founder to decide without guidance.

8.33 Approval Actions

The founder should be able to:
Approve.
Reject.
Edit and approve.
Request more evidence.
Request an alternative.
Defer.
Escalate to Deep Executive Analysis.
Each action should preserve auditability.

8.34 Approval Batching

Low-risk, similar approvals may be batched.
A batch should share:
Project.
Workflow.
Action category.
Risk class.
Approval conditions.
Destination.
Review period.
The founder should be able to inspect individual items before batch approval.

8.35 Approval Burden Indicator

The brief should show approval burden when material.
Example:
Approval load:
6 items
Estimated review effort:
20 minutes
Potential batch candidates:
4
The estimate should help the founder plan attention.

8.36 Approval Delay

The brief should explain the consequence of delay.
Examples:
No immediate consequence.
Blocks publication today.
Delays weekly mission.
Creates customer response risk.
Prevents workflow continuation.
Expires at 16:00.
This improves prioritization.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.37 Risk Summary

The brief should surface material risks.
Risk levels may be:
Critical.
High.
Moderate.
Watch.
Each risk should contain:
Project or portfolio scope.
Cause.
Potential impact.
Current control.
Required action.
Owner.
Review time.

8.38 Critical Risk

Critical risks should appear before the normal Executive Snapshot.
Critical risks may include:
Security incident.
Customer data exposure.
Unauthorized spending.
Wrong-project publication.
Serious customer harm risk.
Shared authorization failure.
Uncontrolled external action.
The brief should make the required immediate action explicit.

8.39 High Risk

High risks require action during the current operating day.
Examples:
Sensitive customer response waiting.
Major publishing error before release.
Repeated workflow failure.
Autonomy license breach.
Critical provider degradation.

8.40 Moderate Risk

Moderate risks should influence daily or weekly planning but may not require immediate action.
Examples:
Approval backlog increasing.
Content quality trending down.
Performance data delayed.
Mission deadline at risk.
Capacity becoming constrained.

8.41 Watch Items

Watch items are early signals.
They should not dominate the brief.
Examples:
Engagement trend weakening.
Provider latency increasing.
Correction rate slightly higher.
Support volume gradually increasing.
Repeated watch items may become moderate risk.

8.42 Risk Suppression

Unchanged low-level risks should not be repeated every day.
They should reappear when:
Severity changes.
A deadline approaches.
A control fails.
New evidence appears.
Founder action becomes necessary.

8.43 Performance Signals

The Daily Brief should include only performance signals that may affect current decisions.
Possible signals include:
Revenue anomaly.
Traffic anomaly.
Subscriber change.
Workflow success rate.
Publishing reliability.
Customer support spike.
Cost anomaly.
Trust Score change.
Policy violation.
Routine metrics belong in project dashboards.

8.44 Signal Interpretation

Every performance signal should include interpretation.
Weak:
Traffic increased 18%.
Strong:
The Prompt traffic increased 18%, driven mainly by short news posts.
Recommendation: Maintain the current short-form mix while collecting another week of evidence.
Data without interpretation does not belong in an executive brief.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.45 Data Freshness

Performance signals should state data freshness when relevant.
Possible states:
Current.
Delayed.
Incomplete.
Estimated.
Unverified.
Stale.
Example:
Subscriber data is delayed by 12 hours.
Do not make a growth decision from the current count.

8.46 Confidence

Material recommendations should include confidence.
Suggested levels:
High.
Medium.
Low.
Confidence should reflect:
Evidence quality.
Data freshness.
Consistency.
Historical reliability.
Assumption burden.
Reversibility.

8.47 Confidence Presentation

Confidence should be visible when it materially affects the recommendation.
Example:
Recommendation:
Keep GainPilot hibernated.
Confidence:
High.
Would change if:
New revenue or user traction appears.
Routine high-confidence information does not need a confidence label on every line.

8.48 Evidence

The brief should allow the founder to inspect evidence.
Evidence may include:
Performance measurements.
Manager reports.
Decision Ledger entries.
Memory records.
Calendar capacity.
Approval history.
Risk signals.
Customer feedback summaries.
The top layer should summarize.
Evidence should remain one step away.

8.49 Assumptions

Material recommendations should identify important assumptions.
Example:
Assumption:
Founder capacity remains limited this week.
Assumption:
The Prompt website workflow remains the highest-value proving ground.
Hidden assumptions reduce trust.

8.50 What Would Change the Recommendation

Important recommendations should state what could change them.
Example:
Would change if:
The Prompt publishing workflow records a serious policy violation.
This makes reasoning dynamic rather than absolute.

8.51 Decisions Due for Review

The brief should surface decisions whose review dates have arrived.
Each item should show:
Decision.
Scope.
Original reason.
Current evidence.
Recommended outcome.
Available actions.
Available outcomes may include:
Renew.
Revise.
Expire.
Reverse.
Escalate.

8.52 Decision Continuity

The brief should connect current recommendations to previous decisions.
Example:
Current recommendation:
Keep newsletters approval-gated.
Previous decision:
Approval required until 30 successful drafts.
Current evidence:
18 successful drafts completed.
This prevents the system from restarting strategic reasoning every day.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.53 Do-Not-Start

The Do-Not-Start section should protect daily focus.
Items may include:
New projects.
New epics.
Unapproved autonomy expansion.
Unnecessary platform work.
Low-priority redesign.
Premature Growth operating mode.
New external integrations.
Each item should include a brief reason.

8.54 Do-Not-Start Relevance

The section should appear only when useful.
It should not become a permanent list of everything not being done.
The brief should surface the distractions most likely to interfere with today’s objective.

8.55 Recommended Calendar Blocks

The brief may propose calendar blocks.
Examples:
09:00–10:00
Memory review.
13:30–13:50
Approval batch.
15:00–15:30
The Prompt strategy check.
The brief should not create calendar events without approval unless a future calendar mandate explicitly allows it.

8.56 Calendar Proposal Logic

Calendar proposals should consider:
Existing events.
Deep-work windows.
Task type.
Decision fatigue.
Approval deadlines.
Personal commitments.
Transition time.
Recovery.
The system should avoid filling every free space.
Unscheduled capacity has value.

8.57 Calendar Approval

The founder should be able to:
Approve all blocks.
Approve selected blocks.
Edit times.
Move blocks.
Reject the schedule.
Request a lighter plan.
After approval, events may be created.

8.58 Upcoming Decision Points

The brief should show decisions or reviews approaching soon.
Examples:
Autonomy license review in 3 days.
Weekly Plan review on Sunday.
Project mode review at month end.
Newsletter decision required by 16:00.
MCP permission expires tomorrow.
This prevents surprise.

8.59 Time Horizon Labels

Items should indicate their horizon when useful:
Today.
This week.
This month.
Quarter.
Condition-based.
The founder should understand whether an item is immediate or strategic.

8.60 Overnight Automation Summary

The morning brief should summarize relevant overnight activity.
It may include:
Workflows completed.
Content published.
Failures.
Approval items created.
Performance anomalies.
Customer messages requiring attention.
Cost changes.
Healthy repetitive automation should be compressed.

8.61 Successful Automation

Successful automation should be reported as:
Operating normally.
Within policy.
No intervention required.
The brief should not celebrate every normal run as an event.
Normal operation should become quiet.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.62 Failed Automation

A failure should include:
Workflow.
Project.
Failure point.
Impact.
Retry status.
External side effect.
Recommended action.
The founder should not need to inspect technical logs unless deeper troubleshooting is required.

8.63 Partial Failure

Partial failures should be represented accurately.
Example:
The Prompt video was generated successfully.
Instagram publishing succeeded.
YouTube publishing failed.
Facebook is waiting for retry.
No duplicate publication detected.
The system should avoid labeling a partially completed workflow as simply successful or failed.

8.64 External Action Summary

The brief may summarize external actions such as:
Content published.
Emails sent.
Customer replies sent.
Spend executed.
Integrations connected.
Data exported.
Only material or unusual external actions should appear.
All external actions should remain auditable.

8.65 Revenue-Affecting Events

Revenue-affecting events should be highlighted when material.
Examples:
New subscriber threshold reached.
Subscription churn increased.
Refund spike detected.
Campaign conversion improved.
Revenue source failed.
Payment provider issue detected.
The brief should explain the likely business impact.

8.66 Customer-Affecting Events

Customer events may include:
Complaint pattern.
Support backlog.
Refund request.
Safety-sensitive question.
Service outage.
Subscription issue.
Negative feedback.
Sensitive cases should be prioritized according to Damage Boundary.

8.67 Project Mode Changes

A recommended project mode change should be clearly marked.
Example:
Recommendation:
Move The Prompt from Build toward Growth.
Reason:
Publishing workflow is stable and traffic measurement is reliable.
Approval required:
Yes.
Mode changes should not be hidden inside general commentary.

8.68 Autonomy Changes

Autonomy recommendations should show:
Project.
Workflow.
Current level.
Proposed level.
Evidence.
Risk.
Trial period.
Rollback.
Approval requirement.
Example:
Workflow:
The Prompt short news publishing.
Current:
L2 — Prepare.
Proposed:
L4 — External Low-Risk.
Recommendation:
Do not approve yet.
Reason:
Successful run threshold is not reached.

8.69 Trust Score Changes

A Trust Score change should appear when material.
Example:
The Prompt article workflow Trust Score increased from 72 to 81.
Driver:
Higher unchanged approval rate.
Limitation:
Only 18 successful runs completed.
Executive interpretation:
Improving, but not ready for autonomy increase.
The score should not speak for itself.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.70 Policy Violations

Policy violations should be shown according to severity.
The brief should include:
Project.
Workflow.
Severity.
Violation.
External impact.
Containment.
Autonomy impact.
Required action.
Minor style issues should not be presented like critical boundary failures.

8.71 Isolation Health

Project isolation health should appear when:
A violation occurred.
A validation failed.
A migration affected ownership.
A cross-project access grant exists.
Autonomy expansion is being considered.
Poor isolation health should block autonomy recommendations.

8.72 Dependency Changes

The brief should surface dependencies that materially changed.
Examples:
A hard dependency was completed.
A dependency became blocked.
A soft dependency was incorrectly treated as hard.
A shared capability became available.
A provider dependency failed.
Dependency changes often affect focus.

8.73 Opportunity Cost

The brief should state opportunity cost when recommending a significant focus change.
Example:
Recommendation:
Prioritize project isolation review today.
Opportunity cost:
The Prompt article automation moves one day later.
Executive judgment:
The delay is acceptable because isolation is a hard dependency for broader autonomy.

8.74 Alternatives

For significant decisions, the brief should provide alternatives.
Example:
Option A:
Approve all five articles.
Option B:
Approve three and return two for edits.
Option C:
Defer the batch.
Recommended:
Option B.
Alternatives should be limited to realistic options.

8.75 Founder Override

The founder may reject the recommendation.
When that happens, Executive Intelligence should:
Record the decision when material.
State the impact.
Update plans.
Adjust missions.
Preserve the original recommendation.
Set a review date if appropriate.
The system should not argue endlessly.
It should remain honest and adaptive.

8.76 Conversational Tone

Atlas should present the brief in a direct, human tone.
Example:
Good morning André.
Today’s best use of your focus is the Memory review. The Prompt workflows are running normally, and there is no reason to interrupt them.
You have one article batch to approve. I would leave GainPilot alone today.
The tone may contain light humor when appropriate.
The decisions themselves should remain precise.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.77 Executive Mode

The brief should use Executive Mode.
Executive Mode is:
Structured.
Evidence-based.
Direct.
Prioritized.
Serious about uncertainty.
Clear about decisions.
The founder may switch into Conversation Mode for discussion.
The underlying reasoning should remain the same.

8.78 Voice Briefing

A future voice briefing should present:
Primary focus.
Critical approval.
Material risk.
Founder capacity.
Do-Not-Start item.
It should remain short.
Detailed evidence should be available visually.
Voice should not attempt to read the entire brief aloud.

8.79 Mobile Notification

A mobile notification should contain only urgent executive value.
Example:
Today: Finish Memory review.
1 approval waiting.
The Prompt is operating normally.
No GainPilot work recommended.
Critical incidents should use a separate alert format.

8.80 Dashboard View

The dashboard should allow the founder to scan:
Primary focus.
Project status.
Approvals.
Risks.
Capacity.
Do-Not-Start.
Decision reviews.
The visual hierarchy should match executive priority.
Important items should not compete equally with routine status.

8.81 Expandable Evidence

Every material item should support expansion into:
Evidence.
Source.
Timestamp.
Data freshness.
Assumptions.
Confidence.
Decision history.
Related missions.
Related risks.
Transparency should be available without making the default view dense.

8.82 Brief Actions

The founder should be able to act directly from the brief.
Actions may include:
Approve.
Reject.
Edit.
Defer.
Open project.
Open mission.
View evidence.
Create calendar block.
Ask Atlas why.
Request alternative.
Escalate analysis.
Pause workflow.
Activate Crisis Mode.
The brief should be an action surface, not a passive report.

8.83 Ask Atlas Why

Every recommendation should support a natural question:
Why are you recommending this?
Atlas should respond with:
Evidence.
Assumptions.
Opportunity cost.
Risk.
Confidence.
What would change the recommendation.
The founder should not need to inspect internal logs to understand the reasoning.

8.84 Brief Generation Inputs

The Daily Executive Brief may use governed inputs from:
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executives.
Manager reports.
Workforce reports.
Performance Intelligence.
Memory.
Decision Ledger.
Approval Queue.
Risk register.
Autonomy licenses.
Calendar capacity.
External event signals.
Each input should preserve scope and freshness.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.85 Input Priority

The brief should prioritize inputs according to authority and materiality.
A conceptual hierarchy:
Critical policy or security event.
Human-approved decisions.
Current verified performance.
Project Executive recommendations.
Manager operational reports.
Workforce outputs.
Historical Memory.
Forecasts and hypotheses.
Historical context should not override verified current reality.

8.86 Missing Data

The brief should state when important data is unavailable.
Example:
The Prompt revenue data is unavailable this morning.
No revenue recommendation is made.
The system should not silently fill gaps with assumptions.

8.87 Conflicting Data

When sources conflict, the brief should show:
The conflict.
The likely cause.
Which source is more trusted.
What decision is delayed.
What verification is required.
Conflicting data should reduce confidence.

8.88 Data Quality

The brief may include a data quality warning when poor data materially affects decisions.
Example:
Data quality warning:
Familje-Stunden product usage tracking is incomplete.
Growth recommendations remain low confidence.

8.89 Materiality Filter

An item belongs in the brief when it may affect:
Founder focus.
Strategy.
Revenue.
Cost.
Risk.
Customer trust.
Project mode.
Autonomy.
Major mission outcome.
Approval need.
Calendar.
Routine operational detail should remain outside the brief.

8.90 Redundancy Filter

Before including an item, the system should ask:
Was this already communicated?
Has anything changed?
Does the founder need to act?
Does it affect today’s focus?
Would omission create risk?
Repeated unchanged information should be suppressed.

8.91 Report Suppression

The brief may be shortened when:
No material changes occurred.
No approvals are waiting.
No risks changed.
Founder capacity is limited.
The organization is operating normally.
A short brief may be:
Primary focus remains unchanged.
No approvals required.
All active workflows are operating normally.
Silence or brevity can be a sign of healthy automation.

8.92 Escalation Override

Critical incidents should override normal brief structure.
The brief should begin with:
Critical Incident.
Immediate impact.
Actions already taken.
Founder decision required.
Recommended response.
Normal daily content may follow afterward.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.93 Crisis Brief

During Crisis Mode, the brief should focus on:
Incident status.
Containment.
Affected projects.
External impact.
Decisions required.
Recovery actions.
Next review time.
Routine performance and planning content should be reduced.

8.94 Recovery Brief

After crisis containment, the brief should show:
What is restored.
What remains restricted.
What tests remain.
What autonomy is reduced.
What decisions are pending.
When normal cadence may resume.

8.95 Positive Opportunity Briefing

Material positive opportunities should appear when:
Revenue opportunity is time-sensitive.
Customer growth changes strategy.
A partnership requires action.
A content format performs significantly better.
A project reaches a readiness threshold.
Opportunity should be evaluated with the same discipline as risk.

8.96 Opportunity Evaluation

The brief should include:
Evidence.
Potential upside.
Required capacity.
Risk.
Urgency.
Opportunity cost.
Recommended action.
Excitement should not replace analysis.

8.97 Personalization

The founder should be able to personalize:
Brief length.
Delivery time.
Voice or text.
Project detail.
Risk threshold.
Notification threshold.
Approval grouping.
Calendar recommendations.
Personalization should not hide critical events.

8.98 Learning from Founder Behavior

The brief should learn from:
Which sections are opened.
Which recommendations are accepted.
Which approvals are edited.
Which risks are dismissed.
Which calendar blocks are moved.
Which brief items are repeatedly ignored.
Behavior may improve prioritization and presentation.
It should not grant new authority automatically.

8.99 Founder Feedback

The founder should be able to give simple feedback:
Useful.
Too detailed.
Too brief.
Wrong focus.
Correct focus.
Risk overstated.
Approval should have been batched.
Feedback should improve future briefs.

8.100 Brief Quality Metrics

Brief quality may be measured through:
Founder usefulness rating.
Recommendation acceptance.
Primary focus completion.
Approval decision time.
Risk detection accuracy.
Redundancy rate.
Brief reading time.
Missed material event rate.
Founder correction rate.
The brief should improve over time.

8.101 Brief Burden

The system should monitor burden.
Burden may include:
Time required to read.
Number of decisions.
Number of interruptions.
Number of expanded details.
Repeated requests for missing context.
Approval volume.
A useful brief reduces organizational burden.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.102 Brief Success

A Daily Executive Brief is successful when the founder can answer:
What should I focus on?
What is running without me?
What needs my decision?
What risk matters?
What should I avoid starting?
If the founder still needs to inspect several systems before understanding the day, the brief has failed.

8.103 Brief Retention

Daily briefs may be retained for a limited or medium period.
Durable elements should be extracted into:
Memory.
Decision Ledger.
Risk history.
Planning accuracy.
Founder preferences.
Approval history.
Not every daily sentence deserves permanent memory.

8.104 Brief Versioning

If the brief changes materially during the day, Omnira should preserve:
Original brief.
Updated brief.
Reason for change.
New evidence.
Affected focus.
Affected decisions.
Silent mutation weakens trust.

8.105 Midday Update

A midday update should be created only when:
A material change occurs.
A critical approval appears.
Founder capacity changes.
The primary focus becomes invalid.
A crisis or opportunity emerges.
It should not become a second routine briefing.

8.106 End-of-Day Recap

The end-of-day recap should remain lightweight.
It may include:
Primary focus result.
Decisions made.
Open carryover.
New risk.
Tomorrow’s likely focus.
It should not repeat the full morning brief.

8.107 Brief and Weekly Plan Alignment

Every daily focus should connect to the Weekly Executive Plan.
The brief should identify:
Weekly objective supported.
Mission supported.
Dependency unlocked.
Reason for deviation if applicable.
Daily work should not drift away from weekly direction without explanation.

8.108 Brief and Monthly Objectives

The brief should not need to mention monthly strategy every day.
However, the system should be able to trace daily focus to:
Weekly goal.
Monthly objective.
Quarterly direction.
Annual thesis.
This relationship should be visible in the Intelligence Graph.

8.109 Brief and Decision Ledger

The brief should reference material decisions.
Examples:
Current approval policy.
Project mode decision.
Autonomy limit.
Do-Not-Start decision.
Budget mandate.
Routine brief content should not create unnecessary Decision Ledger entries.

8.110 Brief and Memory

Memory may support the brief with:
Founder preferences.
Previous recommendations.
Repeated blockers.
Past project decisions.
Approval patterns.
Risk history.
Planning lessons.
Memory should support continuity without overloading the prompt context.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.111 Brief and Project Isolation

The brief must preserve project isolation.
It should use governed project summaries.
It should not combine raw customer data.
It should identify project origin.
It should hide unnecessary sensitive details.
It should respect founder-private boundaries.

8.112 Brief and Future Customer Projects

Future customer projects may have their own Daily Executive Brief.
The brief should respect:
Customer ownership.
Customer roles.
Project permissions.
Approved metrics.
Notification preferences.
Portfolio visibility rules.
Data retention.
An internal Omnira brief should not automatically include external customer details.

8.113 Multi-User Briefs

Future organizations may require several views:
Founder Brief.
Portfolio Owner Brief.
Project Owner Brief.
Approver Brief.
Operator Brief.
Board Brief.
These views should derive from one governed source of truth.
They should not become conflicting reports.

8.114 Brief Object

The Daily Executive Brief should eventually exist as a structured object.
Conceptually, it may contain:
Brief identifier.
Date.
Timezone.
Audience.
Scope.
Generation time.
Data freshness.
Executive snapshot.
Primary focus.
Capacity.
Project summaries.
Mission summaries.
Approvals.
Risks.
Performance signals.
Decisions due.
Do-Not-Start items.
Calendar proposals.
Confidence.
Evidence references.
Version.
The exact implementation may evolve.
The structure should support both human reading and machine action.

8.115 Brief Scope

A brief may be:
Portfolio brief.
Project brief.
Crisis brief.
Approval-focused brief.
Founder capacity brief.
The default Daily Executive Brief is portfolio-level with governed project summaries.

8.116 Brief Status

A brief may have status:
Draft.
Ready.
Delivered.
Updated.
Acknowledged.
Superseded.
Archived.
This may support reliable delivery and versioning.

8.117 Acknowledgement

The founder should not be required to acknowledge every brief.
Acknowledgement may be useful when:
Critical risk exists.
A high-impact decision is waiting.
Crisis Mode is active.
A deadline requires confirmation.
Routine brief delivery should not create unnecessary interaction.

8.118 Brief Generation Timing

The brief should be generated after enough overnight data is available.
Generation should consider:
Scheduled workflow completion.
Performance data freshness.
Calendar updates.
Approval queue.
Risk events.
Timezone.
If data remains incomplete, the brief should state that.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.119 Brief Regeneration

The brief may regenerate when:
A critical event occurs.
A major approval is resolved.
The founder changes the plan.
A project enters Crisis Mode.
The primary focus changes materially.
Regeneration should create a new version rather than silently replacing history.

8.120 The Daily Brief Decision Test

Before including a recommendation, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Does this require founder attention today?
Is the evidence current?
Is the action within founder capacity?
What will happen if delayed?
What is the opportunity cost?
Is approval actually required?
What would change the recommendation?

8.121 The Daily Brief Materiality Test

Before including information, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Did something meaningful change?
Does it affect strategy, risk, revenue, cost, customer trust, autonomy, or founder capacity?
Does the founder need to know now?
Can it wait until the Weekly or Monthly Review?
Would omission create harm?

8.122 The Daily Brief Burden Test

Before finalizing the brief, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Can the founder understand the day quickly?
Are there too many priorities?
Are approvals grouped appropriately?
Is repeated information suppressed?
Are project summaries concise?
Does every section create value?

8.123 The Focus Test

The primary focus is valid when:
It supports the current Weekly Objective.
It fits founder capacity.
It has clear expected value.
It has acceptable opportunity cost.
It is more important than the alternatives.
It is specific enough to complete or advance today.

8.124 The Approval Test

An approval item is ready when:
Project scope is explicit.
Action is explicit.
Risk is clear.
Evidence is available.
Recommendation is provided.
Consequence of delay is known.
Approval authority is valid.
Incomplete approval requests should not reach the founder.

8.125 The Risk Test

A risk belongs in the brief when:
Severity is material.
Founder action may be required.
A threshold changed.
A control failed.
The risk affects today’s plan.
A deadline is approaching.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.126 Failure Modes

The Daily Executive Brief architecture must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Activity Feed
The brief lists events without executive interpretation.
Failure Mode 2 — Too Many Priorities
The brief presents several equal priorities and avoids ranking.
Failure Mode 3 — Approval Dump
The founder receives approval items without enough context.
Failure Mode 4 — Risk Spam
Unchanged low-level risks appear every day.
Failure Mode 5 — Dashboard in Text Form
The brief reproduces metrics without meaning.
Failure Mode 6 — Calendar Blindness
The recommended workload ignores founder capacity.
Failure Mode 7 — False Confidence
Recommendations appear certain despite weak or stale evidence.
Failure Mode 8 — Project Blending
Project summaries expose or combine inappropriate data.
Failure Mode 9 — Repetitive Briefing
Stable information is repeated daily.
Failure Mode 10 — Hidden Opportunity Cost
A recommendation does not explain what it delays.
Failure Mode 11 — No Action Surface
The brief describes decisions but does not allow action.
Failure Mode 12 — Excessive Detail
The default view becomes too long to use.
Failure Mode 13 — Excessive Brevity
The brief lacks enough context to trust.
Failure Mode 14 — Missing Decision Continuity
Recommendations ignore previous decisions.
Failure Mode 15 — Notification Duplication
The same event appears in several channels unnecessarily.
Failure Mode 16 — Healthy Automation Noise
Normal automation generates constant status chatter.
These failure modes should be treated as product and architecture constraints.

8.127 Design Requirements

Any implementation of the Daily Executive Brief should preserve these requirements:
Every brief must recommend one primary focus.
Every brief must consider founder capacity.
Every material recommendation must be evidence-based.
Every material recommendation should expose confidence when relevant.
Every approval item must be decision-ready.
Every risk must be prioritized by severity and materiality.
Every project summary must preserve project scope.
Every performance signal must include interpretation.
Every material change must identify what changed.
Every Do-Not-Start item must protect current focus.
Every calendar block must require appropriate approval.
Every stable workflow should remain quiet unless intervention is needed.
Every brief should connect to the Weekly Executive Plan.
Every material decision should reference relevant decision history.
Every brief must be concise by default and expandable for evidence.
Every critical incident must override normal presentation.
Every brief must reduce founder coordination burden.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
8.128 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the product and leadership contract, not a specific interface or database schema.
The Daily Executive Brief may later be implemented through:
Executive Brief objects.
Scheduled generation.
Event-driven regeneration.
Atlas messages.
Dashboard cards.
Mobile notifications.
Voice summaries.
Approval components.
Risk components.
Project summary components.
Calendar integration.
Evidence drawers.
Decision Ledger links.
Performance queries.
Manager reports.
The interface may evolve.
The executive function must remain stable.

8.129 The Daily Executive Brief Contract

The Daily Executive Brief must:
Explain the current organizational position.
Recommend the highest-value daily focus.
Show what is running without founder intervention.
Surface only material changes.
Make approvals easy to decide.
Make risks easy to understand.
Respect founder capacity.
Protect project boundaries.
Expose uncertainty honestly.
Make opportunity cost visible.
Suppress routine noise.
Connect today’s work to longer-term direction.
Allow immediate action.
Remain concise by default.
Provide evidence on demand.
Reduce the need for manual coordination.
If a feature does not support this contract, it should not dominate the Daily Executive Brief.

8.130 Closing Principle

The Daily Executive Brief is where Executive Intelligence proves whether it can lead usefully.
Not through abstract intelligence.
Not through long reports.
Not through constant notifications.
Through clarity.
The founder should begin the day knowing:
What matters.
What changed.
What needs a decision.
What can continue autonomously.
What risk requires attention.
What should not be started.
A strong brief turns complexity into direction.
It makes autonomy visible without making it noisy.
It protects focus without hiding reality.
It gives the founder control without requiring constant supervision.
The Daily Executive Brief is not the place where Omnira shows everything it knows.
It is the place where Omnira shows what the founder needs to know now.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Founder Capacity as an Executive Resource
text:
9.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Executive Intelligence cannot lead well if it plans for an imaginary founder with unlimited time, energy, attention, and availability.
The founder is not an abstract resource.
The founder has:
Work.
Education.
Family responsibilities.
Appointments.
Health needs.
Meetings.
Recovery needs.
Personal commitments.
Limited deep-work capacity.
Limited decision capacity.
Executive Intelligence must understand those constraints.
It must plan Omnira around the founder’s real life instead of forcing the founder’s real life to absorb unrealistic plans.
At the same time, founder-private information must remain protected.
Project Executives, Manager, Workforce, agents, and tools should not receive detailed private calendar context merely because that context affects planning.
This chapter defines how Atlas and Executive Intelligence should use calendar and capacity information to improve prioritization, scheduling, approval timing, mission planning, and founder workload while preserving privacy and human authority.

9.2 The Core Thesis

Founder capacity is a strategic input.
It is not an afterthought.
The quality of an executive plan depends not only on whether the work is valuable, but on whether the organization has the real capacity to carry it out.
The core rule is:
A plan that ignores founder capacity is not ambitious.
It is inaccurate.
Executive Intelligence should therefore transform private founder context into governed operational signals.
Atlas may understand the detailed context.
Executive systems may use derived capacity.
Projects and Workforce should receive only the minimum information required to plan safely.

9.3 Founder Capacity as an Executive Resource

Founder capacity should be treated like any other constrained organizational resource.
Omnira already needs to reason about:
Money.
Workforce capacity.
Agent capability.
Infrastructure.
Model budget.
Review capacity.
Approval authority.
Founder capacity belongs in the same executive model.
It includes more than hours available.
It also includes:
Attention.
Energy.
Cognitive load.
Decision quality.
Emotional bandwidth.
Deep-work readiness.
Interruption tolerance.
Approval availability.
Recovery state.
Two calendar hours are not always equal.
A free hour after a demanding day may not support deep strategic architecture work.
A short morning block may be more valuable than several fragmented hours later.
Executive Intelligence must learn this difference.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.4 Calendar Time vs Usable Capacity

Calendar availability and usable capacity are related but not identical.
Calendar availability answers:
Is time technically free?
Usable capacity answers:
Can the founder perform this type of work effectively during that time?
A calendar may show two free hours.
Those hours may still be unsuitable because of:
Travel.
Transition time.
Fatigue.
Family obligations.
Recent meetings.
Decision overload.
Interrupted attention.
Insufficient preparation.
Recovery need.
Executive Intelligence should avoid equating empty calendar space with available deep work.

9.5 Capacity Dimensions

Founder capacity should be evaluated across several dimensions.
Time Capacity
How much usable time exists?
Deep-Work Capacity
How much uninterrupted strategic or creative work is realistic?
Decision Capacity
How many meaningful decisions can be made well?
Approval Capacity
How many approval items can be reviewed without overload?
Communication Capacity
How much meeting, email, or customer interaction is realistic?
Emotional Capacity
How much difficult, sensitive, or high-stakes work is appropriate?
Recovery Capacity
How much rest or unscheduled space is required?
Capacity should not be reduced to one number when several dimensions materially differ.

9.6 Capacity Classification

For everyday planning, Executive Intelligence may use a simple top-level capacity classification:
High.
Moderate.
Low.
Unavailable.
This classification should summarize the founder’s overall usable capacity.
High
The founder has meaningful deep-work availability and sufficient decision capacity.
Moderate
The founder can complete one focused task and routine approvals.
Low
The founder should handle only short decisions, urgent approvals, or light work.
Unavailable
The founder should not be scheduled for normal work. Only critical escalation should interrupt.
The classification should remain explainable.

9.7 Capacity Profile

A richer internal capacity profile may include:
Overall capacity.
Deep-work capacity.
Approval capacity.
Meeting tolerance.
Decision fatigue.
Preferred work windows.
Hard unavailability.
Soft unavailability.
Recovery need.
Confidence.
Example:
Overall: Moderate
Deep work: High between 09:00–11:00
Approval capacity: Low after 15:00
Meeting tolerance: Low
Hard unavailable: 13:00–14:30
Recovery need: Moderate
Confidence: High
The founder does not need to see every internal field every day.
The profile supports better planning.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Atlas as the Private Context Holder
text:
9.8 Founder-Private Context

Founder-private context may include:
Personal calendar event titles.
Family events.
Health-related appointments.
Education schedule.
Private meetings.
Travel.
Personal communications.
Recovery needs.
Personal financial obligations.
Sensitive life events.
This information should be treated as Founder Private.
It must not be exposed simply because Omnira uses it for planning.

9.9 The Privacy Transformation Principle

Founder-private information should be transformed before it moves into operational systems.
Example:
Private input:
Dentist appointment at 14:00.
Derived executive signal:
Founder unavailable 13:30–15:30.
No deep work recommended afterward.
Project-visible signal:
Approval response may be delayed this afternoon.
Workforce-visible signal:
Do not block workflow on founder review before tomorrow.
The detailed reason remains private.
The operational consequence is shared.
This is the correct direction of information flow.

9.10 Privacy Tiers

Calendar and capacity access should use several privacy tiers.
Tier 1 — Atlas Private Access
Atlas may access detailed calendar context when authorized.
Tier 2 — Executive Capacity Access
Portfolio Executive and relevant planning functions receive derived capacity signals.
Tier 3 — Project Planning Access
Project Executives receive only project-relevant availability and approval constraints.
Tier 4 — Workforce Scheduling Access
Manager and Workforce receive task timing constraints without private reasons.
Tier 5 — External Access
External tools or collaborators receive only explicitly approved scheduling information.
Each lower tier should receive less detail.

9.11 Atlas as the Private Context Holder

Atlas should be the primary user-facing system allowed to understand detailed private context.
Atlas may use that context to:
Prepare Daily Executive Briefs.
Recommend workload.
Protect family and personal time.
Suggest calendar blocks.
Delay noncritical approvals.
Explain capacity changes.
Warn against overload.
Coordinate weekly planning.
Atlas should not automatically store every personal calendar detail as durable Memory.
Use does not imply permanent retention.

9.12 Executive Capacity Signals

Executive Intelligence should receive derived signals such as:
Available.
Unavailable.
Deep-work window.
Approval window.
High-load day.
Low-load day.
Decision capacity constrained.
Recovery required.
Founder response delay expected.
These signals should be sufficient for most executive planning.
Detailed event titles should remain unnecessary.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.13 Project-Level Capacity Signals

Project Executives may receive signals such as:
Founder review available this morning.
No founder input expected today.
Approval window closes at 14:00.
Project work requiring founder judgment should be deferred.
Light founder involvement available this week.
A project should not know why the founder is unavailable unless the founder explicitly chooses to share it.

9.14 Workforce-Level Capacity Signals

Manager and Workforce should receive only execution-relevant constraints.
Examples:
Continue autonomous work.
Do not wait for approval today.
Prepare items for tomorrow’s approval batch.
Escalate only Critical issues.
Founder decision unavailable until Monday.
Workforce does not need access to private life details.

9.15 Calendar Event Classification

Calendar events may be classified by planning effect rather than by private content.
Possible classifications:
Hard unavailable.
Soft unavailable.
Deep-work block.
Meeting block.
Travel block.
Personal commitment.
Recovery block.
Approval window.
Flexible block.
This classification supports planning without exposing unnecessary event meaning.

9.16 Hard Unavailability

Hard unavailability means the founder should not be scheduled.
Examples may include:
Appointments.
Education sessions.
Family obligations.
Travel.
Important meetings.
Sleep or recovery.
Events explicitly marked protected.
Executive Intelligence should not schedule over hard unavailability.
It should not recommend that the founder ignore a protected commitment for routine work.

9.17 Soft Unavailability

Soft unavailability means work may be technically possible but should not be assumed.
Examples:
Low-energy periods.
Transition time.
Flexible personal tasks.
Commute.
Post-meeting decompression.
Light administrative windows.
Executive Intelligence may suggest optional light work.
It should not schedule deep strategic work automatically.

9.18 Protected Time

The founder should be able to mark time as protected.
Protected time may include:
Family time.
Recovery.
Exercise.
Education.
Sleep.
Personal projects.
Unscheduled rest.
Protected time should be respected as a strategic boundary.
It should not be treated as unused capacity.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.19 Unscheduled Capacity

Empty calendar space has value.
Executive Intelligence should not fill every free block.
Unscheduled capacity provides:
Flexibility.
Recovery.
Buffer for delays.
Room for opportunities.
Reduced stress.
Space for reflection.
A calendar optimized to 100% utilization is usually fragile.
The goal is not maximum calendar density.
The goal is effective capacity.

9.20 Buffer Time

Executive planning should include buffer.
Buffer may be needed for:
Task overrun.
Context switching.
Unexpected family needs.
Technical problems.
Approval delays.
Recovery.
Travel.
The amount of buffer may depend on the day’s uncertainty.
High-uncertainty days require more buffer.

9.21 Transition Time

Executive Intelligence should consider transition cost between activities.
Examples:
Meeting to deep architecture work.
Travel to approval review.
Family obligation to customer escalation.
Exercise to strategic planning.
A five-minute calendar gap is not a meaningful work block.
Transitions should be treated realistically.

9.22 Deep-Work Windows

Deep-work windows should be treated as high-value resources.
They should be reserved for work such as:
Architecture decisions.
Strategy.
Complex reviews.
Major implementation planning.
Board-level analysis.
Difficult writing.
High-impact decision-making.
Routine approvals and administrative work should not consume the best deep-work blocks unless urgent.

9.23 Approval Windows

Approvals should be grouped into suitable windows.
Approval windows may be:
Morning review.
Midday batch.
End-of-day check.
Weekly approval session.
Batching reduces context switching.
Sensitive or high-risk approvals may require dedicated attention.

9.24 Decision Fatigue

Executive Intelligence should account for decision fatigue.
Decision fatigue may increase when:
Many approvals are pending.
Several architecture choices are open.
The founder has attended many meetings.
Sensitive customer cases require judgment.
Personal obligations are heavy.
The day already included high-stakes decisions.
The system should not continuously add nonurgent choices.
It should batch, defer, recommend, or reduce options when appropriate.

9.25 Decision Budget

The founder may have a practical daily decision budget.
This is not necessarily a fixed number.
The concept means:
High-impact decisions consume more capacity.
Ambiguous decisions consume more capacity.
Sensitive customer decisions consume more capacity.
Routine approvals consume less capacity.
Executive Intelligence should prioritize decision quality over decision volume.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.26 Approval Budget

The approval budget represents how much approval work the founder can reasonably complete.
The system should consider:
Number of items.
Complexity.
Risk.
Required evidence review.
Expected edit burden.
Deadline.
Ten simple content approvals may be easier than one difficult strategy approval.
Volume alone is insufficient.

9.27 Capacity and Cognitive Budget

Executive reasoning depth should align with founder capacity.
On a high-capacity day, Atlas may propose:
Deep Executive Analysis.
Architecture review.
Strategy comparison.
Long-form planning.
On a low-capacity day, Atlas may propose:
Short approval batch.
Simple yes/no decisions.
Deferred deep analysis.
Autonomous continuation of existing workflows.
The system should not deliver a board-level decision package when the founder cannot review it properly, unless urgency requires it.

9.28 Capacity and Risk

Low founder capacity does not reduce risk.
It changes response strategy.
When capacity is low:
Critical risks still escalate.
High-risk external actions may pause.
Noncritical decisions may defer.
Existing safe automation may continue.
Approval-dependent workflows may queue.
Crisis rules may override normal availability.
The organization should not become unsafe because the founder is unavailable.

9.29 Capacity and Autonomy

Safe autonomy should reduce founder dependence.
If the founder is unavailable, workflows with valid autonomy licenses may continue.
Workflows requiring approval should wait unless:
An emergency mandate applies.
A pre-approved fallback exists.
The action can be safely downgraded.
The action can be prepared without external execution.
Founder unavailability must not be interpreted as implied approval.

9.30 Capacity and Do-Not-Start

Founder capacity should influence Do-Not-Start recommendations.
Examples:
Do not begin a new architecture chapter on a low-capacity day.
Do not restart a project during a high-load week.
Do not schedule customer strategy decisions after several major reviews.
Do not open a new epic before current approvals are resolved.
The founder may still override.
Executive Intelligence must state the capacity risk honestly.

9.31 Capacity and Project Priorities

Projects may compete for founder attention.
Executive Intelligence should allocate attention based on:
Portfolio priority.
Urgency.
Revenue.
Risk.
Dependency.
Founder expertise required.
Decision deadline.
Opportunity cost.
Not every active project deserves founder attention every day.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.32 Capacity and Project Modes

Project mode should influence founder involvement.
Active / Build
May require focused review or architecture decisions.
Active / Growth
May require performance and commercial decisions.
Observer / Learning
May require periodic interpretation, not daily intervention.
Hibernate
Should require minimal founder attention.
Crisis
May temporarily dominate founder capacity.
Mode should shape planning burden.

9.33 Capacity and Weekly Planning

Sunday planning should evaluate the founder’s full upcoming week.
It should consider:
Hard calendar commitments.
Expected deep-work windows.
Approval windows.
Study schedule.
Family responsibilities.
Recovery.
Known deadlines.
Travel.
Existing project commitments.
The weekly plan should be built around usable capacity.
It should not create work first and look for time afterward.

9.34 Capacity Forecast

Executive Intelligence should forecast capacity for the week.
A conceptual forecast:
Monday: Moderate
Tuesday: High
Wednesday: Low
Thursday: Moderate
Friday: Unavailable
Weekend: Light planning only
The forecast should include confidence.
Unexpected life events may change it.

9.35 Capacity Confidence

Capacity estimates should include confidence when uncertainty is material.
Examples:
High confidence:
Calendar is stable and known.
Medium confidence:
Several flexible commitments exist.
Low confidence:
Family or work demands may change quickly.
Low-confidence capacity should create more buffer.

9.36 Capacity-Based Work Placement

Work should be placed according to cognitive demand.
High-Capacity Windows
Strategy.
Architecture.
Difficult reviews.
Major writing.
Complex decisions.
Moderate-Capacity Windows
Planning.
Standard reviews.
Approval batches.
Project check-ins.
Structured analysis.
Low-Capacity Windows
Routine approvals.
Light administration.
Status checks.
Simple responses.
Review of prepared summaries.
Unavailable Windows
No routine founder work.

9.37 Workload Shaping

Executive Intelligence should shape workload to fit capacity.
Possible actions include:
Reduce scope.
Split a task.
Move work.
Delegate preparation.
Batch approvals.
Delay noncritical decisions.
Create a lighter alternative.
Continue automation without founder involvement.
The system should not simply label the founder overloaded.
It should redesign the plan.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.38 Task Splitting

A large founder task may be split into:
Evidence review.
Decision review.
Approval.
Follow-up.
Implementation handoff.
Example:
Instead of:
Review the full autonomy architecture.
Split into:
1. Review risk model.
2. Approve autonomy levels.
3. Review The Prompt application.
Task splitting should reduce burden without fragmenting the decision beyond usefulness.

9.39 Preparation Before Founder Review

Workforce should prepare founder decisions.
Before a founder review, Omnira should ideally provide:
Recommendation.
Alternatives.
Evidence.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Requested decision.
Estimated review effort.
The founder should not spend high-value capacity gathering context that the system could prepare.

9.40 Founder-Only Work

Executive Intelligence should identify work that genuinely requires the founder.
Examples:
Final strategic choice.
High-impact autonomy approval.
Sensitive customer judgment.
Major budget decision.
Personal preference.
Vision definition.
Constitutional policy.
Work that does not require the founder should be delegated.

9.41 False Founder Dependency

Omnira should detect unnecessary founder dependency.
Examples:
Routine approvals repeated unchanged.
Requests for information already in Memory.
Manual status collection.
Low-risk internal choices.
Formatting decisions.
Workflow retries.
Standard scheduling.
False dependency should be removed over time.

9.42 Founder Leverage

Founder leverage increases when the founder spends more time on:
Vision.
Strategy.
High-impact judgment.
Creative direction.
Critical relationships.
Unique decisions.
and less time on:
Status collection.
Routine coordination.
Repeated approvals.
Manual scheduling.
Operational troubleshooting.
Context reconstruction.
Calendar-aware planning should improve founder leverage, not only calendar efficiency.

9.43 Capacity and Revenue Work

Revenue-related work may deserve priority.
However, revenue work must still fit capacity.
Examples:
A high-value customer decision may override routine architecture work.
A revenue opportunity may justify rescheduling.
A low-confidence campaign decision may wait for a high-capacity window.
Routine revenue reporting should not consume deep-work time.
Executive Intelligence should distinguish urgent revenue activity from merely revenue-adjacent activity.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.44 Capacity and Strategic Work

Strategic work requires quality attention.
Executive Intelligence should avoid scheduling strategic decisions:
Between meetings.
Late after decision-heavy days.
During expected interruptions.
Without sufficient preparation.
When critical evidence is missing.
Poor timing can reduce decision quality even when the strategy process is technically complete.

9.45 Capacity and Sensitive Decisions

Sensitive decisions may include:
Unhappy customer responses.
Refunds.
Child-related issues.
Health-related recommendations.
Security incidents.
Staff or collaborator conflict.
Project termination.
These decisions may require emotional as well as cognitive capacity.
The system should not batch them casually with routine approvals.

9.46 Capacity and Crisis

During Crisis Mode, normal capacity rules may be overridden.
However, Executive Intelligence should still:
Minimize unnecessary decisions.
Present the smallest viable decision set.
Delegate containment.
Separate facts from uncertainty.
Protect rest where possible.
Schedule the next review time.
Avoid continuous interruption.
Crisis leadership must not destroy founder effectiveness through information overload.

9.47 Capacity Recovery After Crisis

After a crisis, the system should expect reduced capacity.
Recovery planning may include:
Lighter workload.
Deferred strategic decisions.
Reduced meeting load.
Post-mortem scheduled later.
Temporary approval support.
Continued automation at safe scope.
The end of an incident does not instantly restore cognitive capacity.

9.48 Capacity and Personal Boundaries

The founder should be able to define personal boundaries.
Examples:
No work after a specific time.
No meetings during family blocks.
No Sunday implementation.
Only light planning on weekends.
Protected training time.
Protected education time.
Executive Intelligence should treat these as planning rules.
Personal boundaries should not need to be renegotiated every day.

9.49 Boundary Exceptions

The founder may define exceptions for:
Critical incidents.
High-value revenue opportunities.
Security issues.
Customer harm.
Time-sensitive legal matters.
Exceptions should remain narrow.
Everything should not become urgent enough to override personal boundaries.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.50 Calendar Proposal Model

Executive Intelligence may propose calendar blocks.
A proposal should include:
Task.
Purpose.
Project.
Duration.
Preferred time.
Cognitive demand.
Deadline.
Flexibility.
Expected outcome.
Example:
Task:
Review The Prompt article batch.
Purpose:
Unblock today’s publication.
Duration:
20 minutes.
Preferred time:
13:30.
Cognitive demand:
Moderate.
Flexibility:
May move before 15:00.

9.51 Calendar Approval Model

Calendar changes require approval unless the founder grants a future scheduling mandate.
The founder should be able to:
Approve.
Edit.
Move.
Shorten.
Split.
Reject.
Request a lighter schedule.
The scheduling interface should preserve control.

9.52 Calendar Mandates

Future bounded scheduling autonomy may be granted.
A calendar mandate could define:
Allowed event types.
Maximum duration.
Allowed hours.
Protected time.
Maximum weekly load.
Projects included.
Notification rules.
Review date.
Example:
Atlas may automatically schedule up to two 30-minute approval blocks per week between 09:00 and 15:00, excluding protected family and study time.
Scheduling autonomy must be scoped like any other autonomy.

9.53 Calendar Conflict Detection

Before proposing or creating events, Omnira should detect:
Hard conflicts.
Travel conflicts.
Insufficient transition time.
Double booking.
Protected time violation.
Excessive daily load.
Repeated context switching.
Approval deadline mismatch.
The system should not treat technical availability as scheduling quality.

9.54 Calendar Conflict Resolution

When conflicts exist, Executive Intelligence should offer alternatives.
Example:
Option A:
Move Memory review to Tuesday morning.
Option B:
Split review into two 30-minute blocks.
Option C:
Defer The Prompt strategy review.
Recommended:
Option A.
The system should explain the tradeoff.

9.55 Calendar Priority

Calendar proposals should follow executive priority.
Higher priority may be given to:
Critical risk.
Revenue deadline.
Founder-only decision.
Hard dependency.
Customer-sensitive issue.
Weekly objective.
Low-priority work should not occupy the best capacity windows.

9.56 Calendar Stability

The calendar should not be continuously reorganized.
Executive Intelligence should avoid:
Moving approved blocks without cause.
Frequent micro-adjustments.
Filling every cancellation immediately.
Replanning for minor workflow changes.
Calendar stability supports execution.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.57 Rescheduling Threshold

Rescheduling should occur when:
Priority materially changes.
Capacity changes.
A hard dependency is delayed.
A crisis emerges.
A time-sensitive opportunity appears.
The original block becomes impossible.
Small changes should not trigger full replanning.

9.58 Founder-Initiated Calendar Changes

When the founder changes the calendar, Executive Intelligence should update:
Capacity forecast.
Approval windows.
Mission timing.
Weekly plan.
Expected decision dates.
The system should not interpret every manual change as a strategic signal.
It should assess materiality.

9.59 Calendar Context and Daily Brief

The Daily Executive Brief should show derived capacity.
Example:
Founder Capacity:
Moderate.
Best deep-work window:
09:00–10:30.
Approval availability:
Before 14:00.
Recommendation:
Complete one strategic review and one approval batch.
The brief should not reveal private calendar detail unnecessarily.

9.60 Calendar Context and Weekly Plan

The Weekly Plan should map major founder commitments to realistic windows.
It should identify:
Deep-work blocks.
Approval blocks.
Decision deadlines.
Protected time.
Buffer.
Unavailable periods.
The weekly Gantt view should reflect these constraints.

9.61 Calendar Context and Workforce

Workforce should know when to expect founder input.
Examples:
Submit approval batch by 12:00.
Do not block on founder feedback before Tuesday.
Prepare alternatives before the review window.
Escalate Critical issues immediately.
Workforce should not know the private reason for timing.

9.62 Calendar Context and Manager

Manager may coordinate around:
Approval windows.
Founder review deadlines.
Blocked missions.
Submission timing.
Escalation windows.
Calendar-created milestones.
Manager should receive operational timing, not personal context.

9.63 Calendar Context and Portfolio Executive

Portfolio Executive should use capacity to:
Allocate founder attention.
Reduce active priorities.
Delay project reactivation.
Protect deep-work windows.
Balance project demands.
Recommend Do-Not-Start items.
Portfolio planning that ignores the calendar is incomplete.

9.64 Calendar Context and Project Executives

A Project Executive should adapt its plan based on founder availability.
Examples:
The Prompt prepares a batch for the next approval window.
Familje-Stunden defers a nonurgent strategy review.
GainPilot remains hibernated.
Omnira schedules architecture work in a high-capacity block.
Projects should compete through executive priority, not through constant notifications.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.65 Capacity Events

Capacity changes may be event-driven.
Examples:
Calendar event added.
Meeting cancelled.
Family obligation added.
Founder marks low energy.
Critical deadline appears.
Crisis occurs.
Travel changes.
A capacity event may trigger plan adjustment.
It should not always trigger a new notification.

9.66 Manual Capacity Input

The founder should be able to tell Atlas:
I have low energy today.
I can work deeply this morning.
Do not schedule anything tonight.
I only want to handle approvals today.
This week is overloaded.
Manual input should override inferred capacity when current and explicit.
The system should not argue with the founder’s self-assessment.

9.67 Inferred Capacity

Executive Intelligence may infer capacity from:
Calendar density.
Meeting load.
Recent work patterns.
Approval completion.
Repeated rescheduling.
Time of day.
Task completion.
Founder feedback.
Inferences should remain probabilistic.
They should not be presented as medical or psychological facts.

9.68 Capacity Uncertainty

When capacity is uncertain, the system should:
Use a lower-confidence label.
Recommend more buffer.
Avoid hard scheduling.
Ask only when the answer materially changes the plan.
Prefer reversible proposals.
Uncertainty should not force unnecessary questioning.

9.69 Capacity Learning

The system should learn from:
Accepted calendar blocks.
Moved calendar blocks.
Rejected schedules.
Completed deep-work sessions.
Approval timing.
Founder feedback.
Repeated overload.
Preferred work windows.
Learning should improve future planning.
It should not create rigid assumptions.

9.70 Capacity Preferences

The founder may have stable preferences such as:
Best deep work in the morning.
Approvals after lunch.
No major decisions late at night.
Sunday planning preferred.
Shorter blocks on study days.
Protected family evenings.
Stable preferences may be remembered.
Temporary conditions should not become permanent preferences.

9.71 Preference vs Constraint

The system should distinguish:
Preference:
Morning deep work is usually better.
Constraint:
Founder is unavailable from 09:00–12:00.
Boundary:
No work during protected family time.
Emergency exception:
Critical security incident.
These categories have different authority.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.72 Capacity Feedback

The founder should be able to provide feedback:
Too much work.
Too little work.
Wrong time.
Good workload.
Too many approvals.
This block was useful.
Do not schedule this type of work then.
Feedback should improve calibration.

9.73 Capacity Calibration

Executive Intelligence should compare predicted capacity with actual outcomes.
Possible measures:
Planned work completed.
Calendar blocks used.
Approval window accuracy.
Reschedule rate.
Founder overload feedback.
Decision quality correction.
Carryover.
The system should become better at planning realistically.

9.74 Overload Detection

Potential overload signals include:
High carryover.
Repeated rescheduling.
Large approval backlog.
Several high-impact decisions in one day.
Too many active projects.
Founder feedback indicating overload.
Protected time repeatedly invaded.
Long periods without recovery.
Overload should trigger plan reduction, not merely another warning.

9.75 Overload Response

Executive Intelligence may recommend:
Freeze new initiatives.
Reduce project focus.
Batch approvals.
Delegate preparation.
Delay noncritical decisions.
Protect recovery time.
Shorten the Daily Brief.
Increase Do-Not-Start restrictions.
The goal is to restore sustainable leadership.

9.76 Underload Detection

The system should also detect underused capacity carefully.
Possible signals:
High capacity.
Low approval burden.
No major blockers.
Weekly objective ahead of schedule.
Founder requests more work.
Underload may justify advancing a planned task.
It should not automatically trigger new epics.

9.77 Capacity Reserve

Executive Intelligence should preserve some reserve capacity.
Reserve supports:
Unexpected risk.
Customer issues.
Opportunities.
Technical failures.
Personal changes.
A fully allocated founder is a fragile single point of failure.

9.78 Founder Dependency Risk

Omnira should measure how dependent projects are on founder availability.
Possible indicators:
Number of founder-only decisions.
Approval waiting time.
Missions blocked on founder input.
Sensitive actions requiring review.
Unresolved strategic ambiguity.
High founder dependency should be treated as an organizational risk.

9.79 Reducing Founder Dependency

The system may reduce dependency by:
Improving Mission Briefs.
Creating clearer policies.
Batching approvals.
Granting earned autonomy.
Improving Memory.
Adding review roles.
Creating better defaults.
Preparing decision alternatives.
Defining budget mandates.
Founder dependency should fall as governance matures.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.80 Founder Authority

Reducing dependency does not reduce founder authority.
The founder retains authority to:
Override plans.
Protect personal time.
Reject calendar proposals.
Change priorities.
Revoke autonomy.
Require approval.
Enter or exit Crisis Mode.
Change capacity preferences.
Automation should create leverage, not loss of control.

9.81 Personal Time as Strategic Infrastructure

Personal time should not be viewed as time stolen from Omnira.
It supports:
Health.
Family.
Recovery.
Creativity.
Decision quality.
Long-term sustainability.
Executive Intelligence should protect the human system that leads the AI system.
Founder burnout is a portfolio risk.

9.82 Recovery Planning

Recovery may be scheduled or protected after:
High-load weeks.
Crisis response.
Major launches.
Intensive strategy work.
Travel.
Illness.
Repeated late work.
The system should not require detailed health disclosure to recommend lighter capacity.

9.83 Sustainable Pace

Executive Intelligence should prefer sustainable execution over repeated intensity cycles.
A sustainable pace:
Produces consistent progress.
Preserves decision quality.
Allows recovery.
Reduces strategic whiplash.
Supports family and personal commitments.
Improves long-term founder leverage.
Maximum short-term output is not always the optimal executive strategy.

9.84 Capacity and Ambition

Capacity-aware planning should not reduce ambition.
It should improve sequencing.
The system may say:
This goal remains valid.
The current timing is unrealistic.
Here is a safer sequence.
Here is what can be delegated.
Here is what must wait.
Ambition without sequencing becomes overload.

9.85 Capacity and Opportunity Cost

Founder time has opportunity cost.
If the founder spends two hours on:
Dashboard styling.
those hours cannot be spent on:
Revenue strategy.
Autonomy approval.
Customer insight.
Architecture review.
Executive Intelligence should make this visible.

9.86 Capacity Value Classification

Founder work may be classified by value.
Unique Founder Value
Only the founder can do it well.
High-Leverage Founder Work
Founder judgment creates disproportionate value.
Reviewable Work
Others can prepare; founder approves.
Delegable Work
Founder should not need to do it.
Avoidable Work
The organization should remove it.
This classification supports leverage.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.87 Founder Work Audit

Monthly review may examine:
Where founder time went.
Which work created value.
Which work should be delegated.
Which approvals were unnecessary.
Which projects consumed disproportionate attention.
Which calendar blocks were ineffective.
This is not employee time tracking.
It is executive leverage analysis.

9.88 Calendar-Aware Prioritization

Priority should consider both value and timing.
A high-value task may still be poorly placed today if:
The founder lacks capacity.
Required evidence is missing.
A better deep-work window exists tomorrow.
The task would disrupt a critical commitment.
The deadline is not urgent.
The system should distinguish priority from immediate scheduling.

9.89 Time-Sensitive Work

Time-sensitive work may include:
Publishing deadlines.
Customer response deadlines.
Revenue opportunities.
Security actions.
Expiring approvals.
Provider migrations.
Legal deadlines.
Time sensitivity should be explicit.
It should not be inferred from emotional urgency.

9.90 Flexible Work

Flexible work may include:
Architecture reading.
Long-term strategy.
Noncritical documentation.
Future product ideation.
Optional research.
Flexible work should move around hard commitments.
It should not continuously displace important but time-bound work.

9.91 Calendar Block Types

Omnira may support several block types:
Deep Work.
Approval Batch.
Executive Review.
Project Review.
Planning.
Meeting.
Recovery.
Protected Personal.
Buffer.
Crisis Response.
Each type may have default duration and preparation needs.

9.92 Deep-Work Block Design

A deep-work block should include:
Clear outcome.
Required context prepared.
No unnecessary notifications.
Sufficient duration.
Transition buffer.
Defined stopping point.
Executive Intelligence should not schedule vague deep-work blocks.

9.93 Approval Block Design

An approval block should include:
Approval count.
Estimated review time.
Priority order.
Batch candidates.
Sensitive items separated.
Decision-ready evidence.
The founder should know what the block contains before accepting it.

9.94 Executive Review Block Design

An Executive Review block may include:
Decision to make.
Recommendation.
Alternatives.
Evidence.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Expected duration.
Review preparation should be complete before the block begins.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.95 Recovery Block Design

A recovery block should not contain hidden work.
It should remain free from:
Routine approvals.
Project notifications.
Planning requests.
Status checks.
Only authorized emergency escalation should interrupt.

9.96 Notification Timing

Notifications should respect capacity and calendar.
Noncritical notifications may be:
Grouped.
Delayed.
Delivered before an approval window.
Included in the next Daily Brief.
Critical notifications remain immediate.

9.97 Notification Quiet Periods

The founder may define quiet periods.
During quiet periods:
Routine notifications are suppressed.
Approval requests queue.
Workflows continue within authority.
Only Critical alerts interrupt.
Quiet periods support focus and personal boundaries.

9.98 Approval Deadline Design

Approval deadlines should reflect real business need.
The system should avoid artificial urgency.
A deadline should state:
Why the time matters.
What happens if missed.
Whether the action can defer.
Whether a fallback exists.

9.99 Founder Response Expectations

Workflows should not assume immediate founder response.
Response expectations may vary by:
Risk.
Project.
Action type.
Day.
Capacity.
Service commitment.
A clear response model reduces unnecessary escalation.

9.100 Capacity-Aware Escalation

Escalation should consider both severity and availability.
Examples:
Critical:
Interrupt immediately.
High:
Notify during current available window.
Moderate:
Add to Daily Brief.
Low:
Include in Weekly Review.
Founder unavailability should not turn every waiting item into High severity.

9.101 Delegated Approval

Future approval authority may be delegated to another human role.
A delegated approval model should define:
Project.
Action category.
Risk level.
Approver role.
Limit.
Duration.
Escalation rule.
Founder capacity may improve through safe delegation.

9.102 Substitute Decision Paths

When the founder is unavailable, a workflow may have a pre-approved substitute path.
Examples:
Prepare draft only.
Pause publication.
Use approved template.
Queue for later review.
Escalate to secondary approver.
Take no external action.
The fallback should be defined before it is needed.

9.103 No-Response Policy

Each approval-dependent workflow should define what happens when no response arrives.
Possible outcomes:
Wait.
Expire.
Defer.
Pause.
Use approved fallback.
Escalate.
Cancel.
No response must never equal approval by default.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.104 Calendar Data Freshness

Calendar-aware planning depends on current data.
The system should understand whether calendar information is:
Current.
Partially synchronized.
Delayed.
Incomplete.
Unavailable.
If calendar data is stale, capacity confidence should fall.

9.105 Conflicting Calendar Sources

The founder may have several calendars.
When sources conflict, the system should determine:
Which calendar is authoritative.
Whether events overlap.
Whether one calendar is personal.
Whether duplicate events exist.
Whether an event is tentative.
The system should not expose private calendars to project systems during reconciliation.

9.106 Tentative Events

Tentative events should reduce confidence but not always block time.
A tentative event may be treated as:
Soft unavailable.
Conditional.
Needs confirmation.
The founder should be able to define preferred handling.

9.107 All-Day Events

All-day events may not mean full unavailability.
The system should distinguish:
Informational all-day event.
Protected all-day event.
Travel day.
Birthday reminder.
Deadline.
Calendar semantics require interpretation.

9.108 Recurring Events

Recurring events may define stable capacity patterns.
Examples:
Education sessions.
Weekly planning.
Training.
Family routines.
Regular meetings.
Executive Intelligence may learn these patterns.
Exceptions should override the recurrence.

9.109 Personal Event Titles

Personal event titles should remain private.
Derived planning may use:
Unavailable.
Personal commitment.
Protected time.
Travel.
Appointment.
The exact title should not flow into project reports.

9.110 Capacity History

The system may preserve capacity history for planning improvement.
Useful durable information may include:
Preferred work windows.
Typical weekly load.
Planning accuracy.
Common overload patterns.
Approval timing preference.
It should avoid storing unnecessary private event history.

9.111 Data Minimization

Calendar and capacity systems should retain only what is necessary.
Possible derived records:
Capacity classification.
Available windows.
Protected windows.
Approval windows.
Confidence.
Planning outcome.
Raw personal details should have stricter retention and access.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.112 Consent and Control

The founder should control:
Which calendars Atlas may access.
Which event details may be interpreted.
Which details may be retained.
Which capacity signals may reach projects.
Whether calendar proposals may be created.
Whether approved events may be added automatically.
Calendar access should remain understandable and revocable.

9.113 Revocation

If calendar access is revoked:
Atlas stops reading the calendar.
Future plans use manual or limited availability.
Existing private details are handled according to retention policy.
Project systems retain only necessary operational constraints.
Scheduling autonomy is suspended if required.
The system should degrade safely.

9.114 Future Multi-User Capacity

Future organizations may include several human leaders.
Capacity planning may then consider:
Founder.
Project owner.
Approver.
Specialist.
Customer contact.
Executive team.
Each person’s calendar and private context should remain separately governed.

9.115 Team Availability

Project systems may receive team-level availability summaries.
Examples:
Editorial approval available Tuesday.
Customer support coverage limited Friday.
Technical review capacity full this week.
Raw personal calendar details should remain unnecessary.

9.116 Capacity and Customer Projects

Future customer projects should control whether Omnira may use human availability data.
Customer-controlled settings may include:
Calendar source.
Availability detail.
Planning scope.
Notification times.
Approval windows.
Retention.
Internal founder rules must not be imposed on external customer organizations.

9.117 Capacity Object

Founder capacity should eventually exist as a structured object.
Conceptually, it may contain:
Capacity identifier.
User.
Date or time range.
Timezone.
Overall classification.
Deep-work capacity.
Approval capacity.
Unavailable windows.
Preferred windows.
Protected windows.
Confidence.
Source freshness.
Privacy classification.
Version.
The exact implementation may evolve.
The concept should remain stable.

9.118 Calendar Proposal Object

A calendar proposal may contain:
Proposal identifier.
User.
Project.
Task.
Purpose.
Start.
End.
Duration.
Block type.
Priority.
Flexibility.
Dependencies.
Approval status.
Version.
The object should support editing and auditability.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.119 Capacity Event Object

A material capacity event may contain:
Event type.
Affected time range.
Capacity change.
Plan impact.
Projects affected.
Recommended response.
Confidence.
Privacy classification.
This allows plans to update without exposing private details.

9.120 Capacity Status

Capacity information may have status:
Draft.
Estimated.
Confirmed.
Updated.
Superseded.
Unavailable.
Plans should understand whether capacity is inferred or confirmed.

9.121 Capacity Versioning

When capacity changes materially, the system should preserve:
Previous estimate.
New estimate.
Reason category.
Affected plans.
Affected approvals.
Time of change.
The detailed private reason may remain outside the executive record.

9.122 The Capacity Decision Test

Before assigning founder work, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Does this truly require the founder?
Does the founder have the right type of capacity?
Is the work time-sensitive?
Can preparation reduce review time?
Can the decision be batched?
Can a safe fallback handle delay?
What will be displaced?

9.123 The Calendar Proposal Test

Before proposing a calendar block, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Is the outcome clear?
Is the duration realistic?
Is this the right cognitive window?
Does it respect protected time?
Is buffer included?
Is the block more valuable than keeping the time free?
Does it require approval?

9.124 The Privacy Test

Before sharing calendar-derived information, Omnira should ask:
Who needs this information?
Can a capacity signal replace the private detail?
Is the recipient authorized?
Is the information necessary?
How long should it be retained?
Could disclosure create personal harm?

9.125 The Overload Test

Before finalizing a plan, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Are too many projects requesting founder attention?
Are there too many high-impact decisions?
Is recovery protected?
Is unscheduled buffer preserved?
Is carryover already high?
Can work be delegated or deferred?

9.126 The Founder Leverage Test

Before assigning work to the founder, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Is this a unique founder contribution?
Could Workforce prepare or complete it?
Could policy replace repeated approval?
Could a clearer decision rule remove this burden?
Does this use founder judgment well?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
9.127 Failure Modes

Founder Capacity and Calendar-Aware Planning must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Calendar Equals Capacity
The system treats every free calendar slot as usable work time.
Failure Mode 2 — Private Detail Leakage
Personal calendar titles reach Project Executives, Workforce, agents, or external systems.
Failure Mode 3 — Over-Scheduling
The system fills every free block.
Failure Mode 4 — Deep-Work Misuse
High-value cognitive windows are consumed by routine approvals.
Failure Mode 5 — Decision Overload
Too many high-impact decisions are scheduled together.
Failure Mode 6 — Approval Overload
The founder receives more approvals than can be reviewed well.
Failure Mode 7 — No Buffer
Plans fail because no space exists for delays or unexpected events.
Failure Mode 8 — Protected-Time Violation
Omnira repeatedly schedules over family, education, health, or recovery boundaries.
