A decision may have outcome status:
Not yet measurable.
On track.
Mixed.
Successful.
Unsuccessful.
Inconclusive.
Harmful.
Superseded before evaluation.
Outcome status should not overwrite the original decision.

11.97 Outcome Evidence

Outcome evidence may include:
Revenue.
Traffic.
Retention.
Quality.
Risk incidents.
Approval burden.
Founder capacity.
Workflow reliability.
Customer feedback.
Cost.
The relevant metrics depend on the decision.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.98 Expected vs Actual

A review should compare:
Expected impact.
Actual impact.
Expected cost.
Actual cost.
Expected risk.
Observed risk.
Expected timeline.
Actual timeline.
This supports organizational learning.

11.99 Good Decision, Bad Outcome

A decision may have been reasonable based on available evidence but still produce a poor outcome.
The ledger should preserve that distinction.
The review should ask:
Was the reasoning sound at the time?
Was uncertainty acknowledged?
Were controls appropriate?
Was the bad outcome foreseeable?

11.100 Bad Decision, Good Outcome

A weak decision may produce a lucky result.
The system should not reward unsafe reasoning merely because damage did not occur.
Decision quality and outcome quality must remain separate.

11.101 Decision Quality Rating

Omnira may later evaluate decision quality through:
Question clarity.
Evidence quality.
Assumption transparency.
Risk analysis.
Alternative analysis.
Authority correctness.
Review design.
Outcome calibration.
This is separate from the business result.

11.102 Decision Learning

Review may produce lessons such as:
The evidence threshold was too low.
The trial scope was too broad.
The founder review burden was underestimated.
The risk control worked.
The recommendation was overly conservative.
A dependency was incorrectly classified.
Lessons may enter Memory when durable.

11.103 Decision Ledger and Trust Score

Ledger outcomes may inform Trust Score.
Relevant evidence includes:
Recommendations approved unchanged.
Recommendations requiring correction.
Autonomy decisions later reversed.
Risk predictions.
Policy compliance.
Decision outcome quality.
Trust Score must not be based only on approval rate.

11.104 Decision Ledger and Executive Calibration

The ledger enables Executive Intelligence to learn:
Where it was overconfident.
Where it was too cautious.
Which assumptions repeatedly fail.
Which risk models are accurate.
Which founder preferences are stable.
Which types of decisions require deeper analysis.

11.105 Decision Ledger and Founder Feedback

The founder may attach feedback:
Correct recommendation.
Wrong priority.
Insufficient evidence.
Too much detail.
Good alternatives.
Risk overstated.
Decision should have been batched.
Feedback should improve future Decision Intelligence.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.106 Decision Review Queue

The ledger should produce a queue of decisions due for review.
The queue may prioritize by:
Risk.
Authority.
Expiration.
Impact.
Project mode.
Autonomy.
Evidence change.
Dependency change.
Chapter 12 defines the complete review model.

11.107 Upcoming Decision Reviews

The Daily Executive Brief may show:
Autonomy decision review due in three days.
Project mode decision due at month end.
Temporary access expires tomorrow.
The founder should not be surprised by expiring authority.

11.108 Automated Review Preparation

Omnira may prepare review packages automatically.
A review package may include:
Original decision.
Original evidence.
Current evidence.
Outcome.
Assumption status.
Risk changes.
Recommended renewal, revision, expiration, or reversal.
Preparation may be autonomous.
Material review decisions remain governed.

11.109 Decision Renewal

Renewal should create a new version or linked decision event.
It should identify:
Evidence supporting renewal.
Changes in scope.
New review date.
Authority.
Updated risk.
Renewal should not erase the original decision period.

11.110 Decision Revision

Revision occurs when the decision remains conceptually valid but terms change.
Examples:
Reduce budget limit.
Narrow autonomy categories.
Extend trial duration.
Add a QA requirement.
A revision should preserve lineage.

11.111 Decision Expiration

Expiration means the decision no longer governs.
The ledger should identify:
Expiration time.
Fallback state.
Affected systems.
Whether renewal was considered.

11.112 Decision Reversal

Reversal should include:
Trigger.
Evidence.
Authority.
Immediate operational effect.
Required rollback.
Customer or project impact.

11.113 Decision Supersession

A new decision may replace an old one.
The new decision should explicitly state:
Supersedes Decision X.
The old entry should state:
Superseded by Decision Y.

11.114 Decision Archival

Completed, expired, superseded, or reversed decisions may move to historical views.
They should remain searchable and linked.
Archival must not mean deletion.

11.115 Retention

Material Decision Ledger entries should normally have long-term retention.
Especially:
Constitutional decisions.
Portfolio strategy.
Autonomy decisions.
Budget mandates.
Crisis decisions.
Project lifecycle changes.
Security and isolation incidents.
Retention rules must respect legal, privacy, and customer obligations.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.116 Permanent Deletion

Permanent deletion of ledger entries should be exceptional.
If deletion is legally or operationally required, the system should preserve an appropriate audit marker when permitted.
Decision history is a core accountability asset.

11.117 Redaction

Sensitive information may require redaction.
The system should distinguish:
Decision existence.
Decision meaning.
Sensitive evidence.
Restricted personal details.
Customer-identifying information.
Redaction should preserve as much decision continuity as safely possible.

11.118 Customer-Controlled Ledger

Future customer projects may have their own Decision Ledger.
Customers should control:
Access.
Retention.
Approvers.
Visibility.
Export.
Review cadence.
Integration with customer policies.
Internal Omnira leadership should not automatically access detailed customer decisions.

11.119 Multi-User Organizations

Future organizations may require:
Decision owner.
Decision sponsor.
Approver.
Reviewer.
Implementer.
Observer.
Each role should have explicit rights.

11.120 Decision Ownership

Decision ownership identifies who is responsible for ensuring the decision is implemented and reviewed.
The owner may differ from the approver.
Example:
Approver:
Founder.
Decision Owner:
The Prompt Project Executive.

11.121 Decision Sponsor

A sponsor may be responsible for the strategic importance of the decision.
This may be useful in future multi-user organizations.

11.122 Decision Reviewer

A reviewer may validate:
Evidence.
Risk.
Security.
Financial impact.
Editorial quality.
Customer impact.
Reviewer authority should remain scoped.

11.123 Decision Implementer

The implementer applies the decision through missions, workflows, or system changes.
Implementation authority is not decision authority.

11.124 Decision Observer

An observer may read the decision but not modify or act on it.
Visibility must not imply authority.

11.125 Decision Ledger Search

The founder should be able to search naturally:
Why is GainPilot paused?
When did we decide newsletters require approval?
Which autonomy decisions expire this month?
What decisions affect The Prompt publishing?
Which decisions were reversed?
Search results should preserve scope and authority.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.126 Semantic Retrieval

Semantic retrieval may help find related decisions.
However:
Relevance must never override authorization.
A semantically similar decision from another project should not be surfaced if access is not permitted.

11.127 Decision Ledger Timeline

A timeline may show:
Decision proposed.
Decision approved.
Decision activated.
Decision amended.
Decision reviewed.
Decision superseded.
This supports historical understanding.

11.128 Decision Ledger Dashboard

The dashboard may include:
Active decisions.
Decisions awaiting approval.
Decisions due for review.
Temporary decisions expiring.
Recently changed decisions.
Decisions with failed conditions.
Decisions linked to active risks.
The dashboard should prioritize action over volume.

11.129 Decision Graph

The Intelligence Graph should connect:
Decision.
Evidence.
Assumptions.
Approvals.
Policies.
Missions.
Workflows.
Risks.
Outcomes.
Reviews.
Successor decisions.
The graph should answer:
Why is this work happening?
Which decision authorized it?
What evidence supported the decision?
What result changed the next recommendation?

11.130 Decision Ledger and Operating Graph

The Operating Graph shows:
Project → Mission → Workflow → Task → Output
The Decision Ledger explains why that chain exists.
Together:
The Operating Graph shows what happened.
The Decision Ledger shows what authorized it.
The Intelligence Graph shows why.

11.131 Decision Ledger Notifications

Notifications should occur when:
Approval is required.
Review date approaches.
Decision expires.
Condition fails.
Conflicting decision appears.
Implementation fails.
Risk changes materially.
Routine entry creation should not create unnecessary notifications.

11.132 Decision Ledger Permissions

Permissions should distinguish:
Create draft.
Submit proposal.
Approve.
Reject.
Amend.
Activate.
Reverse.
View restricted evidence.
Export.
Archive.
A user or agent should receive only the permissions required.

11.133 Executive Creation Authority

Executive Intelligence may create draft or proposed decisions.
It may activate decisions only within granted authority.
It may not create its own higher authority.

11.134 Workforce Ledger Interaction

Workforce may:
Reference decisions.
Report implementation.
Attach outcomes.
Flag conflicts.
Request clarification.
Workforce should not rewrite executive decisions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.135 Manager Ledger Interaction

Manager may:
Read mission-relevant decisions.
Coordinate implementation.
Report application status.
Surface blockers.
Detect operational conflicts.
Manager should not change strategic rationale.

11.136 Performance Intelligence Interaction

Performance Intelligence may:
Attach outcome metrics.
Compare expected and actual results.
Detect threshold failure.
Trigger review recommendations.
Performance Intelligence measures.
Executive Intelligence interprets.

11.137 Memory Interaction

Memory may preserve durable lessons extracted from decisions.
The Decision Ledger remains the authoritative formal record.
Memory should reference the ledger when a memory depends on a formal decision.

11.138 Governance Interaction

Governance should use active decisions to determine:
Allowed action.
Required approval.
Autonomy level.
Budget limit.
Project mode.
Temporary exception.
Crisis restriction.
A ledger entry should not bypass the policy engine.
The two systems must remain consistent.

11.139 Policy Promotion

Repeated decisions may justify a policy.
Example:
Repeated approved behavior:
Low-risk short news posts repeatedly approved unchanged.
Proposed policy:
Approved categories may publish under a governed autonomy license.
Policy promotion requires explicit authority.

11.140 Decision Ledger Integrity

The ledger must protect:
Authenticity.
Completeness.
Chronology.
Scope.
Version history.
Authority.
Relationships.
Compromised ledger integrity undermines Executive Intelligence.

11.141 Integrity Checks

The system should detect:
Missing authority.
Invalid project scope.
Broken references.
Decision without review condition.
Expired decision still enforced.
Conflicting active decisions.
Unapplied approved decision.
Changed evidence without version record.

11.142 Missing Decision Detection

Omnira may detect material organizational states without a supporting decision.
Examples:
A project is active without an activation decision.
A workflow publishes autonomously without an autonomy decision.
A budget is being spent without a mandate.
A project mode changed without a ledger entry.
These are governance gaps.

11.143 Unapplied Decision Detection

A decision may be active in the ledger but not reflected in systems.
Example:
Decision:
Newsletter sending requires approval.
Observed behavior:
Newsletter sent autonomously.
This is a serious control failure.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.144 Orphaned Decision Detection

A decision may reference:
Missing project.
Deleted workflow.
Completed mission.
Expired policy.
Disconnected approval.
Orphaned decisions should be reviewed.

11.145 Conflicting Decision Detection

The system should detect semantic and structural conflicts.
Examples:
Two active autonomy levels.
Different budget limits.
Contradictory project modes.
Approval required and approval waived simultaneously.

11.146 Decision Ledger Health

Ledger health may evaluate:
Percentage of material actions with supporting decisions.
Decisions with valid authority.
Decisions with review dates.
Expired decisions still applied.
Conflicts.
Unapplied decisions.
Outcome coverage.
Review completion.
Poor ledger health should reduce autonomy confidence.

11.147 Decision Completeness

A material decision should not become Active when critical fields are missing.
Required fields may depend on impact.
High-impact decisions should require stronger completeness than low-impact internal decisions.

11.148 Decision Quality Gates

Before activation, a material decision may require:
Scope validation.
Authority validation.
Risk review.
Evidence sufficiency.
Approval.
Review condition.
Implementation plan.

11.149 Decision Ledger Automation

Omnira may autonomously:
Draft entries.
Extract decisions from approved conversations.
Link evidence.
Detect related decisions.
Schedule reviews.
Attach outcomes.
Identify conflicts.
Prepare renewal recommendations.
Automatic extraction should not silently create active decisions.

11.150 Conversation-to-Decision Extraction

When a founder conversation contains a material decision, Atlas may propose:
I detected a material decision. Save it to the Decision Ledger?
Future bounded mandates may allow automatic logging of clearly authorized decisions.
The founder should be able to correct the interpretation.

11.151 Explicit vs Implicit Decisions

Explicit decisions are directly stated.
Implicit decisions are inferred from action or repeated behavior.
Material implicit decisions should not automatically become formal authority.
The system should request confirmation or create a proposed entry.

11.152 Decision Confirmation

A confirmation interface may show:
Detected decision.
Scope.
Authority.
Effective date.
Review condition.
Affected systems.
The founder may:
Confirm.
Edit.
Reject.
Mark as non-material.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.153 Decision Import

Existing architecture documents or historical records may contain decisions.
Import should distinguish:
Confirmed decision.
Historical proposal.
Deprecated decision.
Unverified statement.
Imported decisions should not become Active without validation.

11.154 Legacy Decision Migration

Legacy decisions may lack:
Scope.
Authority.
Review date.
Evidence.
Version history.
They should be classified and normalized carefully.
Unknown details should remain unknown.

11.155 Decision Quarantine

Ambiguous legacy decisions may enter quarantine.
Quarantined entries:
Do not authorize action.
Remain visible for review.
May inform historical context cautiously.
Require classification before activation.

11.156 Decision Export

Decision export should preserve:
Scope.
Authority.
Versions.
Relationships.
Redactions.
Evidence references.
Outcome.
Exports must respect project and customer boundaries.

11.157 Decision Ledger Backup

The Decision Ledger is critical organizational infrastructure.
Backup and recovery should preserve:
Chronology.
Version history.
Relationships.
Permissions.
Project scope.
Audit integrity.

11.158 Decision Ledger Recovery

Recovery should verify that:
Active decisions are complete.
Expired decisions remain expired.
Superseded decisions are not reactivated.
Relationships are intact.
Permissions remain correct.

11.159 Crisis Mode and the Ledger

Crisis Mode decisions should be logged immediately or as soon as safely possible.
The record should include:
Trigger.
Authority.
Immediate actions.
Affected systems.
Temporary overrides.
Next review time.
Emergency speed should not eliminate accountability.

11.160 Break-Glass Decisions

Break-glass decisions should have enhanced requirements:
Explicit reason.
Limited scope.
Automatic expiration.
Enhanced audit.
Founder notification.
Mandatory review.
Post-mortem.

11.161 Autonomy Decisions

Autonomy decisions must always enter the ledger.
They should include:
Project.
Workflow.
Current level.
New level.
Action categories.
Evidence.
Trust Score.
Violations.
Controls.
Duration.
Review.
Rollback.

11.162 Budget Decisions

Budget decisions should include:
Project.
Amount.
Purpose.
Vendor scope.
Duration.
Authority.
Reporting.
Stopping conditions.
Review.
Unused budget does not create authority outside scope.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.163 Project Mode Decisions

Mode decisions should include:
Previous lifecycle mode.
New lifecycle mode.
Previous operating mode.
New operating mode.
Reason.
Impact.
Required missions.
Review date.

11.164 Strategy Decisions

Strategy decisions should include:
Strategic question.
Chosen direction.
Rejected alternatives.
Evidence.
Assumptions.
Opportunity cost.
Expected impact.
Review horizon.

11.165 Architecture Decisions

Major architecture decisions should include:
Problem.
Chosen architecture.
Alternatives.
Constraints.
Security impact.
Project impact.
Migration implications.
Review or replacement condition.
The Decision Ledger may reference a more detailed architecture record.

11.166 Publishing Decisions

Publishing decisions may include:
Content categories.
Source requirements.
Approval rules.
Autonomy.
Channels.
Correction policy.
Archive policy.
Permanent deletion restrictions.

11.167 Customer Communication Decisions

These may include:
Allowed response categories.
Sensitive topics.
Refund authority.
Discount authority.
Escalation.
Brand tone.
Human review requirements.

11.168 Tool Connection Decisions

Tool or MCP connection decisions should include:
Project.
Business purpose.
Permissions.
Data accessed.
External actions.
Cost.
Risk.
Approval.
Revocation.
Review.

11.169 Data Access Decisions

Data access decisions should include:
Actor.
Project.
Resource.
Purpose.
Allowed operations.
Duration.
Retention.
Audit.
Expiration.

11.170 Cross-Project Decisions

Cross-project decisions require:
Projects affected.
Minimum data required.
Shared capability.
Authority.
Risk.
Duration.
Data minimization.
Revocation.

11.171 Founder Capacity Decisions

Material planning decisions may include:
Freeze new initiatives for one week.
Protect defined deep-work blocks.
Reduce founder approval load.
Defer project reactivation due to limited capacity.
The ledger should preserve operational capacity signals, not unnecessary private detail.

11.172 Do-Not-Start Decisions

A material Do-Not-Start decision may be logged when it affects strategic sequencing.
It should include:
Prohibited initiative.
Reason.
Scope.
Review date.
Condition for removal.
Daily temporary suggestions do not always require ledger entries.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.173 Decision Ledger User Experience

The founder should experience the ledger as a strategic memory system.
It should not feel like legal paperwork.
The interface should answer:
What have we decided?
What is active now?
What needs review?
What changed?
Why does this rule exist?
What happened afterward?

11.174 Decision Cards

A decision card may show:
Title.
Status.
Scope.
Authority.
Summary.
Effective date.
Review date.
Outcome.
The founder may expand for deeper reasoning.

11.175 Decision Filters

Useful filters may include:
Project.
Status.
Decision type.
Authority.
Review due.
Autonomy.
Budget.
Risk.
Date.
Outcome.

11.176 Decision Comparison

The interface may compare:
Original decision.
Current version.
Changed fields.
Reason for change.
Outcome differences.

11.177 Decision Timeline View

The timeline may show major portfolio and project decisions in chronological order.
It should support understanding organizational evolution.

11.178 Decision Review View

The review view should show:
Original rationale.
Current evidence.
Expected vs actual.
Assumptions still valid.
Risk changes.
Recommended action.

11.179 Decision Outcome View

The outcome view should show:
Success criteria.
Measured outcomes.
Unintended consequences.
Cost.
Founder burden.
Next recommendation.

11.180 Decision Explainability

Every active decision should be explainable.
The system should never answer:
Because the database says so.
It should answer:
Because this decision was approved under this authority for these reasons and remains active until this review condition.

11.181 Decision Ledger and Voice

Atlas may answer through voice:
We kept GainPilot hibernated because The Prompt and Omnira foundations had higher leverage. That decision is due for review at the next quarterly portfolio review.
Voice should summarize.
Detailed records should remain visual.

11.182 Decision Ledger and Mobile

Mobile views should prioritize:
Decisions awaiting approval.
Reviews due.
Expiring authority.
Critical conflicts.
Recently changed decisions.

11.183 Decision Ledger and Daily Brief

The Daily Executive Brief should surface:
Decisions requiring approval.
Decisions due for review.
Decisions whose conditions failed.
Decisions changed by new evidence.
It should not list every active decision.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.184 Decision Ledger and Weekly Planning

Sunday planning should check:
Which decisions constrain the week?
Which decisions require implementation?
Which reviews are due?
Which Do-Not-Start rules remain active?

11.185 Decision Ledger and Monthly Review

Monthly review should assess:
Material decisions made.
Decisions renewed.
Decisions reversed.
Expected vs actual impact.
Decision quality.
Approval burden.
Repeated decision categories.

11.186 Decision Ledger and Quarterly Review

Quarterly review should examine:
Strategic decision quality.
Portfolio mode decisions.
Autonomy decisions.
Project investment decisions.
Systemic risk decisions.
Outdated assumptions.

11.187 Decision Ledger and Annual Review

Annual review should use the ledger to understand:
How strategy evolved.
Which projects changed mode.
How autonomy matured.
Where risk was accepted.
Which decisions created value.
Where founder burden changed.

11.188 Anti-Log-Spam Principle

The ledger must remain selective.
If every minor action becomes a decision entry:
Important decisions become harder to find.
Review burden grows.
Executive meaning is diluted.
The system becomes bureaucratic.
Materiality is essential.

11.189 Anti-Amnesia Principle

The ledger must also avoid under-recording.
If major decisions live only in chat:
They may be forgotten.
They may be contradicted.
They may never be reviewed.
They may not reach execution systems.

11.190 Anti-Retrospective-Rewrite Principle

The system must not rewrite old decisions to make history appear cleaner.
Mistakes, uncertainty, and disagreement are valuable organizational evidence.

11.191 Anti-Authority-Ambiguity Principle

Every active decision must have valid authority.
A statement from an agent, workflow, or model is not automatically a decision.

11.192 Anti-Orphan-Decision Principle

Every active material decision should connect to relevant:
Project.
Policy.
Mission.
Workflow.
Review.
Outcome.
A decision that affects nothing may be incomplete or obsolete.

11.193 Anti-Decision-Contradiction Principle

Conflicting active decisions must be surfaced and resolved.
The system should not choose silently.

11.194 Anti-Permanent-Temporary-Decision Principle

Trials, exceptions, and emergency mandates must expire or be reviewed.
Temporary authority must not become permanent through inactivity.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.195 The Ledger Entry Test

Before creating an entry, Omnira should ask:
Is this a material decision?
Would forgetting it create future confusion or risk?
Does it affect strategy, authority, autonomy, money, risk, customers, or project mode?
Is another system a better place for the record?

11.196 The Scope Test

Before activation, Omnira should ask:
Is the scope explicit?
Which projects are affected?
Which workflows are affected?
Could the decision be misapplied elsewhere?

11.197 The Authority Test

Omnira should ask:
Who made the decision?
Why did they have authority?
Did the authority have limits?
Was approval required?

11.198 The Completeness Test

A material entry should answer:
What was decided?
Why?
Based on what?
Under which authority?
For how long?
What should happen next?
When should it be reviewed?

11.199 The Conflict Test

Before activation, Omnira should ask:
Does this conflict with an active decision?
Does it conflict with policy?
Does it conflict with project mode?
Does it conflict with an autonomy license?

11.200 The Implementation Test

After activation, Omnira should ask:
Was the decision applied?
Which systems changed?
Did any application fail?
Is behavior consistent with the decision?

11.201 The Outcome Test

At review, Omnira should ask:
What was expected?
What happened?
Which assumptions held?
Which risks materialized?
Was the decision quality sound?
What should change?

11.202 Failure Modes

The Decision Ledger architecture must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Decision Amnesia
The organization forgets why a rule or priority exists.
Failure Mode 2 — Log Spam
Minor operational activity overwhelms material decisions.
Failure Mode 3 — Chat-Only Decisions
Important decisions remain trapped in conversations.
Failure Mode 4 — Missing Authority
A decision is active without valid authority.
Failure Mode 5 — Scope Leakage
A project decision is applied to another project.
Failure Mode 6 — Silent Mutation
Decision meaning changes without a new version.
Failure Mode 7 — Conflicting Active Decisions
Contradictory rules govern the same action.
Failure Mode 8 — Unimplemented Decisions
The ledger says one thing while systems behave differently.
Failure Mode 9 — Permanent Temporary Authority
Trials and exceptions never expire.
Failure Mode 10 — Missing Review
Material decisions remain active indefinitely.
Failure Mode 11 — Outcome Blindness
The organization never evaluates whether the decision worked.
Failure Mode 12 — Retrospective Rewriting
History is modified to hide uncertainty or error.
Failure Mode 13 — Raw Private Detail
Founder or customer-private information is stored unnecessarily.
Failure Mode 14 — Approval Confusion
An approval is mistaken for a broader policy decision.
Failure Mode 15 — Recommendation Confusion
An Executive recommendation is treated as an authorized decision.
Failure Mode 16 — Decision Without Execution Trace
No connection exists between decision, mission, workflow, and outcome.
These failure modes should be treated as architectural constraints.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.203 Design Requirements

Any implementation of the Decision Ledger should preserve these requirements:
Every material decision must have a stable identifier.
Every decision must have explicit scope.
Every active decision must have valid authority.
Every recommendation must remain distinguishable from the final decision.
Every material decision must preserve its rationale.
Every material decision should link relevant evidence and assumptions.
Every high-impact decision must preserve risk and opportunity cost.
Every temporary decision must have expiration or review.
Every active decision must be versioned rather than silently edited.
Every superseded or reversed decision must remain historically visible.
Every decision must respect project isolation and privacy.
Every material decision should connect to implementation.
Every material decision should connect to outcomes when measurable.
Every conflict between active decisions must be surfaced.
Every expired decision must stop granting authority.
Every ledger entry must remain both human-readable and machine-readable.
The ledger must remain selective enough to preserve executive meaning.

11.204 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the institutional decision-memory contract.
It does not require a particular database schema, graph database, event system, or interface.
The Decision Ledger may later be implemented through:
Decision records.
Version tables.
Evidence references.
Approval links.
Policy relationships.
Mission references.
Workflow references.
Outcome events.
Review schedules.
Graph relationships.
Search indexes.
Audit logs.
Atlas interfaces.
The technical model may evolve.
The ledger contract must remain stable.

11.205 The Decision Ledger Contract

The Decision Ledger must:
Preserve what was decided.
Preserve why it was decided.
Preserve who had authority.
Preserve the evidence and assumptions that mattered.
Preserve the difference between recommendation and final decision.
Preserve project scope.
Preserve review and expiration conditions.
Preserve amendments, reversals, and supersession.
Connect decisions to missions and workflows.
Connect decisions to outcomes.
Expose conflicts.
Support human understanding.
Support machine enforcement.
Avoid unnecessary private detail.
Avoid log spam.
Prevent decision amnesia.
A feature that does not support this contract should not define the institutional decision record.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
11.206 Closing Principle

An organization does not become intelligent merely because it can make decisions.
It becomes intelligent when it can remember:
What it decided.
Why it decided it.
What it expected.
What authority existed.
What happened afterward.
What it should learn.
The Decision Ledger is the institutional backbone of Executive Intelligence.
Memory gives Omnira continuity.
The Decision Ledger gives Omnira accountability.
Performance shows what happened.
Review determines whether the decision should survive.
Without a Decision Ledger, Omnira may act intelligently in isolated moments while remaining organizationally forgetful.
With a Decision Ledger, every material decision can become part of a continuous chain:
Evidence
→ Recommendation
→ Authority
→ Decision
→ Mission
→ Action
→ Outcome
→ Review
→ Learning
That chain is how Omnira stops repeating decisions and starts building institutional judgment.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.1 Purpose of This Chapter

A decision may be correct when it is made and become incorrect later.
Evidence changes.
Assumptions fail.
Projects change mode.
Customers behave differently.
Technology evolves.
Costs change.
Risks increase.
Founder capacity changes.
Authority expires.
A decision that remains active indefinitely may gradually become disconnected from reality.
Executive Intelligence therefore requires a formal system for:
Review dates.
Decision expiration.
Evidence decay.
Assumption decay.
Authority expiration.
Condition-based review.
Decision renewal.
Decision revision.
Decision supersession.
Decision reversal.
This chapter defines how Omnira ensures that decisions remain valid over time.
The goal is not to constantly reopen every decision.
The goal is to prevent outdated decisions from silently governing the organization.

12.2 The Core Thesis

Decisions are not permanent truths.
They are authorized judgments made under specific conditions.
Every material decision exists inside a context:
Available evidence.
Accepted assumptions.
Current strategy.
Current project mode.
Current risk.
Current authority.
Current resources.
Current time horizon.
When that context changes materially, the decision may need review.
The core principle is:
A decision remains valid only while its authority, assumptions, evidence, and operating conditions remain sufficiently valid.

12.3 Decision Decay

Decision decay is the gradual reduction in a decision’s reliability or relevance over time.
Decay may occur because:
Evidence becomes stale.
Assumptions become weaker.
The environment changes.
Expected outcomes fail to appear.
Authority expires.
A dependency changes.
Risk increases.
The decision is repeatedly overridden.
The project changes mode.
A newer strategy emerges.
Decision decay does not mean the original decision was poor.
It means the decision must be reconsidered under current conditions.

12.4 Decision Decay vs Decision Failure

Decay and failure are different.
Decision Decay
The conditions supporting the decision have weakened or changed.
Decision Failure
The decision produced unacceptable outcomes or violated its success criteria.
Example of decay:
A publishing policy was created six months ago using an outdated workflow and old risk assumptions.
Example of failure:
The workflow created a serious policy violation during its current trial.
Failure may require immediate reversal.
Decay may require scheduled review.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.5 Review Dates

A review date defines when a decision should be reconsidered.
A review date does not automatically invalidate the decision.
It creates a required decision point.
At review, Omnira should determine whether to:
Renew.
Revise.
Narrow.
Expand.
Expire.
Supersede.
Reverse.
Request more evidence.

12.6 Review Conditions

Not every review should depend on a calendar date.
A decision may be reviewed when a condition occurs.
Examples:
After 30 successful workflow runs.
When revenue reaches a defined threshold.
After the next customer cohort.
When a project changes operating mode.
When a serious policy violation occurs.
When a provider changes pricing.
When project isolation health falls.
When a strategic dependency is completed.
Condition-based reviews are often more meaningful than arbitrary dates.

12.7 Review Types

Omnira should support several review types.
Time-Based Review
Triggered at a specific date or interval.
Threshold-Based Review
Triggered when a measurement crosses a threshold.
Outcome-Based Review
Triggered when expected results can be evaluated.
Event-Based Review
Triggered by an incident or material event.
Dependency-Based Review
Triggered when a related decision or capability changes.
Mode-Based Review
Triggered when the project enters a new lifecycle or operating mode.
Authority-Based Review
Triggered when permission, delegation, or mandate expires.

12.8 Time-Based Review

Time-based review may be appropriate for:
Project strategy.
Budget mandates.
Temporary policies.
Operating modes.
Roadmaps.
Portfolio priorities.
Founder capacity rules.
External tool permissions.
Examples:
Review in 30 days.
Review at month end.
Review quarterly.
Review annually.
The interval should reflect how quickly the decision context may change.

12.9 Threshold-Based Review

Threshold-based review is appropriate when the decision depends on measurable performance.
Examples:
Review autonomy after 30 successful runs.
Review Growth operating mode after 1,000 monthly users.
Review budget when 75% has been consumed.
Review approval policy when unchanged approval rate exceeds 95%.
Review provider choice when cost increases by 20%.
The threshold must be measurable and project-scoped.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.10 Outcome-Based Review

Outcome-based review occurs when enough evidence exists to evaluate the expected impact.
Example:
Decision:
Increase short-form content production.
Expected outcome:
Higher website traffic and newsletter conversion.
Review:
After four weeks of comparable performance data.
The review should compare expected and actual outcomes.

12.11 Event-Based Review

Material events may require immediate reconsideration.
Events may include:
P0 or P1 policy violation.
Security incident.
Customer harm.
Project isolation failure.
Unauthorized spending.
Major provider outage.
Significant revenue loss.
Unexpected customer growth.
Founder override.
New legal requirement.
Event-based review should not wait for the normal review date.

12.12 Dependency-Based Review

A decision may rely on another capability or decision.
Example:
Decision:
Prepare The Prompt for L4 website publishing.
Dependency:
Reliable project isolation.
If the dependency fails or changes, the decision must be reviewed.
Dependency links should therefore be machine-readable.

12.13 Mode-Based Review

A decision created under one project mode may become inappropriate under another.
Example:
Build operating mode:
Prioritize architecture and controlled experimentation.
Growth operating mode:
Prioritize distribution and revenue.
Crisis Mode:
Pause external autonomy.
A mode change should trigger review of decisions affected by the new mode.

12.14 Authority-Based Review

Authority may expire independently of the decision rationale.
Examples:
Temporary budget mandate.
Delegated approval authority.
Autonomy trial.
Emergency exception.
Temporary cross-project access.
Calendar scheduling mandate.
When authority expires, the system must return to a safe default unless renewed.

12.15 Review Horizon

Every material decision should have a review horizon.
Possible horizons:
Immediate.
Daily.
Weekly.
Monthly.
Quarterly.
Annual.
Condition-based.
Event-triggered.
The horizon should reflect decision volatility.
A crisis restriction may require hourly review.
A constitutional principle may require review only through a formal governance process.

12.16 Decision Volatility

Decision volatility describes how quickly a decision may become outdated.
High Volatility
Examples:
Daily campaign allocation.
Provider routing.
Temporary approval policy.
Crisis restrictions.
Founder workload plan.
Medium Volatility
Examples:
Project operating mode.
Workflow autonomy.
Monthly strategy.
Budget mandate.
Low Volatility
Examples:
Project purpose.
Global project-isolation rules.
Constitutional authority boundaries.
Review cadence should match volatility.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.17 Decision Half-Life

Decision half-life is a conceptual measure of how quickly confidence in a decision should decline without new confirmation.
Examples:
Daily focus:
Very short half-life.
Weekly priorities:
Short half-life.
Project strategy:
Medium half-life.
Architecture principles:
Long half-life.
Constitutional rules:
Very long half-life.
The concept helps Omnira avoid treating all decisions as equally durable.

12.18 Evidence Decay

Evidence decay occurs when evidence becomes less useful over time.
Evidence may decay because:
The data becomes stale.
The measurement model changes.
The market changes.
The workflow changes.
The customer population changes.
The source loses reliability.
The sample becomes unrepresentative.
An old metric may remain historically true while becoming strategically irrelevant.

12.19 Evidence Freshness Rules

Evidence should include:
Collected time.
Relevant time period.
Source.
Freshness status.
Decision relevance.
Expiration or revalidation condition.
Possible freshness states:
Current.
Recent.
Historical.
Stale.
Superseded.
Invalid.

12.20 Evidence Relevance Decay

Evidence may remain accurate but lose relevance.
Example:
A content format performed well before a platform algorithm change.
The historical result remains true.
Its predictive value may decline.
Decision Intelligence should separate factual validity from current relevance.

12.21 Evidence Replacement

New evidence may:
Confirm.
Strengthen.
Weaken.
Contradict.
Replace.
Invalidate.
The Decision Ledger should preserve both the original evidence state and later evidence.
History must not be rewritten.

12.22 Assumption Decay

Assumptions should not survive indefinitely without validation.
An assumption may decay because:
No evidence confirms it.
Contradictory evidence appears.
The context changes.
The assumption depended on a temporary condition.
The expected result fails to appear.
Example:
Assumption:
Founder capacity will remain high this month.
Reality:
Capacity becomes constrained.
Impact:
Roadmap and approval timing require review.

12.23 Assumption Status

Assumptions may have status:
Unvalidated.
Partially supported.
Supported.
Weakened.
Contradicted.
Invalidated.
No longer relevant.
Material assumption changes should trigger review.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.24 Assumption Expiration

Some assumptions should have explicit expiration.
Examples:
Market demand remains stable for the next quarter.
Provider pricing remains unchanged during the trial.
Founder capacity remains moderate this week.
Source quality remains acceptable during the publishing test.
Expired assumptions require revalidation.

12.25 Assumption Dependency

Decisions should identify which assumptions are critical.
A critical assumption is one whose failure changes the recommendation.
Example:
Critical assumption:
Project isolation is reliable.
If false:
Autonomy expansion must stop.
Noncritical assumptions may affect expected impact without invalidating the decision.

12.26 Critical Assumption Failure

When a critical assumption fails, the system should:
Pause affected authority if necessary.
Create an immediate review.
Notify the relevant Executive.
Assess external impact.
Apply safe fallback.
Record the assumption failure.

12.27 Authority Decay

Authority may decay or expire even if the strategy remains valid.
Authority decay may result from:
Mandate expiration.
Role change.
Ownership change.
Project transfer.
Policy update.
Crisis end.
Revocation.
Security concern.
An expired authority cannot continue authorizing actions.

12.28 Autonomy License Decay

Autonomy should decay when trust or operating conditions weaken.
Potential triggers:
Correction rate increases.
Policy violations occur.
Rollback fails.
Project isolation health declines.
Performance becomes unstable.
Source quality weakens.
Workflow configuration changes materially.
Autonomy should not remain fixed merely because it was previously earned.

12.29 Budget Mandate Decay

A budget mandate may require review when:
Time period ends.
Budget is mostly consumed.
Cost assumptions change.
Purpose changes.
Vendor risk changes.
Project mode changes.
Expected value does not appear.
Remaining funds do not automatically justify continued spending.

12.30 Strategy Decay

Strategy may decay when:
Customer evidence changes.
Revenue fails to develop.
The market changes.
A competitor changes the landscape.
Project purpose changes.
Cost becomes unsustainable.
A stronger opportunity emerges.
Strategy should not be changed casually.
It should not survive indefinitely through inertia.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.31 Roadmap Decay

A roadmap may become outdated when:
Dependencies change.
Milestones fail.
New risks emerge.
Capability becomes unnecessary.
Project priority changes.
Founder capacity shifts.
A better sequence appears.
Roadmaps should be reviewed as hypotheses, not treated as permanent contracts.

12.32 Project Mode Decay

A project may remain in a mode longer than appropriate.
Examples:
Build operating mode continues despite readiness for Growth.
Observer lifecycle mode continues despite strong traction.
Hibernate continues despite a time-sensitive opportunity.
Crisis Mode continues after recovery.
Mode decisions require review conditions.

12.33 Temporary Decisions

Temporary decisions must define:
Start.
End.
Scope.
Safe fallback.
Renewal process.
Authority.
Review.
A temporary decision without expiration is not truly temporary.

12.34 Default Fallback

Every expiring authority decision should define a fallback state.
Examples:
Autonomy trial expires:
Return to previous autonomy level.
Temporary budget expires:
Stop new spending.
Cross-project access expires:
Revoke access.
Crisis exception expires:
Return to standard governance.
Calendar mandate expires:
Require manual approval.
The fallback should normally be safer than the temporary state.

12.35 Renewal

Renewal continues an existing decision.
A renewal should require:
Current evidence.
Outcome review.
Assumption review.
Risk review.
Authority confirmation.
New review date.
Renewal should not merely update the date.

12.36 Automatic Renewal

High-impact authority should not renew automatically.
Automatic renewal may be acceptable only when:
Risk is low.
Scope is narrow.
The action is reversible.
Monitoring is reliable.
No policy violations occurred.
The founder explicitly authorized automatic renewal.
Even then, renewal should remain visible and revocable.

12.37 Manual Renewal

Manual renewal should be required for:
High-impact autonomy.
Material budget authority.
Cross-project access.
Customer-sensitive policy.
Crisis exceptions.
Constitutional or governance exceptions.

12.38 Revision

Revision changes part of a decision while preserving its overall purpose.
Examples:
Reduce the budget.
Narrow autonomy categories.
Extend the review period.
Add a QA requirement.
Change the success threshold.
Revision creates a new version.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.39 Expansion

A decision may be expanded when evidence supports broader scope.
Example:
Original:
The Prompt may prepare short news posts.
Expanded:
The Prompt may publish approved low-risk short news categories.
Expansion requires new authority when impact increases.

12.40 Narrowing

A decision may be narrowed when:
Risk increases.
Evidence weakens.
Performance becomes unstable.
Founder capacity falls.
Project mode changes.
Policy violation occurs.
Narrowing may be temporary or permanent.

12.41 Expiration

Expiration ends the decision’s active authority.
Expiration should:
Change status.
Apply fallback.
Notify affected systems.
Update missions.
Update workflows.
Preserve history.

12.42 Supersession

A decision is superseded when replaced by a newer decision.
Supersession should identify:
New decision.
Reason.
Authority.
Effective time.
Affected systems.
The old decision remains historically visible.

12.43 Reversal

Reversal actively undoes a decision.
Reversal may be triggered by:
Failure criteria.
Critical assumption failure.
Serious policy violation.
Unexpected harm.
Founder override.
Strategy change.
Invalid authority.
Reversal should include rollback and recovery.

12.44 Emergency Reversal

A high-risk decision may need immediate reversal before a complete review.
Emergency reversal may:
Pause external actions.
Reduce autonomy.
Stop spending.
Revoke access.
Return to safe defaults.
Create a crisis review.
The full rationale may be completed after containment.

12.45 Review Package

A review should use a structured package.
It should include:
Original decision.
Original evidence.
Original assumptions.
Expected impact.
Current evidence.
Actual outcome.
Risk changes.
Authority status.
Dependency changes.
Recommended next state.

12.46 Review Recommendation

The Executive recommendation should be one of:
Renew unchanged.
Renew with revised review date.
Revise.
Expand.
Narrow.
Expire.
Supersede.
Reverse.
Request more evidence.
The recommendation should include confidence.

12.47 Review Authority

Review authority may differ from original decision authority.
However, a lower authority should not renew or expand a higher-level decision without permission.
Example:
A Project Executive may recommend renewal.
The founder may be required to approve it.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.48 Review Ownership

Every material decision should have a review owner.
The owner ensures that:
Evidence is collected.
Review occurs.
Affected systems are updated.
Expired authority stops.
Outcome is recorded.
The review owner may be a Project Executive, Portfolio Executive, or designated human role.

12.49 Review Queue

Omnira should maintain a review queue.
The queue should include:
Decision.
Scope.
Review trigger.
Deadline.
Impact.
Authority.
Recommended review depth.
Current evidence status.

12.50 Review Queue Priority

Review priority should consider:
Damage potential.
Expiration proximity.
Authority level.
Autonomy.
Financial impact.
Customer impact.
Evidence change.
Failed conditions.
Dependency impact.
The oldest review should not automatically be first.

12.51 Review Preparation Automation

Omnira may automatically:
Collect current evidence.
Compare expected and actual outcomes.
Check assumptions.
Detect failed conditions.
Identify related incidents.
Calculate decision age.
Prepare a recommendation.
Automatic preparation does not equal automatic renewal.

12.52 Review Depth

Review depth should match the decision.
Fast Review
For low-impact, stable decisions.
Standard Review
For routine project policy and operating decisions.
Deep Review
For autonomy, strategy, budgets, major architecture, and risk.
Board-Level Review
For portfolio direction, project lifecycle, and constitutional matters.

12.53 Review Effort

A review package should estimate founder effort.
Example:
Estimated review:
Five minutes.
Required decision:
Renew or expire.
Recommended:
Renew for 30 days.
Review burden should remain visible.

12.54 Review Deferral

A review may be deferred when:
Evidence is incomplete.
The outcome is not yet measurable.
Founder capacity is insufficient.
A related dependency is pending.
Deferral should define:
Interim state.
Risk of waiting.
New review date.
Authority for the interim state.

12.55 Safe Deferral

Deferral should not silently extend risky authority.
Possible safe responses:
Maintain current low-risk state.
Reduce autonomy.
Pause spending.
Continue preparation only.
Require manual approval.

12.56 Overdue Review

A review becomes overdue when its required time or condition has passed.
Overdue decisions should be classified by risk.
Possible responses:
Notify owner.
Escalate.
Freeze expansion.
Apply fallback.
Expire authority.
Reduce autonomy.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.57 Grace Period

Some decisions may allow a grace period.
A grace period should define:
Duration.
Allowed actions.
Restrictions.
Escalation.
Fallback.
High-risk authority should have little or no grace period.

12.58 Review Failure

Review failure occurs when the system cannot complete the review.
Reasons may include:
Missing data.
Broken performance integration.
Unknown authority.
Unavailable approver.
Conflicting decisions.
Missing project ownership.
The safe response should depend on impact.

12.59 Decision Age

Decision age is the time since activation or last material review.
Age alone does not make a decision invalid.
It is one signal among:
Volatility.
Evidence change.
Assumption status.
Outcome.
Authority.
Risk.

12.60 Decay Score

Omnira may eventually calculate a Decision Decay Score.
The score may consider:
Decision age.
Decision volatility.
Evidence freshness.
Assumption validity.
Outcome deviation.
Dependency changes.
Override frequency.
Policy changes.
Project mode changes.
Authority age.
The score should prioritize reviews.
It should not automatically invalidate decisions without policy.

12.61 Decay Score Interpretation

A conceptual classification may be:
Stable.
Review approaching.
Review recommended.
Review required.
Invalid or expired.
The system should explain why the score changed.

12.62 Decay Is Not Universal

Different decision components may decay at different rates.
Example:
Project purpose:
Stable.
Current publishing frequency:
Volatile.
Approved source list:
Moderately volatile.
Constitutional privacy rule:
Highly stable.
The system should not apply one expiration period to everything.

12.63 Evidence Change Trigger

A material evidence change may trigger review when it:
Contradicts the rationale.
Changes expected impact.
Changes risk.
Changes opportunity cost.
Invalidates a critical assumption.
Minor metric movement should not reopen major decisions constantly.

12.64 Outcome Deviation Trigger

Review may trigger when actual outcomes differ materially from expected outcomes.
Examples:
Revenue remains below threshold.
Founder burden increases instead of decreasing.
Correction rate exceeds expectation.
Customer trust declines.
Cost becomes materially higher.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.65 Risk Change Trigger

Risk review should trigger when:
Severity increases.
Risk velocity increases.
A control fails.
Residual risk becomes unacceptable.
A new category of harm appears.

12.66 Authority Change Trigger

Review should trigger when:
Project ownership changes.
Approver role changes.
Mandate expires.
Founder revokes authority.
Security access changes.
Customer contract changes.

12.67 Policy Change Trigger

A policy change may affect existing decisions.
Example:
New global rule:
All customer-sensitive communication requires human approval.
Affected autonomy decisions must be reviewed.

12.68 Constitutional Change Trigger

A constitutional change may invalidate lower-level decisions.
The system should identify all affected:
Policies.
Projects.
Autonomy licenses.
Budget mandates.
Workflows.
Temporary exceptions.

12.69 Project Mode Trigger

When a project changes mode, related decisions should be reviewed.
Examples:
Growth to Crisis:
Review publishing autonomy.
Build to Growth:
Review resource allocation.
Observer to Active:
Review Workforce missions.
Hibernate to Active:
Review old strategy and credentials.

12.70 Workflow Change Trigger

Material workflow changes may invalidate prior evidence.
Examples:
New model.
New provider.
New prompt.
New source.
New tool permission.
New external channel.
New QA process.
Trust earned under the old workflow may not transfer completely.

12.71 Model or Provider Change

Changing the AI model or provider may affect:
Quality.
Cost.
Latency.
Safety.
Consistency.
Tool use.
Risk.
AI Intelligence should notify Decision Intelligence when the change materially affects decisions.

12.72 Personnel or Role Change

Future multi-user organizations may require review when:
Approver changes.
Project owner changes.
Reviewer leaves.
Delegated authority changes.
Customer representative changes.

12.73 Founder Preference Change

A stable founder preference may influence decisions.
When the founder explicitly changes the preference, dependent decisions should be reviewed.
The system should not infer major preference change from one isolated action.

12.74 Capacity Change Trigger

A material founder capacity change may trigger review of:
Weekly priorities.
Approval expectations.
Project activation.
Calendar mandates.
Founder-dependent missions.
It should not automatically reopen unrelated long-term strategy.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.75 Opportunity Change Trigger

A new opportunity may justify reviewing a previous Do-Not-Start or hibernation decision.
The review should evaluate:
Evidence.
Urgency.
Expected value.
Capacity.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Novelty alone is insufficient.

12.76 Repeated Override Trigger

If the founder repeatedly overrides an active decision, the system should review whether:
The decision is outdated.
The policy is too strict.
The founder preference changed.
The implementation is inconvenient.
The decision is misunderstood.
Repeated overrides are evidence.

12.77 Repeated Exception Trigger

Frequent temporary exceptions may indicate:
A bad base policy.
A missing workflow category.
Insufficient authority design.
A new operating reality.
The system should review the rule rather than normalize endless exceptions.

12.78 Review and Decision Ledger

Every review should create a linked Decision Ledger event.
It should preserve:
Review date.
Evidence considered.
Assumption status.
Outcome.
Recommendation.
Final review decision.
New review condition.
The original decision remains unchanged.

12.79 Review Versioning

Review outcomes should create:
Renewal version.
Revision version.
Expiration event.
Reversal event.
Superseding decision.
Silent date updates are insufficient.

12.80 Review and Memory

Memory may preserve durable lessons such as:
Autonomy reviews require larger sample sizes.
Founder approval burden was underestimated.
Quarterly strategy reviews work better than monthly changes.
Temporary exceptions often indicate missing policy.
The formal review remains in the Decision Ledger.

12.81 Review and Performance Intelligence

Performance Intelligence should provide:
Outcome metrics.
Trend changes.
Threshold status.
Cost changes.
Trust Score changes.
Policy violation history.
Founder burden.
Performance Intelligence measures.
Executive Intelligence decides renewal or change.

12.82 Review and Governance

Governance should enforce:
Expiration.
Fallback.
Authority limits.
Review requirements.
Renewal conditions.
Reversal triggers.
A review date that exists only in a document is insufficient.

12.83 Review and Manager

Manager should receive operational consequences such as:
Mission paused.
Approval rule changed.
Workflow autonomy reduced.
Deadline extended.
New QA step required.
Manager does not own the review decision.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.84 Review and Workforce

Workforce should receive the current operational rule.
It does not need the entire review history unless relevant to execution.

12.85 Review and Daily Executive Brief

The Daily Executive Brief should surface:
Reviews due today.
Reviews approaching.
Overdue high-impact decisions.
Conditions that failed.
Recommended review action.
Routine low-impact reviews may be batched.

12.86 Review and Weekly Planning

Sunday planning should identify:
Decisions expiring during the week.
Reviews requiring founder capacity.
Missions affected by review.
Authority that may disappear.
Evidence collection required.

12.87 Review and Monthly Review

Monthly Executive Review should examine:
Decisions renewed.
Decisions revised.
Decisions expired.
Decisions reversed.
Overdue reviews.
Decay patterns.
Repeated exceptions.

12.88 Review and Quarterly Strategy

Quarterly review should challenge:
Portfolio strategy.
Project viability.
Long-running operating modes.
Major autonomy decisions.
Shared capability priorities.
Risk acceptances.

12.89 Review and Annual Direction

Annual review should examine whether major long-term decisions still support the organization Omnira is becoming.
It should not simply renew the previous year by default.

12.90 Review Notifications

Notifications should occur when:
Review approaches.
Authority is about to expire.
A condition fails.
Evidence materially changes.
Review becomes overdue.
Safe fallback activates.
Notifications should identify required action and consequence.

12.91 Notification Lead Time

Lead time should depend on review complexity.
Examples:
Routine low-risk review:
One day.
Budget or autonomy review:
Several days.
Quarterly strategy review:
One or two weeks.
Annual review:
Several weeks.

12.92 Review Batching

Similar low-risk reviews may be batched.
A batch should share:
Project.
Decision category.
Risk level.
Review authority.
Time horizon.
High-impact reviews should remain individually visible.

12.93 Review Burden

Review burden should be measured.
It may include:
Number of reviews.
Estimated time.
Evidence volume.
Decision complexity.
Approval requirements.
Founder effort.
The system should avoid creating unnecessary review bureaucracy.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.94 Review Burden Reduction

Burden may be reduced through:
Better review intervals.
Condition-based reviews.
Automatic evidence preparation.
Batching.
Delegated review authority.
Clear renewal criteria.
Safe automatic expiration.

12.95 Review Quality

Review quality may be measured through:
Completion rate.
Overdue rate.
Evidence completeness.
Outcome evaluation.
Expired authority still used.
Reversal speed.
Founder correction rate.

12.96 Review Health

The review system should have a health status.
Possible indicators:
Upcoming reviews prepared.
High-risk reviews overdue.
Expired decisions still active.
Failed conditions unresolved.
Unknown review owners.
Missing fallback states.
Poor review health should reduce autonomy confidence.

12.97 Decision Staleness Dashboard

A dashboard may show:
Stable decisions.
Reviews due soon.
Overdue reviews.
Expired authority.
Decisions with stale evidence.
Decisions with failed assumptions.
Decisions awaiting outcomes.
The dashboard should prioritize risk, not merely age.

12.98 Decision Decay Graph

The Intelligence Graph may connect:
Decision.
Evidence age.
Assumption status.
Dependencies.
Review conditions.
Outcome.
Renewal.
Supersession.
Reversal.
The founder should be able to understand why a decision is considered stale.

12.99 Decision Review Card

A review card may show:
Decision.
Original reason.
Current state.
Evidence change.
Assumption change.
Expected vs actual.
Recommended action.
Authority.
Estimated review time.

12.100 Conversational Review

Atlas may say:
We decided three months ago to keep GainPilot hibernated. That decision is due for review. No meaningful new traction has appeared, and founder capacity remains committed elsewhere. I recommend renewing hibernation for another quarter.
The conversational summary should reflect the structured record.

12.101 Review Explanation

The founder should be able to ask:
Why is this decision being reviewed?
What changed?
What happens if we do nothing?
Why are you recommending renewal?
What evidence is stale?
Atlas should answer from the review package.

12.102 Stale Decision Warning

A stale decision warning should state:
Which decision is stale.
Why.
What authority remains.
What risk exists.
Recommended action.
Fallback.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.103 Expiration Warning

An expiration warning should identify:
Decision.
Expiration time.
Affected workflow.
Safe fallback.
Required approver.
Consequence of no response.

12.104 No-Response Review Policy

When a review receives no response, the system should follow a defined policy.
Possible outcomes:
Renew low-risk decision temporarily.
Expire.
Reduce authority.
Maintain safer state.
Escalate.
Pause external action.
No response should not automatically renew high-impact authority.

12.105 Safe Default Principle

When uncertainty exists at expiration, Omnira should prefer the safer valid state.
Examples:
Autonomy:
Return to lower level.
Spending:
Stop new spend.
Publishing:
Require approval.
Access:
Revoke temporary grant.
Project mode:
Maintain current mode until reviewed, unless harmful.

12.106 Continuity vs Safety

Expiration rules must balance continuity and safety.
An abrupt expiration may interrupt healthy operations.
Automatic continuation may preserve unsafe authority.
The system should classify decisions by:
Operational continuity need.
Damage potential.
Reversibility.
External impact.
Monitoring quality.

12.107 Graceful Degradation

When authority expires, workflows may degrade gracefully.
Example:
Before expiration:
Autonomous publishing.
After expiration:
Prepare drafts and queue for approval.
This preserves work without preserving unauthorized external action.

12.108 Review During Founder Unavailability

If a review becomes due while the founder is unavailable:
Critical authority may expire.
Low-risk decisions may receive a short governed extension.
External high-risk actions may pause.
Preparation may continue.
The review enters the next available approval window.
Founder unavailability must not imply renewal.

12.109 Crisis Review Cadence

During Crisis Mode, review frequency should increase.
Crisis decisions may require:
Hourly review.
Daily review.
Review after each containment milestone.
Review before restoring external action.

12.110 Ending Crisis Mode

Crisis Mode should end only when:
Containment is confirmed.
Required tests pass.
Risk falls.
Affected authority is reviewed.
Recovery plan is active.
Founder or authorized authority approves exit.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.111 Post-Crisis Decision Review

After crisis, Omnira should review:
Which decisions contributed.
Which assumptions failed.
Which controls failed.
Which temporary restrictions remain.
Which autonomy should be restored.
Which policy should change.

12.112 Review of Hibernated Projects

A hibernated project should have periodic review.
The review should ask:
Why is it hibernated?
Are restart conditions met?
Has strategic fit changed?
What capacity would reactivation require?
What opportunity cost would reactivation create?
The absence of activity is not itself a reason to reactivate.

12.113 Review of Observer Projects

Observer projects should be reviewed for:
New evidence.
Customer signals.
Readiness.
Risk.
Required maintenance.
Potential mode change.

12.114 Review of Active Projects

Active projects should review:
Strategy.
Operating mode.
Goals.
Autonomy.
Performance.
Capacity.
Major dependencies.

12.115 Review of Archived Projects

Archived projects may require:
Retention review.
Access review.
Legal review.
Knowledge extraction.
Deletion eligibility.
They should not re-enter active operation without explicit reactivation.

12.116 Review of Do-Not-Start Decisions

A Do-Not-Start decision should not become permanent avoidance.
Review should ask:
Does the reason remain valid?
Has the blocking dependency changed?
Has opportunity cost changed?
Is capacity available?
Should the item remain deferred?

12.117 Review of Founder Capacity Policies

Stable personal boundaries may remain durable.
Scheduling preferences may require periodic calibration.
The system should not repeatedly ask the founder to reconfirm protected family or recovery boundaries unless the founder changes them.

12.118 Review of Tool Permissions

External tool access should be reviewed for:
Current business need.
Permissions used.
Unused access.
Security risk.
Cost.
Project scope.
Credential health.
Unused high-impact access should be removed.

12.119 Review of Cross-Project Access

Cross-project grants should be temporary by default.
Review should assess:
Is access still required?
Can a summary replace it?
Was the data used correctly?
Did any boundary incident occur?
Should access be revoked?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.120 Review of Delegated Authority

Delegated human authority should be reviewed for:
Scope.
Usage.
Decision quality.
Conflicts.
Role status.
Duration.

12.121 Review of Architecture Decisions

Architecture decisions may have long half-lives.
They should still be reviewed when:
Scale assumptions change.
Security requirements change.
The technology becomes obsolete.
Migration cost increases.
A repeated workaround appears.
A new platform direction emerges.

12.122 Review of Model Selection Policies

AI Intelligence may update provider and model choices frequently.
Executive review is required when changes affect:
Cost materially.
Quality materially.
Security.
Data handling.
Project risk.
External commitments.

12.123 Review of Performance Definitions

Metrics themselves may decay.
Review should ask:
Does the metric still represent project value?
Has measurement changed?
Is the metric being gamed?
Does portfolio comparison remain valid?

12.124 Review of Trust Score Rules

Trust Score design should be reviewed when:
Scores fail to predict quality.
Approval rate dominates incorrectly.
Risk is underweighted.
Project differences are ignored.
Autonomy decisions repeatedly require correction.

12.125 Review of Approval Policies

Approval policies may be too strict or too loose.
Review should examine:
Approval rate.
Edit rate.
Rejection rate.
Founder burden.
Missed risk.
Workflow delay.
Readiness for batching or autonomy.

12.126 Review of Spending Authority

Spending review should compare:
Approved purpose.
Actual spend.
Actual value.
Unused budget.
Unexpected vendors.
Risk.
Future need.

12.127 Review of Publishing Authority

Publishing review should examine:
Accuracy.
Corrections.
Brand impact.
Source quality.
Performance.
Policy violations.
Rollback.
Customer response.

12.128 Review of Customer Communication Authority

Review should examine:
Tone consistency.
Customer satisfaction.
Escalation accuracy.
Sensitive-case handling.
Refund or discount errors.
Trust impact.

12.129 Review of Project Strategy

Strategy review should not occur from one noisy metric.
It should use:
Trend evidence.
Customer evidence.
Revenue.
Cost.
Risk.
Capacity.
Strategic fit.
Opportunity cost.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.130 Review of Portfolio Strategy

Portfolio review should ask:
Are these still the right projects?
Is attention allocated correctly?
Are shared capabilities producing leverage?
Is founder dependency falling?
Is revenue direction credible?

12.131 Anti-Perpetual-Decision Principle

No temporary authority should survive indefinitely without review.

12.132 Anti-Constant-Reopening Principle

Stable decisions should not be reopened without material reason.
Review discipline must prevent both staleness and strategic whiplash.

12.133 Anti-Automatic-Renewal Principle

High-impact authority should not continue merely because no one reviewed it.

12.134 Anti-Calendar-Arbitrariness Principle

Review dates should be connected to meaningful volatility, evidence, outcomes, or authority—not chosen randomly.

12.135 Anti-Outcome-Only Principle

A positive outcome does not automatically justify renewal if the reasoning, authority, or controls were unsafe.

12.136 Anti-Age-Only Principle

An old decision is not necessarily wrong.
A recent decision is not necessarily valid.
Age must be interpreted with evidence and context.

12.137 Anti-Review-Theatre Principle

A review should produce:
Renewal.
Revision.
Expiration.
Reversal.
More evidence.
Explicit continuation.
A review that only repeats the original decision adds little value.

12.138 The Review Trigger Test

Before triggering review, Omnira should ask:
Did a review condition occur?
Did evidence change materially?
Did a critical assumption weaken?
Did risk change?
Did authority change?
Did a dependency change?
Did project mode change?

12.139 The Renewal Test

Before renewal, Omnira should ask:
Did the decision produce the expected value?
Do assumptions remain valid?
Is risk still acceptable?
Does authority remain valid?
Should scope remain unchanged?
What is the new review condition?

12.140 The Expiration Test

Before expiration, Omnira should ask:
What stops?
What safe fallback applies?
Which missions or workflows are affected?
Does the founder need notification?
Could abrupt expiration create harm?

12.141 The Reversal Test

Before reversal, Omnira should ask:
Which condition failed?
What damage exists?
What must be rolled back?
Who has authority?
What recovery is required?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.142 The Decay Test

Omnira should ask:
How old is the decision?
How volatile is its context?
How fresh is the evidence?
Which assumptions remain valid?
Did expected outcomes occur?
Did dependencies change?
Has the decision been repeatedly overridden?

12.143 The Safe Fallback Test

Omnira should ask:
What is the safest valid operating state?
Can internal preparation continue?
Should external action pause?
Should authority narrow?
How can continuity be preserved without unauthorized action?

12.144 Failure Modes

Review Dates and Decision Decay must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Permanent Temporary Authority
Trials and exceptions never expire.
Failure Mode 2 — Stale Evidence
Old evidence continues supporting current action.
Failure Mode 3 — Hidden Assumption Failure
Critical assumptions fail without review.
Failure Mode 4 — Automatic High-Risk Renewal
Authority continues because no one responded.
Failure Mode 5 — Review Spam
Stable decisions are reopened too frequently.
Failure Mode 6 — Review Theatre
Reviews occur but produce no meaningful judgment.
Failure Mode 7 — No Safe Fallback
Expiration causes uncontrolled failure or continued unauthorized action.
Failure Mode 8 — Overdue High-Impact Review
Autonomy, budget, or access continues after review deadlines.
Failure Mode 9 — Age-Only Decay
Decisions are treated as invalid merely because they are old.
Failure Mode 10 — Outcome-Only Renewal
Lucky outcomes justify unsafe decisions.
Failure Mode 11 — Silent Renewal
Dates change without versioning or authority.
Failure Mode 12 — Dependency Blindness
Related decisions change without triggering review.
Failure Mode 13 — Project Mode Blindness
Old decisions remain active after mode changes.
Failure Mode 14 — Founder Unavailability Equals Renewal
Missing response extends authority automatically.
Failure Mode 15 — Crisis Restriction Persistence
Emergency restrictions remain after recovery without review.
Failure Mode 16 — Strategic Whiplash
Every small signal reopens long-term strategy.
These failure modes should be treated as architecture and governance constraints.

12.145 Design Requirements

Any implementation of Review Dates and Decision Decay should preserve these requirements:
Every material decision must have a review date or condition.
Every temporary authority must have expiration.
Every expiration must define a fallback.
Every high-impact renewal must require current evidence.
Every review must assess assumptions.
Every review must assess authority.
Every review must assess risk.
Every review must compare expected and actual outcomes when available.
Every material review must create a versioned Decision Ledger event.
Every expired decision must stop granting authority.
Every dependency change must be able to trigger affected reviews.
Every project mode change must review affected decisions.
Every failed critical assumption must escalate.
Every overdue high-impact review must become visible.
Every review must preserve project scope and privacy.
Stable decisions should not be reopened without material reason.
The system must balance continuity with safety.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
12.146 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the temporal governance contract.
It does not require a specific scheduler, scoring model, database, or notification system.
The architecture may later be implemented through:
Review schedules.
Condition monitors.
Decision versioning.
Expiration jobs.
Decay scores.
Evidence freshness metadata.
Assumption status records.
Review queues.
Fallback policies.
Decision Ledger events.
Performance triggers.
Governance enforcement.
The technical model may evolve.
The temporal contract must remain stable.

12.147 The Review and Decay Contract

Executive Intelligence must:
Treat decisions as contextual judgments.
Track when decisions require review.
Track when authority expires.
Detect stale evidence.
Detect weakened assumptions.
Detect changed dependencies.
Detect mode and policy changes.
Prepare reviews automatically.
Renew only with sufficient authority and evidence.
Expire risky authority safely.
Use fallback states.
Preserve version history.
Avoid unnecessary strategic reopening.
Learn from expected and actual outcomes.
Prevent outdated decisions from silently controlling the organization.
A feature that does not support this contract should not govern decision longevity.

12.148 Closing Principle

The danger of organizational memory is not only forgetting.
It is remembering something for too long.
A decision may once have been correct.
A policy may once have been necessary.
A restriction may once have protected the organization.
An autonomy level may once have been appropriate.
But Omnira must continuously ask:
Is this still true?
Is the evidence still current?
Are the assumptions still valid?
Does the authority still exist?
Did the expected outcome occur?
Should this decision survive?
The Decision Ledger preserves history.
Review Dates create accountability.
Decision Decay creates adaptation.
Together, they allow Omnira to maintain continuity without becoming trapped by its own past.
A mature Executive system does not constantly change its mind.
It also does not mistake an old decision for a permanent truth.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Vision vs Strategy vs Roadmap vs Plan
text:
13.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Executive Intelligence must convert long-term vision into coordinated action.
Vision alone does not create progress.
Tasks alone do not create strategy.
A roadmap must connect:
Vision
→ Strategic thesis
→ Objectives
→ Outcomes
→ Milestones
→ Executive Missions
→ Workflows
→ Measured results
→ Review
This chapter defines Strategic Planning and Roadmap Intelligence: the system through which Omnira chooses direction, sequences major initiatives, manages dependencies, allocates limited capacity, identifies decision gates, and adapts plans without losing strategic continuity.
The goal is not to predict the future perfectly.
The goal is to create a coherent path through uncertainty.

13.2 The Core Thesis

A roadmap is not a list of features.
It is an executive argument about sequence.
It explains:
Where are we going?
Why does that direction matter?
What must become true first?
What should happen next?
What should wait?
What evidence will determine the next step?
What would cause the roadmap to change?
The core principle is:
A roadmap should express strategic intent, dependencies, and decision gates—not false certainty.

13.3 Vision vs Strategy vs Roadmap vs Plan

These concepts must remain distinct.
Vision
Describes the future Omnira is trying to create.
Strategy
Defines how Omnira expects to create value and reach that future.
Roadmap
Sequences the major capabilities, outcomes, and decisions required.
Plan
Defines what will be executed within a defined time horizon.
Mission
Translates part of the plan into bounded delegated work.
Task
Represents a specific unit of execution.
The hierarchy is:
Vision
→ Strategy
→ Roadmap
→ Plan
→ Mission
→ Task
Confusing these levels creates either vague ambition or excessive micromanagement.

13.4 The Strategic Planning Function

Strategic Planning should help Executive Intelligence decide:
Which outcomes matter most?
Which capabilities are prerequisites?
Which projects should receive investment?
Which opportunities should wait?
What is the correct sequence?
What risks must be reduced first?
Which assumptions must be tested?
What should the founder review?
When should strategy change?
Strategic Planning is not the same as generating more work.
It is the discipline of deciding which work deserves to exist.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
13.5 Roadmap Intelligence

Roadmap Intelligence is the ability to understand and continuously evaluate:
Strategic direction.
Project and portfolio objectives.
Dependencies.
Readiness.
Capacity.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Evidence.
Decision history.
Milestone progress.
Changing conditions.
It should detect when a roadmap is:
On track.
Blocked.
Overloaded.
Under-specified.
Outdated.
Strategically inconsistent.
Missing a dependency.
No longer worth pursuing.

13.6 Roadmaps as Strategic Hypotheses

A roadmap represents a hypothesis:
If we build or achieve these things in this order, we expect to reach the desired strategic outcome.
Every roadmap therefore contains assumptions.
Examples:
Project isolation will enable broader autonomy.
Performance Intelligence will improve executive decisions.
The Prompt can become the first autonomous project.
Better analytics will make Familje-Stunden reactivation safer.
Founder burden will fall as approval and delegation improve.
These assumptions must remain visible and reviewable.

13.7 Roadmap vs Backlog

A backlog contains possible work.
A roadmap contains strategically sequenced commitments and hypotheses.
A backlog may include:
Feature ideas.
Technical improvements.
Design refinements.
Future experiments.
Unprioritized requests.
A roadmap should include only work that connects to:
Strategic objectives.
Required capabilities.
Milestones.
Dependencies.
Decision gates.
Risk reduction.
Revenue or learning outcomes.
