Which historical actions would have been allowed?
Which would have required approval?
How many denials occur?
What founder burden is reduced?
Which edge cases appear?

18.197 Dry Run

A workflow may operate in shadow mode.
It decides what it would do without creating the external effect.
The system can compare its decisions with human approvals.

18.198 Historical Replay

Historical workflow data may be replayed against a proposed license.
This can test:
Scope.
False allows.
False denials.
Volume.
Damage classification.
Policy conflicts.

18.199 License Testing

Tests should verify:
Allowed action succeeds.
Forbidden action fails.
Wrong-project action fails.
Expired license fails.
Volume limit works.
Budget limit works.
Fallback activates.
Monitoring failure suspends action.
Material workflow change invalidates authority.

18.200 Adversarial Testing

Testing should attempt:
Approval reuse.
Scope broadening.
Action renaming.
Tool substitution.
Workflow copying.
Scale fragmentation.
Project spoofing.
License self-modification.
Prompt injection.

18.201 Action Fragmentation Evasion

A workflow must not avoid volume or financial limits by splitting one action into many small actions.
Aggregate intent should be evaluated.

18.202 Semantic Evasion

Renaming:
Refund
as:
Customer goodwill adjustment
must not bypass financial policy.

18.203 Tool Substitution

Using a different tool for the same external effect should not bypass the license.

18.204 Workflow Copying

Copying a licensed workflow should not copy its active authority automatically.

18.205 Agent Replacement

Replacing the executing agent may require review when agent behavior materially affects quality or risk.

18.206 License Import

Imported licenses should be classified as:
Historical.
Proposed.
Unverified.
Expired.
Active only after validation.

18.207 Legacy Permission Migration

Legacy permissions should not become licenses merely because they exist.
They should be audited and normalized.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.208 License Export

Exports should preserve:
Scope.
Authority.
Version.
Conditions.
Redactions.
Review status.
Decision references.

18.209 License Retention

Material autonomy records should have long-term retention.
They are required for:
Audit.
Learning.
Incident review.
Trust calibration.
Authority history.

18.210 License Redaction

Sensitive evidence may be redacted.
The meaning, authority, scope, and history of the license should remain understandable.

18.211 Multi-User Organizations

Future organizations may separate:
License requester.
Executive recommender.
Risk reviewer.
Security reviewer.
Financial approver.
Final approver.
License owner.

18.212 Separation of Duties

High-impact autonomy may require different actors to:
Propose.
Review.
Approve.
Activate.
Audit.

18.213 Dual Approval

Dual approval may be required for:
Large financial authority.
Sensitive customer communication.
Cross-project autonomy.
High-scale publishing.
Strategic autonomy.
Constitutional exceptions.

18.214 License Owner

Every active license should have an owner.
The owner is responsible for:
Monitoring.
Review.
Incident response.
Scope accuracy.
Renewal.
Revocation.

18.215 Review Owner

The review owner ensures the evidence package is prepared before expiration.

18.216 Technical Owner

A technical owner may maintain:
Controls.
Monitoring.
Rollback.
Tool integrations.
Version compatibility.
Technical ownership is not approval authority.

18.217 Business Owner

A business owner may evaluate whether the autonomy creates actual project value.

18.218 Founder Authority

The founder retains authority to:
Approve.
Reject.
Narrow.
Suspend.
Revoke.
Require more evidence.
Change review cadence.
Return any workflow to approval mode.

18.219 Founder Override

A founder may override a license decision where authority permits.
Material overrides should preserve:
Reason.
Scope.
Duration.
Risk accepted.
Review.

18.220 License Recommendation Explanation

Atlas should explain:
Why autonomy is recommended.
What evidence supports it.
What exact actions become autonomous.
What remains approval-gated.
What could go wrong.
How rollback works.
When the license expires.

18.221 “Why Not More Autonomy?”

Atlas should be able to answer:
Which evidence is missing?
Which control is weak?
Which damage category is too high?
Which violation blocks promotion?
Which founder decision is required?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.222 “Why Not Less Autonomy?”

Atlas should be able to explain:
Which founder burden is unnecessary?
Which actions are repeatedly approved unchanged?
Which controls are proven?
Which business value is being delayed?

18.223 Autonomy Recommendation Card

A card may show:
Workflow.
Current level.
Recommended level.
Allowed actions.
Evidence.
Risk.
Controls.
Trial duration.
Fallback.
Estimated founder burden reduction.

18.224 License Timeline

The timeline may show:
Proposed.
Approved.
Activated.
Restricted.
Renewed.
Promoted.
Demoted.
Suspended.
Revoked.

18.225 Autonomy Graph

The Intelligence Graph should connect:
Workflow.
License.
Decision.
Policy.
Trust Score.
Violations.
Performance.
Reviews.
Outcomes.

18.226 Operating Graph Integration

The Operating Graph should show which active workflow instances operate under which licenses.

18.227 Autonomy Heatmap

A future dashboard may visualize:
Projects.
Workflows.
Autonomy levels.
Damage profiles.
License health.
Review status.
It should not reduce autonomy to one global percentage.

18.228 Autonomy Portfolio

Portfolio Executive should understand:
Where autonomy exists.
Where founder bottlenecks remain.
Where risk is concentrated.
Which workflows are promotion candidates.
Which licenses are unhealthy.

18.229 Autonomy Concentration Risk

Too much high-impact autonomy in one shared component may create systemic risk.

18.230 Autonomy Fragmentation

Too many small inconsistent licenses may create governance complexity.
The system should identify opportunities to standardize safe patterns.

18.231 Policy Promotion from Licenses

Repeated successful licenses may support a reusable project or global policy template.
Promotion still requires authority.

18.232 License Demotion into Policy

A workflow-specific license may be replaced by a stricter project-wide policy if incidents show a broader risk.

18.233 Autonomy Review Cadence

Reviews may occur:
Daily for crisis-restricted autonomy.
Weekly during trials.
Monthly for stable L4 licenses.
Quarterly for mature L5 licenses.
Event-driven after violations or material changes.

18.234 Daily Review

Daily review should focus on:
Violations.
Unexpected actions.
Control health.
Current external effects.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.235 Weekly Review

Weekly review should examine:
Quality.
Correction rate.
Business value.
Founder burden.
Risk.
Trial progress.

18.236 Monthly Review

Monthly review should examine:
License portfolio.
Promotion candidates.
Demotion candidates.
Governance burden.
Project-mode fit.
Business outcomes.

18.237 Quarterly Review

Quarterly review should challenge:
Autonomy strategy.
Systemic risk.
Cross-project patterns.
Policy maturity.
Founder-role reduction.
Long-term L5 readiness.

18.238 Annual Review

Annual review should evaluate:
How autonomy matured.
Which workflows became reliable.
Where founder dependence remains.
Which incidents changed governance.
Whether strategic autonomy should expand.

18.239 Autonomy Success

Autonomy is successful when it:
Creates business value.
Reduces founder burden.
Maintains policy compliance.
Maintains project isolation.
Keeps risk acceptable.
Remains explainable.
Can be stopped.

18.240 Autonomy Failure

Autonomy fails when it:
Creates uncontrolled external effects.
Requires constant human correction.
Consumes more governance than it saves.
Hides incidents.
Expands beyond scope.
Cannot be reversed.
Creates no meaningful business value.

18.241 Autonomy Maturity

A workflow’s maturity may be described as:
Unproven.
Observed.
Reliable internally.
Externally trialed.
Stable low-risk autonomous.
Conditionally business-autonomous.
Strategically autonomous.
Maturity is evidence.
The license remains the authority.

18.242 Anti-Global-Autonomy Principle

No general autonomy score should automatically authorize all behavior.

18.243 Anti-Agent-Autonomy Principle

An agent does not own autonomy independently of project, workflow, and license.

18.244 Anti-Tool-Access Principle

Tool access does not equal operating authority.

18.245 Anti-Time-Served Principle

A workflow does not earn promotion merely by existing for a long time.

18.246 Anti-Success-Count-Only Principle

Many successful runs do not erase one severe boundary failure.

18.247 Anti-Self-Promotion Principle

No system component may grant itself more authority.

18.248 Anti-Permanent-Trial Principle

Trial licenses must expire or be reviewed.

18.249 Anti-Approval-Fatigue-Promotion Principle

Founder overload alone is not sufficient evidence for autonomy expansion.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.250 Anti-Volume Principle

More autonomous actions do not prove higher organizational value.

18.251 Anti-Silent-Demotion Principle

Material autonomy reductions should be visible and explained.
Emergency suspension may occur immediately, but must still be recorded.

18.252 Anti-License-Evasion Principle

Actions may not bypass the license through renaming, splitting, copying, or tool substitution.

18.253 Anti-Context-Transfer Principle

Trust and authority must not transfer automatically between projects, workflows, agents, models, or channels.

18.254 Anti-Unmonitored-Autonomy Principle

Autonomy without functioning monitoring should suspend or degrade safely.

18.255 The Scope Test

Before issuing or using a license, Omnira should ask:
Which project?
Which workflow?
Which action?
Which object?
Which destination?
Which audience?

18.256 The Authority Test

Omnira should ask:
Who approved this license?
Why did they have authority?
Does the authority cover this scope?
Has it expired?

18.257 The Readiness Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the workflow stable?
Is policy clear?
Is monitoring active?
Is rollback tested?
Is project isolation reliable?

18.258 The Evidence Test

Omnira should ask:
How many successful runs exist?
What corrections occurred?
What violations occurred?
What business value was created?
Is the evidence from the same workflow version?

18.259 The Damage Test

Omnira should ask:
Which Damage Boundary categories apply?
What is the maximum permitted damage class?
What causes escalation?

18.260 The Control Test

Omnira should ask:
Which controls are mandatory?
Are they active?
Can the workflow detect control failure?
What happens if a control is unavailable?

18.261 The Monitoring Test

Omnira should ask:
What is measured?
Who receives alerts?
Which thresholds suspend autonomy?
Can monitoring fail silently?

18.262 The Rollback Test

Omnira should ask:
Can the action be reversed?
Can the consequences be recovered?
How quickly?
Who owns rollback?

18.263 The Value Test

Omnira should ask:
What business value does autonomy create?
What founder burden does it remove?
Does the value justify governance and risk?

18.264 The Trial Test

Omnira should ask:
Can the scope be smaller?
Can the audience be smaller?
Can the period be shorter?
Can stronger monitoring reduce uncertainty?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.265 The Promotion Test

Omnira should ask:
What new authority is requested?
Why is current authority insufficient?
Does evidence support the exact expansion?

18.266 The Demotion Test

Omnira should ask:
Which authority must stop?
Which safe work may continue?
What fallback applies?
What evidence would support restoration?

18.267 The Expiration Test

Omnira should ask:
When does authority end?
What happens automatically?
Who is notified?
Can the workflow degrade gracefully?

18.268 The Mode Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the license compatible with project lifecycle and operating mode?
Would the action create a hidden mode change?

18.269 The Conflict Test

Omnira should ask:
Does policy prohibit any licensed action?
Does another license conflict?
Does the Damage Boundary require stronger authority?

18.270 The Self-Promotion Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the requesting system also attempting to approve the change?
If yes, separate recommendation from authority.

18.271 Failure Modes

The Autonomy Licensing Model must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Global Autonomy
One autonomy level is applied across unrelated projects and actions.
Failure Mode 2 — Capability Equals Authority
A workflow acts because it can.
Failure Mode 3 — Tool Access Equals Autonomy
A connected integration becomes broadly usable.
Failure Mode 4 — Self-Promotion
Executive Intelligence or a workflow grants itself greater authority.
Failure Mode 5 — Scope Leakage
A license is reused across projects, channels, or workflows.
Failure Mode 6 — Workflow-Version Leakage
Authority survives a material workflow change.
Failure Mode 7 — Permanent Trial
Temporary authority never expires.
Failure Mode 8 — Promotion by Approval Fatigue
Autonomy increases only because the founder is overloaded.
Failure Mode 9 — Success-Count Blindness
Many successful runs hide one severe failure.
Failure Mode 10 — Unmonitored Autonomy
External action continues without reliable monitoring.
Failure Mode 11 — No Fallback
Expiration or violation creates uncontrolled behavior.
Failure Mode 12 — Scale Blindness
Small-scope authority expands to large scale.
Failure Mode 13 — License Evasion
Actions are renamed, split, copied, or rerouted.
Failure Mode 14 — Shadow Autonomy
Legacy workflows act without formal licenses.
Failure Mode 15 — Autonomy Without Value
The workflow acts independently but creates little business benefit.
Failure Mode 16 — Crisis Persistence
Normal autonomy remains active during a serious incident.
These failure modes should be treated as foundational governance constraints.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.272 Design Requirements

Any implementation of the Autonomy Licensing Model should preserve these requirements:
Every autonomous external action must be covered by a valid license or specific approval.
Every license must have explicit project scope.
Every license must identify a specific workflow instance.
Every license must define allowed and forbidden actions.
Every license must define channels, data, tools, scale, frequency, and time scope where relevant.
Every license must define its maximum permitted damage class.
Every license must define required controls and monitoring.
Every license must define expiration or review conditions.
Every license must define a fallback level.
Every material license must connect to the Decision Ledger.
Every promotion must require evidence and valid authority.
No component may promote its own autonomy.
Every material workflow change must trigger license review.
Every expired license must stop granting authority.
Every serious violation must suspend, reduce, or revoke authority according to policy.
Every project-mode change must review affected licenses.
Every autonomous action must remain traceable to its license.
Every license must be revocable.
Every autonomy decision must consider business value and founder burden, not only technical success.
Full autonomy must remain governed, auditable, bounded, and reversible where possible.

18.273 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the autonomy-authority contract.
It does not require a specific database schema, policy language, authorization service, or interface.
The architecture may later be implemented through:
Autonomy-license records.
Policy evaluation.
Workflow identities.
Action envelopes.
Tool-level authorization.
Trust Scores.
Performance metrics.
Review queues.
Violation events.
Fallback controls.
Decision Ledger links.
Dashboards.
Atlas explanations.
The technical implementation may evolve.
The licensing contract must remain stable.

18.274 The Autonomy Licensing Contract

Omnira must:
Treat autonomy as licensed authority.
Keep authority project-, workflow-, action-, risk-, and time-scoped.
Separate capability from permission.
Separate recommendation from approval.
Require valid human or constitutional authority for promotion.
Use trials to reduce uncertainty.
Require monitoring and rollback.
Reduce autonomy when conditions weaken.
Expire temporary authority safely.
Prevent authority transfer between unrelated contexts.
Preserve every grant, renewal, restriction, suspension, and revocation.
Measure business value as well as technical reliability.
Reduce founder burden without weakening safety.
Keep human override and emergency control real.
Ensure that greater autonomy always creates stronger accountability, not less.
A feature that does not support this contract should not grant repeated autonomous authority.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
18.275 Closing Principle

Autonomy should not be something Omnira claims.
It should be something a workflow earns and the organization grants.
A valid autonomy license must make it possible to answer:
What may this workflow do?
For which project?
Using which tools?
To which audience?
At what scale?
Within which budget?
Under which controls?
For how long?
Who approved it?
What stops it?
What happens when it fails?
At low maturity, workflows should observe, recommend, and prepare.
As trust grows, they may execute internally.
When evidence, controls, and value are strong, they may perform bounded external actions.
Eventually, selected workflows may receive conditional business autonomy.
But no workflow should become more autonomous than its governance, monitoring, rollback, and demonstrated judgment can support.
Autonomy in Omnira is not the absence of permission.
It is permission made precise.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Autonomy should increase only when demonstrated behavior justifies greater trust.
A workflow may complete many runs.
A model may produce impressive output.
An agent may receive repeated approvals.
A project may benefit from faster execution.
None of these signals alone prove that broader autonomy is safe or valuable.
Omnira therefore requires a Trust Score system that converts observed workflow behavior into structured evidence for autonomy decisions.
The Trust Score should help answer:
How reliably does this workflow operate?
How often are its outputs approved unchanged?
What kinds of corrections are required?
Does it remain inside project and policy boundaries?
Does it create meaningful business value?
Does it reduce founder burden?
How stable is its performance?
How serious are its violations or near misses?
Is the available evidence sufficient?
Is the workflow ready for more autonomy?
Should its current autonomy be maintained, restricted, or reduced?
The Trust Score supports autonomy progression.
It does not grant autonomy.

19.2 The Core Thesis

Trust must be earned through observable behavior.
It must remain:
Scoped.
Evidence-based.
Version-aware.
Risk-sensitive.
Time-sensitive.
Explainable.
Reversible.
The foundational principle is:
Trust Score is evidence for an autonomy decision.
Trust Score is not authority.
A high score may support a recommendation for broader autonomy.
Only a valid governance decision and autonomy license may grant that authority.

19.3 Trust Is Contextual

Trust should not exist as one global score for Atlas, an agent, or a model.
Trust belongs to a defined operating context.
That context may include:
Project.
Workflow instance.
Workflow version.
Action category.
Channel.
Audience.
Tool configuration.
Data scope.
Damage class.
Operating mode.
Example:
The Prompt short-news workflow may be highly trusted for drafting low-risk AI news.
That trust does not transfer automatically to:
Newsletter sending.
Customer support.
Political content.
Financial claims.
Familje-Stunden communication.
Another workflow version.

19.4 Trust Score vs Autonomy Level

Trust Score estimates demonstrated reliability.
Autonomy level defines the category of authority that may be licensed.
A workflow may have:
High Trust Score.
L2 autonomy.
because:
The action category remains sensitive.
Rollback is incomplete.
Policy is missing.
The Damage Boundary is too high.
The founder has not approved a broader license.
A score does not determine the level automatically.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.5 Trust Score vs Business Performance

A workflow may perform technically well but create little business value.
Another workflow may create strong revenue but require frequent policy correction.
Trust Score should consider both operational reliability and organizational value.
However, business success must not erase unsafe behavior.
High revenue does not cancel a serious policy violation.

19.6 Trust Score vs Model Quality

Model quality is only one input.
Trust also depends on:
Workflow design.
Context quality.
Source quality.
Policy checks.
Tool behavior.
Project isolation.
Human review.
Monitoring.
Recovery.
The same model may produce different trust outcomes in different workflows.

19.7 Trust Score vs Founder Confidence

Founder confidence is valuable evidence.
It should not become an unstructured substitute for measured behavior.
Founder confidence may be influenced by:
Experience.
Observed consistency.
Communication quality.
Strategic fit.
Personal preference.
Recent incidents.
The Trust Score should combine behavioral data with explicit founder feedback where appropriate.

19.8 The Trust Unit

The canonical Trust Score unit should normally be:
Project
+
Workflow Instance
+
Material Workflow Version
+
Action Category
Additional dimensions may include:
Channel.
Audience.
Damage class.
Tool set.
Data classification.
This prevents trust from becoming dangerously broad.

19.9 Trust Scope Example

A valid trust record may state:
Project:
The Prompt.
Workflow:
Short-News Publishing v3.
Action Category:
Publish low-risk AI news summaries.
Channel:
theprompt.nu.
Audience:
Public website visitors.
It should not mean:
This workflow is trusted for all publishing.

19.10 The Trust Score Object

A Trust Score should eventually exist as a structured object.
Conceptually, it may contain:
Trust identifier.
Project.
Workflow.
Workflow version.
Action category.
Channel.
Audience.
Current score.
Confidence.
Sample size.
Observation window.
Trend.
Dimension scores.
Violation penalties.
Near-miss penalties.
Business-value evidence.
Founder-feedback evidence.
Current autonomy level.
Promotion readiness.
Demotion risk.
Last material event.
Review date.
Version.

19.11 Trust Score Dimensions

The canonical Trust Score should evaluate several dimensions:
1. Execution Reliability.
2. Output Quality.
3. Approval Alignment.
4. Correction Severity.
5. Policy Compliance.
6. Scope Integrity.
7. Stability.
8. Business Value.
9. Founder Burden Reduction.
10. Monitoring and Recovery Readiness.
No single dimension should dominate every context.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.12 Execution Reliability

Execution Reliability measures whether the workflow completes correctly.
It may include:
Successful completion rate.
Timeout rate.
Retry rate.
Partial-failure rate.
Duplicate-action rate.
Destination accuracy.
State consistency.
Tool-call reliability.
Technical completion alone is not enough.

19.13 A Successful Run

A successful run should satisfy:
Correct project.
Correct workflow version.
Correct input.
Correct action.
Correct object.
Correct destination.
Correct scale.
Correct policy result.
Correct external outcome.
No hidden side effect.
A technically completed wrong-project action is not successful.

19.14 Partial Success

A run may be partially successful when:
Draft created correctly.
Publication failed.
One channel succeeded.
Another channel failed.
External result is uncertain.
Partial success should not be counted as full reliability.

19.15 Unknown Outcome

When Omnira cannot verify the external result, the run should be classified as unknown.
Unknown outcomes should not increase trust as if successful.

19.16 Output Quality

Output Quality measures whether the workflow’s result meets project requirements.
Possible factors include:
Factual accuracy.
Completeness.
Relevance.
Brand fit.
Tone.
Formatting.
Source quality.
Customer usefulness.
Strategic alignment.
Quality criteria should be project- and action-specific.

19.17 Approval Alignment

Approval Alignment measures how often human reviewers accept the workflow output.
Possible outcomes:
Approved unchanged.
Approved with minor edits.
Approved with material edits.
Rejected.
Deferred for missing evidence.
Escalated due to risk.
These outcomes should have different trust effects.

19.18 Unchanged Approval Rate

An unchanged approval indicates that:
The output was acceptable.
The scope was correct.
The reviewer found no material correction necessary.
Repeated unchanged approvals are strong evidence for trust.
They are not sufficient alone for autonomy promotion.

19.19 Minor Edit Rate

Minor edits may include:
Formatting.
Punctuation.
Small tone adjustment.
Non-material title improvement.
Cosmetic structure.
Minor edits should reduce trust less than factual or policy corrections.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.20 Material Edit Rate

Material edits may include:
Factual correction.
Changed recommendation.
Removed unsupported claim.
Changed customer promise.
Changed financial term.
Changed project scope.
Removed sensitive content.
Material edits are important evidence against promotion.

19.21 Rejection Rate

A rejection should record its reason.
Possible categories:
Low quality.
Incorrect facts.
Wrong strategy.
Insufficient evidence.
Policy violation.
Scope failure.
Brand mismatch.
Customer risk.
Duplicate or unnecessary action.
Different rejection reasons should have different weights.

19.22 Correction Severity

Corrections should be classified by severity.
C0 — Cosmetic
No material meaning changed.
C1 — Quality
Clarity, style, or usefulness improved.
C2 — Material Content
Facts, recommendation, or important meaning changed.
C3 — Governance or Scope
Policy, authority, project, or Damage Boundary issue corrected.
C4 — Prevented Serious Harm
The reviewer prevented a severe or systemic action.
A C4 correction should outweigh many successful runs.

19.23 Rare Severe Errors

A low average correction rate may hide rare severe failures.
Example:
999 acceptable runs.
1 cross-project data publication attempt.
The workflow should not be considered highly trusted merely because 99.9% of runs appeared successful.
Severity must outweigh volume where appropriate.

19.24 Policy Compliance

Policy Compliance measures whether the workflow respects:
Constitutional rules.
Global policy.
Project policy.
Mission constraints.
Autonomy-license scope.
Tool restrictions.
Budget mandates.
Approval requirements.
Policy compliance is a core trust dimension.

19.25 Scope Integrity

Scope Integrity measures whether the workflow consistently remains inside:
Correct project.
Correct workflow.
Correct action category.
Correct channel.
Correct audience.
Correct data scope.
Correct financial scope.
Correct volume.
Scope failure should carry a strong penalty.

19.26 Project Isolation Integrity

Project isolation should be treated as a minimum trust floor.
A workflow that cannot reliably preserve project boundaries should not receive external autonomy.
One serious isolation failure may require immediate suspension.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Burden Reduction Is Not Safety Evidence Alone
text:
19.27 Stability

Stability measures whether performance remains consistent over time.
It may include:
Variance in quality.
Variance in latency.
Failure clustering.
Provider instability.
Model-output inconsistency.
Performance after context changes.
Performance under higher volume.
A high average with extreme instability may be less trustworthy than a slightly lower but consistent performance.

19.28 Trend

The Trust Score should include direction.
Possible trends:
Improving.
Stable.
Declining.
Volatile.
Insufficient data.
A declining score may require review before the absolute score becomes low.

19.29 Business Value

Business Value measures whether the workflow creates meaningful organizational outcomes.
Possible evidence:
Revenue created.
Revenue protected.
Customer response improved.
Publishing speed increased.
Founder waiting time reduced.
Cost reduced.
Learning accelerated.
Risk reduced.
Project milestone advanced.

19.30 Value Is Not Volume

More outputs do not necessarily mean more value.
Examples:
More articles without traffic or quality.
More support replies with lower satisfaction.
More reports no one uses.
More recommendations without decisions.
The Trust Score should not reward activity for its own sake.

19.31 Founder Burden Reduction

A workflow should receive positive trust evidence when it reduces unnecessary founder effort.
Possible measurements:
Approvals avoided.
Review time reduced.
Context switching reduced.
Waiting time reduced.
Repeated decisions eliminated.
Corrections reduced.
Escalations improved.

19.32 Burden Reduction Is Not Safety Evidence Alone

Reducing founder burden is valuable.
It does not justify autonomy when:
Policy violations remain high.
Damage risk is uncontrolled.
Monitoring is weak.
Rollback is absent.

19.33 Monitoring Readiness

Monitoring Readiness measures whether Omnira can reliably observe autonomous behavior.
It may include:
Complete action logging.
Outcome verification.
Threshold alerts.
Cost tracking.
Violation detection.
Near-miss detection.
Project-scope checks.
License traceability.

19.34 Recovery Readiness

Recovery Readiness measures whether the workflow can be stopped and its effects addressed.
Possible evidence:
Pause works.
Rollback works.
Credentials can be revoked.
External action can be corrected.
Duplicate action can be prevented.
Affected customers can be identified.
Fallback level is functional.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Scores Should Not Imply False Precision
Trust Band Is Not Autonomy Level
text:
19.35 The Trust Score Is Composite

The total Trust Score may combine dimension scores.
A conceptual structure may be:
Positive Evidence
−
Risk-Weighted Corrections
−
Policy Penalties
−
Scope Penalties
−
Instability Penalties
The exact formula should remain implementation-specific.

19.36 Scores Should Not Imply False Precision

A numerical score may support internal comparison.
It should not imply scientific certainty where the evidence is limited.
The human-facing system may use bands such as:
Unproven.
Low Trust.
Developing Trust.
Operationally Reliable.
High Trust.
Mature Trust.

19.37 Suggested Trust Bands

A conceptual Trust Score scale may use 0–100.
0–19 — Untrusted
Insufficient or strongly negative evidence.
20–39 — Low Trust
Limited reliability or material weaknesses.
40–59 — Developing Trust
Useful behavior but meaningful correction or stability issues remain.
60–74 — Operationally Reliable
Reliable within current internal or preparation scope.
75–89 — High Trust
Strong evidence for narrow external autonomy consideration.
90–100 — Mature Trust
Sustained high-quality behavior with strong controls and business value.
These bands should not directly authorize autonomy.

19.38 Trust Band Is Not Autonomy Level

A Mature Trust score does not automatically produce L5 or L6 authority.
Autonomy still depends on:
Damage class.
Policy.
Project sensitivity.
Rollback.
Monitoring.
Business need.
Approving authority.

19.39 Minimum Floors

Promotion should require minimum scores in critical dimensions.
Example:
Overall Trust:
85.
Policy Compliance:
100.
Scope Integrity:
100.
Monitoring Readiness:
95.
Recovery Readiness:
90.
A high overall average should not hide failure in a critical category.

19.40 Hard Blockers

Certain conditions should block promotion regardless of score.
Possible blockers:
Unresolved P0 violation.
Unresolved P1 violation.
Cross-project failure.
Missing rollback.
Monitoring unavailable.
Expired policy.
Invalid license.
Unknown workflow version.
Project mode incompatibility.
Critical data-quality gap.

19.41 Score Confidence

Every Trust Score should have a confidence level.
Possible levels:
High.
Medium.
Low.
Insufficient Evidence.
Confidence should depend on:
Sample size.
Observation duration.
Data completeness.
Scenario diversity.
Measurement reliability.
Workflow-version stability.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.42 Sample Size

Small sample sizes should limit confidence.
Example:
Five successful runs:
Encouraging evidence.
Five hundred successful runs:
Stronger evidence.
Five hundred identical low-risk runs:
Not necessarily evidence for broader action categories.

19.43 Scenario Diversity

Trust should consider whether the workflow has operated across:
Normal cases.
Edge cases.
Different sources.
Different times.
Different volumes.
Different content categories.
Failure conditions.
Repeated identical cases produce narrower trust.

19.44 Observation Duration

Trust should include sustained behavior over time.
A short period of strong results may be suitable for a trial.
Longer sustained evidence is required for mature autonomy.

19.45 Recency

Recent evidence should generally carry more weight than old evidence.
However, historical severe violations should not disappear merely because time passed.

19.46 Recency Weighting

A conceptual model may weight:
Recent normal runs:
Strongly.
Older normal runs:
Moderately.
Severe historical incidents:
Persistently.
Old workflow versions:
Weakly or separately.

19.47 Evidence Decay

Trust evidence should decay when:
Workflow is inactive.
Model changes.
Provider changes.
Policy changes.
Project mode changes.
Audience changes.
Data source changes.
Monitoring changes.
Long time passes without validation.

19.48 Trust Decay

Trust Score may decline gradually without new evidence.
This does not mean the workflow became bad.
It means the organization has less current evidence that the workflow remains reliable.

19.49 Inactivity

A workflow inactive for a long period should not resume at full autonomy automatically.
The system may require:
Revalidation.
Dry run.
Reduced scale.
Updated policy check.
New license review.

19.50 Workflow-Version Boundaries

A material workflow version change should create a new or inherited-but-reduced trust record.
The new version may receive:
Historical reference.
Reduced initial trust.
Lower confidence.
Trial requirements.
Stronger monitoring.

19.51 Minor Version Change

A minor change may preserve more trust.
Examples:
Formatting improvement.
Non-material prompt clarification.
Performance optimization without behavior change.
The system should still record the change.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.52 Material Version Change

A material change may include:
New model.
New provider.
New tool.
New agent.
New prompt strategy.
New source type.
New output schema.
New destination.
New policy behavior.
Material changes require stronger revalidation.

19.53 Trust Inheritance

Trust should never transfer fully by default.
Possible inheritance levels:
No inheritance.
Limited historical reference.
Partial inherited score with low confidence.
Full inheritance only for verified non-material changes.

19.54 Cross-Project Trust

Trust from one project should not automatically transfer to another.
The workflow may have similar technical behavior but different:
Customers.
Brand.
Policies.
Data.
Risk.
Channels.
Damage profile.

19.55 Template Trust

A workflow template may accumulate design evidence.
That evidence may support:
Recommended controls.
Expected failure modes.
Initial testing strategy.
License template.
It should not create active autonomy in a new project.

19.56 Agent Trust

Agent-level behavior may be measured.
However, autonomy should remain attached to the workflow context.
An agent may perform well in one role and poorly in another.

19.57 Model Trust

Model performance may inform workflow trust.
It should remain separate because:
Prompts differ.
Tools differ.
Context differs.
Output validation differs.
Risk differs.

19.58 Tool Trust

Tool reliability may affect workflow trust.
Examples:
API consistency.
Idempotency.
Response correctness.
Destination accuracy.
Authentication stability.
Tool trust is not action authority.

19.59 Positive Trust Events

Positive events may include:
Successful run.
Unchanged approval.
Accurate escalation.
Correct refusal.
Correct project-scope detection.
Successful rollback.
Reliable incident containment.
Business-value milestone.

19.60 Negative Trust Events

Negative events may include:
Failure.
Material correction.
Rejection.
Policy violation.
Scope failure.
Near miss.
Duplicate action.
Wrong destination.
Monitoring failure.
Hidden side effect.

19.61 Correct Refusal as Positive Evidence

A workflow should gain trust when it correctly refuses or escalates an action beyond its authority.
Autonomy maturity includes knowing when not to act.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.62 Correct Escalation

A correct escalation may be more trustworthy than a confident answer.
Examples:
Sensitive customer complaint.
Unsupported news claim.
Budget beyond mandate.
Project-scope ambiguity.
Health-adjacent question.

19.63 False Escalation

Excessive escalation may create:
Founder burden.
Execution delay.
Low throughput.
Reduced autonomy value.
False escalation should reduce efficiency evidence but not as severely as unsafe action.

19.64 False Allow

A false allow occurs when the workflow acts autonomously when approval or denial was required.
This should carry a strong penalty.

19.65 False Denial

A false denial occurs when safe permitted work is blocked.
This may reduce:
Operational usefulness.
Founder leverage.
Business throughput.
It should influence calibration without being treated like a safety violation.

19.66 Policy Violation Penalties

Violation penalties should reflect severity.
Conceptually:
P3:
Small penalty.
P2:
Meaningful penalty.
P1:
Large penalty and likely suspension.
P0:
Trust collapse for the affected scope and immediate revocation review.

19.67 Violations Should Not Average Away

A severe violation should not disappear because the workflow later completes many easy runs.
The system should preserve:
Severity memory.
Incident status.
Remediation status.
Post-remediation evidence.

19.68 Near-Miss Penalties

Near misses should reduce trust based on:
Potential damage.
Why harm was avoided.
Whether the workflow detected the issue.
Whether an external control detected it.
Likelihood of recurrence.
A near miss caught by the workflow itself is different from one caught only by the founder.

19.69 Self-Detected Near Miss

Self-detection may demonstrate:
Boundary awareness.
Monitoring quality.
Correct escalation.
Recovery capability.
It still reveals a failure path but may preserve more trust.

19.70 Externally Detected Near Miss

A near miss detected only through founder or external review indicates weaker autonomous control.

19.71 Hidden Incident

Failure to report an incident should carry a stronger penalty than the underlying operational error alone.
Transparency is a trust requirement.

19.72 Incident Recovery

Trust may recover when:
Root cause is understood.
Controls are improved.
Tests pass.
The workflow operates safely under reduced scope.
No recurrence appears.
Review is completed.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.73 Trust Recovery

Trust should be recoverable.
A single incident should not necessarily permanently destroy a workflow’s future value.
Recovery must require evidence, not time alone.

19.74 Recovery Stages

A conceptual recovery path may be:
Suspended.
Observed.
Dry Run.
Prepare Only.
Internal Execution.
Limited External Trial.
Restored License.

19.75 Trust Recovery Is Scope-Specific

A workflow may recover trust for one action category while remaining restricted for another.

19.76 Trust Score Update Frequency

Trust may update:
After each material run.
After each approval.
After each violation.
Daily for active workflows.
At review boundaries.
After workflow changes.
The interface need not show constant minor fluctuations.

19.77 Score Smoothing

The score should avoid extreme movement from one ordinary event.
Smoothing may be useful for:
Normal successes.
Minor edits.
Routine latency changes.
Severe events should bypass smoothing.

19.78 Event Weighting

Events should be weighted by:
Severity.
Relevance.
Recency.
Confidence.
Action category.
Damage potential.
Detection source.

19.79 Baseline

A new workflow should begin with:
No trust.
Not distrust.
The initial state should be:
Unproven.
This avoids treating missing evidence as either safety or failure.

19.80 Cold Start

During cold start, the workflow may operate through:
L0 observation.
L1 recommendation.
L2 preparation.
Dry runs.
Human approvals.
Shadow-mode comparison.

19.81 Cold-Start Evidence

Early evidence may include:
Historical replay.
Simulation.
Test cases.
Adversarial tests.
Human-reviewed drafts.
Safe internal execution.
Simulation should not count as strongly as real production behavior.

19.82 Shadow Mode

In shadow mode, the workflow predicts what it would do.
Its decisions can be compared with human decisions.
Metrics may include:
Agreement rate.
False allows.
False denials.
Risk classification accuracy.
Escalation accuracy.

19.83 Historical Replay

Historical cases can test:
Policy interpretation.
Scope decisions.
Output quality.
Edge-case handling.
Failure detection.
Replay evidence should be marked as simulated evidence.

19.84 Test Evidence vs Production Evidence

A mature score should distinguish:
Unit-test evidence.
Simulation evidence.
Shadow-mode evidence.
Human-approved production evidence.
Autonomous production evidence.
Production evidence should generally carry more weight.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.85 Approval History

Approval history should preserve:
Approver.
Decision.
Edits.
Rejection reason.
Response time.
Risk class.
Workflow version.

19.86 Approver Consistency

Different approvers may apply different standards.
The system should account for:
Approver role.
Project expertise.
Policy authority.
Historical consistency.

19.87 Founder Approval Signal

Founder approvals are important but should not become the only quality signal.
A founder may approve quickly due to:
Time pressure.
Trust.
Low attention.
Low materiality.
High workload.
Unchanged approval should be interpreted with context.

19.88 Founder Corrections

Founder corrections may reveal:
Preference mismatch.
Strategic mismatch.
Quality problem.
Risk issue.
Missing context.
Policy weakness.
Not all founder edits indicate workflow unreliability.

19.89 Preference Corrections

Stable preference corrections may suggest that the workflow needs better personalization.
They should not carry the same penalty as factual or policy corrections.

19.90 Strategy Corrections

Repeated strategy corrections indicate the workflow may not understand project direction.
This should affect Executive trust more strongly.

19.91 Manual Trust Adjustment

The founder may manually adjust trust evidence.
Manual adjustment should:
Preserve the original computed score.
Record the adjustment.
Record the reason.
Record duration.
Trigger review where material.

19.92 Manual Adjustment Is Not Authority

Increasing a Trust Score manually does not grant autonomy.
A license decision remains necessary.

19.93 Trust Override

A founder may state that the score overstates or understates trust.
The system should use the feedback to:
Review data.
Review weighting.
Review context.
Create a temporary interpretation note.
It should not silently rewrite history.

19.94 Score Transparency

The founder should be able to inspect:
Current score.
Confidence.
Trend.
Dimension scores.
Positive evidence.
Negative evidence.
Violations.
Sample size.
Workflow version.
Promotion blockers.

19.95 Explainable Trust

Atlas should be able to answer:
Why is this score high?
Why did it fall?
Why is promotion blocked?
Which evidence matters most?
What would improve trust?
What would cause demotion?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.96 Trust Score Summary

A human-readable summary may look like:
Trust Score:
82 — High Trust.
Confidence:
Medium.
Strengths:
Strong approval alignment, stable output, no policy violations.
Weaknesses:
Limited production sample and untested rollback at higher volume.
Autonomy Recommendation:
Maintain L3 and begin a small L4 trial.

19.97 Trust Score Card

A card may show:
Workflow.
Current score.
Confidence.
Trend.
Current autonomy.
Promotion readiness.
Blocking issue.
Next review.

19.98 Dimension View

The detailed view may show:
Reliability:
High.
Quality:
High.
Approval Alignment:
High.
Policy Compliance:
Perfect.
Scope Integrity:
Perfect.
Business Value:
Moderate.
Recovery Readiness:
Developing.

19.99 Promotion Readiness

Promotion readiness should be a separate conclusion.
Possible statuses:
Not Eligible.
Evidence Developing.
Eligible for Trial.
Eligible for Narrow Promotion.
Eligible for Renewal.
Blocked by Governance.
Blocked by Risk.
Blocked by Missing Controls.

19.100 Promotion Is a Decision Package

A promotion recommendation should include:
Current level.
Requested level.
Score.
Confidence.
Evidence.
Critical dimensions.
Violations.
Business value.
Founder burden reduction.
Damage analysis.
Controls.
Trial proposal.
Fallback.
Review date.

19.101 Promotion Thresholds

Thresholds may vary by transition.
Example:
L1 → L2:
Moderate evidence may be sufficient.
L2 → L3:
Strong internal reliability required.
L3 → L4:
Strong policy, scope, monitoring, and rollback evidence required.
L4 → L5:
Sustained business value and mature operational control required.
L5 → L6:
Constitutional mandate and extensive strategic evidence required.

19.102 Promotion Thresholds Are Contextual

A low-risk internal workflow may progress faster than a customer-sensitive or financial workflow.

19.103 Promotion Requires Business Need

A workflow should not receive higher autonomy merely because it qualifies technically.
The system should ask:
Will broader autonomy create meaningful value?
Will it reduce a real bottleneck?
Will it reduce founder burden?
Will it improve customer outcomes?
Does the benefit justify governance cost?

19.104 Promotion Requires Stable Scope

A workflow with frequently changing purpose or output should not receive broad autonomy.
Stable scope is necessary for meaningful evidence.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.105 Promotion Requires Monitoring

A high score without functioning monitoring should not support promotion.

19.106 Promotion Requires Rollback

External autonomy should require proven fallback and rollback appropriate to the action.

19.107 Promotion Requires Policy Coverage

The action category must have clear policy.
Trust cannot fill a governance gap.

19.108 Promotion Requires Damage Compatibility

The requested autonomy must remain within the permitted Damage Boundary and authority.

19.109 Trial Recommendation

When evidence is promising but incomplete, the preferred outcome may be:
Do not grant permanent autonomy.
Grant a narrow trial license.

19.110 Trial Trust Threshold

A trial may tolerate:
Lower sample size.
Lower confidence.
Narrower audience.
Lower scale.
Stronger monitoring.
Shorter duration.

19.111 Promotion Evidence Window

The evidence window should match the action.
Examples:
High-frequency publishing:
Recent weeks may produce enough runs.
Low-frequency budget decisions:
A longer period may be required.
Rare crisis actions:
Simulation and adversarial testing may matter more.

19.112 No Automatic Promotion

Crossing a score threshold should create:
A promotion candidate.
It should not activate a new license.

19.113 No Self-Promotion

The workflow may report evidence and propose promotion.
It may not approve or activate the higher authority.

19.114 Demotion Readiness

The system should also calculate demotion risk.
Possible statuses:
Stable.
Watch.
Review Recommended.
Restriction Recommended.
Immediate Suspension Required.
Revocation Required.

19.115 Demotion Triggers

Possible triggers:
P0 violation.
P1 violation.
Repeated P2 violations.
Scope failure.
Monitoring failure.
Rollback failure.
Sharp quality decline.
Project-mode change.
Workflow-version change.
Trust confidence collapse.

19.116 Automatic Demotion

Automatic demotion may be appropriate when explicitly defined by policy.
Examples:
Monitoring failure:
L4 → L2.
Budget threshold reached:
Disable spending action.
Project enters Crisis:
External licenses suspended.
P1 violation:
Immediate suspension pending review.

19.117 Demotion Is Safer Than Promotion

Automatic restriction can reduce damage.
Automatic authority expansion increases exposure.
Therefore:
Automatic demotion may be policy-driven.
Promotion must remain governed.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: High Trust, Low Founder Burden Reduction
text:
19.118 Demotion Scope

Demotion should remove only the affected authority where possible.
Example:
Website publishing remains active.
Social publishing is suspended.
Newsletter preparation continues.
Newsletter sending remains blocked.

19.119 Trust Collapse

A Trust Score may collapse for a specific scope after:
Critical violation.
Cross-project action.
Hidden incident.
Intentional policy bypass.
Irrecoverable external harm.
This should not necessarily erase unrelated internal trust evidence.

19.120 Trust Recovery Review

A recovery review should include:
Original incident.
Root cause.
Control changes.
Test results.
Reduced-scope performance.
New evidence.
Recommended restoration path.

19.121 Score Trend Alerts

Alerts may trigger when:
Trust declines materially.
One dimension falls below a floor.
Confidence decreases.
Violation rate rises.
Correction severity increases.
Business value disappears.

19.122 Trust and Autonomy License Renewal

License renewal should consider:
Current Trust Score.
Score confidence.
Trend.
Violations.
Business value.
Control health.
Project mode.
Workflow version.

19.123 Stable Score, Weak Value

A workflow may remain technically reliable while producing little value.
The recommendation may be:
Do not reduce trust.
Do not renew broad autonomy.
Retire or redesign the workflow.

19.124 High Value, Weak Trust

A high-value workflow with weak trust may require:
More human review.
Narrower scope.
Stronger controls.
More preparation authority.
No external autonomy yet.

19.125 High Trust, High Value

This is the strongest autonomy-promotion candidate.
It still requires:
Policy.
Authority.
Damage compatibility.
Monitoring.
Rollback.
License review.

19.126 Low Trust, Low Value

The likely recommendation is:
Stop.
Redesign.
Retire.
Return to observation.

19.127 High Trust, Low Founder Burden Reduction

A workflow may be reliable but not remove a meaningful bottleneck.
Autonomy expansion may have low priority.

19.128 Trust Score and Project Modes

Project mode should affect score interpretation.
Build operating mode
Trust focuses on correctness, learning, and internal reliability.
Growth operating mode
Business value, scale, and customer impact become more important.
Stabilize operating mode
Reliability, policy compliance, and variance receive greater weight.
Learning operating mode
Experiment quality and uncertainty reduction matter.
Maintenance operating mode
Consistency and low operating cost matter.
Crisis Mode
Trust progression pauses; containment and recovery dominate.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.129 Lifecycle Mode

Active
Normal trust accumulation.
Observer
Mostly observation and preparation evidence.
Hibernate
Trust may decay due to inactivity.
Archived
Operational trust becomes historical only.

19.130 Mode Change Review

A project-mode change should trigger review of:
Trust weights.
Relevant evidence.
Current autonomy.
Promotion candidates.
License validity.

19.131 Trust Score and Damage Profile

Different projects require different minimum floors.
The Prompt may emphasize:
Accuracy.
Source quality.
Brand consistency.
Correction behavior.
Familje-Stunden may emphasize:
Child sensitivity.
Customer trust.
Data minimization.
Support escalation.
GainPilot may emphasize:
Safety.
Injury escalation.
Health-claim avoidance.
Conservative recommendations.

19.132 The Prompt Trust Profile

For low-risk short-news publishing, key evidence may include:
Source validation.
Factual accuracy.
Duplicate prevention.
Correct project publication.
Correction rate.
SEO and brand quality.
Stale-content handling.
Rollback.

19.133 Familje-Stunden Trust Profile

For support drafting, key evidence may include:
Correct classification.
Tone.
Sensitive-topic escalation.
No unapproved promises.
No child-sensitive overreach.
Accurate account guidance.
Customer satisfaction.

19.134 GainPilot Trust Profile

For training recommendations, key evidence may include:
Injury detection.
Conservative escalation.
No medical claims.
Training-context accuracy.
Load progression safety.
User feedback.

19.135 Omnira Platform Trust Profile

For platform workflows, key evidence may include:
Project isolation.
Authorization correctness.
Migration safety.
Audit integrity.
Rollback.
Production-impact containment.

19.136 Trust Score and Governance

Governance should use Trust Score as one evidence source.
It should never treat the score as a bypass around:
Policy.
Approval.
Damage Boundary.
Constitutional rules.
Authority.

19.137 Trust Score and Decision Ledger

Material trust-based decisions should link to the Decision Ledger.
Examples:
Autonomy promotion.
Autonomy demotion.
License renewal.
Workflow suspension.
Trust-weight change.
Manual score override.

19.138 Trust Score and Performance Intelligence

Performance Intelligence should provide:
Reliability metrics.
Quality outcomes.
Revenue impact.
Cost.
Latency.
Customer results.
Founder burden.
Trend data.
Executive Intelligence interprets the evidence.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.139 Trust Score and Memory

Memory may preserve durable lessons such as:
This workflow becomes unstable above five publications per day.
Founder edits are usually stylistic, not factual.
Two-source validation materially improves accuracy.
Newsletter sending remains more sensitive than website publication.
Memory should not overwrite current trust evidence.

19.140 Trust Score and Knowledge

Knowledge may define:
Domain quality standards.
Risk categories.
Required validations.
Expected failure modes.
Industry constraints.

19.141 Trust Score and AI Intelligence

AI Intelligence may inform:
Model reliability.
Provider performance.
Fallback quality.
Cost-quality tradeoffs.
Reasoning-depth needs.
A provider change may reduce score confidence.

19.142 Trust Score and Manager

Manager may use trust evidence to:
Route work.
Increase review.
Reduce concurrency.
Escalate edge cases.
Prefer stable workflows.
Manager may not change autonomy authority independently.

19.143 Trust Score and Workforce

Workforce may receive operational consequences:
More review required.
Reduced scope.
Increased validation.
Trial limits.
Escalation changes.
Workforce does not need to manipulate the Trust Score.

19.144 Trust Score and Agents

Agents should not be allowed to alter their own trust records.
They may produce telemetry and incident reports.
The score should be computed by a separate trusted process.

19.145 Separation of Measurement and Execution

The workflow being measured should not control:
Its success classification.
Its violation classification.
Its sample selection.
Its score weighting.
Its promotion decision.
This prevents self-serving measurement.

19.146 Trust Score Gaming

Potential gaming behaviors include:
Selecting only easy cases.
Avoiding difficult cases without reporting.
Splitting failures.
Hiding incidents.
Inflating activity volume.
Routing risky work to humans while claiming full success.
Changing labels to reduce penalties.

19.147 Case-Mix Adjustment

A workflow handling only simple cases should not receive the same trust interpretation as one handling complex edge cases.
The score should preserve:
Case difficulty.
Risk category.
Escalation rate.
Coverage.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.148 Selective Escalation

Correctly escalating hard cases is positive.
Avoiding all difficult work may limit the scope of earned trust.

19.149 Coverage

Trust should identify which portion of the action space has been tested.
Example:
Trusted for:
Routine AI product news.
Unproven for:
Breaking news, allegations, politics, financial claims.

19.150 Score Manipulation Detection

The system should detect:
Unusual drops in reported failures.
Missing logs.
Sudden case-mix changes.
High success with low outcome verification.
Mismatch between approvals and reported quality.
Unreported manual corrections.

19.151 Independent Verification

High-impact workflows may require independent checks from:
Policy engine.
Performance Intelligence.
Audit system.
Human review.
External outcome verification.

19.152 Trust Data Integrity

Trust evidence should preserve:
Source.
Timestamp.
Workflow version.
Project.
Action category.
Outcome.
Confidence.
Audit trace.

19.153 Missing Trust Data

Missing data should not be interpreted as positive performance.
The score should become:
Lower confidence.
Review required.
Potentially restricted.

19.154 Monitoring Failure

When monitoring fails:
Score updates stop.
Confidence falls.
External autonomy may degrade.
Review is triggered.

19.155 Data Freshness

Trust data should include freshness.
Possible states:
Current.
Recent.
Stale.
Incomplete.
Invalid.

19.156 Score Calculation Version

The scoring method should be versioned.
A score under one model may not be directly comparable with a later model without normalization.

19.157 Weight Versioning

Changes to trust weights should preserve:
Previous weights.
New weights.
Reason.
Affected workflows.
Authority.
Effective date.

19.158 No Silent Weight Change

Changing the importance of violations, approvals, or business value may materially alter autonomy recommendations.
Such changes should be reviewable.

19.159 Project-Specific Weights

Project-specific weighting may be valid.
Examples:
Familje-Stunden:
Customer sensitivity and escalation accuracy weighted heavily.
The Prompt:
Accuracy, source validation, and correction behavior weighted heavily.
GainPilot:
Safety and conservative escalation weighted heavily.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.160 Global Minimum Rules

Project-specific weights must not weaken global minimum requirements for:
Project isolation.
P0 violations.
Authority.
Audit.
Monitoring.
Constitutional compliance.

19.161 Trust Score Review Cadence

Trust may be reviewed:
Continuously for active metrics.
Daily for violations and anomalies.
Weekly during trials.
Monthly for stable L4 workflows.
Quarterly for mature L5 workflows.
Event-driven after material changes.

19.162 Daily Trust Review

Daily review should focus on:
Violations.
Near misses.
Control failures.
Unexpected external outcomes.
Sharp score changes.

19.163 Weekly Trust Review

Weekly review should examine:
Approval alignment.
Correction categories.
Quality trend.
Founder burden.
Business value.
Trial progress.

19.164 Monthly Trust Review

Monthly review should examine:
Promotion candidates.
Demotion candidates.
Stale scores.
Workflow-version changes.
Project-mode fit.
Value produced.

19.165 Quarterly Trust Review

Quarterly review should challenge:
Weighting.
Calibration.
Cross-project patterns.
Systemic risk.
Autonomy maturity.
Founder-dependency reduction.

19.166 Trust Score Calibration

Calibration compares trust predictions with later outcomes.
Questions include:
Did high-trust workflows perform reliably?
Did low-trust workflows create more corrections?
Were violations predicted?
Did promotion candidates succeed?
Were demotions too late?

19.167 Overconfidence

The score is overconfident when:
High Trust repeatedly precedes correction or incidents.
Confidence remains high with limited samples.
Workflow-version changes are underweighted.
Severe rare errors are averaged away.

19.168 Underconfidence

The score is underconfident when:
Stable workflows remain approval-bound unnecessarily.
Minor stylistic edits dominate scoring.
Business value is ignored.
Repeated correct escalations are underrewarded.

19.169 False Promotion Candidate

A workflow may appear ready but fail after promotion.
Review should ask:
Was the sample too narrow?
Was scale underestimated?
Did the channel change risk?
Did monitoring fail?
Was business pressure allowed to override evidence?

19.170 Missed Promotion Candidate

A workflow may remain overly restricted despite strong evidence.
This creates:
Founder burden.
Execution delay.
Lost value.
Lower learning speed.
The system should identify missed autonomy opportunities.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.171 Calibration Metrics

Possible metrics include:
Promotion success rate.
Demotion accuracy.
Incident rate by trust band.
Correction rate by trust band.
Founder override rate.
Business value by autonomy level.
False escalation rate.

19.172 Trust Score Accuracy

Accuracy is not whether the score predicts every individual run.
It is whether the score reliably supports better autonomy decisions over time.

19.173 Trust Score Dashboard

A dashboard may show:
Workflow.
Project.
Trust band.
Confidence.
Trend.
Current autonomy.
Promotion status.
Demotion risk.
Last violation.
Next review.

19.174 Trust Heatmap

A heatmap may visualize:
Projects.
Workflows.
Action categories.
Trust.
Autonomy.
Damage sensitivity.
License health.
It should not imply that one color authorizes action.

19.175 Trust Timeline

The timeline may show:
Score changes.
Workflow versions.
Promotions.
Demotions.
Violations.
Reviews.
Recoveries.
Business milestones.

19.176 Trust Graph

The Intelligence Graph should connect:
Workflow.
Trust Score.
Evidence.
Approvals.
Corrections.
Violations.
License.
Performance.
Decision.
Outcome.

19.177 Approval Inbox Integration

An autonomy request should show:
Trust Score.
Confidence.
Trend.
Sample size.
Critical dimension floors.
Violations.
Promotion blockers.
Recommended license scope.

19.178 Daily Executive Brief Integration

The Daily Brief should surface Trust Score only when material.
Examples:
Workflow became eligible for trial.
Trust declined sharply.
Serious violation occurred.
License review is due.
Founder burden can be reduced safely.

19.179 Weekly Planning Integration

Weekly planning may include:
Trust-building trials.
Evidence collection.
Control improvements.
Promotion reviews.
Recovery work.

19.180 Roadmap Integration

Autonomy roadmaps should include trust milestones.
Example:
Twenty successful internal runs.
Two weeks of approval-equivalent quality.
No serious violations.
Rollback validated.
Eligible for L4 trial.

19.181 Prioritization Integration

Trust-building work should be prioritized when:
It removes a founder bottleneck.
It unlocks meaningful business value.
The workflow has a stable use case.
The required evidence can be gathered safely.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.182 Opportunity Cost Integration

Increasing trust may require:
More review.
More testing.
Monitoring work.
Controlled trials.
The expected autonomy value should justify the investment.

19.183 Trust Score and Founder Capacity

Low founder capacity should not cause:
Lower review standards.
Manual score inflation.
Premature promotion.
It may justify:
Better batching.
More internal preparation.
Temporary safe restrictions.
Focused trust-building trials.

19.184 Trust Score and Crisis Mode

During Crisis Mode:
Promotion pauses.
External trust may be restricted.
Incident evidence dominates.
Monitoring increases.
Recovery evidence is collected.

19.185 Post-Crisis Trust

After crisis, trust should not return automatically to the prior level.
Restoration should require:
Root-cause resolution.
Control repair.
Testing.
Reduced-scope success.
Authorized review.

19.186 Trust Score Alerts

Alerts should occur when:
Critical floor fails.
P0 or P1 violation occurs.
Confidence collapses.
Score declines sharply.
Promotion criteria are met.
License scope exceeds supported trust.
Monitoring stops.

19.187 Trust Score Notifications

Routine score movement should remain quiet.
Only material changes should interrupt the founder.

19.188 Trust Score Search

The founder should be able to ask:
Why is this workflow trusted?
What prevents promotion?
Which workflows are ready for L4 trials?
Which scores are stale?
Which workflow lost trust this month?
What evidence would restore autonomy?

19.189 Conversational Trust Explanation

Atlas may say:
The Prompt short-news workflow has High Trust with medium confidence. Its drafts are usually approved unchanged, it has no policy violations, and its output quality is stable. Promotion is still limited to a small L4 trial because rollback at higher volume has not been tested.

19.190 Formal Trust Summary

A formal summary may look like:
Project:
The Prompt.
Workflow:
Short-News Publishing v3.
Trust Score:
84 — High Trust.
Confidence:
Medium.
Current Autonomy:
L3.
Strengths:
Strong approval alignment, perfect scope integrity, stable quality.
Risks:
Limited production scale and untested high-volume rollback.
Recommendation:
Grant a fourteen-day L4 trial for website publication only.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.191 Trust Score Ownership

The Trust Score system should have an owner responsible for:
Model integrity.
Weight review.
Calibration.
Data quality.
Conflict resolution.
Auditability.

19.192 Project Trust Owner

Project Executive should own contextual interpretation.
It should not be able to manipulate raw evidence or approve its own promotion.

19.193 Portfolio Trust Oversight

Portfolio Executive should monitor:
Cross-project consistency.
Systemic trust patterns.
Autonomy concentration.
Founder burden.
Governance health.
Shared workflow risks.

19.194 Human Review Authority

The founder or authorized approver retains final authority over material autonomy changes.

19.195 Specialist Review

Future workflows may require specialist review for trust interpretation in:
Security.
Legal.
Privacy.
Finance.
Child safety.
Health-adjacent domains.

19.196 Trust Score Export

Exports should preserve:
Scope.
Score version.
Evidence window.
Confidence.
Dimension scores.
Redactions.
Workflow version.
Authority references.

19.197 Trust Score Retention

Historical trust records should be retained for:
Calibration.
Incident review.
Autonomy history.
Workflow comparison.
Decision accountability.

19.198 Trust Score Privacy

Trust evidence may contain:
Customer outcomes.
Founder feedback.
Sensitive incident information.
Internal performance.
Access should remain project- and role-scoped.

19.199 Future Multi-User Organizations

Future organizations may define:
Trust reviewer.
Risk reviewer.
Project owner.
Autonomy approver.
Audit viewer.
Specialist approver.

19.200 Customer-Controlled Trust Models

Customer organizations may define their own:
Trust dimensions.
Weights.
Minimum floors.
Promotion requirements.
Review cadence.
Autonomy ceilings.
Global Omnira safety requirements should still apply where relevant.

19.201 Trust Score Simulation

Before production use, Omnira may simulate scores using historical data.
Simulation should test:
Promotion candidates.
Violation penalties.
Rare severe errors.
Score volatility.
Confidence behavior.
Project-specific weighting.

19.202 Historical Backtesting

Backtesting should ask:
Would the model have promoted unsafe workflows?
Would it have restricted reliable workflows?
Did severe incidents reduce trust early enough?
Did business value receive appropriate weight?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.203 Adversarial Testing

Testing should attempt:
Hiding failures.
Inflating easy-case volume.
Splitting incidents.
Changing labels.
Manipulating approval records.
Reusing evidence across versions.
Claiming another project’s trust.

19.204 Negative Testing

The system should verify that:
One P0 event blocks promotion.
Missing monitoring lowers confidence.
Wrong-project action collapses Scope Integrity.
Workflow-version change triggers review.
Expired evidence cannot support promotion.

19.205 Score Resilience

The score should remain stable against ordinary noise while reacting quickly to material risk.

19.206 Trust Score Debt

Trust Score debt occurs when:
Scores exist without reliable evidence.
Weights are undocumented.
Workflow versions are ignored.
Violations are missing.
Scores are used as authority.
Manual overrides are unlogged.

19.207 Shadow Trust

Shadow trust occurs when humans informally allow autonomy because a workflow “usually works” without formal measurement.
Shadow trust should be converted into:
Explicit evidence.
Trust record.
Governed license decision.

19.208 Trust Inflation

Trust inflation occurs when:
Success volume is overweighted.
Minor approvals dominate.
Severe rare failures are ignored.
Business pressure influences scoring.
Evidence is copied across contexts.

19.209 Trust Deflation

Trust deflation occurs when:
Minor stylistic edits are overweighted.
Correct escalations are treated as failures.
Low-risk experiments never count.
Historical incidents never allow recovery.
Business value is ignored.

19.210 Anti-Global-Trust Principle

No workflow, agent, model, or Executive should receive one universal Trust Score that governs all contexts.

19.211 Anti-Automatic-Authority Principle

Trust Score must never activate autonomy automatically.

19.212 Anti-Average-Only Principle

Average performance must not hide severe rare failures.

19.213 Anti-Volume Principle

High run count alone does not prove trust.

19.214 Anti-Time-Served Principle

A workflow does not become trusted merely because it has operated for a long time.

19.215 Anti-Success-Only Principle

Trust must include failures, corrections, violations, near misses, and business value.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.216 Anti-Approval-Fatigue Principle

Founder overload should not inflate trust or lower promotion standards.

19.217 Anti-Context-Transfer Principle

Trust must not transfer automatically across projects, versions, channels, audiences, or action categories.

19.218 Anti-Score-Gaming Principle

The measured workflow should not control its score, evidence selection, or promotion outcome.

19.219 Anti-Permanent-Penalty Principle

Trust should be recoverable through remediation and new evidence where appropriate.

19.220 Anti-False-Precision Principle

Numerical scores must communicate confidence and evidence limitations.

19.221 Anti-Business-Value-Override Principle

Strong revenue or output does not erase safety, policy, or scope failure.

19.222 Anti-Safety-Only Principle

A workflow that never causes harm but creates no value should not automatically receive broader autonomy.

19.223 The Scope Test

Before calculating or using trust, Omnira should ask:
Which project?
Which workflow?
Which version?
Which action category?
Which channel?
Which audience?

19.224 The Evidence Test

Omnira should ask:
How many relevant cases exist?
How recent are they?
Are outcomes verified?
Does the evidence match the current version?

19.225 The Quality Test

Omnira should ask:
How often is output approved unchanged?
What kinds of corrections occur?
Are factual or policy corrections present?

19.226 The Compliance Test

Omnira should ask:
Were policies respected?
Was project scope correct?
Were approvals and license conditions followed?
Did any violation occur?

19.227 The Severity Test

Omnira should ask:
Do averages hide rare severe failures?
What is the worst correction or violation?
Was material harm prevented only through human review?

19.228 The Stability Test

Omnira should ask:
Is performance consistent?
Does quality change with scale?
Does the workflow fail in clusters?
Is the provider stable?

19.229 The Value Test

Omnira should ask:
What business value was created?
Was founder burden reduced?
Did customer or project outcomes improve?

19.230 The Monitoring Test

Omnira should ask:
Can every action be observed?
Are outcomes verified?
Can failures remain hidden?
Are alerts reliable?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.231 The Recovery Test

Omnira should ask:
Can autonomy be stopped?
Can actions be rolled back?
Can customers and systems recover?
Has recovery been tested?

19.232 The Confidence Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the sample large enough?
Is the observation period long enough?
Were enough scenarios tested?
Is the score method current?

19.233 The Promotion Test

Omnira should ask:
Does evidence support the exact requested authority?
Are critical dimension floors met?
Are blockers absent?
Does broader autonomy create meaningful value?

19.234 The Demotion Test

Omnira should ask:
Did trust decline materially?
Did a hard blocker appear?
Which authority should be removed?
What safe scope may continue?

19.235 The Recovery Test After Violation

Omnira should ask:
Was root cause addressed?
Were controls improved?
Did reduced-scope operation remain stable?
Is restoration justified?

19.236 The Gaming Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the workflow selecting only easy cases?
Are failures missing?
Did case mix change?
Does reported success match independent outcomes?

19.237 Failure Modes

The Trust Score architecture must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Trust Equals Authority
A high score activates autonomy automatically.
Failure Mode 2 — Global Trust
One score applies across unrelated projects and actions.
Failure Mode 3 — Average Hides Severity
Many easy successes hide one serious failure.
Failure Mode 4 — Volume Inflation
Large run count is mistaken for quality.
Failure Mode 5 — Version Leakage
Trust survives a material workflow change.
Failure Mode 6 — Project Transfer
Trust from one project is reused in another.
Failure Mode 7 — Approval Fatigue Promotion
Founder overload is interpreted as trust.
Failure Mode 8 — Business Value Override
Revenue hides policy or safety failure.
Failure Mode 9 — Safety Without Value
A useless workflow receives autonomy because it rarely fails.
Failure Mode 10 — Missing Confidence
A precise-looking score is based on weak evidence.
Failure Mode 11 — Score Gaming
The workflow manipulates cases, logs, or labels.
Failure Mode 12 — Hidden Incidents
Failures are omitted from trust evidence.
Failure Mode 13 — Permanent Distrust
A remediated workflow can never recover.
Failure Mode 14 — Trust Inflation
Positive evidence is overweighted.
Failure Mode 15 — Trust Deflation
Minor edits and correct escalations are over-penalized.
Failure Mode 16 — Uncalibrated Progression
Trust bands do not predict safe autonomy outcomes.
These failure modes should be treated as foundational governance constraints.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.238 Design Requirements

Any implementation of Trust Score and Autonomy Progression should preserve these requirements:
Every Trust Score must have explicit project and workflow scope.
Every Trust Score must identify the workflow version.
Trust must remain action- and context-specific.
Trust Score must remain separate from autonomy authority.
Every score must include confidence.
Every score must identify its evidence window and sample size.
Successful runs must require correct scope, policy, destination, and outcome.
Corrections must be classified by severity.
Policy and scope failures must carry stronger penalties than cosmetic edits.
Severe violations must not average away.
Business value and founder burden reduction must be measured.
High business value must not override safety or policy failure.
Monitoring and recovery readiness must influence promotion.
Critical dimensions must have minimum floors.
Hard blockers must prevent promotion regardless of total score.
Material workflow changes must trigger trust review.
Trust must decay when evidence becomes stale.
Trust may recover only through remediation and new evidence.
No workflow may alter its own score or promotion authority.
Promotion must create a governed decision package.
Demotion may occur automatically only under explicit policy.
Every material trust-based autonomy decision must connect to the Decision Ledger.
The Trust Score system must be calibrated against actual autonomy outcomes.

19.239 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the behavioral trust contract.
It does not require a particular formula, numerical range, database schema, or machine-learning model.
The architecture may later be implemented through:
Trust records.
Behavioral event streams.
Approval analytics.
Correction classification.
Violation records.
Performance metrics.
Confidence models.
Score bands.
Promotion gates.
Demotion triggers.
Review queues.
Decision Ledger links.
Autonomy-license integrations.
Dashboards.
Atlas explanations.
The technical implementation may evolve.
The trust contract must remain stable.

19.240 The Trust Score Contract

Omnira must:
Measure demonstrated behavior rather than claimed capability.
Keep trust scoped to project, workflow, version, action, and context.
Distinguish technical success from safe and valuable success.
Weight correction and violation severity appropriately.
Treat correct refusal and escalation as positive evidence.
Include business value and founder burden reduction.
Communicate confidence and evidence limitations.
Prevent severe failures from disappearing inside averages.
Prevent trust from transferring automatically.
Use Trust Score to prepare autonomy recommendations.
Require governance and valid authority for promotion.
Reduce or suspend autonomy when trust conditions weaken.
Support evidence-based recovery.
Detect gaming and missing evidence.
Continuously calibrate trust against real autonomy outcomes.
A feature that does not support this contract should not influence autonomy progression.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
19.241 Closing Principle

Autonomy should grow at the same speed as demonstrated judgment.
Not at the speed of technical capability.
Not at the speed of founder impatience.
Not at the speed of workflow volume.
Not at the speed of AI confidence.
A trusted workflow should repeatedly demonstrate:
I act in the correct project.
I remain inside my authority.
I produce useful outcomes.
I require few material corrections.
I respect policy.
I recognize when to escalate.
I remain stable.
I report failures honestly.
I can be monitored.
I can be stopped.
I reduce human burden without increasing unacceptable risk.
Trust Score makes that evidence visible.
Autonomy Licensing converts approved trust into bounded authority.
Governance ensures that authority remains legitimate.
The Damage Boundary ensures that trust never becomes permission to create uncontrolled harm.
The mature Omnira system should therefore promote autonomy carefully, demote it quickly when required, and preserve the founder’s ability to understand exactly why every workflow is trusted—or why it is not.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Mission Brief as an Execution Contract
text:
20.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Executive Intelligence must convert decisions into executable organizational work.
A recommendation is not a mission.
A roadmap milestone is not a mission.
A priority is not a mission.
A founder instruction is not necessarily a sufficiently defined mission.
Before Manager and Workforce can act, Omnira must translate executive intent into a bounded execution contract.
That contract is the Executive Mission Brief.
A Mission Brief should make it possible to answer:
