What must be achieved?
Why does it matter?
Which project owns the work?
What does success look like?
What is inside scope?
What is outside scope?
Which authority exists?
Which tools and data may be used?
Which actions are forbidden?
Where are the approval gates?
What is the deadline?
How should progress be reported?
When should work stop or escalate?
The Mission Brief is the bridge between strategy and execution.

20.2 The Core Thesis

Executive Intelligence should define the outcome.
Manager should coordinate the execution.
Workforce should perform the work.
The canonical separation is:
Executive Intelligence:
Defines purpose, outcome, constraints, authority, and success.
Manager:
Plans, routes, sequences, and supervises execution.
Workforce:
Executes bounded work and reports evidence.
Governance:
Determines what may be done.
Founder:
Retains final authority where required.
The foundational principle is:
Workforce should never need to invent the strategic meaning, authority, or success criteria of its own mission.

20.3 Mission Brief as an Execution Contract

A Mission Brief is more than a prompt.
It is a structured contract.
It should define:
Objective.
Context.
Desired outcome.
Success criteria.
Scope.
Constraints.
Authority.
Resources.
Tools.
Forbidden actions.
Approval gates.
Deadline.
Reporting.
Escalation.
Completion conditions.
The Mission Brief should remain understandable to humans and executable by systems.

20.4 Mission Brief vs Prompt

A prompt instructs a model.
A Mission Brief governs organizational work.
A prompt may say:
Analyze our publishing workflow.
A Mission Brief should say:
Project:
The Prompt.
Objective:
Determine why short-news publication fails to persist reliably.
Success:
Root cause identified, evidence provided, safe fix plan prepared.
Constraints:
Read-only investigation. No production changes.
Approval Gate:
Implementation requires founder approval.
Deadline:
Before the next publishing window.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.5 Mission Brief vs Task

A Mission Brief defines a meaningful outcome.
A task is a specific unit of work inside the mission.
Example:
Mission:
Validate project isolation before broader autonomy.
Tasks:
Audit RLS.
Test cross-project queries.
Inspect credentials.
Review cron behavior.
Produce remediation plan.
Manager may create tasks from the mission.

20.6 Mission Brief vs Roadmap Milestone

A roadmap milestone describes what must become true.
A Mission Brief delegates work intended to make it true.
Example:
Milestone:
Approval architecture is operational and validated.
Mission:
Design and validate a project-scoped Approval Inbox with decision-ready context, action controls, and auditability.

20.7 Mission Brief vs Decision

A decision authorizes direction.
A Mission Brief operationalizes that direction.
Example:
Decision:
The Prompt will become the first autonomy proving ground.
Mission:
Prepare the short-news workflow for a bounded L4 publishing trial.

20.8 Mission Brief vs Workflow

A workflow is a repeatable execution mechanism.
A Mission Brief may:
Create a workflow.
Use an existing workflow.
Modify a workflow.
Validate a workflow.
Retire a workflow.
The mission remains the higher-level executive contract.

20.9 Mission Brief vs Project

A project is an enduring organizational scope.
A mission is temporary and outcome-specific.
A project may contain many missions.

20.10 Mission Brief vs Role

A Workforce role describes a reusable capability.
A mission assigns that capability to a bounded objective.
Example:
Role:
Editorial Researcher.
Mission Assignment:
Validate sources for The Prompt short-news autonomy trial.

20.11 Mission Types

Executive Mission Briefs may include:
Strategic Mission.
Build Mission.
Investigation Mission.
Validation Mission.
Growth Mission.
Stabilization Mission.
Risk-Reduction Mission.
Recovery Mission.
Learning Mission.
Operational Mission.
Governance Mission.
Autonomy Mission.

20.12 Strategic Mission

A Strategic Mission may:
Evaluate a new project direction.
Prepare a portfolio decision.
Compare strategic alternatives.
Design a roadmap.
Assess project reactivation.
Strategic Missions usually require Executive review before external action.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.13 Build Mission

A Build Mission creates or changes a capability.
Examples:
Build an Approval Inbox.
Create a performance collector.
Implement project-scoped memory retrieval.
Prepare a new publishing workflow.
Build Missions should define technical and governance constraints.

20.14 Investigation Mission

An Investigation Mission seeks evidence without changing the system.
It should normally define:
Read-only scope.
Evidence requirements.
Systems to inspect.
Questions to answer.
No-change constraints.
Reporting format.

20.15 Validation Mission

A Validation Mission determines whether an existing capability is safe, correct, or ready.
Examples:
Validate project isolation.
Validate rollback.
Validate migration safety.
Validate publishing persistence.
Validate autonomy readiness.

20.16 Growth Mission

A Growth Mission seeks measurable commercial or audience improvement.
It should define:
Target outcome.
Baseline.
Experiment scope.
Budget.
Channels.
Customer boundaries.
Success and stop criteria.

20.17 Stabilization Mission

A Stabilization Mission improves:
Reliability.
Quality.
Security.
Operational consistency.
Cost control.
Incident resistance.
It should generally avoid unnecessary feature expansion.

20.18 Risk-Reduction Mission

A Risk-Reduction Mission addresses a known exposure.
It should define:
Risk.
Current severity.
Affected systems.
Required control.
Residual-risk target.
Escalation threshold.

20.19 Recovery Mission

A Recovery Mission follows:
Incident.
Failed rollout.
Policy violation.
Autonomy suspension.
Data problem.
Customer harm.
It should prioritize containment, restoration, evidence preservation, and safe restart.

20.20 Learning Mission

A Learning Mission reduces uncertainty.
It should define:
Question.
Hypothesis.
Experiment.
Evidence.
Decision affected.
Timebox.
Stopping condition.

20.21 Operational Mission

An Operational Mission maintains or executes an established process.
Examples:
Prepare the weekly newsletter.
Run the monthly performance review.
Maintain content freshness.
Process standard support requests.
Operational Missions should usually use existing policies and workflows.

20.22 Governance Mission

A Governance Mission may:
Create a policy proposal.
Audit permissions.
Review autonomy licenses.
Map approval authority.
Test the Damage Boundary.
Remove governance debt.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.23 Autonomy Mission

An Autonomy Mission prepares or validates a workflow for increased authority.
It should include:
Current autonomy level.
Target level.
Evidence required.
Trial design.
Controls.
Rollback.
Trust thresholds.
Approval requirement.

20.24 The Mission Brief Object

A canonical Mission Brief should eventually exist as a structured object.
Conceptually, it may contain:
Mission identifier.
Title.
Project.
Mission type.
Executive owner.
Mission owner.
Objective.
Strategic context.
Expected outcome.
Success criteria.
Scope.
Out-of-scope items.
Dependencies.
Assumptions.
Risks.
Constraints.
Authority.
Allowed tools.
Allowed data.
Forbidden actions.
Approval gates.
Budget.
Deadline.
Priority.
Reporting cadence.
Escalation triggers.
Stop conditions.
Completion evidence.
Review date.
Status.
Version.
Decision Ledger reference.

20.25 Mission Identifier

Every mission should have a stable identifier.
It should be referenced by:
Tasks.
Workflow runs.
Approvals.
Reports.
Decisions.
Incidents.
Performance results.
Completion records.

20.26 Mission Title

A strong title should describe the intended outcome.
Weak:
Work on publishing.
Strong:
Prepare The Prompt Short-News Workflow for an L4 Publishing Trial.

20.27 Project Scope

Every mission must identify its project.
A mission without clear project scope should not activate.
Project scope determines:
Data.
Credentials.
Policies.
Budget.
Brand.
Customers.
Approvers.
Autonomy.

20.28 Cross-Project Missions

Cross-project missions should be exceptional.
They should define:
Participating projects.
Shared objective.
Minimum data exchange.
Portfolio authority.
Isolation controls.
Project-specific outputs.
Duration.

20.29 Executive Owner

The Executive owner is responsible for the mission’s strategic validity.
Possible owners:
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Founder.
Authorized governance role.
The Executive owner does not necessarily perform the work.

20.30 Mission Owner

The Mission owner is accountable for delivering the mission outcome.
This may be:
Manager.
Workforce lead.
Human project owner.
Specialized agent team.
One mission should have one accountable owner.

20.31 Mission Objective

The objective should state what the mission is intended to achieve.
It should be:
Outcome-oriented.
Specific.
Strategically relevant.
Bounded.
Verifiable.
Weak:
Improve Memory.
Strong:
Resolve the Stage 1 Memory schema and ownership conflicts so implementation can proceed safely on the dedicated branch.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.32 Strategic Context

Strategic context explains why the mission matters.
It may include:
Related objective.
Roadmap milestone.
Decision.
Risk.
Revenue opportunity.
Project mode.
Portfolio tradeoff.
Workforce should understand enough context to make correct local choices.

20.33 Context Minimization

The mission should include the context required for execution.
It should not expose unnecessary:
Founder-private information.
Other project data.
Sensitive strategy.
Unrelated Decision Ledger history.
Confidential customer details.

20.34 Expected Outcome

The expected outcome describes the future state that should exist after successful completion.
Example:
The publishing persistence defect is understood, a safe remediation is prepared, and no production changes have been made without approval.

20.35 Deliverables

Deliverables are concrete artifacts or outputs.
Examples:
Audit report.
Implementation plan.
Code change.
Test results.
Policy proposal.
Workflow configuration.
Decision package.
Performance analysis.
Deliverables support the outcome.
They are not always the outcome itself.

20.36 Success Criteria

Success criteria define how completion is judged.
They should be:
Observable.
Relevant.
Sufficient.
Non-contradictory.
Connected to the objective.

20.37 Quantitative Success Criteria

Examples:
All project-isolation tests pass.
Zero cross-project query leakage.
Correction rate below 5%.
Workflow completes thirty successful trial runs.
Build and typecheck pass.

20.38 Qualitative Success Criteria

Examples:
The root cause is supported by evidence.
The recommendation is implementation-ready.
The policy is understandable and enforceable.
The user experience remains coherent.
Qualitative criteria should still be reviewable.

20.39 Minimum Success

A mission may define the minimum acceptable outcome.
Example:
Minimum:
Identify the root cause and produce a safe fix plan.
Target:
Implement and validate the fix after approval.

20.40 Target Success

Target success describes the desired complete result.

20.41 Stretch Success

Stretch outcomes may be included where they do not compromise the core mission.
They must not silently expand scope.

20.42 Scope

Scope defines what the mission includes.
Examples:
Specific files.
Specific workflows.
Specific customer category.
Specific time period.
Specific channels.
Specific data sources.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.43 Out-of-Scope Items

Out-of-scope items should be explicit where confusion is likely.
Example:
Out of scope:
Homepage redesign.
Newsletter sending.
Pricing changes.
Cross-project content reuse.
Production deployment.

20.44 Scope Boundaries

Scope should limit:
Projects.
Systems.
Actions.
Data.
Tools.
Time.
Budget.
External effects.

20.45 Scope Change

A material scope change should require:
Mission revision.
Authority review.
Capacity review.
Deadline review.
Approval where required.
Manager should not silently expand the mission.

20.46 Mission Constraints

Constraints define how the mission must be performed.
Examples:
Read-only.
No production changes.
No external publishing.
Use existing architecture.
Do not create new dependencies.
Remain on the dedicated branch.
Do not push to main.
Preserve project isolation.
Use reversible changes.

20.47 Technical Constraints

Technical constraints may include:
Required environment.
Repository.
Branch.
Framework.
Schema boundaries.
Testing requirements.
Migration restrictions.
Deployment restrictions.

20.48 Product Constraints

Product constraints may include:
Brand tone.
User experience.
Customer promise.
Accessibility.
Mobile behavior.
Approval experience.
Project identity.

20.49 Governance Constraints

Governance constraints may include:
Approval required before implementation.
No spending.
No external side effects.
No policy modification.
No autonomy expansion.
No permanent deletion.

20.50 Capacity Constraints

Capacity constraints may include:
Founder review limited to one decision package.
No interruption of current production workflow.
Use existing Workforce roles.
Timebox investigation.
Limit AI cost.

20.51 Time Constraints

A deadline may be:
Exact.
Target.
Conditional.
Event-driven.
Review-based.
The mission should distinguish these.

20.52 Budget

The mission should define:
No spend.
Approved maximum.
Allowed vendors.
Model-cost ceiling.
Infrastructure ceiling.
Approval threshold.

20.53 Authority

Authority defines what the mission may decide or change.
Possible authority includes:
Read.
Analyze.
Prepare.
Create internal records.
Modify development code.
Run tests.
Create drafts.
Deploy to preview.
Publish.
Spend.
Contact customers.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.54 Authority Source

The mission should identify the source of authority.
Examples:
Founder instruction.
Decision Ledger decision.
Active project policy.
Budget mandate.
Autonomy license.
Portfolio decision.

20.55 No Implied Authority

A mission should not imply authority from vague wording.
Example:
“Fix publishing”
does not automatically mean:
Deploy to production.
Delete data.
Change policy.
Publish content.

20.56 Allowed Actions

Allowed actions should be explicit.
Example:
Inspect code.
Read database schema.
Run tests.
Prepare patch.
Commit to the dedicated branch.
Create implementation report.

20.57 Forbidden Actions

Forbidden actions should be explicit where risk is material.
Example:
Do not merge to main.
Do not deploy.
Do not alter production data.
Do not disable RLS.
Do not widen tool permissions.
Do not create unapproved migrations.

20.58 Tools

The mission should define which tools may be used.
Examples:
Repository tools.
Supabase read-only access.
Browser testing.
Analytics.
Approved MCPs.
Internal reporting tools.

20.59 Tool Restrictions

Tool restrictions may define:
Read-only mode.
No external sends.
No destructive operations.
Project-specific credentials only.
No tool installation.
No new MCP connection.

20.60 Data Access

The mission should define:
Allowed data.
Required data.
Restricted data.
Retention.
Export restrictions.
Project scope.

20.61 Minimum Necessary Data

Workforce should receive only the data required for the mission.

20.62 Dependencies

Dependencies may include:
Prior decisions.
Other missions.
Technical capabilities.
Founder approval.
External providers.
Project modes.
Data availability.

20.63 Hard Dependencies

A hard dependency blocks activation or completion.
Example:
Implementation cannot begin until the architecture plan is approved.

20.64 Soft Dependencies

A soft dependency improves execution but does not block it.

20.65 Dependency Owner

Every material dependency should have an owner or source.

20.66 Assumptions

The Mission Brief should state important assumptions.
Example:
Assumption:
The current main branch contains the latest merged isolation changes.

20.67 Critical Assumptions

A critical assumption is one whose failure changes the mission.
Example:
Assumption:
The issue can be reproduced without production writes.
If false:
Pause and request revised authority.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.68 Risks

The mission should identify material risks.
Examples:
Data leakage.
Production outage.
Scope expansion.
Duplicate external action.
Unexpected spend.
Founder overload.
Brand damage.

20.69 Risk Controls

Each material risk should have:
Preventive control.
Detection.
Escalation.
Fallback.
Owner.

20.70 Damage Boundary

The Mission Brief should state whether any planned action may cross the Damage Boundary.
If yes, it should define:
Approval gate.
Required authority.
Safer alternative.
Rollback.
Residual risk.

20.71 Approval Gates

Approval gates define where execution must pause.
Examples:
Before implementation.
Before migration.
Before deployment.
Before publishing.
Before spending.
Before customer contact.
Before scope expansion.
Before autonomy activation.

20.72 Gate Inputs

An approval gate should receive a decision-ready package.
It may include:
Recommendation.
Evidence.
Alternatives.
Risk.
Opportunity cost.
Changes.
Tests.
Rollback.
Decision required.

20.73 Gate Outcomes

Possible outcomes:
Approve.
Approve with conditions.
Edit and approve.
Reject.
Request more evidence.
Request alternative.
Defer.
Escalate.

20.74 Pre-Approved Actions

Some actions may already be covered by:
Policy.
Mission authority.
Autonomy license.
Budget mandate.
The Mission Brief should identify them.

20.75 Approval Expiration

Approval should expire if:
The object changes materially.
Scope expands.
Risk changes.
The deadline passes.
The workflow version changes.
The project mode changes.

20.76 Reporting Requirements

The Mission Brief should define how Manager reports progress.
Possible reporting modes:
Event-driven only.
Daily summary.
Milestone report.
Approval-gate report.
Completion report.
Incident report.

20.77 Quiet Execution

Healthy routine execution should remain quiet.
Reports should focus on:
Material progress.
Blockers.
Risk.
Decision requirements.
Scope change.
Completion.

20.78 Progress Report

A progress report may include:
Current status.
Work completed.
Evidence.
Remaining work.
Blockers.
Risk changes.
Next step.
Decision required.

20.79 Completion Report

A completion report should include:
Objective.
Outcome.
Success criteria.
Deliverables.
Tests.
Changes.
Known limitations.
Risks.
Follow-up.
Decision required.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.80 Evidence Requirements

The mission should define what evidence proves completion.
Examples:
Test output.
Screenshots.
Logs.
Metrics.
Diff.
User validation.
Policy evaluation.
Production observation.

20.81 Evidence Quality

Evidence should be:
Relevant.
Current.
Traceable.
Reproducible where possible.
Project-scoped.
Sufficient for review.

20.82 Reporting to Executive Intelligence

Manager should compress operational detail into executive-relevant information.
Executive Intelligence should not need to inspect every task.

20.83 Reporting to the Founder

The founder should receive:
What changed.
Why it matters.
What remains.
What decision is needed.
What risk exists.

20.84 Escalation Triggers

The mission should define when Workforce or Manager must escalate.
Examples:
Scope is ambiguous.
A critical assumption fails.
A policy conflict appears.
The Damage Boundary is crossed.
A deadline becomes impossible.
Required data is missing.
A serious defect is discovered.
The project is wrong.
Cost exceeds limit.

20.85 Escalation Destination

The mission should define whether escalation goes to:
Manager.
Project Executive.
Portfolio Executive.
Founder.
Governance.
Specialist reviewer.
Crisis process.

20.86 Escalation Package

An escalation should include:
Issue.
Impact.
Evidence.
Attempted resolution.
Options.
Recommendation.
Decision required.
Urgency.

20.87 No Silent Blockers

A blocked mission should not remain active without reporting.

20.88 Stop Conditions

Stop conditions define when execution must cease.
Examples:
P0 or P1 violation.
Wrong-project access.
Uncontrolled production effect.
Budget exhausted.
Approval denied.
Critical dependency failure.
Monitoring unavailable.
Mission objective becomes invalid.

20.89 Pause Conditions

Pause may be appropriate when:
More evidence is required.
Founder review is pending.
External provider is unstable.
Risk is temporary.
Scope requires clarification.

20.90 Safe Continuation

When external execution is blocked, safe work may continue.
Examples:
Drafting.
Testing.
Evidence collection.
Documentation.
Alternative preparation.
Internal simulation.

20.91 Kill Switch

Every high-impact mission should define who may stop it.
Possible authorities:
Founder.
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Governance engine.
Manager under explicit policy.
Crisis process.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Task Completion Is Not Mission Completion
text:
20.92 Completion Conditions

A mission is complete when:
The outcome exists.
Success criteria are met.
Required evidence exists.
Approvals are resolved.
Known limitations are documented.
Ownership is transferred where needed.

20.93 Task Completion Is Not Mission Completion

All tasks may be complete while the mission outcome remains unmet.
Example:
All implementation tasks completed.
Production validation failed.
Mission remains incomplete.

20.94 Partial Completion

A mission may close as partially complete when:
Minimum outcome achieved.
Target outcome blocked.
Remaining work is explicitly transferred.
Risk is acceptable.
Executive owner approves closure.

20.95 Failed Mission

A mission may fail when:
Objective cannot be achieved.
Critical assumptions fail.
Risk becomes unacceptable.
Authority is withdrawn.
Success criteria are not met.
The strategic need disappears.
Failure should produce learning.

20.96 Cancelled Mission

A mission may be cancelled because:
Priority changes.
Roadmap changes.
Project mode changes.
Opportunity cost increases.
The work is no longer valuable.
Cancellation is not necessarily failure.

20.97 Superseded Mission

A mission may be replaced by a newer mission with:
Different scope.
Different objective.
Different approach.
Different authority.

20.98 Mission Status

A mission may have status:
Draft.
Proposed.
Awaiting Approval.
Approved.
Ready.
Active.
Blocked.
Paused.
At Risk.
Awaiting Review.
Completed.
Partially Completed.
Failed.
Cancelled.
Superseded.
Archived.

20.99 Draft Mission

A Draft Mission grants no execution authority.

20.100 Approved Mission

An Approved Mission has valid executive authority but may still wait for dependencies.

20.101 Ready Mission

A Ready Mission has:
Valid authority.
Available dependencies.
Assigned owner.
Required tools.
Active policy.
No unresolved blocker.

20.102 Active Mission

An Active Mission is currently being executed.

20.103 Blocked Mission

A Blocked Mission cannot progress because of a specific dependency or decision.
The blocker should be explicit.

20.104 At-Risk Mission

An At-Risk Mission may continue but is likely to miss outcome, deadline, cost, or quality expectations.

20.105 Mission Activation

Before activation, Omnira should verify:
Project scope.
Objective.
Owner.
Authority.
Constraints.
Dependencies.
Tools.
Data access.
Approval gates.
Budget.
Deadline.
Reporting.
Stop conditions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.106 Activation Failure

If activation requirements are incomplete:
The mission remains inactive.
Missing elements are reported.
No external execution begins.

20.107 Mission Decomposition

Manager may decompose the mission into:
Workstreams.
Tasks.
Checkpoints.
Role assignments.
Workflow runs.
Review gates.

20.108 Decomposition Boundaries

Manager may not change:
Strategic objective.
Project scope.
Authority.
Forbidden actions.
Budget ceiling.
Approval gates.
Damage Boundary.
without an approved mission revision.

20.109 Workstreams

A complex mission may contain several workstreams.
Example:
Architecture.
Implementation.
Testing.
Governance.
UX.
Rollout.
Measurement.

20.110 Task Creation

Tasks should inherit:
Project.
Mission.
Authority.
Constraints.
Priority.
Reporting.
Traceability.

20.111 Task-Level Narrowing

A task should receive less authority than the mission where possible.

20.112 Role Assignment

Manager should assign roles based on:
Capability.
Availability.
Trust.
Tool access.
Project context.
Risk.

20.113 Separation of Duties

High-risk missions may separate:
Builder.
Reviewer.
Approver.
Deployer.
Auditor.

20.114 Agent Selection

Agent selection should consider:
Relevant skill.
Context.
Trust evidence.
Model requirements.
Cost.
Risk.
Tool compatibility.

20.115 Model Selection

AI Intelligence may select models according to:
Reasoning depth.
Quality needs.
Latency.
Cost.
Data policy.
Fallback.
The Mission Brief should express intent, not necessarily hard-code model names.

20.116 Mission Cognitive Depth

A mission may require:
Fast Executive Response.
Standard Executive Review.
Deep Executive Analysis.
Board Review.
Manager should not downgrade required reasoning depth for speed.

20.117 Mission Priority

The mission should have a priority classification.
Possible classifications:
P0 — Immediate Critical.
P1 — Executive Priority.
P2 — Planned Priority.
P3 — Prepared Opportunity.
P4 — Parked.

20.118 Priority Is Not Permission

A P0 mission still requires valid authority.
Urgency does not override governance.

20.119 Mission Capacity

The brief may estimate:
Founder effort.
Workforce effort.
Technical effort.
Approval effort.
AI cost.
Operational maintenance.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.120 Founder Capacity

Founder-dependent moments should be identified.
Examples:
Strategy approval.
Architecture decision.
Budget approval.
Production release.
Sensitive customer judgment.

20.121 Approval Window

Where possible, founder decisions should be batched into defined approval windows.

20.122 Mission Deadline

The deadline should identify:
Exact date.
Target range.
Decision gate.
External event.
Dependency condition.

20.123 Deadline Consequence

The Mission Brief should state what happens if the deadline is missed.
Examples:
Revenue delayed.
Autonomy trial postponed.
Customer impact continues.
Risk remains active.
No material consequence.

20.124 Deadline Confidence

The mission may include:
High confidence.
Medium confidence.
Low confidence.
based on dependency and capacity certainty.

20.125 Mission Assumption Review

Critical assumptions should be reviewed when:
Evidence changes.
A dependency fails.
The deadline moves.
Scope changes.
The project mode changes.

20.126 Mission Change Control

A material mission change should produce a new version.
Material changes include:
Objective.
Scope.
Authority.
Budget.
Deadline.
Success criteria.
Approval gate.
Risk.
Project.

20.127 Mission Versioning

Version history should preserve:
Previous brief.
Changes.
Reason.
Authority.
Effective date.
Affected tasks.

20.128 Silent Mission Mutation

Manager or Workforce must not silently rewrite the mission.

20.129 Mission Revision Request

A revision request should include:
Current constraint.
Proposed change.
Reason.
Impact.
Opportunity cost.
Risk.
Decision required.

20.130 Scope Expansion Request

A scope expansion should state:
What new work is added?
Why is it required?
What authority changes?
What deadline changes?
What capacity is displaced?

20.131 Mission Reprioritization

Portfolio or Project Executive may reprioritize a mission.
The system should record:
Previous priority.
New priority.
Reason.
Interrupted work.
Opportunity cost.
Review condition.

20.132 Mission Pause

A pause should define:
What stops.
What may continue.
Why.
Review date.
Restart conditions.

20.133 Mission Restart

Restart should verify:
Objective remains valid.
Authority remains valid.
Dependencies remain current.
Brief version is current.
Risks are acceptable.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.134 Mission Handoff

A mission may be handed from one owner to another.
Handoff should include:
Current state.
Evidence.
Outstanding work.
Risks.
Decisions.
Access.
Authority.

20.135 Mission Continuity

The new owner should not need to reconstruct the mission from scattered chat history.

20.136 Mission Memory

Durable mission lessons may enter Memory.
Examples:
This workflow requires two-source validation.
This type of migration needs additional isolation testing.
Founder review works best as one consolidated package.
Mission state should remain in the operational system.

20.137 Mission and Decision Ledger

Material mission creation may link to the Decision Ledger when it implements a strategic decision.
Material changes, cancellations, or failures may also require ledger entries.
Routine task changes usually do not.

20.138 Mission and Roadmap

Every strategic mission should link to:
Objective.
Roadmap phase.
Milestone.
Decision gate.

20.139 Mission and Prioritization

The mission should explain why it deserves capacity now.

20.140 Mission and Opportunity Cost

A material mission should identify:
What it delays.
Which project loses capacity.
Which founder work is displaced.
Which alternative was rejected.

20.141 Mission and Governance

Governance should evaluate:
Mission authority.
Allowed actions.
Approval gates.
Tool permissions.
Data access.
Budget.
Project mode.
before activation.

20.142 Mission and Damage Boundary

The Mission Brief should identify high-impact actions before Workforce reaches them.

20.143 Mission and Autonomy License

An active autonomy license may allow part of the mission to proceed without individual approval.
The brief should state:
Which license applies.
Which actions it covers.
Which actions remain gated.
When it expires.

20.144 Mission and Trust Score

Trust Score may influence:
Role assignment.
Review intensity.
Trial scale.
Autonomy recommendation.
Monitoring.
Trust does not modify mission authority by itself.

20.145 Mission and Performance Intelligence

Performance Intelligence should measure:
Progress.
Outcome.
Cost.
Quality.
Delay.
Founder burden.
Business value.
Risk.

20.146 Mission and AI Intelligence

AI Intelligence should support:
Reasoning-tier selection.
Provider selection.
Cost estimation.
Fallback.
Quality monitoring.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.147 Mission and Manager

Manager owns operational orchestration.
Manager should:
Decompose work.
Assign roles.
Sequence tasks.
Track dependencies.
Collect evidence.
Enforce checkpoints.
Escalate exceptions.
Report progress.

20.148 Manager Must Not Redefine Strategy

Manager may optimize the route.
It may not redefine the destination.

20.149 Mission and Workforce

Workforce should understand:
What outcome matters.
What it may do.
What it must not do.
What evidence is required.
When to escalate.
When to stop.

20.150 Mission and Agents

Agents should receive task-specific instructions derived from the Mission Brief.
They should not receive broad unused authority.

20.151 Mission and Tools

Tool calls should carry:
Mission identifier.
Project.
Task.
Actor.
Authority.
Action.
Trace identifier.

20.152 Mission Traceability

The system should connect:
Decision.
Mission.
Tasks.
Workflow runs.
Approvals.
Actions.
Evidence.
Outcome.

20.153 Mission Graph

The Operating Graph should show:
Project.
Mission.
Owner.
Roles.
Workflows.
Tasks.
Dependencies.
Status.

20.154 Intelligence Graph

The Intelligence Graph should connect:
Decision.
Mission rationale.
Evidence.
Outcome.
Performance.
Learning.
Next recommendation.

20.155 Mission Dashboard

A Mission dashboard may show:
Active missions.
Project.
Objective.
Owner.
Priority.
Status.
Next gate.
Risk.
Deadline.
Decision required.

20.156 Mission Detail View

The detail view should include:
Brief.
Progress.
Tasks.
Evidence.
Approvals.
Changes.
Reports.
Incidents.
Completion.

20.157 Mission Search

The founder should be able to ask:
What is Workforce doing?
Why is this mission active?
What is blocked?
Which mission needs my approval?
What does success look like?
What is The Prompt waiting for?

20.158 Atlas Mission Explanation

Atlas should explain missions in executive language.
Example:
The active mission is validating News Hunter persistence. Workforce may inspect and prepare a fix on the dedicated branch, but it may not deploy or merge to main. Success means the duplicate persistence path is handled safely and covered by tests.

20.159 Mission Recommendation Card

A proposed mission card may show:
Objective.
Why now.
Expected value.
Owner.
Capacity.
Deadline.
Risk.
Approval required.
Opportunity cost.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.160 Mission Approval

Mission approval should confirm:
Objective.
Scope.
Authority.
Constraints.
Budget.
Deadline.
Approval gates.
Owner.

20.161 Mission Batch Approval

Several low-risk missions may be approved as a batch when:
They share project.
They share policy.
They have similar risk.
Authority is clear.
Capacity is available.

20.162 Mission Templates

Templates may exist for:
Read-only audit.
Bug investigation.
Implementation.
Migration.
Publishing experiment.
Autonomy trial.
Customer-support analysis.
Crisis containment.
Roadmap design.
Templates should never replace project-specific context.

20.163 Read-Only Audit Template

A read-only mission should emphasize:
No changes.
Evidence collection.
Scope.
Questions.
Output format.
Escalation.

20.164 Implementation Template

An implementation mission should emphasize:
Branch.
Files.
Architecture constraints.
Tests.
Migration rules.
Review gate.
No-main rule.
Deployment gate.

20.165 Migration Template

A migration mission should define:
Schema scope.
Data impact.
Rollback.
Compatibility.
RLS.
Deployment order.
Validation.
Production approval.

20.166 Autonomy Trial Template

An autonomy-trial mission should define:
Workflow.
Current level.
Target level.
Trial scope.
Volume.
Evidence.
Controls.
Failure criteria.
Fallback.
Review.

20.167 Crisis Template

A crisis mission should define:
Incident.
Containment objective.
Immediate authority.
Forbidden actions.
Evidence preservation.
Communication.
Recovery gate.

20.168 Mission Simulation

Before activation, Omnira may simulate:
Required tasks.
Tool access.
Approval count.
Founder burden.
Likely blockers.
Policy conflicts.
Capacity.

20.169 Mission Pre-Mortem

Before a major mission, Executive Intelligence should ask:
Assume this mission failed. Why?
Possible failure causes:
Unclear scope.
Missing authority.
Wrong dependency.
Insufficient capacity.
Weak evidence.
Tool limitation.
Policy conflict.
Founder bottleneck.

20.170 Mission Post-Mortem

After failure or major deviation, review:
Was the objective wrong?
Was the brief incomplete?
Was scope unclear?
Did Manager decompose poorly?
Did Workforce lack capability?
Did governance block late?
Was capacity unrealistic?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.171 Mission Quality

Mission quality may be measured through:
Objective clarity.
Scope clarity.
Authority clarity.
Success measurability.
Change frequency.
Blocker rate.
Completion rate.
Founder correction rate.
Outcome quality.

20.172 Brief Completeness

The system should detect missing:
Owner.
Project.
Objective.
Success criteria.
Authority.
Approval gate.
Deadline.
Stop condition.

20.173 Mission Ambiguity

Ambiguity may exist when:
Objective is vague.
Scope is open-ended.
Authority is implied.
Success cannot be measured.
Project ownership is unclear.
Constraints conflict.
Ambiguous missions should not activate.

20.174 Mission Over-Specification

The brief should not prescribe every implementation detail unless necessary.
Over-specification may:
Prevent better execution.
Increase maintenance.
Turn Executive into Manager.
Slow adaptation.

20.175 Mission Under-Specification

Under-specification forces Workforce to invent:
Strategy.
Scope.
Authority.
Success.
Risk tolerance.
This is unsafe.

20.176 Outcome Freedom

Within valid constraints, Manager and Workforce should have freedom to choose the best execution path.

20.177 Mission Drift

Mission drift occurs when work gradually moves away from the objective.
Signals include:
New unrelated tasks.
Changed deliverables.
Expanded systems.
Different project.
New external effects.
Unapproved architecture.

20.178 Drift Detection

Manager should compare active work with:
Objective.
Scope.
Success criteria.
Roadmap.
Authority.

20.179 Hidden Work

Unplanned work should not appear inside a mission merely because capacity is available.
It should be proposed separately.

20.180 Mission Creep

Repeated small additions may materially expand the mission.
Aggregate changes should trigger revision.

20.181 Orphaned Mission

A mission becomes orphaned when:
Owner disappears.
Objective is removed.
Roadmap is superseded.
Project is hibernated.
Decision expires.

20.182 Zombie Mission

A Zombie Mission remains Active but has:
No progress.
No owner.
No deadline.
No current value.
No review.
It should be paused, cancelled, or rewritten.

20.183 Mission Congestion

Too many simultaneous missions create:
Context switching.
Delayed completion.
Founder overload.
Workforce fragmentation.
Priority confusion.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.184 Mission Work-in-Progress Limits

Portfolio and Project Executives should limit active missions.
A project may have:
One primary mission.
A small number of supporting missions.
Several prepared missions.
Many parked ideas.

20.185 Mission Dependency Conflict

The system should detect when:
Two missions require the same unavailable capacity.
One mission changes a dependency used by another.
A mission invalidates another mission’s assumptions.
Two missions modify the same system.

20.186 Mission Authority Conflict

The system should detect:
Conflicting approvals.
Overlapping write authority.
Different project scope.
Contradictory forbidden actions.
Expired mandate.

20.187 Mission Integrity

A healthy mission should maintain:
One project scope.
One objective.
One accountable owner.
Clear authority.
Measurable success.
Traceable execution.

20.188 Mission Health

Mission health may evaluate:
Progress.
Dependency health.
Capacity.
Risk.
Approval status.
Deadline confidence.
Scope stability.
Evidence quality.

20.189 Mission Health Status

Possible statuses:
Healthy.
Watch.
At Risk.
Blocked.
Invalid.
Recovery.

20.190 Mission Alerts

Alerts should occur when:
Approval is required.
Critical dependency fails.
Mission becomes at risk.
Scope changes.
Budget approaches limit.
Damage Boundary is crossed.
Deadline becomes impossible.
Mission completes.

20.191 Notification Discipline

Routine task updates should not interrupt the founder.
Manager should aggregate operational detail.

20.192 Mission Review Cadence

Mission review may be:
Continuous for incidents.
Daily for critical missions.
Weekly for normal active missions.
At milestone gates.
At approval gates.
At completion.

20.193 Daily Mission Review

Daily review should focus on:
Material change.
Blocker.
Risk.
Founder decision.
Completion probability.

20.194 Weekly Mission Review

Weekly review should examine:
Outcome progress.
Capacity.
Dependencies.
Scope.
Opportunity cost.
Next gate.

20.195 Completion Review

Completion review should ask:
Did the mission achieve its objective?
Are criteria met?
Is evidence sufficient?
Did it remain within authority?
What follows?

20.196 Mission Closure

Closure should record:
Outcome.
Status.
Evidence.
Decision.
Lessons.
Residual work.
Ownership transfer.
Review date.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.197 Residual Work

Unfinished work should become:
New mission.
Follow-up task.
Known limitation.
Risk.
Backlog item.
Do-Not-Start item.
It should not remain hidden.

20.198 Mission Outcome Types

Possible outcomes:
Capability Created.
Issue Resolved.
Decision Prepared.
Risk Reduced.
Evidence Produced.
Workflow Validated.
Project Stabilized.
Opportunity Rejected.
Mission Failed Safely.

20.199 Failed Safely

A mission may still create value if it:
Tests an assumption.
Avoids damage.
Produces decisive evidence.
Stops an unviable initiative.
Improves future planning.

20.200 Mission Learning

Omnira should learn:
Which briefs produced clear execution.
Which constraints were missing.
Which success criteria predicted value.
Which dependencies were underestimated.
Which founder gates created delay.
Which missions should have been stopped sooner.

20.201 Founder Feedback

The founder should be able to say:
This mission was clear.
This scope was too broad.
This should not have needed me.
The report contained too much detail.
The result did not answer the objective.
The constraints were correct.

20.202 Mission Calibration

Mission design should improve through:
Completion outcomes.
Scope-change frequency.
Founder corrections.
Manager questions.
Workforce escalations.
Missed deadlines.
Risk incidents.

20.203 Mission Reusability

Successful mission structures may become templates.
Project-specific authority and context must still be added.

20.204 Mission Brief Privacy

A Mission Brief should contain only the private context required for execution.
Founder-private context should normally be transformed into:
Capacity signal.
Deadline constraint.
Unavailable window.
Approval timing.

20.205 Customer Data in Mission Briefs

Customer data should be minimized.
Use identifiers and scoped fields rather than full histories where possible.

20.206 Multi-User Mission Rights

Future roles may include:
Mission proposer.
Executive owner.
Mission owner.
Contributor.
Reviewer.
Approver.
Viewer.
Auditor.

20.207 Customer-Owned Missions

Future customer organizations should control:
Objective.
Approvals.
Data scope.
Tools.
Budgets.
Reporting.
Autonomy.
Omnira may provide structure without taking ownership of customer strategy.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.208 Mission Export

Exports should preserve:
Scope.
Version.
Authority.
Status.
Redactions.
Evidence references.
Decision links.

20.209 Mission Import

Imported missions should be classified:
Historical.
Proposed.
Unverified.
Active only after validation.

20.210 Legacy Work Conversion

Existing informal work should be converted into Mission Briefs when it is:
Strategic.
Long-running.
High-risk.
Cross-functional.
Approval-dependent.
Externally consequential.

20.211 Shadow Missions

Shadow Missions exist when meaningful work proceeds without an explicit brief.
Signals include:
Unplanned agent activity.
Recurring external action.
No owner.
No success criteria.
No project scope.
No authority record.

20.212 Mission Quarantine

Ambiguous missions may be quarantined.
Quarantine may permit:
Read-only investigation.
Evidence collection.
No external action.
No spending.
No production change.

20.213 Anti-Prompt-Only Principle

A model prompt is not a sufficient organizational contract.

20.214 Anti-Task-List Principle

A list of tasks does not explain strategic outcome or authority.

20.215 Anti-Vague-Objective Principle

“Improve,” “fix,” or “optimize” without measurable meaning is insufficient.

20.216 Anti-Implied-Authority Principle

The ability to perform work does not authorize external effects.

20.217 Anti-Scope-Creep Principle

Workforce may not expand the mission through accumulated small additions.

20.218 Anti-Manager-Strategy Principle

Manager coordinates execution but does not redefine strategic direction.

20.219 Anti-Executive-Micromanagement Principle

Executive Intelligence should define outcomes and boundaries, not every low-level step.

20.220 Anti-Hidden-Dependency Principle

Critical dependencies must be explicit.

20.221 Anti-Hidden-Approval Principle

Approval requirements must appear before the action reaches the gate.

20.222 Anti-Reporting-Noise Principle

Routine execution detail should not overwhelm Executive or founder attention.

20.223 Anti-Silent-Change Principle

Material mission changes must be versioned.

20.224 Anti-Zombie-Mission Principle

Inactive, unowned, or unjustified missions should not remain Active.

20.225 Anti-Completion-Theatre Principle

Completed tasks do not prove mission success.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.226 Anti-Context-Leakage Principle

Mission context must not expose unrelated project or founder-private information.

20.227 The Objective Test

Before activation, Omnira should ask:
What must become true?
Is the objective outcome-oriented?
Why does it matter?

20.228 The Project Test

Omnira should ask:
Which project owns the mission?
Which policies, data, credentials, and budget apply?

20.229 The Success Test

Omnira should ask:
How will success be verified?
Are criteria sufficient?
Can task completion be distinguished from outcome success?

20.230 The Scope Test

Omnira should ask:
What is included?
What is excluded?
Could the scope be interpreted too broadly?

20.231 The Authority Test

Omnira should ask:
What may Workforce do?
What is the source of authority?
Which actions remain approval-gated?

20.232 The Constraint Test

Omnira should ask:
Which technical, governance, budget, time, and product constraints apply?

20.233 The Tool Test

Omnira should ask:
Which tools are required?
Which operations are permitted?
Are credentials project-scoped?

20.234 The Data Test

Omnira should ask:
Which data is required?
What is restricted?
Can a summary replace raw data?

20.235 The Dependency Test

Omnira should ask:
What must exist first?
Who owns each dependency?
What happens if it fails?

20.236 The Risk Test

Omnira should ask:
What can go wrong?
Does the Damage Boundary apply?
What controls and fallback exist?

20.237 The Approval Test

Omnira should ask:
Where must execution stop?
What evidence must be presented?
Who may approve?

20.238 The Capacity Test

Omnira should ask:
Does founder and Workforce capacity exist?
What active work is displaced?
Is reserve preserved?

20.239 The Reporting Test

Omnira should ask:
What does Executive need to know?
What should remain operational detail?
When should the founder be interrupted?

20.240 The Escalation Test

Omnira should ask:
Which events require escalation?
To whom?
With which evidence?

20.241 The Stop Test

Omnira should ask:
Which conditions require pause or termination?
What safe work may continue?

20.242 The Completion Test

Omnira should ask:
What evidence closes the mission?
Who confirms completion?
What follows afterward?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.243 Failure Modes

Executive Mission Briefs must prevent several failure modes.
Failure Mode 1 — Prompt as Mission
A vague model prompt replaces an execution contract.
Failure Mode 2 — Task List Without Outcome
Work is completed without achieving strategic value.
Failure Mode 3 — Undefined Authority
Workforce does not know what it may change.
Failure Mode 4 — Scope Creep
The mission expands without review.
Failure Mode 5 — Hidden Approval Gate
Work reaches a consequential action before approval requirements are known.
Failure Mode 6 — Manager Redefines Strategy
Operational coordination changes the objective.
Failure Mode 7 — Executive Micromanagement
The brief dictates every implementation detail.
Failure Mode 8 — Missing Success Criteria
Completion cannot be judged.
Failure Mode 9 — Wrong-Project Execution
Work uses the wrong data, credentials, or systems.
Failure Mode 10 — Missing Stop Conditions
Unsafe work continues.
Failure Mode 11 — Reporting Overload
Founder receives excessive operational detail.
Failure Mode 12 — Silent Mission Mutation
Scope or authority changes without versioning.
Failure Mode 13 — Zombie Mission
Inactive work remains Active indefinitely.
Failure Mode 14 — Completion Theatre
Tasks are marked done while the objective remains unmet.
Failure Mode 15 — Context Leakage
Unnecessary private or cross-project information reaches Workforce.
Failure Mode 16 — Orphaned Mission
No one remains accountable for the outcome.
These failure modes should be treated as organizational and architecture constraints.

20.244 Design Requirements

Any implementation of Executive Mission Briefs should preserve these requirements:
Every mission must have explicit project scope.
Every mission must have one clear objective.
Every mission must explain strategic context.
Every mission must define expected outcome and success criteria.
Every mission must define scope and relevant exclusions.
Every mission must define authority and its source.
Every mission must define constraints and forbidden actions.
Every mission must define required tools and data boundaries.
Every mission must define dependencies and critical assumptions.
Every high-impact mission must define Damage Boundary controls.
Every approval gate must be known before execution reaches it.
Every mission must define reporting and escalation requirements.
Every mission must define pause, stop, and completion conditions.
Every mission must have an accountable owner.
Every material mission change must create a new version.
Manager may decompose and optimize execution but may not redefine strategy or authority.
Workforce should receive only mission-relevant context and permissions.
Task completion must remain distinct from mission success.
Material missions should connect to roadmap, priority, and Decision Ledger context.
Mission execution must remain traceable from decision to outcome.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
20.245 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the executive delegation contract.
It does not require a specific project-management tool, workflow engine, agent framework, database, or user interface.
The architecture may later be implemented through:
Mission records.
Structured Mission Briefs.
Manager planning.
Task graphs.
Role assignments.
Approval gates.
Policy checks.
Tool permissions.
Progress reports.
Evidence records.
Mission dashboards.
Decision Ledger links.
Performance integrations.
Atlas explanations.
The technical implementation may evolve.
The mission contract must remain stable.

20.246 The Executive Mission Brief Contract

Executive Intelligence must:
Translate decisions and priorities into bounded missions.
Define what must become true.
Explain why the mission matters.
Assign the correct project and owner.
Define measurable success.
Define scope and exclusions.
Define authority and constraints.
Identify tools, data, dependencies, and assumptions.
Make approval gates visible before execution.
Protect the Damage Boundary.
Define reporting, escalation, and stop conditions.
Allow Manager flexibility inside approved boundaries.
Prevent Workforce from inventing strategy or authority.
Preserve version history and traceability.
Evaluate outcomes rather than task volume.
Turn executive intent into coordinated, accountable execution.
A feature that does not support this contract should not govern Executive-to-Workforce delegation.

20.247 Closing Principle

Executive Intelligence should not hand Workforce an idea and hope it interprets the idea correctly.
It should hand Workforce a mission.
A valid mission must make it possible to say:
This is the outcome.
This is why it matters.
This is the project.
This is what success means.
This is what you may do.
This is what you must not do.
This is where you must stop and ask.
This is the evidence I need.
This is when the mission is complete.
Executive Intelligence provides direction.
Governance provides authority.
Manager provides coordination.
Workforce provides execution.
Performance Intelligence provides evidence.
The Mission Brief keeps every layer aligned.
A mature Omnira organization should not depend on agents guessing what leadership meant.
Leadership intent should arrive as a precise, bounded, explainable, and executable contract.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Delegation as Transfer of Bounded Responsibility
text:
21.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Executive Intelligence must be able to delegate meaningful work without losing strategic control.
If Executive Intelligence manages every task directly, Omnira cannot scale.
If Workforce operates without clear supervision, Omnira cannot remain safe or coherent.
The organization therefore requires a formal model for:
Delegation.
Operational planning.
Execution.
Monitoring.
Escalation.
Reprioritization.
Intervention.
Pause.
Cancellation.
Emergency shutdown.
This chapter defines how Executive Intelligence delegates missions to Manager and Workforce, how operational freedom is bounded, and when leadership must intervene.
The goal is neither constant supervision nor uncontrolled independence.
The goal is accountable execution inside a clearly defined mission envelope.

21.2 The Core Thesis

Executive Intelligence should control:
Purpose.
Priority.
Outcome.
Authority.
Risk boundaries.
Approval gates.
Strategic changes.
Manager should control:
Operational sequencing.
Task decomposition.
Role assignment.
Routine scheduling.
Safe retries.
Execution coordination.
Operational escalation.
Workforce should control:
Task execution.
Evidence production.
Local problem-solving.
Permitted tool use.
Accurate reporting.
Escalation when boundaries are reached.
The foundational principle is:
Executive defines what must be achieved and within which boundaries.
Manager determines how permitted work is coordinated.
Workforce performs the work.

21.3 Delegation Is Not Abandonment

Delegation does not mean:
Give work to Workforce.
Stop observing.
Assume completion.
Intervene only after failure.
Delegation requires:
Clear Mission Brief.
Valid authority.
Assigned ownership.
Progress visibility.
Escalation paths.
Intervention rules.
Completion review.

21.4 Delegation Is Not Micromanagement

Delegation also does not mean:
Executive chooses every task.
Executive chooses every agent.
Executive approves every retry.
Executive receives every status update.
Executive dictates every technical method.
Manager and Workforce need operational freedom within valid boundaries.

21.5 Delegation as Transfer of Bounded Responsibility

A delegation transfers responsibility for an outcome or workstream.
It does not transfer unlimited decision authority.
The delegated envelope should define:
Objective.
Scope.
Priority.
Allowed actions.
Constraints.
Budget.
Tools.
Data.
Approval gates.
Escalation triggers.
Stop conditions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.6 Delegation Layers

A canonical delegation chain is:
Founder
→ Executive Intelligence
→ Manager
→ Workforce Role
→ Agent or Workflow
→ Tool Action
Authority should narrow at every layer.

21.7 Founder to Executive Delegation

The founder may delegate:
Portfolio review.
Priority recommendations.
Mission preparation.
Roadmap maintenance.
Risk monitoring.
Internal reprioritization.
Decision preparation.
Founder delegation does not automatically include:
Unbounded spending.
Constitutional change.
Unrestricted publishing.
Project activation.
Self-granted autonomy.

21.8 Executive to Manager Delegation

Executive Intelligence delegates a Mission Brief to Manager.
Manager receives authority to:
Plan execution.
Decompose work.
Assign available roles.
Sequence tasks.
Track dependencies.
Use permitted workflows.
Collect evidence.
Escalate exceptions.

21.9 Manager to Workforce Delegation

Manager delegates work packages to Workforce roles.
Each work package should include:
Mission reference.
Project.
Task objective.
Inputs.
Expected output.
Authority.
Constraints.
Deadline.
Reporting.
Escalation.

21.10 Workforce to Agent Delegation

A Workforce role may use one or more agents or workflows.
The agent should receive only:
Task-relevant context.
Task-relevant data.
Task-relevant tools.
Task-level authority.
Required output format.
Escalation rules.

21.11 Tool-Level Delegation

The final tool action should be narrower than the task.
Example:
Mission:
Prepare a publishing fix.
Task:
Inspect the persistence path.
Tool authority:
Read specified repository files.
Not:
General repository write access.

21.12 Delegation Envelope

The Delegation Envelope is the operational boundary surrounding delegated work.
It may include:
Mission identifier.
Project.
Delegating authority.
Receiving role.
Allowed decisions.
Allowed actions.
Forbidden actions.
Budget.
Time horizon.
Tools.
Data scope.
Approval gates.
Escalation path.
Revocation.

21.13 Delegated Authority

Delegated authority should be explicit.
Possible categories include:
Observe.
Analyze.
Prepare.
Modify internal state.
Execute approved internal work.
Use approved external action.
Spend within mandate.
Escalate.
Pause subordinate work.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.14 Delegation Scope

Delegation should be scoped by:
Project.
Mission.
Workflow.
Action category.
Time.
Risk.
Budget.
Data.
Channel.

21.15 No Implied Delegation

Delegation must not be inferred merely from:
Past assignments.
Role title.
Tool access.
Previous success.
Project membership.
User silence.
An agent volunteering to act.

21.16 Delegation Acceptance

The receiving Manager or Workforce role should validate:
Objective is clear.
Authority is sufficient.
Required data exists.
Required tools exist.
Dependencies are available.
Constraints are consistent.
Deadline is feasible.
Escalation is defined.

21.17 Delegation Rejection

Manager should reject or escalate a Mission Brief when:
Objective is ambiguous.
Project scope is missing.
Authority is insufficient.
Constraints conflict.
Success cannot be verified.
Required capacity does not exist.
The mission crosses policy boundaries.

21.18 Delegation Is a Two-Sided Contract

Executive Intelligence must provide a valid mission.
Manager must verify it can be executed safely.
Workforce should not be forced to guess around missing authority or context.

21.19 Operational Planning

After accepting a mission, Manager should produce an operational plan.
The plan may include:
Workstreams.
Tasks.
Sequence.
Dependencies.
Roles.
Checkpoints.
Approval gates.
Evidence requirements.
Fallbacks.

21.20 Operational Plan vs Executive Mission

The Mission Brief defines the destination and boundaries.
The operational plan defines the route.
Manager may change the route.
Manager may not change the destination without approval.

21.21 Operational Freedom

Manager may autonomously adjust:
Task order.
Role assignment.
Safe retry timing.
Internal scheduling.
Parallelization.
Checkpoint frequency.
Evidence-gathering method.
provided that the mission envelope remains intact.

21.22 Operational Constraints

Manager may not autonomously change:
Mission objective.
Project scope.
Budget ceiling.
External authority.
Approval gates.
Forbidden actions.
Damage Boundary.
Strategic priority.
Success criteria.

21.23 Local Optimization

Manager should optimize execution for:
Speed.
Quality.
Cost.
Reliability.
Capacity fit.
Dependency efficiency.
Low founder burden.
Optimization must remain subordinate to mission success and governance.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.24 Manager Replanning

Manager may replan when:
A task fails.
A role becomes unavailable.
A dependency is delayed.
A safer method appears.
A tool becomes unavailable.
A task can be parallelized.
Evidence shows a local approach is inefficient.

21.25 Replanning Boundary

Replanning remains operational when it does not materially alter:
Outcome.
Scope.
Authority.
Risk.
Budget.
Deadline commitment.
External effect.

21.26 Material Replanning

Material replanning requires Executive review when it:
Changes the expected outcome.
Adds a new system.
Expands scope.
Changes risk.
Requires more budget.
Creates new external action.
Moves a major deadline.
Displaces another mission.

21.27 Replanning Report

Material replanning should explain:
What changed.
Why.
Operational impact.
Strategic impact.
Risk.
Capacity.
Recommendation.
Decision required.

21.28 Task Decomposition

Manager should decompose missions into tasks that are:
Bounded.
Traceable.
Assignable.
Verifiable.
Properly authorized.
Small enough to monitor.
Large enough to create useful progress.

21.29 Task Dependencies

Tasks should identify:
Predecessors.
Inputs.
Outputs.
Owner.
Blocking state.
Fallback.

21.30 Workstream Coordination

Manager may coordinate several workstreams.
Example:
Investigation.
Architecture.
Implementation.
Testing.
Governance.
Deployment preparation.

21.31 Parallel Work

Parallel work is appropriate when:
Capacity types differ.
Tasks do not modify the same resource unsafely.
Dependencies permit it.
Review burden remains manageable.
Project focus remains coherent.

21.32 False Parallelism

Work is not truly parallel when tasks compete for the same:
Founder attention.
Repository area.
Database schema.
Approval gate.
Shared agent.
Tool quota.
Technical owner.

21.33 Work-in-Progress Limits

Manager should limit active tasks and workstreams.
Excessive work in progress creates:
Longer completion time.
Context switching.
Coordination cost.
Hidden blockers.
Lower quality.
Incomplete missions.

21.34 Role Assignment

Manager should assign work according to:
Capability.
Trust.
Availability.
Project familiarity.
Tool access.
Risk.
Cost.
Required reasoning depth.

21.35 Role Fitness

A role is fit when it has:
Relevant competence.
Sufficient context.
Valid authority.
Required tools.
Available capacity.
Acceptable trust.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.36 Role Substitution

Manager may replace a role or agent when:
Capability is equivalent.
Authority remains valid.
Context is transferred safely.
Risk does not increase materially.
The mission remains unchanged.

21.37 Material Role Change

Executive review may be required when a role change:
Changes independence of review.
Removes separation of duties.
Introduces external access.
Changes risk materially.
Uses a different provider or trust profile.

21.38 Separation of Duties

High-impact work may separate:
Researcher.
Builder.
Reviewer.
Approver.
Deployer.
Auditor.
One agent should not automatically perform every role.

21.39 Reviewer Independence

A reviewer should be sufficiently independent from the builder where:
Security is affected.
Data integrity is affected.
Production is affected.
Customer harm is possible.
Autonomy is being expanded.

21.40 Workforce Operating State

A Workforce unit may be:
Available.
Assigned.
Executing.
Waiting.
Blocked.
Escalated.
Paused.
Completed.
Failed.
Quarantined.

21.41 Available

The role has capacity and valid access but is not assigned.

21.42 Assigned

The role has received a work package but may not yet have started.

21.43 Executing

The role is actively performing permitted work.

21.44 Waiting

The role is waiting for:
Dependency.
Tool.
Approval.
Data.
Another task.
Defined execution window.

21.45 Blocked

The role cannot progress safely.
A Blocked state should include an explicit cause.

21.46 Escalated

The role has submitted an issue requiring higher authority or judgment.

21.47 Paused

The work has been deliberately stopped temporarily.

21.48 Completed

The assigned work package has produced its required output.
This does not necessarily mean the mission is complete.

21.49 Failed

The work package cannot deliver its required output under current conditions.

21.50 Quarantined

The role or workflow is restricted because:
Authority is unclear.
Project scope is uncertain.
A violation occurred.
Monitoring failed.
Tool behavior is untrusted.

21.51 Workforce Autonomy

Workforce may operate autonomously only within:
Mission authority.
Project policy.
Task assignment.
Tool permissions.
Active autonomy licenses.
Damage Boundary.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Workforce Does Not Own Strategic Priority
Workforce Does Not Own Project Mode
Workforce Does Not Own Its Own Autonomy
text:
21.52 Workforce Does Not Own Strategic Priority

Workforce may report urgency.
It may not independently decide that its own work should outrank the portfolio.

21.53 Workforce Does Not Own Project Mode

Workforce may recommend a mode change.
It may not activate or hibernate a project independently.

21.54 Workforce Does Not Own Policy

Workforce may identify policy gaps and propose changes.
It may not rewrite active policy.

21.55 Workforce Does Not Own Its Own Autonomy

Workforce may produce evidence supporting higher autonomy.
It may not grant itself a broader license.

21.56 Manager Authority

Manager may be authorized to:
Assign tasks.
Sequence work.
Pause unsafe subordinate tasks.
Retry safe work.
Replace equivalent agents.
Collect reports.
Escalate.
Reduce concurrency.

21.57 Manager Prohibitions

Manager should not:
Change strategy.
Broaden project scope.
Approve its own higher authority.
Ignore governance.
Spend outside mandate.
Create external commitments.
Override the Damage Boundary.
Reuse unrelated project permissions.

21.58 Routine Retry

Manager may retry work autonomously when:
The action is idempotent.
No duplicate external effect can occur.
The failure is understood.
Retry is within budget.
Policy permits it.
Retry limits remain.

21.59 Unsafe Retry

Retry should require escalation when:
External state is uncertain.
Duplicate action is possible.
Money may move twice.
A customer may receive repeated communication.
Data may be corrupted.
The prior failure cause is unknown.

21.60 Retry Limits

Every recurring workflow should define:
Maximum attempts.
Backoff.
Cost ceiling.
Escalation threshold.
Duplicate protection.

21.61 Operational Monitoring

Manager should monitor:
Progress.
Task state.
Dependencies.
Failures.
Cost.
Quality.
Policy status.
License status.
External outcomes.

21.62 Executive Monitoring

Executive Intelligence should monitor:
Mission outcome.
Strategic alignment.
Material risk.
Capacity conflict.
Approval requirements.
Priority changes.
Intervention triggers.

21.63 Founder Monitoring

The founder should normally see:
Material progress.
Decisions required.
Risks.
Blocked outcomes.
Important changes.
Completion.
Routine task telemetry should remain hidden unless requested.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.64 Reporting Compression

Each layer should compress detail for the layer above.
Agent:
Task evidence.
Workforce Role:
Work-package status.
Manager:
Mission progress.
Project Executive:
Project outcome.
Portfolio Executive:
Portfolio consequence.
Founder:
Decision-relevant summary.

21.65 Evidence Preservation

Compression should not destroy traceability.
Detailed evidence should remain accessible when required.

21.66 Healthy Silence

A healthy workflow should not need constant reporting.
Silence is acceptable only when:
Monitoring is active.
No material change occurred.
The workflow remains within scope.
No deadline is at risk.
No decision is needed.

21.67 Silent Failure

Silence becomes dangerous when:
Monitoring is missing.
The workflow stopped unexpectedly.
External outcome is unknown.
A deadline passed.
A violation was hidden.

21.68 Progress Checkpoints

Checkpoints may be:
Time-based.
Milestone-based.
Risk-based.
Approval-based.
Event-based.

21.69 Checkpoint Purpose

A checkpoint should answer:
Is the mission still valid?
Is execution on track?
Do assumptions remain valid?
Is intervention needed?
May the next phase begin?

21.70 Escalation

Escalation transfers an issue to a layer with sufficient authority or judgment.
Escalation is correct when local resolution would exceed the delegation envelope.

21.71 Escalation Triggers

Possible triggers include:
Scope ambiguity.
Policy conflict.
Missing authority.
Critical assumption failure.
High-impact defect.
Budget risk.
Wrong-project data.
Deadline failure.
Customer harm risk.
Uncertain external state.

21.72 Escalation Is Not Failure

Correct escalation is evidence of mature execution.
A system that always proceeds without escalating may be less trustworthy.

21.73 Escalation Quality

A high-quality escalation should include:
Issue.
Evidence.
Impact.
Urgency.
Attempted resolution.
Options.
Recommendation.
Decision required.

21.74 Escalation Destination

Escalation may go to:
Manager.
Project Executive.
Portfolio Executive.
Governance.
Founder.
Specialist reviewer.
Crisis response.

21.75 Local Escalation

Operational issues should first go to Manager when Manager has authority to resolve them.

21.76 Executive Escalation

Strategic, scope, priority, risk, or authority issues should go to Executive Intelligence.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.77 Founder Escalation

Founder escalation is appropriate for:
Strategic decision.
Material spend.
Project mode.
High-impact autonomy.
Customer-sensitive judgment.
Constitutional question.
Residual risk acceptance.

21.78 Specialist Escalation

Specialist review may be required for:
Security.
Privacy.
Legal.
Finance.
Child safety.
Health-adjacent content.

21.79 Escalation Overload

Excessive escalation may indicate:
Mission under-specification.
Policy gaps.
Insufficient delegation.
Weak role capability.
Overly strict controls.
Poor task decomposition.

21.80 Escalation Avoidance

Workforce must not hide issues to preserve performance metrics or trust.
Hidden escalation need is a serious trust problem.

21.81 Intervention

Intervention occurs when Executive Intelligence changes or stops ongoing execution.
Intervention may include:
Clarify.
Constrain.
Reprioritize.
Redirect.
Pause.
Reduce autonomy.
Replace owner.
Cancel.
Activate Crisis Mode.

21.82 Intervention Is Exceptional

Executive intervention should occur when the current execution path is no longer safely or strategically acceptable.
It should not be used for routine operational preference.

21.83 Intervention Threshold

Executive Intelligence should intervene when:
Mission objective is threatened.
Strategic conditions changed.
Risk materially increased.
Scope drift occurred.
Policy is violated.
Project mode changed.
Capacity conflict became material.
External harm may occur.
Manager cannot resolve the issue.

21.84 Non-Intervention Principle

Executive Intelligence should not intervene merely because:
A different task order seems preferable.
A safe retry is occurring.
A minor delay exists.
A stylistic execution preference differs.
The workflow is functioning within its envelope.

21.85 Minimum Necessary Intervention

Intervention should be as narrow as possible.
Preferred sequence:
Clarify.
Adjust one task.
Restrict one action.
Pause one workflow.
Pause one mission.
Reduce project autonomy.
Activate project crisis.
Activate portfolio crisis.

21.86 Clarification Intervention

Executive Intelligence may clarify:
Objective.
Priority.
Success criteria.
Scope.
Decision intent.
Clarification should not silently rewrite the mission.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.87 Constraint Intervention

A new constraint may be added when:
Risk changes.
Policy changes.
New customer sensitivity appears.
A provider becomes unreliable.
A project boundary issue emerges.
Material constraint changes require versioning.

21.88 Reprioritization Intervention

Executive Intelligence may reprioritize Workforce when conditions materially change.
Examples:
Critical revenue failure.
Security risk.
Customer harm.
Hard dependency completion.
Time-sensitive opportunity.
Founder capacity change.

21.89 Reprioritization Discipline

Reprioritization should identify:
What moves up.
What moves down.
What is interrupted.
Why the change is material.
What opportunity cost is accepted.
When the priority is reviewed.

21.90 Protected Execution Window

Active missions may receive a protected execution window.
During that period, unrelated work should not interrupt them unless:
P0 or P1 risk appears.
Material customer harm is possible.
Revenue loss is immediate.
Critical dependency changes.
Founder explicitly reprioritizes.

21.91 Unrelated Support Issue

An unrelated support issue should not automatically interrupt a healthy automation workflow.
The correct response may be:
Notify the founder.
Assign support handling separately.
Create a parallel bounded mission.
Queue for the next approval window.

21.92 Workflow-Caused Support Issue

The workflow should be interrupted when the support issue indicates that the workflow:
Caused customer harm.
Sent incorrect information.
Created account problems.
Produced repeated complaints.
Broke a promise.
Created public damage.

21.93 Damage-Coupled Intervention

Intervention should be directly connected to the affected workflow or mission where possible.
Do not stop unrelated safe operation without reason.

21.94 Redirect Intervention

Executive Intelligence may redirect a mission when:
The original method is no longer viable.
The objective remains valid.
A safer or higher-value route exists.
Redirecting the method should preserve the objective.

21.95 Scope Reduction

Executive Intelligence may narrow scope to:
Reduce risk.
Meet deadline.
Preserve budget.
Protect capacity.
Enable partial value.
Keep work reversible.

21.96 Scope Expansion

Scope expansion requires explicit review of:
Authority.
Risk.
Budget.
Capacity.
Deadline.
Opportunity cost.
Success criteria.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.97 Pause

Pause temporarily stops execution.
A pause should define:
Affected work.
Reason.
Effective time.
Safe state.
Allowed continuation.
Review date.
Restart conditions.

21.98 Task Pause

A Task Pause affects one task.
Other mission work may continue.

21.99 Workflow Pause

A Workflow Pause stops a repeatable execution mechanism.
Preparation or related analysis may continue.

21.100 Mission Pause

A Mission Pause stops the active mission.
Dependent tasks should move to a safe waiting state.

21.101 Project Pause

A Project Pause may stop most active execution.
This may imply an operating-mode or lifecycle decision.

21.102 Portfolio Pause

A Portfolio Pause is exceptional and generally related to systemic crisis.

21.103 Safe Pause State

A pause should avoid leaving:
Partial external transactions.
Uncommitted migrations.
Unknown customer state.
Open write operations.
Untracked drafts.
Inconsistent workflow checkpoints.

21.104 Pause Receipt

The system should record:
What stopped.
What completed before stop.
What remains uncertain.
Which tools were disabled.
Which external effects occurred.
Who authorized the pause.

21.105 Restart

Restart should verify:
Mission remains valid.
Authority remains active.
Policy remains current.
Dependencies are restored.
Risk is acceptable.
Workflow state is known.
Duplicate action is prevented.

21.106 Restart Is Not Resume Blindly

Restart should not repeat external actions unless their previous state is verified.

21.107 Cancellation

Cancellation permanently ends the delegated mission.
Cancellation may occur when:
Objective is no longer valuable.
Strategy changes.
Project is hibernated.
Risk becomes unacceptable.
Opportunity cost becomes too high.
Mission repeatedly fails.
A superior replacement exists.

21.108 Cancellation Consequences

Cancellation should identify:
Tasks stopped.
Resources released.
Artifacts retained.
External commitments affected.
Residual risk.
Replacement plan.
Decision Ledger requirement.

21.109 Mission Termination vs Workflow Revocation

Mission termination ends the mission.
Workflow revocation removes authority from a reusable workflow.
They are related but distinct.

21.110 Kill Switch

A kill switch immediately stops or isolates execution that may create serious harm.
It may affect:
Task.
Workflow.
Mission.
Project.
Tool connection.
External channel.
Entire Workforce.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.111 Kill Switch Authority

Authorized triggers may include:
Founder.
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Governance engine.
Security process.
Crisis process.
Manager under narrow emergency authority.

21.112 Kill Switch Triggers

Possible triggers:
Unauthorized spend.
Wrong-project data.
Serious public error.
Customer harm.
Credential compromise.
Uncontrolled external action.
Repeated policy violation.
Systemic workflow failure.

21.113 Kill Switch Behavior

The kill switch should:
Stop new actions.
Contain active work.
Revoke or suspend permissions.
Preserve evidence.
Report affected state.
Prevent automatic restart.
Escalate.

21.114 Kill Switch Scope

The narrowest effective scope should be used.
A single failed workflow should not automatically stop all projects unless systemic risk exists.

21.115 Emergency Brake

The Emergency Brake is the broader governance mechanism that may:
Pause several workflows.
Freeze spend.
Disable external actions.
Restrict tools.
Activate Crisis Mode.
Require human approval.

21.116 Manager-Initiated Pause

Manager may pause subordinate work when:
A stop condition is met.
External state is uncertain.
Policy evaluation fails.
Duplicate risk exists.
A dependency becomes unsafe.

21.117 Manager Cannot Restore High-Risk Authority

Manager may pause.
Manager should not restore high-impact authority without the required Executive or human approval.

21.118 Workforce Self-Pause

Workforce should be able to self-pause when:
Scope is unclear.
Authority is missing.
Project identity is uncertain.
Sensitive content appears.
External result is unknown.
A serious risk emerges.

21.119 Correct Self-Pause

Correct self-pause should be positive trust evidence.

21.120 False Self-Pause

Repeated unnecessary self-pauses may indicate:
Weak confidence.
Poor policy.
Incomplete Mission Brief.
Insufficient capability.
Excessively strict controls.

21.121 Intervention Levels

A conceptual intervention ladder is:
I0 — Observe.
I1 — Clarify.
I2 — Adjust Operations.
I3 — Constrain Scope.
I4 — Reprioritize.
I5 — Pause.
I6 — Cancel or Revoke.
I7 — Crisis Intervention.

21.122 I0 — Observe

No action is taken beyond monitoring.

21.123 I1 — Clarify

Executive Intelligence resolves ambiguity without changing strategic intent.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
21.124 I2 — Adjust Operations

Manager is directed to change sequencing or assignment.

21.125 I3 — Constrain Scope

Authority, volume, channel, or task scope is reduced.

21.126 I4 — Reprioritize

Capacity is moved between missions or projects.

21.127 I5 — Pause

Execution temporarily stops.

21.128 I6 — Cancel or Revoke

Mission or authority is terminated.

21.129 I7 — Crisis Intervention

Crisis Mode and emergency controls activate.

21.130 Intervention Evidence

Before material intervention, Executive Intelligence should consider:
Current mission state.
Evidence.
Risk.
Manager assessment.
Performance trend.
Opportunity cost.
Available alternatives.
Urgency.

21.131 Immediate Intervention

Immediate intervention is appropriate when delay may cause:
Customer harm.
Financial loss.
Data exposure.
Security compromise.
Public damage.
Systemic failure.

21.132 Deliberate Intervention

Non-urgent intervention should include analysis of:
Disruption cost.
Mission value.
Alternative route.
Capacity.
Founder burden.
Review timing.

21.133 Intervention Without Full Evidence

Executive Intelligence may pause first and investigate second when the worst credible outcome is severe.
The pause should be narrow and reviewable.

21.134 Intervention Receipt

Every material intervention should record:
Trigger.
Authority.
Scope.
Action taken.
Affected missions.
Affected workflows.
Reason.
Evidence.
Fallback.
Review.

21.135 Intervention Review

After intervention, Omnira should determine:
Was intervention necessary?
Was it timely?
Was it too broad?
Was harm prevented?
What should change?
May work resume?

21.136 Intervention Cost

Intervention creates cost through:
Lost progress.
Context switching.
Delayed outcomes.
Replanning.
Reduced trust.
Founder attention.
The cost should be justified by avoided harm or higher value.

21.137 Over-Intervention

Over-intervention occurs when Executive Intelligence:
Changes task order unnecessarily.
Interrupts healthy workflows.
Overrides local expertise.
Creates constant reprioritization.
Requests excessive reporting.
Removes operational freedom.
