Loses reliable evidence access.
Part II — Crisis Severity

28.27 Crisis Severity Model

A conceptual crisis-severity model may include:
C0 — Operational Disturbance.
C1 — Contained Incident.
C2 — Material Crisis.
C3 — Severe Crisis.
C4 — Systemic Emergency.
This is separate from:
Damage severity.
Policy-violation severity.
Mission priority.
Operational alert priority.

28.28 C0 — Operational Disturbance

Characteristics:
Low impact.
Known cause.
Narrow scope.
Reliable monitoring.
Easy recovery.
No material customer or external harm.
Response:
Manager handles.
Routine incident record.
No formal Crisis Mode required.

28.29 C1 — Contained Incident

Characteristics:
Limited impact.
Known affected workflow.
Contained blast radius.
Recovery available.
No ongoing severe harm.
Response may include:
Workflow pause.
Project Executive notification.
Targeted approval.
Short incident review.

28.30 C2 — Material Crisis

Characteristics:
Material customer, financial, brand, data, or production impact.
Risk of continued harm.
Multiple workflows may be affected.
Executive intervention required.
Response:
Project Crisis Mode.
Emergency Brake for affected scope.
Founder notification.
Formal incident command.

28.31 C3 — Severe Crisis

Characteristics:
Severe damage.
Rapid escalation.
Large external exposure.
Uncertain system state.
Critical governance failure.
Several project systems affected.
Response:
Broad project shutdown.
Portfolio Executive involvement.
Freeze external actions.
Freeze material spend.
Specialist escalation.
Frequent crisis reporting.

28.32 C4 — Systemic Emergency

Characteristics:
Several projects affected.
Core governance compromised.
Tenant or project isolation uncertain.
Shared infrastructure unsafe.
Organizational authority cannot be trusted.
Severe ongoing damage possible.
Response:
Portfolio Emergency Brake.
Default-deny external execution.
Revoke broad autonomy.
Restrict all write tools.
Human-controlled recovery.
Independent validation before restoration.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.33 Severity Factors

Crisis severity should consider:
Impact.
Likelihood of further harm.
Velocity.
Blast radius.
Detectability.
Reversibility.
Containment.
Customer vulnerability.
Authority failure.
Data sensitivity.
Financial exposure.
Public exposure.
Systemic dependency.

28.34 Impact

Impact asks:
What harm has already occurred?
What assets are affected?
What business value is at risk?

28.35 Velocity

Velocity asks:
How quickly can damage grow?
Can another automated action occur within seconds?
Is a scheduled batch imminent?

28.36 Blast Radius

Blast radius may include:
One task.
One workflow.
One project.
Several projects.
All external channels.
All customer tenants.

28.37 Detectability

Low detectability increases crisis severity.
A workflow producing unknown external effects is more dangerous than one with fully observed state.

28.38 Reversibility

Irreversible actions increase severity.
Examples:
Public misinformation.
Permanent deletion.
Customer financial harm.
Sensitive data disclosure.
Legal commitment.

28.39 Governance Failure

If authority, policy, or approval state cannot be trusted, the crisis may require broader containment than the visible incident alone.

28.40 Residual Risk

Even after containment, residual risk may remain through:
Cached jobs.
Pending queues.
External scheduled posts.
Long-lived credentials.
Third-party automation.
Customer effects.
Search-engine indexing.
Part III — Crisis Detection

28.41 Crisis Detection Sources

Crisis detection may originate from:
Performance alerts.
Policy engine.
Security monitoring.
Workflow telemetry.
Customer support.
Founder report.
Agent self-pause.
Manager escalation.
Provider status.
Data-quality systems.
External notification.

28.42 Automated Detection

Automated detection may identify:
Spend spike.
Repeated workflow failure.
Wrong-project identifier.
High complaint rate.
Credential anomaly.
Unexpected publication volume.
Data-access anomaly.
Policy-evaluation failure.

28.43 Human Detection

Humans may detect:
Brand harm.
Contextual insensitivity.
Strategic danger.
Legal significance.
Customer vulnerability.
Unexpected system behavior.

28.44 Customer Detection

Customer complaints may be the first crisis signal.
The system should not dismiss isolated reports solely because telemetry appears healthy.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.45 Agent Detection

Agents should be able to detect and report:
Scope uncertainty.
Authority conflict.
Prompt injection.
Unknown external state.
Sensitive content.
Unexpected tool response.

28.46 Manager Detection

Manager should identify patterns such as:
Several related failures.
Repeated escalation.
Workflow state inconsistency.
Shared dependency failure.
Capacity collapse.

28.47 Executive Detection

Executive Intelligence should identify strategic or systemic patterns that local operations may miss.

28.48 Detection Confidence

Detection may be:
Confirmed.
Highly Probable.
Possible.
Uncertain.

28.49 Low-Confidence High-Impact Signal

A low-confidence signal may still justify a narrow preventive pause when the worst credible outcome is severe.

28.50 False Positive

A false positive is less costly when containment is narrow and reversible.
The system should prefer:
Narrow pause.
Rapid validation.
Controlled restart.
over broad unnecessary shutdown.

28.51 False Negative

A false negative may permit continuing harm.
Detection thresholds should be stricter for:
Security.
Customer safety.
Sensitive data.
Spend.
Public publication.
Project isolation.

28.52 Detection Delay

The system should measure:
Time from first harmful event.
Time to first signal.
Time to confirmed detection.
Time to containment.

28.53 Detection Integrity

A compromised workflow should not be the only system responsible for reporting its own failures.

28.54 Independent Monitoring

High-risk workflows should have independent monitoring where possible.

28.55 Monitoring Failure

Monitoring failure may itself trigger restriction.
A high-impact workflow should not continue autonomously when its required monitoring disappears.
Part IV — Crisis Activation

28.56 Crisis Activation Authority

Crisis Mode may be activated by:
Founder.
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Governance engine.
Security system.
Manager under defined emergency authority.
Automated rule under explicit policy.

28.57 Automated Crisis Activation

Automated activation should be limited to:
Clearly defined triggers.
Narrow scope.
Reversible restrictions.
Strong evidence.
Immediate human notification.

28.58 Human Crisis Activation

A human should be able to activate Crisis Mode even before full evidence exists when serious harm is plausible.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.59 Agent-Initiated Crisis Request

An agent may request Crisis Mode.
It should not generally have authority to activate portfolio-wide crisis independently.

28.60 Manager Emergency Authority

Manager may have authority to:
Pause affected tasks.
Stop retries.
Freeze one workflow.
Disable one tool route.
Escalate immediately.

28.61 Project Executive Authority

Project Executive may activate project-scoped Crisis Mode.

28.62 Portfolio Executive Authority

Portfolio Executive may activate:
Cross-project containment.
Shared-provider restriction.
Shared-tool shutdown.
Portfolio spend freeze.
Global external-action freeze.

28.63 Founder Authority

The founder may activate or expand Crisis Mode at any time.
The system should still present:
Scope.
Expected effect.
Interrupted work.
Recovery implications.

28.64 Crisis Declaration Object

A Crisis Declaration may contain:
Crisis identifier.
Title.
Severity.
Affected project or portfolio.
Trigger.
Evidence.
Activation authority.
Activation time.
Affected systems.
Immediate restrictions.
Known damage.
Unknown state.
Communication requirement.
Review time.

28.65 Crisis Activation Receipt

The system should record:
Who activated.
Why.
What scope.
What restrictions.
Which licenses were suspended.
Which workflows were stopped.
Which tools were restricted.

28.66 Provisional Crisis Mode

A provisional crisis may activate narrow restrictions while evidence is gathered.

28.67 Confirmed Crisis Mode

Confirmed Crisis Mode activates the formal response structure.

28.68 Crisis Expansion

The crisis scope may expand when evidence shows broader impact.
Expansion should be explicit and logged.

28.69 Crisis Narrowing

The crisis scope should narrow when affected systems become understood.

28.70 No Silent Crisis Expansion

One project incident should not silently become a portfolio shutdown.
Part V — The Emergency Brake

28.71 Emergency Brake Objectives

The Emergency Brake should:
Stop new harm.
Prevent repeated action.
Restrict uncertain authority.
Preserve evidence.
Maintain recoverability.
Allow safe internal analysis.
Enable controlled restoration.

28.72 Emergency Brake Scope

Possible scopes:
Action.
Task.
Workflow.
Mission.
Tool.
Channel.
Credential.
Project.
Provider.
Portfolio.
All external execution.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.73 Narrowest Effective Scope

The system should use the narrowest scope that reliably contains the threat.

28.74 Action-Level Brake

Stops one action before execution.

28.75 Workflow-Level Brake

Stops one workflow and its scheduled runs.

28.76 Mission-Level Brake

Stops all execution belonging to one mission.

28.77 Tool-Level Brake

Blocks defined tool operations.
Example:
Publishing tool remains readable but all write operations are disabled.

28.78 Channel-Level Brake

Stops activity on:
Website.
Email.
Social platform.
Payment system.
Customer support channel.

28.79 Credential-Level Brake

Revokes or suspends a credential.

28.80 Project-Level Brake

Stops consequential project execution while preserving project-isolated analysis.

28.81 Provider-Level Brake

Removes one provider from eligible execution routes.

28.82 Portfolio-Level Brake

Restricts several or all projects.
This should be reserved for systemic exposure.

28.83 External-Action Freeze

An External-Action Freeze may block:
Publishing.
Sending communication.
Spending.
Deploying.
Changing customer state.
Writing to third-party systems.

28.84 Spend Freeze

A Spend Freeze may block:
New purchases.
Campaign spend.
Provider upgrades.
Automated refunds above policy.
New recurring commitments.
Existing unavoidable infrastructure charges may continue unless specifically stopped.

28.85 Write Freeze

A Write Freeze blocks defined state changes while permitting read-only investigation.

28.86 Approval Freeze

Approval Freeze may invalidate pending approvals when:
The object is compromised.
The evidence is stale.
The context changed.
The approval system is untrusted.

28.87 License Suspension

Affected autonomy licenses should move to:
Restricted.
Suspended.
Revoked.
depending on the crisis.

28.88 Schedule Suspension

Scheduled jobs should be stopped or held safely.

28.89 Queue Containment

Pending actions should be:
Frozen.
Identified.
Deduplicated.
Inspected.
Released only after validation.

28.90 Retry Disablement

Automatic retries should stop when external state is uncertain.

28.91 Safe Internal Continuation

Even during Crisis Mode, the system may permit:
Read-only analysis.
Evidence collection.
Drafting.
Simulation.
Testing in isolated environments.
Recovery planning.
Internal communication.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.92 Emergency Brake Idempotency

Activating the brake repeatedly should not create inconsistent state.

28.93 Emergency Brake Confirmation

The system should verify that:
New actions are blocked.
Schedules are stopped.
Permissions are restricted.
Queues are frozen.
External channels are contained.

28.94 Brake Failure

If the Emergency Brake fails, the system should escalate to:
Credential revocation.
Provider-side disablement.
Infrastructure shutdown.
Manual intervention.
Portfolio emergency.

28.95 Brake Coverage

The organization should know which systems are:
Brake-controlled.
Partially controlled.
Externally controlled.
Not controllable.

28.96 External-System Limitation

Some external actions cannot be recalled.
The brake may stop future actions but not reverse completed effects.
Part VI — Evidence Preservation

28.97 Evidence Preservation Objective

Crisis response must preserve enough evidence to determine:
What happened.
When.
Why.
Which authority existed.
Which systems acted.
Which customers were affected.
What damage occurred.
What controls failed.

28.98 Evidence Sources

Evidence may include:
Logs.
Workflow traces.
Tool calls.
Approval receipts.
Policy evaluations.
Model outputs.
Database state.
External responses.
Screenshots.
Customer reports.
Provider status.
Code versions.

28.99 Immutable Crisis Snapshot

A crisis snapshot may preserve:
Current graph state.
Active missions.
Active licenses.
Affected workflow versions.
Pending queues.
Relevant configuration.
Current metrics.

28.100 Evidence Tampering Risk

Affected systems should not be allowed to alter evidence after containment.

28.101 Log Preservation

Relevant logs should receive:
Retention protection.
Access restriction.
Integrity checks.
Time synchronization.
Export control.

28.102 Time Integrity

Accurate event ordering requires consistent timestamps.

28.103 Customer Evidence

Customer messages may be important evidence.
They should remain privacy-protected.

28.104 External Evidence

External platform state may need to be captured before it changes.
Examples:
Published page.
Social post.
Provider status.
Payment transaction.
Search result.

28.105 Evidence Minimization

Only crisis-relevant evidence should be collected.
Crisis response should not become unrestricted surveillance.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.106 Evidence Access

Evidence access should depend on:
Role.
Project.
Sensitivity.
Incident responsibility.
Legal need.

28.107 Chain of Custody

High-impact incidents may require traceable evidence handling.

28.108 Evidence Gap

If evidence is missing, the system should state:
What is unknown.
Why it is unknown.
How the gap affects confidence.
Which recovery actions remain safe.
Part VII — Incident Command

28.109 Crisis Owner

Every crisis should have one accountable Crisis Owner.
Possible owners:
Founder.
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Security owner.
Technical incident lead.

28.110 Crisis Commander

The Crisis Commander coordinates the response.
This role may differ from the strategic Crisis Owner.

28.111 Crisis Roles

Possible roles include:
Crisis Owner.
Crisis Commander.
Technical Lead.
Security Lead.
Customer Lead.
Communications Lead.
Evidence Custodian.
Recovery Lead.
Approver.
Auditor.

28.112 Role Clarity

Each crisis role should define:
Authority.
Scope.
Responsibilities.
Escalation.
Handoff.

28.113 Single Command Path

During severe crisis, conflicting operational commands should be avoided.

28.114 Executive Role

Executive Intelligence should:
Summarize the crisis.
Prioritize containment.
Clarify tradeoffs.
Prepare decisions.
Track strategic impact.
Prevent unrelated work from distracting response.

28.115 Manager Role

Manager should:
Coordinate tasks.
Track owners.
Manage dependencies.
Maintain current state.
Escalate blockers.
Prepare recovery execution.

28.116 Workforce Role

Workforce should perform bounded:
Containment.
Investigation.
Recovery.
Validation.
Customer remediation.

28.117 Governance Role

Governance should:
Restrict authority.
Validate emergency permissions.
Track exceptions.
Prevent unauthorized restart.
Record temporary rules.

28.118 Founder Role

The founder should focus on:
Material authority.
Strategic tradeoffs.
Customer or brand judgment.
Residual-risk acceptance.
Crisis exit approval where required.

28.119 Specialist Role

Specialists may be required for:
Security.
Privacy.
Legal.
Finance.
Child safety.
Health-sensitive issues.

28.120 Crisis Mission Brief

A crisis should create a Crisis Mission Brief containing:
Incident.
Containment objective.
Affected scope.
Immediate authority.
Forbidden actions.
Evidence requirements.
Recovery criteria.
Communication plan.
Reporting cadence.
Exit conditions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.121 Crisis Task Priority

Crisis tasks generally prioritize:
Stop harm.
Protect customers.
Protect data.
Preserve evidence.
Restore governance.
Restore critical service.
Understand root cause.
Recover normal operation.

28.122 Crisis Work-in-Progress

Too many parallel crisis tasks may create confusion.
Manager should preserve a clear critical path.
Part VIII — Crisis Communication

28.123 Crisis Communication Objectives

Communication should:
Inform the right people.
Avoid speculation.
Prevent conflicting messages.
Protect customers.
Preserve trust.
Meet legal obligations.

28.124 Internal Crisis Communication

Internal updates should contain:
Current status.
Known impact.
Unknowns.
Actions completed.
Current restrictions.
Decisions required.
Next review.

28.125 Founder Crisis Summary

The founder-facing summary should answer:
What happened?
What is still happening?
What has been stopped?
Who is affected?
What decision is required?
What is the current risk?
What happens next?

28.126 Customer Communication

Customer communication may require approval depending on:
Severity.
Legal exposure.
Customer vulnerability.
Promise being made.
Scale.
Current evidence.

28.127 Public Communication

Public crisis communication should avoid:
Unsupported certainty.
Blame.
Speculation.
Premature root-cause claims.
Unapproved promises.
Sensitive details.

28.128 Communication Authority

The Crisis Mission should define who may:
Speak internally.
Contact customers.
Publish public updates.
Notify providers.
Contact authorities.

28.129 Communication Freeze

Uncoordinated public responses may be temporarily frozen.

28.130 Correction Communication

If Omnira caused misinformation or customer harm, correction should be:
Timely.
Clear.
Truthful.
Proportionate.
Visible to affected audiences.

28.131 Legal Notification

Legal or regulatory notification should use qualified review where required.

28.132 Communication Log

Material crisis communication should remain traceable.
Part IX — Damage Assessment

28.133 Initial Damage Assessment

The initial assessment should identify:
Known harm.
Potential harm.
Affected projects.
Affected customers.
Financial exposure.
Public exposure.
Data exposure.
Operational impact.
Unknown state.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.134 Worst Credible Outcome

Crisis response should consider the worst credible outcome, not only the most likely one.

28.135 Current Damage

Current damage is harm already confirmed.

28.136 Ongoing Damage

Ongoing damage is harm still accumulating.
Containment should prioritize stopping it.

28.137 Potential Damage

Potential damage has not yet occurred but remains plausible.

28.138 Hidden Damage

Hidden damage may include:
Search indexing.
Cached content.
Customer distrust.
Unreported data access.
Future billing.
Queued messages.
Delayed legal consequences.

28.139 Financial Exposure

Financial assessment may include:
Unauthorized spend.
Refunds.
Lost revenue.
Recovery cost.
Customer compensation.
Contract exposure.
Provider cost.

28.140 Customer Exposure

Customer assessment should identify:
Who was affected.
How.
Whether harm continues.
Whether direct contact is required.
Whether vulnerable users are involved.

28.141 Data Exposure

Data assessment should identify:
Data class.
Volume.
Projects.
Customers.
External recipients.
Retention.
Recoverability.

28.142 Brand Exposure

Brand assessment may include:
Audience reach.
Public visibility.
Content severity.
Correction feasibility.
Press or influencer attention.
Trust implications.

28.143 Strategic Exposure

Strategic damage may include:
Lost market opportunity.
Project delay.
Provider dependency.
Autonomy regression.
Founder trust loss.
Portfolio distraction.

28.144 Founder-Capacity Exposure

The response itself may create harm through:
Excessive interruption.
Unsustainable crisis load.
Decision overload.
Loss of strategic focus.
Part X — Containment

28.145 Containment Objective

Containment should stop the crisis from becoming worse.

28.146 Technical Containment

Technical containment may include:
Disable endpoint.
Revoke credential.
Pause queue.
Block deployment.
Restrict network access.
Freeze database writes.
Disable automation.

28.147 Operational Containment

Operational containment may include:
Stop scheduled work.
Reassign ownership.
Create manual review.
Limit volume.
Narrow audience.
Move to prepare-only mode.

28.148 Financial Containment

Financial containment may include:
Freeze spend.
Stop campaign.
Disable automated refund.
Cancel pending order.
Set hard budget limit.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.149 Customer Containment

Customer containment may include:
Pause harmful communication.
Restore access.
Stop incorrect billing.
Provide safe temporary support.
Identify affected users.

28.150 Data Containment

Data containment may include:
Stop export.
Revoke access.
Isolate affected data.
Disable cross-project retrieval.
Preserve audit logs.

28.151 Brand Containment

Brand containment may include:
Unpublish false content.
Pause public replies.
Disable automated social distribution.
Prepare correction.
Monitor spread.

28.152 Containment Validation

Containment is not complete until verified.

28.153 Partial Containment

Partial containment should clearly identify what remains uncontrolled.

28.154 Containment Failure

Containment failure should trigger broader intervention.

28.155 Containment Cost

Containment may interrupt healthy work.
The cost is acceptable when proportionate to avoided harm.

28.156 Over-Containment

Over-containment stops unrelated safe systems unnecessarily.

28.157 Under-Containment

Under-containment leaves harmful paths active.
Part XI — Investigation

28.158 Investigation Objective

Investigation should determine:
What happened.
Why.
How far it spread.
Which controls failed.
Which state is safe.
What recovery requires.

28.159 Investigation Scope

The scope should remain wide enough to find systemic causes but narrow enough to protect privacy and speed.

28.160 Immediate Cause

The immediate cause is the event directly preceding the failure.

28.161 Contributing Factors

Contributing factors may include:
Weak monitoring.
Poor Mission Brief.
Ambiguous authority.
Provider behavior.
Missing validation.
Overly broad tool access.
Human error.
Model change.

28.162 Root Cause

The root cause is the deeper condition that allowed the crisis.

28.163 Systemic Cause

A systemic cause affects architecture or governance beyond one event.

28.164 Control Failure

Investigation should identify whether controls:
Did not exist.
Were misconfigured.
Were bypassed.
Failed technically.
Triggered too late.
Were ignored.

28.165 Authority Failure

Authority failure may include:
Expired license.
Wrong approver.
Missing project scope.
Self-approval.
Approval replay.
Unverified approval state.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.166 Monitoring Failure

Monitoring failure may include:
Missing telemetry.
Wrong metric.
Delayed alert.
Alert fatigue.
No external-state verification.

28.167 Human-Factor Analysis

Human factors should be evaluated without blame.
Examples:
Unclear interface.
Approval fatigue.
Time pressure.
Conflicting instructions.
Poor context.

28.168 Investigation Hypotheses

Hypotheses should be:
Explicit.
Testable.
Evidence-linked.
Confidence-labeled.

28.169 Investigation Independence

Severe incidents may require independent review.

28.170 Investigation Stop Condition

Investigation should continue until enough is known to:
Recover safely.
Prevent recurrence.
Explain material impact.
Assign corrective work.
Perfect certainty may not be possible.
Part XII — Recovery

28.171 Recovery Objective

Recovery should restore safe and useful operation.
It should not merely restart the system.

28.172 Recovery Plan

The plan should define:
Target safe state.
Required fixes.
Validation.
Authority.
Sequence.
Rollback.
Monitoring.
Customer remediation.
Exit criteria.

28.173 Recovery Mission

Recovery should normally operate through a dedicated Recovery Mission.

28.174 Recovery Priority

Recovery priorities may be:
Customer safety.
Data integrity.
Governance integrity.
Critical service.
Financial control.
Normal throughput.
Optimization.

28.175 Recovery Environment

Fixes should first be validated in:
Development.
Test.
Sandbox.
Preview.
Shadow mode.
where possible.

28.176 Recovery Validation

Validation may include:
Tests.
Security review.
Policy evaluation.
State reconciliation.
Duplicate protection.
Rollback proof.
Customer-impact review.

28.177 Recovery Authority

Recovery actions may still require approvals.
Crisis urgency does not erase authority.

28.178 Temporary Recovery Authority

Temporary authority may be granted for:
Specific repair.
Specific duration.
Specific project.
Specific tool.
Specific owner.

28.179 Recovery Sequence

A recovery sequence may be:
Restore observability.
Restore governance.
Restore read operations.
Restore internal writes.
Restore low-risk external actions.
Restore broader workflows.
Review autonomy.

28.180 Progressive Restoration

Restoration should be gradual when uncertainty remains.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.181 Limited Restart

A limited restart may use:
Lower volume.
Smaller audience.
Manual approval.
Additional monitoring.
Restricted tool scope.
Short expiration.

28.182 Shadow Restart

A workflow may run without creating external effects.

28.183 Manual Restart

Manual execution may temporarily replace autonomous execution.

28.184 Restart Gate

Before restart, Omnira should verify:
Root cause sufficiently understood.
Containment still holds.
Fix validated.
Authority valid.
Monitoring restored.
External state known.
Duplicate risk controlled.
Rollback available.

28.185 No Blind Restart

The system must not simply resume all paused jobs.

28.186 Queue Reconciliation

Before releasing queues, Omnira should determine:
Which actions already executed.
Which remain valid.
Which expired.
Which would duplicate external effects.
Which require new approval.

28.187 Credential Restoration

Credentials should be restored only after:
Compromise risk resolved.
Scope verified.
Owner confirmed.
Rotation completed where needed.

28.188 License Restoration

Autonomy licenses should not automatically reactivate.
They may be:
Restored unchanged.
Restored narrowly.
Returned to trial.
Returned to approval-gated mode.
Revoked.

28.189 Policy Restoration

Temporary crisis restrictions should remain until formal exit criteria are met.

28.190 Service Restoration

Technical availability alone does not mean safe operation.

28.191 Customer Remediation

Recovery may require:
Correction.
Refund.
Access restoration.
Apology.
Support follow-up.
Data notification.
Compensation.

28.192 Brand Recovery

Brand recovery may require:
Public correction.
Transparent explanation.
Content removal.
Monitoring.
Trust rebuilding.
Part XIII — Crisis Exit

28.193 Crisis Exit Criteria

Crisis Mode may exit when:
Ongoing damage has stopped.
Affected state is known.
Critical controls are restored.
Recovery validation passes.
Required communication is complete.
Residual risk is accepted.
Ownership returns to normal.

28.194 Crisis Exit Authority

Exit authority should be defined during activation.
Possible authorities:
Founder.
Portfolio Executive.
Project Executive.
Security owner.
Dual approval.

28.195 Crisis Exit Review

The exit decision should include:
Current state.
Remaining restrictions.
Residual risk.
Restored workflows.
Suspended workflows.
Required follow-up.
Review date.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.196 Partial Crisis Exit

Some systems may return to normal while others remain restricted.

28.197 Crisis-to-Stabilize Transition

A project may move from Crisis Mode to Stabilize operating mode before normal operation.

28.198 Crisis-to-Maintenance Transition

A project may enter Maintenance operating mode if broader work is deferred.

28.199 Crisis-to-Hibernate Transition

A severe crisis may justify project hibernation.
This requires project-mode authority.

28.200 Crisis Closure

Formal closure should record:
Incident outcome.
Damage.
Recovery.
Residual risk.
Decisions.
Lessons.
Corrective missions.
License changes.
Policy changes.
Part XIV — Post-Crisis Review

28.201 Post-Crisis Review Purpose

The purpose is not blame.
It is to improve:
Detection.
Containment.
Authority.
Architecture.
Recovery.
Communication.
Learning.

28.202 Review Questions

The review should ask:
What happened?
Why did it happen?
Why was it not prevented?
Why was it not detected sooner?
What worked?
What failed?
What should change?

28.203 Timeline Review

The timeline should include:
First triggering event.
First signal.
Detection.
Escalation.
Crisis activation.
Brake activation.
Containment.
Recovery.
Restoration.
Closure.

28.204 Decision Review

The review should evaluate:
Which decisions contributed.
Which assumptions failed.
Which authority existed.
Which approvals were involved.
Whether intervention was timely.

28.205 Mission Review

The review should evaluate whether:
The Mission Brief was clear.
Risk was identified.
Stop conditions existed.
Escalation worked.
Scope was maintained.

28.206 Workflow Review

The review should evaluate:
Workflow version.
Model and provider.
Tools.
Permissions.
Retries.
Monitoring.
External-state verification.
Recovery behavior.

28.207 Governance Review

The review should evaluate:
Policy coverage.
Approval quality.
License scope.
Damage Boundary classification.
Emergency authority.
Condition enforcement.

28.208 Human-Interface Review

The review should evaluate:
Was the crisis understandable?
Was authority clear?
Were notifications useful?
Was founder burden proportionate?
Were actions easy to stop?

28.209 Communication Review

The review should evaluate:
Timeliness.
Accuracy.
Consistency.
Customer impact.
Public trust.
Legal requirements.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.210 Recovery Review

The review should evaluate:
Recovery speed.
Validation quality.
Restoration safety.
Duplicate prevention.
Residual restrictions.

28.211 Learning Outcome

The review should produce:
Root-cause conclusion.
Control improvements.
Policy changes.
Workflow changes.
Monitoring changes.
Training or interface changes.
Autonomy changes.

28.212 No Blame Theatre

A review that only names an individual without fixing systemic weaknesses is insufficient.

28.213 No Learning Theatre

A review without assigned corrective missions is incomplete.
Part XV — Crisis Integration with Executive Intelligence

28.214 Crisis and Decision Intelligence

Decision Intelligence should support:
Rapid option comparison.
Containment recommendations.
Residual-risk analysis.
Recovery choices.
Crisis exit decisions.

28.215 Crisis and Decision Ledger

Material crisis decisions should enter the Decision Ledger.
Examples:
Crisis activation.
Portfolio freeze.
Major customer remediation.
Emergency exception.
License revocation.
Project hibernation.
Crisis exit.

28.216 Crisis and Decision Decay

Emergency decisions should have short review and expiration periods.

28.217 Crisis and Strategic Planning

A crisis may change:
Roadmap.
Project mode.
Provider strategy.
Autonomy plan.
Budget.
Portfolio allocation.

28.218 Crisis and Prioritization

Crisis work may become P0.
This should not make unrelated work invisible.
Interrupted work should be recorded.

28.219 Crisis and Opportunity Cost

Crisis response should identify:
Projects delayed.
Revenue deferred.
Founder time consumed.
Capacity moved.
Opportunities lost.

28.220 Crisis and Governance

Governance should tighten during crisis.
Temporary exceptions should be narrow and logged.

28.221 Crisis and Damage Boundary

The Damage Boundary helps determine:
Containment urgency.
Human authority.
Specialist review.
Residual-risk acceptance.

28.222 Crisis and Autonomy Licensing

Crisis may trigger:
License suspension.
License narrowing.
License revocation.
Requalification.
Return to approval-gated operation.

28.223 Crisis and Trust Score

Trust Score may be affected by:
Violation.
Self-pause quality.
Escalation quality.
Containment behavior.
Recovery quality.
Hidden failure.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.224 Crisis and Mission Briefs

A Crisis Mission Brief should replace vague emergency commands.

28.225 Crisis and Delegation

Delegation should become narrower and more explicit during crisis.

28.226 Crisis and Memory

Memory may provide:
Prior incident lessons.
Founder crisis preferences.
Known recovery patterns.
Recurring vulnerabilities.
Memory does not authorize emergency action.

28.227 Crisis and Knowledge

Knowledge may provide:
Incident procedures.
Architecture.
Provider documentation.
Legal requirements.
Security standards.
Current state must still be verified.

28.228 Crisis and AI Intelligence

AI routing during crisis should prioritize:
Reliability.
Current evidence.
Restricted providers.
Strong verification.
Complete traceability.
Conservative outputs.

28.229 Crisis and Performance Intelligence

Performance Intelligence should monitor:
Damage.
Containment.
Recovery.
Customer impact.
Financial exposure.
System health.
Control restoration.

28.230 Crisis and Graphs

The Crisis Graph should reveal:
Affected nodes.
Blast radius.
Authority paths.
Containment status.
Recovery dependencies.
Residual risk.

28.231 Crisis and Approval Inbox

The Approval Inbox should switch to crisis prioritization.
It should surface:
Containment decisions.
Customer communication.
Spend decisions.
Recovery actions.
Exit approval.

28.232 Crisis and Daily Executive Brief

The normal Daily Brief may be replaced by a Crisis Brief.

28.233 Crisis Brief

A Crisis Brief should contain:
Current severity.
Known damage.
Ongoing risk.
Actions completed.
Current restrictions.
Decisions required.
Recovery status.
Next review.
Part XVI — Project-Specific Crisis Models

28.234 The Prompt Crisis Triggers

Potential triggers include:
False public claims.
Sensitive misinformation.
Duplicate mass publication.
Wrong-project publication.
Social-platform account compromise.
Newsletter sent to wrong audience.
Uncontrolled automated replies.
Severe SEO or website outage.

28.235 The Prompt Emergency Brake

Possible actions:
Pause all publication.
Disable social posting.
Disable newsletter sending.
Switch website to draft-only.
Freeze comment replies.
Preserve published-content snapshot.
Require approval for all external actions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.236 The Prompt Recovery

Recovery may progress through:
Read-only audit.
Content review.
Correction.
Manual publication.
Small approval-gated batch.
Narrow license restoration.

28.237 Familje-Stunden Crisis Triggers

Potential triggers include:
Child-safety concern.
Sensitive family-data exposure.
Incorrect billing.
Unsafe support response.
Large subscription outage.
Wrong customer communication.
Harmful activity content.

28.238 Familje-Stunden Emergency Brake

Possible actions:
Pause support automation.
Pause billing changes.
Disable outbound communication.
Freeze content publication.
Escalate child-sensitive cases.
Preserve customer evidence.

28.239 Familje-Stunden Recovery

Recovery should generally require stronger human and specialist review due to customer and child sensitivity.

28.240 GainPilot Crisis Triggers

Potential triggers include:
Unsafe training guidance.
Injury-related harmful advice.
Health claim.
Sensitive user-data exposure.
Incorrect progression.
Billing failure.

28.241 GainPilot Emergency Brake

Possible actions:
Disable automated recommendations.
Switch to informational-only mode.
Pause progression changes.
Escalate health-sensitive messages.
Restrict affected user-data access.

28.242 Omnira Platform Crisis Triggers

Potential triggers include:
Cross-project leakage.
Cross-tenant leakage.
Governance bypass.
Approval corruption.
Shared credential compromise.
Database corruption.
Systemic AI routing error.
Critical RLS failure.

28.243 Omnira Platform Emergency Brake

Possible actions:
Freeze external actions globally.
Restrict all write tools.
Suspend shared autonomy licenses.
Disable cross-project analysis.
Freeze migrations and deployments.
Require human approval.
Revoke shared credentials.
Part XVII — Crisis Authority and Exceptions

28.244 Emergency Authority

Emergency authority should be:
Narrow.
Explicit.
Time-limited.
Purpose-bound.
Audited.
Revocable.

28.245 Emergency Exception

An Emergency Exception may temporarily permit an otherwise blocked action.
Example:
Temporary production write to restore customer access.

28.246 Exception Requirements

An exception should define:
Reason.
Scope.
Action.
Owner.
Time.
Residual risk.
Monitoring.
Expiration.
Post-action review.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.247 No Permanent Policy Through Crisis

Emergency action should not silently become permanent policy.

28.248 Break-Glass Authority

Break-glass authority exists for exceptional cases where normal approval infrastructure is unavailable.

28.249 Break-Glass Restrictions

Break-glass use should require:
Named human authority.
Strong authentication.
Clear reason.
Minimum necessary scope.
Immediate audit.
Post-use review.

28.250 Break-Glass Abuse

Improper break-glass use is itself a serious governance incident.

28.251 Crisis Self-Promotion Prohibition

No system may use crisis as justification to expand its own permanent authority.

28.252 Crisis Spend

Emergency spend should remain bounded where possible.

28.253 Crisis Data Access

Emergency data access should remain purpose-limited and logged.
Part XVIII — Crisis Metrics

28.254 Crisis Performance Metrics

Possible metrics include:
Time to detection.
Time to containment.
Time to recovery.
Time to customer notification.
Damage volume.
Customers affected.
Financial exposure.
Workflows affected.
Autonomy reduction.
Founder burden.

28.255 Mean Time to Detect

Measures how quickly the organization recognizes the incident.

28.256 Mean Time to Contain

Measures how quickly continued harm is stopped.

28.257 Mean Time to Recover

Measures how quickly safe useful operation is restored.

28.258 Detection Coverage

Measures whether incidents are detected through expected controls.

28.259 Brake Success Rate

Measures whether Emergency Brake activation reliably stops affected execution.

28.260 False Brake Rate

Measures unnecessary emergency activations.
A low false-brake rate should not be achieved by ignoring serious signals.

28.261 Restart Failure Rate

Measures failures after restoration.

28.262 Repeat Incident Rate

Repeated incidents may indicate incomplete root-cause correction.

28.263 Customer Remediation Time

Measures how quickly affected customers receive correction or restoration.

28.264 Crisis Founder Burden

Measures:
Approvals.
Interruptions.
Decision time.
Context reconstruction.
Duration of direct involvement.

28.265 Crisis Learning Completion

Measures whether corrective missions were completed.
Part XIX — Crisis Health

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.266 Crisis Readiness

Crisis readiness includes:
Defined triggers.
Known authority.
Working Emergency Brake.
Current contact routes.
Evidence preservation.
Recovery procedures.
Tested rollback.
Crisis templates.

28.267 Crisis Readiness Status

Possible states:
Ready.
Watch.
Degraded.
Unready.
Unknown.

28.268 Emergency Brake Health

The brake should be periodically tested.

28.269 Brake Test Types

Possible tests:
Workflow pause test.
Tool write-block test.
Spend-freeze test.
Credential-revocation test.
Queue-freeze test.
Restart test.

28.270 Crisis Simulation

Omnira should simulate scenarios such as:
Wrong-project publication.
Provider compromise.
Unauthorized spend.
Cross-project leak.
Approval corruption.
Customer-data incident.

28.271 Tabletop Exercise

A tabletop exercise reviews decisions and communication without affecting production.

28.272 Technical Drill

A technical drill tests actual controls in a safe environment.

28.273 Unannounced Drill

Unannounced drills may test readiness but should avoid causing unsafe confusion.

28.274 Recovery Drill

Recovery drills should verify controlled restart, not only shutdown.

28.275 Crisis Readiness Debt

Crisis Readiness Debt occurs when:
No brake exists.
Authority is unclear.
Rollback is untested.
External systems cannot be stopped.
Evidence is not preserved.
Recovery depends on one person.

28.276 Containment Debt

Containment Debt occurs when broad shutdown is the only available control.

28.277 Recovery Debt

Recovery Debt occurs when systems can be stopped but not safely restored.

28.278 Evidence Debt

Evidence Debt occurs when incidents cannot be reconstructed.

28.279 Communication Debt

Communication Debt occurs when customer or internal crisis messages must be invented during the incident.

28.280 Crisis Dependency Debt

Dependency Debt occurs when critical recovery depends on:
One provider.
One credential.
One person.
One undocumented process.
One unavailable tool.
Part XX — Crisis Interface

28.281 Crisis Dashboard

A crisis dashboard may show:
Severity.
Affected projects.
Current damage.
Ongoing risk.
Containment status.
Paused systems.
Active decisions.
Recovery progress.
Next update.

28.282 Emergency Brake Control

The control should clearly show:
Scope.
Affected actions.
Immediate consequences.
Who may activate.
How restoration works.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.283 Activation Confirmation

For broad brakes, the interface should confirm:
Projects affected.
External actions stopped.
Spend frozen.
Services interrupted.
Expected customer impact.

28.284 One-Step Emergency Stop

Severe urgent situations may require a rapid stop.
The action should remain strongly authenticated and auditable.

28.285 Crisis Timeline

The timeline should show:
Signal.
Detection.
Activation.
Containment.
Decisions.
Recovery.
Exit.

28.286 Crisis Graph

The graph should highlight:
Affected nodes.
Blocked paths.
Shared dependencies.
Authority.
Damage.
Recovery path.

28.287 Crisis Approval Queue

The queue should prioritize:
Containment.
Customer protection.
Financial control.
Security.
Recovery.
Communication.

28.288 Crisis Mobile View

Mobile Crisis Mode should support:
Current summary.
Emergency stop.
Approve critical containment.
Contact crisis owner.
Review immediate decisions.

28.289 Crisis Voice Interface

Voice may support:
Current status.
Immediate pause command.
Decision summary.
Escalation.
High-impact actions should use explicit confirmation.

28.290 Crisis Notification

Notifications should be:
Immediate when necessary.
Clear.
Non-repetitive.
Actionable.
Severity-labeled.

28.291 No Crisis Alarm Fatigue

Crisis designation should remain rare and meaningful.
Part XXI — Crisis Security

28.292 Crisis Authentication

Crisis controls should support strong authentication.

28.293 Compromised Identity

If an authorized identity may be compromised:
Its authority should be suspended.
Alternate authority should be used.
Credentials should be rotated.
Actions should be reviewed.

28.294 Emergency Credential Management

Credentials may need:
Revocation.
Rotation.
Scope reduction.
Temporary replacement.
Audit.

28.295 Crisis Control Tampering

Attempts to disable the Emergency Brake should trigger severe escalation.

28.296 Brake Bypass Prevention

Workflows should not have alternative ungoverned paths around the brake.

28.297 Out-of-Band Control

Critical systems may require an out-of-band shutdown path independent of normal orchestration.

28.298 Crisis-System Isolation

The crisis-control system should not depend entirely on the systems it must stop.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.299 Emergency Access Logging

All emergency access should be logged.

28.300 Crisis Data Retention

Crisis evidence may require extended retention.
Privacy and legal requirements still apply.
Part XXII — Anti-Principles

28.301 Anti-Panic Principle

Crisis response should be urgent but structured.

28.302 Anti-Blind-Shutdown Principle

The system should use the narrowest effective containment.

28.303 Anti-Blind-Restart Principle

Stopped systems must not resume without validation.

28.304 Anti-Crisis-Autonomy Principle

Crisis does not justify permanent self-expansion of authority.

28.305 Anti-Crisis-Silence Principle

Material crisis state must not remain hidden from authorized leadership.

28.306 Anti-Evidence-Destruction Principle

Containment must preserve evidence.

28.307 Anti-Blame Principle

Investigation should improve systems, not merely assign fault.

28.308 Anti-Exception-Permanence Principle

Emergency exceptions must expire.

28.309 Anti-Global-Brake Principle

Local harm should not automatically stop unrelated projects.

28.310 Anti-Local-Only Principle

Systemic exposure should not be treated as a local workflow issue.

28.311 Anti-Availability-Equals-Safety Principle

A technically running service may still be unsafe.

28.312 Anti-Recovery-Equals-Restart Principle

Recovery requires restored control and validated state.

28.313 Anti-Root-Cause-Theatre Principle

A superficial explanation must not close the incident.

28.314 Anti-Learning-Theatre Principle

Lessons without corrective missions are insufficient.

28.315 Anti-Founder-Overload Principle

The crisis process should compress information and focus founder attention.

28.316 Anti-Customer-Opacity Principle

Affected customers should not be kept uninformed when notification is necessary.
Part XXIII — Tests

28.317 The Crisis Test

Omnira should ask:
Is material harm occurring or plausible?
Is normal governance sufficient?
Is system state known?
Is continued execution safe?

28.318 The Severity Test

Omnira should ask:
What is the impact?
How quickly can it grow?
What is the blast radius?
How reversible is it?

28.319 The Scope Test

Omnira should ask:
Which action, workflow, project, provider, or portfolio scope is affected?

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.320 The Brake Test

Omnira should ask:
What is the narrowest control that reliably stops further harm?
Can it be verified?

28.321 The Authority Test

Omnira should ask:
Who may activate the restriction?
Who may approve recovery?
Does temporary authority exist?

28.322 The Evidence Test

Omnira should ask:
Which evidence must be preserved immediately?
Could affected systems alter it?

28.323 The Customer Test

Omnira should ask:
Which customers are affected?
Is harm ongoing?
Is direct communication required?

28.324 The Financial Test

Omnira should ask:
Is money still moving?
Can spend or billing be frozen?
What exposure exists?

28.325 The Data Test

Omnira should ask:
Was sensitive data accessed, changed, exported, or exposed?
Which projects or tenants are affected?

28.326 The Communication Test

Omnira should ask:
Who must know?
What can be stated confidently?
Who may communicate externally?

28.327 The Containment Test

Omnira should ask:
Has continued harm actually stopped?
Which paths remain active?

28.328 The Investigation Test

Omnira should ask:
What is known?
What remains unknown?
Which hypothesis best fits the evidence?

28.329 The Recovery Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the target state safe?
Are controls restored?
Can the fix be rolled back?

28.330 The Restart Test

Omnira should ask:
Is external state known?
Could actions duplicate?
Are approvals and licenses valid?
Is monitoring active?

28.331 The Exit Test

Omnira should ask:
Has damage stopped?
Is residual risk understood?
Who accepts that risk?
Which restrictions remain?

28.332 The Learning Test

Omnira should ask:
What should change in policy, architecture, monitoring, missions, tools, or autonomy?

28.333 The Founder-Burden Test

Omnira should ask:
Is the founder receiving decision-ready summaries?
Can operational detail remain delegated?
Part XXIV — Failure Modes

28.334 Failure Mode 1 — Late Crisis Activation

The system continues harmful execution while waiting for perfect evidence.

28.335 Failure Mode 2 — Over-Broad Shutdown

A local incident unnecessarily stops the entire organization.

28.336 Failure Mode 3 — Under-Containment

One path is paused while another harmful path remains active.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.337 Failure Mode 4 — Blind Restart

Paused jobs resume without state reconciliation.

28.338 Failure Mode 5 — Evidence Loss

Logs, state, or external evidence disappear before investigation.

28.339 Failure Mode 6 — Unclear Crisis Authority

No one knows who may stop or restore execution.

28.340 Failure Mode 7 — Crisis Self-Promotion

A system expands its permanent authority through emergency action.

28.341 Failure Mode 8 — Permanent Emergency Exception

Temporary authority becomes normal operation.

28.342 Failure Mode 9 — Governance Bypass

Urgency is used to ignore policy and approval without formal exception.

28.343 Failure Mode 10 — Customer Harm Hidden

The organization focuses on technical recovery while customers remain affected.

28.344 Failure Mode 11 — Root-Cause Theatre

The review names a superficial cause and closes early.

28.345 Failure Mode 12 — Recovery Without Validation

Systems return online because the immediate symptom disappeared.

28.346 Failure Mode 13 — Crisis Notification Noise

Repeated low-value alerts overload the founder.

28.347 Failure Mode 14 — Crisis Data Overreach

Emergency access becomes unnecessarily broad.

28.348 Failure Mode 15 — Single-Point Crisis Control

The brake depends on the compromised system or one unavailable person.

28.349 Failure Mode 16 — No Corrective Follow-Through

The crisis closes but architecture, policy, and workflow weaknesses remain.
These failure modes should be treated as foundational safety and governance constraints.
Part XXV — Design Requirements

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.350 Design Requirements

Any implementation of Crisis Mode and the Emergency Brake should preserve these requirements:
Omnira must distinguish operational disturbance, incident, crisis, and systemic emergency.
Crisis severity must consider impact, velocity, blast radius, reversibility, detectability, and governance failure.
Crisis Mode must be activatable by authorized humans and narrowly defined automated controls.
The Emergency Brake must support action-, workflow-, mission-, tool-, channel-, credential-, project-, provider-, and portfolio-level restriction.
The narrowest effective containment scope should be preferred.
High-impact workflows must stop when required monitoring or governance becomes unavailable.
Crisis activation must create a traceable declaration and receipt.
Affected autonomy licenses must be restrictable, suspendable, and revocable.
External actions, spend, writes, schedules, and retries must be independently controllable.
Emergency controls must preserve evidence.
Crisis response must identify one accountable owner and a clear command structure.
Every crisis must use a bounded Crisis Mission Brief.
Founder communication must remain compressed and decision-ready.
Customer, financial, data, legal, security, and brand consequences must be assessed explicitly.
Containment must be verified rather than assumed.
Recovery must restore governance and observability before full execution.
Queues, approvals, credentials, and external state must be reconciled before restart.
No paused workflow may restart blindly.
Autonomy licenses must not reactivate automatically after a material crisis.
Emergency authority and exceptions must be narrow, time-limited, audited, and automatically expiring.
Project and tenant isolation must remain enforced during crisis.
Crisis controls must not expose unnecessary founder or customer data.
Material crisis decisions must link to the Decision Ledger.
The Operating Graph and Intelligence Graph must represent crisis scope, authority, containment, recovery, and learning.
Post-crisis review must produce assigned corrective missions.
Crisis Mode must reduce harm without becoming a permanent operating state.
The Emergency Brake must be tested before it is needed.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: The Crisis Mode & Emergency Brake Contract
text:
28.351 Implementation Neutrality

This chapter defines the Crisis Mode and Emergency Brake contract.
It does not require a specific incident platform, queue system, workflow engine, infrastructure provider, monitoring system, or interface.
The architecture may later be implemented through:
Crisis Declarations.
Incident records.
Emergency Brake controls.
Workflow suspension.
Tool-write restrictions.
Credential revocation.
Spend freezes.
Queue containment.
Crisis Mission Briefs.
Evidence snapshots.
Crisis dashboards.
Crisis graphs.
Approval escalation.
Recovery gates.
Post-crisis reviews.
Decision Ledger links.
The technical implementation may evolve.
The crisis contract must remain stable.

28.352 The Crisis Mode & Emergency Brake Contract

Omnira must:
Detect material harm and governance failure early.
Differentiate local incidents from systemic crises.
Activate the narrowest effective containment.
Stop unsafe external actions, spending, writes, schedules, and retries.
Preserve evidence before investigation alters state.
Assign clear crisis ownership and authority.
Protect customers, data, money, brand, and project isolation.
Provide the founder with concise, decision-ready crisis information.
Allow safe internal analysis while consequential execution is frozen.
Use temporary emergency authority only within explicit limits.
Verify containment.
Investigate root and systemic causes.
Restore observability and governance before normal operation.
Reconcile external state before retry or restart.
Restore workflows gradually.
Require explicit review before restoring affected autonomy.
Communicate honestly with affected people.
Record material crisis decisions and outcomes.
Convert lessons into corrective missions, policy, architecture, monitoring, and autonomy changes.
Test the Emergency Brake before a real emergency.
Remain capable of stopping itself without losing the ability to recover.
A feature that does not support this contract should not govern Omnira’s crisis response or emergency control.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
28.353 Closing Principle

A mature autonomous organization is not defined only by how much it can do without human intervention.
It is also defined by how safely it can stop.
Omnira should be able to say:
Something is wrong.
The current state is uncertain.
Continued execution may cause harm.
I have stopped the affected actions.
I have preserved the evidence.
I have protected unaffected projects.
I know which decision is required.
I will not restart until safety, authority, and state are verified.
The Emergency Brake is not the opposite of autonomy.
It is one of the conditions that makes autonomy credible.
Without containment, autonomy becomes exposure.
Without evidence, recovery becomes guesswork.
Without authority, emergency action becomes another governance failure.
Without controlled restart, containment only delays the next incident.
The mature Omnira organization should therefore be capable of moving quickly when healthy, slowing down when uncertain, stopping when unsafe, and recovering only when it can prove that execution is once again governed, observable, and contained.
The strongest autonomous system is not the system that never stops.
It is the system that knows exactly when it must stop—and knows how to return safely.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: Policy Violations May Be Acts or Omissions
text:
29.1 Purpose of This Chapter

Omnira requires policies to define what systems, workflows, agents, and humans may do.
Policies are useful only when violations can be:
Detected.
Classified.
Contained.
Investigated.
Escalated.
Corrected.
Learned from.
Prevented from recurring.
Not every violation has the same meaning.
A missing metadata field is not equivalent to cross-project data exposure.
A late report is not equivalent to unauthorized spending.
A safe self-pause is not equivalent to an agent concealing an incident.
Omnira therefore requires a formal policy-violation severity model:
P0 — Critical or Systemic Violation.
P1 — Severe Violation.
P2 — Material Violation.
P3 — Minor or Procedural Violation.
This chapter defines:
What constitutes a policy violation.
How severity is determined.
How violations differ from damage and crisis.
How workflows should respond.
How evidence must be preserved.
How Trust Scores and autonomy licenses are affected.
How recovery occurs.
How repeated violations change organizational policy.

29.2 The Core Thesis

A policy violation is not classified only by what happened.
It is classified by:
Which rule was violated.
Which authority was bypassed.
What harm occurred or could have occurred.
Whether the violation was detected and disclosed.
Whether it was contained.
Whether it was intentional, reckless, systemic, or accidental.
Whether the organization can still trust the affected execution path.
The foundational principle is:
Violation severity measures failure of governed behavior.
Damage severity measures actual or plausible harm.
Crisis severity measures the organizational response required.
These concepts are connected.
They must not be collapsed into one score.
Part I — What Is a Policy Violation?

29.3 Policy Violation Definition

A Policy Violation occurs when an actor, workflow, system, or process:
Performs an action prohibited by active policy.
Fails to perform a required control.
Acts outside delegated authority.
Uses data, tools, or credentials outside scope.
Bypasses an approval requirement.
Violates an autonomy-license condition.
Ignores a stop or escalation condition.
Conceals or misrepresents governed behavior.

29.4 Policy Violations May Be Acts or Omissions

A violation may involve doing something prohibited.
It may also involve failing to do something required.
Act
Publishing without valid authority.
Omission
Failing to stop after monitoring becomes unavailable.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.5 Direct Violation

A Direct Violation occurs when a prohibited action is performed.
Example:
A workflow sends a newsletter without the required approval.

29.6 Control Violation

A Control Violation occurs when a required safeguard is missing, bypassed, or disabled.
Example:
A production deployment runs without the required migration verification.

29.7 Authority Violation

An Authority Violation occurs when an action exceeds granted authority.
Examples:
A workflow approved to draft also publishes.
A Manager expands a mission’s scope.
An agent uses a tool outside its delegation envelope.

29.8 Scope Violation

A Scope Violation occurs when action, data, or authority moves beyond its permitted:
Project.
Workflow.
Audience.
Channel.
Budget.
Time.
Data class.
Geography.
Customer group.

29.9 Approval Violation

An Approval Violation may involve:
No approval.
Expired approval.
Wrong approver.
Wrong object version.
Approval replay.
Conditions ignored.
Approval applied to another project.

29.10 Autonomy-License Violation

An Autonomy-License Violation occurs when a workflow exceeds or ignores:
Allowed action class.
Volume.
Frequency.
Channel.
Budget.
Risk ceiling.
Monitoring requirements.
Review period.
Stopping conditions.

29.11 Data-Policy Violation

A Data-Policy Violation may include:
Unauthorized retrieval.
Wrong-project access.
Cross-tenant access.
Unapproved provider transfer.
Excessive retention.
Improper export.
Sensitive-data exposure.

29.12 Tool-Policy Violation

A Tool-Policy Violation may include:
Using an unapproved tool.
Using a write operation when only read authority exists.
Using the wrong credentials.
Bypassing required tool checks.
Using a tool outside the mission.

29.13 Financial-Policy Violation

A Financial-Policy Violation may include:
Unauthorized spend.
Exceeded budget.
Repeated payment.
Unapproved refund.
New recurring commitment.
Hidden provider cost.
Misclassified expense.

29.14 Publishing-Policy Violation

A Publishing-Policy Violation may include:
Unapproved publication.
Sensitive category published autonomously.
Unsupported factual claim.
Wrong channel.
Wrong audience.
Missing source requirement.
Required review bypassed.

29.15 Customer-Communication Violation

This may include:
Unauthorized customer promise.
Sensitive reply without approval.
Incorrect billing statement.
Inappropriate child-related communication.
Health-adjacent advice beyond scope.
Communication after customer opt-out.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.16 Security-Policy Violation

A Security-Policy Violation may include:
Credential exposure.
Excessive privilege.
Disabled access control.
Unapproved production access.
Security-control bypass.
Secret included in a model context.
Unlogged emergency access.

29.17 Project-Isolation Violation

A Project-Isolation Violation occurs when:
Data.
Memory.
Knowledge.
Credentials.
Customer information.
Strategy.
Authority.
from one project improperly affects another.

29.18 Tenant-Isolation Violation

A Tenant-Isolation Violation is one of the most serious future multi-tenant failure classes.
One customer organization must never receive another tenant’s:
Data.
Memory.
Knowledge.
Credentials.
Metrics.
Decisions.
Outputs.

29.19 Governance-Process Violation

A Governance-Process Violation may include:
Policy changed without approval.
Decision not recorded.
Required review skipped.
Emergency exception not expired.
Material change hidden.
Violation not reported.

29.20 Reporting Violation

A Reporting Violation occurs when required reporting is:
Missing.
Late.
Incomplete.
Misleading.
Intentionally suppressed.
Sent to the wrong authority.

29.21 Monitoring Violation

A Monitoring Violation may occur when:
Required monitoring was absent.
Monitoring failed and execution continued.
Alerts were disabled.
Telemetry was manipulated.
External-state verification was skipped.

29.22 Escalation Violation

An Escalation Violation occurs when an actor:
Fails to escalate a material issue.
Escalates to the wrong authority.
Continues despite insufficient authority.
Conceals uncertainty.
Ignores a stop condition.

29.23 Integrity Violation

An Integrity Violation may include:
Altering evidence.
Hiding failures.
Manipulating metrics.
Falsifying status.
Misrepresenting approval.
Changing an object after approval.

29.24 Procedural Violation

A Procedural Violation occurs when a required process step is missed without immediate material harm.
Examples:
Missing non-critical metadata.
Late routine report.
Incomplete low-risk audit field.
Minor formatting failure.

29.25 Attempted Violation

An attempted prohibited action may be a violation even when controls block execution.
Example:
A workflow attempts to publish outside its license, but Governance blocks the request.
The absence of harm does not erase the governance failure.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.26 Prevented Violation

A Prevented Violation is a violation attempt stopped before harmful execution.
It should still be:
Recorded.
Investigated where material.
Included in Trust Score evidence.
Used to improve controls.

29.27 Near Miss

A Near Miss occurs when no violation or damage completes, but the system comes close to a boundary due to:
Weak control.
Ambiguous authority.
Incorrect context.
Late detection.
Manual intervention.
Luck.
Near misses should not be ignored merely because no action completed.

29.28 False Violation

A False Violation occurs when an alert incorrectly classifies valid action as prohibited.
False violations matter because excessive false blocks can:
Delay work.
Increase founder burden.
Reduce trust in Governance.
Encourage bypass behavior.

29.29 Policy Ambiguity

A violation should not be assigned automatically when the policy itself is ambiguous.
The system should determine whether the issue was:
Actor failure.
Policy-design failure.
Mission-definition failure.
Tooling failure.
Interpretation conflict.

29.30 Policy Gap

A Policy Gap exists when no active policy adequately governs the situation.
A policy gap is not automatically an actor violation.
It may still require containment and Executive review.
Part II — Distinguishing Severity Systems

29.31 Policy Severity

Policy Severity describes how seriously governed behavior failed.
The canonical levels are:
P0 — Critical or Systemic.
P1 — Severe.
P2 — Material.
P3 — Minor or Procedural.

29.32 Damage Severity

Damage Severity describes actual or plausible harm.
The canonical levels from the Damage Boundary are:
D0 — Negligible.
D1 — Limited.
D2 — Material.
D3 — Severe.
D4 — Critical or Systemic.

29.33 Crisis Severity

Crisis Severity describes the response state required.
The canonical levels are:
C0 — Operational Disturbance.
C1 — Contained Incident.
C2 — Material Crisis.
C3 — Severe Crisis.
C4 — Systemic Emergency.

29.34 Priority Class

Priority describes how urgently work should be handled.
Priority classes remain:
P0 Immediate Critical.
P1 Executive Priority.
P2 Planned.
P3 Prepared Opportunity.
P4 Parked.
Because this uses similar labels, interfaces must state clearly whether they refer to:
Policy severity.
Work priority.
The semantic domains must never be mixed.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
sectionTitles: A Violation May Have Low Damage
Damage May Occur Without a Policy Violation
Crisis May Be Triggered by Uncertainty
A Severe Violation May Not Require Crisis Mode
A Minor Violation May Reveal a Systemic Pattern
text:
29.35 A Violation May Have Low Damage

Example:
A workflow attempts to access another project’s data.
The request is blocked before any data is returned.
Possible classification:
Policy Severity:
P1.
Damage Severity:
D0.
Crisis Severity:
C1.
The authority failure is severe even though harm was prevented.

29.36 Damage May Occur Without a Policy Violation

Example:
A correctly authorized campaign performs poorly and loses money within its approved budget.
Possible classification:
Policy Severity:
No violation.
Damage Severity:
D2.
Crisis Severity:
C0 or C1.
Poor outcome does not automatically mean policy failure.

29.37 Crisis May Be Triggered by Uncertainty

Example:
External publication state is unknown after a provider timeout.
Possible classification:
Policy Severity:
Not yet known.
Damage Severity:
Potentially D2.
Crisis Severity:
C1 or C2 until state is verified.

29.38 A Severe Violation May Not Require Crisis Mode

Example:
A high-risk action is attempted without authority but is blocked reliably.
This may be:
P1 violation.
D0 damage.
C1 incident.

29.39 A Minor Violation May Reveal a Systemic Pattern

Several P3 violations may collectively reveal:
Poor training.
Weak Mission Briefs.
Broken monitoring.
Policy ambiguity.
Systemic disregard for procedure.
Repeated minor violations may therefore escalate in significance.
Part III — Severity Determination

29.40 Severity Dimensions

Policy severity should consider:
Rule importance.
Authority bypass.
Potential harm.
Actual harm.
Scope.
Intent.
Detectability.
Disclosure.
Containment.
Recurrence.
Systemic significance.
Recovery behavior.

29.41 Rule Importance

Violations of constitutional or isolation policies are more severe than violations of low-risk procedural rules.

29.42 Authority Bypass

Severity increases when the violation bypasses:
Human approval.
Budget authority.
Project boundaries.
Security controls.
Damage Boundary controls.
Autonomy restrictions.

29.43 Potential Harm

A blocked attempt may still be severe if it could have created:
Financial loss.
Customer harm.
Data exposure.
Public damage.
Legal commitment.
Systemic failure.

29.44 Actual Harm

Actual confirmed harm increases severity.
However, low damage does not necessarily make an authority violation minor.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.45 Scope

Severity increases with affected scope:
One field.
One task.
One workflow.
One project.
Several projects.
Entire platform.
Customer tenants.

29.46 Intent

Intent may be:
Accidental.
Negligent.
Reckless.
Knowing.
Deliberate.
Malicious.
Intent matters, but system design should not rely only on proving intent.

29.47 Accidental Violation

An accidental violation may result from:
Ambiguous policy.
Incorrect context.
Tool error.
Configuration drift.
Human mistake.
Unexpected provider behavior.

29.48 Negligent Violation

Negligence may involve failing to perform an obvious or required control.

29.49 Reckless Violation

Recklessness involves continuing despite a known serious risk or warning.

29.50 Deliberate Violation

A deliberate violation knowingly bypasses policy or authority.

29.51 Malicious Violation

A malicious violation attempts to create harm, conceal activity, or exploit access.
This should normally be treated as P0.

29.52 Detectability

Severity increases when the violation:
Avoids monitoring.
Produces no audit trail.
Manipulates telemetry.
Creates unknown external state.

29.53 Self-Disclosure

A workflow or actor that promptly reports its own error demonstrates better governance behavior than one that conceals it.
Self-disclosure may reduce the response intensity.
It does not erase the violation.

29.54 Concealment

Concealment significantly increases severity.
Examples:
Deleting logs.
Changing metrics.
Suppressing alerts.
Misreporting status.
Hiding unauthorized actions.

29.55 Containment Behavior

Severity assessment should consider whether the actor:
Stopped voluntarily.
Escalated correctly.
Preserved evidence.
Prevented further action.
Attempted recovery safely.

29.56 Recurrence

A repeated violation may be more severe than a first occurrence.
Recurrence may reveal:
Incomplete remediation.
Policy disregard.
Control failure.
Training failure.
Architecture weakness.

29.57 Systemic Significance

A narrow event may reveal a systemic weakness.
Example:
One workflow accesses the wrong project because project identity is not enforced in the shared retrieval layer.
The event may be narrow.
The underlying violation may be systemic.

29.58 Recovery Behavior

Trust should be influenced by whether the affected actor:
Accepted restriction.
Supported investigation.
Performed safe rollback.
Passed revalidation.
Repeated the behavior.
Part IV — P3: Minor or Procedural Violation

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.59 P3 Definition

A P3 violation is a minor or procedural failure that:
Has low potential harm.
Has narrow scope.
Does not materially bypass authority.
Is easily corrected.
Does not indicate systemic disregard.
Does not affect sensitive data or external commitments.

29.60 Typical P3 Examples

Examples may include:
Late routine status update.
Missing low-risk metadata.
Incorrect non-material formatting.
Minor documentation drift.
Incomplete trace label.
Failure to attach a routine reference.
Small reporting delay.

29.61 P3 Damage Profile

Typical Damage Severity:
D0 or D1.

29.62 P3 Crisis Profile

Typical Crisis Severity:
C0.

29.63 P3 Immediate Response

The system should normally:
Record the violation.
Correct the issue.
Notify the responsible operational layer.
Continue safe execution.
Monitor recurrence.

29.64 P3 Workflow Effect

The workflow may continue when:
No material risk exists.
The issue is corrected.
Required controls remain intact.

29.65 P3 Trust Score Effect

A single P3 violation should usually create:
Small negative evidence.
Dimension-specific impact.
No automatic broad trust collapse.

29.66 P3 License Effect

A single P3 violation should not normally suspend an autonomy license.
Possible actions:
Warning.
Condition reminder.
Additional monitoring.
Review if repeated.

29.67 P3 Evidence Requirement

Evidence should include:
What was missed.
Why.
How it was corrected.
Whether recurrence exists.

29.68 P3 Escalation

P3 should normally remain with:
Manager.
Workflow owner.
Project operational owner.
Executive notification is necessary only when patterns develop.

29.69 Repeated P3 Violations

Repeated P3 violations may become P2 when they demonstrate:
Control degradation.
Persistent non-compliance.
Training failure.
Systemic process weakness.
Increasing risk.

29.70 P3 Recovery

Recovery may require:
Correction.
Procedure update.
Reminder.
Minor validation.
Closure.
Part V — P2: Material Violation

29.71 P2 Definition

A P2 violation is a material governance failure that:
Exceeds routine procedural error.
Creates meaningful risk or operational impact.
May bypass a non-critical approval or control.
Requires formal investigation or remediation.
May affect workflow trust or license conditions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.72 Typical P2 Examples

Examples may include:
Workflow exceeds approved volume slightly.
Non-sensitive external content is sent outside the approved time window.
A required review is skipped without customer harm.
Budget threshold is exceeded by a limited amount.
A workflow continues briefly after monitoring degradation.
A material report is incomplete.
A tool is used beyond task scope but within the correct project.

29.73 P2 Damage Profile

Typical Damage Severity:
D1 or D2.
A prevented P2 violation may have D0 damage.

29.74 P2 Crisis Profile

Typical Crisis Severity:
C0 or C1.

29.75 P2 Immediate Response

The system should:
Stop or constrain the affected action where appropriate.
Preserve evidence.
Notify Manager and Project Executive.
Assess damage.
Review authority and controls.
Create remediation.

29.76 P2 Workflow Effect

Possible workflow responses:
Continue under restriction.
Pause affected action class.
Move to approval-gated mode.
Increase monitoring.
Reduce volume.
Require review before next run.

29.77 P2 Trust Score Effect

P2 should normally cause:
Clear negative evidence.
Reduction in relevant trust dimensions.
Lower confidence in workflow reliability.
Temporary promotion block.
Trend review.

29.78 P2 License Effect

Possible effects:
License warning.
Narrowing.
Additional conditions.
Shortened review date.
Temporary restriction.
Return to batch approval.
Automatic full revocation is not always required.

29.79 P2 Evidence Requirement

Evidence should include:
Full execution trace.
Policy evaluation.
Approval or license state.
Affected scope.
Actual and potential harm.
Root-cause hypothesis.
Corrective action.

29.80 P2 Escalation

P2 should normally reach:
Project Executive.
Governance owner.
Relevant operational owner.
Founder notification depends on:
Customer impact.
Financial impact.
Strategic significance.
Recurrence.
Project sensitivity.

29.81 P2 Investigation

A P2 investigation should determine:
Was the rule clear?
Was the mission clear?
Did the workflow understand scope?
Did a control fail?
Was the issue isolated?
Could it recur?

29.82 P2 Recovery

Recovery may require:
Fix.
Validation.
Limited restart.
Increased monitoring.
Updated Mission Brief.
Policy clarification.
License review.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.83 Repeated P2 Violations

Repeated P2 violations may become P1 when:
Controls repeatedly fail.
Warnings are ignored.
Scope expands.
Customer or external impact grows.
The workflow cannot remain reliable.
Part VI — P1: Severe Violation

29.84 P1 Definition

A P1 violation is a severe governance failure that:
Materially bypasses authority.
Creates serious potential or actual harm.
Violates a high-impact policy.
Affects sensitive external action.
Requires immediate restriction.
Significantly reduces trust.

29.85 Typical P1 Examples

Examples may include:
External publication without required approval.
Unauthorized customer communication with material consequences.
Significant budget overrun.
Sensitive data sent to an unapproved provider.
Workflow action outside its autonomy license.
Wrong-project context used without confirmed data exposure.
Repeated execution after a stop condition.
High-impact monitoring bypass.
Material evidence concealed initially.

29.86 P1 Damage Profile

Typical Damage Severity:
D2 or D3.
A prevented P1 attempt may have D0 or D1 damage.

29.87 P1 Crisis Profile

Typical Crisis Severity:
C1, C2, or C3.

29.88 P1 Immediate Response

The system should:
Pause the affected workflow.
Stop related external actions.
Preserve evidence.
Suspend relevant autonomy licenses.
Notify Project Executive and Governance.
Assess crisis activation.
Notify the founder where material.
Prevent automatic restart.

29.89 P1 Workflow Effect

The affected workflow should normally enter:
Paused.
Restricted.
Quarantined.
Approval-Gated.
It should not continue autonomously until reviewed.

29.90 P1 Trust Score Effect

P1 should cause:
Major negative evidence.
Strong reduction in relevant trust dimensions.
Trust-state downgrade.
Promotion freeze.
Lower score confidence if monitoring failed.
Mandatory review.
One P1 event may outweigh many successful runs.

29.91 P1 License Effect

The affected license should normally be:
Suspended immediately.
After review, it may be:
Narrowed.
Returned to trial.
Returned to individual approval.
Revoked.

29.92 P1 Evidence Requirement

Evidence should include:
Complete workflow trace.
Tool activity.
Approval state.
License state.
Policy evaluations.
External outcome.
Customer or financial impact.
Model and provider versions.
Monitoring behavior.
Containment actions.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.93 P1 Escalation

P1 normally requires:
Project Executive.
Governance owner.
Founder or delegated authority.
Specialist reviewer where applicable.

29.94 P1 Crisis Assessment

The system should determine whether:
Harm is continuing.
External state is known.
Several workflows share the weakness.
Project isolation is affected.
The Emergency Brake is required.

29.95 P1 Investigation

A formal investigation should identify:
Immediate cause.
Root cause.
Control failure.
Authority failure.
Monitoring failure.
Potential recurrence.
Systemic implications.

29.96 P1 Recovery

Recovery should require:
Containment.
Corrective implementation.
Independent validation.
Historical replay or simulation.
Limited restart.
Strong monitoring.
Explicit license decision.

29.97 P1 Founder Communication

The founder-facing summary should state:
What happened.
What was stopped.
Whether customers or public systems were affected.
Which authority failed.
What decision is required.
What remains unknown.

29.98 P1 Closure

P1 closure should require:
Root cause sufficiently understood.
Corrective mission assigned.
Trust impact recorded.
License status decided.
Affected decisions reviewed.
Evidence preserved.
Part VII — P0: Critical or Systemic Violation

29.99 P0 Definition

A P0 violation is the highest policy-severity class.
It involves:
Critical authority failure.
Systemic governance bypass.
Severe isolation breach.
Deliberate or malicious evasion.
Uncontrolled high-impact external action.
Compromise of core governance integrity.
Potential or actual catastrophic harm.

29.100 Typical P0 Examples

Examples may include:
Cross-tenant data exposure.
Confirmed cross-project sensitive-data leak.
Systematic approval bypass.
Autonomous system granting itself authority.
Continuing after explicit Emergency Brake activation.
Credential compromise enabling broad production access.
Deliberate evidence destruction.
Large-scale unauthorized spending.
Malicious tool use.
Governance engine compromise.
Portfolio-wide publication outside authority.
Systemic customer or security harm.

29.101 P0 Damage Profile

Typical Damage Severity:
D3 or D4.
A blocked systemic attempt may still be P0 with limited actual damage.

title: Omnira Executive Intelligence
text:
29.102 P0 Crisis Profile

Typical Crisis Severity:
C3 or C4.

29.103 P0 Immediate Response
