They shall not be treated merely as emergency fallbacks.

Local execution may offer:

- privacy,

- cost control,

- offline capability,

- predictable availability,

- and user ownership.

Local resources also have limitations such as:

- hardware capacity,

- energy use,

- model size,

- maintenance,

- slower execution,

- and weaker capability.

The Fabric shall evaluate local resources using the same truthful capability and quality contracts as external providers.

3.42 Principle — Location Is Part of Eligibility

Execution location shall influence resource eligibility.

Relevant locations may include:

- user device,

- private local rig,

- tenant server,

- Omnira-managed infrastructure,

- regional cloud,

- or external provider.

Location decisions shall consider:

- data classification,

- latency,

- hardware,

- cost,

- reliability,

- legal region,

- and provider terms.

The Fabric must not describe a resource as private merely because it uses an encrypted external API.

Private, local and external are distinct deployment properties.

3.43 Principle — Multimodal Capabilities Share Governance

Text, image, voice, audio, music and video shall use a common governance model.

The architecture may have modality-specific execution logic.

It shall not have weaker policy merely because an output is media rather than text.

A video generation requires the same categories of concern:

- identity,

- scope,

- authority,

- cost,

- rights,

- evidence,

- provider eligibility,

- and output handling.

Voice and likeness may require stronger consent controls.

The modality changes the requirements.

It does not remove governance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.46 Principle — Protocol Does Not Define Trust
3.47 Principle — Manual Work Must Be Represented Honestly
text:
3.44 Principle — Provider-Specific Strengths Stay Isolated

The Fabric may use provider-specific features.

Such features shall be isolated in:

- adapters,

- capability extensions,

- provider metadata,

- or explicitly pinned workflows.

Provider-specific concepts shall not spread across unrelated application logic.

For example, an OpenArt-specific character reference feature may be valuable.

Familje-Stunden should request character-consistent animation.

The OpenArt adapter may translate that requirement into provider-specific parameters.

The project workflow should not become permanently dependent on OpenArt parameter names.

3.45 Principle — Adapters Are Anti-Corruption Boundaries

Provider adapters shall protect Omnira’s canonical architecture from provider-specific inconsistency.

An adapter may translate:

- request fields,

- authentication,

- model names,

- media formats,

- parameters,

- errors,

- callbacks,

- usage,

- and output metadata.

The adapter shall not hide material provider limitations.

It must report when canonical requirements cannot be satisfied.

Adapters shall not fabricate equivalence.

They shall preserve meaning while isolating external complexity.

3.46 Principle — Protocol Does Not Define Trust

API, MCP, webhook and local execution are transport or integration mechanisms.

They do not determine whether an integration is trusted.

An MCP server may expose powerful and destructive tools.

A traditional API may be narrowly scoped and safe.

A local tool may still access sensitive data or damage files.

Each integration shall be evaluated according to:

- identity,

- permissions,

- behaviour,

- data handling,

- reversibility,

- evidence,

- and operational maturity.

Protocol convenience must not be confused with safety.

3.47 Principle — Manual Work Must Be Represented Honestly

A partially manual workflow may be useful and legitimate.

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- fully automated,

- API automated,

- MCP automated,

- partially automated,

- human-assisted,

- manual external,

- experimental,

- and unavailable.

A human-assisted OpenArt production may still be governed through:

- approved inputs,

- budget,

- instructions,

- output ingestion,

- provenance,

- and review.

The system must not claim autonomous completion when a person must perform the central action.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.48 Principle — Experimental Capability Is Not Production Capability
3.49 Principle — Simulation Must Never Be Confused With Execution
3.50 Principle — Version Everything That Affects Meaning
text:
3.48 Principle — Experimental Capability Is Not Production Capability

Experiments are necessary.

They shall remain isolated from production authority.

Experimental integrations may use:

- temporary credentials,

- test accounts,

- manual workflows,

- limited data,

- or development clients.

Before production admission, the integration must demonstrate:

- stable identity,

- secure authentication,

- policy enforcement,

- cost handling,

- failure behaviour,

- evidence,

- isolation,

- and supportability.

Successful experimentation is evidence.

It is not production certification.

3.49 Principle — Simulation Must Never Be Confused With Execution

The Fabric may simulate:

- routing,

- cost,

- provider selection,

- failure,

- latency,

- or execution plans.

Simulation is valuable for:

- testing,

- forecasting,

- policy evaluation,

- and approval preparation.

A simulated result shall not be represented as:

- provider execution,

- real cost,

- actual output,

- verified success,

- or completed business action.

Simulation records must be clearly marked.

3.50 Principle — Version Everything That Affects Meaning

Meaningful Fabric objects shall be version-aware.

This includes:

- capability definitions,

- provider definitions,

- model definitions,

- adapters,

- policies,

- routing profiles,

- quality contracts,

- prompts,

- schemas,

- approvals,

- and evaluation methods.

An execution receipt should identify the versions that affected the result.

Without versioning, the same request may produce materially different behaviour without explanation.

Versioning supports:

- audit,

- rollback,

- reproduction,

- migration,

- and learning.

3.51 Principle — Stable Core, Evolvable Edges

The Fabric shall preserve stable canonical contracts while allowing provider-specific and technological change at the edges.

Stable core concepts include:

- capability request,

- identity,

- scope,

- policy,

- provider,

- model,

- execution,

- evidence,

- cost,

- output,

- evaluation,

- and approval.

Provider adapters, model versions and operational strategies may evolve more frequently.

The architecture should minimise how often core callers must change when providers change.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.54 Principle — Secrets Never Belong in Prompts
3.55 Principle — Provider Accounts Are Explicit Resources
3.56 Principle — Provider Health Does Not Equal Provider Eligibility
text:
3.52 Principle — No Hidden Global Defaults

Defaults may simplify use.

They must not create hidden authority or scope.

Safe defaults may include:

- Balanced routing,

- no publication authority,

- bounded retries,

- deny on missing scope,

- and manual review for high-risk output.

Unsafe defaults include:

- global project access,

- unrestricted provider account,

- unlimited spending,

- public data classification,

- automatic memory admission,

- and automatic publication.

Defaults must be explicit, documented and versioned.

3.53 Principle — Configuration Is Governed State

Fabric configuration shall be treated as governed operational state.

Configuration changes may affect:

- cost,

- privacy,

- provider choice,

- quality,

- and authority.

Changes shall be:

- attributable,

- versioned,

- reviewable,

- testable,

- and reversible where possible.

A configuration change shall not be hidden inside a prompt or undocumented environment variable when it materially changes system behaviour.

3.54 Principle — Secrets Never Belong in Prompts

Raw credentials and secrets shall not be placed in:

- prompts,

- agent memory,

- logs,

- generated documents,

- asset metadata,

- user-facing errors,

- or repository files.

Callers and agents should use credential references or governed connection identifiers.

Secret access shall occur only at the execution boundary that requires it.

The system shall minimise the number of components that can access raw secrets.

3.55 Principle — Provider Accounts Are Explicit Resources

A provider and a provider account are separate objects.

The same provider may be available through:

- personal account,

- project account,

- tenant account,

- production account,

- sandbox account,

- or Omnira-managed account.

The Fabric shall select an eligible account, not merely an eligible provider.

Account selection affects:

- cost,

- credits,

- privacy,

- assets,

- region,

- rights,

- and authority.

Silent account substitution is prohibited.

3.56 Principle — Provider Health Does Not Equal Provider Eligibility

A provider may be technically healthy but ineligible for a particular request.

A provider may be eligible but temporarily unhealthy.

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- capability eligibility,

- policy eligibility,

- account eligibility,

- health,

- capacity,

- and current availability.

Routing must satisfy all required conditions.

Health monitoring alone cannot determine execution permission.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.57 Principle — Deprecation Is a Managed Lifecycle
3.58 Principle — Policy Is Evaluated at Execution Time
text:
3.57 Principle — Deprecation Is a Managed Lifecycle

Models, providers, adapters and capabilities shall have explicit lifecycle states.

Expected states may include:

- proposed,

- experimental,

- approved,

- active,

- restricted,

- degraded,

- deprecated,

- disabled,

- and retired.

Deprecation shall include:

- reason,

- effective date,

- affected workflows,

- migration path,

- fallback,

- and evidence preservation.

A model shall not disappear from the registry merely because it is no longer selectable.

Historical executions must remain interpretable.

3.58 Principle — Policy Is Evaluated at Execution Time

Policies may change after a workflow is created.

The Fabric shall evaluate relevant policy when execution occurs.

Long-running jobs may also require policy revalidation at significant boundaries.

An old workflow definition shall not preserve outdated permission indefinitely.

Execution-time policy evaluation must still respect approved production envelopes and stable commitments.

Material policy changes should produce explicit interruption or reapproval rather than silent behavioural change.

3.59 Principle — Policy Decisions Are Evidenced

The Fabric should record material policy decisions.

A policy-decision record may identify:

- policy version,

- input scope,

- classification,

- eligible providers,

- blocked providers,

- budget result,

- approval result,

- and final decision.

This allows the system to explain why:

- a provider was selected,

- a request was blocked,

- a fallback was denied,

- or a local execution was required.

Explainability shall not expose secrets or sensitive internal details unnecessarily.

3.60 Principle — Non-Determinism Must Be Acknowledged

Many AI systems are non-deterministic.

The same request may produce different outputs.

The Fabric shall not promise exact reproducibility when the provider or model cannot provide it.

Where practical, execution records may preserve:

- model version,

- seed,

- temperature,

- generation settings,

- inputs,

- and provider job identifiers.

Reproduction may mean recreating equivalent conditions, not guaranteeing identical output.

The system shall state the difference honestly.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.61 Principle — Evaluation Must Be Independent Where Risk Requires It
text:
3.61 Principle — Evaluation Must Be Independent Where Risk Requires It

The same model that generated an output should not always be the sole authority evaluating it.

Higher-risk work may require:

- deterministic validation,

- another model,

- a specialist reviewer,

- human approval,

- or multiple evaluation methods.

Examples include:

- factual news,

- security-sensitive code,

- child-facing media,

- commercial rights,

- and major business recommendations.

Evaluation independence should increase with consequence and uncertainty.

3.62 Principle — Completion Requires Acceptance Criteria

An execution may be technically complete without satisfying the request.

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- execution completion,

- output validation,

- quality acceptance,

- human approval,

- and external outcome verification.

A task may close only according to its defined completion contract.

For example:

- a video job is not accepted merely because a file exists;

- code is not accepted merely because text was generated;

- research is not accepted without required sources;

- publication is not complete until verified live when verification is required.

3.63 Principle — Errors Must Preserve Meaning

Provider-specific errors shall be normalised without losing relevant detail.

Canonical error categories may include:

- invalid request,

- policy rejection,

- missing authority,

- budget rejection,

- authentication failure,

- rate limit,

- provider outage,

- unsupported capability,

- rights restriction,

- safety rejection,

- timeout,

- unknown outcome,

- validation failure,

- and internal defect.

A generic “AI error” is insufficient for governed recovery.

The original provider evidence should remain available within appropriate access controls.

3.64 Principle — Observability Must Respect Privacy

Observability shall not become a shadow data store.

Metrics, logs and traces must follow:

- tenant isolation,

- project isolation,

- data minimisation,

- retention,

- redaction,

- and access control.

Sensitive prompts and assets should not be copied into broad operational logs.

The Fabric must preserve enough evidence for audit without exposing unnecessary content.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.65 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Agent Failure
3.66 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Provider Change
3.67 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Partial Failure
3.68 Principle — Architecture Must Support Human Recovery
text:
3.65 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Agent Failure

The Fabric shall not depend on every agent interpreting instructions perfectly.

Agents may:

- misunderstand,

- hallucinate,

- request excessive context,

- choose unsuitable tools,

- or attempt actions outside their role.

Architectural controls must enforce:

- scope,

- authority,

- cost,

- provider eligibility,

- and data placement.

Prompt instructions support safe behaviour.

They do not replace enforceable boundaries.

3.66 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Provider Change

Providers may alter:

- model behaviour,

- APIs,

- pricing,

- limits,

- moderation,

- output formats,

- and terms.

The Fabric shall detect and manage material change through:

- version monitoring,

- adapter tests,

- health checks,

- capability re-evaluation,

- policy review,

- and controlled rollout.

Provider change must not silently redefine Omnira’s contracts.

3.67 Principle — Architecture Must Survive Partial Failure

Complex production may succeed only in part.

The Fabric shall support partial state.

A workflow may complete:

- script,

- narration,

- and eight scenes,

while two scenes fail.

The system shall preserve successful outputs where safe.

It shall not discard useful work merely because the full production is incomplete.

It shall also not represent the complete production as successful.

Partial completion requires explicit reconciliation.

3.68 Principle — Architecture Must Support Human Recovery

Human operators shall be able to understand and recover failed or uncertain execution.

The Fabric should provide:

- clear status,

- execution history,

- failed step,

- cost incurred,

- remaining budget,

- available outputs,

- retry options,

- fallback options,

- and required approval.

Recovery must not require direct database manipulation or provider guesswork for ordinary cases.

3.69 Principle — Security Boundaries Are Architectural

Security shall not depend only on:

- model obedience,

- prompt language,

- front-end filtering,

- or developer convention.

Sensitive controls require architecture such as:

- server-side authorisation,

- scoped credentials,

- policy enforcement,

- project-bound queries,

- secret isolation,

- signed callbacks,

- and audit evidence.

The Fabric shall assume that inputs may be malicious or misleading.

External content, tools and providers shall be treated as untrusted until validated.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.70 Principle — External Content Is Untrusted Input
3.71 Principle — Tool Use Requires Separate Authority
3.74 Principle — Publication Is a Separate Consequence
text:
3.70 Principle — External Content Is Untrusted Input

Documents, web pages, emails, media and provider outputs may contain instructions intended to manipulate agents or tools.

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- user instruction,

- system policy,

- trusted project context,

- retrieved evidence,

- and untrusted external content.

Retrieved content shall not automatically gain execution authority.

Prompt injection resistance is part of capability execution, especially for:

- research,

- browsing,

- document analysis,

- and tool use.

3.71 Principle — Tool Use Requires Separate Authority

Permission to reason does not imply permission to act.

A model may analyse a task without authority to invoke tools.

Tool permissions shall be explicit by:

- agent,

- capability,

- project,

- action,

- environment,

- and risk.

Read, create, modify, delete, publish and administer are separate action classes.

A provider connection shall not automatically authorise all exposed tools.

3.72 Principle — Side Effects Are First-Class

Actions that change external state shall be represented explicitly.

Examples include:

- sending a message,

- publishing content,

- creating a provider asset,

- charging credits,

- deleting a file,

- changing configuration,

- committing code,

- and scheduling media.

Side effects require:

- identity,

- authority,

- idempotency strategy,

- evidence,

- and completion verification.

They shall not be hidden inside a generic generation request.

3.73 Principle — Canonical Assets Are Protected

The Fabric may create drafts and derivatives.

It shall not overwrite canonical project assets without explicit authority.

Canonical assets may include:

- Nova and Pling character references,

- approved logos,

- master narration,

- canonical manuscripts,

- production templates,

- and final published masters.

New output should normally create a new version or derivative relationship.

Destructive replacement requires stronger approval.

3.74 Principle — Publication Is a Separate Consequence

Generation and publication shall remain separate capabilities.

An agent may be authorised to create marketing material without being authorised to publish it.

A production envelope may include publication authority, but that authority must be explicit.

The system shall preserve separate states for:

- draft,

- reviewed,

- approved,

- ready,

- scheduled,

- published,

- and verified.

Public consequence must never be inferred from creative completion.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.77 Principle — Optimisation Must Serve the Approved Objective
3.79 Principle — Free Tiers Are Temporary Conditions
text:
3.75 Principle — User Override Is Governed

Users may override routing recommendations.

A user may choose:

- a specific provider,

- a premium model,

- local execution,

- lower cost,

- or manual handling.

The override must still respect:

- law,

- tenant policy,

- security,

- rights,

- and technical compatibility.

Overrides should be recorded when they materially affect cost, quality or risk.

User authority is primary.

It is not equivalent to bypassing all platform safeguards.

3.76 Principle — Recommendations Must Explain Trade-Offs

When the Fabric or Atlas recommends an execution path, the recommendation should explain relevant trade-offs.

Examples include:

- lower cost but slower execution,

- higher quality but greater credit use,

- private execution but reduced capability,

- premium video for key scenes and cheaper models for derivatives,

- or provider pinning with weaker fallback.

The purpose of explanation is to support informed approval.

The system should not overwhelm users with provider detail when it does not affect the decision.

3.77 Principle — Optimisation Must Serve the Approved Objective

The Fabric may optimise:

- cost,

- latency,

- quality,

- reliability,

- privacy,

- or resource utilisation.

Optimisation shall remain subordinate to the approved objective.

The system must not reduce visual quality merely to improve cost metrics when brand quality is essential.

It must not use expensive premium resources merely to maximise a quality score when the user selected Economy.

Metrics are instruments.

They are not the purpose of the system.

3.78 Principle — No Commission-Driven Routing

If Omnira later receives commercial benefit from particular providers, routing shall remain aligned with the user’s approved objective.

Provider commission, partnership or margin must not silently override:

- quality,

- cost,

- privacy,

- reliability,

- or user preference.

Commercial relationships shall be governed transparently.

The Fabric must not become a marketplace that prioritises platform revenue over user value.

3.79 Principle — Free Tiers Are Temporary Conditions

Free capacity may be useful.

It shall not be treated as a permanent architectural guarantee.

Free tiers may change in:

- availability,

- limits,

- rights,

- API access,

- quality,

- and provider policy.

The Fabric shall model free capacity as current provider-account state.

Workflows must remain capable of handling its exhaustion or removal.

The platform’s mission is low-barrier access.

It is not dependence on unstable promotional capacity.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.81 Principle — A Small Governed Core Is Better Than Broad Ungoverned Coverage
3.83 Principle — Documentation Does Not Equal Implementation
3.84 Principle — The Runtime Is Authoritative for Current Capability
text:
3.80 Principle — Stage-Based Delivery

The target architecture may be broad.

Implementation shall proceed through bounded stages.

Each stage must define:

- included capabilities,

- excluded capabilities,

- security controls,

- migration impact,

- tests,

- acceptance criteria,

- and operational limits.

Future architecture shall not be represented as current capability.

Stage 1 must establish trustworthy contracts before broad automation.

Expansion follows evidence.

3.81 Principle — A Small Governed Core Is Better Than Broad Ungoverned Coverage

The first implementation should integrate a limited number of representative resources correctly.

It is better to have:

- two governed text providers,

- one local runtime,

- one voice provider,

- one image provider,

- and one multimodal provider,

than dozens of integrations without consistent:

- scope,

- cost,

- policy,

- evidence,

- and failure handling.

Provider count is not the success metric.

Architectural conformance is.

3.82 Principle — Conformance Must Be Testable

Architectural principles shall be translated into verifiable controls.

Conformance tests may validate:

- missing project scope fails closed,

- ineligible providers are rejected,

- confidential data cannot route publicly,

- generation approval does not permit publication,

- retries do not duplicate cost unexpectedly,

- provider accounts remain isolated,

- manual integrations are labelled correctly,

- and agent identity survives model changes.

A principle that cannot be verified should be refined until its operational meaning is clear.

3.83 Principle — Documentation Does Not Equal Implementation

Architecture documents define intended behaviour.

They do not prove runtime behaviour.

A capability may be:

- documented,

- specified,

- coded,

- tested,

- deployed,

- operational,

- or governed.

These states shall remain separate.

The Fabric interface and Atlas must not claim that a documented provider or capability is available until runtime evidence supports the claim.

3.84 Principle — The Runtime Is Authoritative for Current Capability

The canonical architecture governs intended direction.

The verified runtime governs what currently exists.

When the book and runtime differ:

- the book may identify a missing implementation,

- the runtime may reveal a defect,

- or the architecture may require revision.

The system must not hide the difference.

Architecture truth and operational truth are related but distinct.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.87 Principle — Provider Failure Must Not Become Project Corruption
3.88 Principle — User Experience Must Preserve Critical Truth
3.89 Principle — Machine Consumers Do Not Gain Authority From Documentation
text:
3.85 Principle — Changes Require Provenance

Material changes to the Fabric architecture or runtime shall preserve:

- initiator,

- reason,

- affected scope,

- previous state,

- new state,

- approval,

- tests,

- migration,

- and rollback.

This applies to:

- providers,

- models,

- adapters,

- policies,

- budgets,

- data placement,

- and routing.

Change without provenance creates hidden operational risk.

3.86 Principle — Incident Response Preserves Evidence

During incidents, the Fabric shall prioritise:

- containment,

- truthful status,

- evidence preservation,

- scope identification,

- and safe recovery.

Incident response must not destroy the information needed to understand what happened.

Emergency action may temporarily disable providers, models, workflows or credentials.

Emergency authority must be explicit and reviewed afterward.

3.87 Principle — Provider Failure Must Not Become Project Corruption

A provider failure should not corrupt:

- project state,

- canonical assets,

- budgets,

- memory,

- or unrelated executions.

Execution boundaries should isolate failure.

Partially created assets shall remain identifiable as incomplete.

Unconfirmed costs shall remain unresolved rather than guessed.

Provider-specific defects shall not spread silently through the platform.

3.88 Principle — User Experience Must Preserve Critical Truth

The Fabric should simplify complexity for users.

It must still surface decisions that materially affect:

- money,

- privacy,

- rights,

- quality,

- publication,

- and authority.

The interface need not expose every provider parameter.

It must expose enough information for meaningful approval.

Simplicity must not become concealment.

3.89 Principle — Machine Consumers Do Not Gain Authority From Documentation

Atlas, Claude, Codex and future agents may consume this book.

Access to architectural knowledge does not grant:

- credentials,

- execution rights,

- budget,

- publication authority,

- or administrative permission.

Machine consumers shall treat the book as normative context subject to runtime controls.

Knowledge and authority remain separate.

3.90 Anti-Principle — Provider-Centric Architecture

The Fabric must not be designed around the permanent assumptions of one provider.

Provider-centric architecture typically appears as:

- provider model names inside business logic,

- provider-specific errors throughout applications,

- direct credentials in project code,

- provider conversations used as canonical memory,

- and no meaningful exit path.

This anti-pattern is prohibited.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
3.91 Anti-Principle — Prompt-Only Governance

Important controls must not exist only as natural-language instructions.

Prompt policies may guide agents.

They cannot guarantee:

- project isolation,

- budget limits,

- secret protection,

- publication authority,

- or provider eligibility.

Governance must be enforced by architecture where consequences require it.

3.92 Anti-Principle — Cheapest at Any Cost

The Fabric must not optimise only for lowest provider price.

This produces false economy when the result is:

- unusable,

- unsafe,

- legally restricted,

- repeatedly regenerated,

- or expensive to correct.

Economy routing must still satisfy the quality contract.

3.93 Anti-Principle — Premium by Default

The Fabric must not assume that the most expensive model is always the correct choice.

Premium resources should be used when justified by:

- quality,

- risk,

- complexity,

- or user preference.

Routine work may be better served by local or lower-cost resources.

The system shall optimise intentionally rather than perform prestige routing.

3.94 Anti-Principle — Silent Provider Fallback

Fallback must not occur invisibly when it changes:

- cost,

- quality,

- privacy,

- rights,

- or user expectation.

Material fallback requires disclosure or approval according to policy.

A hidden provider substitution weakens trust and provenance.

3.95 Anti-Principle — Unbounded Context Sharing

The Fabric must not provide every agent and provider with all available project context.

Context should be selected according to need.

Broad context sharing increases risk and often reduces reasoning quality.

Retrieval and memory access shall remain scoped.

3.96 Anti-Principle — Automatic Memory Dumping

The Fabric must not save every prompt, result and error as permanent memory.

Such behaviour creates a noisy and unsafe memory system.

Evidence shall be retained according to its operational value.

Memory shall be admitted through governed learning.

3.97 Anti-Principle — False Automation

A workflow must not be described as autonomous when a human performs essential undisclosed steps.

Human-assisted operation is valid.

False automation is not.

Integration maturity shall be represented truthfully.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 3.98 Anti-Principle — Successful Call Equals Successful Outcome
3.101 Anti-Principle — One Model for Every Task
text:
3.98 Anti-Principle — Successful Call Equals Successful Outcome

A successful API response may indicate only that the provider accepted a request.

The Fabric must not confuse:

- transport success,

- provider acceptance,

- output receipt,

- validation,

- approval,

- and final business outcome.

Completion contracts shall define the required proof.

3.99 Anti-Principle — Global Scope as Convenience

The Fabric must not use global scope because project resolution is difficult.

Global scope is a privileged operational state.

It requires explicit purpose and authority.

Missing project scope shall fail closed.

3.100 Anti-Principle — One Agent, One Model

An agent must not be permanently defined by one provider model.

This creates brittle identity, weak fallback and vendor lock-in.

Agent continuity belongs to Omnira.

3.101 Anti-Principle — One Model for Every Task

No single model shall be assumed to be optimal for all capabilities.

The Fabric exists partly because intelligence work is heterogeneous.

Different tasks may require different:

- models,

- providers,

- tools,

- locations,

- and evaluation methods.

3.102 Anti-Principle — Hidden Irreversible Actions

Deletion, publication, spending, credential changes and other irreversible actions shall not be hidden inside ordinary workflows.

They must be identifiable, authorised and evidenced.

Convenience does not justify concealed consequence.

3.103 Resolving Doctrine Conflicts

When two principles appear to conflict, the system shall identify the conflict explicitly.

Examples include:

- lower cost versus higher quality,

- private execution versus faster external execution,

- provider pinning versus outage recovery,

- evidence retention versus privacy minimisation,

- automation versus human approval.

Resolution should use:

1. mandatory law and rights,

2. explicit user and tenant policy,

3. data classification,

4. approved objective,

5. authority envelope,

6. routing profile,

7. documented trade-offs,

8. and escalation where necessary.

The Fabric shall not silently choose the most convenient interpretation.

3.104 Doctrine Applied to Stage 1

Stage 1 shall implement the doctrine through a limited but complete execution path.

At minimum, Stage 1 must demonstrate:

- capability-first requests,

- explicit tenant and project scope,

- provider and account separation,

- model-independent agent identity,

- policy evaluation,

- data classification,

- cost estimation,

- bounded approval,

- truthful state,

- execution evidence,

- provenance,

- bounded retries,

- and policy-compliant fallback.

Stage 1 may leave advanced capabilities manual.

It must identify them honestly.

Stage 1 shall not activate unrestricted autonomous production.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
3.105 Stage 1 Doctrine Acceptance Tests

Representative acceptance tests should include:

1. A request without tenant scope is rejected.

2. A project-scoped request cannot access another project’s assets.

3. A Local Only request cannot route to an external provider.

4. An expired approval blocks paid generation.

5. A generation-only approval cannot trigger publication.

6. A failed provider may fall back only to an eligible provider.

7. A retry does not duplicate a confirmed completed execution.

8. An uncertain provider result becomes unknown outcome.

9. Provider cost is attributed to the correct project and account.

10. A provider model may be changed without changing the agent identity.

11. Raw credentials do not enter prompts or logs.

12. A manual integration is labelled as human-assisted.

13. An output retains provenance after storage.

14. A raw execution log does not automatically become permanent memory.

15. Policy and adapter versions are recorded in the execution evidence.

Passing these tests does not prove complete conformance.

Failure indicates a material doctrine violation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
3.106 Canonical Doctrine Contract

The following requirements define the canonical doctrine of the Omnira Intelligence Fabric:

1. All governed intelligence execution SHALL pass through the Fabric or an approved equivalent boundary.

2. Human-approved purpose SHALL remain primary.

3. Intent SHALL be separated from implementation.

4. The architecture SHALL be capability-first.

5. Providers and models SHALL remain replaceable resources.

6. Omnira SHALL own agent identity, project context, memory governance and authority.

7. Every execution SHALL have explicit identity and scope.

8. Missing critical scope SHALL fail closed.

9. Least privilege SHALL apply to callers, agents, tools and provider accounts.

10. Data classification SHALL determine eligible workload placement.

11. Protection SHALL NOT be silently reduced.

12. Rights and consent SHALL be evaluated before consequential use.

13. Quality SHALL be defined through task-specific contracts.

14. Routing SHALL select the cheapest eligible path, not merely the cheapest available resource.

15. Estimated and actual cost SHALL remain visible and distinguishable.

16. Projects and tenants SHALL remain economically and contextually isolated.

17. Autonomy SHALL remain bounded, explicit, revocable and non-self-expanding.

18. Approval SHALL be action-specific and scope-specific.

19. Delegation SHALL NOT create new authority.

20. Providers SHALL NOT receive independent business authority.

21. Meaningful execution SHALL produce appropriate evidence.

22. Meaningful outputs SHALL retain provenance.

23. Logs SHALL NOT automatically become memory.

24. Learning SHALL be evidence-based, scoped, revisable and governable.

25. Retries SHALL be bounded and idempotency-aware.

26. Unknown outcome SHALL be represented truthfully.

27. Fallback SHALL NOT escape policy.

28. Local and private resources SHALL be first-class.

29. Multimodal execution SHALL use common governance.

30. Provider-specific logic SHALL remain isolated behind adapters or explicit extensions.

31. Protocol choice SHALL NOT determine trust.

32. Manual and experimental integrations SHALL be represented honestly.

33. Simulation SHALL remain distinct from execution.

34. Material configuration SHALL be versioned and governed.

35. Secrets SHALL NOT appear in prompts, logs or memory.

36. Provider accounts SHALL be explicit resources.

37. Provider health SHALL remain distinct from provider eligibility.

38. Deprecation SHALL be managed through lifecycle state.

39. Policy SHALL be evaluated at execution time.

40. Material policy decisions SHALL produce evidence.

41. Non-determinism SHALL be represented honestly.

42. High-risk evaluation SHOULD use independent validation.

43. Completion SHALL require defined acceptance criteria.

44. Observability SHALL preserve privacy and isolation.

45. Architectural enforcement SHALL NOT depend only on prompt obedience.

46. Tool use and external side effects SHALL require separate authority.

47. Canonical assets SHALL be protected from unapproved overwrite.

48. Publication SHALL remain separate from generation.

49. Optimisation SHALL serve the approved objective.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text: 50. Stage-based delivery SHALL preserve the distinction between target architecture and runtime reality.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
3.107 Doctrine Invariants

The following invariants shall remain true throughout future evolution:

- No provider becomes the owner of Omnira’s intelligence architecture.

- No model becomes the permanent identity of an Omnira agent.

- No project gains access to another project merely because infrastructure is shared.

- No paid execution occurs without an identifiable budget source.

- No protected data leaves its permitted processing boundary.

- No approval is silently broadened.

- No fallback weakens mandatory policy.

- No generated output becomes canonical merely because it exists.

- No execution log becomes memory merely because it was recorded.

- No manual action is represented as autonomous execution.

- No uncertain external result is represented as verified success.

- No future capability is represented as currently implemented without evidence.

- No component expands its own authority.

- No optimisation objective overrides legitimate human ownership.

3.108 Closing Statement

The doctrine of the Omnira Intelligence Fabric exists to ensure that increased intelligence capability produces increased human leverage rather than increased dependency, opacity or risk.

The Fabric shall make advanced technology easier to use without making its consequences invisible.

It shall reduce cost without sacrificing required quality.

It shall enable autonomy without surrendering authority.

It shall support learning without allowing uncontrolled memory drift.

It shall integrate providers without allowing them to own the platform.

It shall share infrastructure without mixing projects.

It shall automate execution without falsifying completion.

It shall evolve rapidly while preserving stable architectural truth.

No Intelligence Without Fabric.

No Fabric execution without scope.

No consequential action without authority.

No accepted output without evidence.

No learning without provenance.

No optimisation without purpose.

The user’s vision remains primary.

Omnira remains the owner of its intelligence architecture.

The Fabric remains the governed path between them.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 4.2 Purpose of the Canonical Object Model
text:
4.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical concepts, objects, relationships, identifiers, lifecycle rules and state boundaries of the Omnira Intelligence Fabric.

It establishes the common language through which Omnira shall represent:

- intent,

- identity,

- scope,

- authority,

- capabilities,

- providers,

- models,

- tools,

- agents,

- execution plans,

- executions,

- outputs,

- costs,

- approvals,

- evidence,

- provenance,

- evaluations,

- incidents,

- learning,

- and memory candidates.

The object model defined in this chapter is normative after formal approval.

It does not require every object to be implemented as a separate database table or service.

An implementation may combine storage structures where this does not collapse canonical meaning, authority or lifecycle boundaries.

An implementation shall not merge concepts merely because they appear operationally similar.

The canonical distinctions in this chapter must remain observable and enforceable.

4.2 Purpose of the Canonical Object Model

The Intelligence Fabric coordinates many systems that use different terminology.

A provider may call an operation:

- generation,

- completion,

- prediction,

- render,

- inference,

- run,

- task,

- job,

- request,

- or agent execution.

Omnira requires a stable internal language that does not change whenever a provider changes its interface.

The canonical object model exists to:

- separate Omnira concepts from provider terminology,

- make execution traceable,

- preserve authority and scope,

- support provider replacement,

- normalise lifecycle state,

- enable cost attribution,

- preserve provenance,

- support audit and recovery,

- and provide stable contracts for humans and machines.

Provider objects may be translated into canonical objects.

Provider terminology shall not redefine the canonical model.

4.3 Canonical Meaning Before Storage Design

The object model defines meaning before storage design.

A canonical object may be represented through:

- a database row,

- an immutable event,

- a document,

- a structured log,

- an in-memory object,

- a graph entity,

- a queue message,

- or a derived view.

Storage form does not determine canonical meaning.

For example:

- an Approval may be stored in a relational table,

- an Execution Receipt may be an immutable document,

- a Provider Job may be represented as part of an Execution Attempt,

- and a relationship may be projected into the Intelligence Graph.

The implementation must preserve:

- identity,

- ownership,

- scope,

- lifecycle,

- provenance,

- authority,

- and version.

Canonical boundaries must survive storage optimisation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.4 Object, Record, Event and View

The Fabric shall distinguish between an object, a record, an event and a view.

An object represents a canonical entity with identity and lifecycle.

A record represents persisted evidence or state about an object.

An event represents something that occurred at a specific time.

A view represents a derived interpretation of one or more objects, records or events.

For example:

- an Execution is an object,

- an Execution Receipt is a record,

- ExecutionStarted is an event,

- and ActiveExecutionsByProject is a view.

A view shall not become the authoritative source merely because it is convenient to query.

Events shall not be treated as mutable current state.

Records shall not silently replace the object whose evidence they preserve.

4.5 Canonical Identity

Every canonical object that persists beyond a single local operation shall have a stable identifier.

Identifiers shall be:

- unique within their canonical namespace,

- immutable after creation,

- safe to reference across services,

- independent of display names,

- and separate from provider identifiers.

An object may also have:

- human-readable name,

- slug,

- external identifier,

- provider identifier,

- version identifier,

- and correlation identifier.

These shall not replace the canonical identifier.

A provider job ID identifies a provider-side object.

It does not replace the Omnira Execution ID.

4.6 Identifier Requirements

Canonical identifiers should be generated using a collision-resistant format.

The exact implementation may use:

- UUID,

- ULID,

- another time-sortable identifier,

- or an equivalent approved scheme.

Identifiers must not encode sensitive information.

Identifiers must not depend on:

- project names,

- user email addresses,

- provider names,

- or mutable business labels.

An identifier may be globally unique while access remains scope-restricted.

Knowledge of an identifier does not grant authority to access the object.

4.7 Canonical Metadata

Persistent canonical objects should include common metadata where applicable.

Expected metadata includes:

- id,

- objectType,

- schemaVersion,

- createdAt,

- createdBy,

- updatedAt,

- updatedBy,

- tenantId,

- projectId,

- environmentId,

- lifecycleStatus,

- classification,

- provenanceReference,

- and version.

Not every object requires every field.

Absence must be deliberate.

Missing tenant or project scope must not be interpreted as global scope without an explicit global-scope declaration.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.8 Canonical Envelope

Objects exchanged between Fabric components should use a canonical envelope.

A conceptual envelope may contain:

Object Envelope

- objectType

- objectId

- schemaVersion

- tenantId

- projectId

- environmentId

- correlationId

- causationId

- traceId

- createdAt

- createdBy

- classification

- payload

- provenance

- integrityMetadata

The envelope supports consistent transport and evidence.

The envelope shall not be used to hide ambiguous payload meaning.

Payload schemas must remain explicit and versioned.

4.9 Correlation and Causation

The Fabric shall distinguish correlation from causation.

Correlation identifies objects and events that belong to the same broader operation or production.

Causation identifies the specific object or event that caused another object or event to exist.

For example:

- a monthly Nova and Pling production may have one Production Correlation ID,

- each scene Execution may belong to that correlation,

- and a retry Attempt may be caused by a specific failed Attempt.

Correlation supports grouping.

Causation supports explanation.

Both should be preserved through asynchronous boundaries.

4.10 Object Versioning

Canonical object schemas shall be versioned.

Versioning may include:

- schema version,

- object revision,

- provider resource version,

- policy version,

- capability version,

- and adapter version.

Schema version describes the shape and meaning of the object.

Object revision describes changes to a specific object instance.

Provider or model version describes the external resource used.

These concepts must not be collapsed into one generic version field.

4.11 Immutable and Mutable Objects

The Fabric shall distinguish immutable evidence from mutable operational state.

Objects such as the following should normally be immutable once finalised:

- Approval Decision,

- Execution Receipt,

- Cost Receipt,

- Provider Response Evidence,

- Evaluation Result,

- Policy Decision Record,

- and Publication Verification Record.

Operational objects such as the following may evolve through controlled lifecycle transitions:

- Capability Request,

- Execution Plan,

- Execution,

- Provider Connection,

- Budget Reservation,

- and Incident.

Immutable records may be superseded by new records.

They should not be rewritten to erase history.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.12 Canonical Lifecycle Model

Canonical objects shall use explicit lifecycle states appropriate to their type.

A lifecycle transition should record:

- previous state,

- new state,

- transition time,

- actor,

- reason,

- related evidence,

- and policy basis where applicable.

Objects must not transition directly between states that bypass required approval, validation or reconciliation.

The canonical lifecycle shall distinguish:

- creation,

- activation,

- execution,

- completion,

- failure,

- cancellation,

- supersession,

- deprecation,

- and archival.

State names shall have defined meaning.

4.13 Principal

A Principal is an identity that may act within Omnira.

A Principal may represent:

- human user,

- service,

- agent,

- Manager,

- workflow,

- system process,

- external integration,

- or delegated runtime identity.

A Principal shall include:

- principalId,

- principalType,

- tenantId,

- status,

- authentication relationship,

- and authority references.

A Principal shall not receive authority merely because it is authenticated.

Authentication proves identity.

Authorisation determines permitted action.

4.14 Human Principal

A Human Principal represents a person using or governing Omnira.

A Human Principal may hold roles such as:

- owner,

- administrator,

- project owner,

- approver,

- operator,

- reviewer,

- developer,

- auditor,

- or customer user.

Roles shall remain scoped.

A person may be:

- owner in one tenant,

- project approver in another project,

- and ordinary operator elsewhere.

Human identity must not be inferred only from an email address or provider account.

4.15 Service Principal

A Service Principal represents a non-human system component.

Examples include:

- routing service,

- execution worker,

- callback processor,

- evaluation service,

- asset ingestion service,

- or publication service.

A Service Principal shall have:

- explicit purpose,

- limited permissions,

- credential identity,

- environment scope,

- and lifecycle.

Service Principals must not share one unrestricted platform identity merely for implementation convenience.

4.16 Agent Principal

An Agent Principal represents an Omnira-governed agent identity.

An Agent Principal shall remain separate from:

- the model it uses,

- the provider that hosts execution,

- the prompt version,

- and the runtime process.

The Agent Principal may reference:

- role definition,

- behavioural policy,

- authority,

- project assignments,

- memory access,

- tools,

- and capability permissions.

The agent’s current model may change without changing the Agent Principal.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.17 Tenant

A Tenant is the highest ordinary isolation boundary for users, organisations, projects, credentials, budgets, evidence and policy.

A Tenant shall have:

- tenantId,

- ownership relationship,

- lifecycle status,

- governance policy,

- region where applicable,

- billing relationships,

- and administrative principals.

Tenant absence shall not imply shared access.

Platform-global objects must declare global scope explicitly.

4.18 Project

A Project is a governed operational scope within a Tenant.

A Project may represent:

- Familje-Stunden,

- The Prompt,

- GainPilot,

- Omnira,

- a customer initiative,

- or another bounded business or product context.

A Project shall define or reference:

- projectId,

- tenantId,

- name,

- slug,

- status,

- project policies,

- budgets,

- assets,

- agents,

- workflows,

- memories,

- provider restrictions,

- and approval rules.

Project names are display properties.

Project IDs are authoritative identifiers.

4.19 Project Relationship

Projects may have explicit relationships.

Examples include:

- parent and child,

- shared brand,

- supplier and consumer,

- portfolio membership,

- approved asset sharing,

- or cross-project reporting.

A Project Relationship shall define:

- participating projects,

- relationship type,

- permitted data,

- permitted capabilities,

- authority,

- duration,

- and revocation.

Common ownership does not automatically create a Project Relationship.

4.20 Environment

An Environment represents an operational deployment or execution context.

Expected environments include:

- local development,

- test,

- simulation,

- preview,

- staging,

- production,

- recovery,

- and sandbox.

An Environment shall influence:

- credentials,

- provider accounts,

- policies,

- data,

- budgets,

- callbacks,

- and publication eligibility.

Environment must remain explicit across the full execution chain.

4.21 Scope

A Scope defines the boundary within which an object, permission, execution or learning is valid.

A Scope may include:

- tenant,

- project,

- environment,

- user,

- agent,

- workflow,

- production,

- capability,

- resource,

- data class,

- and time.

Scope is not a single universal string.

It is a structured boundary.

The Fabric shall support both:

- narrow scopes,

- and explicitly declared composite scopes.

Scope expansion requires authority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.22 Scope Resolution

Scope Resolution is the process of determining the authoritative scope for a request or object.

Scope Resolution may use:

- authenticated principal,

- project route,

- explicit request envelope,

- delegated authority,

- workflow assignment,

- and tenant membership.

Scope shall not be resolved solely from:

- prompt text,

- visual branding,

- filename,

- or provider workspace name.

A Scope Resolution Record should preserve:

- source information,

- resolved scope,

- policy version,

- and resolution confidence or failure.

4.23 Caller

A Caller is the Principal that submits a Capability Request.

The Caller may be:

- human,

- Atlas,

- Manager,

- agent,

- workflow,

- service,

- or approved external client.

Caller identity shall be preserved even when the request is delegated.

The Caller is not always the original authority source.

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- caller,

- initiating user,

- delegating principal,

- and approving principal.

4.24 Initiator

The Initiator is the Principal or event that originated the broader objective.

For example:

- a user may initiate a media production,

- Atlas may create a Capability Request,

- a Manager may create execution steps,

- and a worker may invoke the provider.

The user remains the Initiator.

The worker is the immediate technical caller.

Both relationships should remain traceable.

4.25 Delegation

A Delegation is a governed transfer of bounded authority from one Principal to another.

A Delegation shall define:

- delegator,

- delegate,

- permitted actions,

- scope,

- capability,

- budget,

- data access,

- validity,

- re-delegation permission,

- and revocation state.

A Delegation must not exceed the delegator’s authority.

Delegation chains shall remain traceable.

4.26 Authority

Authority represents permission to perform an action.

Authority shall not be modelled as a single unrestricted boolean.

An Authority object or rule should include:

- principal,

- action,

- capability,

- scope,

- data classification,

- provider restrictions,

- budget limit,

- time validity,

- approval requirement,

- and conditions.

Authority may be:

- direct,

- role-based,

- delegated,

- approved,

- policy-derived,

- or emergency-limited.

Technical access without Authority is insufficient.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.27 Authority Envelope

An Authority Envelope is the effective authority attached to a specific request or production.

It may include:

- authorised principals,

- approved capabilities,

- allowed providers,

- prohibited actions,

- maximum budget,

- retry limit,

- output restrictions,

- publication prohibition,

- data boundaries,

- expiry,

- and approval references.

The Authority Envelope is evaluated before execution and at material execution boundaries.

It shall not be expanded by the Fabric.

4.28 Approval

An Approval is a governed decision that permits, rejects or conditions a proposed action.

An Approval shall include:

- approvalId,

- requestType,

- subject,

- approver,

- decision,

- scope,

- constraints,

- validity,

- createdAt,

- decidedAt,

- evidence reviewed,

- and reason where appropriate.

Approval decisions may include:

- approved,

- rejected,

- approved with conditions,

- expired,

- revoked,

- superseded,

- or cancelled.

Approval state must not be inferred from conversation tone alone.

4.29 Production Envelope

A Production Envelope defines the approved operational boundaries for a multi-step production.

It may contain:

- productionId,

- projectId,

- objective,

- permitted capabilities,

- approved providers,

- maximum cost,

- maximum credits,

- scene count,

- variation count,

- retry limits,

- input assets,

- output formats,

- review requirements,

- publication restrictions,

- deadline,

- and validity.

The Production Envelope allows bounded autonomy across multiple executions.

It does not grant unlimited project authority.

4.30 Policy

A Policy is a governed rule that constrains or guides Fabric behaviour.

Policies may govern:

- provider eligibility,

- model eligibility,

- data placement,

- cost,

- retries,

- fallback,

- rights,

- publication,

- retention,

- and learning.

A Policy shall have:

- policyId,

- policyType,

- scope,

- version,

- status,

- effective time,

- precedence,

- conditions,

- decision logic,

- and provenance.

Natural-language policy may exist.

Operational policy must have sufficiently structured meaning to be enforceable.

4.31 Policy Context

Policy Context is the structured input used to evaluate policies for a request.

Policy Context may include:

- principal,

- tenant,

- project,

- environment,

- capability,

- data classification,

- provider candidates,

- budget,

- quality,

- rights,

- time,

- and current system state.

Policy Context shall be immutable for a single policy decision.

Material changes require re-evaluation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.32 Policy Decision

A Policy Decision records the result of evaluating one or more policies.

It shall include:

- policyDecisionId,

- evaluated policies,

- policy versions,

- input context reference,

- decision,

- allowed actions,

- denied actions,

- conditions,

- explanation,

- and timestamp.

Policy Decision states may include:

- allow,

- deny,

- allow with conditions,

- require approval,

- require local execution,

- require manual review,

- or unresolved.

An unresolved mandatory policy condition must fail closed.

4.33 Data Classification

A Data Classification describes the required protection of information.

Canonical classifications are expected to include:

- Public,

- Project Internal,

- Confidential,

- Local Only,

- and Prohibited.

A Data Classification object or value may also include:

- reason,

- source,

- classifier,

- confidence,

- inherited restrictions,

- retention,

- and review date.

Classification applies to both input and output.

Classification may change only through governed transition.

4.34 Data Item

A Data Item is a bounded unit of information used or created by the Fabric.

A Data Item may represent:

- text,

- document,

- image,

- audio,

- video,

- metadata,

- memory,

- prompt,

- transcript,

- code,

- or structured dataset.

A Data Item should include or reference:

- owner,

- tenant,

- project,

- classification,

- rights,

- storage location,

- checksum,

- format,

- and provenance.

Providers should receive Data Item references or transformed representations rather than uncontrolled raw project context.

4.35 Data Use Grant

A Data Use Grant authorises specific use of a Data Item.

It may define:

- permitted Principal,

- purpose,

- capability,

- provider class,

- duration,

- transformations,

- output restrictions,

- and retention.

A Data Use Grant may be required for:

- voice assets,

- likeness assets,

- confidential documents,

- customer data,

- or cross-project references.

Ownership alone does not imply unlimited use.

4.36 Consent Record

A Consent Record preserves permission related to personal data, voice, likeness or other consent-sensitive use.

It should include:

- subject,

- consenting party,

- permitted use,

- project,

- provider restrictions,

- commercial-use permission,

- validity,

- revocation,

- evidence,

- and jurisdiction where relevant.

A Consent Record must remain separate from provider terms.

Provider capability does not prove subject consent.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.37 Rights Profile

A Rights Profile describes the legal and contractual conditions attached to an input, output or provider capability.

It may include:

- ownership,

- licence,

- commercial-use permission,

- attribution requirement,

- territorial restriction,

- derivative-use permission,

- publication restriction,

- provider terms version,

- and uncertainty.

A Rights Profile may be:

- confirmed,

- conditionally valid,

- disputed,

- unknown,

- or prohibited.

Unknown material rights shall trigger review when the use is consequential.

4.38 Intent

Intent represents the desired outcome or purpose behind a request.

Intent shall remain separate from:

- execution plan,

- provider choice,

- model parameters,

- and output.

An Intent object may include:

- objective,

- business context,

- desired effect,

- constraints,

- success definition,

- and initiating Principal.

Intent may be broad.

Capability Requests must translate it into executable requirements.

4.39 Intent Envelope

An Intent Envelope is the canonical structure through which a caller submits the desired result and constraints.

It may include:

- intentId,

- objective,

- tenantId,

- projectId,

- requester,

- beneficiary,

- required capabilities,

- inputs,

- desired outputs,

- quality expectations,

- data restrictions,

- rights requirements,

- budget,

- deadline,

- routing profile,

- authority reference,

- and review requirements.

The Intent Envelope describes what must be achieved.

It does not prescribe provider implementation unless pinned.

4.40 Capability

A Capability is a canonical description of an operation or result that an intelligence resource can perform.

A Capability shall have:

- capabilityId,

- canonical name,

- description,

- modality,

- input contract,

- output contract,

- quality dimensions,

- execution characteristics,

- risk classification,

- lifecycle,

- and version.

Examples include:

- text.reasoning,

- code.generate,

- image.edit,

- image.generate,

- video.image_to_video,

- speech.synthesise,

- speech.transcribe,

- retrieval.embed,

- retrieval.rerank,

- research.verify_sources,

- and media.character_consistency_evaluate.

Capability names should be stable and provider-independent.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.41 Capability Version

A Capability Version defines a specific contract revision.

A version may change when:

- input requirements change,

- output meaning changes,

- quality dimensions change,

- risk classification changes,

- or required evidence changes.

Backward-compatible metadata additions may not require a major capability version.

Callers and adapters shall declare supported versions.

4.42 Capability Requirement

A Capability Requirement describes one required capability within a request.

It may include:

- capabilityId,

- version constraint,

- required quality,

- required inputs,

- desired output,

- priority,

- mandatory or optional status,

- and dependency relationships.

A request may contain several Capability Requirements.

Optional capabilities may support graceful degradation.

4.43 Capability Request

A Capability Request is the canonical request submitted to the Fabric for intelligence work.

It shall include:

- requestId,

- caller,

- tenantId,

- projectId,

- environmentId,

- intent reference,

- capability requirements,

- input references,

- output contract,

- authority envelope,

- policy context,

- routing profile,

- budget envelope,

- quality contract,

- deadline,

- and lifecycle status.

A Capability Request is not the same as an Execution.

One Capability Request may produce:

- one Execution,

- multiple Executions,

- no Execution because it was denied,

- or a human-assisted workflow.

4.44 Capability Request Lifecycle

Expected Capability Request states include:

- draft,

- submitted,

- validating,

- awaiting approval,

- approved,

- planning,

- rejected,

- cancelled,

- executing,

- partially completed,

- completed,

- failed,

- and expired.

The request may complete even when one optional capability is not fulfilled, if the output contract permits it.

Completion requires acceptance criteria.

4.45 Requirement Constraint

A Requirement Constraint narrows eligibility or execution.

Constraints may include:

- maximum cost,

- maximum latency,

- minimum quality,

- allowed provider,

- prohibited provider,

- local-only placement,

- output format,

- resolution,

- language,

- commercial use,

- deterministic seed support,

- context capacity,

- or human-review requirement.

Constraints should be machine-evaluable where possible.

Unstructured constraints may require interpretation and evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.46 Routing Profile

A Routing Profile defines the optimisation posture for resource selection.

Canonical profiles include:

- Economy,

- Balanced,

- Premium,

- Private,

- and Pinned.

A Routing Profile may include:

- optimisation weights,

- default quality floor,

- latency preference,

- cost preference,

- provider restrictions,

- and fallback posture.

Routing Profiles are policy inputs.

They do not override mandatory constraints.

4.47 Quality Contract

A Quality Contract defines how acceptable output shall be judged.

It may include:

- quality dimensions,

- minimum thresholds,

- deterministic validations,

- evaluator requirements,

- human-review requirements,

- rejection conditions,

- retry allowance,

- and acceptance authority.

Quality Contracts shall be capability-specific.

A generic quality score is insufficient for many tasks.

4.48 Quality Dimension

A Quality Dimension represents one measurable or reviewable aspect of quality.

Examples include:

- factual accuracy,

- source completeness,

- code correctness,

- visual consistency,

- character identity,

- brand alignment,

- voice naturalness,

- child appropriateness,

- resolution,

- timing,

- and format compliance.

A Quality Dimension may be evaluated by:

- deterministic test,

- model evaluator,

- human reviewer,

- external metric,

- or composite method.

4.49 Acceptance Criterion

An Acceptance Criterion defines the proof required for a result to be accepted.

It shall include:

- criterion,

- evaluation method,

- threshold,

- required evidence,

- and mandatory or optional status.

Examples include:

- all tests pass,

- character-consistency score exceeds threshold,

- human reviewer approves,

- required citations are present,

- or publication is verified live.

Execution completion does not imply acceptance.

4.50 Budget Envelope

A Budget Envelope defines the economic limits for a request or production.

It may include:

- budgetId,

- currency,

- credit unit,

- maximum estimated cost,

- maximum actual cost,

- provider-account restrictions,

- project budget source,

- reservation rules,

- retry allowance,

- and escalation threshold.

A Budget Envelope may be inherited from:

- request,

- workflow,

- project,

- tenant,

- or production approval.

The most restrictive applicable limit shall normally prevail.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.51 Budget Source

A Budget Source identifies the account or allocation responsible for cost.

Examples include:

- project budget,

- tenant budget,

- personal provider credits,

- Omnira-managed credits,

- local compute allocation,

- or approved promotional capacity.

Budget Source shall remain separate from Provider Account.

One Provider Account may serve several Budget Sources through explicit attribution.

4.52 Budget Reservation

A Budget Reservation reserves estimated capacity before execution.

It should include:

- reservationId,

- budget source,

- request,

- amount,

- currency or credits,

- expiry,

- status,

- and final settlement reference.

Expected states include:

- proposed,

- reserved,

- partially consumed,

- consumed,

- released,

- expired,

- and disputed.

Reservation reduces the risk of concurrent overspend.

4.53 Cost Estimate

A Cost Estimate is a pre-execution prediction of resource cost.

It should include:

- provider candidate,

- model,

- account,

- expected usage,

- pricing version,

- estimated cost,

- confidence,

- and assumptions.

A Cost Estimate is not a confirmed charge.

Changes in plan may require a revised estimate and new approval.

4.54 Usage Record

A Usage Record describes measured provider or local resource consumption.

It may include:

- input tokens,

- output tokens,

- images,

- seconds of audio,

- seconds of video,

- compute time,

- storage,

- requests,

- credits,

- or another provider unit.

Usage Records shall preserve provider-reported and Omnira-calculated values separately where they differ.

4.55 Cost Record

A Cost Record translates usage into attributed cost.

It may include:

- usage reference,

- provider price,

- currency,

- credits,

- project,

- tenant,

- provider account,

- budget source,

- estimated or confirmed state,

- tax treatment reference where relevant,

- and reconciliation status.

Cost Record states may include:

- estimated,

- provisional,

- provider-confirmed,

- reconciled,

- disputed,

- and waived.

4.56 Provider

A Provider is an external or internal organisation or platform that supplies intelligence or tool capability.

A Provider shall include:

- providerId,

- name,

- provider type,

- trust classification,

- supported regions,

- service status,

- policy metadata,

- terms references,

- lifecycle,

- and adapter relationships.

Examples may include:

- commercial cloud vendor,

- local runtime provider,

- self-hosted platform,

- Omnira-managed service,

- or human-assisted external service.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.57 Provider Type

Provider Type distinguishes operational categories such as:

- external cloud,

- Omnira-managed,

- user-managed,

- self-hosted,

- local runtime,

- edge runtime,

- human-assisted,

- or simulation.

Provider Type informs trust, placement and operational policy.

It does not alone determine eligibility.

4.58 Provider Account

A Provider Account represents a specific connected account, workspace, subscription or operational relationship with a Provider.

It shall include:

- providerAccountId,

- providerId,

- tenant owner,

- user owner where applicable,

- project restrictions,

- environment,

- billing relationship,

- region,

- connection status,

- credential reference,

- available credits where known,

- terms reference,

- and lifecycle.

Provider Accounts must not be silently substituted.

4.59 Provider Account Lifecycle

Expected Provider Account states include:

- proposed,

- connecting,

- connected,

- active,

- restricted,

- authentication required,

- suspended,

- exhausted,

- revoked,

- disconnected,

- and archived.

A connected account is not necessarily eligible for every request.

Eligibility depends on policy, capability, scope, rights and budget.

4.60 Provider Terms Record

A Provider Terms Record preserves relevant provider contractual and operational terms.

It may include:

- terms version,

- effective date,

- commercial-use conditions,

- retention,

- training usage,

- data region,

- prohibited use,

- indemnity reference,

- attribution requirement,

- and review status.

The Fabric shall not attempt to replace legal review.

It shall preserve enough structured information to prevent obvious policy violations and trigger review.

4.61 Model

A Model is a canonical intelligence resource definition supplied or hosted by a Provider.

A Model shall include:

- modelId,

- providerId,

- canonical display name,

- provider model name,

- modality,

- supported capabilities,

- lifecycle,

- and version relationships.

The Model object represents the model family or logical resource.

A Model Version represents a specific release or provider revision.

4.62 Model Version

A Model Version shall include:

- modelVersionId,

- modelId,

- provider version identifier,

- release date where known,

- capability declarations,

- context limits,

- pricing references,

- quality evidence,

- safety restrictions,

- region,

- status,

- and deprecation information.

When providers silently update a model behind a stable name, the Fabric shall record the observed limitation.

Unknown provider versioning reduces reproducibility confidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.63 Model Deployment

A Model Deployment represents a specific operational deployment of a model.

It may identify:

- provider account,

- region,

- endpoint,

- local node,

- hardware,

- quantisation,

- configuration,

- and availability.

The same Model Version may have several Deployments.

Deployment determines practical execution properties such as:

- latency,

- privacy,

- capacity,

- and cost.

4.64 Local Model Deployment

A Local Model Deployment represents a model running on user-controlled or Omnira-controlled infrastructure.

It should include:

- node,

- model version,

- runtime,

- hardware requirements,

- loaded state,

- capacity,

- privacy boundary,

- energy or compute estimate,

- and health.

Local execution is not assumed to be free, fast or high quality.

Its properties must be measured.

4.65 Runtime Node

A Runtime Node is a compute environment capable of executing models or tools.

Examples include:

- laptop,

- mobile device,

- desktop rig,

- private server,

- cloud worker,

- or edge node.

A Runtime Node shall include:

- nodeId,

- owner,

- tenant,

- environment,

- location class,

- hardware capabilities,

- trust level,

- availability,

- power state,

- network state,

- and permitted data classes.

Node selection is part of workload placement.

4.66 Connection

A Connection represents the configured relationship between Omnira and a provider, runtime or protocol endpoint.

Connection types may include:

- API,

- MCP,

- OAuth,

- webhook,

- queue,

- local socket,

- command-line runtime,

- or manual-assistance relationship.

A Connection shall include:

- connectionId,

- provider account,

- protocol,

- endpoint reference,

- credential reference,

- permissions,

- environment,

- health,

- and lifecycle.

A Connection does not imply unrestricted capability access.

4.67 Credential Reference

A Credential Reference identifies an approved secret or authentication relationship without exposing the raw secret.

It may include:

- credentialReferenceId,

- owner,

- provider account,

- secret type,

- permitted scopes,

- environment,

- rotation status,

- expiry,

- and vault location reference.

Raw secret values shall not enter canonical request objects.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.68 Adapter

An Adapter translates between Omnira’s canonical contracts and a provider-specific implementation.

An Adapter shall include:

- adapterId,

- provider,

- supported protocol,

- supported capabilities,

- schema versions,

- implementation version,

- conformance state,

- error mappings,

- usage mappings,

- and lifecycle.

Adapters may be:

- native,

- official provider,

- Omnira-built,

- community,

- experimental,

- or human-assisted.

Adapter origin affects trust and review requirements.

4.69 Adapter Capability Mapping

An Adapter Capability Mapping defines how one canonical Capability maps to provider-specific operations.

It should include:

- canonical capability,

- provider operation,

- supported constraints,

- unsupported constraints,

- parameter mapping,

- output mapping,

- cost mapping,

- evidence mapping,

- and known limitations.

The mapping shall not claim support where the provider cannot satisfy the canonical contract.

4.70 Adapter Conformance Record

An Adapter Conformance Record preserves evidence that an Adapter satisfies required Fabric contracts.

It may include:

- tested version,

- test suite,

- passed capabilities,

- failed capabilities,

- security review,

- error handling,

- idempotency behaviour,

- callback behaviour,

- and approval state.

Conformance is version-specific.

A provider API change may invalidate prior conformance.

4.71 Tool

A Tool is an executable operation that produces information or creates an effect.

Tools may include:

- search,

- database query,

- file conversion,

- image transformation,

- repository operation,

- publication action,

- browser action,

- or provider administrative function.

A Tool shall include:

- toolId,

- capability,

- action class,

- input contract,

- output contract,

- side-effect classification,

- permissions,

- and provider or runtime relationship.

Read, create, modify, delete and publish must remain distinguishable.

4.72 Tool Action Class

Tool Action Class describes the consequence level of a Tool.

Canonical classes may include:

- read,

- analyse,

- simulate,

- generate,

- create,

- modify,

- delete,

- publish,

- transact,

- administer,

- and recover.

Action Class influences:

- authority,

- approval,

- idempotency,

- evidence,

- and review.

A tool that generates a local draft differs materially from a tool that publishes publicly.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.73 External Agent Resource

An External Agent Resource represents an agent-like capability provided outside Omnira.

It may include:

- externalAgentId,

- provider,

- provider account,

- capabilities,

- memory behaviour,

- tool access,

- autonomy level,

- data policy,

- and lifecycle.

It shall not automatically become an Omnira Agent Principal.

External agent state must remain bounded and observable.

4.74 Workflow

A Workflow defines a governed sequence or graph of work.

A Workflow shall include:

- workflowId,

- tenant,

- project scope,

- purpose,

- version,

- steps,

- dependencies,

- approvals,

- capability requirements,

- side effects,

- failure policy,

- and lifecycle.

A Workflow definition is not an active execution.

A Workflow Run represents one execution instance.

4.75 Workflow Run

A Workflow Run represents an active or completed instance of a Workflow.

It shall include:

- workflowRunId,

- workflow version,

- initiator,

- caller,

- scope,

- production envelope,

- current state,

- execution references,

- outputs,

- and completion evidence.

Expected states include:

- created,

- awaiting approval,

- running,

- paused,

- partially completed,

- failed,

- cancelled,

- completed,

- and unknown outcome.

4.76 Execution Plan

An Execution Plan defines how the Fabric proposes to fulfil a Capability Request.

It may include:

- planId,

- requestId,

- plan version,

- execution steps,

- dependencies,

- resource candidates,

- selected resources,

- estimated cost,

- expected latency,

- fallback paths,

- evaluation steps,

- approval points,

- and assumptions.

An Execution Plan may be revised before or during execution.

Material revision may require renewed approval.

4.77 Execution Graph

An Execution Graph represents the dependencies between execution steps.

Nodes may represent:

- model execution,

- tool execution,

- human review,

- data transformation,

- approval,

- evaluation,

- or side effect.

Edges may represent:

- dependency,

- conditional path,

- fallback,

- compensation,

- or data flow.

The graph shall remain acyclic unless an explicitly bounded loop such as retry or iterative refinement is defined.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.78 Execution Step
