An Execution Step is one bounded unit of planned work.

It shall include:

- stepId,

- planId,

- capability,

- inputs,

- required authority,

- resource requirement,

- budget allocation,

- retry policy,

- fallback policy,

- output contract,

- and dependencies.

One Execution Step may produce one or more Execution objects over its lifecycle.

4.79 Resource Requirement

A Resource Requirement describes the properties a selected resource must satisfy.

It may include:

- capability,

- model class,

- provider restrictions,

- region,

- privacy,

- quality,

- latency,

- cost,

- context capacity,

- media limits,

- rights,

- and availability.

Resource Requirements are matched against Resource Candidates.

4.80 Resource Candidate

A Resource Candidate represents one eligible or potentially eligible execution resource.

It may combine:

- provider,

- provider account,

- model version,

- model deployment,

- adapter,

- connection,

- runtime node,

- and estimated cost.

A Resource Candidate shall record both:

- eligibility result,

- and ranking evidence.

Ineligible resources may remain in decision evidence without being selectable.

4.81 Eligibility Decision

An Eligibility Decision determines whether a Resource Candidate may be used.

It should include:

- candidate,

- request,

- capability compatibility,

- policy result,

- authority result,

- data-placement result,

- rights result,

- account result,

- budget result,

- health result,

- and final eligibility.

Eligibility is distinct from ranking.

A resource may be eligible but not preferred.

4.82 Selection Decision

A Selection Decision records why one Resource Candidate was chosen.

It shall include:

- selected candidate,

- considered candidates,

- routing profile,

- optimisation criteria,

- policy constraints,

- quality evidence,

- cost estimate,

- health,

- fallback order,

- decision time,

- and decision actor or service.

Selection Decisions support explanation, audit and future learning.

4.83 Execution

An Execution is the canonical object representing one governed attempt to perform intelligence work.

It shall include:

- executionId,

- requestId,

- planId,

- stepId,

- selected resource,

- caller,

- scope,

- authority reference,

- policy decision,

- budget reservation,

- status,

- createdAt,

- startedAt,

- completedAt,

- and output references.

An Execution may contain several Attempts.

The Execution represents the Fabric-level work.

Attempts represent individual technical submissions or retries.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.84 Execution Status

Canonical Execution states should include:

- created,

- validating,

- authorised,

- queued,

- submitting,

- accepted,

- running,

- awaiting provider,

- awaiting callback,

- awaiting approval,

- output received,

- validating output,

- partially completed,

- completed,

- failed,

- cancelled,

- timed out,

- unknown outcome,

- and reconciled.

Not every provider exposes every state.

The adapter shall map provider evidence into the nearest truthful canonical state.

4.85 Execution Attempt

An Execution Attempt represents one technical attempt within an Execution.

It shall include:

- attemptId,

- executionId,

- attempt number,

- selected resource,

- provider request identifier,

- idempotency key,

- submittedAt,

- response evidence,

- status,

- error,

- usage,

- cost,

- and output references.

Retries create new Attempts.

They do not erase prior Attempts.

4.86 Attempt Status

Expected Attempt states include:

- prepared,

- submitted,

- provider accepted,

- processing,

- succeeded,

- failed,

- rejected,

- cancelled,

- timed out,

- duplicate suppressed,

- and unknown outcome.

Attempt state may differ from Execution state.

An Attempt may fail while the Execution later succeeds through fallback.

4.87 Provider Job

A Provider Job represents a provider-side asynchronous job.

It shall include:

- providerJobId within Omnira,

- provider account,

- external job identifier,

- execution attempt,

- submitted parameters reference,

- status,

- polling or callback configuration,

- and reconciliation evidence.

Provider Job state is provider-specific evidence.

Canonical Execution state remains owned by Omnira.

4.88 Idempotency Key

An Idempotency Key identifies operations that should not be duplicated.

It may be attached to:

- Capability Request,

- Execution,

- Attempt,

- side effect,

- provider submission,

- callback,

- or asset ingestion.

Idempotency scope and validity must be explicit.

A key that is safe for provider submission may not be safe for an entire multi-step production.

4.89 Retry Policy

A Retry Policy defines whether and how failed or uncertain operations may be retried.

It may include:

- retryable errors,

- maximum attempts,

- backoff,

- jitter,

- budget limit,

- deadline,

- idempotency requirement,

- and escalation.

Retry Policy shall distinguish:

- safe retry,

- unsafe retry,

- reconciliation required,

- and permanent failure.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.90 Fallback Policy

A Fallback Policy defines eligible alternative resources or plans.

It may include:

- fallback candidates,

- trigger conditions,

- quality floor,

- cost limit,

- data restrictions,

- provider restrictions,

- and approval requirement.

Fallback must preserve the original request’s mandatory constraints.

4.91 Callback

A Callback is an inbound provider or service notification related to an asynchronous operation.

A Callback object or record should include:

- callbackId,

- provider,

- provider account,

- external event identifier,

- receivedAt,

- signature verification,

- event type,

- related job,

- deduplication result,

- and processing status.

Callbacks are untrusted until authenticated and correlated.

Duplicate callbacks must not duplicate completion effects.

4.92 Callback Status

Expected Callback processing states include:

- received,

- verifying,

- verified,

- rejected,

- duplicate,

- correlated,

- uncorrelated,

- processed,

- failed,

- and quarantined.

An uncorrelated callback shall not mutate arbitrary executions.

4.93 Side Effect

A Side Effect is an action that changes external or durable state beyond ordinary internal reasoning.

Examples include:

- spending credits,

- creating provider assets,

- sending messages,

- publishing content,

- modifying files,

- deleting data,

- committing code,

- or changing configuration.

A Side Effect shall include:

- action,

- target,

- authority,

- idempotency,

- expected result,

- actual result,

- and verification.

Side Effects require stronger evidence than non-consequential analysis.

4.94 Side-Effect Receipt

A Side-Effect Receipt records evidence that a side effect was attempted or completed.

It shall distinguish:

- requested,

- submitted,

- accepted,

- completed,

- verified,

- failed,

- and unknown outcome.

A provider acknowledgement may not prove the final external state.

Verification requirements depend on the action.

4.95 Output Contract

An Output Contract defines the expected form and meaning of an execution result.

It may include:

- output type,

- format,

- schema,

- resolution,

- language,

- duration,

- classification,

- quality requirements,

- provenance requirements,

- and storage destination.

Outputs that do not satisfy the Output Contract are not accepted.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.96 Output

An Output is a result produced by an Execution.

An Output may be:

- text,

- structured data,

- code,

- image,

- audio,

- video,

- embedding,

- ranking,

- recommendation,

- report,

- or action result.

An Output shall include:

- outputId,

- executionId,

- type,

- format,

- storage reference,

- checksum,

- classification,

- quality status,

- provenance,

- and lifecycle.

An Output is not automatically a durable Asset.

4.97 Temporary Output

A Temporary Output is an intermediate or disposable result.

Examples include:

- draft prompt,

- low-resolution preview,

- intermediate transcript,

- rejected scene,

- or temporary conversion.

Temporary Outputs should have:

- explicit retention,

- project scope,

- classification,

- and deletion policy.

They must not silently enter the canonical asset library.

4.98 Asset

An Asset is a durable project or platform object intended for reuse, review, distribution or archival.

Assets may include:

- character reference,

- image,

- video,

- audio,

- document,

- prompt template,

- code package,

- or publication master.

An Asset shall include:

- assetId,

- owner,

- tenant,

- project,

- asset type,

- canonical status,

- version,

- classification,

- rights,

- provenance,

- storage,

- and lifecycle.

An Asset may be created from one or more Outputs.

4.99 Asset Version

An Asset Version represents a specific immutable version of an Asset.

It should include:

- assetVersionId,

- assetId,

- version number,

- checksum,

- format,

- dimensions or duration,

- createdFrom,

- approval,

- and storage reference.

Edits create new Asset Versions.

Canonical replacement shall not erase prior versions.

4.100 Asset Relationship

An Asset Relationship connects assets such as:

- derived from,

- variant of,

- translated from,

- resized from,

- animated from,

- narrated by,

- composed with,

- or supersedes.

Relationships support provenance and reuse.

A social-media clip may be derived from a master episode.

It is not an unrelated asset.

4.101 Canonical Asset Status

Expected canonical asset states include:

- draft,

- candidate,

- reviewed,

- approved,

- canonical,

- superseded,

- deprecated,

- archived,

- and rejected.

Existence does not imply canonical status.

Only an authorised process may mark an Asset Version canonical.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.102 Provenance Record

A Provenance Record describes how an object or output came into existence.

It may include:

- source objects,

- source versions,

- prompts,

- instructions,

- provider,

- model,

- adapter,

- execution,

- human contribution,

- transformations,

- rights,

- consent,

- cost,

- and timestamps.

Provenance shall follow meaningful Outputs and Assets.

It must remain queryable after export or publication where practical.

4.103 Prompt Record

A Prompt Record preserves the meaningful prompt or instruction set used for execution.

It may include:

- promptId,

- prompt type,

- project,

- version,

- author,

- source template,

- runtime substitutions,

- provider adaptation,

- classification,

- and checksum.

Sensitive prompt content may be stored separately from general execution evidence.

Prompts shall not include raw credentials.

4.104 Instruction Set

An Instruction Set is a governed collection of reusable behavioural, brand, project or task instructions.

Examples include:

- Nova and Pling character rules,

- The Prompt editorial rules,

- GainPilot Arnold coaching rules,

- global safety policy,

- or provider-specific parameter guidance.

Instruction Sets shall be:

- versioned,

- scoped,

- attributable,

- and distinguishable from temporary prompts.

4.105 Evaluation

An Evaluation is the process or object through which output quality, correctness, safety or compliance is assessed.

An Evaluation shall include:

- evaluationId,

- target output,

- evaluation method,

- evaluator,

- quality dimensions,

- criteria,

- result,

- evidence,

- and timestamp.

Evaluation may be:

- automated,

- deterministic,

- model-based,

- human,

- or composite.

4.106 Evaluator

An Evaluator is the Principal, model, service or method that performs an Evaluation.

An Evaluator shall declare:

- evaluator type,

- competence or capability,

- independence,

- version,

- scope,

- and potential conflicts.

The generating model should not always be the only Evaluator.

4.107 Evaluation Result

An Evaluation Result records measured or reviewed quality.

It may include:

- scores,

- pass or fail,

- reviewer comments,

- confidence,

- detected defects,

- required correction,

- and acceptance recommendation.

Evaluation does not automatically equal approval.

Approval authority remains separate.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.108 Human Review

A Human Review is an Evaluation performed by an authorised person.

It shall include:

- reviewer,

- target,

- criteria,

- decision,

- comments,

- timestamp,

- and scope.

A Human Review may be required for:

- child-facing media,

- publication,

- rights-sensitive output,

- strategic recommendations,

- or production acceptance.

Human review must not be simulated by a model and labelled as human.

4.109 Acceptance Decision

An Acceptance Decision determines whether an Output satisfies its contract.

It may be:

- accepted,

- accepted with conditions,

- rejected,

- revision required,

- or unresolved.

Acceptance Decision shall reference:

- Output,

- Quality Contract,

- Evaluation Results,

- authorised decider,

- and reason.

Acceptance is distinct from publication approval.

4.110 Execution Receipt

An Execution Receipt is an immutable summary of what occurred during an Execution.

It should include:

- executionId,

- request,

- scope,

- selected resource,

- attempts,

- policy decision,

- authority,

- start and end times,

- final state,

- outputs,

- cost,

- evaluation status,

- unresolved issues,

- and integrity metadata.

The receipt supports audit, user explanation, recovery and learning.

It shall not expose raw secrets.

4.111 Provider Receipt

A Provider Receipt preserves provider-originated evidence.

It may include:

- provider request identifier,

- provider response,

- usage,

- cost,

- timestamps,

- status,

- and signature or integrity information where available.

Provider Receipts should be retained in their original form where possible.

Canonical interpretation may be stored separately.

4.112 Boundary Receipt

A Boundary Receipt records the critical scope and authority decisions applied to execution.

It may include:

- tenant,

- project,

- environment,

- caller,

- authority,

- data classification,

- provider account,

- policy version,

- budget source,

- approval,

- and restrictions.

Boundary Receipts help prove that the execution stayed within the intended scope.

4.113 Decision Evidence

Decision Evidence is evidence used by Atlas, Executive Intelligence, Managers or humans to support a decision.

It may include:

- research,

- evaluations,

- costs,

- provider performance,

- audience analytics,

- incidents,

- or previous outcomes.

Decision Evidence shall preserve:

- source,

- date,

- scope,

- confidence,

- and limitations.

Evidence is not itself the final decision.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.114 Incident

An Incident is an event or condition that threatens:

- security,

- privacy,

- rights,

- reliability,

- cost control,

- project isolation,

- or truthful operation.

An Incident shall include:

- incidentId,

- severity,

- scope,

- detectedAt,

- detector,

- affected objects,

- containment,

- status,

- evidence,

- and resolution.

Incident lifecycle shall remain separate from ordinary Execution failure.

4.115 Incident Severity

Incident Severity may include:

- informational,

- low,

- moderate,

- high,

- critical,

- and catastrophic where needed.

Severity should consider:

- affected users,

- data sensitivity,

- financial impact,

- public consequence,

- duration,

- scope,

- and recoverability.

Severity shall not be determined only by technical error type.

4.116 Incident Lifecycle

Expected Incident states include:

- detected,

- triaged,

- contained,

- investigating,

- recovering,

- resolved,

- monitoring,

- and closed.

Closure requires sufficient evidence.

A temporary provider recovery does not automatically resolve the root cause.

4.117 Learning Candidate

A Learning Candidate is a proposed conclusion derived from execution evidence.

It shall include:

- claim,

- supporting evidence,

- scope,

- capability,

- conditions,

- confidence,

- creator,

- and proposed retention.

A Learning Candidate is not yet governed long-term memory.

4.118 Derived Learning

Derived Learning is a reviewed conclusion accepted for operational or decision support.

It may state:

- one provider performs better for a specific capability,

- one workflow configuration reduces cost,

- one quality failure occurs repeatedly,

- or one project audience responds better to a format.

Derived Learning shall include:

- evidence,

- scope,

- confidence,

- validity,

- contradiction handling,

- and review status.

4.119 Memory Candidate

A Memory Candidate is a structured proposal submitted to Atlas Memory or another governed memory system.

It may originate from:

- Derived Learning,

- user instruction,

- decision,

- preference,

- repeated pattern,

- or verified project fact.

A Memory Candidate shall include:

- proposed memory type,

- owner,

- project,

- source,

- confidence,

- sensitivity,

- retention,

- and supersession rules.

The Fabric shall not directly admit Memory Candidates into permanent memory without the memory-governance process.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.120 Governed Memory Reference

A Governed Memory Reference links Fabric work to an approved memory object without making the Fabric the memory owner.

The reference may include:

- memoryId,

- version,

- scope,

- retrieval permission,

- and usage reason.

Memory access shall be minimised and evidenced when relevant.

4.121 Publication Package

A Publication Package is a structured set of approved or publication-ready assets and metadata.

It may include:

- media,

- caption,

- title,

- description,

- thumbnail,

- subtitles,

- target platform,

- scheduling preference,

- rights profile,

- approval state,

- and provenance.

A Publication Package is not proof of publication.

Publication requires a separate side-effect execution.

4.122 Publication Record

A Publication Record preserves evidence of an external publication action.

It may include:

- platform,

- account,

- asset,

- submittedAt,

- external post identifier,

- status,

- public URL reference,

- verification,

- and publication receipt.

Expected states include:

- prepared,

- scheduled,

- submitted,

- published,

- failed,

- removed,

- and verified live.

4.123 Health Observation

A Health Observation records the observed operational state of a Provider, Connection, Adapter, Model Deployment or Runtime Node.

It may include:

- target,

- time,

- status,

- latency,

- error rate,

- capacity,

- and source.

One observation does not permanently define health.

Health state is derived from observations.

4.124 Health State

Health State is the current derived operational condition of a resource.

Expected states may include:

- healthy,

- degraded,

- unavailable,

- unknown,

- maintenance,

- rate limited,

- authentication required,

- and exhausted.

Health State does not equal policy eligibility.

4.125 Benchmark

A Benchmark defines a repeatable evaluation used to measure resource performance.

It shall include:

- benchmarkId,

- capability,

- dataset or task,

- quality dimensions,

- execution conditions,

- scoring method,

- scope,

- and version.

Benchmarks may be:

- platform-wide,

- tenant-specific,

- project-specific,

- or provider-specific.

Benchmark results must remain contextual.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.126 Benchmark Result

A Benchmark Result records one resource’s performance under defined conditions.

It should include:

- resource,

- model version,

- adapter version,

- benchmark version,

- cost,

- latency,

- quality,

- failures,

- date,

- and environment.

Benchmark Results may inform routing.

They do not override mandatory policy.

4.127 Registry

A Registry is a governed collection of canonical resource definitions.

The Fabric shall include or integrate with registries for:

- capabilities,

- providers,

- provider accounts,

- models,

- deployments,

- adapters,

- tools,

- external agents,

- and potentially evaluation methods.

A Registry shall support:

- identity,

- lifecycle,

- versioning,

- discovery,

- eligibility metadata,

- and historical interpretation.

A Registry is not merely a static configuration file.

4.128 Capability Registry

The Capability Registry is the authoritative catalogue of canonical capabilities.

It shall contain:

- capability definitions,

- versions,

- input and output contracts,

- risk classification,

- quality dimensions,

- supported resource mappings,

- and lifecycle.

Provider names must not define the Capability Registry structure.

4.129 Provider Registry

The Provider Registry is the authoritative catalogue of provider organisations and platform relationships.

It shall contain:

- Provider objects,

- trust metadata,

- terms references,

- service regions,

- lifecycle,

- and provider-level policy information.

Provider Accounts remain separate objects.

4.130 Model Registry

The Model Registry is the authoritative catalogue of Model, Model Version and Model Deployment objects.

It shall support:

- capability mapping,

- lifecycle,

- quality evidence,

- context limits,

- pricing references,

- and deprecation.

The Registry must preserve historical versions used by past executions.

4.131 Tool and Agent Resource Registry

The Tool and Agent Resource Registry represents executable non-model resources.

It may contain:

- tools,

- provider-hosted agents,

- workflows,

- local utilities,

- browser actions,

- repository tools,

- and publication tools.

Each resource shall declare:

- capability,

- action class,

- side effects,

- authority requirements,

- and integration maturity.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.132 Canonical Status Vocabulary

Status values shall be defined per object type.

The Fabric must not use one generic status field with ambiguous values across all objects.

For example:

- active for a Provider Account,

- running for an Execution,

- approved for an Approval,

- and canonical for an Asset

represent different lifecycle concepts.

Status vocabularies shall be documented and versioned.

4.133 Terminal State

A Terminal State is a state after which ordinary lifecycle progression ends.

Examples include:

- completed,

- failed,

- cancelled,

- rejected,

- revoked,

- retired,

- and archived.

Unknown outcome may be temporarily terminal for automated execution but remain open to reconciliation.

Terminal does not always mean immutable.

A reconciliation event may supersede prior interpretation without rewriting evidence.

4.134 Unknown State

Unknown shall be treated as an explicit state where the system lacks sufficient evidence.

Unknown may apply to:

- provider job outcome,

- cost,

- health,

- rights,

- classification,

- or publication.

Unknown must not be silently converted into a favourable default.

Resolution may require:

- new evidence,

- human review,

- provider reconciliation,

- or blocking action.

4.135 Unavailable State

Unavailable means the resource or capability cannot currently be used.

Unavailable may result from:

- outage,

- policy,

- authentication,

- quota,

- deprecation,

- environment,

- or missing adapter.

Unavailable must preserve reason.

A capability may be architecturally defined while operationally unavailable.

4.136 Deprecated State

Deprecated means an object remains interpretable but should not be selected for new use.

Deprecation shall include:

- reason,

- effective date,

- replacement,

- migration plan,

- and retirement target where known.

Historical evidence must continue to resolve deprecated objects.

4.137 Retired State

Retired means the object is no longer available for active use.

Retired objects may remain queryable for:

- audit,

- provenance,

- historical cost,

- and incident review.

Retirement shall not erase identity or historical relationships.

4.138 Object Relationships

Canonical relationships shall be explicit.

Expected relationships include:

- belongs to Tenant,

- belongs to Project,

- initiated by,

- called by,

- delegated by,

- approved by,

- constrained by Policy,

- requires Capability,

- fulfilled by Execution,

- selected Provider,

- used Model Version,

- invoked through Adapter,

- charged to Budget Source,

- produced Output,

- created Asset,

- evaluated by,

- derived from,

- supported Decision,

- created Learning Candidate,

- and submitted Memory Candidate.

Relationships may be represented relationally or graphically.

Their meaning must remain stable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.139 Relationship Direction

Relationship direction shall reflect canonical meaning.

For example:

- Execution produced Output,

- Output derived Asset,

- Approval authorised Execution,

- and Learning derived from Evidence.

Inverse queries may be supported.

The canonical relationship direction should remain documented to avoid ambiguous graph semantics.

4.140 Relationship Scope

Relationships inherit or declare scope.

A relationship between objects in different Projects requires:

- an approved cross-project relationship,

- explicit authority,

- or a platform-global object type designed for that purpose.

The system shall not create cross-project relationships merely because identifiers are known.

4.141 Relationship Provenance

Meaningful relationships should preserve provenance.

The system should be able to determine:

- who created the relationship,

- what event caused it,

- when it became valid,

- and whether it remains active.

Derived relationships shall be distinguishable from explicitly approved relationships.

4.142 Canonical Time

Fabric objects shall use consistent time representation.

Timestamps should be:

- timezone-aware,

- stored in a canonical format,

- and attributable to a trusted clock source where consequence requires it.

The architecture shall distinguish:

- createdAt,

- submittedAt,

- acceptedAt,

- startedAt,

- completedAt,

- observedAt,

- effectiveAt,

- expiresAt,

- and verifiedAt.

One generic timestamp is insufficient.

4.143 Effective Time and Recorded Time

Effective Time describes when a fact or policy became valid.

Recorded Time describes when Omnira recorded it.

These may differ.

For example:

- provider terms may become effective before Omnira records them,

- a delayed callback may describe an earlier provider completion,

- and a human may record consent after the consent was originally given.

Both times may be important for audit and reconciliation.

4.144 Integrity Metadata

Important records should preserve integrity metadata.

This may include:

- checksum,

- signature,

- source system,

- immutable storage reference,

- schema version,

- and evidence chain.

Integrity metadata helps detect:

- corruption,

- accidental modification,

- duplicate ingestion,

- and disputed evidence.

Not every low-risk temporary object requires cryptographic signing.

Integrity controls should match consequence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.145 Classification Inheritance

Outputs and derived objects may inherit classification from their inputs.

Inheritance rules should consider:

- highest input classification,

- transformation,

- redaction,

- aggregation risk,

- and output content.

A derived public summary may be eligible for lower classification only through explicit declassification logic.

Classification shall not drop automatically because output is shorter or reformatted.

4.146 Rights Inheritance

Derivative outputs shall preserve relevant rights restrictions from source assets.

A generated animation based on a licensed character reference may remain subject to:

- character ownership,

- provider terms,

- commercial-use restrictions,

- and publication conditions.

Rights inheritance shall be evaluated through the full derivation chain.

4.147 Cost Attribution Chain

Cost shall remain attributable through:

- Capability Request,

- Execution Plan,

- Execution,

- Attempt,

- Provider Account,

- Budget Source,

- Project,

- and Tenant.

The cost chain must support:

- request-level reporting,

- production-level reporting,

- project reporting,

- provider reconciliation,

- and retry analysis.

Shared infrastructure cost may be allocated separately from direct provider cost.

4.148 Evidence Chain

An Evidence Chain links the objects required to explain an outcome.

A valid Evidence Chain may connect:

- Intent,

- Capability Request,

- Authority Envelope,

- Policy Decision,

- Selection Decision,

- Execution,

- Attempts,

- Provider Receipts,

- Outputs,

- Evaluations,

- Acceptance,

- Assets,

- and publication or memory outcomes.

The chain need not be stored in one document.

It must remain reconstructable.

4.149 Object Ownership

Each persistent object shall have an ownership model.

Ownership may belong to:

- user,

- tenant,

- project,

- platform,

- provider,

- or shared governed scope.

Ownership affects:

- access,

- retention,

- deletion,

- export,

- cost,

- and governance.

Ownership shall not be inferred only from who created the object.

4.150 Object Custody

Custody describes which system currently stores or controls an object.

Custody is separate from ownership.

A provider may have temporary custody of an input.

Omnira or the user may retain ownership.

A cloud storage system may have custody of an Asset.

The Project may own it.

Custody transitions should be evidenced for sensitive objects.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.151 Object Authority

Object Authority defines who may:

- read,

- modify,

- approve,

- supersede,

- delete,

- publish,

- or administer an object.

Authority may vary by action.

The creator of an object does not automatically receive every authority over it.

4.152 Object Retention

Persistent objects shall have explicit or inherited retention.

Retention may depend on:

- object type,

- classification,

- legal requirement,

- project policy,

- provider terms,

- incident state,

- and memory status.

Evidence needed for unresolved incidents must not be deleted prematurely.

Temporary outputs should not remain indefinitely by default.

4.153 Object Deletion

Deletion shall distinguish:

- soft deletion,

- archival,

- revocation,

- logical removal,

- physical deletion,

- provider deletion,

- and cryptographic erasure where applicable.

Deletion of a canonical object must preserve required audit evidence without retaining prohibited content beyond policy.

Deletion propagation across providers and derivatives must be deliberate.

4.154 Object Export

Users or authorised systems may require export of:

- Assets,

- provenance,

- execution evidence,

- costs,

- policies,

- provider relationships,

- or memory candidates.

Export shall preserve:

- scope,

- classification,

- rights,

- integrity,

- and relationship references.

Export does not remove the original object unless deletion is separately authorised.

4.155 Object Redaction

Redaction creates a reduced representation that removes protected content while preserving necessary evidence.

Redaction should record:

- source object,

- redaction method,

- actor,

- reason,

- removed categories,

- and resulting classification.

Redaction must not silently modify the original immutable evidence.

4.156 Object Supersession

Supersession means a newer object or version replaces an older one for active use.

The superseded object remains part of history.

Supersession should record:

- superseding object,

- superseded object,

- reason,

- effective time,

- and migration impact.

Examples include:

- new Policy Version,

- new Prompt Version,

- new Model Version,

- or new Canonical Asset Version.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.157 Object Contradiction

A Contradiction Relationship records that two claims, learnings, evaluations or memories conflict.

Contradiction does not require immediate deletion.

The system should preserve:

- both objects,

- conflict reason,

- evidence,

- scope,

- and resolution status.

Contradiction handling is especially important for Derived Learning and Memory Candidates.

4.158 Object Confidence

Confidence may be attached to:

- classification,

- derived learning,

- evaluation,

- source verification,

- rights interpretation,

- or health inference.

Confidence shall not replace evidence.

A high numerical confidence without transparent basis is insufficient.

Confidence scale and meaning must be versioned.

4.159 Canonical Object Minimalism

The canonical model should be expressive without becoming unnecessarily fragmented.

A new object type should be introduced when it has distinct:

- identity,

- lifecycle,

- ownership,

- authority,

- or evidence requirements.

A simple attribute may be sufficient when those distinctions do not exist.

The purpose is clarity, not maximum object count.

4.160 Canonical Object Extensibility

Canonical objects may support extension fields.

Extensions shall be:

- namespaced,

- versioned,

- provider- or project-specific,

- and prevented from redefining canonical fields.

Provider-specific extensions may preserve unique features.

They must not become hidden core semantics.

4.161 Provider Object Translation

Adapters shall translate provider objects into canonical objects.

Examples include:

- provider generation request into Execution Attempt,

- provider job into Provider Job,

- provider asset into Output or Asset Reference,

- provider credit usage into Usage Record,

- provider error into canonical Error,

- and provider callback into Callback.

Translation shall preserve provider identifiers for reconciliation.

4.162 Canonical Error

A Canonical Error represents a normalised failure or rejection.

It may include:

- errorId,

- category,

- source,

- provider code,

- message,

- retryability,

- permanence,

- user action required,

- scope,

- and evidence reference.

Canonical categories may include:

- validation,

- authentication,

- authorisation,

- policy,

- budget,

- unsupported capability,

- rate limit,

- provider outage,

- timeout,

- unknown outcome,

- rights,

- safety,

- data classification,

- quality,

- and internal defect.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.163 Error Causality

Errors may have causal relationships.

For example:

- ProviderAuthenticationExpired may cause ExecutionAttemptFailed,

- which may cause ExecutionPaused,

- which may cause WorkflowRunAwaitingOperator.

The system should preserve root cause where known.

A generic top-level failure must not erase lower-level evidence.

4.164 Compensation

A Compensation is a corrective action intended to reverse or mitigate a completed side effect.

Examples include:

- deleting an unintended provider asset,

- releasing a budget reservation,

- removing a scheduled publication,

- or restoring a prior configuration.

Compensation shall include:

- triggering failure,

- target,

- authority,

- execution,

- result,

- and residual risk.

Compensation is not always equivalent to rollback.

4.165 Reconciliation

Reconciliation is the process of resolving discrepancies between Omnira and an external provider or subsystem.

It may compare:

- job state,

- cost,

- output existence,

- publication state,

- credits,

- or asset records.

A Reconciliation Record should include:

- source states,

- discrepancy,

- resolution,

- evidence,

- and remaining uncertainty.

Reconciliation may convert unknown outcome into completed or failed without rewriting prior evidence.

4.166 Simulation Object

A Simulation represents a non-production evaluation of:

- routing,

- cost,

- policy,

- provider choice,

- or execution plan.

A Simulation shall be clearly marked.

It may produce:

- simulated Selection Decision,

- simulated Cost Estimate,

- simulated Execution Plan,

- or test Output.

Simulation objects must not be included in production performance evidence without explicit classification.

4.167 Test Execution

A Test Execution is an Execution performed for conformance, benchmark or integration testing.

It shall include:

- test purpose,

- environment,

- synthetic or approved data,

- expected outcome,

- and test result.

Test Executions shall not use production side effects unless explicitly approved.

4.168 Experimental Object

An Experimental object or resource has not yet completed production admission.

Experimental status may apply to:

- Provider Account,

- Model Version,

- Adapter,

- Capability Mapping,

- Tool,

- or Workflow.

Experimental resources may have:

- reduced data eligibility,

- low spending limits,

- mandatory human review,

- and sandbox-only use.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.169 Production Admission Record

A Production Admission Record documents the decision to permit a resource in production.

It should include:

- target resource,

- tested version,

- conformance evidence,

- security review,

- policy review,

- approved scope,

- restrictions,

- approver,

- and effective time.

Production admission is not permanent.

Material change may require re-certification.

4.170 Canonical Object Access Pattern

Fabric components should access objects through authorised services or repositories rather than uncontrolled direct storage access.

Access should enforce:

- tenant,

- project,

- environment,

- authority,

- classification,

- and object lifecycle.

A direct database query that bypasses these controls is not canonical merely because it reads canonical tables.

4.171 Object Query Scope

Every object query shall declare or resolve scope.

Queries should distinguish:

- one object by authorised ID,

- project-scoped collection,

- tenant-scoped collection,

- platform-global operational view,

- and cross-project governed query.

Missing scope shall not return all objects.

4.172 Object Mutation Contract

Mutations shall include:

- acting Principal,

- target object,

- expected version,

- requested transition,

- authority,

- reason,

- and correlation.

Optimistic or equivalent concurrency control should prevent silent overwrite.

Mutation failure must preserve current state.

4.173 Object Creation Contract

Creation shall validate:

- identity,

- ownership,

- scope,

- schema,

- classification,

- authority,

- and uniqueness.

Objects created by asynchronous callbacks must still resolve legitimate ownership and scope.

External input must not create unrestricted global objects.

4.174 Object Read Contract

Read access shall be evaluated separately from mutation access.

A Principal may be allowed to:

- see summary metadata,

- but not sensitive payload;

- inspect cost,

- but not prompts;

- review output,

- but not credentials;

- or view project status,

- but not another project’s assets.

Canonical services should support field-level or representation-level restriction where necessary.

4.175 Object Projection

A Projection is a derived read model created for a specific use.

Examples include:

- project execution dashboard,

- provider health summary,

- monthly cost report,

- agent activity view,

- or Intelligence Graph projection.

Projections shall identify:

- source objects,

- freshness,

- scope,

- and derivation.

A stale Projection must not be represented as current truth.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.176 Object Freshness

Objects and views that represent changing external state shall include freshness information.

Freshness may include:

- observedAt,

- sourceUpdatedAt,

- retrievedAt,

- expected refresh,

- and stale threshold.

Unknown freshness shall be represented honestly.

4.177 Canonical Object Search

Search across Fabric objects must preserve scope and classification.

Search indexes shall not become cross-tenant leakage paths.

Index documents should include:

- tenant,

- project,

- classification,

- object type,

- and lifecycle.

Search results must re-check authorisation before content is returned.

4.178 Object Graph Projection

Canonical objects may be projected into the Intelligence Graph.

Graph projection shall preserve:

- object identity,

- relationship type,

- scope,

- provenance,

- and freshness.

The Graph may provide navigation and explanation.

It shall not become the only authoritative storage for objects whose lifecycle belongs elsewhere.

4.179 Canonical Object Event

Material object changes should emit or record canonical events.

Examples include:

- CapabilityRequestSubmitted,

- ApprovalGranted,

- ExecutionStarted,

- ProviderJobAccepted,

- OutputReceived,

- EvaluationFailed,

- AssetCanonicalised,

- LearningCandidateCreated,

- and IncidentDetected.

Events shall include:

- eventId,

- object reference,

- event type,

- occurredAt,

- recordedAt,

- actor,

- correlation,

- causation,

- scope,

- and payload version.

4.180 Event Idempotency

Event consumers shall handle duplicate delivery where the architecture uses at-least-once transport.

Consumers should use:

- event IDs,

- object versions,

- deduplication state,

- or idempotent mutation.

Duplicate event receipt shall not duplicate:

- cost,

- assets,

- memory candidates,

- or publication actions.

4.181 Event Ordering

The Fabric shall not assume global event ordering.

Ordering may be preserved within:

- one object,

- one execution,

- one provider job,

- or one partition.

Consumers shall use:

- object revision,

- occurred time,

- causation,

- and state-transition validation.

Late events must not silently revert newer confirmed state.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.182 Object State and Event Evidence

Current object state and historical events shall remain consistent.

If they differ, the system must:

- identify projection delay,

- repair state,

- or open an Incident.

Events should not be deleted merely to make current state appear correct.

4.183 Canonical Object Security Label

Objects may include a security label beyond general Data Classification.

A security label may express:

- personal data,

- credential-adjacent,

- legal hold,

- child-related,

- financial,

- health,

- proprietary,

- or export-controlled.

Labels may trigger additional policy.

Security labels shall remain scoped and versioned.

4.184 Child-Facing Content Label

Outputs and Assets intended for children may receive a child-facing content label.

This label may require:

- stronger human review,

- age appropriateness,

- visual safety,

- voice suitability,

- advertising restrictions,

- and publication rules.

The label is especially relevant to Familje-Stunden.

It shall not be inferred only from project name when content purpose differs.

4.185 Commercial Asset Label

Commercially used Assets may receive a commercial asset label.

This may require:

- confirmed rights,

- stronger provenance,

- approved quality,

- canonical version,

- publication history,

- and retention.

Disposable experiments should not automatically receive commercial status.

4.186 Canonical Object Schema Governance

Schema changes shall follow governed evolution.

A schema change should include:

- motivation,

- compatibility analysis,

- migration,

- affected services,

- version,

- tests,

- and rollback.

Breaking changes require explicit version transition.

Providers must not force uncontrolled breaking changes into canonical schemas.

4.187 Canonical Naming Rules

Canonical object and field names should be:

- clear,

- stable,

- provider-independent,

- and consistent across services.

Provider terminology may be preserved in extension fields.

Ambiguous names such as:

- item,

- data,

- job,

- result,

- or status

should be avoided without context.

Names should communicate lifecycle and ownership.

4.188 Required and Optional Fields

Schema definitions shall clearly distinguish:

- required,

- conditionally required,

- optional,

- derived,

- and prohibited fields.

Conditionally required fields should state the condition.

For example:

- projectId is required for project-scoped execution,

- globalScopeReason is required for platform-global execution,

- approvalId is required when policy requires approval,

- and providerJobId is optional for synchronous providers.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 4.190 Canonical Object Example — Simple Text Request
4.191 Canonical Object Example — Nova and Pling Scene
text:
4.189 Null, Unknown and Not Applicable

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- null or absent,

- unknown,

- not applicable,

- redacted,

- and unavailable.

These meanings must not be collapsed.

For example:

- cost unknown,

- cost not applicable for a simulation,

- cost redacted from a user view,

- and cost unavailable from the provider

represent different states.

4.190 Canonical Object Example — Simple Text Request

A simple governed request may produce the following object chain:

Human Principal

↓ initiates

Intent

↓ expressed through

Capability Request

↓ constrained by

Authority Envelope

Policy Context

Budget Envelope

Quality Contract

↓ resolved into

Execution Plan

↓ selects

Provider Account

Model Version

Adapter

↓ creates

Execution

↓ contains

Execution Attempt

↓ produces

Output

↓ evaluated by

Evaluation

↓ accepted through

Acceptance Decision

↓ summarised in

Execution Receipt

Even simple execution should preserve the essential chain.

4.191 Canonical Object Example — Nova and Pling Scene

A Nova and Pling scene may include:

Project

Familje-Stunden

Production Envelope

September Episode Production

Capability Request

Animate approved illustration into an eight-second 16:9 scene with stable character appearance.

Input Data Items

- approved Nova reference,

- approved Pling reference,

- approved scene illustration,

- motion instruction,

- brand instruction set.

Rights and Consent

- project ownership record,

- approved commercial-use requirement,

- character asset rights profile.

Quality Contract

- character identity preserved,

- no facial distortion,

- child-appropriate motion,

- correct duration,

- approved resolution.

Budget Envelope

- maximum scene cost,

- maximum two retries.

Execution Plan

- low-cost preview generation,

- evaluation,

- premium retry only if required and approved by policy.

Execution

- selected provider account,

- model version,

- adapter,

- execution attempts.

Outputs

- preview video,

- rejected attempt,

- accepted final scene.

Evidence

- cost,

- quality evaluations,

- human review,

- provenance,

- learning candidate.

This chain preserves the project’s control while allowing provider replacement.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 4.192 Canonical Object Example — The Prompt News Segment
4.195 Canonical Object Example — Local Private Research
text:
4.192 Canonical Object Example — The Prompt News Segment

A The Prompt news segment may include:

Intent

Produce a two-minute verified AI-news segment.

Capability Requirements

- current research,

- source verification,

- script generation,

- voice,

- avatar or reporter video,

- captions,

- quality review.

Data Classification

Public source material and Project Internal editorial instructions.

Quality Contract

- factual claims supported,

- sources current,

- no fabricated quotations,

- clear distinction between fact and interpretation,

- approved reporter identity.

Workflow Run

- research step,

- verification step,

- scripting,

- editorial review,

- media generation,

- final review.

Publication Package

- master video,

- short clips,

- title,

- description,

- citations,

- thumbnail.

Publication remains a separate execution.

4.193 Canonical Object Example — GainPilot Reel

A GainPilot reel may use:

- Economy or Balanced Routing Profile,

- local text model for draft,

- image provider for one still,

- voice provider for narration,

- local tool for motion and captions,

- and human review.

The object model remains the same.

The resource selection and Quality Contract differ.

4.194 Canonical Object Example — Code Change

A software Capability Request may require:

- repository analysis,

- patch generation,

- test execution,

- architecture validation,

- and review.

The Fabric may produce:

- analysis Output,

- patch Asset,

- test Evaluation,

- and Execution Receipt.

Repository mutation, commit, push, pull request and merge remain separate Side Effects with separate authority.

4.195 Canonical Object Example — Local Private Research

A Confidential research request may include:

- Local Only Data Classification,

- Private Routing Profile,

- local Model Deployment,

- local embedding capability,

- no external provider candidates,

- and restricted evidence logging.

If the local resource cannot satisfy the Quality Contract, the request may fail or require explicit authority to change placement.

It must not silently fall back externally.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.196 Canonical Object Invariants

The following invariants shall apply:

1. Every persistent canonical object SHALL have stable identity.

2. Every project-scoped object SHALL reference an explicit Project.

3. Every tenant-scoped object SHALL reference an explicit Tenant.

4. Global scope SHALL require explicit declaration.

5. Every Execution SHALL reference a Capability Request or approved equivalent source.

6. Every paid Execution SHALL reference a Budget Source.

7. Every provider Execution SHALL identify a Provider Account.

8. Every model Execution SHALL identify a Model Version or preserve the provider’s uncertainty.

9. Every Execution Attempt SHALL remain historically visible after retry.

10. Every Output SHALL reference the Execution that produced it.

11. Every durable Asset SHALL preserve provenance.

12. Every Approval SHALL identify approver, scope and decision.

13. Every Policy Decision SHALL identify evaluated policy versions.

14. Every delegated action SHALL preserve its authority chain.

15. Every external side effect SHALL preserve completion evidence.

16. Every Learning Candidate SHALL reference supporting evidence.

17. Every Memory Candidate SHALL remain separate from admitted memory.

18. Every cross-project relationship SHALL be explicit.

19. Every canonical state transition SHALL be valid and attributable.

20. Missing critical scope SHALL fail closed.

4.197 Prohibited Object Collapses

The following conceptual collapses are prohibited:

- Provider and Provider Account.

- Model and Agent.

- Capability Request and Execution.

- Execution and Attempt.

- Output and Asset.

- Evaluation and Approval.

- Approval and Authority.

- Generation and Publication.

- Evidence and Memory.

- Learning Candidate and Governed Memory.

- Provider Job and canonical Execution.

- Authentication and Authorisation.

- Tenant and Project.

- Project ownership and cross-project permission.

- Estimated cost and confirmed cost.

- Provider acceptance and verified completion.

- Object state and event history.

Implementations may store related concepts together.

They must preserve their distinct meaning.

4.198 Stage 1 Minimum Object Set

Stage 1 should implement or explicitly represent at least:

- Principal,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- Capability,

- Capability Request,

- Authority Envelope,

- Approval,

- Policy Decision,

- Data Classification,

- Routing Profile,

- Quality Contract,

- Budget Envelope,

- Provider,

- Provider Account,

- Model,

- Model Version,

- Adapter,

- Credential Reference,

- Execution Plan,

- Execution,

- Execution Attempt,

- Provider Job where asynchronous,

- Output,

- Evaluation,

- Execution Receipt,

- Usage Record,

- Cost Record,

- Provenance Record,

- Incident,

- Learning Candidate,

- and Memory Candidate.

Stage 1 may represent some objects through embedded structures.

It must not lose canonical identity where lifecycle or audit requires it.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.199 Stage 1 Object Acceptance Tests

Representative acceptance tests should include:

1. Provider and Provider Account remain distinct.

2. A Capability Request may exist without an Execution when rejected.

3. One Execution may contain multiple Attempts.

4. A failed Attempt does not erase a later successful Attempt.

5. An Output cannot be accepted without required Evaluation.

6. An Output does not become a canonical Asset automatically.

7. An Approval cannot be reused outside its scope.

8. A Budget Reservation cannot be charged to another Project.

9. A Local Only Data Item cannot be attached to an external Provider Execution.

10. A provider callback cannot mutate an unrelated Execution.

11. A duplicate callback does not duplicate an Output.

12. Unknown provider outcome remains represented as unknown until reconciled.

13. A Model Version may change without changing the Agent Principal.

14. A Learning Candidate does not enter permanent memory automatically.

15. Historical Executions remain interpretable after Model deprecation.

16. A missing Project does not default to global scope.

17. Provider terms and input rights remain separately represented.

18. Estimated and confirmed cost remain distinguishable.

19. Publication Package does not imply Publication Record.

20. Canonical Asset supersession preserves the previous version.

4.200 Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this chapter only when:

- canonical object identities are stable,

- provider terminology is translated rather than leaked into core contracts,

- scope is explicit,

- ownership is explicit,

- authority is explicit,

- lifecycles are defined,

- state transitions are validated,

- evidence remains immutable where required,

- object relationships are reconstructable,

- and critical conceptual distinctions remain enforceable.

A database schema alone does not prove conformance.

Conformance requires runtime behaviour, tests and evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.201 Canonical Object Contract

The following requirements define the canonical object contract:

1. Canonical meaning SHALL remain independent of storage form.

2. Persistent objects SHALL have stable identity.

3. Canonical and provider identifiers SHALL remain distinct.

4. Objects SHALL carry explicit scope where applicable.

5. Schema and object versions SHALL remain distinguishable.

6. Immutable evidence SHALL NOT be silently rewritten.

7. Lifecycle transitions SHALL be explicit and attributable.

8. Principals SHALL remain separate from authority.

9. Tenants and Projects SHALL remain separate scopes.

10. Delegation SHALL preserve its authority chain.

11. Approval SHALL remain separate from general authority.

12. Intent SHALL remain separate from implementation.

13. Capabilities SHALL remain provider-independent.

14. Capability Requests SHALL remain separate from Executions.

15. Providers and Provider Accounts SHALL remain separate.

16. Models, Model Versions and Deployments SHALL remain separate.

17. Agents SHALL remain separate from Models.

18. Adapters SHALL preserve canonical meaning.

19. Execution Plans SHALL remain separate from active Executions.

20. Executions SHALL preserve all Attempts.

21. Provider Jobs SHALL remain external execution evidence.

22. Outputs SHALL remain separate from durable Assets.

23. Evaluations SHALL remain separate from Acceptance and Approval.

24. Estimated cost SHALL remain separate from confirmed cost.

25. Meaningful Outputs and Assets SHALL preserve provenance.

26. Side effects SHALL produce appropriate receipts.

27. Incidents SHALL remain separate from ordinary failures.

28. Learning Candidates SHALL remain separate from permanent memory.

29. Publication preparation SHALL remain separate from publication.

30. Unknown SHALL remain a valid explicit state.

31. Cross-project relationships SHALL require explicit authority.

32. Historical objects SHALL remain interpretable after deprecation.

33. Extensions SHALL NOT redefine canonical fields.

34. Canonical status vocabularies SHALL remain object-specific.

35. Object access SHALL enforce scope and authority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
4.202 Closing Statement

The Omnira Intelligence Fabric requires more than connections to models and providers.

It requires a stable internal language through which every request, resource, execution, output, cost, decision and learning can be understood.

The canonical object model provides that language.

Intent explains what should be achieved.

Capability defines what kind of intelligence is required.

Authority defines what may occur.

Policy defines the rules.

Scope defines where the work belongs.

Providers and models supply replaceable resources.

Plans define how the work may proceed.

Executions record what Omnira attempted.

Attempts preserve every technical submission.

Outputs preserve what was produced.

Evaluations determine quality.

Approvals preserve human authority.

Assets preserve durable value.

Provenance preserves origin.

Receipts preserve operational truth.

Evidence supports decisions.

Learning converts experience into future advantage.

Memory governance determines what should persist.

These objects form the semantic foundation of the Intelligence Fabric.

Without stable objects, routing becomes guesswork.

Without explicit relationships, provenance disappears.

Without lifecycle, state becomes ambiguous.

Without scope, shared infrastructure becomes a leakage risk.

Without authority, technical capability becomes uncontrolled power.

The canonical model shall therefore remain provider-independent, versioned, scoped, observable and governed.

Every future implementation of the Fabric shall preserve these meanings even as the underlying technology changes.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 5.3 Intent and Execution Are Different Objects
text:
5.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical architecture for expressing intent, translating intent into capability requirements and submitting governed work to the Omnira Intelligence Fabric.

It establishes:

- how humans and authorised systems express desired outcomes,

- how broad objectives become executable capability requests,

- how project context and constraints are attached,

- how ambiguity and missing information are handled,

- how quality, budget, time, rights, data and authority are declared,

- how requests are validated before planning,

- how request changes are versioned,

- how recurring and multi-step requests are represented,

- and how the Fabric preserves the difference between desired outcome and technical implementation.

This chapter is normative after formal approval.

It does not require every request to be entered through a single user interface.

Intent may originate through:

- conversation,

- project workflows,

- forms,

- schedules,

- APIs,

- approved automations,

- Managers,

- agents,

- or internal platform events.

Regardless of origin, governed intelligence execution shall converge on the canonical request contracts defined in this chapter.

A natural-language instruction alone is not sufficient authority for consequential execution unless it has been resolved into a valid scoped request and the required approval or delegated authority exists.

5.2 Purpose of Capability Requests

The Intelligence Fabric shall not accept unstructured intent as unrestricted execution authority.

Users should be able to communicate naturally.

The system must then transform that communication into a request that can be:

- understood,

- validated,

- authorised,

- costed,

- planned,

- routed,

- executed,

- evaluated,

- and audited.

The Capability Request is the canonical boundary between:

- what a caller wants,

- and what the Fabric is allowed to execute.

It shall capture the outcome without prematurely coupling the request to one provider or model.

It shall contain enough structure to prevent important requirements from being lost during translation.

5.3 Intent and Execution Are Different Objects

Intent describes the desired purpose or outcome.

Execution describes the technical work performed to fulfil that intent.

The Fabric shall not collapse these concepts.

For example, the intent may be:

Create a monthly Nova and Pling episode connected to the approved Familje-Stunden theme.

The execution may involve:

- script analysis,

- scene segmentation,

- asset retrieval,

- image editing,

- image-to-video generation,

- narration,

- sound effects,

- quality evaluation,

- file conversion,

- and human review.

The user owns the intent.

The Fabric constructs and governs the execution path.

A change in execution method does not necessarily change the intent.

A change in business outcome may require a new or revised intent.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.4 Intent Object

An Intent object represents the purpose that motivates one or more Capability Requests.

An Intent should include:

- intentId,

- tenantId,

- projectId where applicable,

- initiating Principal,

- beneficiary,

- objective,

- business or user context,

- desired outcome,

- success definition,

- importance,

- timing expectations,

- and lifecycle status.

Intent may remain broader than one technical request.

A long-term intent may generate several requests over time.

For example:

Increase discovery and engagement for Familje-Stunden through recurring Nova and Pling video content.

This Intent may later produce:

- one monthly episode request,

- one trailer request,

- several social-media derivative requests,

- one performance-analysis request,

- and one routing-learning request.

The broader intent remains stable while individual requests change.

5.5 Intent Envelope

The Intent Envelope is the structured representation through which broad intent is prepared for translation into governed work.

The canonical Intent Envelope should support:

- intentId,

- tenantId,

- projectId,

- environmentId,

- initiator,

- caller,

- beneficiary,

- objective,

- background context,

- desired outputs,

- success conditions,

- priority,

- time horizon,

- budget posture,

- data classification,

- rights requirements,

- routing preference,

- approval posture,

- and unresolved questions.

The Intent Envelope may begin partially complete.

It must not be treated as execution-ready until required fields have been resolved.

5.6 Capability Request

A Capability Request is the canonical executable request submitted to the Intelligence Fabric.

It shall include or reference:

- requestId,

- intentId,

- request version,

- caller,

- initiator,

- tenant,

- project,

- environment,

- purpose,

- one or more Capability Requirements,

- inputs,

- output contract,

- quality contract,

- authority envelope,

- policy context,

- budget envelope,

- routing profile,

- data classification,

- rights profile,

- deadline,

- review requirements,

- side-effect restrictions,

- lifecycle state,

- and provenance.

The Capability Request defines what the Fabric may attempt.

It does not guarantee that an eligible execution path exists.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.7 Request Origin

A Capability Request may originate from:

- direct human instruction,

- Atlas,

- Executive Intelligence,

- a Manager,

- a specialist agent,

- a workflow,

- a recurring schedule,

- a condition watch,

- a project event,

- an API client,

- or an approved external integration.

The request shall preserve its origin.

The origin shall not determine authority by itself.

A request created by Atlas must still be authorised.

A request created by a schedule must still satisfy current policy.

A request created by an external integration must still resolve tenant, project and caller identity.

5.8 Initiator, Caller and Executor

The Fabric shall distinguish:

- Initiator,

- Caller,

- Planner,

- Executor,

- Approver,

- and Beneficiary.

The Initiator is the Principal or event that began the broader objective.

The Caller submits the Capability Request to the Fabric.

The Planner translates the request into an Execution Plan.

The Executor performs one or more Execution Steps.

The Approver grants required authority.

The Beneficiary is the person, project or system intended to receive value from the result.

These roles may be held by the same Principal.

They must remain distinguishable where they differ.

5.9 Human Intent Capture

Human intent may be expressed through natural language.

The user should not be required to understand Fabric schemas.

The system may ask questions, infer non-consequential defaults and present structured summaries.

However, the final request must preserve the difference between:

- explicitly stated information,

- inferred information,

- defaulted information,

- retrieved project context,

- and unresolved assumptions.

Inferred information shall not silently become user-approved truth when it materially affects:

- cost,

- privacy,

- rights,

- quality,

- publication,

- or authority.

5.10 Intent Interpretation

Intent Interpretation is the process through which natural or broad instructions are translated into structured meaning.

Intent Interpretation may identify:

- objective,

- affected project,

- desired output,

- required capabilities,

- audience,

- constraints,

- timing,

- budget sensitivity,

- quality expectations,

- and risk.

The interpreting system shall preserve uncertainty.

It should distinguish:

- explicit requirement,

- likely preference,

- weak inference,

- and unknown.

The Fabric shall not convert an uncertain inference into a mandatory execution constraint without evidence or confirmation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.11 Clarification Threshold

The system shall not ask unnecessary questions.

It should ask for clarification when missing information could materially change:

- authority,

- privacy,

- cost,

- rights,

- external side effects,

- quality acceptance,

- project scope,

- or irreversible outcome.

It may proceed with safe defaults when the missing information is low-risk and reversible.

For example:

A draft summary may use a default document format.

A public video publication may not assume an account or publication date.

The clarification threshold shall reflect consequence rather than conversational perfection.

5.12 Minimum Necessary Questions

When clarification is required, the system should request the minimum information needed to make the next safe decision.

It should avoid large interview blocks when:

- project context already answers the question,

- a safe default exists,

- the decision can be deferred,

- or the missing detail does not affect the current stage.

For a Nova and Pling episode, the initial questions may only need to resolve:

- approved story,

- target duration,

- output channels,

- maximum budget,

- and publication authority.

Detailed provider selection should remain a Fabric responsibility.

5.13 Explicit and Inferred Requirements

Every meaningful request attribute should identify its origin where consequence requires it.

Possible origins include:

- user explicit,

- user preference,

- project policy,

- tenant policy,

- workflow definition,

- Fabric default,

- system inference,

- provider limitation,

- or legal requirement.

This origin supports:

- explanation,

- conflict resolution,

- approval,

- and revision.

A user-explicit requirement normally takes precedence over a soft system preference.

It does not override mandatory security or legal policy.

5.14 Requirement Confidence

Inferred requirements may include confidence.

Confidence should not be treated as authority.

A high-confidence inference may reduce clarification for reversible work.

It shall not authorise:

- spending,

- publication,

- cross-project access,

- voice cloning,

- or external use of confidential data.

Confidence informs interaction.

Authority governs execution.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.15 Objective

The Objective describes the result the caller wants to achieve.

A good Objective should state:

- desired outcome,

- target context,

- intended audience or beneficiary,

- and relevant business or operational purpose.

Examples include:

Create the approved September Nova and Pling episode for Familje-Stunden.

Produce a two-minute verified AI-news segment for The Prompt.

Create a short GainPilot reel explaining progressive overload.

Audit the Omnira project media architecture for project-isolation defects.

The Objective should not be written only as a provider command such as:

Use OpenArt.

Provider selection may be a constraint or preference, but it is not the objective.

5.16 Purpose

Purpose explains why the request exists.

Purpose may influence:

- quality,

- risk,

- retention,

- evaluation,

- and provider eligibility.

For example, the same image-generation capability may be used for:

- disposable brainstorming,

- internal concept review,

- paid advertising,

- child-facing content,

- or canonical character reference.

The capability is similar.

The governance requirements differ because the purpose differs.

5.17 Beneficiary

The Beneficiary identifies who or what receives the intended value.

The Beneficiary may be:

- the user,

- a project,

- a customer,

- an audience,

- an internal team,

- an agent,

- or the Omnira platform.

Beneficiary identification helps determine:

- project ownership,

- rights,

- output destination,

- quality expectations,

- and cost attribution.

The Beneficiary is not automatically the Caller.

5.18 Success Definition

The request should define what successful fulfilment means.

Success may include:

- required output produced,

- quality threshold met,

- human approval received,

- cost within budget,

- deadline met,

- and side effects verified.

Success must be measurable or reviewable.

A vague success definition such as “make it good” may be translated into project-specific quality dimensions.

The system should preserve the user’s qualitative intent without pretending that all value can be reduced to one numerical score.

5.19 Completion Contract

The Completion Contract defines what evidence is required before the request may be considered complete.

It may require:

- output received,

- schema valid,

- quality evaluation passed,

- human review completed,

- asset stored,

- publication package prepared,

- or external action verified.

Completion differs from provider success.

A provider may complete a generation while the request remains incomplete because evaluation failed.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.20 Capability Requirement

A Capability Requirement defines one type of intelligence or tool operation needed to fulfil the request.

It should include:

- capabilityId,

- capability version,

- mandatory or optional state,

- input requirements,

- output expectations,

- quality constraints,

- placement constraints,

- and dependency relationships.

A simple request may contain one Capability Requirement.

A complex request may contain many.

5.21 Mandatory Capability

A Mandatory Capability is required for successful completion.

If no eligible resource can fulfil it, the request must:

- fail,

- pause,

- degrade through approved revision,

- or escalate.

The Fabric shall not silently remove a mandatory capability.

For example, Swedish narration is mandatory when the approved output contract requires a Swedish audio track.

5.22 Optional Capability

An Optional Capability improves the result but is not required for minimum acceptance.

Optional capabilities may support:

- subtitles,

- additional variants,

- premium visual effects,

- extra research,

- or social-media derivatives.

Optional capabilities should have:

- priority,

- budget limit,

- and omission behaviour.

Their omission must not be represented as failure when the Completion Contract permits it.

5.23 Capability Dependency

Capability Requirements may depend on one another.

Examples include:

- animation depends on approved scene images,

- narration timing depends on final script,

- captions depend on narration or transcript,

- publication package depends on accepted assets.

Dependencies shall be explicit.

The planner shall not infer unsafe execution ordering from provider convenience.

5.24 Capability Alternatives

A request may permit alternative capabilities.

For example:

- image-to-video animation,

- motion-comic composition,

- or human-assisted editing

may all fulfil a broader visual storytelling requirement.

Alternative capabilities shall define:

- equivalence conditions,

- quality differences,

- cost differences,

- and approval requirements.

The Fabric may select among approved alternatives.

It shall not substitute a materially different outcome without disclosure.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.25 Capability Composition

Complex intent may require capability composition.

Composition may include:

- sequential execution,

- parallel execution,

- conditional execution,

- iterative refinement,

- and human checkpoints.

The Capability Request may declare the high-level requirements.

The Execution Planner constructs the detailed graph.

The request should not be forced to contain provider-specific orchestration logic.

5.26 Input Contract

The Input Contract defines what information or assets the request may use.

It may include:

- Data Item references,

- Asset references,

- Memory references,

- source documents,

- structured parameters,

- user instructions,

- and external evidence.

Inputs shall be identified rather than copied unnecessarily.

The Input Contract should preserve:

- owner,

- project,

- classification,

- rights,

- version,

- and required transformation.

5.27 Required Input

A Required Input is necessary for valid execution.

Examples include:

- approved story manuscript,

- canonical character references,

- source document,

- code repository,

- target language,

- or publication platform.

If a Required Input is unavailable, stale or unapproved, the request must not proceed as if it were complete.

5.28 Optional Input

An Optional Input may improve execution.

Examples include:

- previous audience analytics,

- style examples,

- preferred music reference,

- or historical provider evidence.

Optional Inputs should be used only when:

- scope permits,

- classification permits,

- rights permit,

- and retrieval is relevant.

The Fabric shall not indiscriminately attach all available project data.

5.29 Input Version

Requests shall identify relevant input versions.

For canonical assets, the request should reference a specific Asset Version.

A request that uses “the Nova reference image” without version may become ambiguous after the asset changes.

Where the latest approved version is intended, that rule should be explicit.

Execution evidence shall preserve the actual version used.

5.30 Input Freshness

Time-sensitive Inputs may require freshness constraints.

Examples include:

- current news sources,

- pricing,

- provider terms,

- project status,

- availability,

- and analytics.

The request may define:

- maximum age,

- current-as-of time,

- or verification requirement.

Stale input must not be represented as current.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.31 Input Classification

Each Input shall carry or inherit Data Classification.

The request-level classification should normally reflect the most restrictive relevant input unless an approved transformation changes it.

Mixed-classification inputs may require:

- segregation,

- local preprocessing,

- redaction,

- or separate execution paths.

The Fabric must not send a confidential Input merely because the request also includes public data.

5.32 Input Rights

Inputs shall preserve applicable Rights Profiles.

The request must identify whether the input may be:

- analysed,

- transformed,

- used for model generation,

- sent to external providers,

- used commercially,

- published,

- or retained.

Possession of a file does not prove all rights.

5.33 Input Consent

Voice, likeness and personal-data Inputs may require a Consent Record.

The request shall reference valid consent when required.

Consent validity must include:

- permitted use,

- project,

- duration,

- revocation,

- and commercial scope.

A provider’s technical support for cloning does not create consent.

5.34 Memory Inputs

The Capability Request may reference Governed Memory.

Memory retrieval shall be:

- scoped,

- purposeful,

- minimal,

- and evidenced where meaningful.

The request should identify the type of memory required rather than attaching the entire memory store.

Examples include:

- project brand rules,

- user preference,

- prior production learning,

- or approved agent role context.

Unreviewed execution logs shall not be treated as memory inputs.

5.35 Context Package

A Context Package is a scoped collection of information assembled for one request or execution step.

It may contain:

- project context,

- user instruction,

- relevant memory,

- selected assets,

- policy summaries,

- and task-specific evidence.

Context Packages should be:

- minimal,

- versioned,

- classified,

- and attributable.

The same Context Package should not be reused across unrelated projects without explicit authority.

5.36 Context Budget

Some models have limited context capacity.

The request or planner may define a Context Budget.

The Context Budget may constrain:

- token count,

- media count,

- document size,

- retrieval volume,

- or provider limits.

Context selection should prioritise relevance and authority.

It should not silently omit mandatory information to fit a model.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
5.37 Context Reduction

When context exceeds capacity, the Fabric may use:

- retrieval,

- summarisation,

- chunking,

- staged analysis,

- local preprocessing,

- or another eligible model.

Reduction must preserve critical meaning.

The system shall record material transformations.

A summary derived from confidential source material may remain confidential.

5.38 Output Contract

The Output Contract defines the expected result.

It may include:

- output type,

- format,

- schema,

- language,

- dimensions,

- duration,

- resolution,

- count,

- classification,

- rights,

- destination,

- quality requirements,

- and acceptance method.

The Output Contract shall be provider-independent.

The adapter translates it into provider-specific parameters.

5.39 Output Type

Output types may include:

- text,

- structured data,

- code,

- image,

- audio,

- video,

- document,

- embedding,

- ranking,

- plan,

- evaluation,

- or side-effect receipt.

A request may require multiple output types.

Each output should have its own acceptance requirements.

5.40 Output Count

The request may define:

- exact number,

- minimum number,

- maximum number,

- or bounded range of outputs.

For generative work, output count affects:

- cost,

- review burden,

- quality probability,

- and storage.

The Fabric shall not generate unlimited variants when only one is required.

5.41 Output Format

The Output Contract may define required formats such as:

- DOCX,

- PDF,

- Markdown,

- JSON,

- PNG,

- SVG,

- MP4,

- WAV,

- subtitle format,

- or provider-independent structured schema.

Format conversion may be a separate capability.

The Fabric must not claim native format support when it actually relies on post-processing.

5.42 Output Destination
