- or restricted account data.

7.187 Model Search

Search may support:

- canonical name,

- Provider name,

- alias,

- Capability,

- modality,

- licence,

- lifecycle,

- deployment type,

- and language support.

Search results shall remain scope-aware.

7.188 Model Visibility

Model visibility may be:

- platform-wide,

- tenant-visible,

- project-visible,

- administrative,

- experimental,

- or hidden internal.

Visibility does not imply execution authority.

7.189 Model Permission

Permissions may include:

- discover,

- request,

- test,

- approve,

- administer,

- deploy,

- deprecate,

- or retire.

These permissions shall remain separate.

7.190 Project Model Policy

A Project may define:

- allowed Models,

- denied Models,

- preferred Models,

- maximum Model class,

- private-only Models,

- or premium restrictions.

Project policy shall reference canonical Model or Capability identifiers.

7.191 Tenant Model Policy

Tenant policy may constrain:

- Providers,

- Models,

- regions,

- data classes,

- budgets,

- and licences.

Project policy may be stricter.

It shall not weaken mandatory tenant restrictions.

7.192 User Model Preference

A user may prefer:

- local Models,

- certain Providers,

- low cost,

- premium quality,

- or specific Models.

Preferences guide routing.

They do not override safety, policy or rights.

7.193 Model Pinning

A Workflow or request may pin:

- Model,

- Model Version,

- Deployment,

- or Provider alias.

Pinning shall define:

- reason,

- fallback,

- validity,

- and risk.

Pinning to a moving alias should be treated differently from pinning to a fixed Version.

7.194 Model Exclusion

A Model may be excluded by:

- user,

- Project,

- Tenant,

- Capability,

- data class,

- or Incident.

Exclusion shall apply across fallback.

7.195 Model Quota

A Model Deployment may have quotas such as:

- tokens,

- requests,

- images,

- audio minutes,

- or video credits.

Quota belongs to Provider Account and Deployment context.

7.196 Model Rate Limit

Rate limits may be:

- per account,

- per region,

- per Model,

- per endpoint,

- or dynamic.

The Fabric shall preserve current limit and reset evidence where available.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.197 Model Concurrency

Concurrency limits may affect scheduling.

Local Deployments may support one active job.

Cloud Deployments may support many.

Concurrency state belongs to Deployment.

7.198 Model Queue

Some Models or Providers expose queues.

Queue evidence may include:

- position,

- estimated wait,

- current capacity,

- and job priority.

Queue estimates must not be represented as guarantees.

7.199 Model Reservation

The Fabric may reserve:

- local GPU capacity,

- provider quota,

- or budget

for a planned Model execution.

Reservation does not guarantee provider acceptance unless explicitly supported.

7.200 Model Warm-Up

Local or managed Deployments may require warm-up.

Warm-up cost and latency should be considered in routing.

A warm Model may outperform a theoretically faster cold alternative for immediate tasks.

7.201 Model Auto-Unload

Local resource policy may unload Models after inactivity.

Auto-unload should consider:

- memory pressure,

- reload time,

- active schedules,

- and energy use.

7.202 Model Placement

Placement determines where a Model execution should occur.

Factors include:

- data classification,

- hardware,

- latency,

- cost,

- availability,

- energy,

- region,

- and user preference.

Placement is resolved at Deployment selection.

7.203 Workload Suitability

The Registry may derive suitability for workload classes such as:

- quick draft,

- high-quality reasoning,

- long-context analysis,

- confidential local processing,

- child-facing image review,

- or real-time voice.

Suitability remains evidence-based.

7.204 Model Routing Evidence

Selection Decisions should record:

- eligible Models,

- excluded Models,

- selected Deployment,

- Capability compatibility,

- quality evidence,

- cost,

- latency,

- privacy,

- and policy.

This supports explanation and learning.

7.205 Model Feedback

Users and reviewers may provide feedback such as:

- accepted,

- rejected,

- incorrect,

- too slow,

- too expensive,

- stylistically weak,

- or preferred.

Feedback shall remain scoped and not automatically become universal truth.

7.206 Model Learning Candidate

The Fabric may produce Learning Candidates such as:

- Model A performs better for Swedish technical summaries.

- Model B is sufficient for GainPilot caption generation.

- Model C frequently distorts Pling during two-character scenes.

- Local Model D is acceptable for private document extraction.

Each claim shall reference:

- Capability,

- conditions,

- Project scope,

- evidence,

- confidence,

- and validity.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.207 Global Model Learning

Platform-wide learning may be appropriate for:

- Provider outage,

- API instability,

- pricing mismatch,

- or broadly tested Capability performance.

Project-specific quality learning must remain scoped.

7.208 Model Learning Expiry

Model learnings should expire or be reviewed after:

- Model update,

- Adapter update,

- major pricing change,

- benchmark change,

- or defined time.

The Registry shall not use stale evidence indefinitely.

7.209 Model Evidence Conflict

Conflicting evidence may exist.

For example:

- external benchmark strong,

- internal project quality weak.

The Registry shall preserve both and avoid one unsupported universal conclusion.

7.210 Model Confidence

Confidence may be attached to:

- Version identity,

- Capability support,

- quality,

- cost estimate,

- or Deployment equivalence.

Confidence shall not replace evidence.

7.211 Deployment Equivalence

Two Deployments may claim to expose the same Model Version.

They may still differ because of:

- quantisation,

- system configuration,

- hidden Provider adaptation,

- safety settings,

- or runtime.

Equivalence shall be verified, not assumed.

7.212 Hosted Open Model Equivalence

An open Model hosted by a third party may not behave identically to the user’s local artefact.

The Registry shall preserve:

- host,

- runtime,

- configuration,

- and observed behaviour.

7.213 Provider Router Deployment

Some Providers expose an automatic router rather than one fixed Model.

Such a Deployment shall be represented as:

- provider-managed routed resource,

- with declared candidate Models where known,

- routing opacity,

- cost behaviour,

- and reproducibility limits.

It must not be mislabelled as one fixed Model Version.

7.214 Ensemble Model Resource

An Ensemble combines several Models.

It may:

- vote,

- critique,

- route,

- or aggregate.

The Ensemble shall be represented as a composed Resource or Workflow.

It shall not be registered as one ordinary Model unless it has a stable governed contract.

7.215 Mixture-of-Experts Model

A Model internally using mixture-of-experts remains one Model Version if the Provider exposes it as such.

Internal architecture does not require separate Fabric routing unless externally selectable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.216 Model-as-a-Service Product

A Provider product may bundle:

- Model,

- retrieval,

- tools,

- memory,

- and orchestration.

The Registry shall separate the actual components where governance requires it.

A bundled product must not gain unrestricted authority because the Provider presents it as one service.

7.217 Provider Assistant Product

A Provider-hosted assistant may use a Model plus state and tools.

It should normally be represented as an External Agent Resource, not merely a Model.

The underlying Model may remain known or unknown.

7.218 Real-Time Model Session

Real-time voice or multimodal Models may use long-lived sessions.

The Deployment shall declare:

- session limits,

- context retention,

- interruption,

- cost,

- tool permissions,

- and termination.

Session authority must remain bounded.

7.219 Ephemeral Model Session

An Ephemeral Session exists for one request or short task.

It should not become a hidden persistent memory store.

7.220 Persistent Provider Thread

A persistent Provider thread may preserve context.

The Registry or External Agent Resource shall record:

- owner,

- Project,

- retention,

- deletion,

- and synchronisation.

Provider threads shall not become canonical Memory.

7.221 Model Context Isolation

Provider sessions, caches and local runtime state must preserve:

- Tenant,

- Project,

- and user isolation.

Context must not leak between requests.

7.222 Model Cache

Caching may reduce cost or latency.

Model response caching shall consider:

- Input identity,

- classification,

- Project,

- permissions,

- freshness,

- and non-determinism.

A cache hit must not return another Project’s protected result.

7.223 Provider Prompt Cache

Some Providers offer prompt caching.

The Deployment metadata may include:

- cache scope,

- retention,

- pricing,

- privacy,

- and invalidation.

Prompt caching does not remove classification requirements.

7.224 Model Output Cache

Output caching may be suitable for deterministic or reusable tasks.

It must preserve:

- provenance,

- request compatibility,

- rights,

- freshness,

- and scope.

7.225 Model Security

Model execution security includes:

- prompt injection,

- data leakage,

- tool misuse,

- malicious output,

- model supply chain,

- and unsafe artefacts.

Security requirements shall apply at Model, Adapter and Deployment levels.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.226 Model Supply-Chain Security

Self-hosted Models may introduce supply-chain risk through:

- untrusted artefacts,

- malicious code,

- unsafe loaders,

- poisoned weights,

- or compromised containers.

Production admission should verify:

- source,

- checksum,

- licence,

- scanner results,

- and runtime isolation.

7.227 Remote Code Requirement

Some Model repositories require custom code execution.

Custom code increases risk.

The Registry shall identify:

- remote code requirement,

- trust status,

- sandbox need,

- and production restriction.

7.228 Model Sandbox

Untrusted or experimental Models should run in restricted environments where practical.

Sandbox controls may include:

- no network,

- limited file access,

- resource limits,

- and temporary storage.

7.229 Model Data Exfiltration Risk

Models may produce outputs containing sensitive input.

Output classification and review must account for this risk.

A summary does not automatically become safe for public use.

7.230 Prompt Injection Resilience

Models used for retrieval and tool execution should be evaluated for:

- instruction hierarchy,

- external-content handling,

- and tool boundary compliance.

Prompt injection resilience is one quality and security dimension.

7.231 Tool-Use Security

A Model with tool support may request actions beyond its role.

The Fabric shall enforce authority outside the Model.

Model compliance is helpful but not sufficient.

7.232 Model Output Validation

Outputs shall be validated according to Capability and Output Contracts.

Validation may include:

- schema,

- malware scanning,

- media integrity,

- code tests,

- factual grounding,

- or child-safety review.

Provider success is not acceptance.

7.233 Model Refusal

A Model may refuse a request.

Refusal may result from:

- Provider policy,

- safety system,

- unsupported capability,

- ambiguous prompt,

- or model defect.

Refusal shall be normalised and evidenced.

7.234 False Refusal

A benign eligible request may be incorrectly refused.

Repeated false refusals may reduce Model suitability for a Capability.

7.235 Unsafe Compliance

A Model may comply with a request that should have been blocked by Fabric policy.

Fabric enforcement must prevent the execution or side effect before Model willingness matters.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.236 Hallucination Profile

For language and multimodal Models, hallucination risk may be measured by Capability.

Hallucination is not one universal fixed Model property.

Grounded research may differ from creative generation.

7.237 Factuality Evidence

Factuality benchmarks should identify:

- domain,

- date,

- source access,

- and evaluation method.

A Model with strong general factuality may still require current web research.

7.238 Code Correctness Evidence

Code quality shall be measured through:

- tests,

- static analysis,

- type checking,

- security review,

- and architecture conformance.

Model reputation is insufficient.

7.239 Visual Consistency Evidence

For Familje-Stunden, visual Model evidence may include:

- Nova identity,

- Pling identity,

- proportion stability,

- colour consistency,

- clothing,

- expression,

- and multi-character interaction.

7.240 Audio Quality Evidence

Speech Models may be evaluated for:

- Swedish pronunciation,

- naturalness,

- emotional tone,

- pacing,

- artefacts,

- and identity consistency.

7.241 Child-Facing Model Suitability

Models used for child-facing content may require:

- stronger safety evaluation,

- visual artefact review,

- age-appropriate tone,

- and mandatory human acceptance.

A general production approval does not remove these requirements.

7.242 Model Registry Governance

Material Model Registry actions include:

- add Model,

- add Version,

- add Deployment,

- approve,

- restrict,

- deprecate,

- disable,

- retire,

- merge,

- split,

- and correct identity.

Each action shall be attributable.

7.243 Model Proposal

A Model Proposal should include:

- Model identity,

- Provider,

- intended Capabilities,

- use cases,

- licence,

- terms,

- privacy,

- cost,

- risks,

- and reason for addition.

7.244 Model Review

Review should evaluate:

- identity,

- Version stability,

- Capability support,

- licence,

- rights,

- privacy,

- security,

- cost,

- quality,

- operational maturity,

- and need.

7.245 Model Production Admission

Production admission should require:

- approved Model Version,

- eligible Deployment,

- conformant Adapter,

- valid Provider Account,

- security review,

- policy compatibility,

- cost handling,

- quality evidence,

- and operational monitoring.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.246 Model Re-Certification

Re-certification may be required after:

- Version update,

- hidden drift,

- Adapter change,

- runtime change,

- quantisation change,

- licence change,

- or material Provider terms change.

7.247 Model Administrative Separation

The Principal proposing a Model should not necessarily be the only Principal approving production use.

Higher-risk admission may require separation of duties.

7.248 Model Registry Access Control

Read and mutation access shall remain separate.

Many systems may discover approved Models.

Only authorised governance Principals may change lifecycle or production admission.

7.249 Model Registry Audit Trail

The Registry shall preserve:

- creation,

- Version addition,

- evidence updates,

- lifecycle transitions,

- Deployment changes,

- policy restrictions,

- and deprecation.

7.250 Model Registry Snapshot

An immutable Registry Snapshot may be created for:

- execution planning,

- release,

- audit,

- rollback,

- and Atlas Knowledge.

Executions may reference the Snapshot used.

7.251 Model Registry Cache

Caches may accelerate routing.

Caches shall include:

- source Version,

- generated time,

- expiry,

- and invalidation.

Critical disables should invalidate caches rapidly.

7.252 Model Registry Consistency

Control-plane changes may propagate asynchronously.

Security disables and rights restrictions should fail safely during propagation.

7.253 Model Registry Backup

The Registry and history shall be backed up.

Loss would damage:

- historical provenance,

- routing,

- quality evidence,

- and migration.

7.254 Model Registry Export

Exports may support:

- documentation,

- SDKs,

- testing,

- disaster recovery,

- and Atlas Knowledge.

Exports shall declare:

- source Snapshot,

- time,

- scope,

- and completeness.

7.255 Model Registry Import

Imports shall be validated and quarantined before activation.

External packages shall not gain production status automatically.

7.256 Model Registry Federation

Future Omnira deployments may federate Model metadata across:

- user nodes,

- tenant servers,

- Omnira-managed cloud,

- and local runtimes.

Federation shall preserve:

- canonical identity,

- local restrictions,

- Versions,

- and trust.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.257 Local Model Discovery Federation

A local node may report installed Models and capacity.

The platform shall not expose private local Models to other Tenants.

Local metadata visibility shall remain owner-controlled.

7.258 Provider Registry Relationship

The Provider Registry defines Providers and Provider Accounts.

The Model Registry defines Models, Versions and Deployments.

Provider Account state shall not be duplicated as Model identity.

7.259 Capability Registry Relationship

The Capability Registry defines canonical operations.

The Model Registry declares Version-specific support.

Capability meaning remains authoritative outside the Model Registry.

7.260 Adapter Registry Relationship

Adapter metadata defines how Models are invoked.

The Model Registry references compatible Adapters and Versions.

An Adapter change may invalidate support evidence.

7.261 Runtime Node Registry Relationship

Runtime Nodes define available hardware and trust boundaries.

Model Deployments reference compatible Nodes.

Node state determines operational availability.

7.262 Policy Engine Relationship

Policies may target:

- Model,

- Model Family,

- Model Version,

- Deployment,

- ownership class,

- Provider,

- region,

- or Capability.

Policy evaluation occurs at execution time.

7.263 Budget System Relationship

Cost estimates and usage records reference:

- Model Deployment,

- Provider Account,

- and pricing Version.

The Model Registry provides identity and pricing references.

It is not the accounting ledger.

7.264 Quality System Relationship

Benchmarks and Evaluations reference exact Model Versions and Deployments.

The Model Registry exposes evidence for routing.

7.265 Memory Relationship

Governed memory may store Model learnings.

The Model Registry shall not itself become the permanent memory system for every execution observation.

It may reference accepted learning.

7.266 Intelligence Graph Relationship

The Graph may represent:

- Model Families,

- Versions,

- Deployments,

- Capabilities,

- Providers,

- Executions,

- benchmarks,

- incidents,

- and deprecations.

The Registry remains authoritative for model identity.

7.267 Model Registry and Atlas

Atlas may use the Registry to understand:

- eligible capability classes,

- broad trade-offs,

- privacy options,

- and Model restrictions.

Atlas should not need to hard-code Provider Model names.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.268 Model Registry and Managers

Managers may specify:

- quality,

- cost,

- privacy,

- or deadline requirements.

They should not own Model metadata or credentials.

7.269 Model Registry and Agents

Agent definitions may specify:

- required Capabilities,

- preferred routing profile,

- and Model restrictions.

Agents should not define themselves through one Model.

7.270 Model Registry and Workflows

Workflow Steps should reference Capabilities.

They may pin Model Versions only when justified.

The Registry supports validation and migration.

7.271 Model Registry and Provider Routers

If a Provider performs hidden Model routing, the Registry shall represent the resource honestly as routed and partially opaque.

Omnira shall not claim exact Model control it does not possess.

7.272 Model Registry Success Criteria

The Model Registry succeeds when:

- historical Executions can identify their Model resource,

- Agents survive Model replacement,

- Capabilities map to several eligible Models,

- local and cloud Models are represented consistently,

- quality remains task-specific,

- Model updates are detectable,

- deprecation is manageable,

- and routing does not depend on hard-coded Provider names.

7.273 Model Registry Failure Conditions

The Registry is non-conformant when:

- Model and Agent identity are merged,

- Provider aliases are treated as fixed Versions,

- Deployments are omitted,

- local Models lack provenance,

- Capability support is unverified but presented as production-ready,

- Version history is overwritten,

- one global quality score drives all routing,

- or retired Models disappear from historical evidence.

7.274 Stage 1 Model Registry Objective

Stage 1 shall establish the minimum trustworthy Model Registry required for provider-independent routing.

The objective is not to catalogue every Model in the market.

Stage 1 shall prove:

- stable Model identity,

- Version identity,

- Capability mapping,

- Deployment separation,

- lifecycle,

- quality evidence,

- and historical traceability.

7.275 Stage 1 Minimum Model Objects

Stage 1 should implement or represent:

- Model,

- Model Family,

- Model Version,

- Model Alias,

- Model Deployment,

- Model Capability Declaration,

- Model Lifecycle,

- Model Quality Evidence,

- Model Limit Profile,

- and Model Provenance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.276 Stage 1 Initial Model Categories

Stage 1 should include representative Models for:

- local text or reasoning,

- external text or reasoning,

- embeddings,

- image generation,

- speech synthesis,

- and video or multimodal production.

The precise Providers may change during implementation.

7.277 Stage 1 Local Model Support

Stage 1 should support a local runtime such as:

- Ollama,

- NVIDIA NIM,

- or another approved runtime.

The implementation shall represent:

- Model Version,

- Node,

- Runtime,

- hardware,

- privacy,

- and health.

7.278 Stage 1 External Text Models

Stage 1 should include at least two external text or reasoning Provider paths.

The purpose is to prove:

- selection,

- fallback,

- cost,

- and Model independence.

It is not to maximise provider count.

7.279 Stage 1 Embedding Model

Stage 1 should register at least one Embedding Model and preserve:

- dimensions,

- language support,

- context limit,

- and index compatibility.

7.280 Stage 1 Voice Model

Stage 1 should represent at least one speech synthesis Model or Provider-managed voice resource.

Voice identity and consent shall remain separate objects.

7.281 Stage 1 Image Model

Stage 1 should represent at least one image-generation or editing Model path.

The Registry shall preserve:

- Model or routed resource identity,

- supported Capabilities,

- rights,

- and quality evidence.

7.282 Stage 1 Video Model

Stage 1 may represent video generation through:

- exact Model Version where exposed,

- or Provider-routed resource where Model identity remains opaque.

The system must be truthful about the distinction.

7.283 Stage 1 Registry Entry Fields

Stage 1 Model records should include at least:

- modelId,

- Model Family,

- canonical name,

- Provider origin,

- Model Type,

- modality,

- ownership class,

- licence reference,

- lifecycle,

- aliases,

- and provenance.

7.284 Stage 1 Version Fields

Stage 1 Model Version records should include at least:

- modelVersionId,

- modelId,

- provider identifier,

- release or observation date,

- Capability Declarations,

- context limits,

- output limits,

- Feature support,

- quality evidence,

- cost reference,

- lifecycle,

- and known limitations.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.285 Stage 1 Deployment Fields

Stage 1 Deployments should include:

- deploymentId,

- Model Version,

- Provider,

- Provider Account,

- Connection,

- environment,

- region or node,

- health,

- privacy profile,

- pricing reference,

- and Adapter.

7.286 Stage 1 Model Registry API

Stage 1 should support:

- get Model,

- get Model Version,

- list active Versions,

- list Deployments,

- query by Capability,

- inspect limits,

- inspect lifecycle,

- and resolve Provider alias.

7.287 Stage 1 Selection Support

The Registry shall provide routing with:

- exact Version identity,

- Capability support,

- limits,

- health reference,

- cost reference,

- and quality evidence.

Routing remains responsible for final Selection Decision.

7.288 Stage 1 Alias Handling

Stage 1 shall distinguish:

- fixed Version identifier,

- moving Provider alias,

- and unknown routed resource.

Executions shall preserve the actual identifier used.

7.289 Stage 1 Historical Traceability

Historical Executions must remain interpretable after:

- deprecation,

- alias change,

- Provider retirement,

- or local Model removal.

7.290 Stage 1 Acceptance Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Model remains distinct from Provider.

2. Model remains distinct from Provider Account.

3. Model remains distinct from Deployment.

4. Model remains distinct from Agent.

5. Model Version remains distinct from moving alias.

6. Unknown Version is represented explicitly.

7. One Model Version may support several Capabilities.

8. One Capability may be supported by several Model Versions.

9. Partial support is not treated as full support.

10. Model support is Version-specific.

11. Deployment health does not redefine Model identity.

12. Local and external Deployments use the same canonical contract.

13. Deprecated Versions remain historically resolvable.

14. Retired Models cannot be selected.

15. Pinned aliases preserve drift risk.

16. Capability constraints affect eligibility.

17. Provider Account changes do not change Model identity.

18. Cost belongs to Deployment and pricing context.

19. Quality evidence remains Capability-specific.

20. Agent identity survives Model substitution.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 7.294 Applied Example — Nova and Pling Video Model Selection
text:
7.291 Stage 1 Security Tests

Representative security tests should include:

1. Raw credentials do not appear in Model records.

2. Project-specific Models remain scoped.

3. Untrusted local artefacts cannot enter production without admission.

4. Remote custom code requirement is visible.

5. Local Model discovery does not expose private node content across Tenants.

6. Model discovery does not grant execution authority.

7. External Model output remains subject to validation.

8. Tool-capable Models cannot bypass tool permissions.

9. Unknown privacy profile blocks protected routing.

10. Disabled Model cache entries are invalidated.

7.292 Stage 1 Quality Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Benchmark references exact Model Version.

2. Benchmark references Capability Version.

3. Quality evidence references Deployment where relevant.

4. Model Family reputation does not substitute for Version evidence.

5. External benchmark and internal benchmark remain separate.

6. Project-specific quality learning remains Project-scoped.

7. Model update invalidates stale evidence where required.

8. Rejected output affects suitability evidence.

9. Evaluator identity is recorded.

10. Unknown quality does not become high quality by default.

7.293 Stage 1 Reliability Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Provider alias change is detected or represented as uncertain.

2. Deployment outage marks availability without retiring the Model.

3. Fallback selects another eligible Deployment.

4. Local Model load failure produces truthful state.

5. Provider timeout may produce unknown outcome.

6. Model substitution is recorded.

7. Rate limits affect scheduling.

8. Quota exhaustion affects account eligibility.

9. Adapter change triggers conformance review.

10. Historical receipt preserves original Model identifier.

7.294 Applied Example — Nova and Pling Video Model Selection

A future Familje-Stunden scene request may require:

Capability

video.image_to_video.

Mandatory Features

- approved image reference,

- multiple-character support,

- 16:9 output,

- child-safe production,

- commercial-use eligibility,

- and asynchronous job tracking.

Quality Dimensions

- Nova identity,

- Pling identity,

- facial stability,

- body proportion,

- colour consistency,

- motion quality,

- and artefact absence.

The Registry may expose several Resource Candidates:

Candidate A

A lower-cost Model Version supporting image-to-video but weak multi-character evidence.

Candidate B

A premium Model Version with stronger character-consistency evidence.

Candidate C

A Provider-managed routed resource whose exact underlying Model is unknown.

Candidate D

A local video Model that cannot satisfy the required quality floor.

The Model Registry provides:

- identity,

- Version,

- Features,

- limits,

- quality evidence,

- and Deployment relationships.

Routing determines which eligible Candidate should be used.

For a scene containing only a background pan, Candidate A may be sufficient.

For a scene with Nova and Pling interacting, Candidate B may be justified.

The Project does not permanently hard-code either Model.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 7.295 Applied Example — The Prompt Research Models
text:
7.295 Applied Example — The Prompt Research Models

A The Prompt research workflow may use:

- one low-cost Model for source triage,

- one stronger reasoning Model for synthesis,

- one grounding-capable resource for current facts,

- and one evaluator for factual support.

The Model Registry keeps these roles separate.

A visually impressive avatar Model does not become the research Model.

A fluent reasoning Model does not become the source of current facts without verified retrieval.

7.296 Applied Example — GainPilot Content Models

A GainPilot reel may use:

- local text Model for draft,

- low-cost image Model,

- speech Model,

- and local media conversion tools.

The Registry allows the workflow to select inexpensive Models because the Quality Contract differs from Nova and Pling animation.

If one Model’s Swedish tone repeatedly performs poorly, that evidence affects GainPilot routing without creating a universal ban.

7.297 Applied Example — Omnira Code Models

An Omnira code request may compare Models for:

- repository analysis,

- TypeScript generation,

- test generation,

- architecture conformance,

- and debugging.

A Model may be strong at isolated code completion but weak at large-repository reasoning.

The Registry shall preserve Capability-specific evidence.

Code Model output remains subject to:

- tests,

- repository scope,

- and software-delivery authority.

7.298 Applied Example — Local Confidential Model

A Local Only document request may use:

- local Model Version,

- local Deployment,

- Runtime Node,

- private Adapter,

- and local Embedding Model.

The Registry shall preserve:

- artefact checksum,

- Runtime Version,

- quantisation,

- hardware,

- and privacy boundary.

If the local Model cannot satisfy the Quality Contract, the request stops or seeks revised authority.

It does not silently fall back to an external Model.

7.299 Applied Example — Provider-Routed OpenArt Resource

A multimodal Provider may expose several internal Models through one product or router.

When the exact Model can be selected and observed, the Registry should record:

- Model Version,

- Deployment,

- and Adapter mapping.

When the Provider chooses the underlying Model automatically, the Registry should record:

- Provider-routed Resource,

- declared candidate Models where known,

- routing opacity,

- cost,

- quality evidence,

- and reproducibility limitations.

Omnira must not claim exact Model control when it does not possess it.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 7.301 Anti-Pattern — Model Name in Business Logic
7.306 Anti-Pattern — Model Price as Permanent Property
7.309 Anti-Pattern — Provider Marketing Equals Capability Evidence
text:
7.300 Applied Example — ElevenLabs Voice Resource

A speech workflow may use a Provider-managed speech Model and a separate approved Voice Asset.

The Registry shall distinguish:

- speech Model,

- Provider Account,

- Voice identity,

- Consent Record,

- pronunciation settings,

- and output Asset.

The Voice is not the Model.

The Model is not the Agent.

The Provider Account is not the Project owner.

7.301 Anti-Pattern — Model Name in Business Logic

Project code must not contain permanent logic such as:

If project is Familje-Stunden, always use Model X.

Project requirements should become:

- Capability,

- Quality Contract,

- routing profile,

- and provider constraints.

Model selection remains a Fabric decision unless explicitly pinned.

7.302 Anti-Pattern — Model Equals Agent

Atlas, Arnold or another Agent must not be stored as a Model reference.

Agent identity survives Model changes.

7.303 Anti-Pattern — Provider Alias Equals Version

A mutable alias must not be recorded as a fixed Model Version.

Historical execution must preserve uncertainty.

7.304 Anti-Pattern — One Global Best Model

No universal best-Model field shall drive all tasks.

Model suitability depends on:

- Capability,

- quality,

- Project,

- cost,

- privacy,

- latency,

- and current evidence.

7.305 Anti-Pattern — Context Window as Quality

A larger context window must not be treated as proof of stronger reasoning or retrieval.

Practical quality requires evidence.

7.306 Anti-Pattern — Model Price as Permanent Property

Pricing changes by:

- Provider,

- Account,

- region,

- and date.

The abstract Model must not contain one permanent universal price.

7.307 Anti-Pattern — Local Equals Free

Local Models consume:

- hardware,

- energy,

- storage,

- maintenance,

- and time.

The Fabric may report low marginal cost without claiming zero total cost.

7.308 Anti-Pattern — Open Equals Safe

Open-weight or open-source Models may still have:

- licence restrictions,

- unsafe artefacts,

- supply-chain risk,

- or weak safety.

Open status does not remove governance.

7.309 Anti-Pattern — Provider Marketing Equals Capability Evidence

Marketing claims may initiate testing.

They do not establish verified production support.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.310 Anti-Pattern — Silent Model Substitution

Material substitution must be recorded and evaluated.

A Provider-managed silent switch reduces reproducibility confidence.

7.311 Anti-Pattern — Rewriting Historical Version

A Model Version used in past Executions must not be edited to represent current behaviour.

Create new Version or drift record.

7.312 Anti-Pattern — Deployment Hidden Inside Model

Region, endpoint, Account, local node and configuration belong to Deployment.

Collapsing them into Model identity destroys operational truth.

7.313 Anti-Pattern — Model Discovery Grants Access

A discovered Model must not become active merely because an API listed it.

Production admission remains required.

7.314 Anti-Pattern — Agent Stores Model Credential

Agents shall receive capability access.

They shall not own raw Provider credentials.

7.315 Anti-Pattern — Evaluation by Reputation

A famous or expensive Model is not automatically suitable.

Task-specific evidence remains required.

7.316 Anti-Pattern — Model Retirement Deletes Evidence

Retirement blocks new use.

It must not erase:

- Executions,

- receipts,

- costs,

- benchmarks,

- or provenance.

7.317 Anti-Pattern — Hidden Routed Resource

Provider routers must be represented as routed resources.

They must not be falsely labelled as one fixed Model.

7.318 Anti-Pattern — Unbounded Local Installation

Agents must not install large local Models automatically without approval for:

- storage,

- licence,

- bandwidth,

- and compute.

7.319 Anti-Pattern — Model Output as Memory

Model output shall not become governed memory merely because it was generated.

Memory admission remains separate.

7.320 Future Model Registry Evolution

Future versions may support:

- automated Model-card ingestion,

- cryptographic artefact attestation,

- continuous drift detection,

- dynamic benchmark scheduling,

- federated local Model discovery,

- model marketplace packages,

- automatic licence monitoring,

- energy-aware routing,

- carbon-aware placement,

- model distillation governance,

- user-owned fine-tuning,

- and organisation-level Model portfolios.

Future evolution must preserve:

- canonical identity,

- Version traceability,

- Agent independence,

- Capability-first routing,

- and user authority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.321 Canonical Model Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Model contract:

1. A Model SHALL be represented as an intelligence execution resource.

2. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Provider.

3. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Provider Account.

4. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Model Deployment.

5. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Agent.

6. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Capability.

7. A Model SHALL remain distinct from Adapter and endpoint.

8. Every persistent Model SHALL have stable canonical identity.

9. Every materially distinct Model Version SHALL have stable Version identity.

10. Provider aliases SHALL remain separate from Model Versions.

11. Moving aliases SHALL be represented as mutable.

12. Unknown Model Version SHALL remain an explicit valid state.

13. Model Versions SHALL declare supported Capabilities and Features.

14. Claimed, observed, verified, partial and unknown support SHALL remain distinct.

15. Model Versions SHALL declare relevant limits.

16. Input and output modalities SHALL remain explicit.

17. Native and composed Capability support SHALL remain distinct.

18. Model quality SHALL remain Capability-specific.

19. Model pricing SHALL remain Deployment-, Account- and time-aware.

20. Model privacy SHALL remain Deployment- and Provider-contextual.

21. Model lifecycle SHALL be explicit and versioned.

22. Deprecated and retired Models SHALL remain historically interpretable.

23. Model substitution SHALL be evidenced.

24. Provider-routed resources SHALL be represented honestly.

25. Local and external Models SHALL use one canonical identity framework.

26. Self-hosted artefacts SHOULD preserve checksums and lineage.

27. Fine-tuned, distilled and quantised Models SHALL preserve lineage.

28. Model discovery SHALL NOT create production admission.

29. Model availability SHALL remain request- and Deployment-specific.

30. Agent identity SHALL survive Model replacement.

7.322 Canonical Model Deployment Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Model Deployment contract:

1. Every selectable Model execution path SHALL reference a Deployment or equivalent routed resource.

2. A Deployment SHALL identify Model Version where known.

3. A Deployment SHALL identify Provider and Provider Account where applicable.

4. A Deployment SHALL identify Connection or Runtime.

5. A Deployment SHALL identify environment and region or Runtime Node.

6. A Deployment SHALL declare privacy and retention context.

7. A Deployment SHALL declare health and freshness.

8. A Deployment SHALL declare capacity and known limits.

9. A Deployment SHALL reference pricing context.

10. Deployment configuration affecting behaviour SHALL be versioned.

11. Local Deployment SHALL identify artefact, Runtime and hardware where applicable.

12. Deployment health SHALL NOT redefine Model identity.

13. Deployment outage SHALL NOT automatically retire the Model.

14. Deployment equivalence SHALL NOT be assumed.

15. Provider-managed routing opacity SHALL remain visible.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.323 Canonical Model Registry Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Model Registry contract:

1. The Model Registry SHALL be the authoritative catalogue of known Model identities and Versions.

2. The Registry SHALL preserve Model Families, Models, Versions, aliases and Deployments.

3. The Registry SHALL preserve historical lifecycle.

4. The Registry SHALL reference canonical Capability Versions.

5. The Registry SHALL preserve Capability support evidence.

6. The Registry SHALL preserve known limits and Features.

7. The Registry SHALL preserve licence and terms references.

8. The Registry SHALL preserve quality evidence and limitations.

9. The Registry SHALL support local, managed and external Deployments.

10. The Registry SHALL support governed discovery.

11. Registry discovery SHALL NOT grant execution authority.

12. Registry mutation SHALL require explicit governance authority.

13. Registry changes SHALL preserve provenance.

14. Registry projections and caches SHALL declare freshness.

15. Historical Model Versions SHALL remain resolvable after retirement.

16. Provider aliases SHALL NOT overwrite Version identity.

17. Model records SHALL NOT contain raw credentials.

18. The Registry SHALL support Stage-based production admission.

19. The Registry SHALL support Model drift and Incident states.

20. The Registry SHALL remain suitable for human and machine consumers.

7.324 Model Registry Invariants

The following invariants shall remain true:

- No Model becomes an Agent identity.

- No Provider alias becomes unquestioned Version truth.

- No Deployment becomes the abstract Model.

- No Model gains authority by being available.

- No quality score becomes universal across Capabilities.

- No local Model is treated as automatically free or safe.

- No Provider claim becomes verified support without evidence.

- No moving alias rewrites historical execution meaning.

- No Model substitution occurs without evidence.

- No deprecated Model disappears from history.

- No hidden Provider router is described as a fixed Model.

- No model output becomes canonical memory automatically.

- No Model installation bypasses storage, licence and security authority.

- No Capability Request selects a Model before policy and compatibility.

- No Model Registry record exposes raw credentials.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
7.325 Closing Statement

The Model Registry gives Omnira a stable understanding of the intelligence resources available beneath the Intelligence Fabric.

It allows the platform to distinguish:

- Provider from Model,

- Model from Version,

- Version from Alias,

- Model from Deployment,

- Deployment from Account,

- Model from Agent,

- and Capability from implementation.

This distinction is essential.

Providers will rename Models.

Aliases will move.

Prices will change.

Deployments will fail.

Local runtimes will differ.

Open Models will be quantised.

Provider routers will hide implementation.

Quality will vary by task.

New Models will appear faster than application code can safely absorb them.

The Model Registry ensures that this change occurs at the resource layer rather than inside every Agent, Project and Workflow.

For Familje-Stunden, it allows Omnira to compare video Models according to actual Nova and Pling character consistency instead of provider popularity.

For The Prompt, it allows research, editorial reasoning, avatar production and factual evaluation to use different specialised Models.

For GainPilot, it allows inexpensive local or external Models to handle routine content while stronger Models remain available for tasks that justify them.

For Omnira itself, it allows code, reasoning, retrieval, voice, image, video and future modalities to evolve without giving one vendor ownership of the platform.

The Capability Registry defines what must be done.

The Model Registry defines which intelligence resources may be capable of doing it.

The Provider Registry defines who supplies access.

The Deployment defines where and how execution occurs.

The Adapter translates the request.

Policy determines what is permitted.

Routing selects the eligible path.

Evidence records what actually happened.

The Model is powerful.

It is still only a resource.

Omnira retains identity.

The user retains direction.

The Fabric retains governance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical architecture, governance model, lifecycle, contracts and operational responsibilities of the Omnira Intelligence Fabric Provider Registry.

It establishes:

- what a Provider represents within Omnira,

- how Providers differ from Provider Accounts, Models, Deployments, Connections, Adapters and credentials,

- how external, local, self-hosted, user-managed and Omnira-managed providers are represented,

- how provider identity and service boundaries are established,

- how provider accounts, workspaces, subscriptions and billing relationships are separated,

- how trust, privacy, rights, regional processing and operational maturity are recorded,

- how provider capability claims are evaluated,

- how provider health, availability, quotas and incidents are managed,

- how provider onboarding, restriction, deprecation and removal occur,

- how commercial relationships remain subordinate to user value,

- and how Stage 1 shall implement a bounded but extensible Provider Registry.

The Provider Registry is a foundational Intelligence Fabric control-plane component.

It is the authoritative catalogue of organisations, platforms, services and governed resource suppliers known to Omnira.

A Provider Registry entry does not prove that:

- a usable Provider Account exists,

- credentials are connected,

- a requested Capability is supported,

- a Model is eligible,

- current capacity is available,

- current pricing is known,

- current terms are acceptable,

- or the Provider may process the request’s data.

Those conditions must be evaluated through the appropriate canonical objects and runtime evidence.

This chapter is normative after formal approval.

Implementation and operational conformance must be verified separately.

8.2 Purpose of the Provider Registry

The Intelligence Fabric shall interact with many forms of intelligence and tool suppliers.

These may include:

- commercial AI companies,

- cloud platforms,

- model-hosting services,

- creative-production platforms,

- voice providers,

- search providers,

- self-hosted runtimes,

- local execution environments,

- user-controlled servers,

- Omnira-managed infrastructure,

- MCP servers,

- external agent platforms,

- human-assisted services,

- and future intelligence marketplaces.

Without a canonical Provider Registry, Omnira would risk representing provider relationships through:

- scattered environment variables,

- hard-coded endpoint names,

- undocumented subscriptions,

- agent-specific credentials,

- project-specific integrations,

- provider dashboards,

- and unverified assumptions.

The Provider Registry shall provide one governed representation of:

- who supplies a resource,

- under what operational relationship,

- through which accounts and connections,

- with which terms and restrictions,

- for which scopes,

- and under which lifecycle state.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.3 Provider as a Canonical Entity

A Provider is a canonical entity representing an organisation, platform, runtime operator or bounded service source that supplies one or more resources to the Intelligence Fabric.

A Provider may supply:

- Models,

- Tools,

- External Agent Resources,

- search services,

- storage services,

- media-generation systems,

- local runtimes,

- self-hosted capabilities,

- or human-assisted execution.

A Provider shall have stable identity independent of:

- one account,

- one API key,

- one Model,

- one endpoint,

- one billing plan,

- one project,

- or one user.

The Provider represents the supplier relationship.

Operational access is represented through Provider Accounts, Connections, Deployments and credentials.

8.4 Provider Is Not Model

A Provider may expose many Models.

A Model may be available through several Providers.

The Provider Registry shall not use Model names as Provider identities.

For example:

Provider

A model-hosting platform.

Model

A specific language or image Model Version.

Provider Account

The user’s connected account at that platform.

Model Deployment

The specific endpoint or operational access path through which the Model is executed.

These objects remain distinct.

8.5 Provider Is Not Provider Account

A Provider represents the supplier.

A Provider Account represents a specific connected operational relationship with that supplier.

One Provider may have:

- personal account,

- project account,

- business account,

- sandbox account,

- production account,

- Omnira-managed account,

- and several future customer-owned accounts.

Each account may differ in:

- credentials,

- credits,

- billing,

- region,

- assets,

- terms,

- privacy,

- rate limits,

- and permissions.

The Provider Registry shall preserve the Provider independently from every account.

8.6 Provider Is Not Connection

A Connection represents the technical path through which Omnira communicates with a Provider or Provider Account.

Connection types may include:

- API,

- MCP,

- OAuth,

- webhook,

- queue,

- command-line runtime,

- local socket,

- file exchange,

- or human-assisted handoff.

A Provider may have several Connections.

A Connection may fail without changing Provider identity.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.7 Provider Is Not Adapter

An Adapter translates between Omnira’s canonical contracts and Provider-specific behaviour.

A Provider may require:

- several Adapters,

- one Adapter per protocol,

- one Adapter per service family,

- or one human-assisted Adapter.

The Provider Registry identifies the supplier.

The Adapter Registry defines translation and execution behaviour.

8.8 Provider Is Not Credential

A credential authorises access to a Provider Account or Connection.

Credentials may include:

- API key,

- OAuth token,

- service token,

- certificate,

- signed request key,

- local runtime permission,

- or session relationship.

Credentials shall never become Provider identity.

The Provider Registry shall store only credential references or relationship metadata where necessary.

Raw secrets belong in an approved credential or secret-management service.

8.9 Provider Is Not Agent

A Provider may offer agent-like products.

Those products remain external Provider resources unless they are explicitly admitted into Omnira’s Agent architecture.

A Provider shall not become:

- Atlas,

- a Manager,

- Arnold,

- or another Omnira Agent identity.

Provider-hosted agents remain bounded external resources.

8.10 Provider Is Not Capability

A Capability defines what Omnira needs performed.

A Provider may claim or prove support for several Capabilities.

One Capability may be supported by several Providers.

The Provider Registry shall reference canonical Capabilities rather than inventing Provider-specific business logic.

8.11 Provider Is Not Project

A Project may use a Provider.

The Provider does not become part of that Project’s identity.

The same Provider may serve:

- Familje-Stunden,

- The Prompt,

- GainPilot,

- Omnira,

- and future customer Projects

through separate Provider Accounts, policies and budgets.

Shared Provider use must not collapse Project isolation.

8.12 Provider Identity

Every Provider shall have a stable canonical identifier.

The identifier shall remain independent of:

- website URL,

- current brand name,

- account email,

- endpoint,

- Provider Account,

- or Model catalogue.

The Provider may also have:

- legal name,

- trading name,

- former names,

- aliases,

- domains,

- external identifiers,

- and parent-company relationships.

Canonical identity must remain stable across ordinary rebranding.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.13 Provider Naming

Provider display names should be recognisable to users.

Canonical identity shall remain separate from display name.

A Provider rename should normally update:

- display name,

- aliases,

- branding metadata,

- and documentation

without replacing the canonical Provider ID.

A legal entity change may require a new Provider or explicit successor relationship.

8.14 Provider Legal Entity

Where relevant, the Registry should record the legal entity supplying the service.

This may include:

- legal name,

- jurisdiction,

- registered address reference,

- contracting entity,

- and tax or billing entity.

The service brand and legal contracting entity may differ.

This distinction matters for:

- contracts,

- privacy,

- invoices,

- data processing,

- and disputes.

8.15 Provider Parent Relationship

A Provider may belong to a parent organisation.

Parent relationships may include:

- subsidiary of,

- operated by,

- acquired by,

- reseller of,

- infrastructure hosted by,

- or white-labelled from.

Relationships shall preserve:

- effective date,

- source,

- and impact.

A parent relationship does not automatically merge Provider identities.

8.16 Provider Successor Relationship

When one Provider replaces another through:

- merger,

- acquisition,

- service migration,

- or reorganisation,

the Registry shall preserve a successor relationship.

Historical Executions must continue to reference the original Provider identity used at the time.

8.17 Provider Service Family

A Provider may expose several Service Families.

Examples include:

- language Models,

- image generation,

- video generation,

- voice,

- search,

- embeddings,

- storage,

- external agents,

- or developer tools.

Service Families assist organisation.

They shall not replace canonical Capabilities.

8.18 Provider Product

A Provider Product is a commercial or technical offering.

Products may include:

- subscription plan,

- API platform,

- creative studio,

- enterprise workspace,

- model-hosting service,

- MCP package,

- or managed agent.

Products can change more frequently than Provider identity.

They should be represented separately when product differences materially affect:

- access,

- terms,

- pricing,

- capabilities,

- or privacy.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.19 Provider Type

The Registry shall classify Providers by Provider Type.

Types may include:

- external commercial cloud,

- external specialised AI service,

- model-hosting platform,

- tool platform,

- local runtime provider,

- self-hosted platform,

- user-managed service,

- Omnira-managed service,

- infrastructure provider,

- human-assisted provider,

- marketplace,

- or simulation provider.

A Provider may have several relevant types.

Provider Type informs trust and placement but does not determine eligibility alone.

8.20 External Cloud Provider

An External Cloud Provider executes work on infrastructure outside the user’s and Omnira’s direct control.

It may offer:

- APIs,

- hosted Models,

- storage,

- processing,

- and managed agent systems.

External Providers remain outside Omnira’s trusted core.

They require explicit policy, account and data-placement evaluation.

8.21 Specialised AI Provider

A Specialised AI Provider focuses on one or several modalities or production areas.

Examples may include:

- voice,

- video,

- image,

- music,

- avatar,

- search,

- or document processing.

Specialisation may create strong Capability quality.

It may also create:

- narrow account terms,

- unique credit systems,

- limited fallback,

- and Provider lock-in.

The Registry shall preserve both strengths and restrictions.

8.22 Model-Hosting Provider

A Model-Hosting Provider exposes Models that may originate from:

- the Provider,

- third-party creators,

- open-weight communities,

- or customer deployments.

The Registry shall distinguish:

- Provider,

- Model creator,

- Model licence,

- hosted Deployment,

- and Provider terms.

8.23 Local Runtime Provider

A Local Runtime Provider supplies software that enables Models or Tools to run on user-controlled infrastructure.

Examples may include:

- local language-model runtime,

- inference server,

- media-processing runtime,

- or containerised execution system.

The Provider may supply runtime software without receiving user data externally.

The Deployment and Node determine the actual trust boundary.

8.24 Self-Hosted Provider

A Self-Hosted Provider represents a service deployed on infrastructure controlled by:

- user,

- Tenant,

- Omnira,

- or customer organisation.

The software supplier and infrastructure operator may differ.

The Registry shall distinguish:

- software Provider,

- deployment operator,

- Runtime Node,

- and data custodian.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.25 User-Managed Provider

A User-Managed Provider is operated or contracted directly by the user.

Examples include:

- personal AI subscription,

- personal cloud account,

- local compute,

- or private server.

User management does not remove Fabric governance.

The Provider Account remains scoped and cost-attributed.

8.26 Omnira-Managed Provider

An Omnira-Managed Provider relationship uses infrastructure, credits or accounts controlled by Omnira.

It may support:

- bundled services,

- shared capacity,

- managed routing,

- or future customer plans.

Omnira-managed access shall still preserve:

- Tenant attribution,

- Project attribution,

- account isolation,

- privacy,

- terms,

- cost,

- and user authority.

8.27 Human-Assisted Provider

A Human-Assisted Provider requires a person to perform a material Provider operation.

Examples include:

- using a Provider web interface,

- uploading approved references,

- selecting generation settings,

- downloading output,

- or confirming billing.

The Registry shall classify integration maturity honestly.

Human-assisted support is valid.

It is not equivalent to a fully automated API integration.

8.28 Simulation Provider

A Simulation Provider exists for:

- tests,

- routing simulation,

- cost forecasting,

- failure injection,

- or development.

It shall never be represented as production execution.

Simulation Provider outputs and receipts must be explicitly marked.

8.29 Provider Trust Boundary

Every external Provider shall be treated as outside Omnira’s trusted core unless a more specific internal relationship has been established.

Provider approval does not imply unrestricted trust.

The Fabric shall control:

- what data is sent,

- what action is requested,

- which account is used,

- what cost is allowed,

- how output is validated,

- and how evidence is preserved.

The Provider controls its own infrastructure and internal behaviour.

This boundary must remain explicit.

8.30 Provider Trust Level

The Registry may assign Trust Levels such as:

- untrusted,

- discovered,

- experimental,

- reviewed,

- production approved,

- restricted production,

- strategic approved,

- suspended,

- or retired.

Trust Level shall be:

- evidence-based,

- scoped,

- and time-aware.

A trusted Provider may still be ineligible for a specific request.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.31 Provider Trust Evidence

Trust evidence may include:

- security documentation,

- privacy terms,

- contractual commitments,

- operational history,

- incident response,

- audit reports,

- conformance tests,

- Provider reputation,

- and direct experience.

Trust evidence must preserve:

- source,

- date,

- scope,

- and limitations.

8.32 Provider Risk Classification

Provider Risk may consider:

- data handling,

- operational opacity,

- jurisdiction,

- security maturity,

- financial stability,

- rights uncertainty,

- account controls,

- destructive tools,

- and service dependency.

Risk may be classified as:

- minimal,

- low,

- moderate,

- high,

- critical,

- or unknown.

Unknown risk must not default to low.

8.33 Provider Criticality

Provider Criticality describes how strongly Omnira depends on the Provider.

A Provider may be:

- optional,

- useful,

- important,

- critical,

- or single-source.

Criticality affects:

- monitoring,

- fallback,

- contract review,

- incident planning,

- and migration.

8.34 Single-Source Provider

A Single-Source Provider supplies a Capability for which no approved equivalent currently exists.

Single-source dependence may be acceptable when explicit.

It shall require:

- dependency record,

- impact analysis,

- contingency plan,

- data-export plan,

- and regular review.

8.35 Provider Lock-In Profile

The Registry may record lock-in factors such as:

- proprietary asset format,

- Provider-hosted memory,

- irreversible project structure,

- unique reference system,

- non-exportable voices,

- non-transferable credits,

- proprietary workflow,

- or restricted API access.

Lock-in shall be visible rather than accidental.

8.36 Provider Exit Profile

A Provider Exit Profile may define:

- export support,

- asset download,

- metadata portability,

- account deletion,

- credential revocation,

- data deletion,

- workflow migration,

- and replacement options.

Exit readiness is part of long-term governance.

8.37 Provider Operational Maturity

Provider maturity may include:

- experimental,

- preview,

- beta,

- generally available,

- enterprise,

- legacy,

- or unknown.

Provider labels are evidence.

Omnira shall evaluate actual operational maturity separately.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.38 Provider Integration Maturity

Integration maturity describes Omnira’s relationship with the Provider.

Canonical states may include:

- discovered,

- researched,

- manual external,

- human-assisted,

- experimental API,

- experimental MCP,

- partially automated,

- production API,

- production MCP,

- local production,

- restricted production,

- deprecated,

- and disconnected.

Integration maturity shall be truthful.

8.39 Provider Lifecycle

Canonical Provider lifecycle states may include:

- proposed,

- discovered,

- under review,

- experimental,

- approved,

- active,

- restricted,

- degraded,

- suspended,

- deprecated,

- disconnected,

- retired,

- and archived.

Lifecycle state is distinct from current health.

8.40 Proposed Provider

Proposed means the Provider is being considered for future use.

The Registry may contain incomplete information.

No production use is permitted.

8.41 Discovered Provider

Discovered means the Provider was identified through:

- user suggestion,

- web research,

- API metadata,

- installed connector,

- repository package,

- or existing account.

Discovery does not imply approval.

8.42 Provider Under Review

Under Review means governance is evaluating:

- capabilities,

- terms,

- privacy,

- security,

- rights,

- cost,

- integration,

- and operational need.

Testing may occur in a restricted environment.

8.43 Experimental Provider

Experimental means the Provider may be used in bounded tests.

Experimental use should normally require:

- sandbox or development environment,

- non-sensitive data,

- limited budget,

- no automatic publication,

- and enhanced review.

8.44 Approved Provider

Approved means the Provider may be used for defined scopes and service classes.

Approval shall identify:

- permitted Tenants,

- Projects,

- data classes,

- Capabilities,

- environments,

- and restrictions.

Approved does not mean a usable Provider Account currently exists.

8.45 Active Provider

Active means at least one production-admitted Provider Account and Connection exists for an approved scope.

Active state does not imply every Capability or account is available.

8.46 Restricted Provider

Restricted means use is permitted only under additional conditions.

Restrictions may include:

- Public data only,

- selected Projects,

- selected Capabilities,

- low spending limit,

- human review,

- manual operation,

- or no publishing.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.47 Degraded Provider

Degraded means the Provider remains usable but has reduced:

- availability,

- quality,

- account access,

- API functionality,

- speed,

- or service coverage.

Degradation must be reflected in routing.

8.48 Suspended Provider

Suspended means new execution is temporarily blocked.

Reasons may include:

- security Incident,

- rights uncertainty,

- billing dispute,

- terms change,

- authentication compromise,

- severe outage,

- or governance review.

Historical records remain available.

8.49 Deprecated Provider

Deprecated means the Provider should not be selected for new ordinary work.

Deprecation shall identify:

- reason,

- replacement,

- affected accounts,

- affected Capabilities,

- migration plan,

- and retirement timing.

8.50 Disconnected Provider

Disconnected means no active governed Connection remains.

The Provider record may remain for:

- history,

- assets,

- cost,

- and provenance.

8.51 Retired Provider

Retired means the Provider is no longer eligible for new use.

Historical Executions and Assets must remain interpretable.

8.52 Archived Provider

Archived means the Provider record is retained primarily for historical and audit purposes.

It may be hidden from ordinary discovery.

8.53 Provider Lifecycle Transition

Lifecycle transitions shall preserve:

- previous state,

- new state,

- actor,

- reason,

- evidence,

- effective time,

- affected scope,

- and rollback or recovery plan where relevant.

No Provider shall move directly from discovered to unrestricted active use.

8.54 Provider Registry Entry

A Provider Registry entry should include or reference:

- providerId,

- canonical name,

- legal entity,

- aliases,

- Provider Type,

- Service Families,

- ownership relationships,

- trust level,

- risk classification,

- criticality,

- lifecycle,

- regions,

- terms,

- privacy,

- rights,

- security evidence,

- integration maturity,

- Provider Accounts,

- Connections,

- Adapters,

- capability claims,

- health references,

- incidents,

- and provenance.

8.55 Provider Provenance

Provider metadata shall preserve provenance.

Sources may include:

- official documentation,

- contracts,

- privacy policy,

- service terms,

- API metadata,

- user account information,

- operational tests,

- audit reports,

- and human review.

Conflicting sources shall remain visible.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.56 Provider Metadata Freshness

Provider information changes frequently.

Metadata should include:

- observedAt,

- effectiveAt,

- source,

- expected review,

- and stale threshold.

Stale terms, pricing or privacy information must not be represented as current certainty.

8.57 Provider Region

The Registry shall record regions where the Provider:

- contracts,

- operates,

- processes data,

- stores data,

- bills,

- and offers service.

These regions may differ.

Provider marketing location does not prove data-processing location.

8.58 Data-Processing Region

Data-processing region identifies where request data may be processed.

It may be:

- fixed,

- configurable,

- account-dependent,

- model-dependent,

- routed dynamically,

- or unknown.

Unknown region may make the Provider ineligible for protected data.

8.59 Data-Storage Region

Data-storage region identifies where persistent or temporary Provider data may be stored.

Processing and storage regions must remain distinguishable.

8.60 Provider Jurisdiction

Provider jurisdiction may affect:

- contracts,

- privacy,

- law enforcement access,

- dispute resolution,

- and data transfer.

The Registry may preserve:

- legal jurisdiction,

- contracting entity,

- governing law,

- and dispute forum.

The Fabric does not replace legal review.

8.61 Regional Availability

A Provider may offer different:

- Models,

- Capabilities,

- pricing,

- terms,

- and quotas

by region.

Regional support shall be represented through Provider Product, Account or Deployment metadata as appropriate.

8.62 Provider Terms Record

A Provider Terms Record shall preserve material service terms.

It may include:

- terms identifier,

- source,

- version,

- effective date,

- accepted date,

- accepting Principal,

- applicable account class,

- commercial-use terms,

- data-use terms,

- retention,

- prohibited use,

- attribution,

- indemnity,

- and review status.

Terms history shall not be overwritten.

8.63 Terms Version

Terms shall be versioned where possible.

Executions may need to reference the applicable Terms Version.

If the Provider does not expose versions clearly, Omnira shall preserve:

- retrieval date,

- checksum,

- source snapshot,

- or equivalent evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.64 Terms Acceptance

Accepting new Provider terms is an administrative or contractual action.

It may require:

- owner authority,

- legal review,

- cost review,

- and policy update.

An Agent shall not accept materially changed terms autonomously unless explicitly authorised.

8.65 Terms Change

A Terms Change may affect:

- commercial rights,

- data retention,

- training use,

- pricing,

- acceptable use,

- or account ownership.

Material change may trigger:

- suspension,

- review,

- reapproval,

- migration,

- or provider restriction.

8.66 Privacy Policy Record

The Registry shall preserve Provider privacy-policy evidence.

It may include:

- policy version,

- collection practices,

- retention,

- subprocessors,

- training use,

- region,

- deletion,

- data-subject rights,

- and contact path.

Privacy claims must remain Account- and Product-aware where they differ.

8.67 Data Processing Agreement

Enterprise or managed Provider relationships may include a Data Processing Agreement.

The Registry may preserve:

- agreement identifier,

- scope,

- parties,

- effective date,

- subprocessors,

- regional terms,

- and review state.

The agreement itself may remain in a governed document system.

8.68 Provider Subprocessor

A Provider may rely on subprocessors.

The Registry may record material subprocessors where relevant.

Subprocessor changes may affect protected-data eligibility.

8.69 Training-Use Policy

The Registry shall record whether Provider data may be used for:

- training,

- service improvement,

- safety review,

- human review,

- or no such use.

The answer may vary by:

- Product,

- Account,

- enterprise agreement,

- API,

- web interface,

- region,

- and Model.

One general Provider flag is insufficient.

8.70 Retention Policy

Provider retention may differ for:

- prompts,

- Inputs,

- Outputs,

- logs,

- abuse review,

- assets,

- threads,

- and deleted content.

Retention shall be represented at the narrowest correct level.

8.71 Provider Deletion Support

The Registry may record whether the Provider supports:

- account deletion,

- asset deletion,

- job deletion,

- thread deletion,

- data-export deletion,

- and verified erasure.

Provider deletion claims shall not be treated as completed deletion without evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.72 Commercial-Use Terms

The Registry shall preserve Provider-declared commercial-use conditions.

These may depend on:

- subscription tier,

- Model,

- Product,

- output type,

- region,

- attribution,

- and account status.

Commercial-use eligibility at Provider level does not prove rights to every Input.

8.73 Output Ownership Terms

Provider terms may state how output ownership or licence is allocated.

The Registry shall represent:

- user ownership claim,

- Provider licence retention,

- exclusivity,

- non-exclusivity,

- restrictions,

- and uncertainty.

Legal ambiguity must remain visible.

8.74 Input Licence Granted to Provider

Providers may require a licence to process user Inputs.

The Registry should record the scope where material.

A broad Provider licence may affect Provider eligibility for sensitive or proprietary assets.

8.75 Attribution Requirement

Some Providers or Products may require attribution.

Attribution requirements shall propagate into:

- Rights Profiles,

- Asset Provenance,

- and Publication Packages.

8.76 Watermarking Policy

Provider output may include:

- visible watermark,

- invisible watermark,

- metadata marker,

- or provenance signal.

Watermarking may depend on:

- account tier,

- Product,

- Model,

- and output type.

The Registry shall preserve this behaviour.

8.77 Content Restrictions

Providers may prohibit or restrict categories of use.

Restrictions may include:

- child content,

- political content,

- medical advice,

- finance,

- likeness,

- public figures,

- copyrighted characters,

- sexual content,

- violence,

- or regulated industries.

Restrictions influence Capability eligibility.

8.78 Voice and Likeness Terms

Providers supporting voice or likeness may impose:

- consent requirements,

- identity verification,

- commercial restrictions,

- public-figure prohibitions,

- or regional limits.

Provider requirements supplement Omnira governance.

They do not replace it.

8.79 Provider Security Profile

A Provider Security Profile may include:

- authentication methods,

- encryption,

- access controls,

- incident process,

- audit certification,

- vulnerability disclosure,

- data isolation,

- and administrative security.

Security evidence shall be scoped and fresh.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.80 Security Certification

The Registry may reference:

- independent audits,

- security certifications,

- penetration tests,

- or assurance reports.

Certification is evidence.

It is not proof that every Product or Account configuration is secure.

8.81 Provider Authentication Methods

Providers may support:

- API key,

- OAuth,

- service account,

- certificate,

- signed request,

- short-lived token,

- personal session,

- or local trust boundary.

Authentication method affects:

- security,

- revocation,

- scope,

- and automation maturity.

8.82 Provider OAuth Support

OAuth metadata may include:

- authorisation scopes,

- refresh-token support,

- consent screen,

- account identity,

- revocation,

- and token expiry.

Broad OAuth scopes should be avoided where narrower scopes exist.

8.83 API Key Support

API key relationships shall include:

- owning Provider Account,

- environment,

- permitted use,

- rotation,

- expiry where available,

- and vault reference.

Keys must not be stored in Provider Registry payloads.

8.84 Service Account Support

Service Accounts may be preferable for production automation.

The Registry should record:

- account owner,

- delegated scopes,

- Project or Tenant relationship,

- rotation,

- and administrative controls.

8.85 Personal Session Dependence

Some integrations depend on a personal browser or application session.

This creates risks such as:

- session expiry,

- unclear automation rights,

- individual dependency,

- weak audit,

- and poor transferability.

The Registry shall label such integrations honestly.

8.86 Provider Account

A Provider Account represents a specific connected operational relationship.

It shall include or reference:

- providerAccountId,

- providerId,

- account owner,

- Tenant,

- Project restrictions,

- environment,

- account type,

- workspace,

- subscription,

- billing profile,

- region,

- credentials,

- Connections,

- terms acceptance,

- quotas,

- credits,

- lifecycle,

- and provenance.

8.87 Account Owner

Provider Account ownership may belong to:

- user,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Omnira,

- customer organisation,

- or external partner.

Ownership affects:

- billing,

- access,

- export,

- termination,

- and credential control.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.88 Account Scope

A Provider Account may be scoped to:

- one user,

- one Project,

- one Tenant,

- one environment,

- one Capability family,

- or platform-wide managed use.

Scope shall be explicit.

Missing account scope shall not imply global use.

8.89 Personal Provider Account

A Personal Provider Account is owned directly by a human user.

It may be used by Omnira only within explicit permission.

The Fabric shall not silently consume personal credits for Project work.

8.90 Project Provider Account

A Project Provider Account belongs primarily to one Project.

Its assets, credits, credentials and usage should remain Project-scoped.

8.91 Tenant Provider Account

A Tenant Provider Account may serve several Projects.

Usage and cost must still be attributed correctly.

Project policy may restrict access.

8.92 Omnira-Managed Provider Account

An Omnira-managed account may support several Tenants or Projects through governed allocation.

It shall require strong:

- isolation,

- cost attribution,

- credentials,

- quotas,

- and audit.

8.93 Sandbox Provider Account

A Sandbox Account is intended for:

- development,

- tests,

- previews,

- or experimentation.

It shall not be used for production side effects unless explicitly approved.

8.94 Production Provider Account

A Production Account is approved for live governed execution.

It should have:

- appropriate owner,

- secure credential,

- monitoring,

- billing controls,

- incident path,

- and recovery access.

8.95 Provider Workspace

A Provider Workspace is a Provider-defined grouping of:

- users,

- assets,

- credits,

- Models,

- permissions,

- or projects.

Workspace identity shall remain separate from Omnira Project identity.

A Provider Workspace may map to:

- one Project,

- one Tenant,

- or shared managed scope.

8.96 Workspace Mapping

Workspace mapping shall define:

- Provider Workspace,

- Omnira Tenant,

- Omnira Project,

- account owner,

- environment,

- and restrictions.

A workspace named “Familje-Stunden” is not sufficient architectural proof of Project scope.

8.97 Provider Subscription

A Provider Subscription represents the commercial plan attached to an Account.

It may define:

- plan name,

- billing period,

- included capacity,

- API access,

- commercial rights,

- users,

- storage,

- and limits.

Subscriptions change independently from Provider identity.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
8.98 Subscription Tier

Subscription tier may affect:

- Models,

- quality,

- queue priority,

- watermarking,

- retention,

- commercial use,

- API access,

- and support.

The Registry shall preserve tier-specific eligibility.

8.99 Provider Credit System

Providers may bill through:

- currency,

- credits,

- tokens,

- seconds,

- images,

- jobs,

- compute units,

- or subscription capacity.

The Provider Registry shall reference the credit system.

The cost and budget architecture shall normalise usage separately.

8.100 Credit Balance

Credit balance is dynamic Provider Account state.

It may include:

- observed balance,

- source,

- observedAt,

- reset date,

- reserved amount,

- and uncertainty.

A displayed balance may be stale.

8.101 Promotional Credits

Promotional or trial credits may have:

- expiry,

- restricted Models,

- commercial restrictions,

- or separate terms.

They shall not be treated as permanent capacity.

8.102 Included Capacity

Subscription-included capacity may have:

- monthly reset,

- fair-use limits,

- Model restrictions,

- or hidden throttling.

Included capacity shall remain observable where possible.

8.103 Provider Billing Profile

The Billing Profile may include:

- payment owner,

- currency,

- invoice relationship,

- tax details reference,

- spending limits,

- and billing contact.

Sensitive financial data should remain in appropriate systems.

The Provider Registry may store references.

8.104 Provider Account Lifecycle

Provider Account states may include:

- proposed,

- connecting,

- connected,

- active,

- restricted,

- authentication required,
