- read balance,

- read freshness,

- reserve credits,

- record consumption,

- and record refund.

12.425 Cost API

The Cost API should support:

- create estimate,

- create provisional record,

- confirm,

- adjust,

- dispute,

- and aggregate.

12.426 Reconciliation API

The reconciliation interface should support Provider and invoice evidence import.

12.427 Economic Observability

Observability should expose:

- Budget utilisation,

- Reservations,

- provisional cost,

- confirmed cost,

- anomaly state,

- and reconciliation delay.

12.428 Economic Metrics

Metrics may include:

- cost per accepted Output,

- estimate variance,

- retry cost,

- fallback cost,

- subscription utilisation,

- Provider concentration,

- and anomaly frequency.

12.429 Economic Trace Correlation

Every economic record should preserve:

- requestId,

- planId,

- stepId,

- executionId,

- attemptId,

- providerJobId,

- and correlationId where applicable.

12.430 Economic Incident Correlation

Cost Incidents shall link to:

- Credential Incidents,

- Provider Incidents,

- Routing Decisions,

- and affected Assets.

12.431 Economic Performance

Reservation and Budget checks must be fast enough to protect execution without becoming a hidden bottleneck.

12.432 Economic Cache

Read projections may be cached.

Critical remaining-Budget decisions require authoritative or concurrency-safe state.

12.433 Stale Budget Cache Prohibition

A stale cache shall not authorise spending beyond current Budget.

12.434 Pricing Cache

Pricing may be cached within a defined freshness window.

12.435 Credit Cache

Credit balance caching shall be conservative.

12.436 Economic Consistency

The architecture shall define consistency for:

- reservation,

- cost confirmation,

- refund,

- and Budget exhaustion.

Strong consistency or equivalent protection is required at spend boundaries.

12.437 Economic Availability

If the economic control plane is unavailable, paid execution should normally pause.

Direct Provider spending is not the safe fallback.

12.438 Offline Local Execution

Zero-marginal-charge local execution may continue during economic-service outage only when:

- policy permits,

- resource use is bounded,

- and later reconciliation is possible.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.439 Emergency Economic Route

A pre-approved emergency Budget may exist for critical recovery work.

It shall be tightly bounded.

12.440 Economic Simulation

Budget and cost may be simulated before execution.

Simulation shall not reserve or consume real funds unless explicitly configured.

12.441 Cost Dry Run

A Cost Dry Run validates:

- candidate pricing,

- expected usage,

- Budget fit,

- and approval requirements.

12.442 Subscription Scenario

The system may compare:

- current subscription,

- higher tier,

- lower tier,

- and usage-based alternative.

12.443 Provider Migration Scenario

Economic analysis may compare current and replacement Providers including migration cost.

12.444 Stage 1 Economic Objective

Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy economic control plane required for bounded paid intelligence execution.

The objective is not to create complete corporate finance automation.

Stage 1 shall prove:

- explicit Funding Source,

- Project and Plan Budgets,

- Cost Estimates,

- Budget Reservations,

- Provider credit awareness,

- usage and Cost Records,

- retry cost,

- cost attribution,

- approval binding,

- anomaly handling,

- and reconciliation.

12.445 Stage 1 Funding Sources

Stage 1 should support:

- user-owned Provider Account,

- Project-owned Provider Account,

- Omnira-managed or future-managed placeholder,

- subscription-included capacity,

- prepaid Provider credits,

- and local compute classification.

12.446 Stage 1 Budget Types

Stage 1 should support:

- Project Budget,

- Production Budget,

- Plan Budget,

- and Step Budget.

12.447 Stage 1 Budget Object

The Stage 1 Budget object should include:

- budgetId,

- owner,

- Funding Source,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- currency,

- maximum amount,

- remaining amount,

- period,

- lifecycle,

- and approval policy.

12.448 Stage 1 Budget Envelope Object

The Stage 1 Budget Envelope should include:

- budgetEnvelopeId,

- Plan Version,

- maximum authorised cost,

- expected cost,

- Step allocations,

- retry reserve,

- Funding Source,

- approval reference,

- and expiry.

12.449 Stage 1 Reservation Object

The Stage 1 Reservation object should include:

- reservationId,

- Budget Envelope,

- Step,

- Candidate,

- amount,

- currency,

- status,

- expiry,

- and createdAt.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.450 Stage 1 Pricing Object

The Stage 1 Pricing Record should include:

- pricingRecordId,

- Provider,

- Provider Account class,

- Model or Capability,

- Pricing Unit,

- price,

- currency,

- effective or retrieved date,

- source,

- and confidence.

12.451 Stage 1 Cost Estimate Object

The Stage 1 Cost Estimate should include:

- estimateId,

- Step,

- Candidate,

- minimum,

- expected,

- maximum,

- currency,

- retry assumptions,

- pricing references,

- confidence,

- and createdAt.

12.452 Stage 1 Usage Object

The Stage 1 Usage Record should include:

- usageRecordId,

- Execution,

- Attempt,

- Provider,

- Provider Account,

- quantity,

- unit,

- source,

- state,

- and observedAt.

12.453 Stage 1 Cost Record Object

The Stage 1 Cost Record should include:

- costRecordId,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Plan,

- Step,

- Execution,

- Attempt,

- Provider,

- Provider Account,

- Funding Source,

- amount,

- currency,

- state,

- and provenance.

12.454 Stage 1 Credit Object

The Stage 1 Credit Balance should include:

- Provider Account,

- Credit System,

- observed balance,

- reserved amount,

- available amount,

- observedAt,

- and confidence.

12.455 Stage 1 Subscription Object

The Stage 1 Subscription should include:

- owner,

- Provider Account,

- tier,

- recurring cost,

- period,

- included capacity,

- renewal date,

- and lifecycle.

12.456 Stage 1 Cost Estimation

Stage 1 shall estimate cost before paid execution when Provider pricing permits it.

12.457 Stage 1 Unknown Pricing

When pricing is unknown, Stage 1 shall require:

- conservative maximum,

- explicit approval,

- or human-assisted confirmation.

12.458 Stage 1 Reservation Requirement

Every paid automated Provider Execution should require an active Reservation.

12.459 Stage 1 Credit Reservation

Credit-based video, image and voice work should reserve expected credits where practical.

12.460 Stage 1 Local Cost

Local execution may initially report:

- zero marginal Provider charge,

- estimated local compute cost,

- or internal cost unknown.

It shall not report universal zero cost.

12.461 Stage 1 Cost Attribution

Every paid Execution shall identify:

- Project,

- Provider Account,

- Funding Source,

- and Plan Step.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.462 Stage 1 Retry Cost

Every retry shall create a separate Attempt-level cost record.

12.463 Stage 1 Fallback Cost

Fallback shall use a new estimate and remain inside the Budget Envelope.

12.464 Stage 1 Human-Assisted Cost

Manual Provider work shall capture:

- approved maximum,

- reported Provider spend,

- and evidence.

12.465 Stage 1 Cost Approval

The approval summary shall include:

- expected cost,

- maximum cost,

- Funding Source,

- retry allowance,

- and Provider Account or class.

12.466 Stage 1 Autonomous Threshold

Stage 1 may permit low-cost execution within a pre-approved Project allowance.

The threshold shall be explicit and revocable.

12.467 Stage 1 No Auto-Top-Up

Automatic credit purchase or subscription upgrade should remain disabled by default.

12.468 Stage 1 Reconciliation

Stage 1 should reconcile:

- Execution usage,

- Provider charge where available,

- and credit-balance change.

12.469 Stage 1 Cost Dashboard

A simple Project view should expose:

- Budget,

- Reservations,

- provisional cost,

- confirmed cost,

- and remaining amount.

12.470 Stage 1 Alerts

Stage 1 should alert on:

- nearing Budget limit,

- exhausted credits,

- unusual cost variance,

- and repeated failed paid attempts.

12.471 Stage 1 Economic API

Stage 1 should support:

- get Budget,

- create Reservation,

- release Reservation,

- create Estimate,

- record Usage,

- confirm Cost,

- adjust Cost,

- inspect Credit Balance,

- and reconcile.

12.472 Stage 1 Budget Acceptance Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Budget identifies owner.

2. Budget identifies Funding Source.

3. Budget identifies Project and Environment.

4. Child allocation cannot exceed parent capacity.

5. Exhausted Budget blocks new paid work.

6. Suspended Budget blocks new reservations.

7. Expired Budget blocks new execution.

8. Budget increase creates attributable amendment.

9. Budget decrease does not erase existing confirmed cost.

10. Closed Budget remains historically queryable.

11. One Project cannot consume another Project Budget.

12. Tenant shared Budget preserves Project attribution.

13. User-owned Funding Source requires explicit permission.

14. Omnira-managed Funding Source preserves Tenant isolation.

15. Budget approval binds to exact scope.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.473 Stage 1 Reservation Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Paid execution cannot start without required Reservation.

2. Duplicate Reservation request is idempotent.

3. Concurrent Reservations cannot overspend the Budget.

4. Reservation reduces available capacity.

5. Unused Reservation is released.

6. Partial cost consumes part of Reservation.

7. Fully consumed Reservation cannot be reused.

8. Expired Reservation does not vanish while job remains unresolved.

9. Cancelled job releases only unused capacity.

10. Reservation cannot exceed Step Budget.

11. Fallback creates or updates valid Reservation.

12. Reservation identifies selected Candidate.

13. Reservation currency is explicit.

14. Reservation state survives restart.

15. Reservation history remains immutable.

12.474 Stage 1 Pricing Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Pricing identifies Provider.

2. Pricing identifies applicable Model or Capability.

3. Pricing identifies Account tier where material.

4. Pricing identifies currency.

5. Pricing identifies unit.

6. Pricing identifies source.

7. Pricing identifies effective or retrieval date.

8. Stale pricing lowers confidence.

9. Promotional pricing preserves expiry.

10. Minimum charges are included.

11. Failed-request pricing is represented where known.

12. Cancellation pricing is represented where known.

13. Provider credits are not assumed equal to currency.

14. Regional pricing remains distinct.

15. Historical pricing remains queryable.

12.475 Stage 1 Estimate Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Estimate references exact Pricing Records.

2. Estimate distinguishes minimum, expected and maximum.

3. Estimate includes retry allowance.

4. Estimate includes Provider minimum charge.

5. Estimate includes required evaluation.

6. Estimate identifies confidence.

7. Opaque pricing is labelled.

8. Updated estimate creates new version.

9. Material increase requires renewed approval.

10. Exchange-rate source is preserved.

11. Estimate never becomes confirmed cost automatically.

12. Estimate remains Step-specific.

13. Candidate change creates a new estimate.

14. Optional work remains separately visible.

15. Local execution is not falsely represented as universally free.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.476 Stage 1 Cost Record Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Cost Record identifies Project.

2. Cost Record identifies Provider Account.

3. Cost Record identifies Funding Source.

4. Cost Record identifies Execution and Attempt.

5. Estimated and confirmed states remain separate.

6. Missing Provider usage does not become zero.

7. Rejected Output retains cost.

8. Failed Attempt retains cost.

9. Cancelled job retains any incurred cost.

10. Refund creates adjustment rather than deleting original charge.

11. Attribution correction preserves history.

12. Duplicate Provider event does not duplicate cost.

13. Currency remains explicit.

14. Provider and Omnira records remain distinguishable.

15. Historical Cost Record remains immutable except through adjustment.

12.477 Stage 1 Credit Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Credit Balance identifies Provider Account.

2. Balance declares freshness.

3. Stale balance is not treated as exact.

4. Credit Reservation reduces available credits.

5. Credit consumption links to Execution.

6. Returned credits create Refund Record.

7. Promotional credits preserve expiry.

8. User-owned credits are not silent fallback.

9. Project credits cannot fund another Project without authority.

10. Credit value preserves purchase context.

11. Credit purchase requires separate approval.

12. Auto-top-up remains disabled by default.

13. Quota and credit remain distinct.

14. Unknown credit loss triggers anomaly.

15. Credit reconciliation compares expected and observed balance.

12.478 Stage 1 Subscription Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Subscription identifies owner.

2. Subscription identifies Provider Account.

3. Subscription identifies recurring cost.

4. Subscription identifies included capacity.

5. Subscription identifies renewal date.

6. Personal subscription is not platform-wide.

7. Included capacity is not treated as unlimited.

8. Upgrade requires approval.

9. Auto-renewal state is explicit.

10. Cancellation preserves service end date.

11. Tier change updates pricing and rights evidence.

12. Subscription utilisation can be measured.

13. Duplicate subscriptions can be detected.

14. Overage remains separately recorded.

15. Historical subscription periods remain queryable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 12.479 Stage 1 Retry and Fallback Cost Tests
text:
12.479 Stage 1 Retry and Fallback Cost Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Retry consumes retry allocation.

2. Retry stops when allocation is exhausted.

3. Quality retry and transport retry remain separately identified.

4. Unknown outcome does not trigger unsafe paid retry.

5. Fallback receives new estimate.

6. Fallback remains within Plan Budget.

7. Premium fallback requires approval when threshold is crossed.

8. Candidate race reserves full possible cost.

9. Hedged request cost is included.

10. Cancelled duplicate candidate reconciles actual charge.

11. Retry cost affects future Economy routing.

12. Failed fallback remains attributed.

13. Human-assisted fallback captures reported cost.

14. Fallback Funding Source change is disclosed.

15. Unbounded paid retry is impossible.

12.480 Stage 1 Authority Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Connected Provider Account does not create spending authority.

2. Available credits do not create spending authority.

3. Planner cannot increase Budget.

4. Router cannot override maximum cost.

5. Agent cannot purchase credits without authority.

6. Agent cannot upgrade subscription without authority.

7. Bounded approval includes retry limit.

8. Approval binds to Budget Envelope Version.

9. Expired approval blocks new paid execution.

10. Funding Source change may require new approval.

11. User-owned funding requires user permission.

12. Project Manager cannot use Tenant funds beyond delegation.

13. Economic administrator cannot approve own high-risk purchase where separation is required.

14. Spend Stop blocks new cost.

15. Emergency Budget use remains attributable.

12.481 Stage 1 Security Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Payment credentials never enter Agent prompts.

2. Card and bank data never enter ordinary Fabric records.

3. Provider billing credentials remain in approved systems.

4. Cost dashboards respect Tenant isolation.

5. Project spend is not visible to unrelated Projects.

6. Managed-account cost preserves Tenant attribution.

7. Compromised Credential can freeze related spending.

8. Wrong Provider Account triggers Incident.

9. Billing export is validated before import.

10. Cost API cannot mutate Budget without authority.

11. Reconciliation service cannot initiate new Provider spending.

12. Economic logs do not expose raw payment data.

13. Cost exports preserve classification.

14. Shadow Spend is flagged.

15. Hidden commercial margin is prohibited.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.482 Stage 1 Reconciliation Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Provider usage maps to correct Execution.

2. Provider job ID maps to correct Attempt.

3. Credit balance change matches expected consumption.

4. Duplicate charge is detected.

5. Missing charge remains unresolved.

6. Unknown cost does not become zero.

7. Refund reduces confirmed cost through adjustment.

8. Currency mismatch is detected.

9. Wrong Project attribution is corrected with history.

10. Rounding tolerance is applied consistently.

11. Delayed invoice updates provisional cost.

12. Closed Budget waits for required reconciliation.

13. Manual Provider spend requires evidence.

14. Reconciliation discrepancy creates anomaly.

15. Reconciliation result is attributable.

12.483 Stage 1 Anomaly Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Rapid spending triggers velocity alert.

2. Estimate variance beyond threshold triggers review.

3. Repeated paid failure triggers pause.

4. Duplicate Provider charge triggers anomaly.

5. Unexpected credit loss triggers anomaly.

6. Wrong Account usage triggers Incident.

7. Budget overrun remains visible.

8. Provider price change invalidates stale estimate.

9. Suspicious Provider usage may suspend Credential.

10. Anomaly does not delete original records.

11. Critical anomaly can activate Spend Stop.

12. Low-severity anomaly does not halt unrelated Projects.

13. Resolution preserves evidence.

14. Refund pending remains unresolved.

15. Post-Incident policy update is recorded.

12.484 Stage 1 Economic Reporting Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Project report separates estimated and confirmed cost.

2. Report separates reserved and available Budget.

3. Report includes failed-attempt cost.

4. Report includes refunds.

5. Provider report includes subscription and usage cost.

6. Capability report preserves Model and Provider context.

7. User-owned and Omnira-managed spend remain distinguishable.

8. Local compute remains distinguishable from Provider charges.

9. Currency conversion source is visible.

10. Redacted view hides restricted contract rates.

11. Reporting preserves Project isolation.

12. Cost totals equal underlying confirmed records within tolerance.

13. Provisional cost is not presented as final.

14. Unknown cost is visible.

15. Historical report remains reproducible.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 12.485 Applied Example — Nova and Pling Episode Budget
text:
12.485 Applied Example — Nova and Pling Episode Budget

A Familje-Stunden Nova and Pling episode may receive a Production Budget containing:

- scene-planning allocation,

- preview-generation allocation,

- premium-scene reserve,

- Swedish narration allocation,

- local composition allocation,

- evaluation allocation,

- human-review allocation,

- and derivative allocation.

The Production Budget may define:

Expected Cost

The likely total when most scenes pass preview quality.

Maximum Authorised Cost

The hard boundary including approved premium escalation.

Retry Reserve

A bounded amount for failed character-critical scenes.

Optional Allocation

Trailer, short clips and extra thumbnails.

Funding Sources

- Project-owned creative Provider credits,

- Project voice subscription,

- and local compute.

The Plan shall stop before consuming additional personal or Omnira-managed credits unless the Funding Waterfall explicitly permits them.

12.486 Nova and Pling Scene Cost

Each scene should have a Step-level estimate.

A background-motion scene may have:

- low expected cost,

- no premium reserve,

- and Economy routing.

A close-up scene containing both Nova and Pling may have:

- higher expected cost,

- premium reserve,

- stronger evaluation cost,

- and Balanced or Premium routing.

12.487 Nova and Pling Preview Economics

Preview-first production may reduce total expected cost by:

- testing motion,

- identifying character defects,

- and preventing unnecessary premium final generation.

The preview cost shall remain visible.

Savings shall be measured against accepted final output, not only first-call price.

12.488 Nova and Pling Premium Escalation

Premium escalation may occur only when:

- mandatory character evaluation fails,

- remaining premium reserve exists,

- the scene is important,

- and the approved Plan permits escalation.

The Router shall not use premium resources for every scene merely because funds remain.

12.489 Nova and Pling Derivative Economics

Trailer and short-form derivatives may use:

- accepted master footage,

- local editing,

- and lower-cost captioning.

The derivative budget shall remain separate from master production.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 12.490 Applied Example — The Prompt News Production
text:
12.490 Applied Example — The Prompt News Production

A The Prompt episode may use:

- search quota,

- reasoning API cost,

- factual-evaluation cost,

- voice or avatar subscription,

- and local composition.

The Budget should distinguish:

- research cost,

- editorial reasoning cost,

- media cost,

- and publication preparation.

A visually expensive Provider shall not consume research Budget.

12.491 The Prompt Current-Search Cost

Current search may be billed by:

- query,

- document retrieval,

- or included Provider capacity.

The Plan shall estimate the likely number of source queries and verification calls.

12.492 The Prompt Factuality Cost

Independent factual evaluation may add cost.

It remains justified when it reduces publication risk.

12.493 Applied Example — GainPilot Reel

A GainPilot reel may use:

- local script generation,

- one low-cost image,

- included voice credits,

- and local composition.

Economy routing may produce a low direct Provider cost.

The Fabric shall still preserve:

- local compute classification,

- voice-credit consumption,

- and failed image Attempts.

12.494 Applied Example — Omnira Code Audit

A code-audit Budget may include:

- external reasoning allocation,

- local repository-search cost,

- test execution,

- and human review.

The Budget shall exclude:

- deployment,

- paid infrastructure purchase,

- repository subscription upgrade,

- and unrelated implementation.

Those actions require separate approval.

12.495 Applied Example — Private Local Analysis

A Local Only analysis may use local compute.

The Cost Record may state:

- direct Provider charge: zero,

- local compute estimate: provisional,

- storage impact: measured,

- and human review cost: not tracked or estimated.

The system shall not present the work as having no economic footprint.

12.496 Applied Example — User-Owned OpenArt Credits

André may choose to use a personal OpenArt Account for a Familje-Stunden pilot.

The economic objects should identify:

Funding Source

User-owned OpenArt credits.

Project

Familje-Stunden.

Approval

Bounded pilot approval.

Maximum Spend

Defined Provider credits or currency equivalent.

Restrictions

- no automatic top-up,

- no use for another Project,

- no premium retry beyond the approved reserve.

The credits remain André’s personal capacity.

Omnira receives permission to use only the approved amount.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 12.502 Anti-Pattern — Connected Account Means Spend Permission
text:
12.497 Applied Example — Omnira-Managed Credits

A future Omnira-managed plan may allocate monthly managed credits to a Tenant.

The user-facing Cost Record should distinguish:

- managed plan allowance,

- usage consumed,

- remaining allowance,

- overage if permitted,

- and service fee.

Omnira’s internal Provider procurement cost may remain operationally restricted.

The user-facing price and margin structure shall remain truthful.

12.498 Applied Example — Mixed Funding Plan

A future production may use:

- local text generation,

- user-owned video credits,

- Project-owned voice subscription,

- Omnira-managed image credits,

- and Tenant storage.

The Plan shall preserve a Funding Source for every Step.

No aggregate cost shall hide who paid for each part.

12.499 Applied Example — Failed Video Job

A Provider video job times out after submission.

The state may be:

Execution

Unknown outcome.

Reservation

Still active.

Cost

Provisional maximum.

Next Step

Provider reconciliation.

The system shall not submit a duplicate paid job until:

- Provider job state,

- Asset library,

- credit balance,

- and billing evidence

have been checked.

12.500 Applied Example — Provider Refund

A failed Provider job consumes ten credits.

The Provider later returns eight credits.

The economic history should show:

- original consumption: ten credits,

- refund: eight credits,

- final confirmed cost: two credits,

- reason,

- and reconciliation evidence.

The original record shall not be deleted.

12.501 Applied Example — Subscription Review

The Fabric may observe that:

- one Provider subscription costs more than usage-based alternatives,

- but it supplies commercial rights and reliable premium capacity.

The recommendation shall consider:

- direct cost,

- strategic fallback,

- quality,

- and lock-in.

It shall not recommend cancellation from utilisation alone.

12.502 Anti-Pattern — Connected Account Means Spend Permission

A connected Provider Account shall not be used without Budget and Authority.

12.503 Anti-Pattern — Available Credits Mean Free

Credits represent limited economic value.

12.504 Anti-Pattern — Subscription Means Unlimited

Included capacity and fair-use restrictions remain bounded.

12.508 Anti-Pattern — Retry Cost Hidden

12.509 Anti-Pattern — Fallback Cost Hidden

12.510 Anti-Pattern — Failed Output Deletes Cost

12.516 Anti-Pattern — One Budget for Every Project

12.517 Anti-Pattern — One Budget for Development and Production

Estimate treatment shall be explicit.

Automatic purchases require explicit policy.

Autonomous limits should remain scoped by:

- Project,

It shall not increase authority.

Spend boundaries require authoritative state.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.546 Future Economic Architecture

Future versions may support:

- customer billing,

- usage-based Omnira plans,

- prepaid managed credits,

- automatic but bounded plan optimisation,

- enterprise cost centres,

- invoice generation,

- internal transfer pricing,

- energy-aware routing,

- carbon-aware compute placement,

- Provider contract optimisation,

- multi-currency wallets,

- and customer-managed spend policies.

Future evolution must preserve:

- transparency,

- bounded authority,

- Project attribution,

- Funding Source ownership,

- and historical truth.

12.547 Customer Billing

Future customer billing may aggregate Omnira-managed resource use into customer invoices.

Internal Provider cost and customer price shall remain distinct.

12.548 Cost Centre

A Tenant may define organisational cost centres.

Project attribution shall remain available beneath them.

12.549 Chargeback

Chargeback may allocate shared costs to Projects or departments.

The allocation method shall be explicit.

12.550 Showback

Showback reports cost without creating a financial transfer.

12.551 Internal Transfer Price

Omnira may assign an internal price to local or managed resources.

It shall remain distinct from direct external cost.

12.552 Dynamic Budgeting

Future systems may recommend Budget changes based on forecast and value.

They shall not enact increases without authority.

12.553 Value-Aware Budgeting

Business Value evidence may inform where Budget should be allocated.

Value prediction shall remain uncertain and explainable.

12.554 Cost-Aware Scheduling

The scheduler may delay non-urgent work to:

- use lower-cost capacity,

- wait for quota reset,

- or use local idle hardware.

It shall respect deadlines.

12.555 Spot Capacity

Future managed compute may use variable-price or interruptible capacity.

The risk and fallback shall be explicit.

12.556 Reserved Provider Capacity

Enterprise contracts may reserve Provider capacity.

Reservation cost and utilisation shall be tracked.

12.557 Carbon-Aware Cost

Energy source and carbon may become economic or policy dimensions.

They shall not override mandatory quality or privacy unless policy states so.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.558 Economic Success Criteria

The economic architecture succeeds when:

- no paid execution occurs without attributable authority,

- users understand expected and actual cost,

- every cost reaches the correct Project and Funding Source,

- retries and fallbacks remain bounded,

- credits and subscriptions remain visible,

- local cost is represented honestly,

- Provider billing can be reconciled,

- anomalies can stop spending,

- and economic optimisation never weakens governance.

12.559 Economic Failure Conditions

The architecture is non-conformant when:

- Provider access implies spend authority,

- user-owned credits are consumed silently,

- Budgets lack Project scope,

- retries consume unbounded funds,

- estimated and confirmed cost are merged,

- unknown cost becomes zero,

- refunds delete original history,

- Provider Account attribution is missing,

- margin is hidden,

- or economic-service failure permits uncontrolled Provider calls.

12.560 Canonical Funding Source Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Funding Source contract:

1. Every paid Execution SHALL identify a Funding Source.

2. Every Funding Source SHALL have stable identity.

3. Every Funding Source SHALL identify its owner.

4. User-owned Funding Sources SHALL remain user-owned.

5. Project-owned Funding Sources SHALL remain Project-scoped.

6. Tenant-owned Funding Sources SHALL preserve Project attribution.

7. Omnira-managed Funding Sources SHALL preserve Tenant isolation.

8. Funding Source SHALL remain distinct from Provider Account.

9. Funding Source SHALL remain distinct from Budget.

10. Funding Source substitution SHALL be attributable.

11. Personal capacity SHALL NOT become silent shared capacity.

12. Mixed Funding Sources SHALL be identified at Step level.

13. Funding Source availability SHALL NOT create spending authority.

14. Funding Source commercial conditions SHALL remain visible.

15. Historical Funding Source use SHALL remain interpretable.

12.561 Canonical Budget Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Budget contract:

1. Every Budget SHALL have stable identity.

2. Every Budget SHALL identify an owner.

3. Every Budget SHALL identify a Funding Source or permitted source set.

4. Every Budget SHALL identify currency or governed unit.

5. Every Budget SHALL identify maximum amount.

6. Every Budget SHALL identify scope.

7. Project Budgets SHALL identify Project.

8. Environment scope SHALL be explicit where applicable.

9. Periodic Budgets SHALL identify reset or expiry.

10. Budget lifecycle SHALL be explicit.

11. Child allocations SHALL NOT exceed parent capacity.

12. Budget amendment SHALL be attributable.

13. Exhausted Budgets SHALL block new paid execution.

14. Suspended Budgets SHALL block new reservations.

15. Budget closure SHALL NOT erase historical cost.

16. Budget state SHALL survive restart.

17. Budget consumption SHALL preserve confirmed, provisional and reserved values separately.

18. Budget approval SHALL bind to scope and version.

19. Budget caches SHALL NOT authorise overspend.

20. Budget history SHALL remain auditable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.562 Canonical Budget Envelope Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Budget Envelope:

1. Every paid Plan SHALL reference an active Budget Envelope.

2. The Envelope SHALL identify maximum authorised cost.

3. The Envelope SHALL distinguish expected and maximum cost.

4. The Envelope SHALL identify Funding Source priority.

5. The Envelope SHALL identify Step allocations.

6. The Envelope SHALL identify retry allocation.

7. The Envelope SHALL identify fallback allocation where permitted.

8. The Envelope SHALL identify optional-work allocation.

9. The Envelope SHALL identify currency.

10. The Envelope SHALL identify approval and validity.

11. The Envelope SHALL bind to exact Plan Version.

12. Material cost increase SHALL invalidate or amend approval.

13. The Envelope SHALL NOT grant operational authority beyond spending.

14. The Envelope SHALL NOT permit Quality Floor reduction.

15. The Envelope SHALL NOT permit policy bypass.

16. Unused capacity SHALL be released or remain available according to policy.

17. Funding Source change SHALL be evaluated for materiality.

18. Envelope Version SHALL remain historically resolvable.

19. No execution path SHALL expand beyond the Envelope.

20. The Envelope SHALL remain human- and machine-readable.

12.563 Canonical Reservation Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Reservation contract:

1. Paid automated execution SHOULD require a Reservation before Provider submission.

2. Every Reservation SHALL have stable identity.

3. Every Reservation SHALL reference a Budget Envelope.

4. Every Reservation SHALL identify Plan and Step.

5. Every Reservation SHALL identify amount and currency.

6. Every Reservation SHALL identify selected Candidate or resource class.

7. Every Reservation SHALL have lifecycle state.

8. Reservation creation SHALL be concurrency-safe.

9. Duplicate Reservation requests SHALL be idempotent.

10. Reservation SHALL reduce available Budget.

11. Reservation SHALL NOT exceed Step or Plan limits.

12. Reservation SHALL distinguish expected and maximum exposure.

13. Partial consumption SHALL remain visible.

14. Unused capacity SHALL be released.

15. Unknown outcome SHALL preserve possible charge exposure.

16. Reservation expiry SHALL NOT abandon active unresolved jobs.

17. Reservation renewal SHALL remain inside the Budget Envelope.

18. Cancelled work SHALL release only unconsumed capacity.

19. Historical Reservation events SHALL remain immutable.

20. Reservation failure SHALL block paid execution where required.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.564 Canonical Pricing Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Pricing contract:

1. Every material Pricing Record SHALL have stable identity and version.

2. Pricing SHALL identify Provider or local cost model.

3. Pricing SHALL identify applicable Product, Model, Capability or Account class.

4. Pricing SHALL identify unit.

5. Pricing SHALL identify price and currency.

6. Pricing SHALL identify source.

7. Pricing SHALL identify effective or retrieval time.

8. Pricing SHALL identify confidence.

9. Stale pricing SHALL NOT be presented as current certainty.

10. Promotional pricing SHALL preserve expiry and restrictions.

11. Minimum charges SHALL remain visible.

12. Failed-request pricing SHALL remain visible where known.

13. Cancellation and refund behaviour SHALL remain visible where known.

14. Provider credits SHALL preserve original unit.

15. Currency conversion SHALL preserve rate source and time.

16. Historical Pricing Records SHALL NOT be overwritten.

17. Account-tier and regional pricing SHALL remain distinguishable.

18. Opaque pricing SHALL require conservative treatment.

19. Pricing SHALL NOT create spending authority.

20. Pricing evidence SHALL remain attributable.

12.565 Canonical Cost Estimate Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Cost Estimate:

1. Every paid Step SHOULD have a Cost Estimate before execution.

2. Every Estimate SHALL identify its scope.

3. Every Estimate SHALL reference relevant Pricing Records.

4. Every Estimate SHALL identify currency.

5. Every Estimate SHALL distinguish minimum, expected and maximum where appropriate.

6. Every Estimate SHALL include permitted retry assumptions.

7. Every Estimate SHALL include required evaluation and post-processing cost where material.

8. Every Estimate SHALL identify confidence.

9. Opaque estimates SHALL remain explicitly uncertain.

10. Candidate change SHALL create a new or revised Estimate.

11. Material Estimate increase SHALL trigger approval review.

12. Estimated Cost SHALL NOT become Confirmed Cost automatically.

13. Estimate history SHALL remain queryable.

14. Exchange-rate assumptions SHALL remain visible.

15. Optional-work cost SHALL remain distinguishable.

16. Local execution SHALL NOT be represented as universally free.

17. Human-assisted cost SHOULD include material manual expense.

18. No-estimate paid work SHALL require conservative bounded approval.

19. Estimate generation SHALL remain separate from routing authority.

20. Estimates SHALL be explainable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.566 Canonical Usage and Cost Contract

The following requirements define canonical Usage and Cost records:

1. Every paid Execution SHALL create or resolve a Cost Record.

2. Every Cost Record SHALL have stable identity.

3. Every Cost Record SHALL identify Tenant and Project.

4. Every Cost Record SHALL identify Plan, Step and Execution where applicable.

5. Every Cost Record SHALL identify Provider Account for external work.

6. Every Cost Record SHALL identify Funding Source.

7. Usage Records SHALL preserve original Provider units.

8. Estimated, reserved, provisional and confirmed cost SHALL remain distinct.

9. Unknown cost SHALL remain unknown.

10. Failed and rejected Attempts SHALL preserve cost.

11. Retry cost SHALL remain Attempt-specific.

12. Fallback cost SHALL preserve changed Provider and pricing.

13. Refunds SHALL create adjustments rather than erase history.

14. Attribution changes SHALL preserve original state and reason.

15. Duplicate Provider evidence SHALL NOT duplicate cost.

16. Currency SHALL remain explicit.

17. Cost state SHALL be attributable and version-aware.

18. Historical records SHALL remain interpretable after Provider retirement.

19. Cost Records SHALL NOT contain payment secrets.

20. Aggregated totals SHALL remain traceable to underlying records.

12.567 Canonical Credit Contract

The following requirements define canonical credit governance:

1. Every Credit System SHALL identify issuer and unit meaning.

2. Every Credit Balance SHALL identify Provider Account or managed account.

3. Credit Balance SHALL declare observation time and confidence.

4. Stale balance SHALL NOT be treated as exact.

5. Credit Reservation SHALL remain linked to Budget Reservation.

6. Credit consumption SHALL remain linked to Execution and Attempt.

7. Promotional credits SHALL preserve expiry and restrictions.

8. User-owned credits SHALL NOT be consumed silently.

9. Project credits SHALL remain Project-scoped.

10. Managed credits SHALL preserve Tenant and Project attribution.

11. Credit purchase SHALL require separate authority.

12. Auto-top-up SHALL be disabled unless explicitly governed.

13. Credit value SHALL preserve purchase or plan context.

14. Credit refunds SHALL preserve original consumption history.

15. Credit transfer SHALL require explicit support and authority.

16. Credit expiry MAY influence routing only after user value and eligibility.

17. Credit and quota SHALL remain distinct.

18. Credit availability SHALL NOT create spending authority.

19. Credit reconciliation SHALL compare expected and observed balances.

20. Unknown credit movement SHALL trigger anomaly review.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.568 Canonical Economic Approval Contract

The following requirements define economic approval:

1. Spending approval SHALL remain separate from technical access.

2. Approval SHALL identify maximum cost.

3. Approval SHALL identify Funding Source.

4. Approval SHALL identify scope.

5. Approval SHALL identify Plan or Budget Envelope Version.

6. Approval SHALL identify retry allowance.

7. Approval SHALL identify fallback allowance where applicable.

8. Approval SHALL identify optional work where applicable.

9. Approval SHALL identify validity period.

10. Approval conditions SHALL become enforceable controls.

11. Material cost increase SHALL require renewed approval.

12. Material Funding Source change MAY require renewed approval.

13. Credit purchase SHALL require separate approval.

14. Subscription purchase or upgrade SHALL require separate approval.

15. Auto-renewal SHALL remain explicit.

16. Agent autonomy SHALL remain bounded by approved limits.

17. Available Budget SHALL NOT imply operational authority.

18. Expired approval SHALL block new paid work.

19. Revoked approval SHALL stop new spending.

20. Approval evidence SHALL remain immutable.

12.569 Canonical Reconciliation Contract

The following requirements define economic reconciliation:

1. Provider and Omnira economic evidence SHALL be reconciled.

2. Reconciliation SHALL preserve expected and observed values.

3. Reconciliation SHALL identify discrepancies.

4. Missing usage SHALL NOT be interpreted as zero.

5. Duplicate charges SHALL be detected.

6. Credit changes SHALL be compared with expected consumption.

7. Refunds SHALL be verified before final adjustment.

8. Currency mismatches SHALL remain visible.

9. Attribution corrections SHALL preserve history.

10. Rounding tolerance SHALL be explicit.

11. Delayed Provider evidence SHALL update provisional state.

12. Material unresolved discrepancies SHALL create anomaly or Incident.

13. Reconciliation SHALL be attributable.

14. Manual Provider spending SHALL require evidence.

15. Closed Budgets SHOULD complete required reconciliation.

16. Provider retirement SHALL NOT prevent historical reconciliation.

17. Reconciliation imports SHALL be validated.

18. Reconciliation SHALL NOT expose payment secrets.

19. Reconciliation outcomes SHALL remain queryable.

20. Unknown economic state SHALL remain truthful until resolved.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.570 Canonical Economic Governance Contract

The following requirements define overall economic governance:

1. No paid execution SHALL occur without attributable economic authority.

2. No connected Account SHALL create spending authority.

3. No credit balance SHALL create spending authority.

4. No subscription SHALL be treated as unlimited.

5. No local resource SHALL be treated as universally free.

6. No cost optimisation SHALL weaken Quality Floor.

7. No cost optimisation SHALL weaken privacy, rights, safety or authority.

8. User-owned capacity SHALL remain user-owned.

9. Project spending SHALL remain Project-attributed.

10. Shared managed capacity SHALL preserve Tenant isolation.

11. Retry and fallback spending SHALL remain bounded.

12. Unknown outcome SHALL preserve possible economic exposure.

13. Economic records SHALL remain distinct from raw payment credentials.

14. Hidden Provider or Omnira margin SHALL be prohibited.

15. Commercial interest SHALL NOT silently control routing.

16. Economic learning SHALL NOT create authority.

17. Budget, pricing and cost history SHALL remain versioned.

18. Economic-service failure SHALL NOT authorise uncontrolled paid Provider calls.

19. Users SHALL receive meaningful cost transparency.

20. Historical economic truth SHALL remain reconstructable.

12.571 Economic Invariants

The following invariants shall remain true:

- No Provider access becomes spend authority.

- No available credit becomes permission.

- No personal subscription becomes shared infrastructure by convenience.

- No Project pays for another Project without explicit authority.

- No paid Step starts beyond its Budget boundary.

- No retry escapes the retry allocation.

- No fallback hides its changed cost.

- No unknown cost becomes zero.

- No refund erases original spending history.

- No failed Output erases incurred cost.

- No stale price becomes current truth.

- No stale credit balance becomes guaranteed capacity.

- No cheaper Candidate defeats mandatory quality, rights, privacy or security.

- No premium profile becomes unlimited spending.

- No local execution becomes economically invisible.

- No Provider dashboard becomes the sole canonical ledger.

- No managed margin is misrepresented as Provider base price.

- No economic recommendation purchases or upgrades without authority.

- No payment credential enters Agent or Model context.

- No economic-system outage creates uncontrolled Provider spending.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
12.572 Closing Statement

Economic governance determines whether Omnira can use powerful intelligence resources without allowing technical capability to become uncontrolled cost.

The user defines what is worth doing.

The Project defines where the value belongs.

The Funding Source defines who pays.

The Budget defines how much may be consumed.

The Budget Envelope defines the bounded cost of one Plan.

The Reservation protects the limit before spending begins.

The Pricing Record defines what the resource is expected to cost.

The Cost Estimate explains the likely exposure.

The Routing Decision selects the eligible resource.

The Execution consumes measurable usage.

The Provider reports or charges its economic result.

The Cost Record attributes the result to the correct Project and Funding Source.

The Reconciliation process determines what actually happened.

The Refund or Adjustment preserves later corrections without rewriting history.

For Familje-Stunden, this architecture allows Nova and Pling productions to combine:

- local processing,

- Project subscriptions,

- user-owned creative credits,

- premium scene reserves,

- and bounded retries

without losing control of the monthly production budget.

For The Prompt, it allows research, factual verification, narration, avatar production and media composition to remain economically separate and measurable.

For GainPilot, it allows Economy routing to use inexpensive or already-included resources without pretending that low price is the only definition of value.

For Omnira, it allows:

- local Models,

- user-owned Accounts,

- Project credits,

- Tenant Budgets,

- Omnira-managed capacity,

- subscriptions,

- Provider APIs,

- and human-assisted production

to coexist within one transparent economic control plane.

The cheapest call is not always the cheapest completed result.

The most expensive Provider is not always the premium choice.

A free tier is not always commercially usable.

A subscription is not unlimited.

A local Model is not without cost.

A refund does not erase the original charge.

A connected key does not authorise spending.

A Budget does not authorise the underlying action.

Economic optimisation begins only after governance.

No paid execution without a Funding Source.

No Funding Source without ownership.

No Budget without scope.

No Reservation without purpose.

No retry without remaining allocation.

No fallback without a new economic check.

No confirmed cost without evidence.

No economic learning without boundaries.

No margin without transparency.

The user retains financial authority.

The Project retains attribution.

Omnira retains neutrality.

The Fabric converts intelligence spending into controlled, explainable and auditable value.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical architecture, governance model, lifecycle, contracts and operational responsibilities for quality, evaluation, benchmarking and acceptance within the Omnira Intelligence Fabric.

It establishes:

- how quality is defined for intelligence work,

- how Quality Floors, Quality Targets and Acceptance Criteria remain distinct,

- how quality requirements are attached to Capability Requests, Plans, Steps, Outputs and Assets,

- how deterministic, model-based, human and outcome-based evaluation methods coexist,

- how evaluation remains independent from generation where consequence requires it,

- how benchmarks are designed, versioned, executed, interpreted and retired,

- how Model, Provider, Tool, Agent and Workflow performance is measured,

- how Project-specific and platform-wide evidence remain correctly scoped,

- how factuality, grounding, reasoning, code, image, video, voice, audio and multimodal quality are evaluated,

- how child-facing content receives stronger review,

- how evaluator bias, uncertainty and disagreement are represented,

- how quality evidence affects routing without becoming universal truth,

- how rejected Outputs, retries and fallback remain attributable,

- how accepted Outputs become Asset Candidates without bypassing rights or authority,

- how production monitoring detects quality drift,

- how evaluation learning is governed,

- and how Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy quality system.

Quality is not one universal score.

Quality is the degree to which a bounded Output satisfies the requirements of a specific Capability, request, Project and intended use.

A Model may be excellent for one task and unsuitable for another.

A Provider may be operationally reliable while producing weak Project-specific results.

An Output may be technically valid but factually wrong.

An image may be visually attractive but inconsistent with canonical characters.

A narration may be intelligible but unsuitable for Swedish child-facing content.

A code patch may compile while violating architecture.

A generated Asset may pass quality review while lacking commercial rights.

Evaluation therefore determines whether the Output is acceptable for its intended next state.

It does not replace:

- policy,

- authority,

- rights,

- consent,

- security,

- provenance,

- or publication approval.

This chapter is normative after formal approval.

Implementation and conformance must be verified separately.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 13.6 Quality Is Not User Preference Alone
text:
13.2 Purpose of the Quality System

The Intelligence Fabric may generate or transform:

- text,

- code,

- images,

- audio,

- voice,

- music,

- video,

- structured data,

- plans,

- decisions,

- summaries,

- classifications,

- recommendations,

- and external side effects.

Provider success confirms only that the Provider accepted or completed an operation.

It does not prove that the result:

- satisfies the user’s intent,

- meets the Capability Contract,

- is factually supported,

- follows Project identity,

- preserves canonical meaning,

- is safe for the intended audience,

- is commercially usable,

- or is ready for publication.

The quality system exists to create explicit evidence for those decisions.

13.3 Quality Is Contextual

Quality shall always be interpreted relative to:

- Capability,

- Input,

- Output Contract,

- Project,

- audience,

- consequence,

- Quality Contract,

- environment,

- and intended next action.

A concise caption and a canonical architecture chapter require different evaluation.

A background animation and a close-up of Nova and Pling require different visual criteria.

A private draft and a public news report require different factual standards.

A prototype patch and a production merge require different software validation.

13.4 Quality Is Not Provider Reputation

Provider reputation may support initial confidence.

It does not prove suitability for the current task.

The quality system shall prefer:

- direct evidence,

- Capability-specific benchmarks,

- Project-specific evaluations,

- recent production outcomes,

- and attributable human review.

13.5 Quality Is Not Price

Higher price does not prove higher quality.

Lower price does not prove inadequate quality.

Price may correlate with:

- capacity,

- Features,

- latency,

- or Provider positioning.

Quality must still be measured.

13.6 Quality Is Not User Preference Alone

User preference is an important signal.

It may capture:

- style,

- tone,

- familiarity,

- emotional fit,

- and brand alignment.

Preference alone may not prove:

- factual correctness,

- technical validity,

- safety,

- rights,

- or conformance.

13.7 Quality Is Not Acceptance Alone

An Output may be accepted for practical reasons while known limitations remain.

Acceptance shall preserve:

- criteria,

- exceptions,

- reviewer,

- context,

- and intended use.

One accepted Output shall not automatically prove general Model superiority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.8 Quality Is Not Correctness Alone

Correctness is one quality dimension.

Other dimensions may include:

- relevance,

- completeness,

- clarity,

- style,

- consistency,

- usefulness,

- safety,

- latency,

- reproducibility,

- and user effort.

13.9 Quality Is Not Safety

Safety and quality overlap but remain distinct.

An Output may be:

- safe but low quality,

- high quality but unsafe,

- or both acceptable.

Mandatory safety policy shall not be reduced to a quality score.

13.10 Quality Is Not Rights

An excellent Output may still be ineligible for commercial use.

Rights and consent remain separate mandatory controls.

13.11 Quality Is Not Publication Approval

An Output may pass quality evaluation and still require:

- owner approval,

- legal review,

- brand approval,

- or publication authority.

Quality acceptance prepares the Output for its next permitted state.

13.12 Quality Control Plane

The Quality Control Plane is the governed collection of services and objects responsible for:

- Quality Contracts,

- Evaluation Plans,

- Test Cases,

- Test Suites,

- Benchmarks,

- Evaluators,

- Evaluation Runs,

- Evaluation Results,

- Human Reviews,

- Quality Gates,

- Acceptance Decisions,

- Drift Detection,

- Quality Incidents,

- and Quality Evidence.

It shall integrate with:

- Capability Registry,

- Model Registry,

- Provider Registry,

- Planning,

- Routing,

- Execution,

- Asset Management,

- Memory,

- Intelligence Graph,

- and Observability.

13.13 Canonical Quality Objects

The quality architecture should include or reference:

- Quality Dimension,

- Quality Contract,

- Quality Floor,

- Quality Target,

- Acceptance Criteria,

- Evaluation Plan,

- Evaluation Method,

- Evaluator,

- Test Case,

- Test Suite,

- Benchmark,

- Benchmark Run,

- Evaluation Run,

- Evaluation Result,

- Score,

- Threshold,

- Human Review,

- Reviewer,

- Acceptance Decision,

- Quality Gate,

- Quality Evidence,

- Defect,

- Quality Incident,

- Drift Record,

- Calibration Record,

- and Learning Candidate.

13.14 Quality Dimension

A Quality Dimension is one bounded property evaluated for an Output or resource.

Examples include:

- factual accuracy,

- source support,

- relevance,

- completeness,

- instruction adherence,

- schema validity,

- code correctness,

- character consistency,

- pronunciation,

- motion coherence,

- child appropriateness,

- latency,

- or acceptance probability.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.15 Quality Dimension Identity

Every reusable Quality Dimension shall have stable canonical identity.

The identity shall remain independent of:

- evaluator,

- metric,

- Project,

- Model,

- Provider,

- and current threshold.

13.16 Dimension Definition

A Quality Dimension definition should include:

- dimensionId,

- canonical name,

- description,

- applicable Capabilities,

- measurement types,

- direction,

- known limitations,

- and provenance.

13.17 Dimension Direction

A Dimension shall define whether:

- higher is better,

- lower is better,

- exact match is required,

- pass or fail applies,

- or categorical interpretation is used.

13.18 Dimension Applicability

Not every Dimension applies to every Capability.

For example:

- pronunciation applies to speech,

- character identity applies to visual media,

- compilation applies to code,

- citation support applies to grounded research.

13.19 Quality Contract

A Quality Contract is the canonical set of quality requirements for a request, Plan, Step, Output or Asset.

It shall include or reference:

- qualityContractId,

- scope,

- Capability,

- Dimensions,

- Quality Floors,

- Quality Targets,

- Acceptance Criteria,

- evaluator requirements,

- review requirements,

- confidence requirements,

- allowed exceptions,

- and lifecycle.

13.20 Quality Contract Identity

Every persistent Quality Contract shall have stable identity and version.

Executions and Evaluations shall reference the exact version used.

13.21 Quality Contract Scope

A Quality Contract may apply to:

- Platform,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Workflow,

- Production,

- Plan,

- Step,

- Capability,

- Output type,

- Asset type,

- or audience.

13.22 Platform Quality Contract

A Platform Quality Contract defines universal expectations such as:

- no false completion,

- schema conformance where required,

- evidence preservation,

- and truthful uncertainty.

13.23 Tenant Quality Contract

A Tenant may define organisation-level standards.

Project requirements may be stricter.

13.24 Project Quality Contract

A Project Quality Contract defines Project-specific quality requirements.

Examples include:

- Nova and Pling visual identity,

- The Prompt factual sourcing,

- GainPilot training-language accuracy,

- Omnira architecture conformance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.25 Workflow Quality Contract

A Workflow may define quality requirements for every Run.

The Workflow Contract shall not replace request-specific additions.

13.26 Production Quality Contract

A Production Quality Contract applies to a complete deliverable.

It may aggregate:

- master Asset quality,

- derivative quality,

- narration quality,

- technical conformance,

- and human approval.

13.27 Step Quality Contract

A Step Quality Contract evaluates one bounded Output.

Step-level evaluation supports:

- retry,

- fallback,

- and selective correction.

13.28 Asset Quality Contract

An Asset Quality Contract defines the criteria required before an Asset may become:

- accepted,

- canonical,

- publishable,

- or reusable.

13.29 Quality Contract Composition

The effective Quality Contract may compose requirements from:

1. Platform.

2. Tenant.

3. Project.

4. Capability.

5. Workflow.

6. Production.

7. Plan.

8. Step.

9. Request-specific additions.

A lower scope may strengthen requirements.

It shall not weaken mandatory higher-level Floors without authority.

13.30 Quality Floor

A Quality Floor is the minimum acceptable level for one Dimension or composite gate.

A candidate or Output below the Floor is not acceptable for the defined use.

13.31 Quality Target

A Quality Target is the desired level above the minimum Floor.

Routing and Premium optimisation may use the Target.

13.32 Quality Ceiling

A Quality Ceiling may define a point beyond which additional quality effort is not economically justified.

It may help prevent:

- excessive retries,

- unnecessary premium escalation,

- and perfection loops.

13.33 Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance Criteria define the exact conditions under which an Output may advance.

They may include:

- all mandatory checks pass,

- composite score exceeds threshold,

- human reviewer approves,

- no critical defects remain,

- required rights are valid,

- and required evidence exists.

13.34 Acceptance Criteria Versus Quality Floor

A Quality Floor applies to a Dimension.

Acceptance Criteria define the complete decision logic.

For example:

- every technical check must pass,

- character consistency score must exceed threshold,

- and a human reviewer must approve.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.35 Hard Quality Requirement

A Hard Quality Requirement cannot be traded away.

Examples include:

- valid schema,

- correct file format,

- no missing mandatory section,

- exact canonical character identity,

- or successful type check where required.

13.36 Soft Quality Preference

A Soft Quality Preference influences selection or review without causing automatic rejection.

Examples include:

- slightly warmer tone,

- more cinematic motion,

- shorter response,

- or more energetic pacing.

13.37 Critical Quality Dimension

A Critical Dimension is one whose failure blocks acceptance.

Examples may include:

- factual support for public news,

- safety for child-facing media,

- compilation for production code,

- consent for a cloned voice.

13.38 Advisory Quality Dimension

An Advisory Dimension provides useful information but does not alone determine acceptance.

13.39 Composite Quality Requirement

Several Dimensions may form a composite requirement.

The composition rule shall be explicit.

13.40 Quality Threshold

A Threshold maps a Score or categorical result to a decision boundary.

It shall include:

- thresholdId,

- Dimension,

- scope,

- value,

- comparison,

- confidence requirement,

- version,

- and provenance.

13.41 Static Threshold

A Static Threshold remains fixed until governance changes it.

13.42 Calibrated Threshold

A Calibrated Threshold may be adjusted based on validated evaluation evidence.

Changes require versioning.

13.43 Project-Specific Threshold

A Project may require stricter or differently weighted thresholds.

13.44 Audience-Specific Threshold

Public, child-facing, medical, financial or high-impact use may require stronger thresholds.

13.45 Environment-Specific Threshold

Development may permit lower acceptance for experiments.

Production shall use approved production thresholds.

13.46 Evaluation

Evaluation is the governed process of measuring an Output, resource or system against defined criteria.

Evaluation may be:

- deterministic,

- statistical,

- model-based,

- human,

- comparative,

- adversarial,

- operational,

- or outcome-based.

13.47 Evaluation Target

An Evaluation Target may be:

- Output,

- Asset,

- Model Version,

- Model Deployment,

- Provider,

- Tool,

- Adapter,

- Agent,

- Workflow,

- Plan,

- Routing Profile,

- or complete Production.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.48 Evaluation Plan

An Evaluation Plan defines how a target shall be evaluated.

It shall include or reference:

- evaluationPlanId,

- target type,

- Quality Contract,

- Evaluation Methods,

- Evaluators,

- Test Cases,

- sampling,

- thresholds,

- review rules,

- disagreement handling,

- cost,

- deadline,

- and provenance.

13.49 Evaluation Plan Identity

Every persistent Evaluation Plan shall have stable identity and version.

13.50 Evaluation Plan Scope

Evaluation Plans may be:

- production-specific,

- Capability-specific,

- Project-specific,

- benchmark-specific,

- or continuous-monitoring plans.

13.51 Evaluation Method

An Evaluation Method defines the procedure used to measure one or more Dimensions.

Methods may include:

- exact comparison,

- schema validation,

- static analysis,

- test execution,

- metric calculation,

- model grading,

- pairwise comparison,

- rubric review,

- human checklist,

- expert assessment,

- user feedback,

- and business-outcome analysis.

13.52 Deterministic Evaluation

Deterministic Evaluation produces the same result for the same Inputs and evaluator version under defined conditions.

Examples include:

- JSON schema validation,

- checksum verification,

- resolution check,

- duration check,

- compilation,

- type checking,

- and unit tests.

13.53 Statistical Evaluation

Statistical Evaluation measures performance across a sample.

Examples include:

- success rate,

- average score,

- confidence interval,

- error distribution,

- and percentile latency.

13.54 Model-Based Evaluation

Model-Based Evaluation uses one Model or model system to evaluate another Output or resource.

It may assess:

- relevance,

- style,

- factual support,

- visual consistency,

- or rubric conformance.

It shall preserve evaluator identity and limitations.

13.55 Human Evaluation

Human Evaluation uses an authorised person to assess quality.

It may be required for:

- creative judgement,

- brand identity,

- child-facing suitability,

- nuanced language,

- high-consequence claims,

- and publication readiness.

13.56 Comparative Evaluation

Comparative Evaluation ranks or selects among several Outputs.

It may use:

- pairwise preference,

- tournament,

- rubric scoring,

- or human selection.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.57 Adversarial Evaluation

Adversarial Evaluation deliberately tests known weaknesses.

Examples include:

- prompt injection,

- malformed Input,

- ambiguous source,

- edge-case code,

- difficult character pose,

- or multilingual pronunciation.

13.58 Operational Evaluation

Operational Evaluation measures production behaviour such as:

- availability,

- retry rate,

- latency,

- cost variance,

- unknown-outcome rate,

- and acceptance rate.

13.59 Outcome-Based Evaluation

Outcome-Based Evaluation examines whether the Output achieved a later Project or business objective.

Examples include:

- user completion,

- audience engagement,

- reduced editing effort,

- or successful deployment.

Outcome evidence shall not be treated as direct proof of every quality Dimension.

13.60 Evaluation Independence

Evaluation should be independent from generation when consequence or bias warrants it.

Independence may mean:

- separate Model,

- separate Provider,

- deterministic test,

- human reviewer,

- or independent evidence source.

13.61 Generator Self-Evaluation

A generator may perform self-checking.

Self-evaluation may improve output.

It shall not be the sole acceptance evidence for high-consequence work.

13.62 Same-Model Evaluation

The same Model Version may evaluate its own Output only when:

- consequence is low,

- independent checks exist where required,

- and bias limitations are accepted.

13.63 Cross-Model Evaluation

A different Model may evaluate the Output.

Different Models may still share:

- Provider bias,

- training data,

- or similar failure modes.

13.64 Cross-Provider Evaluation

A separate Provider may increase independence.

It also changes:

- cost,

- privacy,

- and data custody.

Eligibility must be evaluated.

13.65 Deterministic and Model Composite

A common pattern is:

1. deterministic technical validation,

2. model-based semantic evaluation,

3. human approval where required.

Each layer provides different evidence.

13.66 Evaluation Cost

Evaluation consumes resources.

The Plan and Budget shall include:

- Model cost,

- Tool cost,

- human effort,

- and latency.

13.67 Evaluation Depth

Evaluation depth should reflect:

- consequence,

- cost,

- public exposure,

- irreversibility,

- and uncertainty.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.68 Lightweight Evaluation

Low-risk drafts may use:

- schema validation,

- simple rubric,

- and user review.

13.69 Standard Evaluation

Ordinary production may use:

- deterministic checks,

- model evaluation,

- and sampled human review.

13.70 High-Assurance Evaluation

High-consequence work may require:

- multiple independent evaluators,

- primary-source verification,

- expert review,

- adversarial tests,

- and strict Completion Gates.

13.71 Evaluator

An Evaluator is a governed resource or Principal performing an Evaluation Method.

An Evaluator may be:

- deterministic Tool,

- Model Version,

- human reviewer,

- expert panel,

- external service,

- or outcome-analysis system.

13.72 Evaluator Identity

Every persistent Evaluator shall have stable identity.

The Evaluator shall remain distinct from:

- Evaluation Method,

- Test Suite,

- and Evaluation Result.

13.73 Model Evaluator

A Model Evaluator record should identify:

- Model Version,

- Provider,

- Deployment,

- prompt or rubric version,

- temperature or deterministic settings,

- and known limitations.

13.74 Tool Evaluator

A Tool Evaluator may perform:

- schema validation,

- code tests,

- malware scan,

- media inspection,

- or metric calculation.

Tool Version shall be preserved.

13.75 Human Reviewer

A Human Reviewer is a Principal authorised to evaluate specified quality Dimensions.

Reviewer metadata may include:

- reviewerId,

- role,

- expertise,

- Project scope,

- permitted data,

- and calibration status.

13.76 Expert Reviewer

An Expert Reviewer has domain expertise relevant to the evaluation.

Examples include:

- Swedish language reviewer,

- child-content reviewer,

- software architect,

- legal reviewer,

- or exercise professional.

13.77 Reviewer Assignment

Reviewer assignment shall consider:

- authority,

- expertise,

- Project scope,

- conflict of interest,

- availability,

- and data access.

13.78 Reviewer Independence

A creator may review their own work for low-risk purposes.

High-consequence acceptance may require another reviewer.

13.79 Reviewer Conflict of Interest

A conflict may exist when the reviewer:

- created the Output,

- owns the Provider relationship,

- benefits from acceptance,

- or lacks independence.

The conflict shall be disclosed where material.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.80 Reviewer Calibration

Human and Model Evaluators may require calibration against:

- known examples,

- expert labels,

- or consensus sets.

Calibration evidence shall be versioned.

13.81 Evaluator Qualification

An Evaluator may be qualified for one Dimension but not another.

A visual Model may assess image artefacts but not commercial rights.

A code compiler can validate syntax but not business intent.

13.82 Evaluator Scope

Evaluator scope shall include:

- applicable Capabilities,

- Projects,

- Dimensions,

- consequence levels,

- and environments.

13.83 Evaluator Lifecycle

Evaluator lifecycle may include:

- proposed,

- calibrating,

- approved,

- active,

- restricted,

- degraded,

- suspended,

- deprecated,

- retired,

- and archived.

13.84 Evaluator Drift

Evaluator behaviour may change because of:

- Model update,

- rubric update,

- Tool update,

- reviewer fatigue,

- or Project-standard change.

Drift shall be monitored where material.

13.85 Evaluation Rubric

A Rubric defines how quality shall be judged.

It should include:

- Dimensions,

- definitions,

- scale,

- examples,

- unacceptable conditions,

- threshold interpretation,

- and reviewer instructions.

13.86 Rubric Identity

Every reusable Rubric shall have stable identity and version.

13.87 Rubric Scale

Scales may include:

- pass or fail,

- categorical,

- ordinal,

- numeric,

- pairwise preference,

- or ranked choice.

13.88 Numeric Scale

A numeric scale shall define:

- minimum,

- maximum,

- meaning,

- direction,

- and threshold.

13.89 Categorical Scale

Categories may include:

- unacceptable,

- weak,

- acceptable,

- strong,

- excellent,

- or unknown.

Category meaning shall be explicit.

13.90 Binary Evaluation

Pass or fail is appropriate for strict requirements.

Binary results may hide nuance and should be supplemented where useful.

13.91 Pairwise Preference

Pairwise evaluation compares Output A with Output B.

It shall define:

- criteria,

- tie handling,

- order randomisation,

- and evaluator identity.

13.92 Ranking Evaluation

Ranking orders several candidates.

Rankings shall remain scoped to the Test Cases and criteria used.

13.93 Rubric Examples

Examples may illustrate:

- passing result,

- borderline result,

- critical failure,

- and known ambiguity.

Examples support consistent evaluation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.94 Rubric Leakage

Benchmark rubrics and expected answers may leak into generation systems.

Leakage can invalidate results.

The architecture should separate production prompts from protected benchmark material where appropriate.

13.95 Evaluation Input

Evaluation Input may include:

- target Output,

- source Inputs,

- Capability Contract,

- Quality Contract,

- rubric,

- reference answer,

- canonical Asset references,

- provenance,

- and allowed context.

13.96 Evaluation Context Minimisation

Evaluators should receive only the context necessary to judge the target.

Excess context may:

- leak protected data,

- bias the evaluation,

- or increase cost.

13.97 Blind Evaluation

Blind Evaluation hides selected information such as:

- Provider,

- Model,

- Candidate order,

- or creator

to reduce bias.

13.98 Provider-Blind Evaluation

Provider labels should be hidden when judging output quality unless Provider identity is itself relevant.

13.99 Model-Blind Evaluation

Model names should be hidden during comparative review where practical.

13.100 Project-Aware Evaluation

Some evaluations require Project context.

Nova and Pling consistency cannot be judged without canonical references.

13.101 Evaluation Run

An Evaluation Run is one execution of an Evaluation Plan or Method.

It shall include or reference:

- evaluationRunId,

- Evaluation Plan,

- target,

- evaluator,

- Inputs,

- rubric,

- Test Cases,

- environment,

- status,

- cost,

- start,

- completion,

- and provenance.

13.102 Evaluation Run Identity

Every Evaluation Run shall have stable identity.

13.103 Evaluation Attempt

An Evaluation Run may contain several Attempts because of:

- evaluator failure,

- retry,

- or independent repetition.

Attempts shall remain visible.

13.104 Evaluation Run Lifecycle

States may include:

- proposed,

- queued,

- running,

- awaiting reviewer,

- partially complete,

- complete,

- failed,

- cancelled,

- disputed,

- superseded,

- and archived.

13.105 Evaluation Result

An Evaluation Result records the outcome of an Evaluation Run.

It shall include or reference:

- evaluationResultId,

- target,

- Evaluator,

- Dimension,

- Score,

- confidence,

- evidence,

- defects,

- threshold result,

- explanation,

- and time.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.106 Score

A Score is a measured or judged value for one Dimension or composite.

It shall identify:

- scale,

- direction,

- evaluator,

- confidence,

- and interpretation.

13.107 Score Confidence

Confidence reflects uncertainty in the Evaluation Result.

It may depend on:

- evaluator calibration,

- evidence sufficiency,

- sample size,

- ambiguity,

- and disagreement.

13.108 Unknown Score

When the Evaluator cannot judge reliably, the result shall be unknown or insufficient evidence.

It shall not be replaced with a neutral passing value.

13.109 Score Explanation

Material Scores should include an explanation or evidence reference.

13.110 Evidence Attachment

Evidence may include:

- test output,

- source citation,

- screenshot,

- waveform analysis,

- frame comparison,

- code diff,

- compiler output,

- reviewer notes,

- or metric calculation.

13.111 Defect

A Defect is a specific observed failure or weakness.

It shall include or reference:

- defectId,

- target,

- Dimension,

- severity,

- description,

- evidence,

- reproducibility,

- affected scope,

- and status.

13.112 Defect Severity

Severity may include:

- informational,

- minor,

- moderate,

- major,

- critical,

- and blocking.

13.113 Blocking Defect

A Blocking Defect prevents acceptance for the intended use.

13.114 Known Limitation

A Known Limitation may be accepted for a bounded use.

It shall remain visible in the Acceptance Decision.

13.115 Defect Reproducibility

Defects may be:

- always reproducible,

- intermittent,

- input-specific,

- resource-specific,

- or unknown.

13.116 Defect Ownership

A Defect may originate from:

- Model,

- Provider,

- Adapter,

- prompt,

- Input,

- Tool,

- Plan,

- data,

- or evaluation system.

Ownership shall not be assumed prematurely.

13.117 Defect Correction

Correction may involve:

- new instructions,

- retry,

- different Model,

- different Provider,

- deterministic post-processing,

- human editing,

- or revised Input.

13.118 Defect Waiver

An authorised reviewer may waive a non-critical Defect for a specific use.

The waiver shall include:

- reason,

- scope,

- validity,

- and residual risk.

13.119 Defect Closure

A Defect closes only when:

- corrected,

- accepted with waiver,

- obsolete,

- or target retired.

Closure shall preserve evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.120 Acceptance Decision

An Acceptance Decision determines whether an evaluated target may advance.

It shall include or reference:

- acceptanceDecisionId,

- target,

- Quality Contract,

- Evaluation Results,

- decision,

- approver or policy,

- conditions,

- exceptions,

- intended next state,

- validity,

- and provenance.

13.121 Acceptance States

Acceptance states may include:

- accepted,

- accepted with conditions,

- accepted for limited use,

- revision required,

- rejected,

- unresolved,

- expired,

- and superseded.

13.122 Accepted

Accepted means the target satisfies the defined Acceptance Criteria for the intended use.

13.123 Accepted With Conditions

The target may advance only under stated conditions.

Examples include:

- human review before publication,

- internal use only,

- one Project only,

- or visible disclaimer.

13.124 Limited-Use Acceptance

An Output may be accepted for:

- draft,

- preview,

- internal discussion,

- or test

but not for final publication.

13.125 Revision Required

The target is not yet acceptable but may become acceptable through correction.

13.126 Rejected

The target fails mandatory criteria or is unsuitable for the intended use.

13.127 Unresolved

Evidence is insufficient or Evaluators disagree materially.

13.128 Acceptance Validity

Acceptance may expire after:

- Output mutation,

- Model or source change,

- rights change,

- Project standard change,

- or defined period.

13.129 Acceptance Scope

Acceptance shall identify whether it applies to:

- one exact Output,

- one Asset Version,

- one derivative class,

- one Project,

- one audience,

- or one use.

13.130 Acceptance Does Not Propagate Automatically

Acceptance of one Output shall not automatically accept:

- edited versions,

- translated versions,

- derivatives,

- or later Provider regenerations.

13.131 Quality Gate

A Quality Gate is an enforceable control that evaluates Acceptance Criteria before progression.

It shall include or reference:

- qualityGateId,

- target,

- Quality Contract,

- required Evaluations,

- decision logic,

- pass path,

- fail path,

- timeout,

- and provenance.

13.132 Gate Types

Quality Gates may be:

- automatic,

- human,

- composite,

- blocking,

- advisory,

- or conditional.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
13.133 Blocking Gate

A Blocking Gate prevents downstream execution until passed.

13.134 Advisory Gate

An Advisory Gate produces warning or recommendation without blocking.

13.135 Composite Gate

A Composite Gate combines several Evaluation Results.

Its decision logic shall be explicit.

13.136 Gate Failure Path

Failure may trigger:

- retry,

- fallback,

- human review,

- revision,

- partial acceptance,

- or rejection.

13.137 Gate Timeout

A Gate awaiting human review or external evaluation may time out.

Timeout shall not fabricate acceptance.

13.138 Gate Re-Evaluation

A corrected target shall receive a new Evaluation Run.

Old results shall remain linked to the prior target version.

13.139 Benchmark

A Benchmark is a governed collection of Test Cases, Evaluation Methods and interpretation rules used to compare resource or system performance.

It shall include or reference:
