14.496 The Prompt Publication Unknown Outcome

A publication request times out after submission.

The system shall:

- block duplicate publication,

- query the platform,

- inspect target account,

- resolve the external post ID,

- and confirm visibility.

A second publication Attempt is unsafe until reconciliation.

14.497 Applied Example — GainPilot Reel Voice Failure

A voice Provider rejects the narration because of temporary quota exhaustion.

The Plan may:

- wait for quota reset,

- use another approved voice Provider,

- use a local voice Model,

- or deliver caption-only draft.

The selected degradation shall remain explicit.

14.498 Applied Example — Omnira Code Worker Crash

A code-analysis worker crashes after generating a patch but before recording completion.

Recovery shall inspect:

- worktree,

- file changes,

- test state,

- Execution records,

- and patch checksum.

The system shall not regenerate blindly or claim no work occurred.

14.499 Omnira Repository Side Effect

If a commit or push operation has uncertain outcome:

- inspect local Git state,

- inspect remote branch,

- inspect commit hash,

- and reconcile before retry.

Repository mutation requires exact evidence.

14.500 Applied Example — Local Model Node Offline

A Local Only analysis is scheduled on a user-controlled Node.

If the Node is offline:

- no external fallback is permitted,

- the Plan may wait,

- notify the user,

- use another approved local Node,

- or fail with no route.

Privacy remains stronger than availability.

14.501 Applied Example — Credential Expiry During Long Job

A Provider job starts with a valid Credential.

The Credential expires before callback reconciliation.

The system shall distinguish:

- Provider job state,

- callback authentication,

- and Account access.

Credential renewal may be required to retrieve the Output.

The job shall not be marked failed merely because later authentication expired.

14.502 Applied Example — Duplicate Webhook

A Provider sends the same completion callback three times.

Deduplication shall ensure that Omnira creates:

- one Output ingestion,

- one Cost reconciliation,

- one Step-completion transition,

- and one Asset candidate.

All callback receipts may remain preserved.

14.503 Applied Example — Provider Returns Success but Missing File

The Provider reports success.

The download URL returns no file.

The operation is not complete.

The system shall enter:

- Output missing,

- reconciliation,

- or Provider Incident

rather than accepting success.

14.504 Applied Example — Provider Charges but Reports Failure

The Provider reports failed generation but consumes credits.

The system shall preserve:

- failed Execution,

- confirmed or provisional cost,

- refund eligibility,

- and Provider evidence.

Failure does not erase economic impact.

14.505 Applied Example — Human-Assisted Recovery

A human operator performs an OpenArt generation during an API outage.

The workflow shall record:

- approved Account,

- instructions,

- manual job reference,

- spend,

- downloaded Output,

- and reviewer.

The recovery path remains human-assisted.

14.506 Anti-Pattern — Retry Every Error

Policy, authority and validation failures shall not be retried blindly.

14.507 Anti-Pattern — Timeout Equals Failure

External work may still have completed.

14.508 Anti-Pattern — Timeout Equals Cancellation

Stopping local waiting does not cancel the Provider job.

14.509 Anti-Pattern — Unknown Outcome Becomes Failed

Unknown shall remain explicit until reconciled.

14.510 Anti-Pattern — Unknown Outcome Becomes Success

Completion requires evidence.

14.511 Anti-Pattern — Retry Without Idempotency

Consequential or paid retries require duplicate-effect protection.

14.512 Anti-Pattern — Unbounded Retry

Every retry path shall terminate or escalate.

14.513 Anti-Pattern — Retry Budget Hidden

Retries consume economic and latency resources.

14.514 Anti-Pattern — Retry Storm

Simultaneous retries shall be controlled.

14.515 Anti-Pattern — Immediate Retry on Rate Limit

Backoff and Provider guidance shall be respected.

14.516 Anti-Pattern — Fallback Without Revalidation

Fallback remains subject to all original mandatory constraints.

14.517 Anti-Pattern — Same Failure Domain Called Redundant

Shared Provider, region or Account may defeat fallback.

14.518 Anti-Pattern — Private Fallback to Ordinary Cloud

Privacy shall not weaken silently.

14.519 Anti-Pattern — Fallback Lowers Quality Floor

Degradation requires explicit permission.

Material alternatives require replanning.

One scoped failure shall not disable unrelated resources.

14.522 Anti-Pattern — Circuit Closes on Timer Alone

Recovery requires fresh evidence.

14.523 Anti-Pattern — Health Without Freshness

Stale health shall not be treated as current.

14.524 Anti-Pattern — Liveness Equals Readiness

A running process may still be unable to serve safe work.

14.525 Anti-Pattern — Readiness Equals Eligibility

Technical readiness does not bypass policy.

14.526 Anti-Pattern — Provider Status as Sole Truth

Observed Account and Connection state remain necessary.

14.527 Anti-Pattern — Queue Means Guaranteed Completion

Queued work may still fail or expire.

14.528 Anti-Pattern — Queue Redelivery Duplicates Effect

Internal state replay must remain separate from external re-execution.

Expired owners may still act.

Concurrent updates require version-aware resolution.

14.533 Anti-Pattern — Compensation Equals Rollback

External effects may remain partially irreversible.

14.534 Anti-Pattern — Recovery Grants New Authority

Emergency restoration remains bounded.

Restart does not repair corrupted or ambiguous state.

14.536 Anti-Pattern — Backup Without Restore Test

14.537 Anti-Pattern — Backup in Same Failure Domain

14.538 Anti-Pattern — Recovered Service Receives Full Traffic Immediately

Readiness and canary validation are required.

14.539 Anti-Pattern — Failover Without State Reconciliation

Duplicate or missing work may result.

14.540 Anti-Pattern — Split-Brain Side Effects

Multiple owners shall not publish or mutate the same target concurrently.

Local hardware and storage require health and recovery.

Human availability is a real dependency.

Failure ownership shall remain accurate.

14.544 Anti-Pattern — Partial Completion Presented as Complete

Completion Contract remains authoritative.

14.545 Anti-Pattern — Partial Failure Deletes Valid Work

Accepted Outputs should be preserved where policy permits.

Provider-wide averages may hide Account or Capability failure.

14.551 Anti-Pattern — Uptime Equals User Success

Output quality and verified completion still matter.

14.556 Future Reliability Architecture

Future versions may support:

- multi-region execution,

- cross-cloud failover,

- federated local-node recovery,

- predictive failure detection,

- adaptive circuit breakers,

- automated rollback,

- state-machine verification,

- formal side-effect modelling,

- Provider reliability markets,

- self-healing infrastructure,

- and privacy-preserving distributed continuity.

Future evolution must preserve:

- truthful state,

- bounded authority,

- exact scope,

- and evidence.

14.557 Predictive Failure Detection

The Fabric may predict:

- Provider degradation,

- credit exhaustion,

- Node failure,

- or queue overload.

Predictions shall not be represented as certainty.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
14.558 Proactive Rerouting

Upcoming failure risk may justify rerouting before failure.

The decision shall preserve evidence and cost.

14.559 Adaptive Timeout

Timeouts may adapt based on recent latency.

Hard maximums remain governed.

14.560 Adaptive Retry

Retry behaviour may adapt to failure evidence.

It shall not exceed approved Attempts or Budget.

14.561 Adaptive Circuit Breaker

Thresholds may adapt to traffic and baseline.

Critical safety controls remain deterministic.

14.562 Multi-Region Provider Routing

Future routing may use multiple regions while preserving:

- data residency,

- Account,

- and pricing.

14.563 Cross-Cloud Recovery

Managed infrastructure may recover across independent cloud Providers.

14.564 Federated Local Recovery

User devices and private servers may share encrypted recovery metadata without sharing prohibited data.

14.565 State-Machine Verification

Critical state transitions may be formally verified or exhaustively tested.

14.566 Recovery Automation

More recovery Steps may become automated after repeated verified success.

14.567 Human Authority in Recovery

Automation shall not eliminate human authority over high-impact recovery actions.

14.568 Reliability Success Criteria

The reliability architecture succeeds when:

- failures are classified accurately,

- retries are bounded,

- timeouts do not create false conclusions,

- duplicate effects are prevented,

- unknown outcomes are reconciled,

- fallback preserves governance,

- partial work remains truthful,

- state survives restart,

- recovery is tested,

- and users can understand what happened.

14.569 Reliability Failure Conditions

The architecture is non-conformant when:

- unknown outcome is collapsed into success or failure,

- retries are unbounded,

- duplicate side effects occur without detection,

- fallback weakens mandatory policy,

- queue replay duplicates external work,

- recovery erases history,

- backups are untested,

- stale workers can commit consequential state,

- or Provider success is treated as durable Omnira completion.

14.570 Canonical Reliability Requirement Contract

The following requirements define the canonical Reliability Requirement:

1. Every consequential Capability SHALL define reliability expectations.

3. It SHALL identify scope.

4. It SHALL identify durability requirements.

5. It SHALL identify retry behaviour.

6. It SHALL identify fallback expectations.

11. Lower-level requirements SHALL NOT weaken mandatory higher-level requirements.

12. Requirements SHALL remain distinct from Routing Profile.

13. Requirements SHALL remain distinct from Quality Contract.

14. Requirements SHALL remain distinct from Budget.

15. Changes SHALL be versioned.

16. Executions SHALL reference the applicable Version.

17. High-consequence side effects SHALL require stronger reliability.

18. Local and external resources SHALL use the same canonical requirement model.

14.571 Canonical Failure Contract

1. Every material Failure Event SHALL have stable identity.

9. Timeout SHALL NOT automatically become failure.

10. Unknown outcome SHALL remain a distinct state.

11. Internal defects SHALL remain distinguishable from Provider failures.

12. Account failures SHALL remain distinguishable from Provider failures.

13. Connection failures SHALL remain distinguishable from Model failures.

14. Quality failure SHALL remain distinguishable from transport failure.

15. Failure cost SHALL remain attributable.

16. Failure history SHALL remain immutable.

17. Reclassification SHALL preserve prior interpretation and reason.

14.572 Canonical Retry Contract

The following requirements define canonical retry behaviour:

1. Every retryable operation SHALL use a Retry Policy.

2. Retry Policy SHALL have stable identity and version.

3. Retryable and non-retryable errors SHALL be explicit.

4. Maximum Attempts SHALL be finite.

5. Retry cost SHALL remain inside Budget.

6. Retry time SHALL remain inside deadline.

7. Retry SHALL preserve Idempotency Key where applicable.

8. Unknown outcome SHALL require reconciliation before unsafe retry.

9. Backoff SHALL be explicit.

10. Retry storms SHALL be prevented.

11. Attempt history SHALL remain visible.

12. Same-resource and fallback Attempts SHALL remain distinguishable.

13. Retry exhaustion SHALL produce terminal, fallback or escalation state.

16. Credential failure SHALL require appropriate recovery.

17. Paid retry SHALL create separate economic evidence.

18. Retry SHALL revalidate current eligibility.

19. Retry policy changes SHALL NOT rewrite completed Attempts.

20. Infinite retry SHALL be impossible.

14.573 Canonical Timeout Contract

The following requirements define canonical timeout handling:

1. Every long-running or external operation SHOULD define a Timeout Policy.

2. Timeout Policy SHALL identify applicable phase.

3. Connection, request, job and callback timeouts SHALL remain distinguishable.

4. Timeout SHALL NOT imply external cancellation.

8. Timeout values SHALL reflect Provider and Capability evidence.

9. Timeout changes SHALL be versioned.

10. Human-step timeout SHALL NOT fabricate a response.

11. Total-Step timeout SHALL include retries and waits.

12. Timeout SHALL remain subordinate to hard deadline.

13. Timeout SHALL preserve possible cost exposure.

14. Callback timeout MAY trigger polling.

15. Timeout SHALL NOT authorise duplicate side effect.

16. Provider-directed timing MAY influence policy.

17. Timeout evidence SHALL remain attributable.

18. Stale timeout assumptions SHALL be reviewed.

19. Timeout Incidents SHALL preserve affected Attempts.

20. Timeout handling SHALL remain explainable.

14.574 Canonical Idempotency Contract

The following requirements define canonical idempotency:

1. Consequential side effects SHALL use an Idempotency Key or equivalent control.

2. Paid external job submission SHOULD use idempotency where possible.

3. Idempotency Keys SHALL have explicit scope.

4. Same key with conflicting Inputs SHALL fail.

5. Duplicate requests SHALL NOT create unintended duplicate effects.

6. Idempotency state SHALL be durable.

10. Idempotency SHALL survive worker restart.

11. Idempotency SHALL survive queue redelivery.

14. Unknown outcome SHALL remain attached to the original key.

15. Idempotency SHALL NOT erase separate paid Attempts when they legitimately occurred.

16. Publication SHALL use target-specific duplicate protection.

17. Repository mutation SHALL preserve exact operation identity.

18. Financial actions SHALL require strong idempotency.

19. Idempotency conflicts SHALL be observable.

20. Historical idempotency state SHALL remain auditable.

14.575 Canonical Deduplication Contract

The following requirements define canonical deduplication:

1. Duplicate callbacks SHALL NOT duplicate state transitions.

2. Duplicate queue deliveries SHALL NOT duplicate external effects.

3. Deduplication keys SHALL identify source and scope.

5. Duplicate cost events SHALL NOT duplicate Cost Records.

6. Duplicate Asset events SHALL NOT duplicate Asset admission.

17. Deduplication SHALL NOT replace Idempotency.

18. Deduplication SHALL NOT hide Provider retry cost.

19. Deduplication state SHALL survive restart.

20. Historical processing results SHALL remain queryable.

14.577 Canonical Unknown-Outcome Contract

14.579 Canonical Recovery Contract

1. Every critical service or Workflow SHALL have an approved Recovery Plan or equivalent procedure.

2. Recovery Plans SHALL have stable identity and version.

3. Recovery SHALL identify scope and trigger.

4. Recovery SHALL identify owner.

The following requirements define continuity:

1. Continuity Modes SHALL be explicit.

14.582 Reliability Invariants

The following invariants shall remain true:

- No timeout becomes automatic failure.

- No timeout becomes automatic cancellation.

- No unknown outcome becomes assumed success.

- No unknown outcome becomes assumed failure.

- No retry occurs without a finite bound.

- No consequential retry occurs without duplicate protection.

- No retry escapes Budget or authority.

- No fallback weakens privacy, rights, quality or scope.

- No fallback silently changes Capability meaning.

- No mandatory Pin silently falls back.

- No duplicate callback creates duplicate completion.

- No queue replay duplicates external side effects.

- No stale worker commits after losing ownership.

- No distributed lock is trusted without expiry and fencing where required.

- No compensation is represented as guaranteed rollback.

- No recovered service receives ordinary traffic before validation.

- No backup is considered sufficient without restore testing.

- No partial completion is represented as full completion.

- No recovery rewrites original execution history.

- No service outage authorises bypass of the Fabric.

14.583 Stage 1 Reliability Objective

Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy reliability foundation required for representative local and external intelligence execution.

The objective is not to provide global active-active infrastructure.

Stage 1 shall prove:

- durable execution state,

- canonical failure classification,

- bounded retries,

- timeouts,

- idempotency,

- deduplication,

- health,

- circuit breakers,

- fallback,

- unknown-outcome handling,

- reconciliation,

- checkpoints,

- recovery,

- and continuity modes.

Stage 1 should implement or represent:

- Reliability Requirement,

- Failure Event,

- Health Observation,

- Retry Policy,

- Timeout Policy,

- Idempotency Record,

- Deduplication Record,

- Circuit Breaker,

- Fallback Decision,

- Unknown-Outcome Record,

- Reconciliation Record,

- Checkpoint,

- Recovery Plan,

- Recovery Run,

- and Incident.

- validation,

- policy,

- authentication,

- authorisation,

- budget,

- quota,

- rate limit,

- timeout,

- network,

- Provider outage,

- data integrity,

- cancellation,

- unknown outcome,

- and internal defect.

2. Simulated duplicate callback remains idempotent.

3. Simulated worker crash preserves state.

4. Simulated queue redelivery does not duplicate effect.

5. Simulated credential expiry blocks new execution.

6. Simulated Provider outage opens circuit.

7. Simulated database unavailability pauses unsafe work.

8. Simulated stale worker write is rejected.

9. Simulated fallback preserves policy.

10. Simulated cost-service outage blocks paid work.

11. Simulated quality-service outage blocks acceptance.

12. Simulated policy-service outage fails closed.

13. Simulated restore returns valid state.

14. Simulated local Node loss preserves private policy.

15. Chaos evidence produces corrective actions.

14.617 Reliability Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this chapter only when:

- execution state is durable,

- failures are classified,

- retries are finite,

- timeouts remain truthful,

- duplicate effects are controlled,

- unknown outcomes are first-class,

- fallback is fully governed,

- recovery preserves history,

- Provider and internal state can be reconciled,

- and continuity modes remain explicit.

A generic try-catch block is not a reliability architecture.

A second Provider is not automatically a valid fallback.

A queue is not automatically durable execution.

A backup is not recovery until restoration is tested.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
14.618 Closing Statement

Reliability is the discipline that allows the Intelligence Fabric to remain trustworthy when the world around it is not.

Providers time out.

Callbacks disappear.

Credentials expire.

Queues redeliver.

Workers crash.

Models are retired.

Local Nodes go offline.

Budgets become exhausted.

Users cancel work.

Networks partition.

Human operators make mistakes.

External systems report success while Outputs are missing.

Charges appear before results.

Results appear after local timeouts.

The Fabric must not hide that uncertainty.

The request defines the objective.

The Plan defines the permitted execution path.

The Reliability Requirement defines the expected resilience.

The Retry Policy defines bounded repetition.

The Timeout Policy defines waiting boundaries.

The Idempotency Record prevents duplicate effects.

The Circuit Breaker limits repeated harm.

The Fallback Policy defines approved alternatives.

The Unknown-Outcome Record preserves uncertainty.

The Reconciliation process compares internal state with external reality.

The Checkpoint preserves safe progress.

The Recovery Plan restores valid operation.

The Incident preserves the complete failure and response history.

For Familje-Stunden, reliability means that one failed video scene does not destroy the entire Nova and Pling production, duplicate credits are not consumed blindly, accepted scenes remain safe and no corrupted character Asset reaches the final master.

For The Prompt, reliability means that search outages do not produce fabricated current news, missing publication callbacks do not create duplicate posts and factual Gates remain binding during disruption.

For GainPilot, reliability means that economical production may pause, reroute or degrade honestly without losing Project state or spending control.

For Omnira, reliability means that code, Providers, Models, local Nodes, queues, credentials, Budgets and human actions can fail without the platform losing truth.

Success is useful.

Failure is expected.

Uncertainty is valid.

Recovery is governed.

No retry without classification.

No fallback without eligibility.

No timeout without truthful state.

No side effect without idempotency.

No unknown outcome without reconciliation.

No recovery without evidence.

No restored service without validation.

The user retains authority.

The Project retains continuity.

Omnira retains operational truth.

The Fabric remains dependable not because failure disappears, but because failure is bounded, visible and recoverable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical architecture, governance model, lifecycle, contracts and operational responsibilities for latency, capacity, scheduling, admission control, concurrency, quotas and workload prioritisation within the Omnira Intelligence Fabric.

It establishes:

- how latency is measured across complete intelligence work rather than only Provider response time,

- how deadlines, target completion times and service objectives remain distinct,

- how interactive, real-time, batch, background, scheduled and long-running workloads are classified,

- how available, reserved, committed and effective capacity remain distinct,

- how Provider, Account, Connection, Deployment, Runtime Node, Tool, queue and human capacity are represented,

- how work is admitted, queued, prioritised, scheduled, paused, resumed and cancelled,

- how Project and Tenant fairness are preserved,

- how concurrency limits prevent overload and economic harm,

- how rate limits, quotas, credits and Budgets remain separate,

- how scarce local and external resources are reserved,

- how scheduling remains subordinate to authority, privacy, rights, quality and Budget,

- how deadline-aware and priority-aware scheduling operate without creating starvation,

- how queue backpressure and load shedding preserve critical work,

- how capacity forecasts support planning without being treated as guarantees,

- how scheduled and recurring work revalidates its conditions before execution,

- how latency and capacity evidence influence routing,

- how human-review and manual-assisted capacity are represented,

- how degraded capacity is handled truthfully,

- and how Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy scheduling and capacity foundation.

The Intelligence Fabric shall not treat every request as equally urgent.

It shall not treat every available Provider slot as authorised capacity.

It shall not treat subscription quota as Budget.

It shall not treat a queue as infinite storage.

It shall not treat a deadline as permission to bypass governance.

It shall not create high priority merely because an Agent requests it.

It shall not allow one Project, Tenant, Provider or Workflow to consume all shared capacity by convenience.

This chapter is normative after formal approval.

Implementation and operational conformance must be verified separately.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
sectionTitles: 15.2 Purpose of Latency and Capacity Governance
text:
15.2 Purpose of Latency and Capacity Governance

Intelligence work consumes bounded resources.

These resources may include:

- Provider request capacity,

- Model Deployment concurrency,

- token throughput,

- image-generation slots,

- video-generation jobs,

- speech-synthesis characters,

- search queries,

- queue workers,

- local CPU,

- local GPU,

- device battery,

- memory,

- storage,

- network bandwidth,

- human review time,

- and Project operating Budget.

Demand may exceed available capacity.

Capacity may also change without warning because of:

- Provider outages,

- quota exhaustion,

- rate limits,

- Account suspension,

- local device shutdown,

- competing Projects,

- scheduled maintenance,

- cost policy,

- or degraded Model Deployment.

The scheduling architecture exists to determine:

- whether work may start,

- when it should start,

- which resource should receive it,

- how much capacity it may consume,

- how long it may wait,

- whether it should be delayed, rerouted or rejected,

- and how other work remains protected.

15.3 Scheduling Is Not Planning

Planning defines:

- required Steps,

- dependencies,

- resource requirements,

- deadlines,

- Budgets,

- and Completion Contracts.

Scheduling determines when a Ready Step may use eligible capacity.

The Scheduler shall not:

- add new Steps,

- remove mandatory Steps,

- increase Budget,

- weaken quality,

- or change Capability meaning.

Scheduling changes time and allocation.

It does not change intent.

15.4 Scheduling Is Not Routing

Routing selects an eligible Resource Candidate.

Scheduling allocates time and capacity to that Candidate or to an eligible candidate class.

Routing may select:

- one external Provider Deployment,

- one local Runtime Node,

- or one human-assisted process.

Scheduling determines when the selected path can execute.

Late scheduling may trigger rerouting when the selected resource is no longer feasible.

15.5 Scheduling Is Not Authority

A high-priority or urgent request does not create:

- Provider permission,

- spending authority,

- publication authority,

- cross-Project access,

- or privacy exception.

The Scheduler may reorder eligible work.

It shall not grant authority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.6 Scheduling Is Not Economic Governance

Budget determines whether economic value may be consumed.

Scheduling determines when capacity may be used.

A request may have Budget but no capacity.

A resource may have capacity but no approved Budget.

Both conditions may be required.

15.7 Scheduling Is Not Reliability

Reliability governs:

- failure,

- retry,

- fallback,

- recovery,

- and continuity.

Scheduling governs:

- admission,

- order,

- capacity allocation,

- and timing.

The two systems interact.

They shall remain conceptually distinct.

15.8 Scheduling Is Not Provider Queueing

A Provider may maintain its own internal queue.

Omnira shall still maintain its own canonical scheduling and execution state.

Provider queue position is external evidence.

It is not the complete scheduling model.

15.9 Latency

Latency is the elapsed time between defined points in a request or execution lifecycle.

Latency shall always identify:

- start event,

- end event,

- scope,

- and measurement source.

Without those properties, a latency value is ambiguous.

15.10 End-to-End Latency

End-to-End Latency measures the complete user- or system-observed time from request acceptance to defined completion.

It may include:

- validation,

- policy evaluation,

- approval,

- planning,

- routing,

- queue wait,

- Provider processing,

- retries,

- ingestion,

- evaluation,

- human review,

- and final delivery.

15.11 Execution Latency

Execution Latency measures the time spent performing a specific Execution.

It may exclude:

- planning,

- approval,

- and earlier queue delay.

15.12 Attempt Latency

Attempt Latency measures one Attempt from dispatch to terminal or unknown state.

15.13 Provider Latency

Provider Latency measures the time attributable to the external Provider operation.

It may include:

- request transport,

- Provider queue,

- processing,

- and response delivery.

15.14 Queue Latency

Queue Latency is the time between a Step becoming eligible for scheduling and the start of execution.

15.15 Planning Latency

Planning Latency is the time required to create and validate an Execution Plan.

15.16 Routing Latency

Routing Latency is the time required to create a Selection Decision.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.17 Approval Latency

Approval Latency is the time spent awaiting valid human or policy approval.

15.18 Evaluation Latency

Evaluation Latency is the time required to produce mandatory Evaluation Results and Acceptance Decisions.

15.19 Human Latency

Human Latency is the time spent awaiting or performing a Human Action or Review Step.

15.20 Ingestion Latency

Ingestion Latency is the time required to retrieve, validate and store external Output after Provider completion.

15.21 Callback Latency

Callback Latency is the time from external state change to receipt and processing of the corresponding callback.

15.22 Publication Latency

Publication Latency is the time from authorised publication submission to verified external visibility or confirmed target state.

15.23 Time to First Result

Time to First Result measures when the first usable partial result becomes available.

15.24 Time to Final Result

Time to Final Result measures when the complete defined Completion Contract is satisfied.

15.25 Time to Accepted Result

Time to Accepted Result includes required evaluation and approval.

It is often more meaningful than Provider completion time.

15.26 Time to Durable Result

Time to Durable Result includes required ingestion, storage and evidence preservation.

15.27 Time to Verified Side Effect

Time to Verified Side Effect includes external submission and reconciliation.

For consequential actions, verification is part of completion.

15.28 Latency Distribution

Latency shall be understood as a distribution rather than one average.

Relevant measures may include:

- median,

- p75,

- p90,

- p95,

- p99,

- maximum,

- and timeout rate.

15.29 Average Latency Limitation

Average latency may hide:

- long-tail delays,

- starvation,

- queue spikes,

- and severe outliers.

Tail latency shall be measured where consequence warrants it.

15.30 Latency Confidence

Latency estimates shall include confidence based on:

- sample size,

- freshness,

- workload similarity,

- resource identity,

- and operational volatility.

15.31 Latency Freshness

Historical latency may become stale after:

- Model update,

- Provider capacity change,

- Account tier change,

- local hardware change,

- Adapter change,

- or queue-policy change.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.32 Latency Objective

A Latency Objective defines a desired completion or response time.

It may be:

- target,

- percentile objective,

- or bounded range.

15.33 Latency Requirement

A Latency Requirement defines a mandatory time constraint.

Examples include:

- interactive response within five seconds,

- first audio chunk within one second,

- final episode by a specific publication window,

- or code analysis before a meeting.

15.34 Latency Target

A Latency Target is preferred but may be missed without automatic request failure.

15.35 Hard Deadline

A Hard Deadline is a latest completion time after which the result no longer satisfies the request.

Hard deadlines shall be explicit.

15.36 Soft Deadline

A Soft Deadline is a preferred completion time.

Missing it may reduce value but does not automatically invalidate the Output.

15.37 Start Deadline

A Start Deadline defines the latest time by which work may begin to remain feasible.

15.38 Completion Deadline

A Completion Deadline defines the latest acceptable completion time.

15.39 Publication Window

A Publication Window defines an approved time interval for external release.

It does not by itself grant publication authority.

15.40 Scheduling Window

A Scheduling Window defines when a Step may be started.

Examples include:

- overnight local processing,

- business hours,

- low-cost Provider window,

- or user-presence requirement.

15.41 Expiry Time

Expiry defines when a request, Plan, approval, Reservation or scheduled action is no longer valid.

15.42 Deadline Feasibility

The Fabric shall evaluate whether the complete request can meet its deadline.

The estimate should include:

- queue time,

- execution,

- retries,

- fallback,

- evaluation,

- human review,

- ingestion,

- and verification.

15.43 Deadline Infeasibility

When a deadline is not feasible, the system shall:

- explain the conflict,

- propose a valid alternative,

- request revised scope,

- degrade only if permitted,

- or reject admission.

It shall not pretend that the deadline remains achievable.

15.44 Deadline Does Not Override Policy

A deadline shall never justify bypassing:

- privacy,

- authority,

- rights,

- consent,

- Quality Floor,

- or Budget.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.45 Deadline and Quality

The user may approve a lower Quality Target to meet a deadline only when:

- the mandatory Quality Floor remains satisfied,

- the Completion Contract permits it,

- and the change is explicit.

15.46 Deadline and Cost

Faster execution may require a more expensive Candidate.

The increased cost requires available Budget and authority.

15.47 Deadline and Reliability

A deadline-aware Plan should preserve enough time for:

- retry,

- fallback,

- and evaluation.

Selecting a resource with fast median latency but severe tail risk may be inappropriate.

15.48 Capacity

Capacity is the bounded amount of work a resource or system can perform within a defined interval and condition.

Capacity shall identify:

- resource,

- unit,

- period,

- scope,

- availability,

- reservation,

- and confidence.

15.49 Capacity Is Not Availability

A resource may be available but have no remaining capacity.

A resource may have theoretical capacity but be unavailable.

Both conditions matter.

15.50 Capacity Is Not Quota

Capacity describes actual or estimated ability to perform work.

Quota describes an imposed limit on permitted or available usage.

A system may have unused technical capacity but exhausted Provider quota.

15.51 Capacity Is Not Budget

Capacity answers:

Can the work be performed now or within the required period?

Budget answers:

May the economic value be consumed?

15.52 Capacity Is Not Concurrency

Concurrency is the number of operations that may run simultaneously.

Capacity may also include:

- throughput,

- memory,

- total daily jobs,

- tokens per minute,

- or human hours.

15.53 Capacity Unit

Capacity units may include:

- requests per second,

- requests per minute,

- tokens per second,

- tokens per minute,

- images per hour,

- video seconds per day,

- concurrent jobs,

- GPU minutes,

- CPU cores,

- gigabytes,

- queue slots,

- human review minutes,

- or generic workload units.

15.54 Capacity Record

A Capacity Record shall include or reference:

- capacityRecordId,

- resource,

- Capability,

- unit,

- total capacity,

- available capacity,

- reserved capacity,

- committed capacity,

- effective period,

- observedAt,

- source,

- confidence,

- and provenance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.55 Capacity Identity

Every material Capacity Record shall have stable identity or versioned observation identity.

15.56 Total Capacity

Total Capacity is the maximum known or configured capacity under defined conditions.

15.57 Available Capacity

Available Capacity is the portion currently usable for new eligible work.

15.58 Reserved Capacity

Reserved Capacity is held for future or pending work.

15.59 Committed Capacity

Committed Capacity is allocated to active work.

15.60 Effective Capacity

Effective Capacity is the usable capacity after accounting for:

- health,

- policy,

- maintenance,

- reliability reserve,

- concurrency,

- and workload overhead.

15.61 Theoretical Capacity

Theoretical Capacity is a maximum under ideal conditions.

It shall not be represented as ordinary production capacity.

15.62 Sustainable Capacity

Sustainable Capacity is the workload level that can be maintained without unacceptable degradation.

15.63 Burst Capacity

Burst Capacity is temporary capacity above the sustainable level.

It shall define:

- duration,

- recovery,

- cost,

- and risk.

15.64 Reserved Reliability Capacity

Some capacity may be withheld to support:

- retries,

- recovery,

- critical work,

- or Provider failover.

This reserve shall remain visible to governance.

15.65 Provider Capacity

Provider Capacity may depend on:

- Product,

- Account tier,

- region,

- Model,

- queue,

- and Provider-wide demand.

15.66 Provider Account Capacity

One Account may have specific:

- concurrency,

- rate limit,

- queue priority,

- credit balance,

- or contractual capacity.

15.67 Connection Capacity

A Connection may impose:

- transport limits,

- Adapter worker limits,

- or protocol-specific concurrency.

15.68 Model Capacity

Model capacity may include:

- maximum concurrent requests,

- token throughput,

- context limits,

- and generation throughput.

15.69 Deployment Capacity

The same Model Version may have different capacity across Deployments.

15.70 Local Runtime Capacity

Local Runtime capacity may depend on:

- CPU,

- GPU,

- memory,

- thermal state,

- battery,

- storage,

- Model size,

- and competing workloads.

15.71 Runtime Node Capacity

A Runtime Node may expose multiple resource pools.

Examples include:

- CPU pool,

- GPU pool,

- memory pool,

- storage pool,

- and network pool.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.72 Tool Capacity

Tools may have capacity limits such as:

- worker count,

- file-size limit,

- process limit,

- or licensed-seat limit.

15.73 Queue Capacity

Queue Capacity includes:

- message count,

- storage,

- throughput,

- retention,

- and consumer capacity.

15.74 Human Capacity

Human Capacity represents bounded availability for:

- review,

- approval,

- manual Provider operation,

- creative direction,

- or Incident response.

15.75 Human Capacity Is Not Infinite

A Workflow shall not assume immediate human response.

Human scheduling shall account for:

- working hours,

- role,

- availability,

- expertise,

- and workload.

15.76 Approval Capacity

Approval queues may become a bottleneck.

The system should distinguish:

- approval waiting,

- review work,

- and decision authority.

15.77 Evaluation Capacity

Evaluator capacity may include:

- Model throughput,

- Tool workers,

- or human reviewers.

15.78 Storage Capacity

Storage capacity affects:

- Output ingestion,

- checkpointing,

- Asset retention,

- and recovery.

15.79 Network Capacity

Network bandwidth and latency may constrain:

- media upload,

- local-to-cloud transfer,

- and remote Model execution.

15.80 Composite Capacity

A complex Step may depend on several capacity dimensions.

Its effective capacity is constrained by the required bottleneck resource.

15.81 Bottleneck

A Bottleneck is the resource or dependency limiting throughput or completion time.

15.82 Bottleneck Identification

The Fabric should identify whether delay originates from:

- queue,

- Provider,

- local compute,

- approval,

- evaluation,

- storage,

- or another dependency.

15.83 Bottleneck Shift

Optimising one component may move the bottleneck elsewhere.

Capacity planning shall consider end-to-end flow.

15.84 Capacity Observation

Capacity observations may come from:

- Provider headers,

- official limits,

- current queue,

- local telemetry,

- configured limits,

- historical throughput,

- or manual records.

15.85 Capacity Confidence

Capacity confidence may be:

- exact,

- high,

- moderate,

- low,

- inferred,

- or unknown.

15.86 Unknown Capacity

Unknown capacity shall be treated conservatively for:

- expensive,

- high-priority,

- or consequential work.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.87 Capacity Freshness

Operational capacity may change rapidly.

Every observation shall include freshness.

15.88 Capacity Forecast

A Capacity Forecast predicts future availability or demand.

It shall include:

- horizon,

- assumptions,

- expected demand,

- expected supply,

- uncertainty,

- and source data.

15.89 Forecast Is Not Reservation

A forecast does not guarantee capacity.

Reservations or contracts may be required.

15.90 Capacity Planning

Capacity Planning determines whether expected future demand can be served.

It may include:

- workload forecast,

- Provider contracts,

- local hardware planning,

- subscription tier review,

- and human staffing.

15.91 Short-Term Capacity Planning

Short-term planning may cover:

- current day,

- current week,

- active Production,

- or campaign window.

15.92 Long-Term Capacity Planning

Long-term planning may support:

- hardware acquisition,

- Provider diversification,

- managed service design,

- or Tenant growth.

15.93 Capacity Headroom

Capacity Headroom is unused sustainable capacity held for:

- spikes,

- retries,

- recovery,

- and uncertainty.

15.94 Minimum Headroom

Critical services may require a minimum headroom percentage or absolute reserve.

15.95 Capacity Saturation

Saturation occurs when demand approaches or exceeds sustainable capacity.

15.96 Saturation Indicators

Indicators may include:

- queue growth,

- latency increase,

- timeout increase,

- rate limiting,

- memory pressure,

- thermal throttling,

- or human backlog.

15.97 Capacity Overcommitment

Overcommitment allocates more logical demand than physical capacity.

It may be safe only when usage patterns and risk are understood.

15.98 Unsafe Overcommitment

Overcommitment is unsafe when:

- deadlines are hard,

- workloads peak together,

- cancellation is costly,

- or side effects are consequential.

15.99 Capacity Degradation

Capacity may be degraded by:

- Incident,

- maintenance,

- reduced Account tier,

- local battery,

- high temperature,

- or competing work.

15.100 Capacity Recovery

Recovered capacity shall be validated before full scheduling resumes.

15.101 Scheduler

The Scheduler is the Fabric component or governed service responsible for assigning eligible work to time, queue and capacity.

The Scheduler shall have a stable Service Principal identity.

It shall operate only on validated canonical state.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.102 Scheduler Responsibilities

The Scheduler is responsible for:

- receiving schedulable Steps,

- evaluating admission,

- resolving effective priority,

- selecting queue or resource pool,

- reserving required capacity,

- ordering Ready work,

- enforcing concurrency and quota,

- dispatching eligible work,

- delaying infeasible work,

- handling cancellation,

- and preserving scheduling evidence.

15.103 Scheduler Non-Responsibilities

The Scheduler shall not:

- create Capability authority,

- alter Data Classification,

- approve spending,

- lower Quality Floor,

- retrieve raw credentials,

- or mark business outcomes complete.

15.104 Scheduling Request

A Scheduling Request is a canonical request to allocate time and capacity to one Step or operation.

It shall include or reference:

- schedulingRequestId,

- Plan Version,

- Step ID,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- Capability,

- selected or eligible Candidate,

- workload class,

- effective priority,

- earliest start,

- deadline,

- expected duration,

- capacity requirements,

- concurrency requirements,

- Budget Reservation,

- approval state,

- and policy versions.

15.105 Scheduling Request Identity

Every material Scheduling Request shall have stable identity.

Material changes shall create a new version or superseding request.

15.106 Scheduling Decision

A Scheduling Decision shall include or reference:

- schedulingDecisionId,

- Scheduling Request,

- selected queue,

- selected resource pool,

- scheduled start,

- expected completion,

- capacity reservation,

- priority,

- policy,

- fairness decision,

- and provenance.

15.107 Scheduling Decision Validity

A Scheduling Decision may become invalid because of:

- resource failure,

- deadline change,

- Plan amendment,

- quota exhaustion,

- capacity loss,

- or Budget invalidation.

15.108 Scheduling Lifecycle

Scheduling states may include:

- proposed,

- validating,

- admitted,

- queued,

- scheduled,

- dispatching,

- running,

- delayed,

- blocked,

- preempted,

- cancelled,

- expired,

- completed,

- failed,

- and archived.

15.109 Proposed Scheduling State

The work has been submitted but not evaluated for admission.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.110 Validating Scheduling State

The system is verifying:

- dependencies,

- authority,

- Budget,

- policy,

- and capacity requirements.

15.111 Admitted State

The work is permitted to enter the scheduling system.

15.112 Queued State

The work awaits capacity or its permitted start time.

15.113 Scheduled State

A future dispatch time or resource allocation has been selected.

15.114 Dispatching State

The Scheduler is transferring responsibility to the execution worker or external resource.

15.115 Running State

Execution has begun.

15.116 Delayed State

Work has been intentionally postponed.

The delay reason shall be explicit.

15.117 Blocked State

A required condition remains missing.

15.118 Preempted State

Execution or queue position has been interrupted for higher-priority or emergency work according to policy.

15.119 Cancelled State

Future scheduling has been stopped by authority or policy.

15.120 Expired State

The request is no longer valid for dispatch.

15.121 Completed Scheduling State

The Scheduler’s responsibility for the dispatch has completed.

This does not imply the business request completed.

15.122 Admission Control

Admission Control determines whether new work may enter the scheduling system.

It protects:

- capacity,

- deadlines,

- reliability,

- Budgets,

- and fairness.

15.123 Admission Decision

An Admission Decision may be:

- admit,

- admit with conditions,

- defer,

- reject,

- require approval,

- require replanning,

- or require rerouting.

15.124 Admission Requirements

Admission should evaluate:

- valid Plan and Step,

- current authority,

- current policy,

- required Inputs,

- Budget Reservation,

- resource eligibility,

- capacity feasibility,

- deadline feasibility,

- quota,

- and concurrency.

15.125 Conditional Admission

Work may be admitted under conditions such as:

- wait until a window,

- use reduced concurrency,

- use a specific queue,

- or require human review.

15.126 Deferred Admission

Deferred Admission postpones entry until:

- capacity returns,

- approval exists,

- Budget renews,

- quota resets,

- or a scheduled time arrives.

15.127 Rejected Admission

Rejection occurs when the work cannot safely or feasibly enter the system under current conditions.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.128 Admission Is Not Execution

Admitted work may still wait.

Admission only confirms that the system accepts responsibility for scheduling it.

15.129 Admission Overload Protection

When capacity is saturated, the system shall not continue accepting unlimited work without:

- queue limit,

- delay,

- load shedding,

- or rejection.

15.130 Admission and Deadline

Work should not be admitted when available evidence shows that the Hard Deadline cannot be met, unless the user explicitly accepts delayed or degraded delivery.

15.131 Admission and Budget

Paid work shall not be admitted without required economic protection.

15.132 Admission and Human Capacity

A Plan requiring human review should not claim feasible completion when no qualified reviewer is available before the deadline.

15.133 Workload Class

A Workload Class describes the timing and interaction characteristics of work.

Canonical classes may include:

- real-time,

- interactive,

- near-interactive,

- asynchronous,

- batch,

- background,

- scheduled,

- recurring,

- long-running,

- maintenance,

- recovery,

- and emergency.

15.134 Real-Time Workload

Real-time work requires continuous or near-continuous response within a strict latency boundary.

Examples include:

- live voice interaction,

- streaming interpretation,

- or real-time control.

Real-time work requires specialised capacity and fallback.

15.135 Interactive Workload

Interactive work is user-facing and expects a response within seconds or a short period.

Examples include:

- chat reasoning,

- search assistance,

- or approval support.

15.136 Near-Interactive Workload

Near-interactive work may take tens of seconds or several minutes while the user remains engaged.

15.137 Asynchronous Workload

Asynchronous work may complete later without holding an active user session.

Examples include:

- video generation,

- document processing,

- or large code analysis.

15.138 Batch Workload

Batch work processes a bounded collection of items.

It may optimise throughput over immediate latency.

15.139 Background Workload

Background work has low urgency and may use spare capacity.

Examples include:

- reindexing,

- benchmark runs,

- or non-urgent derivative generation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.140 Scheduled Workload

Scheduled work should begin within an approved time or window.

15.141 Recurring Workload

Recurring work repeats according to a governed schedule.

Each occurrence shall receive fresh validation.

15.142 Long-Running Workload

Long-running work may span:

- minutes,

- hours,

- days,

- or multiple human interactions.

It requires durable scheduling and state.

15.143 Maintenance Workload

Maintenance includes:

- registry refresh,

- cache rebuild,

- cleanup,

- or model download.

Maintenance shall not silently disrupt higher-priority work.

15.144 Recovery Workload

Recovery work restores valid operation or state.

It may receive elevated priority under Incident policy.

15.145 Emergency Workload

Emergency work addresses severe active harm.

Emergency priority shall be tightly governed and attributable.

15.146 Workload Class Is Not Priority

Workload class describes timing behaviour.

Priority determines relative scheduling preference.

A background recovery verification may be higher priority than an interactive optional request.

15.147 Priority

Priority is the governed relative importance of work within a scheduling scope.

Priority shall be explicit, bounded and attributable.

15.148 Priority Level

Canonical levels may include:

- emergency,

- critical,

- high,

- normal,

- low,

- background,

- and best effort.

15.149 Emergency Priority

Emergency priority is reserved for active severe incidents, safety or security containment.

It shall not be available to ordinary Agents by default.

15.150 Critical Priority

Critical priority may apply to:

- essential production deadline,

- recovery,

- or user-blocking operation.

15.151 High Priority

High priority may apply to important time-sensitive work with valid authority.

15.152 Normal Priority

Normal is the default for ordinary work.

15.153 Low Priority

Low-priority work may wait behind ordinary work.

15.154 Background Priority

Background work should consume spare capacity and yield to higher priorities.

15.155 Best-Effort Priority

Best-effort work may be delayed, cancelled or omitted when capacity is scarce.

15.156 Priority Source

Priority may derive from:

- explicit user request,

- Project policy,

- Workflow,

- Incident,

- deadline,

- or system maintenance.

The source shall remain visible.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.157 Priority Authority

Only authorised Principals or policies may assign elevated priority.

15.158 Agent Priority Limitation

An Agent shall not mark its own work critical merely to reduce latency.

15.159 Priority Escalation

Priority escalation shall be:

- reasoned,

- scoped,

- time-bounded,

- and attributable.

15.160 Priority De-Escalation

Priority may decrease when:

- deadline passes,

- Incident resolves,

- or urgency changes.

15.161 Priority Inversion

Priority Inversion occurs when high-priority work waits behind lower-priority work due to shared locks, capacity or dependencies.

15.162 Priority-Inversion Mitigation

Mitigation may include:

- priority inheritance,

- reserved capacity,

- narrow locks,

- or separate queues.

15.163 Priority Inheritance

A lower-priority dependency may temporarily inherit higher scheduling importance when it blocks critical work.

The inheritance shall be bounded.

15.164 Priority Abuse

Repeated unjustified high priority shall be detected and governed.

15.165 Starvation

Starvation occurs when work waits indefinitely because higher-priority work continually arrives.

15.166 Starvation Prevention

Controls may include:

- ageing,

- fair-share allocation,

- maximum delay,

- reserved low-priority capacity,

- or escalation.

15.167 Priority Ageing

Waiting work may gradually gain scheduling weight.

Ageing shall not raise it above mandatory emergency classes without policy.

15.168 Fairness

Fairness ensures that shared capacity is allocated according to governed policy rather than arbitrary arrival, power or implementation order.

15.169 Tenant Fairness

One Tenant shall not monopolise shared Omnira-managed capacity.

15.170 Project Fairness

One Project shall not consume all capacity needed by other authorised Projects.

15.171 User Fairness

Multi-user Tenants may require fair allocation among users or roles.

15.172 Capability Fairness

High-volume media jobs shall not indefinitely block text, approvals or recovery.

15.173 Fairness Weight

A fairness policy may assign weights based on:

- subscription,

- Project importance,

- reserved capacity,

- or contractual entitlement.

Weights shall be explicit.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.174 Weighted Fair Scheduling

Weighted Fair Scheduling allocates proportional capacity among eligible classes.

15.175 Equal Fairness

Equal share may be appropriate when all participants have equivalent entitlement.

15.176 Reserved Share

A Tenant or Project may hold a reserved capacity share.

15.177 Borrowed Share

Unused reserved capacity may be borrowed by others when policy permits.

Borrowing shall be revocable.

15.178 Fairness Window

Fairness may be measured over a defined time window rather than every individual dispatch.

15.179 Fairness Versus Priority

Priority may temporarily override fair share for urgent work.

Long-term starvation remains prohibited.

15.180 First-In-First-Out

First-In-First-Out scheduling orders work by arrival.

It is simple but may be unsuitable when:

- deadlines differ,

- workloads vary greatly,

- or priority matters.

15.181 Shortest-Job-First

Shortest-Job-First may reduce average wait time.

It can starve long work and relies on duration estimates.

15.182 Earliest-Deadline-First

Earliest-Deadline-First prioritises the nearest deadline.

It requires realistic duration and feasibility estimates.

15.183 Priority Queue

Priority queues order work by effective priority.

They require starvation prevention.

15.184 Weighted Queue

Weighted queues allocate service across workload classes.

15.185 Round-Robin

Round-Robin rotates among queues or Projects.

It may improve fairness.

15.186 Deficit Round-Robin

Deficit Round-Robin can support workloads with different sizes while preserving fair share.

15.187 Hybrid Scheduling

Omnira may combine:

- admission control,

- priority,

- fairness,

- deadline,

- and resource fit.

The algorithm shall be versioned and explainable.

15.188 Scheduling Policy

Scheduling Policy defines how admitted work is ordered and allocated.

It shall include:

- scope,

- workload classes,

- priorities,

- fairness,

- concurrency,

- quotas,

- ageing,

- preemption,

- and load shedding.

15.189 Scheduling Policy Identity

Every reusable Scheduling Policy shall have stable identity and version.

15.190 Policy Scope

Scheduling policies may exist at:

- Platform,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- Capability,

- Provider,

- queue,

- and workload-class level.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.191 Policy Composition

Effective policy is the composition of applicable rules.

Mandatory isolation and safety rules outrank convenience.

15.192 Scheduling Algorithm Version

Every material Scheduling Decision shall preserve the algorithm or policy version used.

15.193 Queue

A Queue is a durable or transient ordered collection of schedulable work.

The queue shall have explicit:

- scope,

- capacity,

- retention,

- ordering,

- priority,

- and ownership.

15.194 Queue Identity

Every persistent queue shall have stable identity.

15.195 Platform Queue

A platform queue may serve shared infrastructure work.

15.196 Tenant Queue

Tenant queues can isolate demand and enforce entitlements.

15.197 Project Queue

Project queues can preserve attribution and prevent cross-Project starvation.

15.198 Provider Queue

Provider-specific queues isolate external capacity and failure.

15.199 Capability Queue

Capability queues may separate:

- text,

- image,

- video,

- voice,

- code,

- and publication.

15.200 Risk Queue

Consequential operations should use separate queues or dispatch controls.

15.201 Human Review Queue

Human review tasks shall have:

- required role,

- deadline,

- estimated effort,

- and assignment state.

15.202 Queue Item

A Queue Item shall include or reference:

- queueItemId,

- Scheduling Request,

- priority,

- enqueue time,

- deadline,

- expected size,

- attempts,

- state,

- and provenance.

15.203 Queue Item Identity

Every durable Queue Item shall have stable identity.

15.204 Queue Item Version

Material changes to priority, deadline or requirements shall create attributable updates.

15.205 Queue Position

Queue position is a derived estimate.

It may change as:

- priorities,

- capacity,

- or deadlines change.

15.206 Estimated Start Time

Estimated Start Time is a forecast.

It shall not be presented as a guarantee.

15.207 Estimated Completion Time

Estimated Completion Time should include:

- expected queue wait,

- execution,

- evaluation,

- and known downstream work.

15.208 Queue Wait Limit

A Queue Item may have a maximum permitted waiting time.

15.209 Queue Expiry

Expired work shall not dispatch without revalidation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.210 Queue Cancellation

Cancellation shall remove future dispatch while preserving history.

15.211 Queue Reprioritisation

Reprioritisation shall be authorised and attributable.

15.212 Queue Migration

Work may move between queues after:

- rerouting,

- priority change,

- or Continuity Mode.

Migration shall preserve identity and wait history.

15.213 Queue Compaction

Completed and expired records may be archived.

Compaction shall not erase required audit history.

15.214 Queue Backlog

Backlog is the amount of admitted unfinished work.

15.215 Backlog Age

Backlog age may reveal starvation or insufficient capacity.

15.216 Queue Depth

Queue depth is the number or weighted size of waiting items.

15.217 Queue Size Limitation

A queue shall have bounded capacity or explicit spillover behaviour.

15.218 Queue Overflow

Overflow may cause:

- rejection,

- alternate queue,

- durable spillover,

- or load shedding.

15.219 Infinite Queue Prohibition

Infinite logical queues create hidden failure and unbounded delay.

Every queue requires bounded operational policy.

15.220 Backpressure

Backpressure slows or rejects new work when downstream capacity is constrained.

15.221 Backpressure Signal

Signals may include:

- queue depth,

- wait time,

- memory pressure,

- Provider rate limit,

- or worker saturation.

15.222 Producer Backpressure

Upstream systems should reduce work submission when the Scheduler signals saturation.

15.223 Agent Backpressure

Agents shall not create unlimited child requests when the Fabric reports constrained capacity.

15.224 Workflow Backpressure

Workflow fan-out shall respect downstream queue and Budget limits.

15.225 Provider Backpressure

Provider rate-limit or queue signals shall reduce dispatch.

15.226 Human Backpressure

Large review backlogs shall reduce new work requiring the same reviewer class where feasible.

15.227 Load Shedding

Load Shedding deliberately drops, rejects, delays or degrades lower-value work to protect essential service.

15.228 Load-Shedding Order

A representative shedding order may be:

1. speculative work,

2. duplicate alternatives,

3. optional derivatives,

4. background benchmarks,

5. best-effort work,

6. low-priority work,

7. normal work where unavoidable.

Critical and emergency work should be protected according to policy.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.229 Load-Shedding Decision

A decision shall record:

- affected work,

- trigger,

- priority,

- user impact,

- and recovery path.

15.230 Silent Load Shedding Prohibition

Dropped work shall receive truthful state.

It shall not disappear.

15.231 Capacity Reservation

A Capacity Reservation commits resource availability for future or immediate work.

It is distinct from a Budget Reservation.

15.232 Capacity Reservation Object

A Capacity Reservation shall include or reference:

- capacityReservationId,

- resource pool,

- Scheduling Request,

- amount,

- unit,

- start,

- end,

- state,

- priority,

- and provenance.

15.233 Capacity Reservation Identity

Every material Capacity Reservation shall have stable identity.

15.234 Reservation Scope

Capacity may be reserved for:

- Provider concurrency,

- local GPU,

- human review,

- queue share,

- or scheduled window.

15.235 Hard Capacity Reservation

A Hard Reservation guarantees capacity only to the extent supported by the underlying resource contract.

The guarantee level shall be explicit.

15.236 Soft Capacity Reservation

A Soft Reservation expresses intended allocation but may be preempted under policy.

15.237 Capacity Reservation Lifecycle

States may include:

- proposed,

- pending,

- active,

- partially consumed,

- consumed,

- released,

- expired,

- cancelled,

- and breached.

15.238 Reservation Breach

A Reservation is breached when the promised capacity is unavailable.

The system shall:

- reroute,

- delay,

- compensate,

- or escalate

according to policy.

15.239 Capacity Reservation Expiry

Unused capacity shall be released after expiry.

15.240 Capacity and Budget Reservation Coordination

Paid work may require both:

- Budget Reservation,

- and Capacity Reservation.

Neither substitutes for the other.

15.241 Resource Pool

A Resource Pool groups capacity that may serve compatible work.

Examples include:

- external text Providers,

- local GPU workers,

- video-generation slots,

- human reviewers,

- or publication workers.

15.242 Resource Pool Identity

Every pool shall have stable identity and scope.

15.243 Homogeneous Pool

A Homogeneous Pool contains equivalent resources.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.244 Heterogeneous Pool

A Heterogeneous Pool contains resources with different:

- speed,

- cost,

- quality,

- or capacity.

Routing and scheduling must coordinate.

15.245 Pool Capacity

Pool Capacity is the sum of usable member capacity after constraints.

15.246 Pool Health

Pool health shall preserve member-level state.

15.247 Pool Membership

Membership changes shall be versioned and observable.

15.248 Pool Isolation

Pools may be isolated by:

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- privacy class,

- or risk.

15.249 Shared Pool

Shared pools require fairness and attribution.

15.250 Dedicated Pool

A Dedicated Pool serves one scoped owner or workload class.

15.251 Concurrency

Concurrency is the number of simultaneous operations permitted within a scope.

15.252 Concurrency Limit

A Concurrency Limit shall identify:

- scope,

- resource,

- maximum,

- burst,

- period,

- and source.

15.253 Global Concurrency

Global concurrency protects the platform or service as a whole.

15.254 Tenant Concurrency

Tenant concurrency prevents one Tenant from monopolising shared resources.

15.255 Project Concurrency

Project concurrency limits parallel work within one Project.

15.256 Provider Concurrency

Provider concurrency respects Account and Product limits.

15.257 Model Concurrency

Model concurrency protects a Deployment from overload.

15.258 Capability Concurrency

Capability-specific concurrency may protect expensive or scarce operations.

15.259 Local Node Concurrency

Local concurrency shall consider:

- memory,

- GPU,

- thermal state,

- battery,

- and responsiveness.

15.260 Human Concurrency

Human reviewers have practical simultaneous-work limits.

15.261 Side-Effect Concurrency

Publication, deletion and canonical mutation may require concurrency of one for a target.

15.262 Target-Specific Concurrency

The same target should not receive conflicting simultaneous actions.

15.263 Concurrency Token

A Concurrency Token grants temporary permission to occupy one concurrency slot.

15.264 Token Acquisition

Execution shall acquire required tokens before dispatch.

15.265 Token Release

Tokens shall be released after terminal or safe suspended state.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.266 Lost Concurrency Token

Lost or expired worker ownership shall not permit continued state mutation.

15.267 Concurrency Leak

A leaked token reduces available capacity incorrectly.

The system shall detect and recover stale allocations.

15.268 Dynamic Concurrency

Concurrency may adjust based on:

- latency,

- error rate,

- resource utilisation,

- and Provider guidance.

Hard maximums remain governed.

15.269 Adaptive Concurrency

Adaptive control may increase or decrease parallelism gradually.

It shall not exceed policy or Budget.

15.270 Concurrency and Latency

Higher concurrency may reduce queue delay but increase:

- processing latency,

- failures,

- rate limits,

- and contention.

15.271 Concurrency and Cost

Parallel paid work may consume more Budget before results can be evaluated.

15.272 Speculative Concurrency

Candidate races and hedged requests require explicit concurrency and Budget reservation.

15.273 Sequential Constraint

Some Steps must remain sequential because of:

- dependency,

- target mutation,

- or review.

15.274 Parallel Eligibility

Steps may run in parallel only when:

- dependencies permit,

- capacity exists,

- Budget is reserved,

- and side effects do not conflict.

15.275 Parallel Group Scheduling

A Parallel Group shall define:

- maximum active children,

- priority,

- shared capacity,

- and join behaviour.

15.276 Fan-Out

Fan-Out creates multiple child operations.

Fan-Out shall be bounded by:

- item count,

- concurrency,

- Budget,

- and deadline.

15.277 Fan-In

Fan-In waits for required child results.

The join policy shall be explicit.

15.278 Unbounded Fan-Out Prohibition

Agents and Workflows shall not create unlimited parallel child requests.

15.279 Rate Limit

A Rate Limit restricts operations over time.

It may be imposed by:

- Provider,

- Omnira,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Account,

- Capability,

- or Environment.

15.280 Rate-Limit Unit

Units may include:

- requests per second,

- requests per minute,

- tokens per minute,

- bytes per second,

- or jobs per hour.

15.281 Hard Rate Limit

A Hard Rate Limit rejects or delays work beyond the configured maximum.

15.282 Soft Rate Limit

A Soft Rate Limit produces warning or reduced priority before a hard boundary.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.283 Burst Limit

A Burst Limit permits short temporary activity above sustained rate.

15.284 Sustained Rate

Sustained Rate defines the ordinary long-term throughput.

15.285 Rate-Limit Window

Windows may be:

- fixed,

- sliding,

- rolling,

- or token-bucket based.

15.286 Token Bucket

A Token Bucket permits bounded bursts while enforcing average rate.

15.287 Leaky Bucket

A Leaky Bucket smooths output at a controlled rate.

15.288 Provider Rate Limit

Provider limits shall be associated with the exact:

- Account,

- Product,

- Model,

- region,

- and operation

where known.

15.289 Rate-Limit Headers

Provider headers may update current capacity and reset time.

They shall be treated as dynamic evidence.

15.290 Rate-Limit Reset

Reset time shall be explicit where known.

15.291 Rate-Limit Backoff

The Scheduler and Reliability system shall coordinate delayed dispatch after rate limiting.

15.292 Rate-Limit Distribution

Shared Provider limits require coordinated allocation across workers.

15.293 Distributed Rate Limiter

A distributed limiter shall use authoritative or safely consistent state.

15.294 Local Rate Limiter

A local limiter may protect one worker or Node.

It may be insufficient for shared Account limits.

15.295 Rate-Limit Bypass Prohibition

New workers shall not bypass a shared Provider rate limit.

15.296 Quota

A Quota is a governed or externally imposed usage allowance within a defined scope and period.

Quota shall include or reference:

- quotaId,

- owner or issuer,

- scope,

- unit,

- limit,

- consumed,

- reserved,

- remaining,

- reset or expiry,

- source,

- freshness,

- and lifecycle.

15.297 Quota Identity

Every persistent Quota shall have stable identity and version or observation history.

15.298 Provider Quota

Provider Quota may limit:

- requests,

- tokens,

- images,

- video,

- audio,

- storage,

- or seats.

15.299 Subscription Quota

Subscription capacity may reset periodically or follow fair-use rules.

15.300 Project Quota

A Project Quota limits resource consumption independently of financial Budget.

15.301 Tenant Quota

A Tenant Quota protects shared platform resources.

15.302 User Quota

A user may receive bounded capacity within a Tenant.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.303 Capability Quota

A Capability Quota may limit costly or scarce operations.

15.304 Environment Quota

Development and test may receive smaller quotas than production.

15.305 Local Quota

Local Nodes may have policy quotas for:

- battery,

- GPU hours,

- storage,

- or background runtime.

15.306 Human Quota

A human-review quota may limit daily or weekly assigned effort.

15.307 Quota Versus Credit

Credits represent economic capacity.

Quota represents usage allowance.

They may be related but shall remain distinct.

15.308 Quota Versus Rate Limit

Quota limits total usage over a period.

Rate limit controls the speed of usage.

15.309 Quota Versus Concurrency

Quota limits cumulative allowance.

Concurrency limits simultaneous work.

15.310 Quota Versus Capacity

Quota may be lower than technical capacity.

Technical capacity may be lower than remaining quota.

15.311 Quota Lifecycle

Quota states may include:

- active,

- nearing limit,

- exhausted,

- suspended,

- reset pending,

- expired,

- and unknown.

15.312 Quota Observation

Provider quota may be observed through:

- API,

- dashboard,

- response header,

- contract,

- or manual verification.

15.313 Quota Freshness

Remaining quota shall include observation time.

15.314 Unknown Quota

Unknown quota requires conservative scheduling for expensive or critical work.

15.315 Quota Reservation

Expected usage may be reserved before dispatch.

15.316 Quota Reservation Identity

Quota Reservation shall remain linked to:

- Step,

- Execution,

- and Provider Account.

15.317 Quota Consumption

Actual consumption shall be reconciled with usage evidence.

15.318 Quota Release

Unused reserved quota shall be released.

15.319 Quota Reset

Reset behaviour shall preserve:

- timezone,

- Provider period,

- and effective time.

15.320 Quota Rollover

Unused quota may or may not roll over.

The policy shall be explicit.

15.321 Quota Borrowing

One Project may borrow another Project’s unused shared quota only when policy permits.

15.322 Quota Transfer

Quota transfer requires explicit ownership and governance.

15.323 Quota Exhaustion

When exhausted, the system may:

- wait for reset,

- use another eligible Account,

- reroute,

- use local capacity,

- request purchase,

- or fail.

It shall not substitute silently.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.324 Quota Nearing Limit

Near-limit state may reduce:

- optional work,

- exploration,

- or speculative execution.

15.325 Quota Alert

Alerts should identify:

- scope,

- remaining amount,

- expected reset,

- and affected work.

15.326 Quota Anomaly

Unexpected quota loss may indicate:

- shadow usage,

- duplicate jobs,

- Provider error,

- or compromised Credential.

15.327 Quota Reconciliation

Observed Provider usage shall be compared with internal usage.

15.328 Quota Shadow Usage

Usage outside governed Fabric paths may consume shared quota.

It shall be identified where possible.

15.329 Scheduled Execution

Scheduled Execution begins at or within a future approved time window.

The schedule shall be represented canonically.

15.330 Schedule

A Schedule shall include or reference:

- scheduleId,

- owner,

- scope,

- recurrence or time,

- timezone,

- start window,

- expiry,

- authority,

- and lifecycle.

15.331 Schedule Identity

Every persistent Schedule shall have stable identity and version.

15.332 Timezone

Every human-facing schedule shall identify timezone.

Ambiguous local times are prohibited.

15.333 One-Time Schedule

A one-time schedule triggers one occurrence.

15.334 Recurring Schedule

A recurring schedule creates repeated occurrences under a defined rule.

15.335 Fixed-Time Schedule

A fixed-time schedule targets a specific clock time.

15.336 Window Schedule

A window schedule permits dispatch within a bounded interval.

15.337 Flexible Schedule

A flexible schedule allows the Scheduler to choose an efficient time within an approved window.

15.338 Event-Triggered Schedule

An event may trigger a scheduled occurrence.

Event authenticity and deduplication remain required.

15.339 Condition-Triggered Schedule

A condition may create an occurrence only when its predicate is satisfied.

15.340 Recurrence Rule

Recurrence shall be represented in a machine-readable form.

15.341 Schedule Version

Changes to recurrence, time, scope or authority shall create a new Version.

15.342 Schedule Lifecycle

Schedule states may include:

- proposed,

- active,

- paused,

- expired,

- cancelled,

- superseded,

- and archived.

15.343 Scheduled Occurrence

Each recurrence shall create a distinct Scheduled Occurrence or request instance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.344 Occurrence Identity

Every occurrence shall have stable identity.

One recurring Schedule shall not hide changing execution state.

15.345 Occurrence Revalidation

Before dispatch, every occurrence shall revalidate:

- authority,

- policy,

- Inputs,

- Budget,

- quota,

- credentials,

- and resource eligibility.

15.346 Missed Occurrence

A missed occurrence may be:

- skipped,

- delayed,

- executed late,

- or escalated

according to policy.

15.347 Catch-Up Policy

Catch-up determines whether missed recurring work runs later.

Unbounded catch-up is prohibited.

15.348 Coalescing

Several missed occurrences may be combined only when semantics permit it.

15.349 Duplicate Occurrence

Duplicate schedule triggers shall not create duplicate consequential work.

15.350 Schedule Drift

Execution may start later than planned because of capacity or dependency delay.

Drift shall remain visible.

15.351 Clock Skew

Distributed clocks may differ.

Time-sensitive scheduling shall use authoritative time and tolerance.

15.352 Daylight-Saving Transition

Recurring local-time schedules shall define behaviour during ambiguous or missing local times.

15.353 Schedule Cancellation

Cancelling a Schedule stops future occurrences.

It does not automatically cancel already-created Executions.

15.354 Schedule Pause

Pausing a Schedule prevents new occurrences while preserving configuration.

15.355 Schedule Resume

Resume shall define whether missed occurrences are skipped or caught up.

15.356 Scheduled Side Effect

Scheduled publication, message or mutation requires valid authority at execution time.

Past approval may expire.

15.357 Scheduled Budget

Recurring paid work should use:

- recurring Budget,

- per-occurrence limit,

- and period limit.

15.358 Scheduled Capacity Reservation

Critical future work may reserve capacity ahead of time.

15.359 Reservation Lead Time

Lead time shall reflect:

- resource scarcity,

- Provider contract,

- human availability,

- and deadline.

15.360 Preemption

Preemption interrupts or delays lower-priority work to release capacity.

Preemption shall be explicit and governed.

15.361 Queue Preemption

Queued work may lose position without execution state impact.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.362 Running-Work Preemption

Running work may be interrupted only when:

- technically safe,

- economically justified,

- and supported by the resource.

15.363 Non-Preemptible Work

Some work cannot be safely interrupted after start.

Examples include:

- paid Provider generation,

- publication,

- file mutation,

- or model loading.

15.364 Preemptible Local Work

Some local batch work may checkpoint and yield.

15.365 Preemption Cost

Preemption may waste:

- compute,

- money,

- time,

- or partial progress.

The decision shall consider these costs.

15.366 Preemption Authority

Emergency or critical policy may permit preemption.

Ordinary Agents shall not preempt unrelated work.

15.367 Preemption Evidence

The system shall record:

- preempted work,

- reason,

- state,

- lost cost,

- and resumption path.

15.368 Resumption After Preemption

Preempted work may:

- resume from Checkpoint,

- restart,

- reroute,

- or be cancelled.

The behaviour shall be defined.

15.369 Priority Reservation

Critical workloads may hold reserved capacity to reduce the need for destructive preemption.

15.370 Resource Affinity

Scheduling may preserve affinity to:

- Runtime Node,

- Provider Account,

- Deployment,

- cached context,

- loaded Model,

- or Provider Asset.

15.371 Node Affinity

Node affinity may reduce data movement or model-loading time.

15.372 Data Affinity

Work may be scheduled near its data when privacy and performance benefit.

15.373 Model Affinity

A loaded Model may receive related work to avoid repeated loading.

15.374 Account Affinity

Provider-side sessions or Assets may require one Account.

15.375 Anti-Affinity

Anti-affinity separates workloads across failure domains.

15.376 Tenant Anti-Affinity

Sensitive Tenants may require isolated workers or pools.

15.377 Failure-Domain Anti-Affinity

Redundant work should avoid shared regions, Accounts or Nodes.

15.378 Affinity Versus Fairness

Affinity may improve performance but shall not create starvation or hidden lock-in.

15.379 Batch Scheduling

Batch scheduling processes a collection efficiently.

It shall preserve item-level identity and results.

15.380 Batch Size

Batch size may affect:

- throughput,

- latency,

- memory,

- Provider limits,

- and error isolation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.381 Dynamic Batch Size

Batch size may adapt to capacity and latency.

Hard limits remain enforced.

15.382 Batch Failure

One item failure shall not necessarily fail the complete batch.

Batch semantics shall be explicit.

15.383 Batch Partial Completion

Successful items remain attributable.

Failed items may retry independently when permitted.

15.384 Batch Deadline

A batch may have:
