- whole-batch deadline,

- item deadlines,

- or both.

15.385 Batch Fairness

Large batches shall not monopolise the queue.

They may be segmented.

15.386 Batch Cost Reservation

Paid batches shall reserve expected maximum cost.

15.387 Micro-Batching

Micro-batching groups small compatible requests for efficiency.

It shall preserve:

- Tenant isolation,

- Project scope,

- and individual provenance.

15.388 Cross-Tenant Batching

Cross-Tenant batching is prohibited unless the architecture proves strict data and output isolation.

15.389 Streaming Scheduling

Streaming workloads consume capacity continuously.

They require:

- session reservation,

- sustained throughput,

- interruption policy,

- and backpressure.

15.390 Streaming Session

A Streaming Session shall have:

- sessionId,

- owner,

- resource,

- start,

- capacity allocation,

- maximum duration,

- and lifecycle.

15.391 Streaming Capacity

Streaming capacity may be measured in:

- concurrent sessions,

- audio seconds,

- tokens per second,

- or bandwidth.

15.392 Streaming Backpressure

The system may:

- reduce quality,

- buffer,

- slow generation,

- or terminate

according to approved policy.

15.393 Streaming Priority

Interactive voice may receive higher scheduling priority than background generation.

15.394 Streaming Interruption

Interruption shall preserve:

- user-visible state,

- partial transcript,

- and recovery path.

15.395 Real-Time Scheduling

Real-time workloads may require:

- dedicated capacity,

- low-latency routing,

- preloaded Models,

- and strict concurrency.

15.396 Real-Time Fallback

Fallback must meet latency as well as quality and policy requirements.

15.397 Real-Time Admission

The system should reject or degrade a real-time session before start when sustainable capacity is unavailable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.398 Real-Time Overload

Overload behaviour may include:

- lower audio quality,

- reduced Features,

- wait,

- or refusal.

It shall not silently violate latency or privacy.

15.399 Local Scheduling

Local scheduling shall account for the user’s device and current activity.

15.400 Local Foreground Protection

Background AI work shall not make the user’s device unresponsive without explicit permission.

15.401 Battery-Aware Scheduling

Mobile or laptop work may be delayed or reduced when:

- battery is low,

- device is unplugged,

- or power policy forbids heavy work.

15.402 Thermal-Aware Scheduling

Thermal throttling may reduce effective capacity.

15.403 Storage-Aware Scheduling

Large media or Model work shall confirm sufficient storage before start.

15.404 Network-Aware Scheduling

External work may require:

- stable network,

- sufficient upload capacity,

- or approved Wi-Fi state.

15.405 Offline Scheduling

Local-only work may continue offline.

External work shall remain queued or blocked.

15.406 User-Presence Scheduling

Some high-risk work may require the user to be present for approval or supervision.

15.407 Quiet-Hour Scheduling

Projects may delay noisy or resource-intensive local work to approved periods.

15.408 Local Model Loading

Model loading consumes:

- time,

- memory,

- and storage bandwidth.

Loading latency shall be part of scheduling.

15.409 Model Eviction

Local Models may be evicted to free memory.

Eviction policy shall consider upcoming work.

15.410 Model Warm Pool

Frequently used Models may remain warm when capacity permits.

15.411 Warm-Pool Cost

Keeping Models loaded consumes memory and energy.

The value shall remain visible.

15.412 External Scheduling

External scheduling shall consider:

- Provider queue,

- Account tier,

- rate limit,

- quota,

- cost,

- and callback behaviour.

15.413 Provider Queue Estimate

Provider queue estimates may influence completion time.

They shall remain uncertain unless contractually guaranteed.

15.414 Provider Priority Tier

Paid Account tiers may receive faster queues.

The selected Account and tier shall be explicit.

15.415 Provider Maintenance Window

Known maintenance may delay or reroute work.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.416 Provider Capacity Reservation

Some contracts may offer reserved capacity.

The reservation terms and scope shall be recorded.

15.417 Provider Batch API

Provider batch APIs may reduce cost but increase latency.

They shall be used only when the deadline permits.

15.418 Provider Asynchronous API

Asynchronous APIs may improve worker utilisation.

They still require durable job tracking.

15.419 Provider Synchronous API

Synchronous APIs may suit interactive work but hold connection and worker capacity.

15.420 Human Scheduling

Human tasks shall be treated as schedulable work with real capacity and deadlines.

15.421 Human Assignment

Assignment may consider:

- role,

- expertise,

- Project,

- workload,

- timezone,

- and conflict of interest.

15.422 Human Review Estimate

Estimated review effort shall be included in completion forecasting.

15.423 Human Queue

Human work may use queues by:

- Project,

- expertise,

- urgency,

- or reviewer.

15.424 Human Priority

Urgent human tasks may be prioritised.

Repeated false urgency shall be controlled.

15.425 Human Availability Window

Availability may include:

- working hours,

- leave,

- and explicit on-call periods.

15.426 Human Overload

The system shall not assign more work than the reviewer can reasonably perform.

15.427 Human Reassignment

Unaccepted or expired tasks may be reassigned according to policy.

15.428 Human Escalation

Missed critical review may escalate to another qualified reviewer or owner.

15.429 Human Capacity Privacy

Reviewer assignment shall not expose protected Project content to unauthorised people.

15.430 Latency and Routing

Routing may use latency evidence after mandatory eligibility.

The selected Routing Profile determines how strongly latency influences ranking.

15.431 Economy Latency Behaviour

Economy may accept slower eligible resources when:

- deadline permits,

- total expected cost is lower,

- and Quality Floor remains satisfied.

15.432 Balanced Latency Behaviour

Balanced considers latency with:

- quality,

- cost,

- reliability,

- and privacy.

15.433 Premium Latency Behaviour

Premium may accept longer processing for higher expected quality when the deadline permits.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.434 Private Latency Behaviour

Private may accept slower local or isolated execution to preserve custody.

15.435 Pinned Latency Behaviour

Pinned routing honours the selected resource when it remains deadline-feasible or the user accepts delay.

15.436 Latency-Based Rerouting

Rerouting may occur when:

- queue grows,

- deadline risk increases,

- or capacity falls.

The new Candidate must remain fully eligible.

15.437 Latency-Based Degradation

A reduced result may be proposed when full completion cannot meet the deadline.

Degradation requires permission.

15.438 Capacity-Based Rerouting

A technically healthy resource may be bypassed when capacity is insufficient.

15.439 Capacity and Failure Domains

Alternate capacity should avoid correlated failure where practical.

15.440 Capacity and Cost

Scarce or priority capacity may have higher cost.

Economic approval remains required.

15.441 Capacity and Quality

Higher-throughput resources may produce different quality.

Capacity optimisation shall not weaken Quality Floor.

15.442 Capacity and Privacy

Shared external capacity shall not be used for data requiring isolated execution.

15.443 Capacity and Rights

Alternate Provider capacity shall preserve commercial-use rights.

15.444 Capacity and Authority

Reserved capacity does not grant operational authority.

15.445 Capacity and Provenance

Scheduling and capacity decisions shall remain linked to resulting Executions.

15.446 Capacity and Reliability

Sustainable capacity should include reliability headroom.

15.447 Capacity and Incidents

Incident response may reduce or reserve capacity.

15.448 Capacity and Continuity Mode

Continuity Modes may change:

- allowed resource pools,

- priorities,

- quotas,

- and concurrency.

15.449 Capacity Learning

The Fabric may create Learning Candidates such as:

- Provider A video queue exceeds two hours during evening peaks.

- Local Model B can support two concurrent short prompts but degrades at three.

- Human review is the dominant Familje-Stunden completion bottleneck.

- The Prompt research work completes reliably when scheduled before media composition.

Learning shall remain scoped and evidence-based.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.450 Latency Learning

Latency learning may improve:

- duration estimates,

- deadline feasibility,

- and Scheduler ordering.

15.451 Capacity Learning Admission

Learning shall not modify quotas, priority or authority automatically without governance.

15.452 Learning Scope

Capacity learning may be:

- Provider,

- Account,

- Deployment,

- Runtime Node,

- Capability,

- Project,

- workload-class,

- or time-window specific.

15.453 Learning Expiry

Learning shall expire after relevant infrastructure or policy change.

15.454 Demand Forecast

Demand Forecast predicts future Scheduling Requests.

It may use:

- historical volume,

- recurring Schedules,

- active Plans,

- Project milestones,

- and seasonal patterns.

15.455 Forecast Scope

Forecasts shall remain scoped to:

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Capability,

- resource pool,

- and horizon.

15.456 Forecast Confidence

Forecasts shall expose uncertainty.

15.457 Seasonal Demand

Projects may have periodic demand such as:

- monthly Familje-Stunden production,

- daily The Prompt content,

- or scheduled benchmark runs.

15.458 Event-Driven Demand Spike

News events, campaigns or Incidents may create sudden demand.

15.459 Demand Shaping

Demand may be shaped by:

- scheduling background work later,

- reducing optional variants,

- or spreading batch work.

15.460 Capacity Procurement Recommendation

The Fabric may recommend:

- Provider tier upgrade,

- local hardware,

- more managed capacity,

- or additional reviewers.

Recommendations do not create purchase authority.

15.461 Capacity Efficiency

Capacity Efficiency measures useful accepted work relative to consumed capacity.

15.462 Utilisation

Utilisation measures committed capacity relative to sustainable capacity.

15.463 Low Utilisation

Low utilisation may indicate excess capacity or necessary reliability reserve.

15.464 High Utilisation

High sustained utilisation may increase:

- queue latency,

- failure,

- and deadline risk.

15.465 Target Utilisation

A target below 100 percent may preserve headroom.

15.466 Effective Throughput

Effective Throughput measures accepted completed work per time unit.

15.467 Raw Throughput

Raw Throughput may include failed or rejected attempts.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.468 Accepted Throughput

Accepted Throughput counts results meeting the Quality Contract.

15.469 Cost-Adjusted Throughput

Cost-adjusted throughput compares accepted work with spend.

15.470 Latency-Adjusted Throughput

Throughput shall not be optimised by allowing unacceptable wait time.

15.471 Queue-Time Metric

Queue-time metrics should be tracked by:

- priority,

- workload class,

- Project,

- Capability,

- and resource pool.

15.472 Deadline-Miss Rate

Deadline-Miss Rate measures the proportion of work missing defined deadlines.

15.473 Admission-Rejection Rate

Admission rejection may reveal insufficient capacity or overly strict policy.

15.474 Preemption Rate

High preemption may indicate poor planning or insufficient reserved capacity.

15.475 Starvation Metric

The system should detect work exceeding expected maximum wait.

15.476 Fairness Metric

Fairness metrics may compare actual allocation with entitlement.

15.477 Quota-Exhaustion Rate

Frequent exhaustion may justify capacity or plan review.

15.478 Rate-Limit Rate

Rate-limit events may reveal poor scheduling or insufficient Provider tier.

15.479 Capacity-Reservation Breach Rate

Reservation breaches indicate unreliable supply or poor forecasting.

15.480 Scheduling Explainability

Every material scheduling outcome should be explainable.

The explanation should answer:

- Why was the work admitted or rejected?

- Which priority applied?

- Which queue was used?

- Which capacity was reserved?

- What is the estimated start?

- What is the deadline risk?

- Which quota or limit constrains it?

- Why did another task run first?

15.481 Human-Readable Scheduling Explanation

A concise explanation may state:

The scene was queued behind two higher-priority character-critical scenes because the selected Provider Account permits only two concurrent video jobs. Expected start is within the approved production window.

15.482 Machine-Readable Scheduling Evidence

The canonical record shall preserve:

- policy,

- queue,

- priority,

- fairness,

- quota,

- capacity,

- estimates,

- and versions.

15.483 Scheduling Receipt

A Scheduling Receipt may contain:

- Scheduling Request,

- Admission Decision,

- Scheduling Decision,

- queue,

- priority,

- reservation,

- expected start,

- actual start,

- delay reasons,

- and provenance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.484 Actual Versus Estimated Time

The system should compare:

- estimated queue time,

- estimated duration,

- actual queue time,

- actual duration,

- and final completion time.

15.485 Delay Reason

Delay reasons may include:

- no capacity,

- quota,

- rate limit,

- approval,

- Budget,

- human review,

- maintenance,

- dependency,

- or policy.

15.486 Delay Ownership

The system should distinguish whether delay originated from:

- Omnira,

- Provider,

- user approval,

- human reviewer,

- local Node,

- or external dependency.

15.487 Scheduling Incident

A Scheduling Incident may involve:

- starvation,

- wrong priority,

- quota bypass,

- overcommitment,

- duplicate dispatch,

- missed Hard Deadline,

- unfair allocation,

- or capacity leak.

15.488 Latency Incident

A Latency Incident occurs when delay materially violates an objective or deadline.

15.489 Capacity Incident

A Capacity Incident occurs when available or reserved capacity becomes insufficient unexpectedly.

15.490 Quota Incident

A Quota Incident may involve:

- unexplained exhaustion,

- wrong Project usage,

- or Provider mismatch.

15.491 Concurrency Incident

A Concurrency Incident may involve:

- limit bypass,

- duplicate side effect,

- or resource overload.

15.492 Priority Incident

A Priority Incident may involve:

- unauthorised escalation,

- starvation,

- or emergency-class abuse.

15.493 Scheduling-Incident Containment

Containment may include:

- stop admission,

- reduce concurrency,

- freeze priority changes,

- shed background work,

- or isolate a Project queue.

15.494 Scheduling-Incident Recovery

Recovery may include:

- rebuild queue state,

- release leaked tokens,

- reconcile dispatches,

- restore capacity,

- and re-estimate deadlines.

15.495 Queue-State Recovery

Queue recovery shall preserve:

- item identity,

- priority,

- enqueue time,

- and dispatch history.

15.496 Capacity-Leak Recovery

Stale reservations or concurrency tokens shall be detected and released only after confirming no active owner remains.

15.497 Deadline-Incident Review

Review should determine whether failure came from:

- inaccurate estimate,

- late admission,

- insufficient capacity,

- Provider delay,

- or human dependency.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.498 Scheduling Policy Governance

Changing scheduling policy may affect:

- fairness,

- latency,

- cost,

- and deadlines.

Changes require versioning and review.

15.499 Priority Policy Governance

Priority classes and escalation authority shall be governed centrally.

15.500 Quota Policy Governance

Quota changes shall identify:

- owner,

- scope,

- reason,

- period,

- and effect.

15.501 Concurrency Policy Governance

Concurrency changes may affect reliability and cost.

They require controlled rollout.

15.502 Capacity Reservation Policy

Reservations shall not be sold or promised beyond provable supply without disclosed risk.

15.503 Load-Shedding Policy

Load-shedding order shall be approved and visible.

15.504 Fairness Policy

Fair-share rules shall be explicit and auditable.

15.505 Emergency Scheduling Policy

Emergency policy may:

- reserve capacity,

- preempt lower-priority work,

- block background work,

- or enter recovery mode.

It shall be temporary and attributable.

15.506 Scheduling Event

Material scheduling events may include:

- SchedulingRequested,

- AdmissionGranted,

- AdmissionRejected,

- QueueItemCreated,

- PriorityChanged,

- CapacityReserved,

- DispatchStarted,

- DispatchDelayed,

- WorkPreempted,

- QuotaExhausted,

- DeadlineAtRisk,

- and ScheduleOccurrenceCreated.

15.507 Scheduling Event Identity

Events shall preserve:

- eventId,

- target,

- object version,

- correlation,

- causation,

- and time.

15.508 Event Deduplication

Duplicate schedule or queue events shall not create duplicate dispatch.

15.509 Event Ordering

Late events shall not revert newer queue or priority state.

15.510 Scheduling State Durability

Queue, Reservation, quota and occurrence state shall survive restart.

15.511 Scheduling Idempotency

Repeated submission of the same Scheduling Request Version shall not create duplicate Queue Items.

15.512 Dispatch Idempotency

Repeated dispatch messages shall not create duplicate Executions.

15.513 Distributed Scheduler

A distributed Scheduler may use multiple instances.

It shall preserve:

- single ownership,

- fencing,

- and consistent capacity accounting.

15.514 Scheduler Leader

Some operations may require a leader or partition owner.

Leadership shall be leased and fenced.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.515 Scheduler Partitioning

Work may be partitioned by:

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Provider,

- Capability,

- or queue.

15.516 Scheduler Failover

Scheduler failover shall not duplicate dispatch or lose Queue Items.

15.517 Scheduler Recovery

Recovery shall reconcile:

- leased items,

- active Executions,

- capacity tokens,

- and Reservations.

15.518 Scheduling Access Control

Permissions may include:

- submit work,

- view queue,

- modify priority,

- create Schedule,

- pause Schedule,

- alter quota,

- alter concurrency,

- and administer policy.

15.519 Queue View Permission

Users may view their own Project queue without seeing other Tenants’ work.

15.520 Priority-Change Permission

Elevated priority requires authorised role.

15.521 Quota-Administration Permission

Quota modification requires owner or administrative authority.

15.522 Concurrency-Administration Permission

Concurrency changes require platform or scoped resource authority.

15.523 Schedule-Creation Permission

A Principal may create Schedules only within its Project and Capability authority.

15.524 Schedule-Side-Effect Permission

Scheduled side effects require explicit authority covering the occurrence or bounded recurrence.

15.525 Capacity-Reservation Permission

Reserved scarce capacity may require budget or contract authority.

15.526 Scheduling API

The Scheduling Control Plane should expose governed operations such as:

- submit Scheduling Request,

- evaluate admission,

- enqueue,

- inspect queue,

- estimate start,

- reserve capacity,

- acquire concurrency,

- dispatch,

- reprioritise,

- delay,

- preempt,

- cancel,

- create Schedule,

- pause Schedule,

- and inspect quota.

15.527 Admission API

The Admission API should return:

- decision,

- conditions,

- capacity feasibility,

- deadline feasibility,

- and blocking reasons.

15.528 Queue API

The Queue API should support:

- enqueue,

- inspect state,

- cancel,

- reprioritise,

- and migrate.

15.529 Capacity API

The Capacity API should support:

- observe,

- reserve,

- commit,

- release,

- forecast,

- and inspect headroom.

15.530 Concurrency API

The Concurrency API should support:

- acquire token,

- renew,

- release,

- and inspect utilisation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.531 Quota API

The Quota API should support:

- inspect,

- reserve,

- consume,

- release,

- reconcile,

- and alert.

15.532 Schedule API

The Schedule API should support:

- create,

- version,

- pause,

- resume,

- cancel,

- and list occurrences.

15.533 Scheduling Observability

Observability should expose:

- queue depth,

- wait time,

- capacity,

- utilisation,

- concurrency,

- quota,

- deadline risk,

- priority,

- preemption,

- and load shedding.

15.534 Scheduling Dashboard

A dashboard may show:

- current queues,

- blocked work,

- active capacity,

- quota remaining,

- and expected completion.

15.535 Scheduling Alerts

Alerts may include:

- deadline at risk,

- queue overflow,

- capacity saturation,

- quota nearing limit,

- priority starvation,

- or leaked reservation.

15.536 Alert Actionability

Alerts should indicate:

- affected scope,

- consequence,

- and possible response.

15.537 Scheduling Logs

Logs shall not expose protected Inputs or raw credentials.

15.538 Scheduling Trace

Traces shall preserve the path from:

- Request,

- Plan,

- Routing,

- Admission,

- Queue,

- Dispatch,

- Execution,

- and completion.

15.539 Capacity Data Classification

Capacity and workload records may reveal:

- Project strategy,

- Provider contracts,

- and infrastructure.

Access shall be scoped.

15.540 Queue Data Privacy

Queue metadata shall minimise exposure of confidential request content.

15.541 Human Queue Privacy

Reviewer queues shall not reveal protected details to unassigned reviewers.

15.542 Scheduling Retention

Historical scheduling state should support:

- audit,

- incident analysis,

- forecasting,

- and fairness review.

15.543 Queue Retention

Completed Queue Items may be archived after required audit periods.

15.544 Schedule Retention

Historical Schedule Versions and occurrences shall remain queryable.

15.545 Capacity History

Capacity history supports forecasting and Incident review.

15.546 Quota History

Quota usage and reset history shall remain attributable.

15.547 Scheduling Backup

Critical queue and schedule state shall be backed up.

15.548 Scheduling Restore

Restore shall not duplicate dispatch or scheduled side effects.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.549 Stage 1 Scheduling Objective

Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy scheduling and capacity foundation required for representative Omnira workloads.

The objective is not to create a globally optimal distributed super-scheduler.

Stage 1 shall prove:

- workload classes,

- Admission Control,

- durable queues,

- explicit priorities,

- Project and Tenant fairness,

- capacity records,

- concurrency limits,

- rate limits,

- quotas,

- scheduled occurrences,

- deadline awareness,

- backpressure,

- load shedding,

- and truthful scheduling evidence.

15.550 Stage 1 Workload Classes

Stage 1 should support:

- interactive,

- asynchronous,

- batch,

- background,

- scheduled,

- long-running,

- recovery,

- and consequential side-effect work.

15.551 Stage 1 Priority Levels

Stage 1 should support:

- critical,

- high,

- normal,

- low,

- background,

- and emergency through restricted policy.

15.552 Stage 1 Scheduling Request Object

The Stage 1 Scheduling Request should include:

- schedulingRequestId,

- Plan Version,

- Step ID,

- Tenant,

- Project,

- Environment,

- workload class,

- priority,

- earliest start,

- deadline,

- expected duration,

- resource requirements,

- Budget Reservation,

- and policy references.

15.553 Stage 1 Queue Item Object

The Stage 1 Queue Item should include:

- queueItemId,

- Scheduling Request,

- queue,

- priority,

- enqueue time,

- deadline,

- state,

- dispatch attempts,

- and provenance.

15.554 Stage 1 Capacity Record

The Stage 1 Capacity Record should include:

- resource,

- Capability,

- unit,

- total,

- available,

- reserved,

- committed,

- observedAt,

- confidence,

- and source.

15.555 Stage 1 Capacity Reservation

The Stage 1 Capacity Reservation should include:

- reservationId,

- resource pool,

- Scheduling Request,

- amount,

- unit,

- start,

- end,

- state,

- and expiry.

15.556 Stage 1 Concurrency Limit

The Stage 1 Concurrency Limit should include:

- scope,

- resource,

- maximum active,

- burst,

- and policy source.

15.557 Stage 1 Quota

The Stage 1 Quota should include:

- quotaId,

- scope,

- unit,

- limit,

- consumed,

- reserved,

- remaining,

- reset,

- observedAt,

- and source.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.558 Stage 1 Schedule

The Stage 1 Schedule should include:

- scheduleId,

- owner,

- Project,

- recurrence or execution time,

- timezone,

- start window,

- expiry,

- lifecycle,

- and authority reference.

15.559 Stage 1 Occurrence

Each scheduled occurrence shall create a distinct:

- request,

- Plan,

- or Scheduling Request

according to Workflow design.

15.560 Stage 1 Admission Control

Stage 1 shall reject or defer work when:

- authority is invalid,

- Budget is unavailable,

- capacity is infeasible,

- deadline is impossible,

- quota is exhausted,

- or queue is full.

15.561 Stage 1 Queue Isolation

Stage 1 should isolate at minimum by:

- Environment,

- Provider class,

- and risk class.

Project attribution is mandatory.

15.562 Stage 1 Fairness

Stage 1 should implement a simple versioned fair-share or weighted queue policy across Projects or Tenants using shared capacity.

15.563 Stage 1 Deadline Awareness

Stage 1 should record:

- earliest start,

- deadline,

- estimated duration,

- and deadline-risk state.

15.564 Stage 1 Capacity Reservation Requirement

Scarce or consequential work should reserve required capacity before dispatch where practical.

15.565 Stage 1 Concurrency

Stage 1 shall enforce concurrency by:

- Provider Account,

- Model Deployment,

- local Runtime Node,

- and consequential target where applicable.

15.566 Stage 1 Rate Limiting

Stage 1 shall support distributed or authoritative limits for shared Provider Accounts.

15.567 Stage 1 Quota Awareness

Stage 1 shall track:

- Provider quota,

- Project quota,

- and quota reset where available.

15.568 Stage 1 Backpressure

Stage 1 shall signal upstream systems when:

- queue depth,

- wait time,

- or capacity

crosses thresholds.

15.569 Stage 1 Load Shedding

Stage 1 should shed:

- speculative,

- optional,

- and background work

before critical or approved user-facing work.

15.570 Stage 1 Scheduled Work

Stage 1 shall support one-time and recurring scheduled work with timezone and occurrence identity.

15.571 Stage 1 Human Capacity

Human Review Steps should enter a visible queue with:

- role,

- deadline,

- and assignment state.

15.572 Stage 1 Local Scheduling

Stage 1 should account for:

- Node online state,

- available memory,

- storage,

- and maximum local concurrency.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.573 Stage 1 External Scheduling

Stage 1 should account for:

- Provider health,

- Account rate limits,

- quota,

- and current concurrency.

15.574 Stage 1 Scheduling API

Stage 1 should support:

- admit,

- enqueue,

- inspect queue,

- estimate start,

- reserve capacity,

- acquire concurrency,

- dispatch,

- delay,

- cancel,

- create Schedule,

- and inspect occurrence.

15.575 Stage 1 Scheduling Acceptance Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Scheduling remains separate from Planning.

2. Scheduling remains separate from Routing.

3. Priority does not create authority.

4. Admitted does not mean running.

5. Queue state survives restart.

6. Duplicate Scheduling Request does not create duplicate Queue Item.

7. Queue Item references exact Plan Version and Step.

8. Expired request does not dispatch.

9. Blocked dependency prevents dispatch.

10. Budget failure prevents paid admission.

11. Impossible Hard Deadline produces rejection or clarification.

12. Optional background work may be delayed.

13. Critical recovery work may receive higher priority.

14. Historical scheduling decisions remain immutable.

15. Actual and estimated times remain distinguishable.

15.576 Stage 1 Capacity Tests

Representative tests should include:

1. Total, available, reserved and committed capacity remain distinct.

2. Capacity observation includes freshness.

Representative tests should include:

15.591 Applied Example — Nova and Pling Monthly Production

A Familje-Stunden monthly production may include:

Workload classes

- scene planning: asynchronous,

- preview generation: batch,

- character-critical final scenes: high-priority asynchronous,

- narration: asynchronous,

- local composition: batch,

- human child-facing review: human review,

- derivatives: low or background.

Capacity constraints may include:

- two concurrent video jobs,

- one local composition worker,

- one approved child-content reviewer,

- limited voice credits,

- and a publication deadline.

The Scheduler may:

1. admit all validated scene Steps,

2. dispatch previews in bounded parallel groups,

3. reserve premium capacity for critical scenes,

4. delay optional derivatives,

5. protect human-review time,

6. update deadline risk continuously,

7. and prevent optional work from consuming the master-production window.

15.592 Nova and Pling Scene Priority

Character-critical close-ups may receive higher production priority than:

- background loops,

- trailer derivatives,

- or additional thumbnail variants.

Priority shall derive from the approved Production Plan.

It shall not be added by the generation Agent independently.

15.593 Nova and Pling Video Concurrency

If the Provider Account permits two concurrent jobs, the Fabric shall not submit ten scene generations simultaneously.

The Scheduler may:

- run two,

- queue the rest,

- preserve fair ordering,

- and reserve retry headroom.

text:
15.594 Nova and Pling Human Review Capacity

The production estimate shall include the real availability of the person reviewing:

- character identity,

- emotional safety,

- and final story coherence.

Provider completion does not remove the human-review bottleneck.

15.595 Nova and Pling Deadline Risk

If premium scenes remain incomplete near the deadline, the Fabric may propose:

- delayed release,

- approved motion-comic substitution,

- fewer optional derivatives,

- or human-assisted correction.

It shall not silently publish an unreviewed master.

15.596 Applied Example — The Prompt Daily News Workflow

The Prompt may contain:

- scheduled topic discovery,

- high-priority current research,

- source verification,

- script generation,

- media production,

- final editorial review,

- and publication preparation.

Current research may receive earlier scheduling than media generation because:

- source freshness is time-sensitive,

- and downstream work depends on verified claims.

Optional thumbnail variants may be shed before factual verification.

15.597 The Prompt Publication Window

A publication window may define when the episode should become public.

The Scheduler shall reserve enough time for:

- factual evaluation,

- human review,

- composition,

- and publication verification.

The window does not grant publication authority.

15.598 The Prompt Breaking-News Spike

A major AI event may create sudden demand.

The Scheduler may:

- elevate one verified breaking-news Workflow,

- delay background research,

- preserve source-verification capacity,

- and restrict speculative media variants.

Urgency shall not permit unsupported claims.

15.599 Applied Example — GainPilot Reel Batch

GainPilot may schedule several reels as a batch.

The Scheduler may:

- generate scripts locally,

- process images with limited external concurrency,

- synthesise voice using remaining quota,

- compose locally,

- and queue human review.

Batch segmentation prevents one large campaign from blocking other Projects.

15.600 Applied Example — Omnira Code Audit

An Omnira repository audit may be:

- long-running,

- local or private,

- read-only,

- and high importance.

The Scheduler may:

- reserve local memory,

- delay non-critical local media work,

- checkpoint repository analysis,

- and protect interactive system responsiveness.

The audit shall not preempt a critical data-recovery operation without policy.

text:
15.601 Applied Example — Private Local Analysis

A Local Only request requires one private Runtime Node.

If the Node is offline:

- admission may be deferred,

- the request may wait,

- another approved local Node may be selected,

- or the request may fail.

The Scheduler shall not use external capacity merely to meet a Soft Deadline.

15.602 Applied Example — User-Owned Video Credits

A user-owned Provider Account has:

- ten remaining video credits,

- concurrency of two,

- and a reset in five days.

The Fabric may reserve:

- six credits for the approved Familje-Stunden production,

- two credits for retry,

- and leave two unallocated.

Another Project shall not consume the remaining capacity without permission.

15.603 Applied Example — Human-Assisted OpenArt Queue

A manual OpenArt workflow may enter a Human Action Queue.

The task shall include:

- Project,

- approved Account,

- spend limit,

- scene package,

- deadline,

- and expected Output.

Human availability is the effective execution capacity.

15.604 Applied Example — Provider Rate-Limit Reset

A text Provider reaches its tokens-per-minute limit.

The Scheduler may:

- delay low-priority requests,

- route eligible urgent work to another Provider,

- preserve the Account’s reset time,

- and avoid retry storms.

The rate limit shall not be misclassified as permanent Provider outage.

15.605 Applied Example — Scheduled Benchmark Run

A large benchmark may be scheduled overnight.

Before occurrence, the Fabric shall revalidate:

- Budget,

- Provider pricing,

- local Node capacity,

- Test Suite Version,

- and production workload.

The benchmark may be delayed when critical production requires the same resources.

15.606 Applied Example — Missed Recurring Occurrence

A recurring The Prompt background scan is missed during outage.

The catch-up policy may:

- skip obsolete scans,

- create one current scan,

- and avoid replaying every missed interval.

Currentness matters more than occurrence count.

Priority inflation destroys meaningful scheduling.

15.608 Anti-Pattern — Agent Sets Its Own Priority

Priority requires governed source and authority.

15.657 Future Scheduling Architecture

Future versions may support:

- predictive admission,

- multi-region capacity markets,

- workload auctions,

- energy-aware scheduling,

- carbon-aware placement,

- federated edge scheduling,

- negotiated Provider reservations,

- dynamic managed-credit capacity,

- adaptive fair sharing,

- and cross-device execution migration.

Future evolution must preserve:

- user authority,

- Project isolation,

- transparent priority,

- bounded quotas,

- and truthful timing.

15.658 Predictive Admission

The Fabric may predict whether new work will meet its deadline.

Predictions shall preserve confidence and shall not become guarantees.

15.659 Adaptive Fairness

Fairness weights may adapt to actual usage and contractual entitlement.

Changes shall remain governed.

15.660 Capacity Marketplace

Future Providers or Omnira services may offer variable-price capacity windows.

Selection shall remain subject to Budget and routing policy.

15.661 Deadline-Aware Economic Scheduling

Flexible work may be delayed to lower-cost capacity when the deadline permits.

15.662 Carbon-Aware Scheduling

Work may be moved to lower-carbon time or location under Project policy.

Privacy and deadline remain binding.

15.663 Cross-Device Scheduling

Work may move among:

- laptop,

- workstation,

- home server,

- and cloud Node

when policy permits.

15.664 Execution Migration

A running operation may migrate only when the Runtime and state model support safe continuation.

15.665 Mobile Scheduling

Mobile Nodes may prioritise:

- approvals,

- notifications,

- lightweight local inference,

- and user-present tasks.

Heavy work may move elsewhere only under approved placement policy.

15.666 Federated Capacity

Several user-controlled Nodes may contribute capacity while preserving:

- identity,

- trust,

- data scope,

- and failure isolation.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.667 Reserved Managed Capacity

Future Omnira plans may provide reserved capacity entitlements.

The entitlement, priority and fair-use policy shall be transparent.

15.668 Capacity Success Criteria

The capacity architecture succeeds when:

- resource limits are explicit,

- queues remain bounded,

- work is admitted only when feasible,

- concurrency is controlled,

- Project and Tenant fairness are preserved,

- deadlines are evaluated honestly,

- quotas and Budgets remain distinct,

- schedules revalidate before execution,

- and critical work remains protected during saturation.

15.669 Capacity Failure Conditions

The architecture is non-conformant when:

- queue depth is unbounded,

- Agents assign unrestricted priority,

- one Project monopolises shared capacity,

- Provider rate limits are enforced only per worker,

- scheduled work uses expired authority,

- quota is confused with Budget,

- capacity reservations are double-allocated,

- stale capacity is represented as current,

- or missed deadlines are hidden.

15.670 Canonical Latency Contract

The following requirements define canonical latency governance:

1. Every latency measurement SHALL identify start and end events.

2. End-to-end, execution, Attempt, Provider and queue latency SHALL remain distinguishable.

3. Time to Provider completion SHALL remain distinct from time to accepted result.

4. Time to accepted result SHALL include required evaluation and review.

5. Latency SHALL be scoped to resource, Capability and workload class.

6. Latency distributions SHOULD include tail measures where material.

7. Average latency SHALL NOT be the sole production metric.

8. Latency evidence SHALL identify freshness.

9. Latency estimates SHALL identify confidence.

10. Hard and Soft Deadlines SHALL remain distinct.

11. Deadline feasibility SHALL include queue, retry, fallback and evaluation.

12. Deadline SHALL NOT override authority, privacy, rights, quality or Budget.

13. Missed deadlines SHALL remain explicit.

14. Estimated and actual start and completion times SHALL remain distinct.

15. Provider latency SHALL NOT be represented as complete user latency.

16. Human review latency SHALL remain visible.

17. Unknown completion time SHALL remain unknown.

18. Latency learning SHALL remain scoped and version-aware.

19. Historical latency evidence SHALL remain queryable.

20. Latency claims SHALL be human- and machine-interpretable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.671 Canonical Capacity Contract

The following requirements define canonical capacity governance:

1. Every material Capacity Record SHALL identify resource and scope.

2. Capacity SHALL identify unit.

3. Total, available, reserved, committed and effective capacity SHALL remain distinct.

4. Capacity SHALL remain distinct from availability.

5. Capacity SHALL remain distinct from quota.

6. Capacity SHALL remain distinct from Budget.

7. Capacity SHALL remain distinct from concurrency.

8. Capacity observations SHALL identify freshness.

9. Capacity observations SHALL identify confidence.

10. Unknown capacity SHALL NOT be treated as full capacity.

11. Provider capacity SHALL remain Account- and Product-aware.

12. Model capacity SHALL remain Deployment-aware.

13. Local capacity SHALL remain Node-aware.

14. Human capacity SHALL remain explicit.

15. Sustainable and burst capacity SHALL remain distinguishable.

16. Reliability headroom SHOULD remain visible.

17. Capacity Reservations SHALL be concurrency-safe.

18. Recovered capacity SHALL require validation.

19. Capacity forecasts SHALL NOT become guarantees.

20. Historical capacity evidence SHALL remain queryable.

15.672 Canonical Admission Contract

The following requirements define canonical Admission Control:

1. Every schedulable Step SHALL receive an Admission Decision or approved equivalent.

2. Admission SHALL validate Plan and Step identity.

3. Admission SHALL validate authority.

4. Admission SHALL validate policy.

5. Paid work SHALL validate Budget protection.

6. Admission SHALL validate required Inputs and dependencies.

7. Admission SHALL evaluate capacity feasibility.

8. Admission SHALL evaluate deadline feasibility.

9. Admission SHALL evaluate quota and concurrency.

10. Admission SHALL distinguish admit, defer, reject and require-change outcomes.

11. Admitted SHALL NOT mean running.

12. Impossible Hard Deadline SHALL NOT be represented as feasible.

13. Queue saturation SHALL influence admission.

14. Human-review capacity SHALL influence feasibility where required.

15. Deferred work SHALL identify its blocking condition.

16. Rejected work SHALL identify the reason.

17. Admission SHALL NOT expose raw credentials.

18. Admission changes SHALL be attributable.

19. Historical Admission Decisions SHALL remain immutable.

20. Admission SHALL fail closed when mandatory conditions are unresolved.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.673 Canonical Scheduling Contract

The following requirements define canonical scheduling:

1. Every Scheduling Request SHALL have stable identity.

2. It SHALL identify Plan Version and Step.

3. It SHALL identify Tenant and Project.

4. It SHALL identify workload class.

5. It SHALL identify effective priority.

6. It SHALL identify earliest start where applicable.

7. It SHALL identify deadline where applicable.

8. It SHALL identify capacity requirements.

9. It SHALL identify Budget Reservation for paid work.

10. Scheduling SHALL remain separate from Planning.

11. Scheduling SHALL remain separate from Routing.

12. Scheduling SHALL remain separate from authority.

13. Scheduling SHALL NOT alter Quality Contract.

14. Scheduling SHALL NOT alter Data Classification.

15. Scheduling Decisions SHALL identify queue and resource pool.

16. Scheduling state SHALL be durable.

17. Duplicate Scheduling Requests SHALL NOT create duplicate dispatch.

18. Expired work SHALL NOT dispatch.

19. Material scheduling changes SHALL be attributable.

20. Historical Scheduling Decisions SHALL remain queryable.

15.674 Canonical Queue Contract

The following requirements define canonical queues:

1. Every persistent Queue SHALL have stable identity.

2. Queue scope SHALL be explicit.

3. Queue capacity SHALL be bounded.

4. Queue ordering policy SHALL be explicit.

5. Queue priority behaviour SHALL be explicit.

6. Queue overflow behaviour SHALL be explicit.

7. Every Queue Item SHALL have stable identity.

8. Queue Item SHALL reference Scheduling Request.

9. Queue Item SHALL preserve enqueue time.

10. Queue Item SHALL preserve deadline.

11. Queue state SHALL survive restart.

12. Duplicate enqueue SHALL be idempotent.

13. Queue cancellation SHALL prevent future dispatch.

14. Queue migration SHALL preserve history.

15. Queue position SHALL be presented as estimate.

16. Starvation SHALL be detected.

17. Project and Tenant isolation SHALL be enforced.

18. Queue recovery SHALL NOT duplicate dispatch.

19. Completed Queue Items MAY be archived without erasing audit evidence.

20. Queue events SHALL remain attributable.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.675 Canonical Priority Contract

The following requirements define canonical priority:

1. Priority SHALL have explicit level and source.

2. Normal SHALL be the ordinary default.

3. Elevated priority SHALL require authority or policy.

4. Agents SHALL NOT self-assign unrestricted elevated priority.

5. Emergency priority SHALL be tightly restricted.

6. Priority escalation SHALL be scoped and time-bounded.

7. Priority changes SHALL be attributable.

8. Priority SHALL NOT create Budget authority.

9. Priority SHALL NOT bypass quota automatically.

10. Priority SHALL NOT bypass privacy, rights or quality.

11. Priority inheritance MAY resolve blocking dependencies.

12. Priority ageing SHOULD prevent starvation.

13. Ageing SHALL NOT create emergency priority.

14. Fairness SHALL remain relevant under sustained high priority.

15. Priority abuse SHALL be detectable.

16. Expired urgency SHALL be de-escalated.

17. Priority policy SHALL be versioned.

18. Historical priority changes SHALL remain queryable.

19. Priority SHALL be human-explainable.

20. One Project SHALL NOT monopolise shared capacity through priority inflation.

15.676 Canonical Fairness Contract

The following requirements define canonical fairness:

1. Shared capacity SHALL use an explicit fairness policy.

2. Tenant and Project attribution SHALL remain intact.

3. One Tenant SHALL NOT monopolise shared capacity by convenience.

4. One Project SHALL NOT indefinitely starve another authorised Project.

5. Reserved share SHALL remain explicit.

6. Borrowed capacity SHALL be revocable.

7. Fairness weights SHALL be versioned.

8. Priority MAY temporarily override fair share.

9. Long-term starvation SHALL remain prohibited.

10. Background work SHALL yield to higher-value work.

11. Fairness SHALL account for workload size where practical.

12. Fairness Decisions SHALL be explainable.

13. Shared Provider Accounts SHALL preserve per-Project allocation.

14. New Tenants SHALL NOT inherit unrelated reservations.

15. Cross-Tenant queue visibility SHALL remain restricted.

16. Fairness metrics SHOULD be measurable.

17. Emergency exceptions SHALL be bounded.

18. Fairness policy changes SHALL be attributable.

19. Historical allocations SHALL remain auditable.

20. Commercial preference SHALL NOT silently override fair entitlement.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.677 Canonical Concurrency Contract

The following requirements define canonical concurrency:

1. Concurrency limits SHALL identify scope and resource.

2. Provider Account concurrency SHALL remain Account-specific.

3. Model concurrency SHALL remain Deployment-specific.

4. Local concurrency SHALL remain Node-specific.

5. Human concurrency SHALL remain explicit where material.

6. Consequential target concurrency SHALL prevent conflicting actions.

7. Required concurrency token SHALL be acquired before dispatch.

8. Tokens SHALL be released after safe terminal state.

9. Token ownership SHALL expire or be recoverable.

10. Stale workers SHALL NOT retain mutation authority.

11. Concurrency state SHALL survive restart.

12. Dynamic concurrency SHALL remain inside hard limits.

13. Parallel work SHALL have sufficient Budget and capacity.

14. Fan-out SHALL be bounded.

15. Candidate races SHALL reserve full potential exposure.

16. Concurrency changes SHALL be versioned.

17. Concurrency limits SHALL interact with rate limits and quota.

18. Leaked tokens SHALL be detectable.

19. Historical concurrency decisions SHALL remain queryable.

20. Maximum concurrency SHALL NOT be treated as the default target.

15.678 Canonical Rate-Limit Contract

The following requirements define canonical rate limiting:

1. Every material Rate Limit SHALL identify scope.

2. Rate Limit SHALL identify unit and window.

3. Burst and sustained limits SHALL remain distinct.

4. Provider limits SHALL identify Account and Product.

5. Shared Account limits SHALL use coordinated enforcement.

6. New workers SHALL NOT bypass shared limits.

7. Rate-limit state SHALL identify freshness.

8. Reset time SHALL remain explicit where known.

9. Provider retry-after guidance SHOULD be respected.

10. Rate limiting SHALL coordinate with retry backoff.

11. Rate limit SHALL remain distinct from quota.

12. Rate limit SHALL remain distinct from concurrency.

13. Rate-limit events SHALL affect scheduling estimates.

14. Development and production limits SHALL remain separate where applicable.

15. Manual override SHALL be restricted.

16. Distributed limit state SHALL be safely consistent.

17. Rate-limit changes SHALL be attributable.

18. Repeated limit events SHOULD create capacity evidence.

19. Historical rate-limit events SHALL remain queryable.

20. Rate-limit exhaustion SHALL NOT be classified as universal Provider failure.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.679 Canonical Quota Contract

The following requirements define canonical quota governance:

1. Every persistent Quota SHALL have stable identity.

2. Quota SHALL identify issuer or owner.

3. Quota SHALL identify scope.

4. Quota SHALL identify unit.

5. Quota SHALL identify limit.

6. Consumed, reserved and remaining SHALL remain distinct.

7. Quota SHALL identify reset or expiry.

8. Quota state SHALL identify freshness.

9. Unknown quota SHALL NOT be treated as full allowance.

10. Quota SHALL remain distinct from Budget.

11. Quota SHALL remain distinct from credits.

12. Quota SHALL remain distinct from rate limits.

13. Quota SHALL remain distinct from concurrency.

14. Quota Reservations SHALL be linked to work.

15. Unused reserved quota SHALL be released.

16. Quota exhaustion SHALL produce explicit wait, reroute or failure.

17. User-owned quota SHALL NOT become silent shared capacity.

18. Project quota SHALL remain Project-scoped.

19. Provider usage SHALL be reconciled against internal consumption.

20. Historical quota state SHALL remain queryable.

15.680 Canonical Schedule Contract

The following requirements define canonical schedules:

1. Every persistent Schedule SHALL have stable identity and version.

2. Schedule SHALL identify owner.

3. Schedule SHALL identify Tenant and Project where applicable.

4. Schedule SHALL identify execution time, recurrence or trigger.

5. Human-facing Schedule SHALL identify timezone.

6. Schedule SHALL identify start window.

7. Schedule SHALL identify expiry or cancellation behaviour.

8. Schedule lifecycle SHALL be explicit.

9. Every occurrence SHALL have distinct identity.

10. Duplicate triggers SHALL NOT duplicate consequential occurrence.

11. Occurrences SHALL revalidate authority.

12. Occurrences SHALL revalidate policy.

13. Paid occurrences SHALL revalidate Budget.

14. Occurrences SHALL revalidate credentials and resource eligibility.

15. Missed-occurrence behaviour SHALL be explicit.

16. Catch-up SHALL be bounded.

17. Schedule pause and cancellation SHALL affect future occurrences only unless specified.

18. Schedule changes SHALL NOT rewrite historical occurrences.

19. Daylight-saving and ambiguous-time behaviour SHALL be defined.

20. Scheduled side effects SHALL require current execution authority.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.681 Canonical Capacity Reservation Contract

The following requirements define canonical Capacity Reservations:

1. Every material Capacity Reservation SHALL have stable identity.

2. It SHALL identify resource pool.

3. It SHALL identify Scheduling Request.

4. It SHALL identify amount and unit.

5. It SHALL identify start and end.

6. It SHALL identify lifecycle.

7. It SHALL reduce available capacity.

8. It SHALL be concurrency-safe.

9. It SHALL NOT exceed allocatable resource capacity.

10. Hard and Soft Reservations SHALL remain distinguishable.

11. Reservation breach SHALL create explicit state.

12. Unused Reservation SHALL be released.

13. Expired Reservation SHALL NOT remain silently committed.

14. Reservation renewal SHALL be attributable.

15. Capacity Reservation SHALL remain distinct from Budget Reservation.

16. Paid work MAY require both Reservations.

17. Reservation preemption SHALL follow policy.

18. Historical Reservation events SHALL remain immutable.

19. Reservation records SHALL NOT expose credentials.

20. Capacity guarantees SHALL not exceed the underlying contract or evidence.

15.682 Canonical Backpressure and Load-Shedding Contract

The following requirements define backpressure and load shedding:

1. Saturation SHALL produce explicit backpressure.

2. Upstream Agents and Workflows SHALL respond to backpressure.

3. Queue depth and wait time SHOULD contribute to backpressure.

4. Fan-out SHALL be reduced under constrained capacity.

5. Backpressure SHALL NOT silently delete admitted work.

6. Load shedding SHALL follow an approved order.

7. Speculative and optional work SHOULD be shed before mandatory work.

8. Background work SHOULD yield to critical recovery and user-facing work.

9. Shed work SHALL receive explicit state.

10. Shed paid work SHALL NOT begin after the decision.

11. Non-preemptible external work SHALL NOT be represented as stopped until confirmed.

12. Load shedding SHALL preserve Project and Tenant attribution.

13. Privacy, rights and Quality Floor SHALL remain binding.

14. User-visible impact SHALL be disclosed when material.

15. Capacity recovery SHALL permit controlled readmission.

16. Backpressure policy SHALL be versioned.

17. Load-shedding policy SHALL be versioned.

18. Emergency exceptions SHALL remain bounded.

19. Historical decisions SHALL remain queryable.

20. Saturation SHALL NOT authorise direct Provider bypass.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.683 Canonical Human-Capacity Contract

The following requirements define human-capacity governance:

1. Human Actions and Reviews SHALL be schedulable work.

2. Human task SHALL identify responsible role.

3. Human task SHALL identify Project scope.

4. Human task SHOULD identify estimated effort.

5. Human task SHALL identify deadline where material.

6. Human availability SHALL NOT be assumed.

7. Reviewer assignment SHALL respect qualification.

8. Reviewer assignment SHALL respect data access.

9. Human concurrency SHALL remain bounded.

10. Human timeout SHALL NOT fabricate a decision.

11. Missed human task MAY be reassigned only to qualified authority.

12. Human queue priority SHALL be explicit.

13. Human overload SHALL be detectable.

14. Human latency SHALL be included in completion estimates.

15. Human reassignment SHALL be attributable.

16. Human-assisted capacity SHALL remain distinct from automation.

17. Reviewer conflicts SHALL remain visible.

18. Human queue data SHALL remain access-controlled.

19. Historical assignments SHALL remain queryable.

20. Human authority SHALL remain separate from scheduling priority.

15.684 Canonical Scheduling Governance Contract

The following requirements define overall scheduling governance:

1. Scheduling Policy SHALL be versioned.

2. Priority Policy SHALL be versioned.

3. Fairness Policy SHALL be versioned.

4. Quota Policy SHALL be versioned.

5. Concurrency Policy SHALL be versioned.

6. Admission SHALL fail closed when mandatory conditions are unresolved.

7. Schedules SHALL revalidate before execution.

8. One Project SHALL NOT monopolise shared resources.

9. User-owned capacity SHALL remain user-owned.

10. Shared managed capacity SHALL preserve Tenant isolation.

11. Deadline SHALL NOT override governance.

12. Queue saturation SHALL be handled explicitly.

13. Capacity forecasts SHALL not become guarantees.

14. Scheduling learning SHALL require governed admission.

15. Emergency scheduling SHALL be temporary and attributable.

16. Scheduler failure SHALL NOT cause uncontrolled direct execution.

17. Scheduling state SHALL be durable.

18. Historical decisions SHALL remain reconstructable.

19. Users SHALL receive meaningful delay and deadline information.

20. The Scheduler SHALL optimise time without changing the user’s authorised objective.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
15.685 Scheduling Invariants

The following invariants shall remain true:

- No Scheduling Decision creates authority.

- No priority bypasses privacy, rights, quality or Budget.

- No Agent assigns itself unrestricted emergency priority.

- No queue grows without a bound or overflow policy.

- No one Project monopolises shared capacity by convenience.

- No quota is treated as Budget.

- No credit balance is treated as quota.

- No concurrency limit is treated as a throughput target.

- No Provider rate limit is enforced only per worker when the Account is shared.

- No scheduled occurrence executes without current revalidation.

- No missed recurrence produces unbounded catch-up.

- No deadline is claimed feasible without end-to-end timing.

- No stale capacity is represented as current certainty.

- No capacity forecast is represented as a guarantee.

- No Capacity Reservation is double-allocated.

- No shed work disappears silently.

- No running non-preemptible job is represented as stopped without evidence.

- No human review capacity is assumed infinite.

- No Scheduler retrieves raw Provider credentials.

- No Scheduler failure authorises bypass of the Fabric.

15.686 Closing Statement

Latency, capacity, scheduling and quotas determine whether the Intelligence Fabric can turn valid Plans into timely work without overwhelming Providers, devices, people, Budgets or Projects.

The Request defines what is needed.

The Plan defines which Steps must occur.

Routing identifies eligible resources.

The Capacity Record defines what those resources can currently support.

The Budget Reservation protects economic authority.

The Capacity Reservation protects scarce execution opportunity.

Admission Control determines whether work may enter.

The Queue preserves waiting work.

Priority reflects governed urgency.

Fairness protects other Projects and Tenants.

Concurrency limits simultaneous pressure.

Rate limits control speed.

Quotas control total allowance.

The Schedule defines when future occurrences should be created.

The Scheduler decides when eligible work may begin.

The Execution system performs the work.

The Quality system determines whether the result is acceptable.

The Reliability system handles disruption.

For Familje-Stunden, this architecture ensures that:

- Nova and Pling master scenes receive enough production and review capacity,

- optional derivatives do not consume the release window,

- Provider concurrency is respected,

- and one monthly production does not create uncontrolled retries or queue saturation.

For The Prompt, it ensures that:

- time-sensitive research occurs before stale media production,

- breaking-news urgency does not bypass factual verification,

- and publication windows include the real cost of review and verification.

For GainPilot, it allows routine content to run in economical batches without monopolising local or external resources.

For Omnira, it allows:

- interactive Atlas requests,

- local Models,

- external Providers,

- asynchronous video jobs,

- scheduled research,

- code analysis,

- recovery work,

- human approvals,

- and future multi-Tenant workloads

to share one governed execution fabric.

Fast is not the same as complete.

Available is not the same as permitted.

Capacity is not quota.

Quota is not Budget.

Priority is not authority.

A deadline is not permission.

A queue is not infinite.

A forecast is not a guarantee.

No admission without feasibility.

No dispatch without capacity.

No paid execution without Budget protection.

No shared capacity without fairness.

No elevated priority without authority.

No recurring execution without revalidation.

No deadline claim without end-to-end evidence.

The user retains urgency.

The Project retains entitlement.

Omnira retains fairness.

The Fabric allocates intelligence capacity without surrendering governance.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.1 Chapter Status

This chapter defines the canonical architecture, governance model, object model, lifecycle, boundaries and conformance requirements for Adapters, Connectors, Connections and integration-facing execution resources within the Omnira Intelligence Fabric.

It establishes:

- how Provider-specific systems are translated into canonical Fabric contracts,

- how Adapters remain separate from Providers, Models, Accounts, Credentials and Connections,

- how Connectors expose governed integration capabilities,

- how external APIs, MCP servers, webhooks, asynchronous queues, local runtimes, tools, browser-assisted systems and human-assisted systems coexist,

- how request and response translation remain deterministic, versioned and observable,

- how capability support is mapped without leaking Provider-specific assumptions into Projects or Agents,

- how Provider-specific identifiers and lifecycle states are preserved,

- how errors, usage, cost, latency, quality and execution evidence are normalised,

- how idempotency, retries, streaming, pagination, callbacks and long-running jobs cross integration boundaries,

- how Assets and multimodal payloads are transferred safely,

- how schema evolution and protocol drift are handled,

- how Provider-managed routing and hidden implementation choices are represented truthfully,

- how security, privacy, Project isolation and authority remain enforceable across every integration,

- how connector health and maturity influence routing,

- how testing, certification, simulation and sandboxing are performed,

- how integration failure is contained,

- how manual-assisted integration paths remain canonical without pretending to be automated,

- and how Stage 1 shall implement the smallest trustworthy adapter and connector foundation.

Adapters and Connectors exist to isolate external variation from Omnira’s canonical architecture.

A Provider-specific API shall not define Omnira’s internal object model.

An MCP server shall not become unrestricted platform authority.

A local tool shall not bypass policy because it runs on a trusted machine.

A browser-assisted Provider shall not be represented as an API.

A webhook shall not be trusted merely because it arrived at an Omnira endpoint.

A Connector shall not contain raw credentials.

An Adapter shall not own Agent identity.

A Provider SDK shall not become the canonical execution contract.

This chapter is normative after formal approval.

Protocol-specific implementation details are expanded in Chapter 17.

Credential, secret and identity mechanics are expanded in Chapter 18.

Implementation and conformance must be verified separately.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.2 Purpose of the Integration Architecture

The Intelligence Fabric must communicate with systems that differ in:

- protocol,

- authentication,

- schema,

- terminology,

- lifecycle,

- error handling,

- billing,

- media formats,

- streaming behaviour,

- job semantics,

- callback design,

- versioning,

- and operational maturity.

Examples may include:

- external language-model APIs,

- image and video generation Providers,

- voice and audio services,

- local Ollama runtimes,

- NVIDIA-hosted or local Models,

- MCP servers,

- search services,

- file-processing tools,

- repository tools,

- publication platforms,

- browser-only creative tools,

- human-assisted production paths,

- and future Agent-to-Agent protocols.

Without a canonical integration layer, Project code would become tightly coupled to:

- Provider model names,

- SDK types,

- endpoint URLs,

- raw API errors,

- Provider billing units,

- callback payloads,

- and hidden Provider assumptions.

That coupling would make it difficult to:

- replace Providers,

- add local resources,

- enforce uniform policy,

- preserve Project isolation,

- compare costs,

- route by Capability,

- recover from failure,

- and maintain truthful provenance.

The Adapter and Connector architecture exists to absorb that variation while preserving canonical semantics.

16.3 Integration Boundary

The Integration Boundary is the controlled interface between canonical Omnira objects and external or implementation-specific systems.

The boundary shall define:

- what enters,

- what leaves,

- which identity is used,

- which policy applies,

- which data may cross,

- which side effects may occur,

- and which evidence must return.

Every external or local execution path shall cross an explicit Integration Boundary.

16.4 Canonical Side

The canonical side uses Omnira-owned objects such as:

- Capability Request,

- Intent Envelope,

- Execution Plan,

- Step,

- Routing Decision,

- Execution,

- Attempt,

- Output,

- Asset,

- Cost Record,

- Evaluation Result,

- and Incident.

Canonical objects shall remain independent from one Provider’s schema.

16.5 Integration Side

The integration side may contain:

- Provider request objects,

- SDK calls,

- HTTP requests,

- MCP messages,

- process invocations,

- local runtime commands,

- browser instructions,

- queue messages,

- webhook payloads,

- or human task packages.

Provider-specific objects shall remain inside the integration boundary unless preserved as evidence.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.6 Integration Translation

Integration Translation converts between:

- canonical request and implementation-specific operation,

- implementation-specific response and canonical Output,

- Provider error and canonical Error Classification,

- Provider usage and canonical Usage Record,

- Provider job state and canonical Execution state,

- Provider Asset and canonical Asset reference,

- and Provider metadata and canonical provenance.

Translation shall not change user intent silently.

16.7 Adapter

An Adapter is a versioned software component that translates between canonical Fabric contracts and one implementation-specific interface.

An Adapter may support:

- one Provider API,

- one Provider Product,

- one local runtime,

- one Tool protocol,

- one MCP server family,

- one queue system,

- one file format,

- or one human-assisted procedure.

An Adapter is an implementation component.

It is not the Provider itself.

16.8 Connector

A Connector is a governed integration capability exposed to the Fabric.

A Connector combines or references:

- one or more Adapters,

- supported Connections,

- Capability mappings,

- policy,

- health,

- maturity,

- and operational constraints.

A Connector describes how Omnira may interact with a resource class.

It is broader than one translation library.

16.9 Connection

A Connection is a configured operational relationship between Omnira and a specific external or local target.

A Connection may identify:

- Provider Account,

- endpoint,

- region,

- workspace,

- Runtime Node,

- repository,

- MCP server,

- queue,

- browser profile,

- or human operator channel.

A Connection is an instance.

A Connector is a governed integration type.

An Adapter is a translating implementation.

16.10 Provider

A Provider is the organisation or system offering a Product or service.

A Provider may expose several:

- Products,

- APIs,

- Models,

- regions,

- Accounts,

- and protocols.

Provider identity shall remain separate from Adapter and Connector identity.

16.11 Provider Product

A Provider Product is one commercial or technical offering.

Examples include:

- text-generation API,

- image-generation workspace,

- voice-synthesis API,

- search product,

- or managed Agent platform.

One Provider may require several Connectors for different Products.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.12 Model

A Model is an intelligence resource.

A Model may be exposed through:

- several Providers,

- several Products,

- several Deployments,

- or several Adapters.

Model identity shall not be embedded into Connector identity unnecessarily.

16.13 Model Deployment

A Model Deployment is one executable placement of a Model.

The Adapter may need deployment-specific translation.

The Connector shall preserve the distinction between:

- Model,

- Model Version,

- Deployment,

- and Provider-managed alias.

16.14 Tool

A Tool is an executable resource that performs a bounded operation.

A Tool may be integrated through:

- local process,

- API,

- MCP,

- SDK,

- queue,

- or human-assisted procedure.

Tool identity shall remain separate from the Connector used to invoke it.

16.15 Runtime Node

A Runtime Node is a machine or environment capable of running local Models or Tools.

A local Connector may target one or more Runtime Nodes.

Node identity and health shall remain explicit.

16.16 External Agent Resource

An External Agent Resource is an external system that performs multi-step or agentic work.

It shall not be treated as an Omnira Agent identity.

Its external autonomy shall remain bounded by:

- Capability,

- Connection,

- data policy,

- authority,

- and evidence.

16.17 Human-Assisted Integration

A Human-Assisted Integration uses a person to operate or mediate an external system.

It remains a valid canonical integration path when:

- no API exists,

- creative direction requires a human,

- login or interface restrictions prevent automation,

- or production maturity is insufficient.

It shall be labelled honestly.

16.18 Integration Object Model

The canonical integration object model should include or reference:

- Adapter,

- Adapter Version,

- Connector,

- Connector Version,

- Connection,

- Connection Profile,

- Endpoint,

- Protocol Profile,

- Capability Mapping,

- Feature Mapping,

- Parameter Mapping,

- Schema Mapping,

- State Mapping,

- Error Mapping,

- Usage Mapping,

- Asset Mapping,

- Callback Mapping,

- Integration Policy,

- Integration Test Suite,

- Conformance Result,

- Integration Incident,

- and Manual Procedure.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.19 Adapter Identity

Every Adapter shall have stable identity.

The identity shall remain stable across implementation versions.

Example:

adapter.openart.director

may have several Versions.

16.20 Adapter Version

Every material Adapter release shall have a distinct Version.

Version changes may reflect:

- Provider API change,

- schema change,

- SDK update,

- new Capability support,

- changed error mapping,

- changed cost mapping,

- or security correction.

16.21 Adapter Version Immutability

Historical Executions shall preserve the exact Adapter Version used.

A new deployment shall not rewrite historical integration evidence.

16.22 Connector Identity

Every Connector shall have stable canonical identity.

Connector identity should describe the governed integration boundary rather than a temporary endpoint.

Examples may include:

- connector.provider.text-api,

- connector.local.ollama,

- connector.mcp.repository,

- connector.human.openart-director.

16.23 Connector Version

Material changes to:

- Capability mappings,

- supported protocols,

- policy,

- maturity,

- or connection requirements

shall create a new Connector Version.

16.24 Connection Identity

Every persistent Connection shall have stable identity.

Connection identity shall remain separate from:

- credential,

- Provider Account,

- endpoint,

- and Adapter Version.

16.25 Connection Version

Material configuration changes should create:

- new Connection Version,

- attributable amendment,

- or new Connection

according to consequence.

16.26 Connection Profile

A Connection Profile defines reusable configuration requirements for one Connector.

It may include:

- protocol,

- endpoint class,

- authentication mechanism,

- region,

- timeout defaults,

- callback requirements,

- supported Environments,

- and health checks.

16.27 Endpoint

An Endpoint is a specific address or invocation target.

An Endpoint may be:

- HTTP URL,

- WebSocket address,

- local socket,

- process command,

- queue topic,

- MCP server address,

- repository path,

- or browser application location.

Endpoint identity shall not be treated as Provider identity.

16.28 Endpoint Environment

Endpoints may be classified as:

- development,

- sandbox,

- staging,

- production,

- local,

- or recovery.

Environment mismatch shall block execution.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.29 Endpoint Region

Region shall remain explicit where relevant to:

- data residency,

- latency,

- pricing,

- and failure domains.

16.30 Protocol Profile

A Protocol Profile defines the communication model used by a Connector.

Protocol classes may include:

- synchronous API,

- asynchronous API,

- streaming API,

- MCP,

- webhook,

- queue,

- local process,

- local runtime,

- file exchange,

- browser-assisted,

- human-assisted,

- or future Agent protocol.

16.31 Protocol Version

Protocol Version shall remain explicit where the external system defines one.

16.32 Protocol Maturity

Protocol maturity may be:

- experimental,

- preview,

- production,

- deprecated,

- legacy,

- or unsupported.

16.33 Adapter Responsibility

An Adapter is responsible for:

- validating canonical invocation inputs,

- resolving Provider-specific parameters,

- serialising requests,

- invoking the target through an approved Connection,

- preserving correlation identifiers,

- parsing responses,

- mapping lifecycle state,

- mapping errors,

- extracting usage,

- extracting Provider identifiers,

- normalising Outputs,

- and emitting evidence.

16.34 Adapter Non-Responsibility

An Adapter shall not:

- decide user intent,

- grant authority,

- select unrestricted Providers,

- increase Budget,

- lower classification,

- approve Outputs,

- create Agent identity,

- or hide external side effects.

16.35 Connector Responsibility

A Connector is responsible for defining:

- supported Capability mappings,

- required Connection properties,

- permitted protocol modes,

- operational maturity,

- policy restrictions,

- health checks,

- conformance expectations,

- and supported Adapter Versions.

16.36 Connector Non-Responsibility

A Connector shall not:

- own business logic,

- own Project memory,

- own Provider billing authority,

- or become the canonical source of Model identity.

16.37 Connection Responsibility

A Connection defines the exact configured path used for execution.

It shall identify or reference:

- Connector,

- Adapter Version,

- Provider Account,

- endpoint,

- Environment,

- region,

- Credential Reference,

- allowed Projects,

- allowed Capabilities,

- and lifecycle.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.38 Connection Non-Responsibility

A Connection shall not contain:

- raw API key,

- raw password,

- payment-card data,

- unrestricted account session,

- or hidden cross-Project authority.

16.39 Integration Separation of Concerns

The canonical separation is:

Provider

offers a service.

Product

defines an offering.

Model or Tool

performs intelligence or action.

Deployment

places the resource.

Connector

defines the governed integration capability.

Adapter

translates canonical contracts.

Connection

configures one operational path.

Credential Reference

allows authorised authentication.

Routing Decision

selects the path.

Execution

uses the path.

Evidence

records what happened.

16.40 Capability Mapping

A Capability Mapping declares that a Connector and resource path can support one canonical Capability or Capability Version.

It shall include or reference:

- capabilityMappingId,

- Connector Version,

- canonical Capability,

- supported Features,

- constraints,

- implementation operation,

- maturity,

- evidence,

- and lifecycle.

16.41 Capability Mapping Identity

Every persistent Capability Mapping shall have stable identity and Version.

16.42 Exact Capability Mapping

An Exact Mapping supports the canonical Capability directly.

16.43 Composite Capability Mapping

A Composite Mapping satisfies one Capability through several implementation operations.

Material composition should normally be represented in the Plan rather than hidden inside the Adapter.

16.44 Approximate Capability Mapping

An Approximate Mapping does not fully implement the canonical Capability.

It shall be marked:

- degraded,

- conditional,

- experimental,

- or unsuitable for certain use.

16.45 Unsupported Capability

Unsupported Capability shall fail explicitly.

The Adapter shall not approximate silently.

16.46 Capability Version Mapping

A Connector may support:

- exact canonical Version,

- compatible Version range,

- or Provider-specific subset.

Compatibility shall be versioned.

16.47 Feature Mapping

A Feature Mapping relates canonical Features to implementation-specific options.

Examples include:

- tool calling,

- structured output,

- reference image,

- voice selection,

- streaming,

- seed,

- transparent background,

- or asynchronous callback.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.48 Mandatory Feature Mapping

Mandatory Features shall map to verified implementation support.

An ignored or unsupported parameter shall not be represented as supported.

16.49 Optional Feature Mapping

Optional Features may be:

- omitted,

- downgraded,

- or emulated

only when the request permits it.

16.50 Feature Evidence

Feature support shall be based on:

- Provider documentation,

- conformance tests,

- production evidence,

- or verified manual procedure.

16.51 Feature Drift

Provider updates may change Feature behaviour.

Feature mappings shall be reviewed after material Provider change.

16.52 Parameter Mapping

A Parameter Mapping translates canonical execution parameters into implementation-specific values.

It shall include:

- canonical parameter,

- target field,

- conversion rule,

- default,

- valid range,

- omission behaviour,

- and Version.

16.53 Canonical Parameter

Canonical parameters express Fabric semantics.

Examples include:

- output format,

- maximum duration,

- quality tier,

- deterministic seed preference,

- response schema,

- reference Asset,

- or streaming preference.

16.54 Provider Parameter

Provider parameters remain implementation-specific.

They shall not leak into Project or Agent contracts unless explicitly pinned.

16.55 Parameter Default

Default values shall be explicit.

The Adapter shall distinguish:

- canonical default,

- Provider default,

- Connection default,

- and request-explicit value.

16.56 Provider Default Risk

Provider defaults may change.

Critical behaviour should not rely on undocumented defaults.

16.57 Parameter Validation

The Adapter shall validate ranges and combinations before dispatch where possible.

16.58 Parameter Rejection

Unsupported or unsafe parameters shall fail before Provider invocation.

They shall not be dropped silently.

16.59 Parameter Normalisation

Units may require conversion.

Examples include:

- milliseconds to seconds,

- pixels to aspect ratio,

- characters to Provider credits,

- or language code transformation.

16.60 Unit Preservation

Original canonical units and Provider units shall remain available in evidence.

16.61 Schema Mapping

A Schema Mapping translates between canonical and implementation-specific data structures.

It may apply to:

- request,

- response,

- callback,

- error,

- usage,

- Asset metadata,

- or Tool input.

title: Omnira Intelligence Fabric
text:
16.62 Schema Mapping Version

Every material Schema Mapping shall be versioned.

16.63 Required Field Mapping

Every canonical mandatory field shall either:

- map directly,

- be derived transparently,

- be unavailable and reject the operation,

- or be satisfied elsewhere in the Plan.

16.64 Derived Field

A derived field shall preserve:

- derivation rule,

- source fields,

- confidence where relevant,

- and provenance.

16.65 Ignored Field

Ignored canonical fields shall be prohibited for mandatory semantics.

Optional ignored fields shall produce evidence or warning.

16.66 Unknown Provider Field

Unknown Provider fields shall not enter canonical objects without validation.

16.67 Schema Validation
